units.la: EX quo tempore, animum adjeci meum, ad Theologiam scribendam Judaicam, illud inprimis mihi semper curæ fuit, ut, quæ, ad hujus pertinerent notitiam, ex ipsis Rabbinorum sectarer monumentis. Cogitabam quippe, quod nunquam certius, tutiusque de Moderna Hebræorum orum Religione institui posit sermo , quam si ex ipsis sapiamus, loquamurque Judeis; Accedit quoque, quod varios Gentis hujus à multis annis consuluimus Doctores, qui consensum suum unanimem sincera testati fuerunt fide: Quod si horum à nobis efflagitares testimonia, profecto rem nobis faceres gratissimam, Sic pariter textum Hebræum
units.tr: Ever since I set my mind to writing a Jewish theology, my first concern has always been to draw from the very writings of the rabbis whatever pertains to knowledge of it. For I reasoned that nothing about the modern religion of the Hebrews can be set forth more surely or safely than by consulting the Jews themselves and speaking with them. Moreover, over many years I have consulted various teachers of this people, who bore witness with sincere faith to their unanimous agreement. If you were to demand their testimonies from us, you would certainly be doing us a most welcome favour. Likewise, we would add the Hebrew text together with a version, sometimes more correct, and certain additions.

units.la: DE MODERNA THEOLOGIA JUDAICA.
units.tr: ON MODERN JEWISH THEOLOGY.

units.la: CAPUT I. De Theologia, Religione, fideique articulis.
units.tr: CHAPTER I. On Theology, Religion, and the Articles of Faith.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: SIcut Gens Judaica disciplinarum aliarum nomina, nostris usitata, feliciter hactenus imitata est, ita pariter suam quoq; fecit Theologiæ vocem, cujus rei post multos testis est A dodomesticus, Rabbi Schabtai Strimesius , luculentus Bibliothecæ Rabbinicæ nuper scriptor,quando sol.7. col.2. refert חכמת הדקדוק הנקראת בלשון לטינא גראמאטיקא scientia accurata duquisitionis vocata est in Lingua Latina Grammatica; חכמת הלצה הנקראת ריטוריקא scientia Eloquentiae nominata Rhetorica ; חכמת הגיון הנקראת דיאלעקטיקא או לוייאיקא scientia meditationis appellata est Dialectica , vel Logica; חכמת החשבון הנקראת אריטמעטיקא scientia Supputationis vocatur Arithmetica; חכמת תשבורת הנקראת יעומעטריאה או אלגעבראא scientia fractionis seu quantitatis appellata est Geometria, vel Algebra; חכמת התכונה או חכמת הכוכבים הנקראת אסטרולוגיאה או אסטרונומיאה Scientia numerationis seu ponderationis, vel scientia stellarum appellatur Astrologia vel Astronomia ; statimque,enumeratis nominibus Musica , Oeconomica, Politica, Mathematica, Physica, Metaphysicaque subjicit : חכמת האלהיית והיא נקראת טעאולוגיאה scientia, divinitatis vero est quae Theologia nuncupatur. II.
units.tr: Since the Jewish nation has happily imitated the names of other disciplines that are in common use among us, it has likewise made the word Theology its own. Of this, after many others, the witness is our countryman Rabbi Shabtai Strimesius, the recent learned writer of the Bibliotheca Rabbinica, where at page 7, column 2, he reports the following: חכמת הדקדוק הנקראת בלשון לטינא גראמאטיקא [chokhmat ha-dikduk] the science of accurate inquiry is called in the Latin tongue Grammar; חכמת הלצה הנקראת ריטוריקא [chokhmat ha-latzah] the science of eloquence is named Rhetoric; חכמת הגיון הנקראת דיאלעקטיקא או לוייאיקא [chokhmat ha-higayon] the science of meditation is called Dialectic, or Logic; חכמת החשבון הנקראת אריטמעטיקא [chokhmat ha-cheshbon] the science of computation is called Arithmetic; חכמת תשבורת הנקראת יעומעטריאה או אלגעבראא [chokhmat tishbores] the science of fractions or quantities is called Geometry, or Algebra; חכמת התכונה או חכמת הכוכבים הנקראת אסטרולוגיאה או אסטרונומיאה [chokhmat ha-tekhunah] the science of numbering or weighing, or the science of the stars, is called Astrology or Astronomy; and at once, after listing the names Music, Economics, Politics, Mathematics, Physics, and Metaphysics, he adds: חכמת האלהיית והיא נקראת טעאולוגיאה [chokhmat ha-elohiyyut] the science of divinity, which is called Theology. II.

units.la: Appellat pariter Natio Theologiam luam Iudaicam התורייה הידיעה scientiam Legalem, peritiamve tiamve Legis, תורה תלמוד doctrinam Legis, חכמת sapientiam divinitatis, חכמה האלהית sapientiam divinam, תורה האלהית Legem, institutionemque divinam, a Deo quippe profectam; nominat Theologum איש האלהים virum Dei הפוסק בתורה Legem secantem, phrasibus in Novi Instrumenti libris obviis, איש האלה virum divinum, איש התורני virum Legalem, חכם האמת sapientem veritatis, aliisque multis, passim inscriptis Hebraicis, maxime Epistolicis, extantibus.
units.tr: In the same way the nation calls its own theology Jewish: התורייה הידיעה [ha-Torah ha-yedu'ah] the known law, the science of the Law, or the skill in the Law; תורה תלמוד [Torah talmud] the teaching of the Law; חכמת [chokhmat] the wisdom of divinity; חכמה האלהית [chokhmah ha-elohit] divine wisdom; תורה האלהית [Torah ha-elohit] the divine Law and institution, since it comes from God. It calls the theologian איש האלהים [ish ha-elohim] the man of God, הפוסק בתורה [ha-posek ba-Torah] one who expounds the Law, and, in the phrases found in the books of the New Testament, איש האלה [ish ha-elohah] a divine man, איש התורני [ish ha-Torani] a man of the Law, חכם האמת [chakham ha-emet] a sage of truth, and many other terms, found everywhere in Hebrew writings, especially in the letters. III.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Agnoscit, probatque cum Majoribus suis Theologiae divisionem in Catechéticam & Acroamaticam. In illa prima, necessariaque Religionis proponuntur rudimenta, ut patet & ex Rabbi Abrahami Jagelis לקח טוב Catechismo Iudaico, pridem Carpzovii, Veilii, Odheliique versionibus Latinis illustrato, & ex Maimonidis tredecim fidei Judaicae articulis, quos non in scholis tantum memoriae mandare jubentur pueri, sed & libellis precum insertos quotidie promiscue omnes recitant. In hac exhibetur, cerniturque prolixior, accuratiorque deductio, expositio, vindicatio, estque rursus varia, nam est vel Masorethica, circa Legis scriptae integritatem tota occupata, perque Eliam Levitam in Masora sua, Buxtorfiumque in Tiberiade descripta; vel est Exegetica, in verum Legis gis utriusque sensum inquirens, in infinitis scriptoribus, recensitis in Buxtorfiorum, Plantavitii, Hottingeri, Bartoloccii, Menasfis Ben Israel, Schabtai Strimesii Bibliothecis Rabbinicis; vel est Dogmatica, fidei vitaeque canones certa methodo formans, apud Rabbi Levi Barzelonitam in תרי"ג quod completitur explicationem 613. praeceptorum; vel Polemica Placita Religionis defendens, refutansque Muhammedanos, Karraitas, Christianos, Gentiles, horumque Philosophos, maxime Aristotelicos, apud Hottingerum in Bibliotheca Orientali; vel Cabbalistica, in mysteriis indagandis, plurima parte circa cognitionem Dei, divinorum attributorum, Angelorum, animae, ex libris Cabbalisticis ab Illustri auctore Cabbalae denudatae editis; vel Practica, poenitentiam, aliasve virtutes commendans, Judaeosque contra mundi vanitatem muniens; vel Liturgica, circa ritus ceremoniasque versans; vel denique Historica, traditiones conservans, vindicansque, Judice horum omnium Doctissimo, Johanne Benedicto Carpzovio, Sacrarum Literarum apud Lipsienses Interprete Celeberrimo, in Introductione ad Theologiam Judaicam.
units.tr: Together with its forebears, it accepts and approves the division of Theology into Catechetical and Acroamatic. The first presents the necessary rudiments of religion, as is clear from Rabbi Abraham Jagel's לקח טוב [Lekach Tov], the Jewish Catechism, long ago illustrated by the Latin versions of Carpzov, Veil, and Odhelius, and from the thirteen articles of Jewish faith of Maimonides, which boys are ordered to commit to memory not only in school but also insert in their prayer books, and which all recite together every day. The second presents a fuller and more accurate deduction, exposition, and defence, and it is again varied in kind. It is either Masoretic, wholly occupied with the integrity of the written Law, as described by Elias Levita in his Masora and by Buxtorf in his Tiberias; or it is Exegetical, inquiring into the true sense of both Laws, among countless writers listed in the rabbinic libraries of the Buxtorfs, Plantavit, Hottinger, Bartolocci, Menasseh ben Israel, and Shabtai Strimesius; or it is Dogmatic, shaping the canons of faith and life by a sure method, as in Rabbi Levi of Barcelona in his תרי"ג [Taryag], which is an explanation of the 613 precepts; or it is Polemical, defending the tenets of religion and refuting Muslims, Karaites, Christians, Gentiles, and their philosophers, especially the Aristotelians, as in Hottinger's Bibliotheca Orientalis; or it is Cabbalistic, searching out mysteries, chiefly concerning the knowledge of God, the divine attributes, angels, and the soul, from Cabbalistic books published by the illustrious author who laid bare the Cabbala; or it is Practical, commending repentance and other virtues and fortifying the Jews against the vanity of the world; or it is Liturgical, dealing with rites and ceremonies; or finally it is Historical, preserving and defending traditions. The most learned judge of all these, Johann Benedict Carpzov, the most celebrated interpreter of the Sacred Letters at Leipzig, sets this out in his Introduction to Jewish Theology. IV.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Divisa quoque Theologia in duas partes, in עיוני חכמה Theoreticam sive speculativam, quæ rerum divinarum solida, exactaque notitia est, & in חכמה המעשית Activam sive Practicam, quæ hominem Judæum ad obedientiam, Deique cultum dirigit, ad pietatem, timoremque hortatur: & quamvis utramque valde commendent, necessariamque judicent, nullaque absque vera fide opera Deo placere scribant, Theoreticamque præcedere ajant, ut Practica sequi possit, tamen hanc Theologiæ partem vehementer urgent, fundamentumque non in nuda Theoria, sed in Praxi consistere referunt, decernentibus Magistris in Tractatu Talmudico פרקי אבות Capitulis Patrum, cap. 1. לא מדרש הוא עיקר אלא המעשה. Non sermo fundamentum est, sed factum; quare quoque Religio, quæ ex Theologia fluit, עבודה cultus, servitium appellata fuit ex Numer. cap. 4 verf. 23. & עבודת אל cultus Dei, ut distingueretur a עבודה זרה cultu alieno sive Idololatria; hinc quoque Religio דת Lex nominata, & דת אלהית Lex Divina, quod Leges præscribat observandas.
units.tr: Theology is also divided into two parts: the Theoretical or speculative, which is the solid and exact knowledge of divine things, עיוני חכמה [iyyuni chokhmah]; and the Active or Practical, חכמה המעשית [chokhmah ha-ma'asit], which directs the Jewish man to obedience and the worship of God and urges him to piety and the fear of God. Although they commend both highly and judge both necessary, and although they write that no works please God without true faith, and say that the Theoretical goes before so that the Practical may follow, nevertheless they press this part of theology hard and declare that the foundation lies not in bare Theory but in Practice. The masters in the Talmudic tractate פרקי אבות [Pirkei Avot], the Chapters of the Fathers, chapter 1, decide: לא מדרש הוא עיקר אלא המעשה [lo midrash hu ikar, ela ha-ma'aseh] Not discourse is the foundation, but deed. For this reason the religion that flows from theology was also called עבודה [avodah], service, worship, from Numbers 4:23, and עבודת אל [avodat El], the worship of God, so that it might be distinguished from עבודה זרה [avodah zarah], alien worship, or idolatry. Hence also religion was named דת [dat], Law, and דת אלהית [dat elohit], Divine Law, because it prescribes what is to be observed. V.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Statuunt præter Revelatam, utraque Lege contentam, Theologiam Naturalem, innatam partim, haustamque ex notionibus communibus, מצוות משכיות Præceptis Intellectualibus. bus, [Hebrew] Notionibus primis, partim ex operibus acquisitam divinis, quae tamen absque illa sit manca, mutilaque, quare ad salutem, vitamque aeternam imperfecta, quod ex solo libro Naturae salutaris Dei cognitio nulla hauriri possit, Chinnuch pag. 9. Quod bona opera ex verbo revelato sint aestimanda, Rabbi Joseph Albo Fundamentorum lib. 3. cap. 7. Quod qui in rebus Theologicis & divinis sequitur rationem & speculationes suas, is incedat sine baculo & scipione, similisque sit homini, qui solus iter facit per desertum in loco obscuro & caliginoso, hic enim certissime vadet ad suum exitium. & in scrobes ac periculà multa incidet, Auctore Rabbi Schem Tof in Praefatione Libri More Nevochim; urgentes propterea ad omnimodam perfectionem, mentisque beatitudinem adsequendam, necessariam maxime esse revelationem, Legisque Mosaicae placita unice sufficere, imo Aristotelem, summum praeteritorum temporum Philosophum multa ignorasse, hinc in fine vitae Revelatam amplexum fuisse Theologiam, Judaeumque factum. Sed ne mirum id videatur Philosophis, juvabit ipsam Aristotelis integram Epistolam ad Alexandrum Regem, discipulum suum missam, cum raro occurrat, ex Rabbi Gedaljae Ben Jachijae [Hebrew] Catena Cabbalae sol. 99. pag. 2. verbis Eruditissimi
units.tr: Besides Revealed theology, which is contained in both Laws, they maintain a Natural theology, partly innate and drawn from common notions, מצוות משכיות [mitzvot sikhiyyot], Intellectual Precepts, First Notions, and partly acquired from the works of God. Yet without revelation this is incomplete and maimed, and therefore inadequate for salvation and eternal life, since the saving knowledge of God cannot be drawn from the book of Nature alone (Chinnuch, p. 9). That good works are to be judged by the revealed word (Rabbi Joseph Albo, Fundamentals, book 3, chapter 7). That whoever in theological and divine matters follows his own reason and speculations goes without staff or guide, and is like a man who alone travels through a desert, in an obscure and misty place, for he will most surely go to his destruction and fall into pits and many dangers, by the author Rabbi Shem Tov in the preface to the book More Nevochim. Therefore they urge that revelation is above all necessary for attaining complete perfection and blessedness of mind, and that the teachings of the Mosaic Law alone are sufficient. Indeed, they say that Aristotle, the greatest philosopher of past times, knew many things not, and so at the end of his life he embraced revealed theology and became a Jew. But lest this seem strange to the philosophers, it will be worthwhile to give the whole letter of Aristotle himself, sent to King Alexander, his pupil, since it rarely occurs. I take it from the Chain of the Cabbala (Rabbi Gedaliah ben Jachiah, p. 99, page 2), in the words of the most learned Mühlius, as follows:

units.la: Muhlii referre sequentibus: Benedictus Deus, qui aperit oculos caecorum, & dirigit peccatores in via, laudetur debita laude, qui retribuit mihi misericordiam suam, ac in multitudine benignitatum suarum, qui liberavit me ab extrema stultitia, in qua haesi omnibus diebus vitae meae, cum occuparer in sapientia Philosophica, ac dijudicarem omnia intellectuali notitia, innumerosque in ea componerem libros, aufugiant omnes quotquot intuentur illos, donec in fine dierum meorum disputarem cum quodam Sapiente ex Sapientibus Israelis, qui probavit mihi manum suam validam in Lege hereditate sibi acquisita ex Sinai, pertraxitque cor meum in verba Legis, ostensis signis ac prodigiis in nominibus tanctis veris & sensu manifestis. Ego autem bardus, brutus nihil capiebam, quippe rerum magnitudo superabat intellectum. Cumque haec vidisset animum appuli, ut quantum possem intelligerem in Lege Judaeorum, ut quae tota fundata est super integros lapides, secus atque falsa sapientia Philosophorum.
units.tr: Blessed be God, who opens the eyes of the blind and directs sinners on the way, let him be praised with due praise, who has shown me his mercy and in the multitude of his kindnesses has freed me from the extreme folly in which I was stuck all the days of my life, when I was occupied with philosophical wisdom, judging all things by intellectual knowledge and composing countless books on it, all of which fled from those who looked at them, until at the end of my days I disputed with a certain sage of the sages of Israel, who showed me his strong hand in the Law, an inheritance acquired from Sinai, and drew my heart to the words of the Law, by signs and wonders displayed in holy names, true and manifest in sense. But I, a dull and brutish man, understood nothing, for the greatness of the things surpassed my understanding. When I saw this, I resolved to understand as far as I could the Law of the Jews, since it is wholly founded on whole stones, unlike the false wisdom of the philosophers.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Itaque carissime discipule, Rex Magne Alexander, ne in errorem te sociosve tuos inducant Philosophorum libri, quoniam si integrum mihi nunc esset colligere omnes li„ libros meos per universum orbem dispersos „ igni comburerem , ne vel unus Principum „ Antistitumque oculis fuperefiet,ipsique per- „ plexi redderentur in hujusmodi scientiis. „ Novi enim gravissimas me poenas Deo datu- „ rum quod ipsemet peccavi , pluresque ad „ peccandum induxi. Quocirca fili mi, Ale- „ xander, confiteor tibi omniquc posteritati „ quamplurima per intellectum cognita men- „ dacia efle, celsus etenim est super excellum „ custos. Atque cum fato meo acciderit, ut „ libri mei dissiparentur per Occidentales re- „ giones,ecce palam ac ingenue indico, nefas „ habendum legere vel meditari in illis, cum „ Logica iniquitas fit , ipsaque Philosophia „ mendax. At ecce ego nunc innocens co- „ ram Deo, quia infcienter peccavi. Vae au- „ tem illis, qui seduli sunt in iis, recta enim via „ gradiuntur ad interitum. Scito autem , „ quemadmodum ista contra sapientiam no- „ stram mihi ostenderat sapiens ille, similiter „ quoque vaticinatum Salomonem filium „ Davidis in Proverbiis suis dicendo, cap. VII, „ verf. 5. Servet te a muliere extera, & verf. 25. „ Ne declinet ad vias illius animus tuus. Item „ cap. II. verf. 19. Qui adeunt eam non revertentur. Vae oculis, qui talia vident, auribus „ quae alia audiunt ! Iterum iterumque vae mihi, qui ita inveteravi, consumfique dies meos in frivolis nocivisque rebus, quæ depri-munt, non elevant. Et quod dixisti mihi no-men meum, quod plurimos conscripserim li-bros, omnes gentes pervagaturum, hosque æternam mihi famam conciliaturos, ita habe, me potius hanc celebritatem in Lege, quam hæreticorum libris elegisse. Quin strangulari magis optasse, quā libros meos sic divulgatos. Nam qui Legi student in luce viventium lu-cem adibunt; at Philosophiæ hujus cultores in interitum commigrabunt, egoque ipsemet coram omnibus etiam pœnis afficiar. Cæ-terum antea hæc talia tibi non significavi, cum certum indubiumque habuerim, si for-te excanduceris, mihique propterea malum intentaveris, antequam hæc Epistola in ma-nus tuas perveniat, me mortuum jam futu-rum depositumque in lignea arca. Interim pacem ab Aristotele Præceptore sepulchro suo jamjam inferendo Regi Magno Ale-xandro.
units.tr: Therefore, most beloved disciple, King Alexander the Great, do not let the books of the philosophers lead you or your companions into error. For if it were now in my power to gather all my books, which are scattered throughout the whole world, I would burn them with fire, so that not even one would remain before the eyes of princes and bishops, and so that those who are perplexed by such sciences would be freed from them. For I know that I shall receive the most grievous punishments from God, because I myself have sinned and have led many into sin. Therefore, my son Alexander, I confess to you and to all posterity that very many falsehoods are known through the intellect, for the Guardian on high is exalted above all. And since it has happened to me by fate that my books have been scattered through the Western regions, behold, I openly and frankly declare that it is wrong to read or meditate on them, since it is a false logic, and philosophy itself is deceitful. But behold, I am now innocent before God, because I sinned in ignorance. Woe, however, to those who are eager for them, for they walk by a straight road to destruction. Know, moreover, that just as that wise man had shown me these things against our wisdom, so also Solomon, son of David, prophesied in his Proverbs, saying (ch. 7, vers. 5): "That he may keep you from the strange woman," and (vers. 25): "Let not your heart decline to her ways." Likewise (ch. 2, vers. 19): "None who go to her return." Woe to the eyes that see such things, and to the ears that hear other things! Again and again woe to me, who have grown so old and have spent my days on trifling and harmful things, which depress and do not raise up. And as to what you said to me, that my name, because I wrote very many books, will pass through all nations and win me eternal fame, be assured that I have chosen this celebrity in the Law rather than in the books of heretics. Indeed I would have preferred to be strangled than to see my books so published. For those who study the Law will come into the light of the living, but the devotees of this philosophy will journey to destruction, and I myself shall be punished before all. Moreover, I did not tell you these things before, since I was certain and sure that, if perhaps you grew angry and on that account threatened me with harm, before this letter reached your hands I would already be dead and laid in a wooden chest. Meanwhile, peace from your teacher Aristotle, who is about to be laid in his tomb, to King Alexander the Great.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Sicut Revelata distincta à Theologia Natu-rali, ita pariter utriusque præcepta nomini-bus sunt divisa, hujus præcepta appellantes מצוות שכליות Præcepta Intellectualia, Illius מצוות מסורה Præcepta traditione accepta, uti patet ex commentario Rabbi Beehai in Le-gem. gem,quando his loquitur dictis: Pracepta Intellectualia sunt ea praecepta, de quibus homines intellectus testatur, eaque explorat, ita ut si vel maxime scripta non essent, tamen intelligens ea suo intellectu inveniret, ut praeceptum de honorandis parentibus, de homicidio, adulterio, furto, falso testimonio, rapina, &c. Praecepta vero accepta traditione sunt, quae homo in aeternum non assequeretur, neque intellectu suo investigaret, sed opus habet traditione, ut praeceptum de clangore tubae, de tabernaculo, frondibus palmarum, & praeceptum de leviratu, & extractione calcei; patebitque magis ex Cofri Rabbi Jehudae Hallevi pag. 113, 114. non solum distinguentis statuta Intellectualia, Leges vel naturae a Lege divina, quam Intellectus humanus capere nequit, quaque filii Israelis donati sunt peculiari privilegio, sed simul observantis, quod Leges naturae, & Progymnasmata sint, vel principia, & praeparatoria ad Legem divinam, praecedentia eam natura & tempore, quodque nulla hominum societas absque illis consistere possit, quodque ille qui Intellectuales non observat, minus observare possit oblationes, Sabbathum, Circumcisionem & alias, quas Intellectus humanus nec affirmat, nec negat.
units.tr: Just as Revealed Theology is distinguished from Natural Theology, so too the precepts of each are named differently: the precepts of the latter are called Intellectual Precepts [מצוות שכליות], and those of the former precepts received by tradition [מצוות מסורה]. This is clear from the commentary of Rabbi Bechai on the Law, where he speaks thus: Intellectual precepts are those precepts to which human intellect bears witness, and which it tests, so that even if they were not written down at all, the one who understands would find them by his own intellect, such as the precept concerning the honouring of parents, concerning murder, adultery, theft, false witness, robbery, etc. But precepts received by tradition are those which a man would never attain, nor investigate by his own intellect, but which need tradition, such as the precept concerning the sound of the trumpet, concerning the tabernacle, the palm branches, the precept concerning levirate marriage, and the drawing off of the shoe. It will become clearer from the Kuzari of Rabbi Judah Halevi, pp. 113, 114, where he not only distinguishes the intellectual statutes, or laws of nature, from the divine Law, which human intellect cannot grasp and with which the sons of Israel were endowed as a special privilege, but also observes at the same time that the laws of nature are the preliminary exercises, or principles and preparations, for the divine Law, preceding it in nature and in time; that no human society can exist without them; and that one who does not observe the intellectual precepts can observe still less the offerings, the Sabbath, circumcision, and the others, which human intellect neither affirms nor denies.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Complectitur Revelata Theologia tum מצוות Præcepta, Dogmatave, fideique Articulos, mox ordine recensendos, tum מנהגים Ritus, Ceremoniasque, partim in Machsorim, Selichot, Thephillot, aliisque hujus generis contentas, partim pluribus descriptas per Antonium Margaritam, Christianum Gersonem, Buxtorfios, Leonem Mutinensem, Abrahamum Cosferum, Lancelottum Addisonem, reliquosque sine numero.
units.tr: Revealed Theology comprises both the precepts [מצוות], the dogmas, and the articles of faith, to be listed in order shortly, and the rites and ceremonies [מנהגים], partly contained in the Machsorim, Selichot, Thephillot, and other works of this kind, and partly described by Antonius Margaritha, Christian Gerson, the Buxtorfs, Leo of Modena, Abraham Cosferus, Lancelot Addison, and countless others.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Appellant fidei luæ articulos עקרים Radices, עקרי האמונה Radices Fidei, ראש אמנה Caput Fidei יסוד האמונה Fundamentum Fidei, שרשים Radices, שרשי אמונה Radices Fidei, quod his Fundamentis tota innitatur Religio Judaica, exque his Radicibus reliquorum firmitas dependeat & soliditas. Audiamus quæso Abarbanelem in libro de Capite Fidei, cap. 6. Certe, si ita sit, nomen יסוד & שרש Radix & Fundamentum, non dicetur nisi de ea re, ex qua stabilitas & firmitas alterius rei dependet, neque habet soliditatem nisi abea; ipsumque Menassen Ben Israel, novissimum Judæorum Doctorem, in Libro de Creatione, Problemate I. Nam sicut rami arboris dependent à radice, ita etiam existimarunt ab ipsis capitibus, sive articulis fidei, legem totam dependere, adeo, ut si quis si quis illos neget, universam legem irritam faciat.
units.tr: They call the articles of their faith the Roots [עקרים], the Roots of Faith [עקרי האמונה], the Head of Faith [ראש אמנה], the Foundation of Faith [יסוד האמונה], the Roots [שרשים], and the Roots of Faith [שרשי אמונה], because the whole Jewish religion rests on these foundations, and the firmness and solidity of the rest depend on these roots. Let us hear, I pray, Abarbanel in his book on the Head of Faith, chapter 6: Certainly, if this is so, the words yesod and sheresh, Root and Foundation, are used only of that thing on which the stability and firmness of another thing depend, and it has no solidity except from it. And Menasseh Ben Israel, the most recent of the Jewish teachers, in his book On the Creation, Problem I: For just as the branches of a tree depend on the root, so too they have thought that the whole Law depends on the articles or heads of faith, so that if anyone denies them, he makes the entire Law void.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: In his articulis suis describendis, determinandisque fuit Synagoga dilcors, non probantibus omnibus, maxime Doctoribus, ex invidia, prurituque dissentiendi, studium illud Maimonidis indefessum, quod rebus impendebat Judaicis, elogiumque, quo magnabatur, divinum, ממשה אי משה לא הי כמשה ד Mose Propheta, usque ad Mosen Maimonidem non fuit sicut Moses Maimonides; videns enim Maimonides articulos fidei per immensa Thalmudicorum aliorumque scriptorum volumina jacere sparsos, hincque optatam genti non apportare utilitatem, statuit primus certum & determinatum dogmatum numerum, quasi fidei & religionis symbolum toti Judæorum coetui praescribere, hæcque tredecim generalioribus completi articulis, quo haberet gens disperta, ut se tum contra Adversarios muniret suos, tum ut veritates clarioribus, distinctioribusque confirmaret verbis, quod ipse in commentario suo super Tractatum Sanhedrin cap. xi. sol. 111. col. 1, postquam articulos recensuisset suos, his fatetur verbis: sed hoc feci, quia summam utilitatem, & fidei ipsius confirmationem continet, & res res utiles per multos & praeclaros libros dispersas tibi hic complexus sum; commendat porro in eodem commentario suam in his concinnandis diligentiam, cum inquit: non enim fortuito & sine judicio ista congessi, sed post maturam cognitionem librorum, & sententiarum verarum falsarumque probam discretionem, ac juxta rationum & argumentorum omnium super re quavis consideratio-nem exactam.
units.tr: In describing and defining these articles the Synagogue was divided. Not everyone approved, and most of all the teachers, from envy and an itch to disagree. The tireless effort that Maimonides devoted to Jewish matters, and the divine praise by which he was magnified, "From Moses to Moses there was none like Moses" [ממשה אי משה לא הי כמשה], were not enough for them. For Maimonides, seeing that the articles of faith lay scattered through the vast volumes of the Talmudists and other writers, and that this brought no useful result to the nation, was the first to fix a certain and determined number of doctrines. He prescribed them to the whole Jewish community as a summary of faith and religion, and he completed them in thirteen more general articles. He did this so that the scattered nation would have something to defend itself with against its adversaries, and so that the truths would be confirmed in clearer and more distinct words. He himself admits this in his commentary on the tractate Sanhedrin, chapter 11, p. 111, col. 1, after he had listed his articles: "But I have done this because it contains the greatest usefulness and the confirmation of the faith itself, and I have gathered together for you here useful matters that were scattered through many famous books." In the same commentary he also commends his diligence in arranging them, saying: "For I have not gathered these things by chance or without judgment, but after a mature knowledge of the books and a sound discernment of true and false opinions, and after an exact consideration of all the reasons and arguments on any subject."

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Non autem haec Maimonidis unquam fuit mens, his suis tredecim articulis, totam absolvi fidem Judaicam, nec plura creditu esse necessaria, cum ingenue fateatur plurima restare credenda, quae tredecim his non sint inserta articulis, inter quae numerat Poenitentiam, de qua sic in More Nevochim Part. 3. cap. 36. pag. 443. ex versione Buxtorfiana loquitur: Porro manifestum est, doctrinam de Poenitentia ad hoc quoque genus pertinere, hoc est, ex illis esse dogmatibus, quae necessario credenda sunt ab illis, qui Legi nostrae nomen dare volunt; Sed voluit per hos informare pueros, plebemque, ipsosque in Lege non exercitatos quasi manu ducere ad claram distinctamque rerum divinarum cognitionem, sic enim rursus inquit in More Nevochim Part. 1. cap. 35. pag. 51. Atque haec mensura sufficit propueris & proplebe, quando sciunt, Deum Deum esse, & esse perfectissimum, sine corpore vel potentia aut facultate aliqua corporea, sine omni imperfectione, ac per consequens nulli passioni obnoxium. Quod idem de Maimonidis quoque propositio testatur Abarbanel, quando in Capite Fidei, his refert verbis cap.33. Interprete Vorstio: Sed intentio eius fuit dirigere homines, qui non sunt solide fundati in scientia Legis, nec dicerunt, aut operam dederunt, quantum illis necesse erat. Quia enim illi non possunt assequi, aut comprehendere omnia fidei dogmata & scientias, quas Lex divina continet, hinc selegit Rab ex omnibus fidei dogmatibus ipsos 13. fidei articulos magis generales, ut compendiose doceret ipsa, quae habent eas doctrinas. Sunt vero hi articuli maxime generales, latissimaeque significationis ac explicationis, proindeque infinita in se continentes; summa junt tantum, unde multi alii articuli oriuntur ac dependent, sicut innuit Judaeus apud Coccejum in Considerationibus ad Quaestiones Judaicas, cap.14.
units.tr: Yet it was never Maimonides' intention that the whole Jewish faith should be completed by these thirteen articles, nor that no more was necessary to be believed. For he frankly admits that very many things remain to be believed which are not included in these thirteen articles, among them repentance. He speaks of this in the More Nevochim, part 3, chapter 36, p. 443, in Buxtorf's version: "Moreover, it is clear that the doctrine of repentance also belongs to this class, that is, it is one of those doctrines which must necessarily be believed by those who wish to give their name to our Law." But he wished through these articles to instruct boys and the common people, and to lead by the hand those not yet trained in the Law to a clear and distinct knowledge of divine things. So he says again in the More Nevochim, part 1, chapter 35, p. 51: "And this measure is sufficient for boys and for the people, when they know that God is God, and is most perfect, without body or power or any corporeal faculty, without any imperfection, and consequently not subject to any passion." Abarbanel also testifies to the same intention of Maimonides when, in the Capita Fidei, chapter 33, he reports these words, in the translation of Vorstius: "But his intention was to direct men who are not solidly grounded in the knowledge of the Law, and who have neither spoken nor labored as much as was necessary for them." For since they cannot grasp or comprehend all the doctrines of faith and the sciences which the divine Law contains, therefore he chose from all the doctrines of faith these thirteen articles of faith, which are more general, so that he might teach briefly those things which contain these doctrines. These articles, however, are most general, and of the widest meaning and explanation, and therefore contain in themselves infinite things. They are only the summaries from which many other articles arise and depend, as a Jew hints in Cocceius, Considerationes ad Quaestiones Judaicas, chapter 14.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Quamvis maxima Gentis Judaicae portio, novi sui Legislatoris Maimonidis admirata fuerit sapientiam, articulosque, ut fidei, Religionisque suae normam libenter amplexata fuerit, reperti tamen diversis temporibus, honoris doctrinaeque Maimonianae Adversarii, rii, qui voce, scriptisque aliam Articulorum fidei constitutionem, numerumque diversum, omnibus suis viribus suadere conati sunt, inter quos excelluerunt Rabbi Chasdai, & Rabbi Ioseph, atro propterea carbone notati ab Abarbanele, qui sic dissensiones Magistrorum inutiles in Capitis fidei Praefatione Rhythmica deplorat, Maimonidisque caulam agit: Fratres nostri liquefecerunt cor da nostra, eosque corruptores vocavimus: nam unus ab altero segregatus est, & iudicium pendet: unusquisque peculiarem viam ingressus est, trita relicta: cuique sua via recta visa, sancta & laudanda, nec unus ad alterius sententiam accessit: omnes vero sibi sapientissimi visi sunt: qua res integros & fideles Iudaeos perturbavit: nulla quies nec laetitia in animis eorum: velut fatui diversis cogitationibus distracti sunt: fidelis quisque horrore & dolore correptus est: dixerunt enim: Quis montem Domini scandet, vel in locum eius sanctum angelis stipatum penetrabit? Nos enim ignoramus, ubi habitat Lux, aut qua via incedent redempti: Numin via aquila caelestis, Principis summi, R. Mosis b. m. Praefecti & Ducis exulum? num fidem ab illo definitam iusti sequentur? At vero in viis Rabbinorum recentiorum, qui litem illi moverunt? tegite urticis faciem eius, ob exactores eius, qui obloquuntur iusto, columnae mundi: cuius cor est instar ianuae palatij: in superbia & contemtu, quis quis cæcus est ut perfectus Spiritus & anima ejus ad me clamant inter viventes in mundo: liberos educavi & exaltavi, omnes inimicos meos factos: Non-ne illi panem meum ederunt, & pane fortium satu-rati sunt? biberunt vinum libaminis mei, hause-runt aquas viventes e fonte meo benedictio, a parvu-lo eorum ad magnum eorum lapidem in me jecerunt, contriverunt & persecuti sunt me, irriserunt me parvuli & pro nugatore habuerunt: Servi adver-sus Dominos suos surrexerunt, erumpentes, exigen-tes, & sagittus pra omnibus jaculatoribus urgentes: Duo viri Hebrei litigantes (nempe Rabbi Chas-dai & Rabbi Joseph Albo) pulli an ova, disci-puli Rabbi Niffim, ad quorum sonum omnes aufuge-runt.
units.tr: Although the greatest part of the Jewish nation admired the wisdom of their new Lawgiver, Maimonides, and gladly embraced his articles as the rule of their faith and religion, nevertheless at various times there were adversaries of Maimonides' honor and teaching, who by voice and writing tried with all their strength to urge a different constitution of the articles of faith and a different number. Among them Rabbi Chasdai and Rabbi Joseph excelled, and for this reason were marked with black charcoal by Abarbanel. Abarbanel deplores the useless disputes of the masters in his rhythmic preface to the Capita Fidei, and pleads the cause of Maimonides: "Our brothers have melted our hearts, and we called them corrupters. For one has separated from another, and judgment hangs in the balance. Each has entered his own path, having abandoned the beaten track. Each has thought his own way right, holy, and praiseworthy, and no one has come round to another's opinion. But all seemed to themselves most wise. This has disturbed the upright and faithful Jews. There is no quiet nor joy in their minds. Like fools they are pulled apart by different thoughts. Every faithful man has been seized with horror and grief. For they said: Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or enter into his holy place surrounded by angels? For we do not know where the Light dwells, or by what way the redeemed shall walk. Is not Maimonides, the heavenly eagle, the Prince supreme, Rabbi Moses of blessed memory, the Prefect and Leader of the exiles? Will the righteous not follow the faith he has defined? But what of the ways of the more recent Rabbis, who have raised a quarrel against him? Cover with nettles the face of him, because of his exactors, who speak against the righteous one, the pillar of the world, whose heart is like the gate of a palace, in pride and contempt. Whoever is blind as the perfect spirit, and his soul cries out to me among the living in the world: I have raised and exalted sons, and all my enemies have become my sons. Have they not eaten my bread, and been satisfied with the bread of the strong? They have drunk the wine of my libation, they have drunk the living waters from my fountain. From their little ones to their great ones they have cast stones at me; they have crushed and persecuted me; the little ones have mocked me and held me for a trifler. Servants have risen against their masters, breaking out, demanding, and pressing with arrows more than all the archers. Two Hebrew men quarreling, namely Rabbi Chasdai and Rabbi Joseph Albo, chicks or eggs, disciples of Rabbi Nissim, at whose sound all have fled away."

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Culpant hi Duumviri Maimonidem multos necessarios omisisse fidei articulos, Præcepta ab Articulis non separasse, Funda-mentalibus annumerasse non Fundamentalia, quare prior Rabbi Chasdai in libro Or Adonai, paulo sibi visus subtilior, quatuor fidei articu-lorum genera, suis propriis distincta quatuor classibus constituit, universumque fidei Judai-cæ systema viginti implevit articulis, quas cum Abarbenel in Capite Fidei cap. 2 enarret, opera pretium erit illos ut mentem Rabbi Chas-dai melius intelligamus, Lectori verbis commumunicare Vorstianis: Certè Rab Chasdai in libro suo, Or Adonai, alia ratione constituit articulos seu fundamenta: Ipse enim scribit, quædam esse fidei legalis capita ac fundamenta in omnibus præceptis, & principia in quolibet præcepto, atque initia in omnifide, uti sunt: Existentia Dei, sub qua comprehenduntur alii fidei articuli, qui sunt: Vnitas ejus, & quod non sit corpus, neque potentia in corpore: Alia autem capita legalia esse fundamenta legis, quia si concipiatur privatio unius ex iis, collapsura sit Lex in generalitate. Sunt autem sex: Notitia Dei de existentibus. Providentia ejus circa ea. Potentia ejus infinita. Prophetia. Liberum arbitrium. Novissimus dies. (Odehlio in Bifronte Synagoga, p. 66. placet Justitia) Sunt denique quidam fidei articuli, quibus credendum est; qui autem unum eorum negat, vocabitur hæreticus; quia sunt articuli fidei non dependentes à præceptis specialibus; & sunt isti octo, Creatio mundi, ψυχή, anima. (Immortalitas) Præmium & pœna. Resurrectio mortuorum. Æternitas legis. Eminentia Prophetiæ Mosis. Quod siat Sacerdoti responsum per Urim & Thummim. Messias. Sunt denique quædam fidei dogmata quibus credendum est; qui vero negaverit unum eorum, appellabitur hæreticus, quia dependent à præceptis particularibus; & sunt tria. Precatio & benedictio Sacerdotum. Utilitas resipiscentia. Principium anni, ac quatuor temporum distinctiones.
units.tr: These two teachers blame Maimonides for omitting many necessary articles of faith, for not separating precepts from articles, and for counting among the fundamentals things that are not fundamental. Therefore the former, Rabbi Chasdai, in his book Or Adonai, seeming to himself somewhat more subtle, distinguished four kinds of articles of faith, arranged in four separate classes, and filled the whole system of Jewish faith with twenty articles. Since Abarbanel sets these out in Chapter 2 of his Capite Fidei, it will be worth while, so that we may better understand the mind of Rabbi Chasdai, to pass them on to the reader in the words of Vorstius: Certainly Rab Chasdai, in his book Or Adonai, set up the articles or foundations on another plan. For he writes that there are certain chief points and foundations of the legal faith in all the precepts, and principles in each precept, and beginnings in all faith, such as: the existence of God, under which other articles of faith are included, namely: his unity, and that he is not a body, nor has power in a body. The other legal chief points, however, are foundations of the law, because if the lack of any one of them were conceived, the Law would collapse as a whole. There are six: knowledge of God concerning existing things; his providence over them; his infinite power; prophecy; free will; the last day. (Odelius in Bifronte Synagoga, p. 66, pleases Justice.) Finally there are certain articles of faith which must be believed; whoever denies one of them will be called a heretic; because they are articles of faith not depending on special precepts. These are eight: the creation of the world, the soul [ψυχή], the anima. (Immortality.) Reward and punishment; the resurrection of the dead; the eternity of the law; the eminence of the prophecy of Moses; that answer be given to the priest through the Urim and Thummim; the Messiah. Finally there are certain dogmas of faith which must be believed; but whoever denies one of them will be called a heretic, because they depend on particular precepts; and there are three: the prayer and blessing of the priests; the usefulness of repentance; the beginning of the year, and the distinctions of the four seasons.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Posterior Rabbi Joseph Albo in libro בעקרים de articulis, quem ex versione Latina sibi servat illustris V Vinckelmannus, tria generalia Fidei posuit fundamenta, ex quibus quasdam deducit radices, quæ rursus suos contineant ramos, octodecimque omnes una colligati faciant Articulos, quos cum valde confuse & negligenter retulerit Abarbanel in Capite Fidei, cap. 2. placuit defectum hunc eruditis Odehlii observationibus illustrare, atque ex ipso in Synagoga sua Bifronte notare, quod Rabbi Joseph Albo Part. 1. tria generalia statuat Religionis divinæ fundamenta, nimirum Existentiam Dei, Legem esse a Deo, & præmium & pœnam; Ex quibus derivet ceu fundamentis radices quasdam, quæ respectu fundamentorum illorum velut species sint sub generibus comprehensæ, quod una radicum sublata non auferatur fundamentum, sublato vero fundamento, radices corruant; Ex primo has quatuor continentes omnia ea, quæ ab existentia Dei dependent, Unitatem Dei, eum non esse corporeum, nec potentiam in corpore, eum nullam habere dependentiam a tempore, & Deum Benedictum ab omni imperfectione immunem esse. Ex secundo tres sequentes, tes, Scientiam Dei, Prophetiam, & missionem legati, scilicet Mosis. Ex tertio unam, nimirum providentiam. Addit his articulum de libero Arbitrio. Præter hos recensitos sex ramos numerat, seu Articulos fidei, quos unusquisque legi Mosaicæ addictus credere tenetur, quique ex tribus illis fundamentis pullulant, licet radicum nomen non mereantur, quia absque his fundamenta & radices legis Mosaicæ concipi possunt, quo refert Creationem mundi ex nihilo, præstantiam Prophetiæ Mosis, immutabilitatem Legis Mosaicæ, fidem qua creditur perfectionem humanam attingi posse per observationem præcepti alicujus Mosaici, articulum de Resurrectione mortuorum, articulum de adventu Messiæ.
units.tr: The later Rabbi Joseph Albo, in his book on the articles [בעקרים], which Mr. Vinckelmann keeps in a Latin version, laid down three general foundations of faith, from which he derives certain roots, which in turn have their own branches; and all of them, bound together, make up eighteen articles. Since Abarbanel reported these very confusedly and carelessly in Chapter 2 of his Capite Fidei, I have thought it good to illustrate this defect with the learned observations of Odelius, and to note from him in his Bifronte Synagoga that Rabbi Joseph Albo, in Part 1, sets up three general foundations of the divine religion, namely: the existence of God; that the Law is from God; and reward and punishment. From these he derives, as from foundations, certain roots, which with respect to those foundations are like species comprehended under genera; so that if one root is removed the foundation is not taken away, but if the foundation is removed the roots collapse. From the first he derives four roots containing all those things which depend on the existence of God: the unity of God; that he is not corporeal, nor has power in a body; that he has no dependence on time; and that the blessed God is free from every imperfection. From the second he derives three following roots: the knowledge of God, prophecy, and the mission of the envoy, namely Moses. From the third he derives one, namely providence. To these he adds the article on free will. Besides these six recounted branches, he counts also certain articles of faith, or branches, which everyone devoted to the Mosaic law is bound to believe, and which spring from those three foundations, although they do not deserve the name of roots, because without them the foundations and roots of the Mosaic law can be conceived. To these he refers the creation of the world out of nothing, the excellence of the prophecy of Moses, the immutability of the Mosaic law, the belief by which it is believed that human perfection can be attained through the observance of some Mosaic precept, the article on the resurrection of the dead, and the article on the coming of the Messiah.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Sunt apud Rabbi Joseph Albo Part. 1. cap. 3. qui viginti sex numerarunt fidei Judaicæ articulos. Extiterunt qui undecim Religionis Judaicæ statuerunt Articulos, teste Rabbi Abraham Jaghel in suo Catechismo Judaico. Autor Hilchot Gedolot in ea est sententia, non nisi unicum in Lege constituendum esse articulum, videlicet Existentiam Dei, vocatque eum receptionem regni divini, uti monet Abarbanel in Capite Fidei, capite 22.
units.tr: In Rabbi Joseph Albo, Part 1, chapter 3, there are those who have numbered twenty-six articles of Jewish faith. There have been some who laid down eleven articles of the Jewish religion, according to Rabbi Abraham Jaghel in his Jewish Catechism. The author of the Hilchot Gedolot is of the opinion that only one article should be laid down in the Law, namely the existence of God, and he calls it the acceptance of the divine kingdom, as Abarbanel advises in the Capite Fidei, chapter 22.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Quamvis Maimoniorum Articulorum varia apud Rabbinos fuerit fortuna, diversisque impetiti fuerintaciebus, vicerunt tamen, habueruntque semper suos admiratores, cultoresque quam plurimos, ita ut hodie tota Rabbinorum sequatur cohors, multis interantur scriptis Rabbinicis, in scholis explicentur, pueris tradantur, commentariis illustrentur, a variis objectionibus vindicentur, sintque proinde hi tredecim articuli summa, tesseraque moderni Judaismi, quibus creditis fiat Judæus, hæresque vitæ æternæ, negatis vero fiat כפר בעקר אפיקורס מ"ן Apostata, negans fundamentum, Epicurœus, hæreticus, sicuti hoc primus horum Autor monuit Maimonides in Commentario Thalmudico Sanhedrin, sol. 121. col. 1. Quod si quis articulos hos omnes credat, & suam fidem eorum professione declaret, recipitur in Ecclesiam Israeliticam, & dignus est amore & benevolentia, & ut præstemus ei, quicquid Deus amoris & charitatis fraternæ alterum alteri exhibere jussit. Et quamvis nimis proterve in peccata incidat ob pravam concupiscentiam & naturæ corruptæ prævalentiam, puniendus quidem est pro ratione delictorum suorum, sed habebit tamen partem in futuro sæculo, quippe qui ex numero tantum transgressorum Israeliticorum est. Quod si quis vero vel unicum horum articulorum vilivilipendat, hoc ipso fit Apostata, & fundamentum negat, vocandusque est haereticus & Epicuræus, plantarumque excisor, quem odio habere & perdere jussi sumus, utpote de quo dictum est Psalmo 139. vers. 21. nonne oderes tuos, Domine, odi? Cum quo egregie convenit Abarbanel, quando in capite Fidei, cap. 6. ici loquitur: Praeterea videbis, ipsos articulos & fundamenta, quæ recenset Rab, non tantum esse articulos & fundamenta legis, sed intendit iis Rab, quod sint articuli Iudaismi, ut qui credat iis, sit in communione Israelis, siquidem de iis ait Mischna: Omnis Israelita habet partem in futuro sæculo, ac si ipse dixisset: Isti articuli sunt fundamenta, quibus superstructa & impositá est hæreditas futuri sæculi spiritualis uniuscujusque qui vocatur nomine Israelis: & credimus illud, quod, etiamsi quis commiserit multa peccata, & propter rebellionem suam sit poenam accepturus, nihilominus habiturus sit partem in futuro sæculo, atque extra hanc fidem & articulos nullus homo poterit hæreditare futurum sæculum; Confirmatur vero quam maxime in Catechismo Judaico, Quæstione 7. qua Doctori Hebræo interroganti, quænam illa sint, quæ illi dixerint, & quæ credere teneantur? respondetur a discipulo: Perplurima dixerunt. Verum tredecim sunt fundamenta, quæ credere oportet quemvis, qui in consortio Israel numerari cupit, & ex illis patefecit fides ejus. Quod si quis in horum fun-
units.tr: Although Maimonides' Articles have had varied fortune among the rabbis, and have been attacked in various ways, they have nonetheless prevailed. They have always had their admirers and very many adherents, so that today the whole company of rabbis follows them. They are set out in many rabbinic writings, explained in the schools, taught to children, illustrated by commentaries and defended against various objections. These thirteen articles are therefore the summary and watchword of modern Judaism: whoever believes them becomes a Jew and has a share in eternal life, but whoever denies them becomes an apostate, a denier of the fundamental principle [כפר בעקר], an Epicurean, a heretic, as Maimonides, the first author of these articles, warned in his Talmudic commentary on Sanhedrin, fol. 121, col. 1. But if anyone believes all these articles and declares his faith by professing them, he is received into the Israelite Church, and he is worthy of love and goodwill, and we should do for him whatever God has commanded one brother to show to another in love and fraternal charity. And although he may fall into sins too recklessly, through depraved desire and the prevalence of corrupt nature, he is indeed to be punished according to the measure of his offences, but he will nevertheless have a share in the age to come, since he is only one of the transgressing Israelites. But if anyone scorns even one of these articles, by that very act he becomes an apostate, denies the fundamental principle, is to be called a heretic and an Epicurean, and a uprooter of plants, whom we are commanded to hate and destroy, as it is said in Psalm 139, verse 21: "Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord?" Abarbanel agrees well with this when, in his Book of Faith, chapter 6, he says: Moreover you will see that these articles and foundations which Rab recounts are not only articles and foundations of the Law, but Rab intends by them that they are the articles of Judaism, so that whoever believes them is in the community of Israel, since the Mishnah says of them: Every Israelite has a share in the age to come, as if he had said: These articles are the foundations on which is built and laid the spiritual inheritance of the age to come of everyone who is called by the name of Israel. And we believe that even if someone has committed many sins and is to receive punishment for his rebellion, he will nevertheless have a share in the age to come; and outside this faith and these articles no man can inherit the age to come. This is confirmed most strongly in the Jewish Catechism, question 7, where the Hebrew teacher asks what those things are that they have said and which they are bound to believe, and the disciple answers: They have said very many things. But there are thirteen foundations which everyone who desires to be counted in the fellowship of Israel must believe, and by these his faith is made manifest. But if anyone strikes against one of these foundations

units.tr: ...of the fundamentals, one of them, he is called an apostate and a heretic, and must not be called by the name of Israelite.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Exhibet Synagoga mox breviores, concisioresque Fidei suae tredecim Articulos, mox latiores, explanatioresque, cum suis commentariis, Illos apud Menaffen Ben Israel in libro de Creatione mundi, Problemate I. Judaeumque Anonymum apud Coccejum in Consideratio-nibus Responsionum Judaicarum, Quaestione 12. cap. 14. Hos apud Rabbi Davidem Vidalium in Michtam LeDavid brevi cum notis, versioneque Latina Wolfii edendum; omnes tamen ex Maimonide petitos, quem ipsis propriis verbis audire juvabit, ut ita ex fonte, veram certissimamque articulorum horum adsequamur mentem; Leguntur vero illi in commentario super Tractatum Talmudicum Sanhedrin, cap. 11. repetunturque ab Abarbanale in Capite Fidei, cap. 1.
units.tr: The Synagogue sets forth its thirteen articles of faith, sometimes in briefer and more concise form, sometimes in fuller and more explanatory form with their commentaries. The former are found in Menasseh ben Israel, in his book on the Creation of the World, Problem I, and in an anonymous Jew cited by Coccejus in his Considerations on Jewish Answers, question 12, chapter 14. The latter are found in Rabbi David Vidal's Michtam LeDavid, which is to be published in a short form with notes and a Latin version by Wolf. All of them, however, are taken from Maimonides, and it will be helpful to hear him in his own words, so that we may reach the true and most certain meaning of these articles from the source. They are read in his commentary on the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin, chapter 11, and are repeated by Abarbanel in his Book of Faith, chapter 1.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Fundamentum primum est Existentia Creatoris excelsi, quod nimirum existat ibi perfectus omni modo perfectionis, & sit supra quaelibet existentia, atque ab eo perpetuitatem eorum esse. Et si concipias illum non existere, cessabit existentia cujuslibet entis: Sin vero tibi imagineris, nulla inveniri existentia præter illum solum, tum ille solum existet, neque desinet aut deficiet existentia Dei, quia ipse in existentia sua non opus habet alio præter se ipsum, sed quicquid præter illum est, sive sint intelligentiæ sepatatæ, sive orbes, aut quod infra illos, istud necessario dependet ab ejus existentia. Hoc autem primum fundamentum discimus ex dicto: (Exod. cap. 20. vers. 2.) Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus; & hoc est præceptum adsirmativum.
units.tr: The first foundation is the existence of the most high Creator, namely that he exists, perfect in every way of perfection, and is above every existence, and that the existence of all other things derives from him. And if you conceive that he does not exist, the existence of every being will cease. But if you imagine that no existence can be found except his alone, then he alone will exist, and the existence of God will neither end nor fail, because in his existence he needs nothing other than himself; but whatever is other than him, whether separate intelligences, or the spheres, or whatever is below them, necessarily depends on his existence. We learn this first foundation from the saying (Exod. ch. 20, verse 2): "I am the Lord your God"; and this is a positive precept.

units.la: Secundum Fundamentum est Vnitas ejus, quod videlicet sit unus: non est autem unus tanquam species generalium, neque unus ut species particularium, nec etiam unus instar compositi, hoc enim dividitur in plures unitates, neque instar corporis simplicis, hoc enim unum est numero suo, atque accipit divisionem in infinitum. Sed Deus est unus unitate, cui nulla similis est. Hoc autem fundamentum secundum discimus ex eo, cum dicitur: (Deuter. cap. 6. vers. 4.) audi Israel, Dominus Deus noster, Deus unus est: atque hoc est præceptum adsirmativum.
units.tr: The second foundation is his unity, namely that he is one. He is not one as a species of genera, nor one as a species of particulars, nor even one like a composite, for that is divided into many unities; nor like a simple body, for that is one in number and admits division to infinity. But God is one with a unity to which none is similar. We learn this second foundation from the saying (Deut. ch. 6, verse 4): "Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one"; and this is a positive precept.

units.la: Fundamentum Tertium est Remotio corporalitatis, quod nimirum unus iste Deus non fit corpus, neque potentia in corpore, neque accidens ad corpora spectans, ut e. c. est motus & quies, non in substantia nec accidente. Et jam ab eo separarunt compositionem & divisionem. Atque hinc ait Propheta: (Esai. cap.40.verf.25) cui assimilabis me, & æqualis ero. Quod si esset corpus, haberet similitudinem cum aliis corporibus: quicquid autem in sacris libris occurrit de attributis corporum, veluti sessionis, stationis, atque id genus alia, omnia ista dicuntur more humano; quemadmodum dixere sapientes cel. mem. Loquitur Lex humana lingua. Plurima autem dixerunt de hoc negotio omnium ætatum sapientes. Atque tertium hoc fundamentum discimus exi-sto: (Deut. cap. 4. verf 15.) non vidistis ullam imaginem, q.d. nulla occurrit in eo figura; quoniam ipse, uti diximus, non est corpus, neque est potentia in corpore.
units.tr: The third foundation is the removal of corporeality: namely, that this one God is not a body, nor a power in a body, nor an accident pertaining to bodies, such as motion and rest, whether in substance or in accident. From this they also separated composition and division. Hence the Prophet says: "To whom then will you liken me, that I should be equal?" (Isa. 40:25). If he were a body, he would have likeness to other bodies. Whatever occurs in the sacred books about the attributes of bodies, such as sitting, standing and the like, all of these are said in the manner of men, as the wise of blessed memory said: "the Law speaks in human language." Indeed, the wise of every age have said very many things on this matter. We learn this third foundation from: "You saw no image" (Deut. 4:15), that is, no figure occurs in him, since he, as we have said, is not a body nor a power in a body.

units.la: Fundamentum Quartum est, quod iste unus sit vere æternus, ac nihil præter illum æter-num, si comparemus eum cum alio, & multæ de hac re probationes occurrunt in libris. Hoc vero fundamentum quartum discimus ex eo: (Deut. cap. 33. verf. 27.) Deus æternus, & infer-ne brachia æterna.
units.tr: The fourth foundation is that this one is truly eternal, and that nothing besides him is eternal, if we compare him with anything else; and many proofs of this matter occur in the books. We learn this fourth foundation from: "The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms" (Deut. 33:27).

units.la: §. Fundamentum Quintum est, quod oportet solum Deum Sanctum Benedictum colere, magnificare, celebrare, atque extollere voce laudis, neque tale quid praestandum esse ulli existenti, praeter illum; sive angelis, sive stellis, vel orbibus aut elementis, aut cuiquam ex iis conflato: quia omnia ista ordinata sunt propter operationes suas, neque inest iis potentia aut voluntas, nisi amor Dei: neque decet constituere mediatores inter Deum sanctum Benedictum & homines; sed omnes cogitationes in eum dirigere & segregare ab alio extra illum. Hoc vero fundamentum discimus ex praecepto nobis lato, ne videlicet serviamus idolis, atque plurima sunt de hoc negotio dicta legis.
units.tr: §. The fifth foundation is that one ought to worship the holy, blessed God alone, magnify him, celebrate him and extol him with the voice of praise, and that no such honour is to be given to any existing thing besides him: whether to angels, or stars, or spheres, or elements, or anything compounded from these; because all of these are ordained for their operations, and in them there is no power or will except the love of God. Nor is it fitting to set up mediators between the holy, blessed God and men, but to direct all thoughts toward him and to separate them from anything outside him. We learn this foundation from the precept laid down for us, namely that we should not serve idols, and very many things are said on this matter in the Law.

units.la: Fundamentum Sextum est Prophetia, quod conveniat scire in isto genere hominum plurimas deprehendi virtutes, atque eximias perfectiones, & reddi animam eorum puram, usque adeo, ut accipiat formam intelligentiae, & postea etiam jungatur intellectus humanus agenti, a quo emanat in illum eximius influxus: & hi ipsi sunt prophetae. Hoc autem est prophetia, ejusque negotium. Accurata autem hujus rei explicatio nimis prolixa foret, neque nobis propositum fuit adducere de-
units.tr: The sixth foundation is Prophecy. It is fitting to know that in this class of men many virtues and outstanding perfections are found, and their souls are made so pure that they receive the form of intelligence. Afterwards the human intellect is joined to the agent intellect, from which an outstanding influx flows into them. These are the prophets. This is prophecy and its function. A precise explanation of the matter would be too lengthy, and it was not our purpose to bring forward a demonstration of each foundation or to explain its truth.

units.la: B monstrationem super quodlibet fundamen-tum, aut explicare ejus veritatem : hoc enim omnem eorum complecteretur scientiam, sed tantum nude vel simpliciter ea commemorabimus ; multum autem versus Legis de Prophetis testantur.
units.tr: B demonstration upon any foundation whatever, or to explain its truth; for that would embrace the whole of their science. We shall simply and merely mention these things, however; and many verses of the Law bear witness concerning the Prophets.

units.la: Fundamentum Septimum est Prophetia Mosis Magistri nostri, super quem pax, quod nimirum oporteat credere, ipsum esse patrem omnium praecedentium prophetarum, qui ante, & subsequentium, qui post illum fuere; illos omnes, infra eum positos esse quoad excellentiam, atque eum solum elegisse Deum ex omni genere humano ; & majori notitia apprehendisse Deum, quam ullus homo qui inventus fuit, aut invenietur. Et ipse, super quem pax, summa sequestratione separatus fuit ab homine, adeo ut, cum apprehenderet aliquid, cessarent in eo potentia imaginationis ac sensus atque accidentia eorum, ut solus relinqueretur intellectus. Idcirco enim dicitur, (Num.cap. 12.verf.8.) quod locutus fuerit cum Deo sine interventu angeli : Ore ad os loquar cum eo.
units.tr: The seventh foundation is the prophecy of Moses our Master, upon whom be peace: namely, that one must believe he is the father of all the prophets, both those who went before him and those who came after him; that all of them are placed below him in excellence; that he alone was chosen by God from the whole human race; and that he apprehended God with greater knowledge than any man who was found or will be found. He himself, upon whom be peace, was separated from man by the highest sequestration, so that when he apprehended something the powers of imagination and sense and their accidents ceased in him, and the intellect alone was left. For this reason it is said (Num. 12:8) that he spoke with God without the intervention of an angel: "Mouth to mouth will I speak with him."

units.la: Declararem autem stupendum hoc negotium, nisi scirem esse materiam hanc valde subtilem, atque idcirco opus esse simplici expositione, problematibus & comparationibus.
units.tr: I would declare this wonderful matter, were I not aware that the material is very subtle and that therefore a simple exposition, with problems and comparisons, is needed.

units.la: Nam prius exponenda effet existentia angelorum,& variatio graduum eorum à creatore: insuper declarandum effet negotium animæ, ejusque potentiarum ; atque fuse tractanda effet revelatio formarum, quæ aptos reddunt prophetas coram Deo ; atque continetur in hac materia mensura altitudinis vel staturæ ejusque negotium, neque perficiet totam hanc materiam, etiamsi quis componeret compendiosissime centum foliis: Idcirco supersedebo isti,ut adducatur suo loco,in libro concionum,quem promisi; vel in libro prophetiæ, quem constitui concinnare; aut in libro peculiari,in quo complectar ista fundamenta.
units.tr: For first the existence of angels and the variation of their degrees from the Creator would have to be set forth; moreover the matter of the soul and its powers would have to be explained, and the revelation of the forms which make prophets fit before God would have to be treated at length. This subject also contains the measure of height or stature and its business, and no one would complete this whole matter even if he compressed it most concisely into a hundred leaves. I will therefore defer it, to be brought forward in its proper place, in the book of sermons which I promised, or in the book on prophecy which I have determined to compose, or in a separate book in which I shall embrace these foundations.

units.la: Fundamentum Octavum est, Legem esse à cælis,atque hoc oportet credere, tam istam legem,quam hodie habemus, esse legem traditam Mosi,atque totam esse ex ore omnipotentis : hoc est quod integram hanc hauserit ex ore Dei Benedicti per apprehensionem, quæ dicitur prolocutio, per modum translationis vel transportationis sermonis, nec quisquam cognovit istam comprehensionem ; atque consignavit istud, quod ipsi dictatum fuit de historiis,seu rebus gestis, ac de negotio legis ejusque præceptis; atque idcirco vocatur Legislator,super quem pax. Non est autem discrimen inter versum (Gen.cap.10. verf.6.) Fi-liiCham,Chuz & Mizraim; atque inter (Deut. cap.6.verf.4.) Ego Dominus Deus tuus. Audi Israel Dominus Deus tuus ; omne hoc ex ore Potentissimi est, atque tota lex Dei est perse-cta,pura,sancta & vera: sed distinctio fit penes omnem abnegatorem, eo quod existimet, lin lege esse fructum vel nucleum & corticem, atque in ea esse res, quibus nulla insit utilitas, quatenus sint a Mose Magistro nostro, super quem pax. Atque hoc ipsum est, legem non esse a Deo. Asserunt sapientes cel. m. (in Cheleck sol.99.) Credens totam legem esse ex ore omnipotentis, excepto unico versiculo, quem non locutus sit Deus Benedictus: sed Moses suo ore, iste est ex genere istius: Quod verbum Domini vilipendit:(Num.cap.15.verf. 31.) exaltetur vero Dominus verbis abnegatorum: sed quaelibet ejus vocula habet in se miraculum sapientiae apud eum, cui Deus dederit sapientiam, atque scientiam, & licet ita sit (scilicet quod sapientes in ea mysteria multa animadvertant) tamen sapientia ejus perfecte attingi non potest, quippe longior terra mensura ejus; neque aliud homini relictum est, quam ut efflagitet a Deo Benedicto quod petiit David unctus Dei Jacobi: (Psalm.119. verf. 1. 2.) Retege oculos meos, ut intueat mirabi-lia lia in lege tua. Sic etiam expositio legis quæ est Talmud, est ex ore Dei, atque hoc, quod hodie nos conficimus formam tabernaculi, & opus palmæ, peniculamenti atque frontalium, atque alia id genus, est exemplar istius ipsius, quod dixit Deus Mosi, & quod ipse nobis indicavit : & ipse fuit fidelis in administratione legislationis suæ. Probatio autem hujus fundamenti octavi est istud, quod dixit : Eo cognoscetis, quod Dominus miserit me.
units.tr: The eighth foundation is that the Law is from heaven. One must believe that this law which we have today, and all of it, was given to Moses and is wholly from the mouth of the Almighty. That is, he received this whole thing from the mouth of God the Blessed by apprehension, which is called speech, by a kind of translation or transport of discourse, and no one knew that apprehension. He recorded what was dictated to him, both the histories or deeds done and the matter of the law and its precepts, and therefore he is called the Lawgiver, upon whom be peace. There is no difference between the verse (Gen. 10:6) "The sons of Ham: Cush and Mizraim" and (Deut. 6:4) "I am the Lord your God. Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God": all of it is from the mouth of the Most High, and the whole law of God is perfect, pure, holy and true. But a distinction is made in the case of every denier, who thinks that in the law there is fruit or kernel and husk, and that there are things in it which have no usefulness, insofar as they come from Moses our Master, upon whom be peace. And this very thing is to say that the law is not from God. The wise of blessed memory assert (in Cheleck, sol. 99): whoever believes the whole law to be from the mouth of the Almighty, except one little verse which God the Blessed did not speak but Moses with his own mouth, is of the kind of the one who despises the word of the Lord (Num. 15:31). Yet the Lord is exalted by the words of the deniers. But every little word of it has within it a miracle of wisdom for him to whom God has given wisdom and knowledge; and although it is so (namely that the wise perceive many mysteries in it), its wisdom nevertheless cannot be fully attained, for its measure is longer than the earth. Nothing else is left to man than to ask of God the Blessed what David, the anointed of the God of Jacob, asked: "Uncover my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things in your law" (Ps. 119:1, 2). So also the exposition of the law, which is the Talmud, is from the mouth of God. And that today we make the form of the tabernacle, and the work of the palm, the phylactery, the fringes and the like, is the pattern of that very thing which God said to Moses, and which he himself indicated to us; and he was faithful in the administration of his legislation. The proof of this eighth foundation is that which he said: "By this you shall know that the Lord has sent me" (Num. 16:28).

units.la: Fundamentum Nonum est radix extirpationis, atque est, quod hæc lex Mosis Magistri nostri, super quem pax, non exterminabitur aut mutabitur, neque ventura sit alia lex præter hanc à Deo, neque futurum sit in ea additamentum aut diminutio, vel in scriptura, vel in explicatione, juxta quod dicitur: (Deut. cap. 12. vers. 31.) Non addes ad eam, neque demes ab ea. Et jam exposuimus in principio hujus syntagmatis, quod opus erat declarare super hoc fundamentum.
units.tr: The Ninth Foundation is the root of uprooting (radix extirpationis): this law of Moses, our Teacher, upon whom be peace, shall not be abolished or changed, and no other law from God shall come after it, nor shall any addition or diminution be made to it, either in the text or in its interpretation, according to what is said: (Deut. 12:31) "You shall not add to it, nor take away from it." We have already explained at the beginning of this treatise that it was necessary to declare this foundation.

units.la: Fundamentum Decimum est, quod Deus cognoscat omnes actiones hominum, & quod in iis non sit negligens, quemadmodum isti opinantur, qui ajunt, (Ezech. cap. 8, 9.) Reliquit DoDominus terram: Sed juxta verba prophetæ dicentis: (Jerem. cap.32. verf.19.) Magnus consilio, & amplus actione, quia oculi tui aperti sunt super omnes vias hominum. Sic quoque dicit: (Gen. cap. 6. verf. 5.) Et vidit Dominus, quod multa esset malitia hominum in terra. Et dicitur: (Genef. cap. 18. verf. 20.) Clamor Sodomæ ac Gomorrhæ, quia multus erat. Atque hoc docet de fundamento hoc decimo.
units.tr: The Tenth Foundation is that God knows all the actions of men, and that he is not careless about them, as those think who say (Ezek. 8:12) "The LORD hath forsaken the earth." Rather, according to the words of the prophet saying (Jer. 32:19) "Great in counsel and mighty in work, for your eyes are open upon all the ways of the sons of men." So also he says (Gen. 6:5) "And the LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth." And it is said (Gen. 18:20) "The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah, because it was great." This is what the tenth foundation teaches.

units.la: II. Fundamentum Undecimum est, quod Deus retributurus sit bonam mercedem observanti præcepta ejus, & puniturus sit eadem violantem, & qui non præstiterit ea; atque retributionem maximam esse futurum seculum, & pœnam gravissimam exterminium. Et jam declaravimus in hoc capite, quantum isti sufficit. Docet autem versus de hoc fundamento, qui est: (Exod. cap. 32. verf. 32,33.) Et jam si reputaveris peccata eorum: Et si non, dele me quæso e libro tuo, quem scripsisti. At respondit ei Deus: Eum, qui provocaverit me, ego delebo ex libro meo. Atque hæc est probatio de præmio justi & pœna impii. 12. Fun-
units.tr: II. The Eleventh Foundation is that God will reward with a good recompense those who keep his precepts, and will punish those who violate them and do not perform them; and that the greatest recompense is in the world to come, and the most grievous punishment is destruction. We have already declared in this chapter as much as suffices for this. A verse teaching about this foundation is (Exod. 32:32-33) "And now, if you will forgive their sin… And if not, blot me, I pray you, out of your book which you have written." But God answered him: "Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot out of my book." This is the proof concerning the reward of the righteous and the punishment of the wicked. 12. Fun-

units.la: Fundamentum Duodecimum, dies Messiæ, quod oporteat credere, illum certissimo venturum, neque moraturum, & si cunctatus fuerit, expectaeum; (Habac. cap. 2. verf. 3.) Non decet autem aliquem supputare tempus, aut curiose elicere ex versibus, ut cognoscatur tempus adventus ejus, quemadmodum dixerunt Sapientes cel. mem. in cap. Cheleck : Illaqueetur animus supputantium terminos. Necesse autem est commemorare liberationem & amorem Dei, atque efflagitare ab eo juxta id, quod venit per manus uniuscujusque prophetæ, à Mose Magistro nostro, super quem tranquillitas, usque ad Malachiam, super quem pax. Quisquis autem dubium de eo movet, aut vile reddit ejus negotium, is falsitatis arguit legem, quæ testatur de eo in Parascha vel Sectione: Bilham, &c. Vos stabilitis hodie: (Num. cap 24. Deut. cap 22.) Comprehendit etiam hoc fundamentum, quod non sit Rex in Israele nisi ex Davide & tantum e semine Salomonis. Quisquis autem contradicit regno hujus familiæ, is negat Deum & verba prophetarum ejus.
units.tr: The Twelfth Foundation is the days of the Messiah: that one must believe that he will surely come and will not delay; and if he tarries, one must wait for him (Hab. 2:3). Yet it is not fitting for anyone to calculate the time, or to extract curiously from the verses the time of his coming, as the Sages of blessed memory said in the chapter Cheleck: "Let the spirit of those who calculate the ends be ensnared." It is necessary, however, to call to mind the deliverance and the love of God, and to beseech him according to what has come through the hand of each prophet, from Moses our Teacher, upon whom be tranquillity, down to Malachi, upon whom be peace. Whoever raises doubt about him, or makes his business cheap, convicts the law of falsehood, which bears witness concerning him in the portion or section Balaam, etc.: "You stand this day" (Num. 24; Deut. 29:14). This foundation also includes that there is no king in Israel except from David and only from the seed of Solomon. Whoever contradicts the kingdom of this family denies God and the words of his prophets.

units.la: Fundamentum Decimumtertium est Resurrectio mortuorum : jam autem exposui- mus ejus negotium atque mysteria. Credunt Judæi fixum esse tempus folique Deo notum, quo reviviscent mortui, quodque ille qui il- lud non credat, religione careat, & quam longissime absit à fide Judaica, quia scriptum est (Esa. cap. 26. verf. 19.) Vivent mortui tui & cadavera resurgent, expergifcite & laudate cubantes in pulvere : & alibi (Dan. cap. 12. verf. 2.) & multi qui dormiunt in terra pulveris evigilabunt. Id au- tem justis contin- gere.
units.tr: The Thirteenth Foundation is the resurrection of the dead; we have already set out its nature and mysteries. The Jews believe that there is a fixed time, known to God alone, at which the dead will be revived; and that whoever does not believe this lacks religion and is far removed from Jewish faith, because it is written (Isa. 26:19) "Your dead shall live, and their bodies shall rise; awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust"; and elsewhere (Dan. 12:2) "And many of those who sleep in the land of dust shall awake." This, moreover, happens to the righteous.

units.la: CAPVT II. De Duplici Religionis Iudaicae Principio, Sacra Scriptura, seu Lege scripta, Lege qȯ Orali Talmude comprehensa, totaq; utriusq; ratione.
units.tr: CHAPTER II. On the Twofold Principle of the Jewish Religion, Holy Scripture or the Written Law, and the Oral Law comprised in the Talmud, and the whole reasoning of each.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Tota, universaque Lex, Mosi in Sinai tradita, ex fidei Judaicae articulo octavo, cum Prophetarum reliquorum vaticiniis, ex fidei articulo sexto, discriminata tum in תורה שבכתב Legem scriptam, quinqÿe Mosis libris comprehensam, tum in תורה שבעל פה, Legem Oralem, in Pandectis Talmudicis Babylonicis, Hierosolymitanisque obviam, à Karraeis, Samaritanis, Saddu-caeisque tamen negatam, Indice Maimonide articulo fidei nono: Lex Mosis Magistri nostri C super quæ pax, nō exterminabitur aut mutabitur, neq; ventura est alia Lex præter hanc à Deo, neque futurum est in ea additamentum aut diminutio, vel in scriptura, vel in explicatione, id est, Lege Orali; Testeque Abarbanele in Capite fidei, cap. 8. Simili quoque modo in fundamento octavo, quod est, Legem esse à Deo, extant duæ sententiæ.
