Una est, totam legem scriptam, quæ hodie in manibus nostris versatur, esse legem traditam Mosi ab Omnipotente, hoc est, quod contineat omne ex ore Dei profectum cum apprehensione vocata pronunciatio. Altera fides est, Expositionem legis traditæ seu Talmud etiam esse ex ore Dei, & Mosen eam accepisse in monte Sinai, atque docuisse eam filios Israelis ore vel viva voce; idcirco etiam vocatur, lex ore tradita.
units.tr: The whole Law, the entire Law, delivered to Moses on Sinai, is distinguished, according to the eighth article of the Jewish faith, together with the prophecies of the other Prophets, according to the sixth article of faith, into the written Law [תורה שבכתב], the Written Law, comprised in the five books of Moses, and the oral Law [תורה שבעל פה], the Oral Law, found in the Babylonian and Jerusalem Talmudic collections. The Karaites, Samaritans and Sadducees, however, deny this. Maimonides indicates it in the ninth article of faith: The Law of Moses our Master, peace be upon him, will not be destroyed or changed, and no other law will come from God besides this one, nor is any addition or subtraction to be made to it, either in the written text or in the explanation, that is, in the Oral Law. Abarbanel also bears witness in the Chapter of Faith, chapter 8: In the same way, in the eighth foundation, which is that the Law is from God, there are two opinions. One is that the whole written Law, which is now in our hands, is the Law given to Moses by the Almighty, that is, that it contains everything that proceeded from the mouth of God, with the understanding of what is called pronouncement. The other belief is that the exposition of the handed-down Law, or the Talmud, is also from the mouth of God, and that Moses received it on Mount Sinai and taught it to the children of Israel by mouth or living voice; for this reason it is also called the Law handed down by mouth.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Credit synagoga Legem Oralem esse divinam, à Deo Benedicto profectam, Mosiquc cum Lege Scripta traditam, sic loquitur fidei suæ articulo octavo, in fine apud Maimonidem: Sic etiam Expositio Legis, quæ est Talmud, est ex ore Dei, atque hoc, quod hodie nos conficimus formam tabernaculis & opus palmæ, peniculamenti atque frontalium, atque alia id genus, est exemplar ipsius ipsius quod dixit Deus Mosi, & quod ipse nobis indicavit; Confirmaturque per Abarbanelem, describentem in Capite fidei, cap. 8. Expositionem legis traditæ seu Talmud esse ex ore Dei omnimnipotentis, traditamque fuisse Mosi in monte Sinai, ut eam filios Israelis doceret, indeque appellatam fuisse Legem ore traditam, seu Oralem; Hinc vult paris, si non superioris, cum Lege scripta authoritatis, fundamentumque unicum esse totius Judaismi; Hinc qui aliquid eradicarit ex verbis, quae traditione accepimus, PseudoProphetam nominat, dignumque censet, qui laqueo stranguletur, apud Maimonidem in Fundamentis Legis cap. 9. §. 8. Unde inter abnegatores legis, Apostatasque recensetur a Majmonide in Tractatu Teschuva cap. 3. Qui negat expositionem Legis scriptae seu Legem ore traditam, atque ejus interpretes falsi arguit, uti Zadock & Baitos.
units.tr: The synagogue believes that the Oral Law is divine, proceeding from the blessed God, and was delivered to Moses along with the Written Law. Thus it speaks in the eighth article of its faith, at the end, in Maimonides: So also the exposition of the Law, which is the Talmud, is from the mouth of God; and what we now make, the form of the tabernacles and the work of the palm, the phylacteries and the fringes, and others of that kind, is the pattern of what God said to Moses, and what he himself showed us. This is confirmed by Abarbanel, who describes in the Chapter of Faith, chapter 8, that the exposition of the handed-down Law, or the Talmud, is from the mouth of the Almighty God, and was delivered to Moses on Mount Sinai so that he might teach it to the children of Israel, and that for this reason it was called the Law handed down by mouth, or the Oral Law. Hence he holds that it has equal, if not greater, authority than the Written Law, and that it is the one foundation of all Judaism. Hence Maimonides calls whoever uproots anything from the words that we have received by tradition a false prophet, and judges him worthy to be strangled with a noose, in the Foundations of the Law, chapter 9, §8. Hence Maimonides also counts among the deniers of the Law and apostates, in the Treatise on Repentance, chapter 3, him who denies the exposition of the Written Law, or the Law handed down by mouth, and charges its interpreters with falsehood, as Zadok and Boethus did.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Credit Judæus Legem Oralem, infallibili traditione Orali per continuam successionem ad posteros propagatam, hincque Cabbalam appellatam, hanc Mosen, in monte Sinai a Deo acceptam, Josuae tradidisse, hinc ad Judices, mox ad Prophetas, dein ad Esram, virosque magnae Synagogae delatam, tum Scribis & sapientibus, qui illi successerunt, Antigono Sochaeo, Josuae Serachiae, Hilleli & Schammai commissam, tandem post destructas per Titum Hierosolymas, ne periculum jacturae metuere haberent, a Rabbi Jehuda sancto, ex variis traditionibus conquisitis conflatam, tabulisque com-
units.tr: The Jew believes that the Oral Law, propagated to posterity by an infallible oral tradition through continuous succession, and for this reason called the Cabbalah, was received by Moses from God on Mount Sinai and handed on to Joshua; from him it passed to the Judges, soon after to the Prophets, then to Ezra and the men of the Great Synagogue, then was committed to the Scribes and wise men who succeeded them: Antigonus of Sochoh, Joshua ben Perachiah, Hillel and Shammai. Finally, after Jerusalem was destroyed by Titus, lest they should have to fear the loss of it, it was gathered from various traditions by Rabbi Judah the Holy, brought together, and committed to tablets

units.la: Nothing further. complexam fuisse Talmudicis, testibus Magi- ftris in Capitulis Patrum cap. 1.§.1. Moses accepit Legem in monte Sina, & tradidit eam Iofua, & Iofua Senioribus, Seniores Prophetis, Prophetae denique tradiderunt eam viri synagogae magnae, Fufiusque totum probantibus Legis oralis negotium, Maimonide in Praefatione summae Thalmudi- cae, quam Iad Chazaka vocavit, Abarbanele in Praefatione libri lui Nachalat Abot, aliis denique bene multis.
units.tr: complexam fuisse Talmudicis, as the Masters testify in the Chapters of the Fathers, chapter 1, §1: Moses received the Law on Mount Sinai, and delivered it to Joshua, and Joshua to the Elders, the Elders to the Prophets, and the Prophets finally delivered it to the men of the Great Synagogue. Fuller still, in proving the whole matter of the Oral Law, are Maimonides in the Preface to his summary of the Talmud, which he called Yad Chazaka, Abarbanel in the Preface to his book Nachalat Abot, and very many others.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Credit Legis oralis mentionem in Lege scripta esse factam, maxime Exod. c. 34. v. 27. Et dixit dominus: scribe tibi verba ista, nam juxta Os horum verborum pepigi foedus tecum & cum Israele, concludens, cum lege scripta in verbis, scribe tibi, Oralem memorari Legem in vocibus, fecundum Os horum verborum foedus pepigi, testibus Talmudicis in Gemara Gittin c. f. & Temura cap. 2. Rabbi Ifaaco Corbelenfi in libro Fol. 39. Rabbi Menafleh Ben Israel in Conciliat. in Exod. Quaest. 50. Qui sic brevibus: Ergo ad duplicem hanc legem respiciens Dominus, diversa illa verba protulit; Pariter Exod. cap. 24. verf. 12. Et dixit Dominus Mosi, adscende ad me in montem, & fis ibi, atque dabo tibi tabulas lapideas legem istam & praeceptum, quod scripsi, ad docendum eas; eas; innuens per תורה Legem scriptam, per משנה Legem oralem, Probantibus Talmudicis in Tractatu Berachot Fol. 5. Quid est illud, quod scriptum legitur: Et dabo tabulas lapideas, & legem & praeceptum, quod scripsi ad docendum ipsos? tabulas, ea sunt decem praecepta, id est, Sacra Scriptura מקרא, & praeceptum, id est Mishna; Consentientibus Maimonide, Raschi, Aben Esra; Sic Exod. cap. 18. verf. 16. Deuter. cap. 17. verf. 8, 9, 10, 11. aliisque locis de Lege Orali fieri verba.
units.tr: The Jew believes that mention of the Oral Law is made in the Written Law, chiefly at Exodus 34:27: And the Lord said: write these words for yourself, for according to the mouth of these words I have made a covenant with you and with Israel. He concludes that the Written Law speaks in the words "write for yourself", and that the Oral Law is recalled in the expression "according to the mouth of these words I made the covenant". Witnesses are the Talmudists in the Gemara of Gittin at the end, and Temura chapter 2; Rabbi Isaac of Corbeil in his book, folio 39; Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel in the Conciliator on Exodus, question 50. He says briefly: Therefore the Lord, looking to this double law, uttered those different words. Likewise Exodus 24:12: And the Lord said to Moses, come up to me into the mountain, and be there, and I will give you tablets of stone, the law and the commandment which I have written, to teach them; implying by תורה [torah] the Written Law, and by משנה [mishnah] the Oral Law. The Talmudists prove this in the Treatise Berachot, folio 5: What is meant by what is written: "And I will give you tablets of stone, and the law and the commandment which I have written to teach them"? The tablets are the Ten Commandments, that is, Holy Scripture (מקרא [miqra]), and the commandment is the Mishnah. Maimonides, Rashi and Aben Ezra agree. In this way, Exodus 18:16, Deuteronomy 17:8, 9, 10, 11, and other places, speak of the Oral Law.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Docet Synagoga Legem Oralem esse summe necessariam, sic in suo Conciliat in Exod. Quæst. 50. Menasse Ben Israel, egregie ab Hornbekio in libris de convincendis & convertendis Judæis propterea castigatus, inquit: Ut dubitandum non sit, Traditiones, seu Legem vocalem, maxime necessariam esse. Eamque ob causam Exod. XVIII. 16. jubetur Israel de gravibus quaestionibus Mosen consulere; quod opus haud erat, si omnia in Lege clara fuissent. Sed quia non omnes aquerete eam intelligebant, necessarium Deut. XVII. 9. esse dicitur, ab unoquoque consuli sui temporis Prophetam. Ideoque Moses Legem sacerdotibus Levi filiis tradidit, ut eam caeteris interpretarentur; neque expositiones illas scribere voluit, quia ore tradita melius intelliguntur; scripta autem saepe ambiguos habeant sensus. Statuit Mosen non scripsisse, nec enunciasse ad popupopulum omnia verba, quæ Deus ad eum locutus est, Exod cap.24. verl.4. Deuter.cap.28. v.58. Sed orali traditione propagasse. Legem scriptam esse imperfectam, defectuosam, obscuram, hinc Oralem ad salutem valde necessariam, quæ perficiat, compleat, obscuritatemque tollat.
units.tr: The Synagogue teaches that the Oral Law is of the highest necessity, as it says in its Conciliator on Exodus, question 50. Menasseh Ben Israel, whom Hornbeck rightly rebuked in his books on convincing and converting the Jews, says: There is no doubt that the Traditions, or the Oral Law, are most necessary. For this reason, Exodus 18:16 orders Israel to consult Moses on difficult questions, which would be unnecessary if everything in the Law were clear. But because not everyone understood it, Deuteronomy 17:9 says that each person must consult the Prophet of his own time. Therefore Moses delivered the Law to the priests, the sons of Levi, so that they might explain it to the rest. He did not wish to write down those explanations, because things handed down by word of mouth are better understood, whereas written things often have ambiguous meanings. They hold that Moses did not write down, nor announce to the people, all the words that God spoke to him (Exodus 24:4; Deuteronomy 28:58), but propagated them by oral tradition. They hold that the written Law is imperfect, defective and obscure, and so the Oral Law is highly necessary for salvation, to complete it, perfect it and remove its obscurity.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Clamat Oralem Lege scripta perfectiorem, hinc plures faciendam, Mosen fundatum esse super Legem Oralem, apud Aben Esram in Præfatione commentarii sui in Pentateuchum.
units.tr: They proclaim that the Oral Law is more perfect than the written Law, and therefore should be given more weight: Moses was founded upon the Oral Law, according to Aben Ezra in the preface to his commentary on the Pentateuch.

units.la: Nominat Legem Oralem Fundamentum Legis scriptæ, apud Bechai in Cad Hakkemach, Fol.77. col.3. Quod scripta Lex Mosis non possit intelligi, exponique, sine hujus Legis Oralis adminiculo; Quod teste Aben Esra loco allegato, non possumus perfectam expositionem adducere, si legis scriptæ præceptorum vestigiis tantum insistamus, nisi fundamentum locemus in verbis sapientum nostrorum piæ memoriæ; Quod monitore Isaaco Corbelensi in גרות שמע Fol.39. Non existimandum fit, Legem scriptam Religionis Judaicæ fundamentum esse, quin potius illius fundamentum esse Legem ore traditam, cum propter Legem Oralem initum sit fœdus à Deo cum Israelitis, sicuti scriptum Exod.cap.34. verf.27. Quia juxta verba hæc pangò fœdus; dus, Hinc in Maflichta Sopherim cap. 15. Ha-lacha 7. Talmud vino, & Scripturam aquæ comparant: Similis est textus Biblicus aquis, Mifchna Vino, Talmud condito; Et in sequenti Halacha 8. comparant Legem Sali, Mifchnam piperi, Talmud Aromatibus; Habet quoque exinde pluris præstantiusque studium Talmudicum, quam quod Sacrorum lectioni impenditur, utntque Rabbini semper magis in Talmude, quam in Bibliis exercitati; Imo eousque nonnulli studium hoc Legis Oralis extulerunt, ut non erubuerint scribere: Quod etiam in Lege scripta studere, nihil aliud sit, quam tempus perdere, ut Ephodeus testatur in Præfatione operis sui Grammatici; Et in Bava Metzia Fol. 33. 1. scribunt: Qui operam dant lectioni Biblicæ, virtus aliqua est, aut potius nulla virtus, qui vero operam dant Traditioni vel Legi secundariæ patrum, virtus est propter quam accipitur præmium: Gemara denique incumbere, virtus est, qua nulla præstantior. Monet quin etiam Synagoga Juventutem suam, ut ad verba scribarum magis attendat, quam ad verba legis, quod graviús circa verba scribarum quæ legis delinquatur, cum dilectiora sint, juxta id quod dicitur, amores tui meliores vino, in Tract. Talmud. Sanhedrin, cap. 10. §. 3. in Gemara Hierosolymitana Tractat. Berachot cap 1. Hinc qui transgreditur verba sapientum, sine numero & æstima-
units.tr: In Bechai's Cad Hakkemach, folio 77, column 3, he calls the Oral Law the foundation of the written Law, because the written Law of Moses cannot be understood or explained without the support of this Oral Law. As Aben Ezra, cited above, testifies: We cannot give a complete explanation if we only keep to the traces of the precepts of the written Law, unless we lay the foundation in the words of our wise men of blessed memory. As Isaac of Corbeil warns in the Ṭur [Yoreh De'ah? Sefer Yere'im], folio 39, we must not think that the written Law is the foundation of the Jewish religion; rather its foundation is the Law delivered by word of mouth, since the covenant that God made with Israel was made on account of the Oral Law, as is written in Exodus 34:27: For according to these words I have made a covenant. Hence in the Masechet Soferim, chapter 15, halakhah 7, they compare the Talmud to wine and Scripture to water: The Biblical text is like water, the Mishnah like wine, the Talmud like spiced wine. And in the following halakhah 8 they compare the Law to salt, the Mishnah to pepper, and the Talmud to spices. From this, the study of the Talmud is also valued more highly and esteemed above the reading of the Holy Writings, and the rabbis have always been more practised in the Talmud than in the Bible. Indeed, some have praised this study of the Oral Law so highly that they were not ashamed to write: To study even the written Law is nothing but a waste of time, as Ephodeus testifies in the preface to his grammatical work. And in Bava Metzia, folio 33, column 1, they write: Those who devote themselves to reading the Bible have some virtue, or rather no virtue at all; but those who devote themselves to the Tradition or to the secondary Law of the Fathers have a virtue for which a reward is received; in short, to devote oneself to the Gemara is a virtue surpassing all others. The Synagogue even warns its youth to attend more to the words of the scribes than to the words of the Law, because transgressing against the words of the scribes is more serious than transgressing the Law, since they are more beloved, according to what is said: your loves are better than wine, in the tractate Sanhedrin, chapter 10, §3; and in the Jerusalem Gemara, tractate Berakhot, chapter 1. Hence whoever transgresses the words of the wise is struck without number or measure, according to Maimonides in [ניין] chapter 6. And whoever transgresses the words of the wise deserves death, Eruvin, folio 21. But whoever mocks them is condemned to the boiling dung of hell, Gittin, chapter 5.

units.la: tione one percutitur, apud Maimonidem in ניין cap. 6. Et quicunque transgreditur verba sapientum, mortis reus esto, Erubhin sol. 21. Qui vero subsannat stercori ferventi in inferno adjudicator, Gittin. cap. 5.
units.tr: ...tione one percutitur (is struck without number or measure), according to Maimonides in ניין ch. 6: "And whoever transgresses the words of the wise shall be liable to death." Erubhin, fol. 21: "But whoever mocks them shall be condemned to boiling dung in hell." Gittin, ch. 5.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Statuit totam Veteris Testamenti scripturam divinam, ex ore omnipotentis Dei profetam, normam, mensuramque fidei, ac controversiarum alteram, secundariamque, esse sanctam, venerabilemque ex communi omnium sententia, distinguens inter libros sacros, referensque, quosdam per Prophetiam נבואה exaratos esse, aliquos per Spiritum Sanctum, רוח הקדש qui infimus sit Prophetiae gradus, quasi Spiritus Sanctus a Spiritu Prophetico, qui omnium autor est Prophetiarum, esset distinctus, utiloquitur Rabbi David Kimchi in Praefatione ad Hymnos Davidis: Paucis nunc explicabimus discrimen inter Prophetiam & Spiritum Sanctum. Prophetia est, cum res aliqua pervenit ad hominem sapientem, moribus integrum. Accidit autem ei Prophetia in Somnio. Quod si vero vigilanti alicui obtigerit Prophetia, facultates ejus sensibiles omnes cessant, & is ab omnibus negotiis hujus mundi abstrahitur, videturque aliquis in visione Prophetica secum loqui, eique hoc vel illud dicere. Aut apparent illi species in visione ista : aut nulla quidem species apparet , sed vocem audit secum loquentem: At Spiritus Sanctus est, cum homo integer rebus divinis occupatus , omnibus suis facultatibus salvus manentibus , loquitur quod loquitur , more reliquorum hominum, nisi spiritus excelsius excitavit ipsum & illuminat , vel instillat super linguam ejus, res nempe verba laudis & confessionis Deo suo, verba intellectus & disciplinarum vel institutionum, Loquitur etiam, auxilio Dei futura.
units.tr: They hold that the whole of the Old Testament Scripture is divine, delivered from the mouth of almighty God, and that it is the norm and measure of faith and the first, and secondary, arbiter of controversies; and that it is holy and venerable by the common judgment of all. They distinguish among the sacred books, and report that some were written through Prophecy [נבואה], and some through the Holy Spirit [רוח הקדש], which is the lowest degree of Prophecy, as if the Holy Spirit were distinct from the Prophetic Spirit, which is the author of all prophecies. So Rabbi David Kimchi speaks in his preface to the Psalms of David: We shall now explain briefly the difference between Prophecy and the Holy Spirit. Prophecy is when something comes to a wise man of upright character. Prophecy comes to him in a dream. But if prophecy comes to someone who is awake, all his bodily senses cease, he is withdrawn from all the affairs of this world, and he seems to speak with himself in a prophetic vision, and to be told this or that. Either forms appear to him in that vision, or no form appears but he hears a voice speaking with him. The Holy Spirit, however, is when a man of integrity, occupied with divine things, with all his faculties remaining intact, speaks as he speaks, in the manner of other men, unless a higher spirit has stirred him and illuminates him, or pours something upon his tongue: namely, words of praise and confession to his God, words of understanding and of instruction and discipline. He also speaks, with God's help, of future things.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Codicem Sacrum variis appellat nominibus, elogiisque exornat, mox מקרא Lectu-ram ab usu antiquo in Synagogis, scholisque usitato, ex Nehemia cap. 8, verf. 8. Sic Elias Levita in Thisbi ad vocem מקרא vocant etiam מקרא ארבע ועשרים לכל viginti quatuor libros Mikra; Effatumque Rabbinicum est, ut in aeternum homo annos suos dividat in tres partes, & tertiam impendat במקרא In Mikra ; Mox תורה Doctrinam, institutionem, quod homini veram prae-scribat metam, ad quam quasi jaculando collimare debeat , sumiturque fere semper pro quinque libris Moßis, aliquando quoque pro universa scriptura; Mox כתב מכתב scripturam, voce parallela in libris Novi instrumenti, tum quod Deus scribendi initium fecerit, Exod. c. 32. verf. 16, tum quod scribendi necessitatem authoritate mandatoque confirmarit, com-menmendaveritque, ita ut appareret, non fortuitis occasionibus, consilioque humano exaratas esse sacras scripturas, sed divino, maxima urgente necessitate; Vocat scripturam מקדש'ה Sanctuarium, Sanctum Domini, apud Ephodaeum in praefatione ad Grammaticam suam, a summa libri veneratione, quem puris lotisque manibus tractare, sanctaque mente versare valde deceth, ספרי הקדש Libros sanctitatis, scripta sanctitatis, quod ab autoribus sanctis sint conscripta, sancta sint exarata lingua, sancta quaeque tractent, complectanturque; מגלה Convolutum, quod libri ut veterum, sic recentiorum, maxime libri Legis manuscripti, fuerint convoluti, cujus testis abunde est hodie na Synagoga, hisce multum superbiens; Tandem עשרים ואربעה viginti quatuor vulgari appellatione, a numero librorum Veteris Testamenti, pro varia eorum dispositione, conjunctione, & separatione, apud Eliam Levitam in Thisbi ad vocem קרא, & in Bibliorum Hebraicorum aliquando frontispiciis.
units.tr: He calls the sacred codex by various names and adorns it with praises. First comes Miqra [מקרא], Reading, from the ancient practice in the synagogues and schools, taken from Nehemiah 8:8. So Elias Levita in the Thisbi, under the word miqra, also calls the twenty-four books Miqra [מקרא ארבע ועשרים לכל]. There is a rabbinic saying that a man should divide his years for ever into three parts and spend the third on the Miqra [במקרא]. Next comes Torah [תורה], Doctrine or Instruction, because it sets before a man the true goal at which he ought to aim, as if throwing a dart. It is taken almost always for the five books of Moses, and sometimes for the whole of Scripture. Next comes Ktav [כתב], or Miktav [מכתב], Writing, a term parallel to the books of the New Testament, both because God made a beginning of writing (Exod. 32:16) and because he confirmed and commended the necessity of writing by his authority and command. It is thus evident that the sacred Scriptures were written not by chance occasions or human counsel, but by divine counsel, under the greatest necessity. He calls Scripture Miqdash-Yah [מקדש'ה], Sanctuary, the Holy Place of the Lord, as Ephodaeus does in the preface to his Grammar, from the highest veneration of the book, which it is very fitting to handle with clean and washed hands and to turn over with a holy mind. He calls it Sifrei ha-Qodesh [ספרי הקדש], Books of holiness, Writings of holiness, because they were written by holy authors, were set down in a holy language, and deal with and embrace holy things. He calls it Megillah [מגלה], Scroll, because the books, both ancient and more recent, and especially the manuscript books of the Law, were rolled up; of this the synagogue today is an ample witness, and it takes great pride in them. Lastly, by the common appellation twenty-four, from the number of the books of the Old Testament, according to their varied arrangement, joining and separating, in Elias Levita's Thisbi under the word qara [קרא], and sometimes on the title pages of Hebrew Bibles.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Clamat synagoga scripturam sacram esse perfectam, appellat scripturam כלה sponsam, a summa perfectione, apud Rabbi Bechai in Commentario ad Pentateuchum pag. 3. col. 1. probat ex Davide Psalmo 19. Legem Domini perperfectam esse, verf. 8. Lex Jehovæ perfecta, convertens animam, testimonium Domini verax, sapientem reddens simplicem, testaturque Rabbi Josephus Albo libro de Fundamentis, Orat. 3. c. 25. Falsum quoque est, & plane veritati dissentaneum, legem, quod ad formam pertinet, imperfectam esse: in cunctis enim partibus omnis generis perfectionum absoluta est; Et rursus: Constat omni genere perfectionis legem nostram cumulatam, absolutamque esse. Ac id quidem à Davide compendiose significatur, dum eam commendat, à quatuor causarum generibus: Lex Domini inquit perfecta, convertens animam; Extemplo tamen stylum vocemque vertit, scripturam imperfectionis accusans, quod tota via justificandi, cumque Deo reconciliandi scripta lege non sit consignata, hinc non sufficiat ad salutem, beatitudinemque ultimam, non contineat omnia quæ scitu sint necessaria, ut Legem sua extollat Oralem necessarias suadeat Magistrorum constitutiones, additionesque, quæ scripturam perficiant, compleantque; Et ne sine teste dicere hoc videar, spiritusque ille contradictionis appareat, necesse erit unum evolvere Menassen Ben Israel, qui sic in Conciliatore suo in Exod. Quaest. 50. loquitur: David Psalm. XIX. ait Legem Domini perfectam esse. Jam vero, cum perfectio cujusque rei in eo consistat, ut neque abundet in ea quidquam, nec desit, legem ore traditam necessariam esse consistendum est: nam multa sunt præcepta in quibus desiderari aliquid videatur; in aliis rursum sunt quæ abundare judicaveris, quippe quæ semel, iterum, tertio repetantur: quod sequentia exempla satis comprobabunt.
units.tr: The synagogue cries out that Scripture is perfect. It calls Scripture kallah [כלה], bride, from its supreme perfection, as Rabbi Bechai says in his commentary on the Pentateuch, p. 3, col. 1. He proves it from David's Psalm 19, that the Law of the Lord is perfect (v. 8): The law of Jehovah is perfect, converting the soul; the testimony of the Lord is true, making wise the simple. Rabbi Joseph Albo also testifies in his book on the Fundamentals, Oration 3, ch. 25: It is also false, and wholly contrary to the truth, that the law is imperfect as to its form. For it is complete in all its parts with every kind of perfection. And again: It is agreed that our law is filled up and complete in every kind of perfection. David indeed signifies this briefly, when he commends the Law from the four kinds of causes: The law of the Lord, he says, is perfect, converting the soul. Immediately, however, he changes his style and voice and accuses Scripture of imperfection, because the whole way of justifying and of reconciliation with God is not set down in the written law; hence it does not suffice for salvation and ultimate blessedness, and does not contain all things that need to be known. Therefore he exalts the Oral Law and urges the necessary constitutions and additions of the Teachers, which perfect and complete Scripture. And lest I seem to say this without a witness, and that spirit of contradiction may appear, it will be necessary to unroll Menasseh ben Israel, who speaks thus in his Conciliator on Exodus, question 50: David in Psalm XIX says that the Law of the Lord is perfect. Now, since the perfection of anything consists in this, that nothing abounds in it and nothing is lacking, it must be held that the law delivered by word of mouth is necessary. For there are many precepts in which something seems to be wanting; in others again there are some which you would judge to abound, since they are repeated once, twice, and three times. The following examples will sufficiently prove this.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Asserit, defenditque Codicis sacri integritatem in vocibus, characteribus, punctisque vocalibus, uno negans ore, corruptam esse sacram scripturam, celebrat in rei probationem Tiberiensium Masoretharum curam assiduam, qua מסורה sepimentum Legi apposuerunt, in annotandis, enumerandisque singulis versibus, vocibus, literis, punctis, prout scribit Rabbi Joseph Albo Part. 3. cap. 22. Judæos enim quod attinet, illi accuratissimi sunt circa Legem suam, imo & circa ejus literas, voces item plenas & defectivas; & gloriantur quod sciant numerum literarum, versuum, distinctionum, & accentuum; hæcque adscribunt marginibus librorum suorum, & vocant Masoreth; quod reliquæ gentes non fecerunt; Sed placet adhuc audire Judæum anonymum de integritate scripturæ mascule differentem apud Coccejum in Considerat. Judaic. Quæst. 16. cap. 18. cujus verba hæc sunt: An Judæi per hæc tempora Hebraicum sacræ scripturæ textum habeant ac retineant in pristina sua veritate? Adsolutionem tionem huius quaestionis sufficiebat solum illud annotasse, quod omnia Bibliorum exemplaria quae usquam extant non una syllaba aut litera differant, quod evidens est argumentum incorruptae eorum veritatis, cum in nostrorum hominum licet toto orbe dispersorum, & diversis terrarum nationibus subiectorum codicibus nulla appareat differentia. Et ne quis scrupulus resteet, adducam testimonia scriptorum qui profide dignissimi & sanctissimi habiti inter Christianos, hoc ipsum aperte profitentur. Augustinus in libro de Civitate Dei scribit, non esse credendum quod Judaei ulla ratione S. Scripturam contaminaverint, & complures adserit rationes huic veritati firmandae. 1. Quia videtur impossibile esse ut omnes ita consentiant in una eademque voluntate & prava intentione, ut cum dispersi sint per universos terrae angulos nemo inter ipsos reperiatur, qui tam insigni injustitia & sacrilegio se opponat, cuiusmodi est S. S. literarum depravatio. II. Quia codices authentici Hebraeorum tam vetusti quam recentiores per omnia convenire deprehenduntur, quamlibet diversis temporibus & longe dissitis regionibus descripti. Hoc est manifestum integritatis eorum argumentum. Nec ullo modo putandum est tam innumerabilem populi multitudinem, cui in captivitate sua nullum maius bonum ac solatium superest codicum sacrorum puritate, eos depravare velle explenda malevolentia & odio adversus aliquem populum aut nationem concepto. cepto. Idem contenàit Hieronymus libro Hebraicarum Quastionum, & Beda libro sexto de atatibus mundi, & Thoma Aquinas super Epistolam Pauli ad Romanos c.9. Alexander de imola in consultatione bussuis eandem veritatem asserit. Idem Augustinus expositione in Ps. 40. appellat nos thesaurarios sacrorum librorum. Idipsum quoque confirmat libro 18. de Civitate Dei c. 43. Porro quoniam confessio ipsa adversariorum plus valet quam centum testes, huic articulo satis solide videmur occurrisse. Paria facit Rabbi Gedalja, Augustini utens testimonio, Aquinamq; in sententiæ adducens probationem, qui in Schalschelet Hakkabala p. 69. consuli potest.
units.tr: He asserts and defends the integrity of the sacred codex in its words, letters, and vowel points, denying with one voice that Holy Scripture has been corrupted. To prove the point he celebrates the constant care of the Tiberian Masoretes, by which they placed a masorah [מסורה] as a hedge around the Law, in noting and numbering each verse, word, letter, and point, as Rabbi Joseph Albo writes in Part 3, ch. 22: As for the Jews, they are most exact concerning their Law, and even concerning its letters, and likewise its full and defective spellings. They boast that they know the number of letters, verses, divisions, and accents, and they write these in the margins of their books and call them Masoreth, which the other nations have not done. But it still pleases me to hear an anonymous Jew, who discourses manfully on the integrity of Scripture, in Coccejus, Considerations on Judaism, question 16, ch. 18, whose words are these: Do the Jews in these times have the Hebrew text of Holy Scripture and keep it in its original truth? For the solution of this question it was enough to note only this: that all the copies of the Bible that exist anywhere do not differ by one syllable or letter. This is clear evidence of their incorrupt truth, since no difference appears among the codices of our people, dispersed over the whole world and subject to diverse nations of the earth. And lest any doubt remain, I will adduce the testimonies of writers who were held most faithful and most holy among Christians, and who openly profess this very thing. Augustine in his book On the City of God writes that one should not believe the Jews to have defiled Holy Scripture in any way, and he asserts several reasons for confirming this truth. First, because it seems impossible that all should so agree in one and the same will and wicked intention that, although they are scattered through every corner of the earth, no one among them should be found who would oppose himself to so great an injustice and sacrilege as the corruption of the Holy Letters. Second, because the authentic codices of the Hebrews, both ancient and more recent, are found to agree in all respects, though written at different times and in very distant regions. This is a clear proof of their integrity. Nor is it to be thought that so innumerable a multitude of people, to whom in their captivity no greater good or comfort remains than the purity of their sacred codices, would wish to corrupt them out of hatred and malice conceived against some people or nation. Jerome in his book of Hebrew Questions, Bede in the sixth book of On the Ages of the World, and Thomas Aquinas on Paul's Epistle to the Romans, chapter 9, held the same. Alexander of Imola in his consultation on the Bible asserts the same truth. Augustine in his exposition of Psalm 40 calls us the treasurers of the sacred books, and he confirms the same in book 18 of On the City of God, ch. 43. Moreover, since the confession of the adversaries themselves is worth more than a hundred witnesses, we seem to have dealt with this article solidly enough. Rabbi Gedaliah does the same, using Augustine's testimony and adducing Aquinas's argument, which can be consulted in his Shalshelet ha-Qabbalah, p. 69.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Vocet licet Synagoga scripturam sacram claram, lucidamque, תורה אור Legem Lucem, נר מצוה Præceptum Lucernam, ex Salomonis Proverbiis, cap.6. vers.23. revera tamen obscuram ultro statuit, sibi sæpe contrariam, secumque pugnantem, ut Legem Oralem, Religioni suæ quam maxime inservientem, constituat tum fidei morumque primum Principium, tum obscuriorum Veteris Testamenti explanatorem fidissimum; Hinc trita Judæorum verba apud Rabbi Mosen Mikkotzi in ספר מצות גדול libro præceptorum magno: Nisi accessisset ad legem scriptam expositio legis Oralis, tota lex obscura & mera cæcitas esset: Nam primo scriptura sibi invicem sunt contraria, & inter se pugnantes. Deinde, quia Lex scripta est imperfecta, neque omnia cognitu necessaria in se comprehendit; Quæ fere totidem repetita videmus vocibus in Rabbi Abrahami Zacuti Pɔnv Libro Prosapiarum, quando sic loquitur p. 158. Absque Lege Orali tota Lex in tenebris esset. Multa enim in Scripturis sunt pugnantia, neque iis inniti aut ea conciliare possumus, nisi per Legem Oralem, quam accepit Moses e Sina.
units.tr: Although the Synagogue may call Scripture clear and luminous, calling the Law "Light" [תורה אור], the commandment "Lamp" [נר מצוה], from Solomon's Proverbs 6:23, it nonetheless itself declares Scripture obscure, often contrary to itself and self-contradictory. So it sets up the Oral Law, which serves its religion most fully, as both the first principle of faith and morals and the most trustworthy interpreter of the obscurer parts of the Old Testament. Hence the familiar saying of the Jews in Rabbi Moses Mikkotzi's great Book of Precepts: "Unless the explanation of the Oral Law had been added to the written Law, the whole Law would be obscure and sheer blindness. For first, the Scriptures are contrary to one another and mutually conflicting. Then, because the written Law is imperfect and does not contain in itself everything that needs to be known." We see nearly the same words repeated in Rabbi Abraham Zacuto's Sefer Yuchasin, the Book of Pedigrees, where on p. 158 he speaks thus: "Without the Oral Law the whole Law would be in darkness. For there are many contradictions in the Scriptures, and we cannot rely on them or reconcile them except through the Oral Law, which Moses received from Sinai."

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: In confesso apud Judæos est, nec minima gentis gloria, ab adversariis ipsis asserta, scripturam sacram conscriptam esse maxima partem lingua Hebræa vernacula, sanctam illa, divinaque lingua, minimam partem Lingua Chaldaica, utpote posterioribus usitata inter ipsos temporibus, in Daniele, Esra & Jeremiæ capitis decimi versu undecimo obvia, hinc Apocryphos rejicientes libros, quod peregrina, non sancta Hebræa exarati fuerint lingua, & ad Hebraicam veritatem, tanquam ad arcem, si opus est in disputationibus, confugientes, hancque maxime, ut decet, extollentes.
units.tr: It is admitted among the Jews, and it is no small glory of the nation, even as their opponents themselves assert, that Scripture was written for the most part in the Hebrew vernacular, that holy and divine language, and only in a very small part in the Chaldee language, which was in use among them in later times, as is found in Daniel, Ezra, and Jeremiah 10:11. Hence they reject the Apocryphal books, because they were written not in holy Hebrew but in a foreign language. And they take refuge in Hebrew truth, as in a citadel, if need be in disputations, and extol it above all, as is fitting.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Libri scripturæ sacræ pro varia tum compositione, tum divisione, aliquando aucti, nonnunquam diminuti, hinc Judæis Antiquioribus bus mox viginti duo, uti refert Josephus contra Appionem lib. 1. mox viginti septem fuerunt. Recentioribus vero viginti quatuor, imitantibus Aben Esram, Salomen Isaacum, Davidem Kimchium, aliosque, unde ipsa scriptura nominibus עשרים וארבעה viginti quatuor passim appellatur.
units.tr: The books of Holy Scripture, varied both in their composition and in their division, were sometimes enlarged and sometimes diminished. Hence, as Josephus reports in his Against Apion, book 1, the ancient Jews counted twenty-two books, and later they counted twenty-seven. More recent authors, following Aben Ezra, Solomon Isaac, David Kimchi and others, count twenty-four, and so Scripture is commonly called by the name "twenty-four" [עשרים וארבעה], twenty-four.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Discriminant Hebraei viginti quatuor libros veteris Testamenti in tres partes, תורה נביאים וכתובים Legem, Prophetas, & Hagiographa, sic Moses Kotzensis testatur in libro praeceptorum magno: quia praeviderat Deus, nationes huius mundi exscripturas libros viginti quatuor, qui Lege, Prophetis, Hagiographis continentur, illisque ad haeresin & impietatem abusuras, expositionem oralem Mosi tradidit, neque a Deo permissum fuit, ut scriptis mandaretur; Sic pariter testatur Elias Levita praefat. 3. p. 19. Non fuerunt viginti quatuor libri una colligati, sed illi eos conjunxerunt, ac fecerunt ex ipsis tres partes, Legem, Prophetas, & Hagiographa; Sic in Bibliis apud Janssonium anno 1639. impressis עשרים ואחד ... תורה נביאים ... viginti quatuor libri sunt quinque quintae Legis, Prophetae anteriores & posteriores, & Hagiographa; Intelligentes per תורה Legem, quae complectitur חמשה חומשי תורה Quinque quintas Legis, seu quinquinque libros Mosis; per נביאים Prophetas, quos dividunt in נביאים ראשונים Prophetas Anteriores, à Mose usque ad mortem Salomonis, qui sunt libri Historici Josuae, Judicum, Samuelis, Regum; Et נביאים אחרונים Prophetas Posteriores, post divisionem Tribuum, Esaias, Jeremias, Ezechiel, & duodecim minores Prophetae, à numero תרי עשר dicti; per כתובים Hagiographa, numero undecim, qualia sunt Chronica, Ester, Esra, Nehemias, Psalmi, Proverbia, Ecclesiastes, Canticum Canticorum, Job, Daniel, Threni.
units.tr: The Hebrews divide the twenty-four books of the Old Testament into three parts: Law, Prophets and Writings [תורה נביאים וכתובים], Law, Prophets, and Hagiographa. So Moses of Kotzk attests in his great Book of Precepts: "Because God foresaw that the nations of this world would copy out the twenty-four books, which are contained in the Law, the Prophets and the Writings, and would abuse them for heresy and impiety, he handed on the oral explanation to Moses, and it was not permitted by God that it should be committed to writing." Likewise Elias Levita attests in his preface, p. 19: "The twenty-four books were not originally bound together as one; but they joined them and made from them three parts, the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings." So too in the Bible printed at Janssonius's press in 1639, the "twenty-four books" are said to be: "the five fifths of the Law [תורה], the Former and Latter Prophets [נביאים], and the Writings." By the Law [תורה] they understand the five fifths of the Law [חמשה חומשי תורה], that is, the five books of Moses; by the Prophets [נביאים] they understand those they divide into the Former Prophets [נביאים ראשונים], from Moses to the death of Solomon, which are the historical books of Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings; and the Latter Prophets [נביאים אחרונים], after the division of the tribes, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the twelve minor Prophets, called the Twelve [תרי עשר]; by the Writings [כתובים] they understand eleven books, namely Chronicles, Esther, Ezra, Nehemiah, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, Job, Daniel and Lamentations.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Inter libros Veteris Testamenti maxime laudant libros Mosis, quod reliquorum sint mensura, fontesque contineant uberrimos, ex quibus Prophetae suos derivaverint rivulos; Quod Moses omnium Prophetarum fit Pater אבות הנביאים Quod omnium Prophetarum Magister רבן של כל הנביאים, caeteris omnibus longe praeferendus Prophetis, ab illisque distinguendus, cum Prophetiam acceperit ipse absque opera Angeli, in vigiliis, ipsa clara diurnaque luce, non sub emblemate, similitudineque, nec attonitus, sed vultu placido, ab ore ad os cum Deo locutus, verba, sensumque acceperit, & omni quidem tempore, quoties voluerit, imo ad mortem usque nointerrupto tempore, sicuti pluribus narrat rat Maimonides, quando in Appendice Articuli feprimi de Fide Judaica sequentibus scribit verbis: Redibo autem ad fundamentum hoc sept[?]imum, atque affero, prophetiam Mosis Magistri nostri super quem pax, distinctam esse a prophetis reliquorum Prophetarum, quatuor istis rebus. Prima est, quod illi prophetarint ope mediatoris; Moses autem Magister noster, super quem pax, sine mediatore, juxta id quod dicitur (Num. cap. 12. verf. 8.) Ore ad os loquar cum eo. Secunda est, quod nulli prophetae prophetarint nisi cum dormirent, visione nocturna vel diurna, postquam sopor obruisset prophetam, et cessarent sensus, atque quiesceret instar dormitantis: Negotium autem hoc dicitur visio, vel contemplatio: Sed accessit ad illum Mosen Magistrum nostrum, super quem pax, loquela vel sermo Dei in die, atque consistebat inter duos Cherubim, quem admodum promiserat ei Deus benedictus: Et revelabor tibi ibi &c. Atque dixit Deus: Si fuerit propheta vester Dei &c. Non ita servus meus, &c. Ore ad os, &c. Num. cap. 12. Tertia est, quod, postquam prophetis obvenisset Prophetia, etiam si esset in visione, tamen natura eorum debilitarentur, atque contremiscerent membra corporis illorum, ac valde perterrefierent, ut vere essent veluti descendentes ad portam mortis, sicut apud Danielem cap. 10. verf. 8, 9. Non fuerunt reliquae in me vires, sed decor meus mutatus est in me ad corruptionem, & sopore obrutus fui. Sed Moses Magister noster super
units.tr: Among the books of the Old Testament they praise the books of Moses most highly, because they are the measure of the rest and contain the richest springs from which the Prophets drew their streams. For this reason Moses is the father of all the Prophets [avot ha-nevi'im: אבות הנביאים] and the teacher of all the Prophets [rabban shel kol ha-nevi'im: רבן של כל הנביאים]. He is to be placed far above all the other Prophets and set apart from them, since he received prophecy without the work of an angel. He received it while awake, in the clear light of day, not through a symbol or likeness, and not dazed, but with a calm countenance; he spoke with God mouth to mouth and received the words and their sense. He did this at every time he wished, indeed without interruption until his death. Maimonides relates this at length in the appendix to the seventh article of the Jewish Faith, where he writes these words: I will return to this seventh foundation and state that the prophecy of Moses our master, on whom be peace, is distinguished from the prophecy of the other Prophets by four things. The first is that they prophesied through the agency of a mediator, but Moses our master, on whom be peace, spoke without a mediator, according to what is said (Num. ch. 12, v. 8): Mouth to mouth I will speak with him. The second is that no other prophets prophesied except while asleep, in a nocturnal or diurnal vision, after sleep had overcome the prophet and his senses had ceased and he lay still like one sleeping. This experience is called vision or contemplation. But to our master Moses, on whom be peace, came speech or word of God by day, and he stood between the two cherubim, just as God the Blessed had promised him: And I will reveal myself to you there, etc. And God said: If there is a prophet among you of the Lord, etc. Not so my servant, etc. Mouth to mouth, etc. Num. ch. 12. The third is that after prophecy came upon the prophets, even if it came in a vision, their natural powers were weakened, the limbs of their bodies trembled, and they were greatly terrified, so that they were truly as those going down to the gate of death, as in Daniel ch. 10, vv. 8, 9: There was no strength left in me, but my comeliness was turned in me to corruption, and I fell into a deep sleep. But Moses our master, on whom

units.la: [Lower part of the page continues with the word "super" at the line end, catchword super quem pax, non fuit hoc modo constitutus; siquidem accedebat Deum sermocinans, neque languescebat aut tremebat; atque hoc est quod ait Exod. cap. 33. verf. 11. Locutus est Dominus ad Mosen facie ad faciem, quemadmodum alloqui quis solet amicum suum, quasi diceret: Sicut homo non formidat aut trepidat a colloquiis socii sui, ita Moses non erat perterrefactus aut turbatus a sermone Dei, quia conjunctus erat intellectui.
units.tr: [Lower part of the page continues with the word "super" at the line end, catchword super quem pax:] was not constituted in this way. For he came to God and spoke with him, and he did not grow faint or tremble. This is what Exodus ch. 33, v. 11 says: The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend. It is as if it said: just as a man does not fear or tremble at the talk of his companion, so Moses was not terrified or disturbed by the word of God, because he was joined to the understanding.

units.la: Quarta est, quod nullus propheta quolibet tempore, quo desiderabat, prophetarit, nisi cum beneplacitum esset Deo Benedicto, potest enim quis multis annis manere propheta, & tamen non prophetizare: Sapissime etiam precibus flagitabit, ut prophetet, & post aliquot dies obveniet ipsi quidem, sed non revelabit ipsi prophetia hac istud quod petierat: jam vero esse potest inter illos, qui diligenter perscrutatus fuerit, atque perspexerit cogitationes suas, sicut fecit Elisah, cum diceret 2. Reg. cap. 3. verf. 15. Jam adducite mihi fidicinem, qui pulseт citharam &c.
units.tr: The fourth is that no prophet prophesied at any time he wished, but only when it pleased God the Blessed. For a man may remain a prophet for many years and yet not prophesy. Very often he will ask in prayer that he may prophesy, and after some days prophecy will come to him, but it will not reveal to him what he had asked for. Indeed, it can happen among those who have carefully searched and examined their thoughts, as Elisha did when he said (2 Kings ch. 3, v. 15): Now bring me a harpist who plays the harp, etc.

units.la: Sita je res habebat, non inerat illis virtus prophetandi omni tempore, quo cupiebant; sed Moses Magister noster super quem quies, prophetizabat quolibet tempore pro beneplacito suo, prout dicitur Num. c. 9. verf. 8. Consistite, & audiam quid praecipiat Dominus, &c. Atque ait Lev. cap. 16. verf. 2. Dicat Aaroni fratri tuo, ne accedat quolibet tempore ad Sanctuarium. Itaque Aaron non veniebat quolibet tempore, Moses autem semper accedebat; Explicatque ulterius Maimonides in Fundamentis Legis cap. 7. §. 6,7,8,9. Illustratque pariter Menafleh Ben Israel in Conciliatore Quæst. 43.
units.tr: Such was the state of affairs: the prophets did not have the power to prophesy at every time they desired. But Moses our master, on whom be rest, prophesied at any time at his own pleasure, as is said in Num. ch. 9, v. 8: Stand still, and I will hear what the Lord commands, etc. And Lev. ch. 16, v. 2 says: Tell Aaron your brother that he must not come into the sanctuary at any time. Thus Aaron did not come at every time, but Moses always came in. Maimonides explains this further in the Foundations of the Law, ch. 7, §§ 6, 7, 8, 9, and Menasseh ben Israel likewise illustrates it in the Conciliator, Question 43.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Distinguunt inter Prophetas reliquos, Hagiographaque ex paragrapho septimo, quod Illorum vaticinia excepta fuerint tum in somnio, auditione vocis, vel visione, tum in ecstasi, aut mentis alienatione, ita ut sensus suum plane amiserint officium; Horum vero oracula tradita fuerint per Spiritum Sanctum, manentibus in scriptoribus sensibus integris, differentiam non solum notante Kimchio, verum rationem quoque reddente in Psalmorum præfatione, שרוח הקדש כתובים Quod scripta sint Hagiographa per Spiritum Sanctum; Cui præivit Maimonides, quando in More Nevochim Part. II. cap. 45. postquam de Prophetia seu primo gradu Prophetiæ egisset, sic de Hagiographis subjungit: Secundus gradus est, cum homo in fe sentit rem vel facultatem quampiam exoriri & super fe quiescere, qua eum impellit ad loquendum; ita ut loquatur vel de scientiis & artibus, vel Psalmos & hymnos, vel utilia ac salutaria recte vivendi præcepta, vel res politicas & civiles, vel denique divinas; & quidem inter vigilandum, & in vigore sensuum ordinario. Et hic est, de quo dicitur, quod quod loquatur per Spiritum Sanctum. Hac specie Spiritus Sancti instinctus, Psalmos suos scripsit David, Proverbia, Ecclesiastes & canticum canticorum Salomon. Hoc afflatu scripti sunt Danielis, Iobi, & Chronicorum Libri & reliqua Hagiographa, unde etiam Cethubhim, hoc est, Hagiographa appellantur, quia Cethubhim, hoc est, scripta sunt per Spiritum Sanctum; Calculum addit Elias Levita Germanus in suo Thisbi pag 178. ad vocem כתב Tertiam quoque partem Bibliorum (quem Judaei a numero 24. librorum עשרים ואחד vocant) כתובים appellant, eo quod undecim isti libri (qui in hac parte continentur) per afflatum Spiritus sancti conscripti fuerunt, & non per prophetiam. Quid vero discriminis sit inter prophetiam & Spiritum Sanctum, declaravit Rabbi David Kimchi in Praefatione sua super librum Psalmorum. Similiter & in Graeca lingua Hagiographa, id est, sacra scripta vocantur. Hinc est, quod & nos dicimus in precationibus nostris. In verbis sanctitatis tuae scriptum est &c. vel, in scriptis sanctitatis dictum est, qua formula loquendi intelligimus כתובים id est, Hagiographa.
units.tr: They distinguish the remaining Prophets from the Hagiographa on the basis of the seventh paragraph: the prophecies of the former were received either in a dream, by hearing a voice, or by a vision, and also in ecstasy or a loss of mind, so that their senses wholly lost their function; whereas the oracles of the latter were delivered by the Holy Spirit, the writers' senses remaining intact. Kimchi notes this difference, and in the preface to the Psalms he also gives the reason, that the Hagiographa were written "by the Holy Spirit" [שרוח הקדש כתובים]. Maimonides went before him. In More Nevochim, Part II, chapter 45, after discussing prophecy, or the first degree of prophecy, he adds the following about the Hagiographa: "The second degree is when a man feels within himself that some matter or faculty arises and rests upon him, impelling him to speak, so that he speaks either of the sciences and arts, or of Psalms and hymns, or of useful and salutary precepts for right living, or of political and civil affairs, or finally of divine things; and this while awake and in the ordinary vigour of the senses. This is what is meant by the saying that he spoke 'by the Holy Spirit.'" By this kind of impulse of the Holy Spirit David wrote his Psalms, and Solomon the Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs. By this breath were written Daniel, Job, the Books of Chronicles and the rest of the Hagiographa; hence they are also called Cethubhim [כתובים], that is, Writings, because they were written by the Holy Spirit. Elias Levita the German adds his weight to this in his Thisbi, p. 178, under the word כתב. The third part of the Bible, which the Jews call the twenty-one books by number [עשרים ואחד], they call Cethubhim, because those eleven books contained in this part were written by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and not by prophecy. What difference there is between prophecy and the Holy Spirit, Rabbi David Kimchi explained in his preface to the book of Psalms. Likewise in Greek the Hagiographa are called sacred writings. Hence we too say in our prayers, "In the words of your holiness it is written," or "In the writings of your holiness it is said," a form of speech by which we understand כתובים, that is, the Hagiographa.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Dividunt Legem Mosaicam in LIV Sectiones, seu Ordinationes majores, פרשיות appellatas, tribus ססס notari solitas, quae pariter primae literae sunt vocis פרשה, vel tribus ססס, quae pariter primae literae sunt vocis סור, D ʒ. תוד , ob annuæ lectionis commoditatem, sicuti testatur Maimonides Hil. Teph. cap. 13. Usu receptum est apud omnes Israelitas, quotannis absolvere legem, facto initio in Sabbatho, Festum Tabernaculorum sequente, à Sidra seu ordine Berefchith; aliitamen post trium demum annorum fluxum absolvunt, quæ consuetudo minus est vulgaris; Intelligens fine dubio Judæos Syros, quos Legem triennio absolvere, scribit Benjamin Tudelensis in Itineratio suo, pag. 115. quod ut optimi Beckii exquisitis doctisque notis, nuper in urbe Augusta a nobis visis, brevi prodeat, optandum esset quam maxime. Retinent Judæi, antiquarum consuetudinum tenacissimi sectiones prophetica, Legalibus respondentes Sectionibus, quas הפטרה voce insigniunt, quasque ex Prophetis defumtas legunt in Synagogis post lectam Mosis Sectionem, sicuti hoc confirmat Elias Levita in Thisbi ad vocem הפטר quando refert pag. 170. Et ecce scribam quanam sit causa quare legant sectionem Propheticam. Juxta id quod inveni scriptum nempe, quod Antiochus impius Rex Græciæ præceperit Israelitis, ut non legerent legem publice. Sed quid fecerunt Judæi? Legerunt Parashcham unam ex Prophetis, cujus materia conformis esset ei materiæ, quæ descripta erat in parashcha, quæ in Sabbatho legi solebat. Exempli gratia, pro parashcha Berefchith &c. legerunt ex Esaia cap. 42. Sic dicit Dominus Deus creator cœli, &c. Et pro Parasçha Noah legerunt secundum dies Noah, Esa. cap. 54. Et sic de singulis Parasçhis. Et quamquam nunc cessaverit decretum illud Regis præfati, tamen consuetudo legendi Haphtara non cessavit, quoniam adhuc hodie legunt istiusmodi Parasçhas ex Prophetis post lectionem Legis. Et vocatur Haphtara, àcessando seu finiendo.
units.tr: The Mosaic Law is divided into fifty-four sections, or major ordinances, called parashoth [פרשיות], which are commonly marked with three samech letters, the initial letters of the word parashah, or with three other letters, likewise initials of a word, for the convenience of the yearly reading. So Maimonides testifies in Hil. Teph., chapter 13: "It is the custom among all Israelites to finish the Law every year, beginning on the Sabbath after the Feast of Tabernacles, from the sidra or order Bereshith; others, however, finish it only after a cycle of three years, which custom is less common." Without doubt he means the Syrian Jews, who, according to Benjamin of Tudela in his Itinerary, p. 115, finished the Law in three years. It would be most desirable that Beck's excellent and learned notes, which we recently saw in the city of Augsburg, should soon appear. The Jews, most tenacious of ancient customs, retain the prophetic sections, corresponding to the Legal sections, which they mark with the word haphtarah [הפטרה], and which they read in the synagogues from the Prophets after the reading of the section of Moses. Elias Levita confirms this in his Thisbi under the word haphtar, where he writes on p. 170: "And behold, I will tell you the reason why they read a prophetic section. According to what I have found written, namely that the impious king Antiochus of Greece commanded the Israelites not to read the Law publicly, what did the Jews do? They read one parashah from the Prophets whose subject matter agreed with the matter described in the parashah which was customarily read on the Sabbath. For example, in place of the parashah Bereshith etc. they read from Isaiah chapter 42: 'Thus says the Lord God, creator of the heavens,' etc. And in place of the parashah Noah they read, according to the days of Noah, Isaiah chapter 54. And so for each of the parashoth. And although that decree of the aforesaid king has now ceased, the custom of reading the haphtarah has not ceased, since even today they still read such parashoth from the Prophets after the reading of the Law. And it is called haphtarah from 'ceasing' or 'finishing'."

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Ajunt Hebræi Legem Mosis completi sexcenta & tredecim præcepta, quia Legem præcepit nobis Moses, Deuter. cap. 33. verf. 4. intelligentes per vocem תורה Legem, sexcenta undecim præcepta, cum secundum supputationem usitatam, quam per quatuor has literas faciunt, numerum contineat 611. Sed quia duo hic desunt præcepta, hinc duo priora Decalogi adjiciunt, quod per Mosen populo non sint data, sed ab ipso Deo toti communicata populo, ut ita sexcenta & tredecim exsurgant præcepta, sicuti refert Rabbi Eliefer in Capitulis, pag. 111. Omnia præcepta in Lege sunt 613, duo vero effatus est sanctus, hinc vocatur תורה, numerus enim in voce תורה continet 611; & duo profatus est Sanctus Benedictus, sicuti dicitur Psalmo 62. verf. 12. Semel locutus est, & duo hæc vel bis audivimus. En hic 613. Distinguunt hæc sexcenta tredecim præcepta in Affirmativa & Negativa; Illa תעשה facies, vocantes, Hæc חטיף לא non facies; Præcepta Affirmativa constituunt 248. secundum numerum membrorum hominis; Negativa ponunt secundum numerum dierum anni solaris, vel quia totidem sunt venæ, nervique in corpore humano, scribente Menaseh Ben Israel de Resurrectione mortuorum l. 2. c. 19.
units.tr: The Hebrews say that the Law of Moses contains six hundred and thirteen precepts, because of the text "Moses commanded us the Law," Deut. 33:4, understanding by the word torah [תורה] "Law" six hundred and eleven precepts, since according to the usual reckoning, made by these four letters, the word makes the number 611. But because two precepts are missing here, they add the first two of the Decalogue, on the ground that these were not given to the people through Moses but were communicated to the whole people by God himself; so that six hundred and thirteen precepts arise. Thus Rabbi Eliezer reports in the Chapters, p. 111: "All the precepts in the Law are 613. But the Holy One spoke two of them, and therefore it is called torah, for the number in the word torah is 611; and the Holy One, blessed be he, spoke two more, as it is said in Psalm 62:12: 'Once God has spoken; twice I have heard this.' Behold, here are 613." They divide these six hundred and thirteen precepts into affirmative and negative: the affirmative ones, which they call "you shall do" [תעשה], and the negative ones, "you shall not do" [לא תעשה]. The affirmative precepts make 248, according to the number of the members of the human body; the negative ones they set at 365, according to the number of the days of the solar year, or because there are as many veins and nerves in the human body, as Menasseh Ben Israel writes in On the Resurrection of the Dead, book 2, chapter 19:

units.la: Imago autem & Simulachrum Dei, est lex divina, per Mosem populo tradita: Illa enim, uti Cabalistæ observant, plena est divinorum nominum. Uti igitur lex constat ex lege CCXLVIII. Præceptis affirmativis, & CCCLXV. negativis: Ita etiam tota corporis humani compages, constat ex CCXLVIII. membris, & CCCLXV nervis. Quo non aliud indicari videtur, quam quod tota hominis perfectio ac consummatio sit accurata ac diligenti præceptorum observatione. In hoc officium numero adsignando conveniunt Hippocrates, Galenus, Rasis, Avicenna, & Averroes, imo medici omnes præstantissimi. Similiter Georgius Venetus in Harmonia sua mundi, sequens Hebræorum opinionem, qui per additionem litera ה ad nomen אברם Abram nihil aliud significatum dicunt, quam præcepta legis 248 observanda esse, inducti hac ratione, quod juxta Hebræum calculum numerus ista efficiatur ex literis nominis ipsius; Et libello de Fragilitate Humana, cap. 10. § 5. Dico itaque 1CXIII præcepta legis dividi, ut omnes sint, in CCCLXV Negantia & CCXLVIII Affirmativa. tiva; Caeterum de praeceptis eorumque ordine egerunt Maimonides in Praefatione operi Jad Chazaka praemissa, Rabbi Moses Mikkotzi in libro praeceptorum magno, Rabbi Isaac Corbelensis in libro praeceptorum parvo, Rabbi Levi Barzelonita in libro Chinuch, aliique multi, omnes hoc observantes, quod praecepta haec nucleus sint & compendium totius historiae ac Theologiae Judaicae.
units.tr: "The image and likeness of God is the divine Law, delivered to the people through Moses. For that, as the Cabalists observe, is full of divine names. Therefore, just as the Law consists of 248 affirmative precepts and 365 negative ones, so the whole structure of the human body consists of 248 members and 365 nerves." By this nothing else seems to be indicated than that the whole perfection and completion of man lies in the careful and diligent observance of the precepts. In assigning this number to the office, Hippocrates, Galen, Rhazes, Avicenna and Averroes agree, indeed all the most distinguished physicians. Likewise Georgius Venetus in his Harmony of the World, following the opinion of the Hebrews, who say that the addition of the letter ה to the name Abram [אברם] signifies nothing else than that the 248 precepts of the Law are to be observed, being led to this by the reasoning that by the Hebrew reckoning this number results from the letters of the name itself; and in his little book On the Frailty of Man, chapter 10, §5: "I say therefore that the 613 precepts of the Law are divided, all of them, into 365 negative and 248 affirmative." Moreover, concerning the precepts and their order, Maimonides in the preface prefixed to his work Jad Chazaka, Rabbi Moses Mikkotzi in his great book of precepts, Rabbi Isaac of Corbeil in his little book of precepts, Rabbi Levi of Barcelona in the book Chinuch, and many others have treated, all observing this: that these precepts are the kernel and compendium of the whole Jewish history and theology.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Formant Canonem Veteris Testamenti ex viginti quatuor libris divinis, scilicet Mosaicis, Propheticis, & Hagiographis, incipiendo a Mose, & desinendo in Malachiam, ex fidei Judaicae articulo duodecimo, statuentes collectum post Captivitatem Babylonicam a Viris Synagogae magnae, אנשי כנסת הגדולה, quibus praefuerit Efra עזרא הסופר Legusperitus doctus, exercitatusque, qui Autore Rabbi Azaria in Meor Enaim, pag. 175. Manum suam admovit libris tantum iis, qui editi sunt a Prophetis per Spir. Sanctum, Lingua Sancta. Proinde etiam sapientes nostri prudenter & premeditate eos tantum confirmarunt, qui stabiliti & confirmati fuerant ab eo; Interfuerint tum Haggaeus, Zacharias, & Malachias, tum alii recensiti in Glossa ad Tractatum Thalmudicum, Pirke Abhot, cap. 1. Zerobabel, Nehemias, Seraja, Raalja, & Mardochaeus; Qui una omnes Veteris Testamenti libros in
units.tr: They form the canon of the Old Testament from twenty-four divine books, namely the Mosaic, the Prophetic and the Hagiographa, beginning with Moses and ending with Malachi, according to the twelfth article of Jewish faith. They hold that it was gathered after the Babylonian Captivity by the men of the Great Synagogue [אנשי כנסת הגדולה], over whom presided Ezra [עזרא הסופר], a skilled, learned and practised scholar of the Law. According to the author Rabbi Azariah in Meor Enaim, p. 175, he laid his hand only on those books which were published by the Prophets through the Holy Spirit in the Holy Tongue. Accordingly our wise men also prudently and deliberately confirmed only those which had been established and confirmed by him. Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi were present at this, and, as listed in the gloss on the Talmudic tractate Pirke Avot, chapter 1, Zerubbabel, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Raaliah and Mordecai.

units.la: unum collegerint volumen, Apocryphos, spuriosque leparaverint, ecclesiamque fortiter reformaverint, sicuti legimus in Talmude Hierosolymitano, Tract. Megilla cap. 3. Quando surrexerunt viri synagogæ magnæ, illi restituerunt magnificentiam, id est, Legis Coronam, in pristinum statum.
units.tr: These men together gathered all the books of the Old Testament into one volume, rejected the Apocryphal and spurious ones, and strongly reformed the Church, as we read in the Jerusalem Talmud, tractate Megillah, chapter 3: When the men of the Great Synagogue arose, they restored the magnificence, that is, the Crown of the Law, to its former state.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Ex Canone Veteris Instrumenti eliminant libros Apocryphos, Tobiæ, Judithæ, Sapientiæ, Ecclesiastici, Maccabæorum, Baruchi, supplementum Danielis, Esteræ, Orationem Manassæ, Appendices Jobi, Psalmum centesimum quinquagesimum primum, Præfationem Jeremiæ, tertium & quartum Esdræ, sequentibus inducti rationibus; Quod nunquam sibi fuerint traditi, quodque nunquam hos agnoverint libros, cum ad ædificationem Ecclesiæ non fuerint scripti lingua Hebræa, sed peregrina, nec à Prophetis, nec per Spiritum Sanctum; Quod Malachias fuerit חותם הנביאים Sigillum Prophetarum, scriptioque divina in libris Prophetarum defecerit, Maimonide teste, cui appellatur האחרון הנביאים Ultimus Prophetarum; Quod Canon scripturæ Veteris Testamenti ab ipso Malachia, sociisque Synagogæ magnæ fuerit conditus, ipso non diffitente Genebrardo, quando in Chronographia sic loquitur: tur: Alioqui enim apud recentes Hebraeos aut non extant, aut certe non sunt authentici. Quoniam eorum Canon jam erat conditus ab illa magna synodo, cujus scriba erat Esras. Accusant pariter Christianos, quod Canonem librorum sacrorum multiplicaverint, & libros abscònditos Bibliis inseruerint sanctis, ita enim inquit Rabbi Azarias in Meor Enaim, pag. 175. Recepti sunt ab iis, & non a nobis; Et Rabbi Gedalja in Schalschelet Hakkabala, pag. 68. Operae pretium est tescire, quod gentes saeculi multiplicarunt scribere alios libros in collectione librorum, qui in manibus nostris non sunt.
units.tr: From the canon of the Old Testament they eliminate the Apocryphal books: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, the Maccabees, Baruch, the supplement to Daniel, Esther, the Prayer of Manasseh, the appendices to Job, Psalm 151, the Preface of Jeremiah, and the third and fourth books of Ezra, led by the following reasons: that these were never handed down to them, and that they never acknowledged these books, since they were not written for the edification of the Church in the Hebrew language but in a foreign one, and not by the Prophets nor through the Holy Spirit; that Malachi was the חותם הנביאים Seal of the Prophets, and divine writing ceased in the books of the Prophets, as Maimonides testifies, who calls him האחרון הנביאים the Last of the Prophets; that the canon of the Scripture of the Old Testament was established by Malachi himself and the companions of the Great Synagogue, Genebrardus not denying it when he speaks thus in his Chronography: Otherwise they are either not extant among the recent Hebrews, or certainly are not authentic, since their canon had already been established by that great synod, whose scribe was Ezra. They likewise accuse Christians of multiplying the canon of the sacred books and inserting hidden books into the holy Bibles; for thus says Rabbi Azariah in Meor Enaim, p. 175: They were received by them, and not by us; and Rabbi Gedaliah in Shalshelet ha-Qabbalah, p. 68: It is worth knowing that the nations of the world have multiplied the writing of other books in the collection of books which are not in our hands.

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Negant Libros Novi Testamenti esse Canonicos, quod tum impugnent Religionem propriam, tum Legis afferant mutationem, gentisque superbae diminuant praerogativas, hinc Evangelium illis contentum variis probrosis afficiunt nominibus, moxque Legem novam nominant, quod novas compleactatur Leges, Mosi non memoratas, sic Rabbi Elias Levita in Lexico Thisbiad vocem ‏יהוה‏, Christiani novam suam Legem vocant Evangelium, Gimel leniter prolato, quod ipsum in Lingua Graeca bonum nuntium significat; mox per ‏און גליון‏ Perversitatis revelationem explicant, vel per ‏און גליון‏ iniquitatis revelationem exponunt, concedentibus Judæorum Magistris familiaribus. Non contenti vero blasphemis excepisse convitiis novam Messiæ Legem, Personam, Officium, Mariam matrem, Apostolos, Discipulos, maximeque Paulum, contra Legem intonantem, ipsas quoque Evangelii veritates, resque allatrarunt gestas, perpetuo objicientibus, auribusque nostris ingerentibus, Jesu verba & facta parum sibi constare, cum tot ceremoniæ, purificationes, delectus ciborum, sacrificia, Judicia, & alia id genus sint ablata per Jesum, & tamen Matthæi cap. 5. dicat se non solvisse Legem & prophetas, testibus Rabbi Josepho Albo in libro de Fundamentis, Rabbi Lipmanno in Nizzachon, Rabbi Isaaco Bar Abraham in Munimine Fidei. Interim, licet negent, calumnienturq; librorum Novi Testamenti veritates, sententiasque, multa ex his mutuata in eorum scriptis tamen obvia sunt, quæ totidem veritatis negatæ egregia sunt argumenta, documentaque, sicuti hoc patet ex instituto parallelismo per Voysinium in Notis ad Raymundi Pugionem Fidei, Lightfotium in Horis Hebraicis & Talmudicis ad Novum Testamentum, Muhlium in Apologia Talmudica.
units.tr: They deny that the books of the New Testament are canonical, because they both attack their own religion and assert a change of the Law, and diminish the privileges of the proud nation; hence they load the Gospel contained in them with various insulting names, and soon call it a new Law, because it contains new laws not mentioned by Moses. So Rabbi Elias Levita in his Lexicon Tishbi, under the word יהוה: Christians call their new Law the Evangelium, pronouncing the Gimel softly, which in the Greek tongue signifies good news; soon they explain it by און גליון revelation of perversity, or expound it by און גליון revelation of iniquity, with the approval of familiar Jewish teachers. Not content, however, to have received the new Law of the Messiah, his Person, Office, Mary his mother, the Apostles, the Disciples, and especially Paul, thundering against the Law, with blasphemous reproaches, they have also assailed the very truths of the Gospel and the deeds recounted, constantly objecting and dinning into our ears that the words and deeds of Jesus are little consistent with themselves, since so many ceremonies, purifications, distinctions of foods, sacrifices, judgments and other things of that kind have been abolished through Jesus, and yet Matthew ch. 5 says that he came not to destroy the Law and the Prophets; witnesses being Rabbi Joseph Albo in the book on the Fundamentals, Rabbi Lipmann in the Nizzachon, and Rabbi Isaac Bar Abraham in the Munimen Fidei. Meanwhile, although they deny and calumniate the truths and sentences of the books of the New Testament, many things borrowed from them are nevertheless found in their writings, which are excellent arguments and proofs of the truth they deny, as is clear from the parallel passages set out by Voisin in the Notes to Raymund's Pugio Fidei, Lightfoot in Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae on the New Testament, and Mühlius in Apologia Talmudica.

units.la: XXII. Urgent librorum Canonicorum Lectionem
units.tr: XXII. They urge the diligent and frequent reading of the canonical books

units.la: nemfedulam, frequentemque, iubentes in Tractatu de Idololatria, cap. 1. ut homo Judaeus distribuat annos suos in tres partes, unam Lectioni Biblicæ impendat, partem alteram Mischnæ, tertiam Talmudi, id est, Gemarae; Et in Optimi Wagenseilii Codice MS Ez. Hechaim Hilch. Talm. Tora: Quisque Judæorum, etiam Senes, Calamitosi, & omnino pauperes, tenentur certum tempus determinare studio divinarum literarum, ad diem usque vitæ supremum. Peccatum enim delet quidem meritum servati præcepti, sed peccatum non delet meritum, contractum ex studio divinæ Legis, uti est in Gemara Sota c. 3. Si quis juis manibus victum parat, tres horas opificio, tres studio scripturæ sacræ, totidem Talmudi, totidemque meditationi ac collationi eorum quæ didicit tributo. Quod si vero quis Doctor insignis exstat, & omnia teneat memoriter, ita ut haud opus sit discere, tamen status temporibus disciplinas suas relegere debet, ne obrepat oblivio, sed major vitæ pars, meditationibus conse-cranda. Monent in Pirke Abhot cap. 5. §. 21. ut trahatur filius quinque annorum ad Biblia, filius decem annorum ad Mischna, filius tredecim annorum ad præcepta, filius quindecim annorum ad Talmud, filio octodecim annorum ad nuptias. Commendat Legis lectione tam publicam, quam privatam, siclo-quuntur in Schulchan Aruch p. 50. Etsi audivit homo singulis Sabbathis in cætu universam Legem, tenetur nihilominus & ipse suam legere Parascham illius illius septimanæ; Legunt quippe Mofeh ex antiqua consuetudine, cum Prophèticis Sectionibus, omnibus diebus Sabbathi in Synagogis, imo iplis Lunæ, Jovisque diebus, notante Maimonide Hilch. Tephill.cap.12. Affirmant apud Maimonidem cap.7. lib.alleg. quod præceptum fit affirmatiwum, omnibus & singulis Israelitis datum, ut prose quisque scribat librum Legis, quasi diceret: Nunc autem scribite vobis Canticum hoc. Quasi diceret: Scribite vobis legem, in qua Canticum illud est, neque enim scribere solent legem separatim per Parafchas.
units.tr: They urge, in the tractate On Idolatry, ch. 1, that a Jewish man should divide his years into three parts: one he should devote to the reading of Scripture, the second to the Mishnah, the third to the Talmud, that is, the Gemara. And in the excellent Wagenseil's manuscript codex of Ez. Hechaim, Hilkhot Talmud Torah: Every Jew, even the aged, the afflicted and altogether the poor, is bound to set a fixed time for the study of the divine letters, until the last day of life. For sin indeed blots out the merit of a precept kept, but sin does not blot out the merit gained from the study of the divine Law, as is said in the Gemara, Sotah ch. 3: If anyone prepares his food by his own hands, three hours are to be given to his work, three to the study of Holy Scripture, as many to the Talmud, and as many to meditation and comparison of what he has learned. But if there is some outstanding teacher who holds everything in memory, so that there is no need to learn, yet at set times he ought to go over his studies again, lest forgetfulness creep in, and the greater part of life be consecrated to meditations. They advise, in Pirke Avot ch. 5, §21, that a son of five years be brought to the Bible, a son of ten years to the Mishnah, a son of thirteen years to the precepts, a son of fifteen years to the Talmud, a son of eighteen years to marriage. They commend the reading of the Law, both public and private, saying in the Shulchan Aruch, p. 50: Although a man has heard the whole Law in the assembly on every Sabbath, he is nevertheless bound to read for himself the Parashah of that week; for they read the Torah, by ancient custom, together with the Prophetic sections, on all days of the Sabbath in the synagogues, and even on the days of the New Moon and on Thursdays, as Maimonides notes in Hilkhot Tefillah ch. 12. They affirm, in Maimonides ch. 7 of the aforementioned book, that it is an affirmative precept, given to all and each of the Israelites, that each one should write for himself a book of the Law, as if it said: Now therefore write this song for yourselves. As if it said: write for yourselves the Law, in which that song is; for they are not accustomed to write the Law separately by Parashot.

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: Mandant Legem dies noctesque meditandam, loquentes in Pirke Abhot cap. 5. §. 22. Versa eam, iterumque versa eam, nam omnia sunt in ea: In ea esto totus, neque unquam discedas ab ea: non enim habes melius ea exercitium. Enumerant elogiis magnificis insignes utilitates, commodaque, in strenuam navantibus Legi operam; Quod gratiam ineant & apud Deum, & apud homines; Quod conciliet veram justitiam, pietatem, humilitatem, gaudium, timorem Dei, odium peccati, studiumq; innocentiæ; Quod inde polleant homines consilio sapientiaque; Quodhinc regna egregie gubernentur, judicia justeexerceantur, causlæq; discutiantur, sicuti illud legimus in Pirke Abhot c. 6. §. 1. Rabbi Meir dicit: Quicunque discit in lege nomine legis, dignus est multis rebus, nec multis solum, imo dignus est toto mundo, vocatur item socius & amicus. Diligit Deum, diligit homines. Laetificat Deum, laetificat etiam homines. Vestit eum Lex humilitate & timore. Idoneum eum reddit ut fiat justus, pius, rectus & fidelis. Etiam Lex elongat eum a peccato, & applicat eum ad innocentiam. Etiam utilitatem capiunt homines ab eo, nempe consilium, sapientiam, prudentiam, & fortitudinem, sicut dicitur Proverbiorum cap. 8. verf. 14. Meum est consilium, & quicquid est, mea est prudentia, meum robur. Insuper Lex tribuit ei regnum, Dominium, & investigationem judicii, & revelatur ei arcana legis, efficitur tanquam fons qui nunquam cessat, & sicut fluvi qui magis atq; magis invalescit. Redditur ite verecundus, & longanimis & condonans ei, qui eu ignominia affecit. Lex tale magnificat & exaltat super omnia opera. Sic contra diras precantur hominibus, & vae intonant ob ignominiam Legis, scribentes in iisdem Capitulis cap. 6. Quod quicunque operam non det studio legis, vocetur reprobus; Sic Maimonides quoque refert in Hilch. Edut, cap. 11. §. 1. Qui nec scripturam, nec Mischnam, nec bonos mores didicit, de eo suspicio est, esse illum hominem nequam, vetantque hunc sapientes admittere ad dicendum testimonium.
