Quisquis enim tam abjectus est, eum verisimile fit patraturum omnia peccata, quorum committendorum occasio se offert; Sic pariter in Excerptis Gemaricis ad Sotæ Mischnam cap. 3. §. 8 illi, qui nec Scripturam, nec Mischnam didicerunt, cum lterantibus commiscentur, itadictis, quod peccatum iterent.
units.tr: They enjoin that the Law be meditated upon day and night, saying in Pirke Abhot, chap. 5, §22: Turn it over, and turn it over again, for all things are in it. Be wholly in it, and never depart from it, for you can have no better occupation than this. They list in magnificent terms the notable advantages and benefits that come to those who labour diligently at the Law: that they find grace both with God and with men; that it brings true righteousness, piety, humility, joy, the fear of God, hatred of sin, and zeal for innocence; that from it men grow strong in counsel and wisdom; that from it kingdoms are well governed, judgments justly executed, and causes decided. So we read in Pirke Abhot, chap. 6, §1: Rabbi Meir says: whoever learns in the Law for the sake of the Law is worthy of many things, indeed not only of many things but of the whole world; he is also called a companion and friend. He loves God, he loves men; he gladdens God, he also gladdens men. The Law clothes him with humility and fear. It makes him fit to become just, pious, upright and faithful. The Law also keeps him far from sin and brings him to innocence. Men too derive benefit from him: namely counsel, wisdom, prudence and fortitude, as it is said in Proverbs 8:14: "Mine is counsel, and sound wisdom; I am understanding; I have strength." Moreover, the Law gives him kingdom, dominion, and the discernment of judgment, and the secrets of the Law are revealed to him; he becomes like a fountain that never fails, and like a river that grows ever stronger. He becomes modest, long-suffering, and forgiving toward one who has done him wrong. The Law so magnifies and exalts such a man above all works. On the other hand, they pronounce curses against men and thunder woe upon the dishonour of the Law, writing in the same chapter (chap. 6) that whoever does not devote himself to the study of the Law shall be called reprobate. So Maimonides also reports in Hilchot Edut, chap. 11, §1: whoever has learned neither Scripture, nor the Mishnah, nor good morals, is under suspicion of being a wicked man, and the sages forbid admitting such a man to give testimony. For since he is so base, it is likely he will commit all the sins whose opportunity presents itself. Likewise in the Gemara excerpts on the Mishnah of Sotah, chap. 3, §8, those who have learned neither Scripture nor the Mishnah are mingled with those who repeat (sins), and so it is said that they will repeat the sin.

units.la: XXIV.
units.tr: XXIV.

units.la: Amant Veteris Testamenti Translationem Chaldaicam, Targum appellatam, commendantque maxime tum Jonathanis, tum Onkelosi versionem, referentes Jonathanem (quam acepisse expositionem ab ultimis Veteris Testamenti Prophetis, Onkelosum vero a Rabbi Eliefere & Rabbi Jehoșua, qui & ipsi a Prophetis acceperint; Sic enim dicitur in Talmude Tract. Megil. cap. 1. Targum quod est Legis, Onkelos proselytus dixit illud ex ore Rabbi Eliefers, & Rabbi Jehoșua. Targum quod est Prophetarum, Jonathan filius Uzielis dixit illud ex ore Haggai, Zachariæ & Malachiæ; Repetiturque de Onkelosi apud Maimonidem in More Nevochim, Part. II. pag. 289. Nosti autem, Onkelum res ist as arduas & sublimes, quas explicavit, accepisse a Rabbi Eleazare, & Rabbi Jehosua, qui fuerunt sapientissimi inter Israelitas; Narrant Talmudistæ miracula, quæ patrata, cum Jonathan Expositionem adornaret Chaldaicam, terram motu concussam ingenti, audita que vocem cœlestem, in Tractatu Megilla, cap. 1. Et commota est terra Israel quadringentis leucis, & ex intervallo quadringentarum. tarum leucarum exivit filia vocis, & dixit: quis est ille, qui revelavit arcana mea filiis hominum? Astitit Jonathan filius Uzielis super pedes suos & dixit: Ego sum ille, qui manifestavit secreta tua filiis hominum. Apertum & notum est coram te, quod non ad honorem meum fecerim, nec in honorem patris, sed ad honorem tuum feci, ut non multiplicarentur disceptationes in Israele; Addunt Magistri omne volatile, quod chartæ vel corpori Jonathani insideret, cum operi intentus esset, illico combustum fuisse, in Thalmudico Tractatu Baba Bathra, cap. 8. Dicunt de illo Jonatha filio Uzielis, quod hora qua sederit & studuerit in lege, omnis avis, quæ volarit super eum, combusta fuerit, Quare harum versionum multus fuit usus apud Hebræos, quod de Onkelosi imprimis memorat Rabbi Elias Levita, quando Præfatione in Methurg. sic inquit: At Thargum Onkelosi semper repertum est affatim. Et hoc ideo, quia nos obligati sumus, ut legamus quavis septimana Parascham bis, semel in texetu, & semel in Thargum; Hinc si non authenticas, divinasque Expositiones has statuunt Chaldaicas, quod revera ex hypothesibus fluit Judaicis, quodque ipsum Menassen Ben Israel movit, quare Jonathanem divinum appellaverit in libro de Creatione, pag. 39. Ad minimum tamen maximæ voluntæ esse authoritatis, ita ut ab illis recedendum non sit, sed consulendum
units.tr: They love the Chaldaic translation of the Old Testament, called the Targum, and especially commend the versions of both Jonathan and Onkelos. They relate that Jonathan's exposition was received from the last prophets of the Old Testament, and Onkelos's from Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Joshua, who themselves received it from the prophets. For so it is said in the Talmud, Tract. Megillah, chap. 1: The Targum of the Law, Onkelos the proselyte said it from the mouth of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Joshua. The Targum of the Prophets, Jonathan the son of Uzziel said it from the mouth of Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi; and the same is repeated about Onkelos by Maimonides in the More Nevochim, Part II, p. 289: You know that Onkelos received those difficult and sublime matters which he explained from Rabbi Eleazar and Rabbi Joshua, who were the wisest among the Israelites; The Talmudists tell of the miracles that happened when Jonathan was preparing his Chaldaic exposition: the land of Israel was shaken by a great earthquake for four hundred leagues, and from a distance of four hundred leagues a heavenly voice went forth, saying: Who is he who has revealed my secrets to the sons of men? Jonathan the son of Uzziel stood up on his feet and said: I am he who has made known your secrets to the sons of men. It is open and known before you that I did it not for my own honour, nor for my father's honour, but I did it for your honour, so that disputes might not multiply in Israel; The masters add that whatever bird alighted on the paper or the body of Jonathan while he was intent on his work was at once burned up, as in the Talmudic Tractate Baba Bathra, chap. 8: They say of that Jonathan the son of Uzziel, that in the hour he sat and studied in the Law, every bird that flew over him was burned up. Hence these versions were in great use among the Hebrews. Rabbi Elias Levita especially remarks on Onkelos, when in his preface to the Methurgeman he says: The Targum of Onkelos is always found in abundance. And this is because we are bound to read the Parashah twice every week, once in the text and once in the Targum; If they do not regard these Chaldaic expositions as authentic and divine, which indeed follows from Jewish presuppositions, and which moved Menasseh Ben Israel to call Jonathan divine in his book on the Creation, p. 39, nevertheless at the least they are held to be of very great authority, so that one must not depart from them but consult them,

units.la: E dæ passim sint, indicantib⁹ Talmudicis in Sanhedrin, Fol. 94. Moed Katon, Fol. 28. Megilla, Fol. 3. Nisi Targum istius loci esset, nesciremus quidnam diceret, non intelligeremus illum.
units.tr: and they are everywhere, as the Talmudists indicate in Sanhedrin, fol. 94; Moed Katan, fol. 28; Megillah, fol. 3. Unless there were a Targum of this passage, we would not know what it says; we would not understand it.

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: Sicut olim in Gentis solatium, cum in peregrino versarentur solo, linguaque Hebræa non amplius esset omnibus vernacula, Veteris Testamenti versiones Chaldaicæ, Græcæque efformabantur, sic Judæi, pariter hodie plebi consulentes promiscuæ, diversas Bibliorum adornarunt versiones, sicuti testantur Biblia Veteris Vestamenti Hispanica, Ferraræ in Italia impressa, hinc Ferrariensia appellata, & nupera Germanica, Amstelodami Anno 1679. excusa, privilegioque Regis Poloniæ Johannis III. munita.
units.tr: Just as of old, for the consolation of the nation when they lived in a foreign land, and the Hebrew tongue was no longer the vernacular of all, Chaldee and Greek versions of the Old Testament were produced, so the Jews, likewise today consulting the common people, have prepared various versions of the Bible, as the Spanish Bible of the Old Testament, printed at Ferrara in Italy and therefore called the Ferrara Bible, and the recent German one, published at Amsterdam in the year 1679 and protected by the privilege of John III, King of Poland, bear witness.

units.la: XXVI.
units.tr: XXVI.

units.la: Commendant Scripturarũ divinarum Interpretationem, quod ex innumeris patet Commentariis, qui tamen omnes, vel ex Lege Orali, vel ex Rabbinorũ desumti sunt placitis; Cũ Lex Oralis ambitu suo completatur uberrimam Legis Scriptæ Explicationem, nec intelligi possit absque Orali, quia fundamentum est Legis Scriptæ, ut supra paragrapho sexto enarratum; Ipsorumque Rabbinorum summa fere, divinaque sit Authoritas, quos [Hebrew: רוח הקדש] Spiritu Sancto statuunt sua exarasse scripta, sicuti testatestatur Rabbi Isaac Avuhaf in Menorat Hammaor, Fol.23.col.1. Iis omnibus quae Rabbini nostri in Homiliis suis docuerunt, eadem a nobis, atque Legi ⳨Mosaicae fides tribuenda est: Et, si quid aliquando illis infit, quod sit vel hyperbolicum, vel praeter naturam, vel ingenii nostri captum excedere videatur; non illorum verbis, sed ingeniorum nostrorum tarditati & infælicitati, culpa est assignanda; Et Rabbi Ezechias in Chaskuni suo, qui commentarius est in quinque libros Moisis: Qui dissentit a Doctore suo, perinde est ac si dissentiret a divina Majestate: Qui autem credit verbis Sapientum, est ac si crederet ipsi Deo; Hinc quoque frequens ad Juventutem Judaicam monitum occurrit passim: Mifili, attende ad verba Scribarum magis, quam ad verba Legis; Non mirū igitur quod solii in divinis sapiat Judaei, cum propriam sibi vindicent Legis Expositionem, uti innuit Judaeus Anonymus apud Coccejum in Considerationibus Responf. Judaic. Quaest.17. An solis Judaeis licitum Scripturas interpretari & sensum eum sequi qui maxime ipsis arridet? Cum Dominus Benedictus promulgaret legem suam in monte Sinai, dicebat Moysi post quam populus Decalogum ex ore ejus audivisset ut populum universum dimitteret in tabernacula sua, ipse vero maneret, percepturus divinam voluntatem ut populum deinde ex ea instruere posset, sicut etiam scriptum est in Deuteronomio cap.5.30. Vade & dic eis, eis, revertimini omnes in tabernacula vestra: Tu contra hic coram me stabis ut edisseram tibi omnes leges, praecepta & instituta quae docebis illos, &c. itaque Moses in monte commoratus est 40 diebus & totidem noctibus, quo tempore Dominus ei revelavit expositionem legis, quam legem mentalem dicimus & hanc Moyses communicavit senatui ac nominatim Josua discipulo suo, idq; ita continuo temporum successu per traditionem fuit observatu, Deo addita poena sanctiete eiut obediretur, his verbis: Si qua difficilis aut ambigua controversia inter vos exsistat in judicio, adscendes in locum, quem Dominus Deus tuus eliget, &c. faciesq; secundum id quod vobis praedicto loco monstrabitur, &c. non recedes a eo neq; ad dextram neq; ad sinistra, &c. & vir qui superbe egerit recusans obedire, morte multabitur, &c. Hae traditiones comprehensae sunt libris Mischna & Talmud dictis: secundum has necesse est S. literas interpretari, nullo- que alio modo.
units.tr: They commend the interpretation of the divine Scriptures, as is clear from innumerable commentaries. Yet all of these are drawn either from the Oral Law or from the opinions of the rabbis. Since the Oral Law, in its compass, fills out the very rich explanation of the Written Law, and the Written Law cannot be understood without the Oral, because the Oral is its foundation, as was explained above in the sixth paragraph; and since the authority of the rabbis themselves is almost supreme and divine. They maintain that they wrote their writings by the Holy Spirit [רוח הקדש], as Rabbi Isaac Avuhaf testifies in Menorat Hammaor, fol. 23, col. 1: To all those things which our rabbis taught in their homilies, the same faith must be given by us as to the Law of Moses. And if at any time something in them seems to be either hyperbolical, or contrary to nature, or to exceed the grasp of our intellect, the fault is not to be assigned to their words but to the dullness and unhappiness of our own minds. And Rabbi Ezechias, in his Chaskuni, which is a commentary on the five books of Moses: Whoever dissents from his teacher is just as if he dissented from the divine Majesty. But whoever believes the words of the wise is as if he believed God himself. Hence also the frequent admonition to Jewish youth occurs everywhere: My son, attend to the words of the Scribes more than to the words of the Law. It is no wonder, then, that the Jews are wise in matters divine alone, since they claim for themselves the proper exposition of the Law, as the anonymous Jew hints in Coccejus, Considerations on the Jewish Responses, question 17: Is it lawful for Jews alone to interpret the Scriptures and to follow that sense which pleases them most? When the Blessed Lord promulgated his law on Mount Sinai, he said to Moses, after the people had heard the Decalogue from his mouth, that he should dismiss the whole people to their tents, but he himself should remain, to receive the divine will so that he could then instruct the people from it, as it is also written in Deuteronomy 5:30: Go and say to them, return all of you to your tents. But you, on the contrary, stand here before me, so that I may set out for you all the laws, precepts and institutions which you shall teach them, etc. Thus Moses remained on the mountain forty days and as many nights, during which time the Lord revealed to him the explanation of the law, which we call the mental law. Moses communicated this to the senate, and especially to Joshua his disciple, and it was so observed by tradition through the successive ages, with a penalty added by God so that it might be obeyed with holiness, in these words: If any difficult or doubtful controversy arises among you in judgment, you shall go up to the place which the Lord your God shall choose, etc., and you shall act according to what shall be shown to you in that said place, etc. You shall not turn aside from it, neither to the right hand nor to the left, etc. And the man who acts proudly, refusing to obey, shall be punished with death, etc. These traditions are contained in the books called the Mishnah and the Talmud. According to these it is necessary to interpret the holy letters, and in no other way.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: Sensum scripturae duplicem constituunt, unum Literalem, Mysticum alterum; illum appellantes שפה vel פשט Sensum nudum, simplicem, literalem, Grammaticum; Hunc מדרש aut מדרש Allegoricum, Arcanum, hinc diligenti inquisitione hauriendum, de quo Elias Levita ad vocem דרש in Thisbi: Vocant item Midrasch omne commentarium, quod non juxta simplicem, sive literalem sensum scriptum est, ut Midrasch Agadah, vel vel Midrasch Rabbinorum nostrorum ; Credunt sensum scripturæ non nisi unicum esse, Literalem, Grammaticum, Historicum, quod regula Rabbinorum communis sit, Stylum scripturæ non cadere in Midrasch, seu expositionem allegoricam ; Nec egrediatur scriptura extra simplicem suum & literalem sensum ; Quo indicare volunt, observante celeberrimo Hottingero in Thesauro Philologico, pag. 233. Sensus nativi, proprii, & Grammatici primam, potissimamque rationem esse habendam; Sed licet scripturæ sensum unicum afferant, commendentque valde Literalem, sive Historicum, revera tamen multiplicem faciunt scripturæ sensum, dedit-que nimium sunt Allegoriis, quibus utramq; fere implent paginam ; Hinc jactant infinita sæpe in sensu simplici latere mysteria, ipsaque verba scripturæ quandoque sensus sustinere septuaginta, totidemque diversis posse applicari modis, sicuti refert Rabbi Levi Barsellonius in Sepher Hachinnuch, p. 39. Manifestum est inter nos Legem septuaginta habere facies, id est, multoties posse applicari, multaque continere Mystica; Ulteriusque probat Raschi, quando præfatione in Canticum Canticorum scribit: Una eademque scriptura in multos deduci potest sen-sus: Summa tamen hæc est tenenda; quemque locum suum certum habere sensum simplicem & literalem; Ut ita non mirum sit, Judæos sensum Mysti-cum cum longe præferre simplici, & illum nominare verbum majus, præstantiusque, hunc vero verbum minus, inferiusque; Imo licet semper delectati fuerint allegoriis, illarumque messis fertilis hodie quoque in eorum sit commentariis, tamen inventi fuerunt cordatiores, numero tamen pauci, qui hanc damnarunt aliquando intemperiem, uti legimus apud Maimonidem in More Nevochim, Part. III. cap. 43. Alii vero irrideven & contemnunt eas, (Allegorias) cum certum sit, non esse eam textus sententiam; Sic quoque monet Menasseh Ben Israel de Resurrectione mortuorum lib. 1. pag. 38, 39. Sciendum est, scripturam semper secundum literam intelligendam & explicandam esse, nisi explicatio contineat aliquid, quod implicat contradictionem: Exempli gratia, cum Deo attribuuntur caput, pedes & affectus, five passiones humanæ. Si enim uniuscuique pro arbitrio suo liceat, sensu allegorico explicare sacras literas, quæ certitudo explicationis erit? Sensum quem quisque volet, sibi fingeт: Unde in infinita ac innumerabilia nos incidere necesse erit absurda. Jactant Judæi suos tredecim Modos מדות appellatos, quos a divino acceperint numine, ad Legis verum eruendum sensum, de quibus Rabbi Josua Hallevi in Halichot Olam, quem versione Latina illustravit Constantinus L' Empereur; Et Rabbi Abraham
units.tr: They set up a twofold sense of Scripture, one Literal, the other Mystical. They call the former the plain sense [פשט], the bare, simple, literal, grammatical sense. The latter they call Midrash, the allegorical, secret sense, which must be drawn out by diligent inquiry. Concerning this Elias Levita, under the word darash, in the Thisbi: They also call every commentary that is not written according to the simple or literal sense a Midrash, such as the Midrash Haggadah, or the Midrash of our rabbis. They believe that the sense of Scripture is only one, the literal, grammatical, historical sense, since it is the common rule of the rabbis that the style of Scripture does not fall into Midrash, that is, allegorical exposition, and that Scripture does not go beyond its plain and literal sense. By this they wish to indicate, as the very famous Hottinger observes in the Philological Thesaurus, p. 233, that the native, proper and grammatical sense must have the first and chief place. But although they assert that Scripture has one sense, and greatly commend the literal or historical sense, in reality they make the sense of Scripture manifold, and they are excessively given to allegories, with which they fill almost every page. Hence they boast that infinite mysteries often lie hidden in the plain sense, and that the very words of Scripture are sometimes able to bear seventy senses and can be applied in as many different ways, as Rabbi Levi Barsellonius reports in Sepher Hachinnuch, p. 39: It is evident among us that the Law has seventy faces, that is, it can be applied many times and contains many mystical things. Raschi further proves this when he writes in his preface to the Song of Songs: One and the same Scripture can be drawn out into many senses. Yet this must be held as the main point: that each place has its own certain simple and literal sense. So it is no wonder that the Jews prefer the mystical sense by far to the simple one, and call it the greater word, more excellent, but the simple sense the lesser word, inferior. Indeed, although they have always delighted in allegories, and their fruitful harvest of them is still present today in their commentaries, nevertheless there have been some more sensible men, though few in number, who at times condemned this excess, as we read in Maimonides, More Nevochim, Part III, chap. 43: But others mock and despise them (the allegories), since it is certain that this is not the sense of the text. So also Menasseh Ben Israel warns, concerning the resurrection of the dead, book 1, pp. 38, 39: It must be known that Scripture is always to be understood and explained according to the letter, unless the explanation contains something which implies a contradiction, for example when a head, feet and human affections or passions are attributed to God. For if each person were free at his own discretion to explain the sacred letters in an allegorical sense, what certainty of explanation would there be? Each would invent whatever sense he wished; hence we would necessarily fall into infinite and countless absurdities. The Jews boast of their thirteen Modes, called middot [מדות], which they say they received from the divine power for drawing out the true sense of the Law, concerning which Rabbi Joshua Hallevi in Halichot Olam, which Constantine L'Empereur illustrated with a Latin version, and Rabbi Abraham

units.la: Bar David, in libello de tredecim modis, quibus Judæi interpretantur Legem suam, Cantabrigiæ Anno 1597 in forma octava, sermone impresso Latino.
units.tr: Bar David, in his little book on the thirteen modes by which the Jews interpret their Law, Cambridge, 1597, in octavo, printed in Latin.

units.la: CAPVT III. De Deo, Essentia, Nominibus, & Attributis Dei.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. Concerning God, the Essence, Names, and Attributes of God.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: CRedit Synagoga fide perfecta, quod Deus Ter Optimus Maximus, non Essentia tantum, sed Personis etiam sit אחד Unus, Unicusque, בדד Solus, ex fidei Judaicæ articulo secundo, qui in precum libellis, sic brevioribus exhibetur verbis, ut sit tum clarior, tum magis in præsenti semper teneatur memoria: אני מאמין באמונה שלמה שהבורא יתברך שמו הוא יחיד ואין יחידות כמוהו בשום פנים והוא לבדו אלהנו היה הוה ויהיה; Fide perfecta credo, Creatorem, cujus nomen sit benedictum, Unicum esse unitate, quæ nullam omnino similem habeat, illumque solum Deum Deum nostrum fuisse, esse, & futurum esse; Repeti- turque in Catechismo Judaico his quæ se- quuntur verbis: Fundamentum secundum est, quod hic Deus, qui condidit & formavit omnia, quæ exi- stunt superius & inferius, sit vere unus & singularis, qualis alter in nullo mundo, nec extra mundos repe- riatur, sicut scriptum est Deuter. cap. 6. vers. 4. Audi Israel Dominus Deus noster, Deus unus est; Hinc confitetur cum Maimonide in Jesode Tora, Fundamentis Legis, cap. 1. §. 4. Hic Deus unus est, non duo, nec plures quam duo, sed unus: Ejus unitati nihil ex iis quod in hoc universo unum est, respondet. Non enim est unus specie, quippe quæ multa continet singularia: Nec est unus corpore, idenim in partes & extrema est divisibile: Sed ita unus est, ut nulla ei similis in mundo reperiatur unitas. Laudat ubiq; admirabile divinæ Essentiæ unitatem, inculcat Essentiæ simplicitatem, & spiritualitatem, nihilque flagrantius detestatur quam Deorum Gentilium pluralitatem, Idololatriamque, ut tacite simul tollat Personarum in divina Essentia Trinitatem, petat, impugnetque Messiæ, Filii Dei incarnationem, sicuti suo monstrabitur loco.
units.tr: The Synagogue believes with perfect faith that God, Best and Greatest, is one [אחד], unique, and alone [בדד], not only in essence but also in persons. This is the second article of Jewish faith, which the prayer books set out in words so brief that it is both clearer and always more readily kept in memory at hand: [אני מאמין באמונה שלמה שהבורא יתברך שמו הוא יחיד ואין יחידות כמוהו בשום פנים והוא לבדו אלהנו היה הוה ויהיה]. With perfect faith I believe that the Creator, blessed be his name, is one, with a unity like which there is no other in any way, and that he alone has been, is, and will be our God. The Jewish Catechism repeats this in the following words: The second foundation is that this God, who created and formed all things that exist above and below, is truly one and singular, such that no other is found in any world or beyond the worlds, as it is written, Deuter. cap. 6. vers. 4: Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one. Hence he confesses, with Maimonides in Jesode Tora, the Fundamentals of the Law, cap. 1, §. 4: This God is one, not two, nor more than two, but one. Nothing in this universe that is one corresponds to his unity. For he is not one in species, since that contains many individuals; nor is he one in body, since that is divisible into parts and extremities. But he is one in such a way that no unity like his is found in the world. Everywhere he praises the wonderful unity of the divine essence and insists on the simplicity and spirituality of the essence, and he detests nothing more vehemently than the plurality of the heathen gods and idolatry. Yet at the same time he tacitly removes the Trinity of persons in the divine essence, and he seeks and attacks the incarnation of the Messiah, the Son of God, as will be shown in its place.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Credit Synagoga quod Dei Essentia, ipsa sit Dei Existentia, cum non sit adventitia, sed necessaria, hinc immane quantum à creaturarum distinćta essentia, quæ libera est, caussamque que suæ habet existentiæ, in existentia illa divina, sicuti probat Maimonides, cum in More Nebochim, Part. 1. cap. 57. de Deo scribit: Existentia nihil aliud est, quam ipsius Essentia & veritas, & vicissim Essentia ejus nihil aliud est, quam ipsius Existentia. Nam Essentia ipsius non est ita comparata, ut Existentia ipsi accidat; Nam ita Existentia foret res adventitia, sed semper & necessario existit, nec quicquam novi unquam in ipso exoritur, neque etiam accidens aliquod ei accidit; Fuseque deducit Rabbi Joseph Albo Fundamentorum lib. 2. cap. 10. ostendens, quod ימצ seu שם' Essentia divina, sit ipsa שם'יס Existentia divina, cum non שבמ contingens, sed הוצ' necessaria sit: Deus solus necessario existit, alia vero entia omnia sunt contingentia; Et in hoc conveniunt quod sint contingentia, nihil vero est quod conveniat cum eo in eo quod necessario existit, neque in aliqua alia re, ne in nomine quidem entis: Jam enim ostendimus fieri non posse ut sint duæ necessariæ existentiæ, nulloque modo ea concipi posse paria: Tum ostendimus Esse dici de Deo Benedicto, & de aliis æquivoce: Ideoque Unitas Dei Benedicti est unitas perfecta, cum qua nihil concurrit, neque simile est ullo modo; Et eodem lib. 2. cap. 24. Itaque compertum est nomen entis vere non posse tribui ulli enti, præter Deum. De aliis enim præter eum entibus dici non potest ea semper esse, sed tantum dum existunt, non post, nec ante. Sed Deus benedictus quia
units.tr: The Synagogue believes that the essence of God is itself the existence of God, since it is not accidental but necessary. Hence the divine existence is immeasurably distinct from the essence of creatures, which is free and has a cause of its existence. Maimonides proves this when he writes about God in More Nebochim, Part 1, cap. 57: Existence is nothing other than his essence and truth, and conversely his essence is nothing other than his existence. For his essence is not so constituted that existence happens to it, for then existence would be an accidental thing; rather he always and necessarily exists, nor does anything new ever arise in him, nor does any accident befall him. Rabbi Joseph Albo also deduces this at length in Fundamentorum lib. 2, cap. 10, showing that the divine essence [the Hebrew word for essence] is the divine existence [the Hebrew word for existence], since it is not contingent but necessary: God alone necessarily exists; all other beings are contingent. They agree in this, that they are contingent; yet there is nothing that agrees with him in what necessarily exists, nor in any other thing, not even in the name of being. For we have already shown that there cannot be two necessary existences, and that in no way can they be conceived as equals. We have also shown that "to be" is said of the blessed God and of other things equivocally. Therefore the unity of the blessed God is a perfect unity, with which nothing coincides and to which nothing is in any way similar. And in the same book, lib. 2, cap. 24: Thus it has been established that the name of true being cannot be attributed to any being except God. For of other beings besides him it cannot be said that they always exist, but only while they exist, not after or before. But the blessed God, because he always remains in the same state, his essence is a true being. For the name of being is rightly given to him whose being depends on nothing other than his own essence. For since his being depends on his own essence, he is in no way contingent.

units.la: E s quia semper permanet in eodem statu, ipsius essentia verum est ens. Vere enim tribuitur nomen entis ei, cujus esse non pendet ab alio, quam ab ipsius essentia. Ex eo enim quod ejus esse pendet ab ipsius essentia, nullo modo contingens est.
units.tr: Because it always remains in the same state, the essence of God is a true being. For the name of being is rightly given to that whose existence depends on nothing but its own essence. Since its being depends on its own essence, it is in no way contingent.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Fundamentum fundamentorum apud Judæos est, quod Deus benedictus sit מקור הכל Causa prima omnium rerum, sit עלת העלות Causa causarum, sit Ens summum, a quo omnia dependeant, uti loquuntur in Catechismo, articulo fidei primo: Fundamentum primum est, credere existentiam Dei, qui sit causa causarum, & fundamendum fundamentorum, quod omnia existentia tam infera quam superna ab illo condita sint, ac in eo consistant; Sic Maimonides in Constitutionib9 de Fundamentis Legis, c. 1. §. 1. Fundamentum fundamentorum, & columna sapientiæ est, cognoscere, esse ipsum primum ens, ipsudque existentiam largiri cuilibet existenti: Omnia enim entia cœli & terræ, quæque intra illa sunt, non existunt nisi ex veritate illius existentiæ. Quod si concipias, illud non existere, nulla respoterit existere: sin autem tibi imagineris, nulla existentia esse præter illud solum, ipsud existet, neque desinet esse propter illorum destructionem: Omnia enim existentia necessario dependent ab illo; ipse autem non opus habet illis, ne quidè ullo eorū; Sic quoque Rabbi Joseph Albo, Fundamentorum lib. 2. cap. 13, Hoc est præceptum legis, Deut. cap. 6. Audi Israel Israel Deus Dominus noster, Deus unus est: Idest, proponitur nobis credendum, Deum, etsi sit Dominus noster, idest, causa multitudinis rerum, ipsum tamen unum esse unitate perfecta.
units.tr: The foundation of foundations among the Jews is that the blessed God is the first source of all things [מקור הכל], the cause of causes [עלת העלות], the highest being on whom all things depend, as they say in the Catechism in the first article of faith: The first foundation is to believe in the existence of God, who is the cause of causes and the foundation of foundations, and that all existing things, both lower and higher, were created by him and consist in him. So Maimonides in the Constitutions on the Fundamentals of the Law, cap. 1, §. 1: The foundation of foundations and the pillar of wisdom is to know that there is a first being, who gives existence to every existing thing. For all beings of heaven and earth, and whatever is within them, exist only from the truth of that existence. If you were to conceive that he does not exist, nothing else could exist; but if you imagine that there is no existence besides him alone, he will still exist, and will not cease to be by their destruction. For all existing things necessarily depend on him, while he has no need of them, nor of any one of them. So too Rabbi Joseph Albo, Fundamentorum lib. 2, cap. 13: This is the precept of the law, Deut. cap. 6, Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one. That is, we are bidden to believe that God, although he is our Lord, that is, the cause of the multitude of things, is himself one with a perfect unity.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Asserit Synagoga mortalium neminem divinam comprehendere Essentiam, nullamque creatura, licet naturale Dei Artificis habeat notitia, assequi Essentiae veritate, quod Lux sit inaccessa, quod definiri non possit, cū careat suo tugenere, tū differentia, quod obstet turbulenta, tenebricolaque materia in creaturis, apprehensionem Essentiae exactam impediens, sicuti restatur. Maimonides in Constitutionibus de Fundamentis Legis, cap. 1. Veritatem hujus scientiae (intelligit Deum) non intelligit homo, neque potest assequi, aut investigare, Job. cap. 11. verf. 7. Num investigatione Deum invenies? Num usque ad perfectionem Omnipotentis invenies? Quid quaerebat comprehendere Moses Magister noster, Exod cap. 33. verf. 18. Fac me videre, quaeso, gloriam tuam? Volebat cognoscere veritatem essentiae Dei, donec esset nota intellectui ejus, tanquam notitia cujusdam ex hominibus, quum contemplatur ejus faciem, & insculpitur ejus menti imago ipsius, ut ipse homo distinctus existat in animo ejus a caeteris hominibus: Sic rogavit Moses Magister noster ut essentia Sancti Benedicti in mente ejus distincta esset ab entium reliquorum essentiis, usque dum cognocognoscere veritatem essentiae ejus, uti in se est; Sed respondit ei Deus: Non potest intellectus hominis vivi, compositi ex corpore & anima, perspicue assequi veritatem hujus rei; Confirmatque Maimonidis Scholiastes ad cap. 1. de Fundamentis Legis: Id cujus essentiam cognoscere volumus, cognosci non potest, nisi ex definitione ejus: Deus autem benedictus definiri non potest: definitio enim composita est ex genere proximo, & differentia; Deus autem non habet genus, sub quo comprehendatur, ideoque non possumus comprehendere essentiam ejus. Quam maxime autem inclarescit sententia, si conferamus Eliam in Tikkune Haffohar, de quo sic Rittangelius in Sepher Iezira pag. 162. Domine Mundorum, Tu Es Ipse Unus extra numerum; Tu es excelsus super omnes excelsos, abscónditus omnium absconditorum: Nulla mens te omnino apprehendere valet. Tu es qui produxisti decem Ordines & vocamus eos Numerationes, ad illuminandum in eis mundos absconditos, qui non revelati sunt, & mundos qui revelati sunt: Et in iis te abscondis a filiis hominum, & tu es qui annexus es eis & uniste iis; Et Rabbi Jedajam Happenini in Bechinat Olam cap. penult. referentem, quod scientia omnium ratione utentium ne minimam ejus partem comprehendere possit, imo quod summum, quod de ipso novimus, sit, quod ipsum non novimus.
units.tr: The Synagogue maintains that none of mortals can comprehend the divine Essence, and that no creature, although it has a natural knowledge of the divine Maker, can attain to the truth of the Essence, because it is an inaccessible Light, and cannot be defined, since it lacks a genus, as it lacks a differentia, and because a turbulent and dark matter in creatures stands in the way and prevents the exact apprehension of the Essence, as is attested. Maimonides, in the Constitutions on the Foundations of the Law, chapter 1: "Man does not understand the truth of this knowledge (he means God), nor can he attain to it or investigate it." Job 11:7: "Can you find out God by searching? Can you find out the Almighty to perfection?" What Moses, our Master, sought to comprehend, Exodus 33:18: "Show me, I pray you, your glory?" He wished to know the truth of the Essence of God, until it should be known to his understanding as the knowledge of a certain man is known when one contemplates his face, and the image of him is engraved on one's mind, so that this man stands out distinctly in one's mind from other men. Thus Moses, our Master, asked that the Essence of the Holy Blessed One might stand out distinctly in his mind from the essences of the other beings, until he should know the truth of His Essence as it is in itself. But God answered him that the understanding of a living man, composed of body and soul, cannot clearly attain the truth of this matter. And the scholiast of Maimonides on chapter 1 of the Foundations of the Law confirms this: "That whose essence we wish to know cannot be known except through its definition. But the Blessed God cannot be defined, for a definition is composed of the nearest genus and a differentia; but God has no genus under which He may be comprehended, and therefore we cannot comprehend His essence." The opinion becomes far clearer if we compare Elijah in the Tikkune Haffohar, of whom Rittangelius, in the Sepher Jetzirah, page 162, speaks thus: "Lord of the worlds, You are One beyond number; You are high above all the high, hidden beyond all the hidden: no mind is able to apprehend You at all. You are He who produced the ten Orders, which we call Numerations, to illuminate in them the hidden worlds that are not revealed, and the worlds that are revealed; and in them You hide Yourself from the sons of men, and You are He who is joined to them and united with them." And Rabbi Jedaiah Happenini, in the Bechinat Olam, last chapter but one, reports that the knowledge of all rational beings cannot grasp even the smallest part of Him, and indeed that the highest thing we know of Him is that we do not know Him.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Licet Mosi petenti negata fuerit per summum Numen clara, distinctaque Essentiae divinae notitia, ipsque Angeli Ministerii, Animaliaq; sanctitatis, sustinentia thronum, nunquam tamen, ex mente Hebraeorum, videant, cognoscantque omnem divinam gloriam, interim tamen non intestatum se reliquisse Mosi, aliisq; divina virtute viris, ultro fatentur; Cum enim Moses, prioris petitionis, ut videret gloriam divinam, comprehenderetque Essentiae veritatem, exasse compos non esset factus; secundo efflagitavit Deum, ut tum nota sibi faceret Essentiae suae Nomina, Attributaque, ex Exod.cap.33.verf.13. Notas fac mihi vias tuas, ut cognoscam te; Quo posset divinae Essentiae aliqualem habere notitiam, cum teste Maimonide in More Nevochim, Part. 1. cap. 54, Deus Benedictus per nomina vel attributa sua possit cognosci, utpote cum is, qui novit vias ejus, novit ipsum summe Deum; Hinc quoque innumera in scriptis Judaicis observabis divina nomina, quae [Hebrew] memoracula vocant, tum Essentialia, tum maximam partem ex operibus, attributisque divinis desumta, partim scripturaria, partim Rabbinica, Cabbalisticaque; Mox vocatur [Hebrew] Jehova, [Hebrew] Jehova Exercituum, [Hebrew] Fortis, [Hebrew] Deus Venerandus, colendusque, & [Hebrew] in plurali, [Hebrew]. Excelsus, שרי sufficiens, אדני Dominus; Mox appellatur השם Hoc nomen, ex Levit. cap. 24. verf. 11, Deuter. cap. 28. verf. 58. Substituentes pro Jehova; Elias Levita in Thisbi ad vocem; המקום Locum, quia Judice Aben Ezra ad Est. 1. Omnis locus repletus est gloria ejus, vel quia ipse est locus mundi, in Midrasch Tillim Fol. 40. Vel quia ex computatione Cabbaliftica מקום in numeris continet 168, & nomen יהוה juxta numerum literarum multiplicatum totidem completur; גבורה potentia; שכינה Majestas divina; שמים Coelum, quod coeli sunt sedes ejus, teste Elia Levita in Thisbi, hinc Talmudistarum vox: כל לשם שמים omnia ad coelum, id est, propter Deum; Et in Medrasch Kohelet c. 9. v. 12. Est qui peccat in terram, sed non peccat in coelum, & est qui peccat in coelum, & non peccat terram; Mox nominatur אגלא Agla, voce Cabbaliftica, quae maximus in restinguendis incendiis usus, quaeque significat אתה גבור לעולם אדני Tu es fortis in aeternum Domine; Mox multis describitur, nominaturque Deus רבינו של עולם Dominus mundi הקדוש ברוך הוא Deus Benedictus; Sanctus Benedictus ille: עלת העולות Caussa causarum: יסוד היסודות Fundamentum fundamentorum. VI.
units.tr: Although the clear and distinct knowledge of the divine Essence was refused to Moses when he asked for it, by the Supreme Power, and although the angels of ministry and the living creatures of holiness that bear the throne never, according to the mind of the Hebrews, see or know the whole of the divine glory, they nonetheless freely admit that God did not leave Moses and others endowed with divine power without some provision. For when Moses, in his first request, asked to see the divine glory and grasp the truth of the Essence, he was not granted this at all. Secondly, he begged God to make known to him the Names and Attributes of his Essence, from Exod. 33:13: "Make known to me your ways, that I may know you," so that he might have some knowledge of the divine Essence. For, as Maimonides testifies in More Nevochim, Part 1, ch. 54, the Blessed God can be known through his names or attributes, since he who knows his ways knows God most high. Hence you will also observe in Jewish writings countless divine names, which they call memorials [Hebrew], both essential names and names taken mostly from God's works and attributes, some from Scripture, some rabbinic and cabbalistic. Soon he is called Jehovah, Jehovah of Hosts, the Strong, the Venerable and Worshipful God, and in the plural [Elohim]; Most High, Shaddai [שדי] sufficient, Adonai [אדני] Lord. Soon he is called This name [ha-Shem], from Lev. 24:11 and Deut. 28:58, substituted for Jehovah (Elias Levita in Thisbi, under the word). He is called the Place [ha-Makom], because, according to Aben Ezra on Esth. 1, every place is filled with his glory, or because he is the place of the world (Midrash Tillim fol. 40), or because by cabbalistic computation the word makom contains 168 in its numerals, and the name Jehovah multiplied by the number of its letters makes the same sum. He is called power [gevurah]; Divine Majesty [shekhinah]; Heaven [shamayim], since the heavens are his seat, as Elias Levita testifies in Thisbi. Hence the saying of the Talmudists: all for heaven [kol le-shem shamayim], that is, for God's sake. And in Midrash Kohelet ch. 9 v. 12: There is one who sins against the earth but not against heaven, and one who sins against heaven and not against the earth. Soon he is named Agla, a cabbalistic word of greatest use in quenching fires, which signifies You are strong for ever, Lord. Soon he is described by many and named Lord of the world [Rabbino shel olam], the Holy One, blessed be he [ha-Kadosh barukh hu], the Blessed Holy One; the cause of causes [ilat ha-ilot]; the foundation of foundations [yesod ha-yesodot]. VI.

units.la: Inter nomina divina summae authoritatis est apud omnes Judaeos, nomen יהוה Jehova, שם הנעצם Nomen Essentia vel subsistentia. tia, שם החויה nomen Existentia, cum notet necessariam existentiam, fecundas tribuentes ה' Iah, & אהיה Ero, illaque pariter יסודות Essentialia appellantes: reliqua vero omnia Accessoria, quod ab operibus, Attributisque defumta sint divinis, כנויים vocantes, sicuti demonstrat Maimonides in More Nebochim, Part.1.cap.61. Omnia Dei Optimi Maximi nomina, quae in libris reperiuntur sacris, derivata sunt, ut palam est, ab operibus ejus, unico excepto Jod He Vau He, quod est nomen Dei proprium, unde vocatur Schem Hammephorasch nomen expositum, quia clare & citra ullam aequivocationem de substantia Creatoris docet; Et Rabbi Jehuda Levita in Iosfi Part.11.p.75.76. Nomina Dei omnia, excepto no-Tetragrammato, sunt proprietates & similitudines accessoria, non exprimentes ipsam Dei essentiam, defumta ab affectionibus creaturarum. secundum ejus decreta, & opera. Appellant nomen Jehova שם המפורש Nomen separatum, distinctum, quod sit peculiare & proprium Deo Benedicto, quod sit שם המיוחד nomen peculiare, cum rationem habeat ipsius esse necessarii, uti legimus apud Josephum Albo in Fundamentis lib. 2. cap. 28. Nomen quod scribitur per Jod He Vau He vocatur Schem Hammephorasch, id est, nomen distinctum. Ideo autem vocatur distinctum, quia est peculiare, & proprium Deo Benedicto prae caeteris nominibus: Alia enim nomina dicuntur De Deo, & de aliis. alius prater Deum: Quia nimirum illa sunt imposita Deo Benedicto, sive habita ratione creaturarum, sive propter aliam rationem: Non autem habita ratione ipsius esse necessarii. Sic Elohim significat potestatem, ideoque tribuitur Deo, & aliis prater Deum: tribuitur enim haec vox Elohim etiam Angelis, & Judicibus. Sic etiam Adonai significat Dominium, ideoque Deo, aliisque prater Deum tribuitur: Et sic de aliis nominibus, quae similiter possunt Deo tribui, & aliis prater Deum, vel perfecte ὁμοιω- μως, vel secundum prius & posterius. At nomen Tetragrammaton nullo modo dici potest de alio, quam de Deo, quia hoc nomen Deo convenit, quatenus est ens necessarium. VII.
units.tr: Among the divine names, the name יהוה Jehovah has the highest authority for all Jews. It is called the name of Essence or subsistence [shem ha-ne'elam], the name of Existence [shem ha-hawyah]. Since it denotes necessary existence, they assign to it the fruitful letters Yah [י"ה] and Ehyeh [אהיה], "I shall be," and they likewise call these Essentials [yesodot]. All the other names, however, they call Accessories [kinnuyim], because they are derived from God's works and attributes, as Maimonides shows in More Nevochim, Part 1, ch. 61: "All the names of God the Best and Greatest that are found in the sacred books are derived, as is plain, from his works, with the single exception of Jod He Vau He, which is the proper name of God, and is therefore called Shem Hammephorasch, the explained name, because it teaches clearly, and without any ambiguity, about the substance of the Creator." And Rabbi Jehuda Levita in Cuzari, Part 2, pp. 75–76: "All the names of God, except the Tetragrammaton, are properties and resemblances, accessories, not expressing the very essence of God, taken from the affections of creatures according to his decrees and works." They call the name Jehovah the separated, distinct name [shem ha-meforash], which is peculiar and proper to the Blessed God, the peculiar name [shem ha-meyuhad], since it has regard to his necessary being, as we read in Joseph Albo, Fundamentals, book 2, ch. 28: "The name written with Jod He Vau He is called Shem Hammephorasch, that is, the distinct name. It is called distinct because it is peculiar and proper to the Blessed God above other names. For other names are said of God and of others besides God, namely because they were imposed on the Blessed God either with regard to creatures or for some other reason, but not with regard to his necessary being. Thus Elohim signifies power, and so is attributed to God and also to others besides God; for this word Elohim is given also to Angels and Judges. So too Adonai signifies dominion, and so is attributed to God and to others besides God; and so with the other names, which can likewise be attributed to God and to others besides God, either perfectly homonymously, or according to prior and posterior. But the name Tetragrammaton can in no way be said of anyone other than God, because this name belongs to God insofar as he is a necessary being." VII.

units.la: Hinc abstinet natio Judaica a pronunciatione Nominis היהו Jehova, persuasa ex nimia vocis tum reverentia, tum superstitione, quod nomen sit longe sanctius habitum, quam reliqua DEI nomina, quod non liceat expungere vel delere, ex Talmudistarum statuto in Erachin, cap. 5. Nomen Dei inscriptum anstis vasorum, aut lecti basibus, exscindatur atque occultetur; Et in Maffechet Sopherim, cap. 5. Et apud Maimonidem in Fund. Leg. c. 6. §. 6. Quod mysteriis plenum sit, virtuteq; polleat infinita, cum ipsa vocis pronunciatio miracula valeat producere, ex physica quoque operatione; Sic Mosen omnia sua patrasse miracula per nomen Jehova inscriptum virgae, qua in deserto pulpulsabat petram, testantur in libro Caphtor, Fol. 56. Moses non est ipsius nisi nomine ipso maximo, & omnia miracula sua, quae fecit, fuerunt per Schem Hamphorasch, id est, Nomen expositum, quod est ipsum nomen יהוה & Ehjeh Asher Ehjeh, Et Messiam nostrum, quem ישוע Jeschu appellant, per rectam nominis Jehova prolationem, sua effecisse miracula, ut ipsius divinitatem, quam ex operibus miraculosis quoque demonstram, eludere pro viribus possint, testibus Talmudistis in Schabbat Fol. 104. Nonne filius Sabda exportavit magias ex Ægypto per cæsuras, quas fecerat in carne sua? Quod severissime interdicta fuerit nominis Jehova enunciatio, imo plebi sub poena mortis nonnunquam a Rabbinis fuerit vetita, sicut legimus in Codice Thalmudico Sanhedrin c. 11. Fol. 90. Quicunque profert nomen Tetragrammaton per literas suas, vel secundum scripturam suam, non est ipsi pars in futuro seculo; Et in Codice Avoda Sarah, cap. 1. Fol. 18. Abduxerunt Rabbi Chaninam filium Teradjon, dicent ei ipsi: Quā ratione set egisti in Lege? respondit ipsis: Sicut praecepit mihi יהוה Deus meus, egi. Quo audito, protinus ipsum ad combustionem, damnarunt, uxorem ejus ad necem, filiam ad Pupanar. Ipsi ad compustionē. propterea quod protulerat nomen Tetragrammaton per literas suas, ex vi decreti per Abba Schaul lati: Quicunque protulerit nomē Tetragrammaton per literas suas, non habebit rē in futuro seculo. Haec quoque ratio videtur fuisse, quare hoc nomen Jehova appellaverint שם הנורא, Nomen terribile, quia non ausi fuerunt illud pronunciare; Quod vera lectio nominis Jehova perierit, sicque hodiernis pene fit incognita, qui injuriosi valde sunt in Judæos Karraitas, qui nomen Jehova per literas suas pronunciant; Hinc ne quotidiano usu vilesceret, & in vanum sumeretur, substituerunt ubique in lectione aliud Dei nomen אדני Adonai, vel expresserunt illud per שם של ארבע אותיות Nomen quatuor literarum, per שם המפורש Nomen separatum, per שמא רבא Nomen magnum, per השם הנכבד Nomen gloriosum, per השם Nomen illud. Ast quamvis abhorret à vocis expressione, non intermittit interim hoc nomine Jehova abuti, dum ad usus magicos adhibet, imaginans sibi firmiter, quod incendia extinguat, exercitus deleat, morbos depellat, ἀσυλίαν inducat, tempestates sedet, abortus impediat, & denique quæ non miracula faciat, sicut clare hoc docet Albo, Autor libri de fundamentis lib. 1. c 18. Nomina divina esse velut instrumenta opificii Dei, quibus dedit virtutem, signa, & miracula fieri per ea. VIII.
units.tr: Hence the Jewish nation abstains from pronouncing the name היהו Jehovah. It is persuaded, from an excessive reverence and superstition about the word, that the name is held far holier than the other names of God, and that it may not be erased or blotted out. This follows the rule of the Talmudists in Erachin ch. 5: The name of God written on the rims of vessels or on the bases of a bed is to be cut off and hidden; and in Massechet Sopherim ch. 5, and in Maimonides, Fundamentals of the Law ch. 6 §6. It is held to be full of mysteries and to possess infinite power, since the bare utterance of the word can produce miracles, even by physical operation. Thus they testify in the book Caphtor, fol. 56, that Moses performed all his miracles through the name Jehovah written on the rod with which he struck the rock in the desert: Moses did nothing except by that very greatest name, and all the miracles he performed were through the Shem Hamphorasch, that is, the explained name, which is the name itself [Jehovah] and Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh. They also say that our Messiah, whom they call Jeshu [ישוע], performed his miracles by the correct pronunciation of the name Jehovah, so that they may, as far as they can, evade his divinity, which he also demonstrated by miraculous works. The Talmudists testify in Shabbat fol. 104: Did not the son of Stada bring magic out of Egypt by the cuts he made in his flesh? That the pronunciation of the name Jehovah was most strictly forbidden, and that the rabbis sometimes forbade it even to the common people under penalty of death, we read in the Talmudic code Sanhedrin ch. 11, fol. 90: Whoever pronounces the Tetragrammaton according to its letters, or according to its written form, has no share in the world to come. And in the code Avoda Zarah ch. 1, fol. 18: They led away Rabbi Chanina son of Teradion. They said to him: "By what means did you act in the Law?" He answered them: "As my God Jehovah commanded me, so I did." On hearing this they at once condemned him to the fire, his wife to death, his daughter to the brothel. They condemned him to the fire because he had pronounced the Tetragrammaton according to its letters, by force of a decree issued by Abba Shaul: Whoever pronounces the Tetragrammaton according to its letters will have no share in the world to come. This also seems to have been the reason why they called this name Jehovah the terrible name [shem ha-nora], because they did not dare to pronounce it. So the true reading of the name Jehovah has perished and is now almost unknown, a point on which the Karaites, who pronounce the name Jehovah according to its letters, are very insulting to the Jews. Hence, lest it become cheap through daily use and be taken in vain, they everywhere substituted another name of God in reading, Adonai [אדני], or expressed it by the name of four letters, by the separated name [shem ha-meforash], by the great name [shema raba], by the glorious name [ha-shem ha-nikhbad], by that name [ha-shem]. But although they shrink from uttering it, they do not stop abusing this name Jehovah, using it for magical purposes and firmly imagining that it quenches fires, destroys armies, drives away diseases, confers immunity, calms tempests, prevents miscarriages, and in short does whatever miracles one likes. Albo clearly teaches this, the author of the book Fundamentals, book 1, ch. 18: The divine names are, as it were, instruments of God's workmanship, to which he gave power, and signs and miracles are done through them. VIII.

units.la: Ex mente Hebræorum Deus Sanctus Benedictus possidet Essentiam Spiritualem, cum sit ipsa substantia spiritualis, distincta tum ab omni corpore, tum à מדות הגוף Proprietatibus, operationibus, & accidentibus corporeis, ire, stare, surgere, sedere, currere, loqui, ex articulo fidei tertio ; Et apud Maimonidem in More Nevochim Part.1 cap.26. Quando ergo a Deo removetur corporeitas, tum omnia quoque ista ab ipso removebuntur, videlicet descedere, ascedere, ambulare, stare, circumire, sedere, habitare, egredi, venire, transire, & similia. Hinc non solum incorporeus sine ullo corpore, & qui ne comprehensibilis quidem sit accidentibus corporis, sed quoque incorporabilis, ut simul tacite sanctam infestare possint filii Dei incarnationem; Probant Deum non esse corporeū, quia est infinit, omne vero corpus sit finitum, finitamq; habeat potentiam, uti cumR. Albo urget Maimonides in Fundam. Leg. c. 1. §. 5, 6. Si Creator esset corpus, haberet finem ac terminum, cumsieri nequeat, ut sit corpus non habens finem: at vero quicquid praeditum est sine aut termino, limitatam & determinatam habet virtutem. Dei autem nostri, cujus benedictum sit nomen, potentia cum non habeat terminum, neque cesset, nam certe orbem perpetuo versat, non erit potentia ejus corporea. Quapropter cum nec ipse sit corpus, etiam corporum accidentia in illo non habebunt locum, ut sit divisibilis aut separabilis abalio; Quia omne corpus est compositum ex materia & forma, quæ cum de Deo prædicari non possint, negat Rabbi Albo Deum esse corporeum, quando scribit in Fundamentis lib. 2. cap. 6. Profecto Deum non esse corpus, neque potentiam corpoream, constat etiam ex fundamento, quo usifumus adprobandum Deum esse. Exeo enim idea-dem ratione consequens est. Quippe omne corpus compositum est ex materia & forma. In omni autem composito, compositio ejus, caussa est existentia ipsius. Probat uterque ulterius omne corpus a Deo esse removendum, quia Deus similem non ha-bet, Deuter.cap. 4. vers.15. Quia non vidistis ul-lam imaginem; Et Esai.cap.40. vers. 25. Cui adsi-milaretis me, aut æqualis essem; Omne autem cor-pus habeat simile. Si itaque esset corpus, simi-litudinem haberet cum reliquis corporibus; Quia Deus est ubique, in cœlis superne, & in terris inferne, juxta illud quod dicitur Deut. cap. 4. vers. 39. Corpus autem in duobus esse locis non possit; Quia corpus non movet aliud, nisi moveatur, Deus autem fit immobilis, pri-mumque illud movens; Sed testis horum omni exceptione major est articulus fidei Judaicæ tertius in compendium redactus in Catechi-smo Judaico: [Hebrew text] Fundamentum tertium est, quod Deus hic unicus & singularis non sit corpus, nec definiendus definitionibus corporis, uti scriptum est Deuter. cap. 4. vers. 15. Quia non vidistis ullam figu-ram.
units.tr: According to the mind of the Hebrews, the Holy and Blessed God possesses a spiritual essence, since he is himself a spiritual substance, distinct both from every body and from the properties, operations, and accidents of body (in Hebrew, מדות הגוף [middot ha-guf]): going, standing, rising, sitting, running, speaking. This is from the third article of faith. Maimonides also says in the More Nevochim, Part 1, chapter 26: When corporeality is removed from God, all these things are removed from him as well, namely to descend, to ascend, to walk, to stand, to go around, to sit, to dwell, to go out, to come, to pass over, and the like. Hence he is not only incorporeal, without any body, and not even comprehensible by the accidents of body, but also incorporable, so that the sons of God can tacitly assail the holy incarnation. They prove that God is not corporeal because he is infinite, while every body is finite and has finite power, as Maimonides, following Albo, urges in the Fundamentals, chapter 1, §§ 5, 6: If the Creator were a body, he would have an end and a limit, since it cannot be that a body does not have an end; but whatever is endowed with an end or limit has a limited and determined power. Since the power of our God, blessed be his name, has no limit and does not cease (for he surely turns the sphere perpetually), his power will not be corporeal. Therefore, since he himself is not a body, the accidents of bodies will not have a place in him either, such as being divisible or separable from another. For every body is composed of matter and form, and since these cannot be predicated of God, Rabbi Albo denies that God is corporeal, when he writes in the Fundamentals, book 2, chapter 6: Indeed, it is established that God is not a body, nor corporeal power, from the same foundation by which we set out to prove that God exists. For by the same reasoning it follows that every body is composed of matter and form. In every composite, its composition is the cause of its existence. Both further prove that every body must be removed from God, because God has no likeness, Deut. 4:15: Because you saw no image; and Isa. 40:25: To whom will you liken me, or who is my equal? Every body, however, has a likeness. If, then, God were a body, he would have a likeness to other bodies. Also, God is everywhere, above in heaven and below on earth, according to what is said in Deut. 4:39. A body, moreover, cannot be in two places, because a body does not move another unless it is itself moved, whereas God is immovable and the first mover. But the witness of these things, greater than any exception, is the third article of Jewish faith, reduced to a summary in the Jewish Catechism: [Hebrew text] The third foundation is that this God, the one and only, is not a body, nor to be defined by the definitions of a body, as it is written, Deut. 4:15: Because you saw no figure.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Est Perfectissimus, possidens [Hebrew text] EssenEssentiam perfectam, absolutamque, nullius rei, nullius auxilii, nulliusque opis indigam; Est numeris, gradibusque perfectissimus, de quo nulla potest perfectio negari, nullaque imperfectio affirmari, unde egregie Maimonides in More Nebochim, Part.1. cap.26. Quicquid a nobis pro perfecto habetur, id quoque attribuitur Deo Benedicto, ad docendum, illum omnibus numeris & gradibus esse perfectissimum, nullumque in ipso esse defectum vel privationem. Econtrario autem nihil eorum DEO attribui legimus, in quibus vulgus hominum imperfectionem esse aliquam existimat; Et cap.35. Atque hæc mensura sufficit pro pueris & pro plebe, quando sciunt, Deum esse, & esse perfectissimum, sine corpore vel potentia aut facultate aliqua corporea, sine omni imperfectione, acper consequens nulli passioni obnoxium. Et Rabbi Joseph Albo Auctor Fundamentorum l.2, c.25. Praterea intelligi debet attributa divina infinita esse secundum numerum, id est, infinita esse multitudinis. Cum enim in Deo sint omnes perfectionum species, quæ excogitari possint, & existat omnis omnino defectus: Mens autem concipere possit esse in Deo infinitas perfectiones; oportet eas re ipsa esse in Deo: Alioqui non esset summe perfectus: Posset enim habere plures perfectiones, quam habeat; Hinc omnem a Deo removent privationem, ostenduntque divinas perfectiones non potentia Deo inesse, sed actu omnes, uti optime rursus loquitur Maimonides in More Nevochim, chim, Part. 1. cap. ss. Sic removenda quoque a Deo est omnis privatio, ac simpliciter negandum, illum una vice perfectione quadam carere, qua alia vice ipsi infit. Nam si hoc statueretur, tum potentia tantum perfectus esset: Cum omni etenim potentia necessario privatio est conjuncta, & quicquid de potentia in actum exit, aliud quid de necessitate habet, quod illud educit, & quod actu existit. Quare consequitur, omnes perfectiones DEO inesse actu, nec quicquam ipsi potentia ulla ex parte inesse.
units.tr: He is most perfect, possessing [Hebrew text] a perfect and absolute essence, in need of no thing, no help, and no aid. He is most perfect in number and degrees, so that no perfection can be denied of him and no imperfection affirmed. Hence Maimonides admirably says in the More Nevochim, Part 1, chapter 26: Whatever is regarded by us as perfect, this too is attributed to the Blessed God, to teach that he is most perfect in every number and degree, and that there is in him no defect or privation. On the contrary, we read that nothing is attributed to God in which the common sort of men think there is some imperfection. And in chapter 35: This measure suffices for boys and for the common people, when they know that God exists, and that he is most perfect, without body or power or any corporeal faculty, without all imperfection, and consequently subject to no passion. And Rabbi Joseph Albo, author of the Fundamentals, book 2, chapter 25: Furthermore, it must be understood that the divine attributes are infinite according to number, that is, infinite in multitude. For since in God are all the kinds of perfections that can be conceived, and there is altogether no defect; and the mind can conceive that there are infinite perfections in God, it is necessary that they really be in God. Otherwise he would not be supremely perfect, for he could have more perfections than he has. Hence they remove from God every privation, and show that the divine perfections are in God not potentially but all actually, as Maimonides again speaks very well in the More Nevochim, Part 1, chapter 58. Thus every privation must also be removed from God, and it must simply be denied that he lacks some perfection at one time which he has at another. For if this were established, he would be perfect only potentially. For privation is necessarily joined with all potentiality, and whatever passes from potency into act has something else of necessity that brings it out, and that which exists actually. Hence it follows that all perfections are in God actually, and that nothing is in him potentially in any respect.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Est Infinitus, ᵴᵻᵭ יאה Sine fine, sicut Essentia infinitus, ita pariter attributis, distinctus quam maxime a creaturis finitis, teste Josepho Albo de Fundamentis lib. 1. cap. 25. Cum enim jam constet ex iis, quae diximus, Deum Benedictum esse æternum, & infinitum: Sive habere infinitam durationem Existentia tam antecedentem, quam subsequentem; necesse est attributa ea, quibus Deus Benedictus denominatur, æterna esse, & infinita, quemadmodum Deus ipse est æternus & infinitus. Quippe fieri non potest, ut de novo ipsi contingant; velita sint in Deo, ut aliquando futura non sint; Possidens infinitam dignitatem, infinitasque, complectens voluptates, juxta illud Ps. 16. v. 11. Delectationes in dextera tua sunt infinita; Habens infinitas cognitiones, infinitamque potentiam, prout mox pluribus.
units.tr: He is infinite, [ᵴᵻᵭ יאה] without end. Just as he is infinite in essence, so too in his attributes, and he is in the highest degree distinct from finite creatures, as Joseph Albo testifies in his Fundamentals, book 1, chapter 25. For since it is already established from what we have said that God, Blessed be he, is eternal and infinite, that is, that he has infinite duration of existence both before and after, it is necessary that the attributes by which God, Blessed be he, is described are eternal and infinite, just as God himself is eternal and infinite. For it cannot happen that they come to him anew, so that they would at some time not be in God. He possesses infinite dignity and infinite pleasures, according to that saying of Ps. 16. 11: "In your right hand there are pleasures forevermore." He has infinite knowledge and infinite power, as will soon be shown at greater length.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Est Simplicissimus, המורם כאחד לא non comcompositus, non divisibilis in suas partes, quia unicus, careatque corpore, quia quicquid in Deo sit ipse Deus; Non compositus ex genere & differentia, cum non habeat genus, sub quo comprehendatur, nec praedicari de ipso possit differentia, quod unus, solusque sit; Neque compositus ex subiecto & accidentibus, quod divina substantia non possit admittere accidentia, sicuti optime explicat Rabbi Joseph Albo Auctor Fundamentorum, lib.2.cap.9. Aut enim substantia per se subsistit, & necessario existere potest sine accidentibus. Sic cum accidens possit esse, & non esse; ipsa vero substantia, per se existat necessario: Deus Benedictus esset compositus ex duobus: ex eo quod necessario existit, & ex eo quod est contingens: quatenus necessario existit, causa est: Quatenus contingens est, effectus est: Et ita causa esset, & effectus simul; etiam si substantia per se subsistat, id est, non sit contingens. Vel substantia per se subsistere, & necessario existere non potest sine accidente. Sic accidens necessario existeret, & substantia ipsi subiecta necessario etiam existeret: Et ita essent duo, quae necessario existerent; aut unum compositum ex duobus, substantia nempe, & accidente. At haec omnia ex iis quae explicata sunt, refelluntur; Neque compositus est ex actu & potentia, cum sit actus purissimus & simplicissimus, imo nihil aliud quam actus perpetuus, judice Maimonide in More Nevochim, Part. 1. cap. 68.
units.tr: He is most simple, [המורם כאחד לא] not composite, not divisible into parts, because he is one and without body, since whatever is in God is God himself. He is not composed of genus and differentia, since he has no genus under which he could be comprehended, nor can a differentia be predicated of him, since he is one and alone. Nor is he composed of subject and accidents, because the divine substance cannot admit accidents, as Rabbi Joseph Albo, author of the Fundamentals, book 2, chapter 9, explains very well. For either the substance subsists through itself and can necessarily exist without accidents, and since an accident can either be or not be, while the substance itself exists necessarily through itself, then God, Blessed be he, would be composed of two things: of that which necessarily exists, and of that which is contingent. Insofar as he necessarily exists, he is a cause; insofar as he is contingent, he is an effect. And so he would be cause and effect at once, even if the substance subsists through itself, that is, is not contingent. Or else the substance cannot subsist through itself and necessarily exist without an accident. Then the accident would necessarily exist, and the substance that is its subject would also necessarily exist. And so there would be two things that necessarily exist, or one composite made of two, namely substance and accident. But all these things are refuted by what has been explained; nor is he composed of act and potency, since he is pure and most simple act, indeed nothing other than perpetual act, as Maimonides judges in More Nevochim, part 1, chapter 68.

units.la: §. Quia ergo certo constat, quod Deus Benedictus sit intellectus in actu perpetuo, nunquam in potentia, ut explicatum est, & ulterius adhuc demonstrabitur, ita ut quandoque apprehendat, quandoque vero non apprehendat, sed sit jemper intellectus actu; Sic consequens est ipsum, & rem, quam comprehendit, unum, idemque esse; Neque compositus est ex substantia & Attributis, cum attributa sint ipse Deus, nec ut distincta sint consideranda in Deo benedicto, sed per modum unius, & sine ulla acquisitione, ita ut nullam in substantiam divinam inferant compositionem, uti docet Albo lib. 2. Fundamentorum, cap. 21.
units.tr: §. Since therefore it is certain that God, Blessed be he, is intellect in perpetual act, never in potency, as has been explained, and will be further demonstrated, so that he does not at one time apprehend and at another not apprehend, but is always intellect in act; it follows that he and the thing he comprehends are one and the same. Nor is he composed of substance and attributes, since the attributes are God himself, and are not to be considered in the Blessed God as distinct, but in the manner of a unity, and without any acquisition, so that they introduce no composition into the divine substance, as Albo teaches in book 2 of the Fundamentals, chapter 21.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Est Immutabilis, שנו מבא, absque ulla mutatione, ex articulo fidei Judaicae primo: Existentia Dei nec minuetur, nec mutabitur; Quod Jehova non mutetur, Malach. cap. 3. verf 6. Ego Jehova non mutor; Quod mutabilitas imperfectionem, defectumque inferat, hinc a Sancto Benedicto removenda, Rabbi Joseph Albo de Fundamentis lib. 2. cap. 3. Hoc scimus libertatem ejusmodi non inferre Deo mutationem: Intelligimus enim mutationem esse defectum, qui in Deum cadere non potest; Quia simplicissimus est, omni carens corpore, omnique compositione, sic Maimonides in Constitutionibus de Fundamentis Legis, cap. 1. §. 12. Postquam autem probatum est, illum illum non esse corpus, manifestum erit nulla reperiri in eo accidentia corporum; non compositionem, neque divisionem; non locum, nec mensuram; non ad-scensum, neque descensum; non dextrum, neque finis-trum; non anterius, neque posterius; non sessionem, neque stationem, neque quicquam existens in tempore, ita ut habeat principium vel finem, atque numerum annorum: Non enim variabilis est, quia nihil in eo est, quod mutationem in ipso efficere posset; Quia quicquid mutatur ab alio & fortiori mu-tatur, uti loquitur Albo, Auctor Fundamen-torum lib. 2. cap. 5. Quicquid mutatur, ab alio mu-tatur. Quod autem necessario exsistit per se, non habet aliam causam a qua mutetur. Neque vero ipsum est mutans, & mutatum simul, sic enim ex duobus constaret: unum scilicet, quo mutaret: Et alio a quo mu-taretur: Et ita esset compositum; Quia Passiones a Benedicto seperandæ, cum necessariam infe-rant mutationem, teste Maimonide in More Nevochim, Part. 1. cap. 55. Pari ratione a Deo re-movenda est Passio omnis, quia omnem Passionem ne-cessario sequitur mutatio, & quia efficiens passionum citra dubium aliud est, quam id, quod patitur. Unde si Deus esset Patiens vel Passibilis, quocunque demum passionis modo, necessario aliquid extraneum in ipsum ageret, eumque mutaret; Et in Constitutio-nibus de Fundamentis Legis, cap. 1. §. 15. Sane ipse inquit Malach, cap. 3. vers. 6. Ego Deus non mutor: Quod si esset aliquando tristis, aliquando latus, esset mutamutabilis : At ista haec omnia reperiuntur nonnisi in corporibus tenebricosis & abjectis, incolentibus domicilia lutea, quorum fundamentum in pulvere; Sed Benedictus ille celebretur, supraque haec omnia extollatur. Quod per creationem non mutetur Deus, quia Deus semper est eodem modo sive ante Creationem mundi, sive post finem mundi, neque ullis mutetur temporibus; Judice Josepho Albo lib. 4. cap. 19.
units.tr: He is unchangeable, [שנו מבא] without any change, from the first article of the Jewish faith: The existence of God will neither be diminished nor changed; and that Jehovah is not changed, Malachi 3. 6: I, Jehovah, do not change. Since changeability implies imperfection and defect, it is to be removed from the Holy Blessed One, as Rabbi Joseph Albo says in the Fundamentals, book 2, chapter 3: We know that such freedom does not bring change to God, for we understand change to be a defect, which cannot fall upon God. Because he is most simple, free of every body and every composition, so Maimonides says in the Constitutions concerning the Fundamentals of the Law, chapter 1, §12: Now, after it has been proved that he is not a body, it will be plain that no accidents of bodies are found in him: no composition or division, no place or measure, no ascent or descent, no right or left, no before or behind, no sitting or standing, nor anything existing in time, so that he has a beginning or end or a number of years. For he is not variable, since there is nothing in him that could effect a change in him. Because whatever is changed is changed by another and by a stronger thing, as Albo, author of the Fundamentals, book 2, chapter 5, puts it: Whatever is changed is changed by another. But that which necessarily exists through itself has no other cause by which it could be changed. Nor indeed is it at once the changer and the changed, for then it would consist of two things: one by which it would change, and another by which it would be changed; and so it would be composite. Because passions are to be separated from the Blessed One, since they bring a necessary change, as Maimonides testifies in More Nevochim, part 1, chapter 55: By the same reasoning every passion is to be removed from God, since every passion necessarily brings change, and since the agent of passions is undoubtedly other than that which suffers. Hence, if God were passive or passible in any mode of passion whatever, he would necessarily act upon something external to himself and would change it. And in the Constitutions concerning the Fundamentals of the Law, chapter 1, §15: Indeed he says, Malachi 3. 6: I, God, do not change. For if he were at one time sad and at another glad, he would be changeable. But all these things are found only in dark and abject bodies, dwelling in houses of clay, whose foundation is in dust; but let that Blessed One be celebrated and exalted above all these things. That God is not changed by creation, because God is always in the same manner, both before the creation of the world and after the end of the world, and he is not changed by any times, as Joseph Albo judges in book 4, chapter 19.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Est Æternus, sine omni principio, fineque, קדמן Antiquus, æternus, אלהי קדם Deus æternitatis, Deuteron. cap. 33. verf. 27. Est Primus & Ultimus; Sic fidei articulo quarto: Fundamentum quartum, quod ante Deum hunc unicum & corporis expertem nulla res extiterit, sed ille primus sit & novissimus, sicut scriptum Esai. c. 44. v. 6. Ego primus & ego novissimus & praeter me non est Deus; Est solus æternus, mundu antecedens, uti operose contra Aristotelem demonstrat Maimonides in More Nevochim, Part. ii. cap. 15, 16, 17, 18. Habet Existentiam perpetuam sive ante creationem mundi, sive post finem mundi, in qua non est illa vicissitudo, quæ percipitur ex motu cœli; In qua non est prius nec posterius, neque successio temporum, quia nimirum est sine ullo motu, uti loquitur Rabbi Joseph Albo de Fundamentis lib 2. cap. 18. Probant Deum æternum, quandoquidem à tempore non dependent. pendeat, cum non sit ens contingens, sed exi-stentiæ necessariæ; Quandoquidem semper idem sit, tam ante creationem mundi, quam post illius interitum, neque ullis mutetur temporibus; Quandoquidem ante omne fuerit tempus, nulloque post tempore possit claudi, finirique; Quandoquidem sub tempus non cadat, reliquæ vero res tempori subjiciantur, & ideo tempus illas immutet, sicuti rursus deducit Albo, Auctor fundamentorum lib.2.cap. 19. omnia quæ præter Deum sunt, tempori subjiciuntur, & ideo tempus illa immutat. Hinc ipsæ etiam intelligentiæ separatæ, et sic ex contrariis minime compositæ sint, ut mutationi obnoxiæ esse queant, cum omnis mutationis causa sit contrarietas, nihilominus mutationem à tempore patiuntur. Exempli gratia, ætate Abrahami, inde à creatione primæ creaturæ, anni erant bis mille, & hodie effluxere anni quinquies mille, & amplius, atque sic omnes res creatæ necessario nunc plus ætatis agunt, quam quæ prædita erant temporibus Davidicis & ideo tempori subjiciuntur. At, de Deo Benedicto dici nequit, eum plus ætatis habere hodie, quam habuit ævo Davidis, aut cum crearet hoc universum. Est enim semper idem, tam ante creationem mundi, quam post illius interitum, neque ullis mutatur temporibus.
units.tr: He is Eternal, without any beginning or end; קדמן [kadmon], "Ancient, eternal"; אלהי קדם [Elohei kedem], "the God of eternity," Deut. 33:27. He is the First and the Last. So the fourth article of faith: "The fourth foundation: before God, who is one and free of body, nothing existed, but he is the first and the last, as it is written in Isa. 44:6: I am the first and I am the last, and besides me there is no God." He alone is eternal, prior to the world, as Maimonides laboriously demonstrates against Aristotle in the More Nevochim, Part II, chapters 15, 16, 17 and 18. He has a perpetual existence, both before the creation of the world and after its end, in which there is no alternation such as is perceived from the motion of the heavens; in which there is no before or after, and no succession of times, since it is without any motion, as Rabbi Joseph Albo says in his Fundamentals, book 2, chapter 18. They prove that God is eternal: since they do not depend on time; since he is not a contingent being but of necessary existence; since he is always the same, both before the creation of the world and after its destruction, and is not changed by any times; since he existed before all time and cannot be enclosed or ended by any time afterward; since he does not fall under time, whereas other things are subject to time and so time changes them, as Albo again deduces, author of the Fundamentals, book 2, chapter 19: all things that are besides God are subject to time, and therefore time changes them. Hence even the separate intelligences themselves, although they are not composed of contraries so as to be liable to change, nevertheless suffer change from time, since every cause of change is contrariety. For example, in the age of Abraham, from the creation of the first creature, there were two thousand years; today five thousand years and more have passed away; and so all created things now necessarily have more age than they had in the days of David, and are therefore subject to time. But it cannot be said of the Blessed God that he has more age today than he had in the age of David, or when he created this universe. For he is always the same, both before the creation of the world and after its destruction, and is not changed by any times.

units.la: XIV. Sic varia Essentiæ simplicissimæ prædicant
