units.tr: XIV. Thus they ascribe various attributes to the most simple Essence

units.la: cant Attributa, tum memorata, tum statim ulterius recensenda, non distinguentes illa ab ipsa Essentia divina, nec illa considerantes, ut res adventitias, externasque, sed ut Essentiae, nominisque explicationes, uti pulchre hoc indicat Rabbi Joseph Albo, Fundamentorum autor, lib. 2. cap. 9. Nihil obstat Deum ejusmodi attributis denominari, quia non sunt res adventitiae Essentiae: Pluralitas enim nominum non designat necessario pluralitatem rerum, sed sunt explicationes conceptuum Essentiae; Removent a Sancto Benedicto omne Attributum Accidentale, negantque illud posse Deo tribui, quod accidens indigeat subjecto, nec semper ad Essentiam requiratur, nunquamque per se subsistat. Statuunt attributa divina non concipienda ut res iplam componentes Essentiam, ut דברים שש, sic enim Deus Benedictus ex rebus esset compositus; Nec Attributa Essentiam multiplicare divinam, sed unitatem formare singularissimam. Demonstrant egregie Attributa Dei esse Essentiae explicationes, imo, quod quamvis in intellectu multa sint ob nostram imperfectionem, re tamen, & substantia, unum idemque esse, nec a se invicem, necab Essentia distincta, sic Rabbi Albo lib. Fundamentorum 2. cap. 21. Itaque dicimus, etsi attributa, quibus Deus Benedictus denominatur, sint in nobis distincta, & separata, debere intelligi in Deo Benedicto per modum unius. uni°. Nos enim quia comprehendimus ea, aut acquirimus ea successive unu post aliud, intelligimus ea ut separata; tu quia acquirimus ea, cuantea non haberemus, concipimus illa ut formas adventitias; Sed in Deo benedicto intelligenda sunt per modum unius, & sine ulla acquisitione, ita ut nullam in substantiam ejus inferant compositionem; Et eodem lib. cap. 25. Ego video omnia illa attributa non esse nisi notiones intellectuales, quibus concipiuntur perfectiones illae esse in Essentia tua, sed verere ipsa nihil sunt praeter Essentiam tuam: hoc est quod dicitur, & adhuc sum tecum: Id est, ea nihil sunt praeter te, neque Essentiam tuam multiplicant; Sic quoque praeclare Maimonides perplexorum Doctor in More Nevochim, l. 1. c. 57. Nam Essentia ipsius non est ita coparata, ut Existentia ipsi accidat; nam ita Existentia foret res adventitia, sed semper & necessario exist it nec quicquam novi unquam in ipso exoritur, neque etiam accidens aliquod ei acciditi. Quare Existit, sed non per Existentiam; Virit, sed non per vitam Scit, sed non per scientiam; Potens est sed non per potentiam; Sapiens est, sed non per sapientiam; verum omnia in ipso sunt unum & idem, nullaque in eo est multitudo.
units.tr: They ascribe attributes, both those already mentioned and those to be listed further on, without distinguishing them from the divine Essence itself, and not considering them as adventitious and external things, but as explanations of the Essence and of the name, as Rabbi Joseph Albo, author of the Fundamentals, book 2, chapter 9, neatly points out: Nothing prevents God from being denominated by such attributes, because they are not adventitious things of the Essence. For a plurality of names does not necessarily designate a plurality of things, but they are explanations of the concepts of the Essence. They remove from the Blessed One every accidental attribute, and deny that anything can be attributed to God which requires a subject as an accident does, which is not always required for the Essence, and which never subsists by itself. They hold that the divine attributes are not to be conceived as things making up the Essence itself, as the so-called "things" [דברים שש], for thus the Blessed God would be composed of things. Nor do the attributes multiply the divine Essence, but form a most singular unity. They demonstrate well that the attributes of God are explanations of the Essence; indeed, although in our understanding there are many because of our imperfection, in reality and substance they are one and the same, and are neither distinct from one another nor from the Essence. Thus Rabbi Albo, Fundamentals, book 2, chapter 21: Therefore we say that, although the attributes by which the Blessed God is denominated are distinct and separate in us, they must be understood in the Blessed God in the manner of one. For we, because we grasp them one after another, or acquire them successively, understand them as separate; and because we acquire them when we did not have them before, we conceive them as adventitious forms. But in the Blessed God they are to be understood in the manner of one, and without any acquisition, so that they introduce no composition into his substance. And in the same book, chapter 25: "I see that all those attributes are nothing but intellectual notions by which those perfections are conceived to be in your Essence, but in truth they are nothing apart from your Essence; this is what is said, and I am still with you: that is, they are nothing apart from you, and do not multiply your Essence." Likewise the excellent Maimonides, teacher of the Perplexed, in the More Nevochim, book 1, chapter 57: "For his Essence is not so constituted that existence happens to it as an accident; for then existence would be an adventitious thing. But he always and necessarily exists, and nothing new ever arises in him, nor does any accident befall him. Therefore he exists, but not through existence; he lives, but not through life; he knows, but not through knowledge; he is powerful, but not through power; he is wise, but not through wisdom; but all these things in him are one and the same, and there is no multiplicity in him."

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Vocant divina Attributa אלהים תוארי Formas Dei, אלהים מדות Proprietates Dei, ספירות Numerationes, vel potius, Luces, aluciditate & splendore, sic Autor Praefationis in librum Scaare Ora: Cabalistae tradiderunt, & ordine disposuerunt nobis Proprietates divinas, vocaruntque eas Sephiroth. roth, à puritate & claritate, ex significatione: Opus lapidis sapphirini, Exod. cap. 24. verf. 10. Statuentes ex Cabbala decem divinas Sephiroth, quæ Sancti Benedicti summæ sint perfectiones & virtutes, quas in mundi tum creatione, tum gubernatione hominibus revelaverit maxime, cum dicant Ens Intelligens, Sapientissimum, Magnificum, Gloriosum, Infinitum, Majestate plenum; Quæq; hac fere semper forma apparent: כתר Corona. בינה Intelligentia. חכמה Sapientia. גבורה Potentia. גדולה Magnificentia. תפארת Gloria. הוד Majestas. נצח Victoria. יסוד Fundamentum. מלכות Regnum.
units.tr: They call the divine attributes [אלהים תוארי] "forms of God," [אלהים מדות] "properties of God," and [ספירות] "numerations," or rather "lights," from their brightness and splendour. So the author of the Preface to the book Scaare Ora says: "The Cabalists handed down and arranged for us the divine properties, and called them Sephiroth [ספירות], from purity and clarity, according to the meaning of 'the work of the sapphire stone,' Exod. ch. 24, v. 10." From the Cabbala they set down ten divine Sephiroth, which are the highest perfections and virtues of the Blessed One, and which he has especially revealed to men both in the creation and in the governance of the world. They call him Intelligent Being, Most Wise, Magnificent, Glorious, Infinite, full of Majesty. These usually appear in this form: Crown [כתר]. Understanding [בינה]. Wisdom [חכמה]. Might [גבורה]. Greatness [גדולה]. Glory [תפארת]. Majesty [הוד]. Victory [נצח]. Foundation [יסוד]. Kingdom [מלכות].

units.la: Notandum quod veteres Hebræi super כתר Coronam posuerint אין סוף non est finis; Et גדולה Magnificentiam expos\uuerint per חסד Bonitatem; promiscueque usurpaverint voces מלכות Regnum, & שכינה Habitatio. Credunt proproinde fere unanimes decem Sephiroth esse divina attributa, perfectionesque, sic Rabbi Moses in Commentariis suis ad cap. 1. libri Jezira: Abraham Pater noster vocavit Sephirot, quasi Saphiros, ad significandum, quemadmodum Saphirus omnes colores recipit, sic Deo omnes formas, benedictiones, emanationesque tribui; Ita tamen, ut haec omnia summam Dei benedicti unitatem praedicent; Sic Rabbi Menachem Rekanat in libro Taame Mitzvot ostendit, quod hae decem Sephiroth sint ipsa Sancti Benedicti Attributa; Extat quoque Caesaris Evoli Neapolitani liber de divinis attributis, quae Hebraei Sephiroth vocant, Venetiis Anno 1573. in 8. Ut adeo mirandum valde sit, Menaslen Ben Israel a Contribulibus abire suis, contrariamque amplecti sententiam, dum in libro de Creatione, Problemate 27. ita scribit: Dicimus illas Sephirot, seu divinas perfectiones, aliud quid esse quam Essentiam Dei; neque etiam dicimus illas esse distinctas creaturas; Sed tantum emanationes quasdam essentiae conjunctas, perinde uti radii solares cum sole, flamma cum prunis ardentibus: Aut uti Plato ait, ultimum lineae punctum cum linea conjunctum est.
units.tr: It should be noted that the ancient Hebrews placed "The Without End" [אין סוף] above Crown, "non est finis," and explained Greatness by Goodness [חסד]. They used the terms Kingdom [מלכות] and Habitation [שכינה] interchangeably. Almost all of them therefore believe that the ten Sephiroth are the divine attributes and perfections. So Rabbi Moses, in his commentary on the first chapter of the book Jezira: Our father Abraham called them Sephirot, as if Sapphires, to signify that as the sapphire receives all colours, so all forms, blessings and emanations are ascribed to God; yet in such a way that all of these proclaim the supreme unity of the Blessed One. Likewise Rabbi Menachem Rekanat, in the book Taame Mitzvot, shows that these ten Sephiroth are the very attributes of the Blessed One. There is also the book by Caesar Evolus of Naples on the divine attributes, which the Hebrews call Sephiroth, published at Venice in 1573, in octavo. So it is truly remarkable that Menasseh Ben Israel departed from his fellow countrymen and embraced the opposite opinion, when in his book On the Creation, Problem 27, he writes: We say that those Sephirot, or divine perfections, are something other than the Essence of God; nor do we say that they are distinct creatures; but only certain emanations joined to the essence, just as the rays of the sun are joined to the sun, or flame to glowing embers: or as Plato says, the last point of a line is joined to the line.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Dividunt divina Attributa in Absoluta, & Relativa; illa interna vocantes, atque ad Deum intrinsece referentes; haec externa concipientes. tes, quæ Dei concernant operationes circa creaturas, uti bene docet Rabbi Joseph Albo in Fundamentis lib.2. cap.24. Alia sunt attributa respectu ipsiusmet, alia respectu operationum ejus. Observant pariter alia Attributa de Deo prædicari ab æterno ante mundi creationem, alia ex tempore nomina mutuari sua; Approbant Attributorum distinctionem in Affirmativa & Negativa, licet non omnes, dum Maimonides inficiatur ullum attributum affirmans Deo posse tribui, & hinc maxime Deo vendicat Attributa negativa, sicuti legimus in More Nevochim Part.1.cap.58. Attributa quae Deo per negationem attribuuntur, sunt attributa vera, utpote in quibus nulla est imminutio, & quae nullam imperfectionem Deo assignant. Verum attributa affirmativa sunt tum communia cum aliis, tum etiam maximopere imperfecta. Urgetque ulterius, quod Deo attributa affirmativa falso attribuantur, cumulatque plurimas rationes, quas discussa cernere licet in Rabbi Iosephi Albo Fundamentis, qui strenue præterea distinctionem hanc tuetur, & utraque Deo tribui debere ostendit l.1.c.30. Ast licet Maimonides in hac Attributorum divisione non consentiat cum aliis, fatetur tamen cum universa hodierna Synagoga, Dei attributa immane quantum à nostris distare, dum sic loquitur in More Nevochim, Part.
units.tr: They divide the divine attributes into Absolute and Relative; calling the former internal, and referring them intrinsically to God; and conceiving the latter as external, which concern God's operations upon creatures, as Rabbi Joseph Albo well teaches in his Fundamentals, book 2, ch. 24: Some attributes are with respect to himself, others with respect to his operations. They likewise observe that some attributes are predicated of God from eternity, before the creation of the world, while others take their names from time. They approve the distinction of attributes into Affirmative and Negative, though not all of them do, since Maimonides denies that any affirmative attribute can be ascribed to God, and for this reason claims for God especially the negative attributes, as we read in the More Nevochim, Part 1, ch. 58: The attributes which are ascribed to God by negation are true attributes, inasmuch as in them there is no diminution, and they assign no imperfection to God. But the affirmative attributes are both common to other things and also very much imperfect. He presses further that affirmative attributes are falsely ascribed to God, and he heaps up very many reasons, which may be seen discussed in Rabbi Joseph Albo's Fundamentals, who also vigorously defends this distinction and shows that both kinds ought to be ascribed to God, book 1, ch. 30. But although Maimonides does not agree with others in this division of the attributes, he nevertheless confesses, together with the whole of today's Synagogue, that the attributes of God differ from ours by an immense degree, as he speaks in the More Nevochim, Part

units.la: Part. 1. cap. 35. Quacunque autem in attributione vel proprietate Deus nobiscum conferatur, toto coelo ipsius proprietates a nostris differre semper observa-bimus, nec utrasque sub una definitione comprehendi posse. Sic Existentia vel Existere dicitur de ipso & de aliis extra ipsum aequivoce.
units.tr: Part 1, ch. 35: Whatever attribute or property God may be compared with us in, we shall always observe that his properties differ from ours by the whole heaven, nor can both be comprehended under one definition. Thus existence, or to exist, is said of him and of other things outside him equivocally.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Omniscientiam Infinita statuunt, nulliscriptam terminis, complectentem suo ambitu tam praesentia, quam praeterita, futuraq;, materialia, immaterialia, libera, necessaria, contingentia, possibilia, absq; discursu, ignorantia, mutatione, errore, oblivione, imaginatione, omnia simul aͤtu unico, infinitoque, ex articulo fidei Judaicae decimo : Fide perfecta credo, Creatorem, cujus nomen sit benedictum, cognoscere omnia opera hominum, & omnes cogitationes eorum, sicut dicitur Psalmo 33. vers. 15. Ipse omnium corda pariter finxit, intelligit omnia opera eorum; Et apud Rabbi Joseph Albo in Fundamentis lib. 2. cap. 25. Quando Deus dicitur sapiens, intelligere oportet Sapientiam illius esse infinitae perfectionis, debet enim cognoscere Essentiam suam, quae est infinite perfecta, eam autem infinite perfectam cognoscere non potest, nisi cognitione infinite perfecta; finitum quippe non potest comprehendere Infinitum; Et apud Maimonidem in Constitutionibus de Fundamentis Legis cap. 2. §. 11, 12. Omnia Existentia, praeter Creatorem... Creatorem, à prima forma usque ad minimum reptile, quod est in umbilico terræ, omnia potentia ejus veritatis existunt. Et quia ipse cognoscit semet ipsum, ac intelligit excellentiam, gloriam atque veritatem suam, ideo cognoscit omnia, & nihil est absconditum ei. Sanctus Benedictus intelligit veritatem suam, [sive Essentiam] atque cognoscit eam, uti reipsa est; neque intelligit notitia distincta à se ipso, uti nos cognoscimus, quia nos & intellectus noster non sunt unum; Sed Creator excelsus, ipse, intellectus atque vita ejus sunt unum omni modo, respectu atque ratione unitatis; Distinguunt quam maxime scientiam divinam ab humana, quod illa infinita sit, hæc finita, imperfectaque, imo ex regula Rabbinica הדעתן שבאנשים צריך עיון, scientissimus hominum indigeat consilio; Quod omnis realitas ex divina fluat scientia, in humana præcedat, sicuti observat Maimonides in More Nevochim Part. III, cap. 21. Magna differentia est inter scientiam ejus, qui rem aliquam facit, & scientiam alterius rei illius factæ. Nam res illa facta, si facta sit convenienter Scientiæ factoris ipsius, est illius opus, ac proinde scientiam ejus sequitur; sed Scientia reliquorum hominum, qui rem factam considerant & scientia definita sciunt, rem factam sequitur; Quod homo omnem moveat lapidem ut investiget, interim tamen rem non comprehendat, sicuti scribit Albo Fundamentorum Autor. ctor lib. 2. cap. 15. Sic docet scientiam Dei diversa esse species a scientia humana: Homo enim investigat, nec comprehendit. Deus vero Benedictus scrutatur corda & renes, cognoscitque, & comprehendit cogitationes: hoc est quod ait Psalm 139. verf. 2. Intellexisti cogitationem meam a longe; Quod sapientia acquiratur ab hominibus per conclusiones elicitas ex principiis, & ita de novo comparetur, proinde Essentiae sit adventitia; In Deo vero sit per se, nec colligatur ex principiis, uti egregie probat Albo lib. 2. cap. 21. Describunt quoque qua ratione Deus cognoscat creaturas, & ita ab his distinguatur, ita Maimonides in Constitutionibus de Fundamentis fidei, cap. 2. §. 15. Idcirco non cognoscit neque intelligit creaturas per creaturas, uti nos apprehendimus eas, sed per semet ipsum: Idcirco quatenus se ipsum intelligit, etiam cognoscit omnia: Cujuslibet enim rei essentia in ipso fundata est.
units.tr: Omniscience they hold to be infinite, not restricted by any limits, embracing within its scope present, past and future things, material and immaterial, free, necessary, contingent, and possible, without discourse, ignorance, change, error, forgetfulness or imagination, all at once, by a single and infinite act. This is from the tenth article of the Jewish faith: "With perfect faith I believe that the Creator, whose name be blessed, knows all the works of men and all their thoughts, as it is said in Psalm 33, verse 15: He who fashioned the hearts of them all alike, understands all their works." And in Rabbi Joseph Albo, Fundamentals, book 2, ch. 25: "When God is called wise, one must understand that his wisdom is of infinite perfection; for he must know his own essence, which is infinitely perfect, yet he cannot know that infinitely perfect essence except by an infinitely perfect knowledge; for the finite cannot comprehend the Infinite." And in Maimonides, in the Constitutions on the Fundamentals of the Law, ch. 2, §§ 11, 12: "All existing things, apart from the Creator... the Creator, from the first form down to the least reptile which is in the navel of the earth, all exist by his power of truth. And because he knows himself, and understands his excellence, glory and truth, therefore he knows all things, and nothing is hidden from him. The Blessed One understands his truth [that is, his Essence], and knows it as it really is; nor does he understand by a knowledge distinct from himself, as we know, because we and our intellect are not one; but the exalted Creator, himself, his intellect and his life are one in every way, with respect to unity and to reason." They distinguish the divine knowledge most sharply from the human, in that the former is infinite and the latter finite and imperfect; indeed, by the Rabbinic rule [הדעתן שבאנשים צריך עיון], "the most learned of men needs counsel." That all reality flows from the divine knowledge and precedes the human, as Maimonides observes in the More Nevochim, Part 3, ch. 21: "There is a great difference between the knowledge of one who makes a thing and the knowledge of another about that thing made. For that made thing, if it is made in agreement with the knowledge of its maker, is his work, and therefore follows his knowledge; but the knowledge of the rest of men, who consider the made thing and know it by defined knowledge, follows the made thing." That man moves every stone in order to investigate, yet still does not comprehend the thing, as the author of the Fundamentals, Albo, writes, book 2, ch. 15. Thus he teaches that God's knowledge is a different kind from human knowledge: "Man investigates, and does not comprehend. But God the Blessed searches the heart and the reins, and knows and comprehends the thoughts; this is what Psalm 139, verse 2 says: Thou understoodest my thought afar off." That wisdom is acquired by men through conclusions drawn from principles, and so is gained anew, and therefore is accidental to the essence; but in God it is through itself, and is not gathered from principles, as Albo excellently proves, book 2, ch. 21. They also describe in what way God knows creatures, and thus distinguish him from them, as Maimonides does in the Constitutions on the Fundamentals of Faith, ch. 2, § 15: "Therefore he does not know or understand creatures through creatures, as we apprehend them, but through himself. Hence, insofar as he understands himself, he also knows all things, for the essence of each thing is founded in him."

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Credunt pariter Omnipotentiam Infinitam, sic Maimonides in Constitutionibus de Fundamentis Legis, cap. 1. §. 2. Istudens est Deus mundi, Dominus totius terrae, gubernans sphaeram potentia, quae caret fine ac termino, & virtute nunquam cessante; Et §. 6. Dei autem nostri, cujus benedictum sit nomen, potentia cum non habeat terminum, neque cesset; Ita quoque Rabbi Joseph Albo in Fun-
units.tr: They likewise believe in an infinite omnipotence. So Maimonides, in the Constitutions on the Foundations of the Law, ch. 1, §. 2: "He is the God of the world, the Lord of the whole earth, who governs the sphere by power, a power that has no end or limit and never ceases." And §. 6: "The power of our God, blessed be his name, has no limit and never ceases." So too Rabbi Joseph Albo in his Fundamentals, [Ikkarim]

units.la: Fundamentis lib. 1. cap. 25. Cum Deus benedictus dicitur potens, oportet simul intelligere potentiam illius infinitam esse, nam si illa finita foret, aliam hac majorem potentiam concipere liceret, atque sic in Deum caderet privatio, quatenus non est in illo major illa potentia, quae concipi potest. Credunt divinam potentiam non limitatam esse ad certum subjectum, locum, tempus, instrumentum; sed absolutam esse, cum jungenda semper sit cum voluntate & Intellectu divino, prout rursus loquitur Albo in Fundamentis lib. 2. cap. 8. Sed quia omne agens perfectum non potest operari quidquam, nisi possit illud operari, & sciat operari, & velit operari: Dicimus Deum velle, posse, & scire. Ita tamen ut illae notiones diversae agentis non inferant illi compositionem. Credunt quod quae contradictionem implicent, quaeque impossibilia sint, potentiae divinae objectum esse non possint, quia pugnant cum ipsa potentiae veritate & efficacia, ita Maimonides in More Nevochim Part. III, cap. 15. Ostensum est juxta quamlibet harum sententiarum, esse res quasdam impossibiles, quarum Exilentia est falsa, & quae a Potentia Dei Optimi maximi [citra tamen naturae ejus imperfectionem, vel Potentiae imminutionem] excipiuntur, cum natura sua falsa sint, nec cadant in operationem agentis. Appellant ipsum Deum a Potentia sua, הבורא, sic in Tractatu Talmudico Schabbath, sol.
units.tr: Book 1, ch. 25: When God is called blessed and powerful, we must at the same time understand that his power is infinite. For if it were finite, it would be possible to conceive of a greater power than this, and thus a privation would fall upon God, inasmuch as there is in him no greater power than can be conceived. They believe that the divine power is not restricted to a certain subject, place, time or instrument, but is absolute, since it must always be joined with the divine will and intellect. Albo speaks to the same effect again in the Fundamentals, book 2, ch. 8: But because every perfect agent cannot do anything unless it is able to do it, and knows how to do it, and wills to do it, we say that God wills, is able, and knows. Yet these different notions of the agent do not imply composition in him. They believe that things which involve a contradiction, and which are impossible, cannot be the object of the divine power, because they are at odds with the very truth and efficacy of power. So Maimonides in the More Nevochim, part 3, ch. 15: It has been shown, according to any of these opinions, that there are certain impossible things whose existence is false, and which are excluded from the power of the best and greatest God [yet without any imperfection in his nature or diminution of his power], since by their own nature they are false and do not fall under the operation of an agent. They call God himself by his Power, [הבורא, the Creator], as in the Talmudic tractate Shabbath, fol.

units.la: 87, מרה השיב משה לפני הגבורה, Quid respondit Moses coram potentia, id est, Deo; Et Rabbi Lipman Mulhufinus in Nizzachon Hannozerim, pag. 36. משה קבל מאת הגבורה התורה, accepit Moses Legem a Potentia, id est, a Deo.
units.tr: 87: מה השיב משה לפני הגבורה, What did Moses answer before the Power, that is, before God. And Rabbi Lipman Mulhufinus in the Nizzachon Hannozerim, p. 36: משה קבל מאת הגבורה התורה, Moses received the Law from the Power, that is, from God.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: De Omniprasentia, seu Immensitate divina masculè loquuntur, Deum nominantes מקום Locum, quod omnem implear locum, nec ullus concipi possit locus, cui non sit intime praesens, ita Rabbi Aben Esra in Praefatione Commentarii super librum Estheris: Majores nostri ipsa memoria cum מקום vocarunt, quia omnis locus plenus est gloria ejus; Et Rabbi David Kimchius ad Psalmum 139. verf. 7. Si dicerem illud me facturum, non possum, tute enim in omni loco deprehenderis, locus vero te minime capit; Non quod proprie in loco sit, cum non sit corpus, sicuti ex re demonstrat Rabbi Iosephi Albo in Fundamentis, lib. 2. cap. 17. Nomen loci tribuitur rei, quae ambit corpora, eaque terminat. Quod vero non est corpus, non dicitur esse in loco; nec enim tribuitur nomen loci, nisi rei, quae impletur corpore aliquo dimensionem habente, quod in ea conquiescat, & quod ea ambiat; ideoque neque de Deo, neque de Intelligentiis separatis dici potest, eas esse in loco; quia non sunt corpus quantum, quod ambiat locus. Hoc docet Scriptura 1. Reg. cap. 8. verf. 27. Ecce cæli & cæli cælorum tum te non capiunt; id est, non indiges loco, in quo consistas; Probant multis Deum rebus omnibus praesentem, non per contactum quantitatis dimensivae, sicut corpora, sed per Influxum, contactumque virtutis, nec solum aliquo tempore, sed semper, cum virtus ipsius sit perpetua, uti optime docet Perplexorum Magister, de quo affirmare saepe possumus, quod ineptire inter suos desierit, quando scribit Part. I. cap. 69. Per Existentiam Dei creatoris omnia existunt, et ipse continuat, et conservat statum ipsorum per rem quandam quae vocatur influentia, sicut in aliquot huius libri capitibus explicabimus. Etsi fieri posset ut creator non existeret, vel interiret, perirent quoque omnia, et interiret quidditas causarum ab ipso remotarum, et effectorum ultimorum, ac quicquid inter haec medium est. Quae cum ita sint, sicut per formam res est id quod est, et per eandem veritas, et quiddidas illius subsistit; Sic Deus se habet ad hunc mundum, et eatenus dicitur esse forma ultima, et forma formarum, quatenus existentia omnis forma mundana, ejusque conservatio ultimo innititur Deo, et in ipsa subsistit, quemadmodum res formam habentes in formis suis subsistunt; Confirmatque Maimonidis Scholiastes ad caput 1. libri de Fundamentis Legis: Deus benedictus est Creator rerum omnium, qui conservat per Influxum, quem illis perpetuo communicat: ideo omnia ipso indigent, ipse vero non indiget illis.
units.tr: Those who write about the omnipresence, or immensity, of God speak in the masculine, calling God מקום [makom, "place"], Place, because he fills every place, and no place can be conceived to which he is not intimately present. So Rabbi Aben Ezra, in the preface to his commentary on the book of Esther: Our forefathers themselves called him by the name מקום [place], because every place is full of his glory. Rabbi David Kimchi, on Psalm 139:7: If I were to say that I would do this, I could not, for you are found in every place, yet place does not contain you at all. Yet he is not in a place in the proper sense, since he is not a body. Rabbi Joseph Albo demonstrates this from the nature of the thing, in the Fundamentals, book 2, chapter 17: The name of place is given to that thing which surrounds bodies and bounds them. What is not a body is not said to be in a place. For the name of place is given only to that which is filled by some body having dimension, so that the body may rest in it and be surrounded by it. Therefore it cannot be said of God, or of the separate Intelligences, that they are in a place, since they are not a body of quantity which a place could surround. Scripture teaches this in 1 Kings 8:27: Behold, the heavens and the heavens of heaven cannot contain you; that is, you have no need of a place in which to stand. Many prove that God is present to all things not by contact of dimensive quantity, as bodies are, but by influx and contact of power, and not only at some time but always, since his power is perpetual. The Teacher of the Perplexed teaches this admirably, and of him we may often affirm that he ceased to be foolish among his own people when he wrote in Part 1, chapter 69: Through the existence of God the Creator all things exist, and he himself continues and preserves their state through a certain thing which is called influence, as we shall explain in several chapters of this book. Even if it could happen that the Creator did not exist, or perished, all things would also perish, and the quiddity of the causes removed from him, and of the ultimate effects, and whatever lies between these, would perish. Since these things are so, just as a thing is what it is through its form, and through the same its truth and quiddity subsist, so God stands in relation to this world, and to that extent he is called the ultimate form and the form of forms, inasmuch as the existence of every worldly form and its preservation ultimately rest upon God and subsist in him, just as things having forms subsist in their forms. The commentator on Maimonides confirms this on chapter 1 of the book of the Fundamentals of the Law: Blessed God is the Creator of all things, who preserves them by the influx which he perpetually communicates to them; therefore all things depend on him, but he does not depend on them.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Ex infinitis Dei Perfectionibus, tandem summam ejus colligunt gloriam, quam non adventitiam, sed essentialem ac æternam, absque ulla variatione ac mutatione concipiunt, & à gloria maximorum Regum distinguunt, sicuti probat Judæus, Autor Libri de Fundamentis, lib. 2. cap. 14. Deus perficit omne ens, nulla vero perfectio illi advenit extrinsecus, secus atque Regibus, quorum perfectio extrinsecus accedit: Regum enim imperium non eminet, nisi secundum gloriam & honorem, qui illis extrinsecus exhibetur: quippe sine honore ejusmodi & gloria non dignosceretur rex esse, nec aliis præstaret. Quam ob rem sic sunt quasi illius gloria dominetur. Sed quod attinet ad Deum benedictum, non itares est. Deus enim gloriæ dominatur. Hinc Psalmo 24. verf. 7. vocatur Rex Gloriæ. Dignitas namque Regis à numero subditorum penaet, ut major illi accedat gloria. Deus vero quia est Rex gloriæ, Regnum ejus ab extrinseco se novit erigit, neque mutatione aut destructione subditorum mutationem recipit.
units.tr: From the infinite perfections of God they finally gather his supreme glory, which they conceive not as something adventitious but as essential and eternal, admitting no variation or change, and they distinguish it from the glory of the greatest kings. So the Jewish author of the book De Fundamentis shows, book 2, chapter 14: God perfects every being, and no perfection comes to him from outside, unlike kings, whose perfection accrues to them from outside. For the rule of kings stands out only according to the glory and honour shown to them from outside. Indeed, without such honour and glory, a king would not be recognised as king, nor would he be of any advantage to others. For this reason, kings are, as it were, governed by their glory. But it is not so with the blessed God, for God governs glory. Hence in Psalm 24:7 he is called the King of Glory. The dignity of a king depends on the number of his subjects, so that greater glory may accrue to him. But God, because he is the King of Glory, does not raise his kingdom from anything external, and it undergoes no change through any alteration or destruction of its subjects.
