Et praco praecedebat ante ipsum 40 diebus clamans: illum lapidandum esse, quod fascinarit, seduxerit & ad lapsum impulerit Israelitas; quisquis vero nosset aliquid pro ipsius innocentia allegare, ut is prodeat atque edoceat. Sed non repererunt quicquam pro ipsius innocentia, quare suspenderunt ipsum vespera Paschatis. Dixit Ula: An cogitandum filium perversum hunc insontem fore, cum seductor fuerit? Sic Aben Esra in Commentario in Genes. cap. 27, vers. 39: memorat, quod Constantinus Magnus in vexillo suo poluerit תלי Figuram Suspensi, Christi crucifixi lignum; sic Rabbi Bechai in Kad Hakkemach in litera ג cap. 1. ad Psalmum 80, verf. 14, refert, quod litera Ain, ex voce עיין, suspensa sit, quia tales sunt cultores suspensi illius, lu-
units.tr: The Jews commonly call Jesus by the blasphemy Jeshu-Jpensum, as one who was a blasphemer and seducer of the people, hanged on the cross for shameful deeds and crimes. For so we read in the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin, chap. 6, fol. 43: On the evening of the Passover they hanged Jesus. And a herald went before him for forty days, crying that he was to be stoned, because he had bewitched, seduced and led Israel into apostasy. Whoever knew anything to allege in his defence, let him come forward and declare it. But they found nothing in his defence, so they hanged him on the evening of the Passover. Ula said: Is it to be thought that this perverse son was innocent, when he was a seducer? So Aben Ezra, in his commentary on Genesis chap. 27, verse 39, records that Constantine the Great had on his standard the Figure of the Hanged [תלי], the wood of the crucified Christ. So Rabbi Bechai, in Kad Hakkemach under the letter Gimel, chap. 1, on Psalm 80, verse 14, reports that the letter Ain, from the word [עיין], is suspended because such are the worshippers of that hanged one, to be scorned likewise.

units.la: ipendendi pariter; Hinc inscriptio virulenti Manuscripti תלוי תולדות Historia suspensi; Et apud Lipmannum in Carmine Memoriali: Num suspensus aliquis sepultus, inque cadaver mutatum rem ullam liberare possit? Hinc Mariam matrem quoque appellant תלוייה suspensam; Et Christianos, qui Christum venerantur & colunt עובדי תלוי Cultores Suspensi. Tandem animo eruciant Diabolico Jesum Nazarenum torqueri in inferno in fervente excremento, sic me dubitantem, num in Tractatu Talmudico Gittin, sol. 56, 57. de Jesu nostro haec horrenda praedicentur blasphemia, informavit nuper Rabbi Sanvel, qui coram facie Dei vivi confessus mihi est, non solum hanc Judaeorum esse mentem, quam callide ob poenae metum tegant, verum etiam quod Mardochai Japhe, ultimus Judaeorum falsus Mellias, de quo nos brevi pluribus secunda editione Historiae nostrae de Pseudo-Messiis Judaeorum, cum esset Baal Schemot, evocaverit ex inferis Jesum nostrum, qui excremento cruciabatur fervente. Quis nunc crederet deret proinde, quod Orobius Judæus, qui eru-ditam, amicamque collationem Amstelodami instituit cum Philippo à Limborch, Arminianorum Doctore primario, veritatem ex corde fuerit prolocutus, quando Doctissimo viro alicui testatus est, quod Jesus Nazarenus vir probus fuerit, quodque innocens mortem crucis passus fuerit, quodque Paulus, qui Legem mutaret, causa fuerit, quare Judæi ipsum Jesum non fuerint secuti. Sed de his satis superque, cum manifesta nimis sint Tela hæc ignea Satanæ, quæ primus, exemplo in omnem memorando posteritatem, non solum evulgavit in Christianorum usum, sed maximo judicio, summaque eruditione simul confregit Optimus Wagenseilius noster, quo Fautore utimur egregio, quando in colligato fasciculo quosq; Scriptores virulentos Judæos, qui id operam unice dederunt, ut Christianæ Religioni dicerent calumniam, in lucem protraxit publicam, quorum hæc sequens est nomenclatio: Rabbi Lipmanni Carmen Memoriale; Autoris incogniti Liber Nizzachon Vetus; Rabbi Iechielis Acta disputationis cum quodam Nicolao; Rabbi Mosis Nachmanidis Acta disputationis cum Fratre Paulo Christiani, & Fatre Raymundo Martini; Rabbi Isaaci Bar Abraham Chiffuk Emuna; Et libellus Toledot Ieschu. Sic paripariter manibus teritur eruditorum Rabbi Lipmanni Nizzachon Hannozerim, quod evulgavit Hackspanius; Sic quoque in propatulo sunt quae ex Rabbi Kimchio, Abarbanele, ex Tractatibus que Talmudicis congesserunt passim Finus Hadrianus, Munsterus, Buxtorfius, Mullerus, Vorstius, & si qui plures. Non negamus interim multos in angulis Bibliothecarum latitare, qui manus expectant obstetricantes; Sic Nathanaelis Eliae scriptum Germanicum de Christo, eiusque regno, contra Christianos, quod Brenius latinitate donavit, notisque, seu animadversionibus illustravit, in Bibliotheca Roterodamensi aliqua abscônditum vidimus & legimus; Sic clam asservatur a Iudaeis Amstelodamensibus Propugnaculum Iudaismi, quod contra Hugonem Grotium de Veritate Religionis Christianae conscripsit Iudaeus Lumbrozo, qui in Dalmatia artem exercuit medicam, de quo Limborchius in Amica Collatione cum Orobio Iudaeo pag. 19. Ne quid nunc de nostro referam Manuscripto, quod הישׁ מגן Historia Suspensi inscribitur.
units.tr: Hence the title of the virulent manuscript [תלוי תולדות] History of the Hanged; and in Lipmann's Memorial Poem: Whether a hanged man, once buried, can deliver anything, even into a changed corpse? Hence they also call Mary the mother [תלוייה] "the hanged woman"; and Christians who venerate and worship Christ, [עובדי תלוי] Worshippers of the Hanged. Finally, with diabolical rage, they imagine that Jesus of Nazareth is tormented in hell in boiling excrement. When I doubted whether such horrid blasphemies about our Jesus are foretold in the Talmudic tractate Gittin, fol. 56, 57, Rabbi Samuel informed me recently. He confessed to me, in the sight of the living God, that this is not only the opinion of the Jews, which they craftily conceal for fear of punishment, but also that Mordecai Japhe, the last false Messiah of the Jews (about whom we shall speak more fully in the second edition of our History of the Pseudo-Messiahs of the Jews), when he was Baal Schemot, called up from the dead our Jesus, who was being tortured in boiling excrement. Who, then, would believe that Orobio the Jew, who held a learned and friendly conference at Amsterdam with Philip van Limborch, the chief doctor of the Arminians, spoke sincerely from his heart when he testified to a most learned man that Jesus of Nazareth was an upright man, that he suffered death on the cross innocently, and that Paul, who altered the Law, was the reason why the Jews did not follow Jesus? But enough, and more than enough, about these things, since these fiery darts of Satan are all too manifest. Our excellent Wagenseil, whose work we use with great benefit, first not only published these for the use of Christians, to be remembered as an example by all posterity, but also with the greatest judgement and highest learning at the same time broke them. In a bound bundle he brought to public light the virulent Jewish writers who devoted their whole effort to uttering calumny against the Christian religion. The list of these is as follows: Rabbi Lipmann's Memorial Poem; the Old Nizzachon of an unknown author; Rabbi Jechiel's Acts of a disputation with a certain Nicholas; Rabbi Moses Nachmanides' Acts of a disputation with Brother Paul of the Christians and Brother Raymund Martini; Rabbi Isaac Bar Abraham's Chiffuk Emuna; and the little book Toledot Jeschu. Likewise the learned Rabbi Lipmann's Nizzachon Hannozerim, which Hackspan published, is worn by hands in common use; so too are the things gathered from Rabbi Kimchi and Abarbanel, and from the Talmudic tractates, scattered everywhere by Finus Hadrianus, Münster, Buxtorf, Müller, Vorstius and several others. We do not deny that many works lie hidden in the corners of libraries, awaiting hands to bring them to birth. Thus Nathanael Elias's German writing about Christ and his kingdom, against the Christians, which Breen turned into Latin and illustrated with notes or comments, we have seen and read as hidden away in the Rotterdam library. Thus the Jews of Amsterdam keep secretly the Bulwark of Judaism, which the Jew Lumbroso, who practised medicine in Dalmatia, wrote against Hugo Grotius's On the Truth of the Christian Religion, of which Limborch speaks in his Friendly Conference with the Jew Orobio, p. 19. Not to mention now our own manuscript, which is entitled [הישׁ מגן] History of the Hanged.

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Inficiantur Spiritum Sanctum tertiam divinitatis formare personam, non Deum ipsum, sed Dei donum, virtutem Dei, operationemque divinam esse, proinde non negant Spiritum San-
units.tr: They deny that the Holy Spirit forms a third person of the Godhead. He is, they say, not God himself but a gift of God, the power of God and a divine operation; accordingly they do not deny the Holy Spirit

units.la: Sanctum, quippe multis disceptant de ruach hakodesh Spiritu Sanctitatis, ruach hakodesh Spiritu Sancto, ruach hannevuah Spiritu Prophetiæ, sed divinam esse Personam, quæ cum Creatore cœli Ter Optimo maximo eandem unamque habet infinitatem perfectissimamque Essentiam, neutiquam concedunt, hinc omnia quæ in sacris Pandectis dicuntur de Spiritu Dei, de Spiritu Sancto, de Spiritu Messiæ, mira, stultaque subtilitate detorquent alio, per Spiritum Dei elohim ruach incubantem aquis in primo omnium rerum principio, Genes. c. 1. v. 2. non intelligentes tertiam divinitatis Personam aquas infinita sua virtute foventem & fœcundantem, ast exponentes vel per aerem, uti Maimonides in More Nevochim Part. I. cap. 40. Vel per ventum, vel per vehementissimum ventum, quem nomine Dei describi putant, cujus operâ materiam Deus ventilaret, exsiccaretque ne putresceret. Quam ad rem citant locum e Psal. 147, v. 18. Flabit yiznu Spiritus ejus, & fluent aquæ. Nec tertiam Personam intelligentes per Spiritum Dei, qui cum homine in seculum contendere non debeat, Gen. 6. v. 3. Et per Spiritum, qui super Mosen residebat, & septuaginta senioribus communicatus erat, Num. 11. v. 25. Non negant tantum Spiritum Sanctum Deum esse, sed quandoque blasphemiam in Spiritum SanSanctum eructant, vocantes Spiritum Sanctum רוח הטומאה Spiritum immundum, sic ore maledico pronunciat Judæus Anonymus Veteris Nizzachon Autor pag.12. ad locum Gen.18.v.2, Ecce tres viros stantes coram eo. Haeretici dicunt: Vidit tres & unum adoravit, iique sunt Pater, Filius, Spiritus Immundus, quem ipsi Sanctum vocant, tres illos unius forma vidit, & eum adoravit; Et pag.14. si autem omnino secundum errorem ipsorum, Pater, Filius, & Spiritus Impurus, qui Sanctus ipsis est, id fuere, quare cibum illis apponit? Itane Deum invenire est, qui comedit & bibit?
units.tr: Spirit. Indeed they dispute much about ruach hakodesh Spirit of Holiness, ruach hakodesh Holy Spirit, ruach hannevuah Spirit of Prophecy, but they utterly refuse to concede that he is a divine Person who has the same and one infinity and most perfect essence as the Creator of heaven and earth, the thrice good and greatest. Hence they twist everything said in the sacred Pandects about the Spirit of God, the Holy Spirit and the Spirit of the Messiah elsewhere, with a strange and foolish subtlety. Thus the Spirit of God elohim ruach brooding over the waters at the very beginning of all things (Gen. 1:2) they do not understand as the third Person of the Godhead cherishing and fertilising the waters with his infinite power, but explain it either as the air, as Maimonides does in More Nevochim, Part I, ch. 40, or as the wind, or as a most vehement wind, which they think is described by the name of God, and by whose work God ventilated and dried the matter lest it rot. To support this they cite Ps. 147:18: He shall blow his wind yiznu and the waters shall flow. Nor do they understand the third Person by the Spirit of God who ought not to strive with man forever (Gen. 6:3), or by the Spirit who rested upon Moses and was communicated to the seventy elders (Num. 11:25). They not only deny that the Holy Spirit is God, but sometimes they belch out blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, calling him the unclean spirit ruach hattumah. So the anonymous Jewish author of the old Nizzachon pronounces with a cursing mouth, p. 12, on the text Gen. 18:2, Behold, three men standing before him: The heretics say: he saw three and adored one, and these are the Father, the Son and the unclean Spirit, whom they call Holy; he saw those three in the form of one and adored him. And p. 14: But if indeed, according to their error, the Father, the Son and the impure Spirit, who is holy to them, were those, why does he set food before them? Is it thus to find God, who eats and drinks?

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: Exilia valde sunt quæ seculi nostri Judæi de Spiritu Sancto comminiscuntur, non celebrantes amplius cum Majoribus melioribus Spiritum Mesiæ, qui super fideles debuerit quiescere, non duos Spiritus ex Spiritu, non tria primordialia capita, non Spiritus Sancti Majestatem, Inhabitationem, non intelligentes per שכינה Schechinah Spiritum Sanctum, nec per Spiritum Sanctum ulterius innuentes ipsam divinitatem, aut ipsum Dei nomen, sed justo Dei judicio caeci facti, ipsoque Spiritu sancto Rectore destituti, qui illos unice in omnem potest ducere veritatem, mox hoc, mox illud indigitant, perque Spiritum Sanctum rem a divinitate & Essentia distinctam, velad summum diversa & magnifica dona interpretantur, quæ Deus homini in supremo perfectionis gradu elargitur, ita Abarbanel in Vaticinio Joelis per Spiritum Sanctum qui effundi debebat super omnem carnem, intelligit tum singulare aliquod donum, divinæ nimirum cognitionis & scientiæ gentibus promissum, tum Prophetiæ donum quod solis Judæorum filiis & filiabus promissum; Sic Rabbi Maimonides in More Nevochim per Spiritum Dei indigitat duos priores Prophetiæ gradus, de quibus Part. II. cap. 45. cum quis agitatur, moveturque vel ad insigne & nobile quoddam factum, & quidem non ad quodvis, verum in specie ad oppressos, sive unum, sive totum cœtum juvandos; Vel ad loquendum, scribendumq;, uti ex iis quæ sequuntur, patet: Primus gradus Prophetiæ est, cum quis auxilio divino ita instructus est & præditus, ut eo moveatur & animetur, ad magnum & heroicum aliquod facinus perpetrandum, ut, verbi gratia, ad Ecclesiam totam, vel insignem aliquem hominem à vi & tyrannide improborum liberandum; vel ad multis hominibus benefaciendum, illumque motum inse sentit & animadvertit. Hoc donum vocatur Spiritus Domini: & de homine virtute illa præadito dicitur 1. Sam. 10. 6. quod in illum irruerit Spiritus Domini; vel Iudicum cap. 6. v. 34. Induerit eum Spiritus Domini: aut Esc. 11. vers. 2. Quiescat super ipsum Spiritus Domini: Aut, Fuit cum ipso Dominus: & similia alia. Et hic est gradus luIudicum Israelis omnium, de quibus in genere dicitur, Iudicum c.2.v.18. Cum autem sufcitasset Dominus eis Iudices, erat Dominus cum Iudice, & servabat eos. Est hic gradus etiam praestantissimorum Consiliariorum Israelis omnium, sicut id specialiter in Regibus & Iudicibus quibusdam declaratur: ut Iudicum c.11.v.29. Et fuit super Iephtachum Spiritus Domini. Sic de Samsone Iudicum c.14.v.19. Et irruit in eum Spiritus Domini. De Saule 1.Sam.11.v.6. Et irruit Spiritus Dei in Saulem, cum audiret verba. Ita de Amasa, cum incitasset eum Spiritus Sanctus ad suppetias Davidi ferendas 1.Chron.12.v.18. Et Spiritus induit Amasam, &c. Hac virtute quoque praeditus fuit Moses inde ab eo tempore, quo virilem aetatem assecutus est. Ideoque illius vi impulsus fuit, ut Aegyptium interficeret, & duorum illorum litigantium alterum, injustam causam habentem, reprimeret. Haec virtus adeo fortis & robusta fuit in ipso, ut eo quoque tempore, cum timeret, & fuga sibi consuleret, atque ut peregrinus & exul in terra Midiam habiret, tamen iniquitatem aliquam committi videns, ab ea vindicanda & amovenda temperare sibi non potuerit, eamque ferre nequiverit, sicut dicitur Exod.2.v.17. Tum surrexit Moses, & servavit eas. Haec virtus exseruit se in Davide, postea quam oleo unctionis unctus fuit, sicut Scriptura de ipso ait 1.Sam.16. verf.13. Et spiritus Domini irruit in Davidem a die illa & deinceps. Propterea praevalebat urso & leoni, & & tandem etiam Philistæo. Veruntamen horum nullum induxit virtus ista ad aliquid loquendum vel dicendum. Et paulo post pergit Maimonides: secundus gradus est, cum homo in se sentit rem vel facultatem quampiam exoriri & super se quiescere, quæ eum impellit ad loquendum, ita ut loquatur velde scientiis & artibus, vel Psalmos & hymnos, vel utilia ac salutaria recte vivendi præcepta, vel res politicas & civiles, vel denique divinas; & quidem inter vigilandum, & in vigore sensuum ordinario. Et hic est, de quo dicitur, quod loquatur per spiritum sanctum. Hac specie spiritus sancti instinctus, Psalmos suos scripsit David; Proverbia, Ecclesiasten & Canticum Canticorum Salomon. Hoc afflatu scripti sunt Danielis, Iobi, & Chronicorum libri, & reliqua Hagiographa, unde etiam Kethubbim hoc est Hagiographa appellantur, quia Kethubbim, hoc est, scripta sunt per spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: The fictions which the Jews of our age devise about the Holy Spirit are very absurd. They no longer celebrate, together with their better ancestors, the Spirit of the Messiah who ought to rest upon the faithful. They do not recognise two Spirits proceeding from the Spirit, nor three first principles, nor the majesty and indwelling of the Holy Spirit. They do not understand by Schechinah the Holy Spirit, nor by the Holy Spirit do they further mean the divinity itself or the very name of God. But, made blind by the just judgment of God and deprived of the Holy Spirit as their guide, who alone can lead them into all truth, they point now at this and now at that. By the Holy Spirit they interpret something distinct from the divinity and essence, or at most various and splendid gifts which God bestows on man at the highest degree of perfection. Thus Abarbanel, in his commentary on Joel, understands by the Spirit who was to be poured out upon all flesh both some singular gift, namely of divine knowledge and learning promised to the nations, and the gift of prophecy promised to the sons and daughters of the Jews alone. So Rabbi Maimonides in More Nevochim indicates by the Spirit of God the two earlier degrees of prophecy, of which he speaks in Part II, ch. 45, when a man is moved and stirred either to some notable and noble deed, and indeed not to any deed but specifically to help the oppressed, whether one person or the whole community, or to speaking and writing, as appears from what follows: The first degree of prophecy is when someone is so instructed and endowed by divine help that he is moved and animated by it to perform some great and heroic deed, for example to free the whole Church or some notable man from the violence and tyranny of the wicked, or to do good to many people; and he feels and perceives that movement in himself. This gift is called Spirit of the Lord, and of a man endowed with that power it is said 1 Sam. 10:6, that the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him; or Judges 6:34, the Spirit of the Lord clothed him; or Isa. 11:2, let the Spirit of the Lord rest upon him; or The Lord was with him; and other similar things. This is the degree of all the judges of Israel, of whom it is said in general (Judges 2:18): When the Lord raised up judges for them, the Lord was with the judge and saved them. It is also the degree of all the most excellent counsellors of Israel, as is declared specially of certain kings and judges: as Judges 11:29, And the Spirit of the Lord was upon Jephthah. So of Samson, Judges 14:19, And the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him. Of Saul, 1 Sam. 11:6, And the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard the words. So of Amasai, whom the Holy Spirit had stirred to bring help to David, 1 Chron. 12:18, And the Spirit clothed Amasai, etc. Moses too was endowed with this power from the time he reached manhood; therefore he was impelled by its force to kill the Egyptian and to restrain the one of those two quarrelling men who had an unjust cause. This power was so strong and robust in him that even at the time when he feared and sought safety in flight, and dwelt as a stranger and exile in the land of Midian, yet seeing some iniquity being committed, he could not restrain himself from avenging and removing it, and could not bear it, as is said Exod. 2:17: Then Moses arose and saved them. This power displayed itself in David after he was anointed with the oil of unction, as Scripture says of him, 1 Sam. 16:13: And the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon David from that day onward. Therefore he prevailed over the bear and the lion, and at last also over the Philistine. Yet this power moved none of these men to say or speak anything. And a little later Maimonides goes on: The second degree is when a man perceives within himself some thing or faculty arising and resting upon him, which impels him to speak, so that he speaks either about the sciences and arts, or Psalms and hymns, or useful and salutary precepts for right living, or political and civil matters, or finally divine things; and indeed while awake and in the ordinary vigour of the senses. This is the one of whom it is said that he speaks through the Holy Spirit. By this kind of impulse of the Holy Spirit David wrote his Psalms, and Solomon the Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs. By this inspiration were written Daniel, Job, the books of Chronicles and the rest of the Hagiographa; whence also the Kethubbim, that is the Hagiographa, are so called, because the Kethubbim, that is, they are written by the Holy Spirit.

units.la: CAPUT V. De Decreto Divino, Electione & Reprobatione.
units.tr: CAPUT V. On the Divine Decree, Election and Reprobation.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Opera Essentiae divinae vocant Decreta, דברי Decreta Divina, quod Deus Benedictus definiverit, expresseque statuerit de omnibus rebus, ordine suo tempore eventuris, אורים Luces, quod decretorum suorum semper lucidam, vivamque teneat memoriam, ita quoque מחשבה Intentio apud Kimchium in Psal. 104. v. 4. Placet tamen maxime vox Praescientia, qua passim usus nuperus Amstelodamensis Synagogae Moderator, Menasseh Ben Israel, in libello de Termino vitæ, pag. 223, 226, 227, 231, 233. Et Eruditus Judæus Orobius in Amica collatione cum Limborchio de veritate Religionis Christianæ, pag. 83. Ne de Rabbi Saadiah Hagaon, Maimonide, Isaaco Sangari in libro Cofri, aliisque Antiquioribus referam, qui frequenquenter hac utuntur voce; Sic contra negantem Praescientiam divinam disputat Menasseh Ben Israel, respondetque ad contraria argumenta, tum in citato libello, tum in Concilia-tore suo super Genesin, ubi abunde ad loca Scripturae.
units.tr: The works of the divine essence they call decrees [דברי, dibrei], that is, divine decrees: what the blessed God has determined and expressly ordained concerning all things that will come to pass in their proper time. They call them lights [אורים, urim], because He always keeps a bright and living memory of His decrees. Likewise they call them intention [מחשבה, machshavah], as Kimchi does on Psalm 104:4. Yet the word foreknowledge is the most favoured, and it is used everywhere by Menasseh Ben Israel, the recent head of the Amsterdam synagogue, in his little book on the term of life, pages 223, 226, 227, 231 and 233. So too does the learned Jew Orobio, in his friendly conference with Limborch on the truth of the Christian religion, page 83. I say nothing of Rabbi Saadiah Hagaon, Maimonides, Isaac Sangari in the book Cosri, and other older writers, who frequently use this word. Menasseh Ben Israel likewise disputes against those who deny divine foreknowledge, and answers the opposing arguments, both in the book already cited and in his Conciliator on Genesis, where he appeals abundantly to passages of Scripture.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Statuunt omnium rerum Praescientiam, quae minima quaeque ambitu quoque completur suo, hinc Infinitam, nullis limitatam terminis, absque ulla exceptione, sic Orobius in Amica cum Limborchio Collatione, pag. 83. Quicquid subtiliter latrent Sociniani contra Dei Infinitam Praescientiam; Et Menasseh Ben Israel in Termino Vitae, pag. 126. Quare proxime ad veritatem accedere mihi videtur, quod R. Isaac Bar Sefat in libris suis Consultationum statuere legimus: Deus, inquit, ab aeterno dispositit totius mundi negotia, & divina sua sapientia, ac perspicacia vidit omnes effectus, qui in tempore futuri essent; Sic in Tractatu Talmudico Cholin sol. 7. col. 2. narratur a Rabbinis, quomodo ne digitus laedi possit humanus sine Decreto divino: Non laedit homo digitum suum infra in terra, nisi id decretum sit super eo supra in caelo, ex Psalmo 37. A Domino stabiliuntur gressus ejus; Hinc celebre quoque Zoharis legimus effatum, quod tale est: Non venit res nulla in mundum, quam non promulgent caelitus, icuseu quae non à Deo in coelo decernatur; Sic quoque Maimonides in More Nevochim, Part.III.cap.21. Sed res omnes sequuntur ipsius scientiam praecedentem, quae eas, prout sunt, ordinat & disponit, sive sint Existentia abstracta, sive Existentia singularia materiata firma, sive Existentia materialia, quorum individua mutantur secundum ordinem, qui nec corrumpitur, nec mutatur, ideoque penes ipsum nulla est scientia vel multiplicatio, vel innovatio, vel mutatio, dum enim substantia sua immutabilis veritatem novit, novit simul omnia sua, quae inde sequuntur, opera. Pari modo demonstrat Rabbi Isac Sangarus in libro Cosri Part.5. §.20. quod omnia quaecunque fiunt ad causam suam primam duobus modis debeant referri, sicque ex decreto oriantur divino, cum ita scribit: Dico ergo, omnia scibilia, vel omnia causata referuntur ad causam primam duobus modis, vel secundum Intentionem primam, vel per concatenationem & dependentiam.
units.tr: They hold that God has foreknowledge of all things, down to the smallest details, and that this foreknowledge is therefore infinite, bounded by no limits, and without any exception. So Orobio, in his friendly conference with Limborch, page 83: Whatever the Socinians snarl subtly against God's infinite foreknowledge. And Menasseh Ben Israel, in On the Term of Life, page 126: It seems to me that the nearest approach to the truth is what we read Rabbi Isaac Bar Sefat stated in his books of Consultations: God, he says, from eternity arranged the affairs of the whole world, and by His divine wisdom and penetration He saw all the effects that were to be in time. So too the Talmudic tractate Chullin, folio 7, column 2, relates from the rabbis how a man cannot even hurt his finger without a divine decree: A man does not injure his finger below on earth, unless it has been decreed about it above in heaven, citing Psalm 37: The steps of a man are established by the LORD. Hence we also read the well-known saying of the Zohar, which runs thus: No thing comes into the world which is not proclaimed from heaven, that is, which is not decreed by God in heaven. Maimonides likewise, in the More Nevochim, part 3, chapter 21: But all things follow His prior knowledge, which orders and disposes them as they are, whether they be abstract existences, or firm material singular existences, or material existences whose individuals change according to an order that is neither corrupted nor changed. Therefore in Him there is no knowledge that is multiplied, renewed or changed; for while His unchangeable substance knows the truth, it knows at the same time all its works that follow from it. In the same way Rabbi Isaac Sangari demonstrates in the Cosri, part 5, §20, that all things that come to be must be referred to their first cause in two ways, and so arise from the divine decree. He writes thus: I say, then, that all knowable things, or all caused things, are referred to the first cause in two ways: either according to the primary intention, or through concatenation and dependence.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Extendunt Divinam Praescientiam ad ipsas res malas, negantes optime cum omnibus sanis, cordatisque Theologis, Deum peccati esse authorem, hinc malum, injustitiamque in ipso quaerentes homine, sicut egregie loquitur Rabbi Maimonides in More Nevochim, Part. III. cap. 17, Ex fundamentis Legis Moysis Doctorus nostri pia pia memoria est & hoc, quod Deo nullo pacto ulla conveniat aut adscribi debeat iniquitas & injustitia:& quod omnia sive mala, quae eveniunt homini, sive bona, quae homini aut toti alicui Ecclesiae, contingunt, procedant secundum justum & aequum Dei judicium, quod est sine ulla iniquitate & injustitia; ita ut, si vel spina homo manum suam laedat, quam statim iterum extrahat, poena loco id ipsi inflictum esse censendum sit; & e contra, si vel minimum bonum ipsi contingat, premii & retributionis loco sit habendum. Omnia haec sunt ex justo illius judicio, de quo dicitur: Omnes viae ejus sunt judicium; sed nos modos & rationes judicii illius ignoramus. Ita passim urgent dicta, in quibus malarum actionum causam, originemque non in Deum conjiciunt, sed in homines ipsos, citantque Malachiam cap. 1. v. 9. Nunc itaque deprecamini jam faciem Dei fortis, ut gratiam faciat nobis, dum e manu vestra est hoc, an suscepturus est ullius ex vobis vultum? Aut Iehova Exercituum; Iesaiam 30. v. 1. Va filiis contumacibus, dictum Iehovae, ad agitandum consilium, at non ex me, & ad obducendum tegumentum, at non spiritus mei; ut adjiciant peccatum peccato; Et Jer. cap. 23. v. 21. Me non mittente Prophetas isti os, ipsos cucurrisse: me non alloquente ipsos, prophetasse ipsos. Sic probat Rabbi Joseph Albo, quod peccata non fiant ex decreti divini necessitate, sed ex liberi arbitrii abusu, quando in Fundamentis suis scribit bit lib. 4. cap. 1. Cum ergo probitas aut malum sint in hominis libero arbitrio, necessario etiam bona, aut mala sequentur liberi arbitrii determinationem, non autem, ut tuputabas, omnia fiunt ex necessitate Decreti.
units.tr: Others extend the divine foreknowledge even to evil things themselves, and so, against all sound and judicious theologians, they deny that God is the author of sin, and seek evil and injustice in man rather than in God. Rabbi Maimonides speaks admirably on this in the More Nevochim, part 3, chapter 17: It is among the foundations of the Law of Moses, of our teacher of blessed memory, that iniquity and injustice cannot in any way belong to God or be ascribed to Him; and that all things, whether the evils that befall man or the goods that befall man or any whole congregation, proceed according to God's just and equitable judgment, which is without any iniquity or injustice. So that if a man hurts his hand even with a thorn, which he at once pulls out again, it must be judged to be a punishment inflicted on him; and conversely, if he meets with even the smallest good, it must be counted as a reward and recompense. All these things come from His just judgment, of which it is said: All His ways are judgment; but we do not know the modes and reasons of that judgment. So the passages press on everywhere in which they place the cause and origin of evil actions not in God but in men themselves, and they cite Malachi 1:9: Now therefore beseech God that He will be gracious unto us; while this is by your hand, will He accept any of your persons? saith the LORD of hosts. They cite Isaiah 30:1: Woe to the rebellious children, saith the LORD, that take counsel, but not of me; and that cover with a covering, but not of my spirit, that they may add sin to sin. And Jeremiah 23:21: I sent not these prophets, yet they ran; I spake not unto them, yet they prophesied. Rabbi Joseph Albo likewise proves that sins do not come about from the necessity of the divine decree but from the abuse of free will, when he writes in his Fundamentals, book 4, chapter 1: Since, then, goodness and evil lie in man's free will, the good or evil that follows must necessarily follow the determination of free will; it is not the case, as you supposed, that all things happen from the necessity of the decree.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Sic pariter contra ipsos disputant Manichaeos, qui duos constituebant Deos adversos, duoque ponebant Principia diversa, duasque naturas somniabant distinctas, tum boni, tum mali, ostendentes mali originem in Deo nullo modo quaerendam, sed per accidens esse malum, ex hominum quae dependere improbitate, voluntatisque abusu, uti liquet ex iis, quae habet Rabbi Joseph Albo Fundamentorum Auctor lib. 2. cap. 13. Apud antiquos fuit qui existimaret prima principia esse duo: unum boni, alterum mali. Dicebant enim ex ore excelsi non prodire bonum, & malum: id est fieri non posse ut principia contrariorum sint unum quid: quia vero contraria universalia, omnem speciem contrariorum complectentia sunt bonum & malum; dicebant duo esse rerum principia: unum principium boni, aliud principium mali, & haec erat opinio viri unius qui vocabatur Manes; Et rursus eodem capite: Quamobrem propter bonum, & malum non est necesse ponere duo eorum principia diversa: etenim ab uno principio existit bonum per se; malum vero per accidens; Et denique coeodem capite: Bonum est per se in omnibus iis, quae existunt: malum vero praeter intentionem primam; neque aliter est, quam per accidens: quemadmodum poena, aut castigatio, qua pater corripit filium malum est propter bonum, non quod primo intendatur, &c. Quibus jungendus erit Rabbi Isaac Bar Abraham, qui in suae fidei Munimine non solum Manichaeorum refert opinionem, sed simul ex Lege & Prophetis refutat, quando pag. 116, 117. sic scribit: Caeterum, cum prisci Haeretici viderent esse in hoc orbe influxus rerum contrariarum, hoc est, tam actiones bonas quam malas promoventes, existimarunt ipsi esse duo Numina, quorum unum bona, alterum mala operetur. Dicebant enim, fieri non posse ut in bona ac mala eadem causa influat. Ad hanc erroneam opinionem tollendam, dixit Deus Benedictus in Lege sua Deut. 32. Videte nunc me meipsum esse, & nullum esse Deum mecum: me morte afficere & vita restituere, frangere me & sanare &c. Eandem ob causam ait Deus apud Esaiam cap. 45. Formo lucem & creo tenebras, facio pacem, & creo malum; ego Dominus facio omnia ista. His duobus dictis docetur, quod idem Deus qui occidit, sit quoque Deus qui vitae reddit; quod idem qui frangit, sanet quoque; quod qui lucem efformat, creet etiam tenebras; quod pacem producens, efficiat quoque malum; & quod non sit aliud praeter eum, ceu Haereticus visum.
units.tr: In the same way they argue against the Manichaeans, who posited two opposing gods, imagined two distinct principles and two natures, one of good and one of evil, and who showed that the origin of evil is not to be sought in God in any way, but that evil is incidental, arising from the wickedness of men and the abuse of the will. This is clear from what Rabbi Joseph Albo, author of the Fundamenta, says in book 2, chapter 13: Among the ancients there was one who thought that the first principles were two, one of good and one of evil. For they said that good and evil do not proceed from the mouth of the Most High, that is, that the principles of contraries cannot be one thing, and since good and evil are universal contraries embracing every kind of contrary, they said there are two principles of things, one principle of good and another principle of evil; and this was the opinion of one man who was called Manes; and again in the same chapter: Therefore, on account of good and evil, it is not necessary to posit two different principles of them; for good exists from one principle per se, but evil per accidens; and finally in the same chapter: Good is per se in all the things that exist, but evil is beyond the primary intention, and it is nothing other than per accidens; just as the punishment or correction with which a father chastises a bad son is an evil on account of the good, not because it is primarily intended, etc. To these must be joined Rabbi Isaac Bar Abraham, who in the Munimen of his faith not only reports the opinion of the Manichaeans but at the same time refutes it from the Law and the Prophets, when at pages 116 and 117 he writes thus: Moreover, since the ancient heretics saw that in this world there are influences of contrary things, that is, those that promote good actions as well as evil ones, they thought there were two divinities, one of which works good things and the other evil. For they said it is impossible that the same cause flows into good and evil. To remove this erroneous opinion, the blessed God said in his Law, Deut. 32: See now that I am myself, and there is no God with me: I put to death and restore to life, I wound and I heal, etc. For the same reason God says in Isaiah 45: I form the light and create darkness, I make peace and create evil; I the Lord do all these things. By these two sayings it is taught that the same God who kills is also the God who restores life; that the one who wounds also heals; that the one who forms the light also creates the darkness; that the one who produces peace also brings about evil; and that there is no other beside him, as the heretic seemed to think.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Non negant Decreta divina aterna esse, cum sint ipsa Dei Scientia, quæ nihil aliud est, quam ipsius divina subsistantia, teste Maimonide in More Nevochim Part. III. cap. 21. Cum per divinam suam Sapientiam totius mundi negotia ab æterno disposuerit Deus Benedictus, Judice Menasseh Ben Israel cum Rabbi Isaac Bar Sclat, de Termino Vitæ pag. 226. Quod quæcunque in tempore fiant, ex voluntate Dei æterna contingant, ipsaque animalia omnia moveantur quoque ex divina voluntate, sicuti scribit Maimonides in More Nevochim Part. III. cap. 17. Fundamentum Legis Mosis Doctoris nostri, omniumque eorum, qui illi adhærent, est, quod homo habeat absolutissimam potestatem, hoc est, quod homo per Naturam, arbitrium & voluntatem suam faciat, quicquid homo facere potest, sine ulla re alia in ipso creata & innovata. Omnia pariter animalia irrationalia moventur Voluntate sua. Et sic voluit Deus Optimus Maximus, hoc est, Voluntas ejus æterna fuit, ut omne animal moveatur per voluntatem suam, & ut homo habeat potestatem ejus, quod vult velleligit, in iis, quæ cadunt sub ipsius potentiam. Huic fundamento unquam ab aliquo in Gente nostra contradictum fuisse, non est auditum; Quod in Deo Benedicto non fit prius & posterius, non tempus sit seu præteritum seu futurum, sed omnia illi maxime sint præsentia, uti loquitur Menasseh Ben Israel in libello de Termino Vitæ, pag. 228, 229. Abiīta enim æternitate res omnes scivit, non aliter ac si in tempore fierent. Rem aliquam similī illustremus: ponamus circulum ex cujus centro aliquot lineæ ducantur in circumferentiam : respectu hujus circumferentiæ potest considerari prius & posterius, sive linearum inter se distantia, quæ ratione centri nulla est : ita etiam respectu Dei non est prius, & posterius tempus, seu præteritum & futurum, sed omnia illi præsentia sunt.
units.tr: The divine decrees are not denied to be eternal, since they are God's own knowledge, which is nothing other than his divine substance, as Maimonides testifies in More Nevochim, Part III, chap. 21. Since the blessed God has disposed all the affairs of the world from eternity by his divine wisdom, as Menasseh Ben Israel, with Rabbi Isaac Bar Sclat, judges in De Termino Vitae, p. 226. Whatever happens in time comes about by the eternal will of God, and all living creatures are also moved by the divine will, as Maimonides writes in More Nevochim, Part III, chap. 17. The foundation of the Law of Moses, our Teacher, and of all who adhere to it, is that man has absolute power, that is, that by his nature, judgment and will man does whatever man can do, without any other thing created or introduced in him. Likewise all irrational animals are moved by their own will. And so God, most good and most great, willed, that is, his will was eternal, that every animal should be moved by its own will, and that man should have the power to will and choose what he wishes, in those things which fall under his power. No one among our people has ever been heard to contradict this foundation; That in the blessed God there is no before and after, nor is there time, whether past or future, but all things are most fully present to him, as Menasseh Ben Israel says in the booklet De Termino Vitae, pp. 228, 229. For from eternity he knew all things, not otherwise than if they were happening in time. Let us illustrate the matter by a likeness: suppose a circle from whose centre several lines are drawn to the circumference. With respect to this circumference one may consider a before and after, or the distance of the lines from one another, but with respect to the centre there is none. So also with respect to God there is no before and after in time, or past and future, but all things are present to him.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Decretum divinum statuunt Vnicum, quod Dei Scientia una sit, quæ ex multitudine variarum rerum decretarum, quas intime semper perspectas sibi habet, non multiplicetur, nec mutetur, prout rursus testatur Maimonides in More Nevochim Part. III. cap. 20. quem proinde audire, maxime hic juvabit: In confesso est apud omnes, non convenire Naturæ Dei Optimi Maximi innovationem scientiæ alicujus, ita ut nunc sciat, quod antea ignoraverit, neque etiam ut habeat scientias multas, juxta illos quoque qui attributa credunt. Hoc itaque demonstrato, dicimus nos legem divinam tenentes, ipsum una scientia scire res multas; neque secundum multitudinem scibilium velscitorum multiplicari in Deo scientias, sicut in nobis. Sic dicimus, ipsum omnes res, quæ innovantur, scire. scire antequam fiant, neque unquam eas nescire, ac per consequens, nullam in ipsò scientiam innovari. Nam notum ipsi est, quod N. nunc non extat, extitu-rus autem sit tempore N. tempore tanto permansu-rus, & deinde iterum non Ens futurum. Cum igitur postea vir ille ita existit, sicut in scientia ejus ante praesciit, sequitur, nullam ei scientiam accessisse, nec quicquam innovatum esse, quod ipsi ignotum fuerit; sed innovatum esse illud ipsum, quod et notum fuerat sicut est, antequam innovaretur; Quod licet res successive eveniant una post alteram, Deus Benedictus tamen ea non cognoscat succes-sive, sed simul, quia notitia ejus aeternitate mensuratur, sicuti in Conciliatore suo in Exodum Quaestione sexta, pag. 113. scribit Menasseh Ben Israel, quem notis & annotatiunculis Manu-scriptis Brenii illustratum nuper vidimus, ita autem ille: Et quanquam contingentia fiant succes-sive, non tamen eo Deus successive illa cognoscit, sed simul. Etenim notitia ejus aeternitate mensuratur, ut & Essentia: sed aeternitas simul, & praesens, com-prehendit universum tempus; eoque omnes res, quae sunt in tempore, ab aeterno praesentes sunt Deo, quia visus ejus ab aeterno se extendit ad omnes res, quatenus sunt in ejus praesentia. Unde manifestum est, contingentia infallibiliter a Deo cognosci, quatenus se subjiciunt divino conspectui, juxta modum praesentiae divinae: & nihilominus esse futura contingentia, comparata causis suis.
units.tr: They hold the divine decree to be one, in that the knowledge of God is one, and it is not multiplied or changed by the multitude of the various things decreed, which it always has intimately before itself. Maimonides again bears witness to this in More Nevochim, Part III, chap. 20, whom it will be especially helpful to hear here: It is agreed by all that it does not befit the nature of God, most good and most great, to have some knowledge newly introduced, so that he now knows what before he did not know, nor that he has many sciences, as those also hold who believe in attributes. Having therefore demonstrated this, we, holding the divine law, say that he knows many things by one knowledge; nor are there multiple sciences in God according to the multitude of knowable and known things, as there are in us. Thus we say that he knows all things which come into being, before they come to be, and never fails to know them; and consequently no knowledge in him is newly introduced. For it is known to him that N. does not now exist, but will exist at time N., will remain for so long a time, and afterwards will again not be. When therefore that man afterwards exists just as he was foreknown in his knowledge, it follows that no knowledge has come to him, nor has anything been introduced which was unknown to him; but that very thing has been introduced which was known just as it is before it was introduced. Although things come about successively, one after another, the blessed God nevertheless does not know them successively but all at once, because his knowledge is measured by eternity, as Menasseh Ben Israel writes in his Conciliator, on Exodus, question six, p. 113, which we recently saw illustrated with notes and little Manuscript annotations of Brenius. He says thus: And although contingent things come about successively, God does not therefore know them successively, but all at once. For his knowledge is measured by eternity, as is also his essence; but eternity, being simultaneous and present, comprehends the whole of time, and so all things which are in time are present to God from eternity, because his sight extends from eternity to all things, insofar as they are in his presence. Whence it is clear that contingent things are known infallibly by God, insofar as they submit themselves to the divine gaze, according to the mode of the divine presence; and nevertheless they are future contingent things, when compared with their causes.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Negant optimo jure Præscientiam necessi-tantem, repudiantes inevitabilem, absolutamque tum necessitatem, tum duram, fatalemque coactionem, quæ omne liberum in humanis tollat arbitrium, contingentiamque, explodentes Stoicum illud Fatum, quod Voluntas divina rebus omnibus non imponat necessitatem, sed potius omnis quoque libertatis humanæ, & contingentiæ existat causa; Hinc necessariam talem dependentiam non solum errorem nominant vetustissimum, quem propugnaverit Secta Assariæ inter Ismaelitas olim famosissima, quæ, teste Maimonide in More Nevochim, Part. III. cap. 17. Credit nullam in hoc mundo rem, nec universalem, nec particularem fieri per contingentiam, sed omnia esse ex certa voluntate, intentione, & gubernatione; Sed multis convellunt Argumentis, demonstrantes per fatalem rerum omnium coactionem tolli ex humanis contingentiam, libertatemque ad utrumque oppositorum, uti loquitur rursus Maimonides in More Nevochim Part. III. cap. 17. Secundum hanc sententiam sequitur etiam, quod omnes motus & quietes animantium sint à Deo decreta, nec penes hominem sit, quicquam vel faciendi, vel intermittendi. Tollitur etiam secundum illam opinionem rerum contingentia, & sequitur quod omnia sint vel necessaria fària vel Impossibilia, id quod agnoscunt, dicunt quo- que illa, quæ vulgo possibilia vocantur, ut ʼnʼstare Ru- benus, venire Simeonis, esse possibilia respectu nostri, sed respectu Dei nullam prorsus in illis esse possibilita- tem, verum esse vel necessaria, vel impossibilia; Po- sito fatali absoluto divino decreto, inutilia, fru- straneaque omnia tum media, tum studia ad rem aliquam vel obtinendam, vel vitandam, sic Rabbi IsacSangarus in libro CofriPart. V. §.20. Non negat naturam possibilis vel contingentis, nisi qui perversi & profani est ingenii, qui dicit ea quæ non credit. Vides enim quomodo se præparet quis- que ad id quod vel sperat, vel timet: Id quod te docet, illum credere, quod res illa sit possibilis, & præparatio ad eam prosit. Quod si crederet, rem illam absolute & necessario futuram, tum exponeret sese libere, non instrueret se armis belliis contra inimicum suum, neque annona contra famem; Inutiles fore omnes leges, admonitiones, promisiones & comminationes; Sic Rabbi Saadiah in Sepher Emu- nah sol. 26. Si Deus hominem necessitaret, inutilia essent præcepta & prohibitiones ipsi factæ; Rabbi Maimonides in More Nevochim Part. III. cap. 17. Insuper sequitur ex hac sententia, nihil quicquam prodesse Leges, quandoquidem homo, cui datæ sunt omnes Leges, nullam sic habet facultatem quicquam vel faciendi eorum, quæ præcipiuntur, vel intermit- tendi eorum, quæ prohibentur; At vero monemur, mur, ut foliciti fimus de vitando malo, & eligendo bono, quia utrumque in potestate nostra est, utiloquitur Menasleh Ben Israel de Termino Vitæ pag. 202; Quod injustus esset Deus, si homines puniret ob id factum, ad quod prædestinati sunt,& quod ex necessitate decreti divini debuerunt facere, sic enim rur-sus Menasleh Ben Israel citato libello pag. 194. Itaque injustum nimis etiam foret, Deum punire homines ob id factum, ad quod prædestinati sunt, & quod ex vi decreti divini non potuerunt non facere; Et pag. 196. Ne dicam injustum Deum fuisse, quod blasphemum est de Deo cogitare, quando eum punivit, si liberam istam potestatem non habuit; Quod nullus præmiis pœnisque concedatur locus, si statuatur, quod omnia ex Decreto fiant; quodque sic impingat homo in fidei articulum de præmio, pœnaque, imo quod iniquitatem, malitiamque Deo imputet, quod peccatorem præter meritum puniat Deus, siquidem aliter quam fecit, facere non potuit, sicuti disputat Fundamentorum lib. 1. cap. 13. Rabbi Joseph Albo, quem latine vertit Matthias Elia, apud Winckelmannum; Quod nulla sit differentia inter virtuosos & vitiosos, nec ulla probi præ repro-bo prærogativa, sed utrique pro cultoribus Dei habendi, cum ea, ad quæ ordinati & impulsi sunt, ambo faciant. Sic pariter ad motas obje-&io{ß}tiones non tantum plurimis respondent apud Rabbi Ifacum Sangarum in Cofri, pag. 369, 370. Editionis & Versionis Buxtorfianæ, sed quandoque immerito, valdeque imperite accusant Reformatos, vel quod media ad decretorum divinorum executionem non judicent esse necessaria, vel quod omnia, quæ ab homine fieri debeant, non libere, sed necessario evenire debeant, sicuti quandoque scripsit Menasseh Ben Israel, cum tamen toties hæc Religionis calumnia per nostros non sine fructu feliciter sit depulsa, nec sibi foli servet schola Calvini, colat, adoretque hoc insigne ac præclarum veritatis & sapientiæ cœlestis mysterium, sicuti nobis non ex amore fraterno objecit in Synagoga lua Bifronte Odehlius pag. 96.
units.tr: They rightly deny a necessitating foreknowledge, rejecting an inevitable and absolute necessity, and a harsh, fatal compulsion which would take away all free choice in human affairs, and they reject contingency, exploding that Stoic fate, namely that the divine will imposes no necessity on all things, but rather is the cause of all human liberty and of contingency. Hence they call such a necessary dependence not only a very ancient error, which was defended by the sect of the Ash'arites, once most famous among the Ismaelites, who, as Maimonides testifies in More Nevochim, Part III, chap. 17, believe that no thing in this world, either universal or particular, comes about by contingency, but that all things are from a fixed will, intention and governance; but they also refute it with many arguments, demonstrating that by the fatal compulsion of all things contingency is removed from human affairs, and liberty to either of two opposites, as Maimonides again says in More Nevochim, Part III, chap. 17. According to this opinion it follows also that all motions and rests of living creatures are decreed by God, nor is it in man's power to do or to omit anything. Contingency of things is also removed according to that opinion, and it follows that all things are either necessary or impossible, which they acknowledge; they also say of those things which are commonly called possible, such as that Reuben should stand or Simeon should come, that they are possible with respect to us, but with respect to God there is no possibility at all in them, but they are either necessary or impossible. Once the fatal and absolute divine decree is posited, all means and efforts, whether for obtaining or avoiding something, are useless and vain. So Rabbi Isaac Sangarus in the book Cofri, Part V, §20: Only one who is of a perverse and profane mind denies the nature of the possible or contingent, who says the things he does not believe. For you see how each man prepares himself for what he either hopes or fears; which teaches you that he believes the thing to be possible, and that preparation for it is useful. But if he believed that the thing would certainly and necessarily happen, he would then expose himself freely, would not arm himself for war against his enemy, nor store grain against famine; all laws, admonitions, promises and threats would be useless. So Rabbi Saadiah in Sepher Emunah, p. 26: If God necessitated man, the precepts and prohibitions given to him would be useless. Rabbi Maimonides in More Nevochim, Part III, chap. 17. Furthermore it follows from this opinion that the laws profit nothing, since man, to whom all the laws are given, has no such faculty to do any of those things which are commanded, or to omit any of those which are forbidden. But indeed we are admonished to be careful to avoid evil and to choose good, because both are in our power, as Menasseh Ben Israel says in De Termino Vitae, p. 202. That God would be unjust if he punished men for that deed to which they are predestined, and which by necessity of the divine decree they were bound to do; for so again Menasseh Ben Israel in the cited booklet, p. 194: Therefore it would be far too unjust for God to punish men for that deed to which they are predestined, and which by force of the divine decree they could not but do; and p. 196: Not to say that God would be unjust, which is blasphemous to think of God, when he punished them, if they did not have that free power. Thus no place is left for rewards and punishments, if it is laid down that all things come about by decree; and thus man stumbles into an article of faith concerning reward and punishment, indeed attributes iniquity and malice to God, in that God punishes a sinner beyond his merit, since he could not have done otherwise than he did; as Rabbi Joseph Albo disputes in Fundamentorum, book 1, chap. 13, which Matthias Elia translated into Latin, in the edition of Winckelmann. Thus there is no difference between the virtuous and the vicious, nor any advantage of the upright over the reprobate, but both must be regarded as worshippers of God, since both do what they were ordained and impelled to do. Likewise, in answering the objections raised, they not only answer in many ways in Rabbi Isaac Sangarus in Cofri, pp. 369, 370, of the Buxtorf edition and translation, but sometimes unjustly and very ignorantly accuse the Reformed, either because they do not judge means to be necessary for the execution of the divine decrees, or because all things which ought to be done by man come about not freely but by necessity, as Menasseh Ben Israel has at times written. Yet this calumny of religion has been happily repulsed by our people many times, not without fruit, and the school of Calvin does not keep this remarkable and illustrious mystery of truth and heavenly wisdom to itself alone; it cultivates and adores it, as Odehlius, in his two-faced Synagogue, p. 96, objected to us not out of brotherly love.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Credunt proinde hodiernæ Synagogæ Judæi, Deum Benedictum liberi arbitrii usum per æternum suum decretum neutiquam tollere, aut subtrahere, vel ipsam cogere, imminuereque libertatem, semper brevem illam Sapientum Veterum recitantes sententiam, quæ legitur in Tractatu Talmudico Pirke Abhot cap. 3. §. 16. הכל צפוי והרשות נתונה Omnia visa & licentia data est; Innuentes, quod licet omnia a Deo vita, ab æterno quæ sint decreta, non tamen exinde homini ademptum sit liberum arbitrium bitrium agendi bene vel male prout placuerit, sicuti multis deducit Menasleh Ben Israel in libello de Termino vitæ pag.218,219. Ad me quod attinet, ego sentio, Deum nunquam cogere, aut subtrahere cuiquam usum liberi arbitrii, sed suaviter semper disponere media prout magis, vel minus appetitui nostro grata sunt. Eodem modo, quo primum mobile rapit inferiores orbes; Sed ita ut suum tamen cuique proprium motum relinquat. Ex. gr. Deus decreverat, ut populus Israelis captivus maneret in Ægypto per aliquot annos, & ut Iosephus supra fratres suos eveheretur in summam dignitatem. Neminem hic coegit Deus, ut finem, quem constituerat, consequeretur: sed suaviter duntaxat media disposuit, occurrere faciendo occasionem, qua Midianiticis mercatoribus Iosephus venderetur, atque ita in Ægyptum veniret. Similiter Deus constituerat inter Ægyptios signa edere admirandæ suæ potentiæ, at quomodo? an indurando cor Pharaonis, ita ut usum libertatis ei adimeret? Nequaquam: Sed rem ita dirigendo & disponendo, ut regi occasio daretur per libertum voluntatis suæ usum, aut potius abusum, animum suum obdurandi; Pergitque Menasseh pag. 221,222. Similiter Deus decreverat dividere regnum Salomonicum. Quomodo id facit? Non cogendo Roboamum, sed occasionem tantum ei dando, per consilia iuniorum, quibus ille passus se adduci, renuit populo concedere imminutionem vectigalium: Atque ita Prophetia ⊂Abiæ completa fuit. Hunc in modum omnia mihi loca exponi posse videntur, quibus videtur indicari, Deum quandoque libertate arbitrii privare eos, quos punire vult. Uti enim illi, qui summa rerum potiuntur, norunt omnia industrie, & prudenter adeo disponere, ut ad finem suum intentum perveniant: Ita etiam Deus Rex cœli & terræ, omnia novit sapienter disponere, absque ulla læsione liberi arbitrii, quo finem suum obtineat, ut hos pro sua gratia præmio, illos pro justitia sua pœna afficiat; Sic quoque Judæus Orobius in Amica nupera collatione cum Limborchio pag. 82. Non quod Deus libero hominis arbitrio vim sit illaturus; sed quod ex affluentia gratiæ homo fere semper inclinabitur in bonum ut sic finis imponatur peccato.
units.tr: Accordingly, the Jews of the present-day synagogue believe that God, blessed be He, by His eternal decree in no way takes away or withdraws the use of free will, nor does He compel or diminish human liberty. They keep repeating that brief saying of the ancient Sages, found in the Talmudic tractate Pirke Abhot, chapter 3, §16: הכל צפוי והרשות נתונה [All is foreseen, and freedom is given]. By this they mean that although all things are decreed by God from eternity, free will is not for that reason taken from man, so that he may act well or badly as he pleases, as Menasseh Ben Israel draws out at length in his booklet De Termino vitae, pp. 218, 219. As for me, I hold that God never compels anyone to use free will, nor withdraws it, but always gently arranges the means, as they are more or less agreeable to our appetite. He does this in the same way that the primum mobile carries the lower spheres, yet leaves each its own proper motion. For example, God had decreed that the people of Israel should remain captive in Egypt for some years, and that Joseph should be raised above his brothers to the highest dignity. God compelled no one here to reach the end he had set; He only gently arranged the means, bringing it about that Joseph was sold to the Midianite merchants, and so came into Egypt. Likewise God had determined to display His wonderful power among the Egyptians. But how? By hardening Pharaoh's heart, so as to take away his use of liberty? By no means. He ordered and arranged the matter so that the king was given the occasion, through the free use, or rather the abuse, of his own will, of hardening his own mind. Menasseh goes on, p. 221, 222: Likewise God had decreed to divide the kingdom of Solomon. How does He do this? Not by compelling Rehoboam, but only by giving him occasion, through the counsel of his young men, to whom he allowed himself to be persuaded, when he refused to grant the people a reduction of taxes. And so the prophecy concerning Abijah was fulfilled. In this way all the passages seem to me capable of explanation, in which it seems to be indicated that God sometimes deprives of freedom of choice those whom He wishes to punish. For just as those who hold supreme power know how to arrange all things diligently and wisely so as to attain their intended end, so God, King of heaven and earth, knows how to arrange all things wisely, without any injury to free will, so that He may attain His end, rewarding these with His grace and punishing those with His justice. So too the Jew Orobio, in his recent friendly conference with Limborch, p. 82: Not that God is going to do violence to man's free will; but that, from the abundance of grace, man will almost always be inclined to good, so that an end is put to sin.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Hinc docent non omnia Decreta esse ⊂Absoluta, sed formant, finguntque innumera Conditionata, quæ quamvis ex æterno, divinoque procedant decreto, dependeant nihilominus ex libero hominis arbitrio, mutabilique voluntate, quæ cum sui sit juris, tum velle possit, tum nolle, uti pluribus ex Judæorum scriptis ostendi possit, si hæc communis, vulgataque opinio non luce clarior esset meridiana, & inferius demonstranda quoque esset ulterius; Quare Menasseh Ben Israel in Termino vitæ pag. 217. reprehendit Don Iacum Abarbanelem, quod in
units.tr: Hence they teach that not all decrees are absolute; they form and imagine countless conditional decrees, which, although they proceed from the eternal and divine decree, nonetheless depend on the free choice of man and his changeable will, which, since it is in its own power, can both will and refuse. This can be shown from many Jewish writings, if this common and popular opinion were not clearer than the midday light, and if it did not also need to be demonstrated further below. For this reason Menasseh Ben Israel, in De Termino vitae, p. 217, rebukes Don Isaac Abarbanel for having dared to write in his book Nachalat Abhot, as if no human care or anxiety could ever delay the divine foreknowledge or hinder the absolute decree. He speaks thus:

units.la: libro suo Nachalat Abhot scribere ausus fuerit, quasi neque cura, neque solicitudo ulla humana quandoque posset morari Præscientiam divinam, ipsumque impedire decretum absolutum, sic autem loquitur: Quando Deus decrevit aliquem punire, vel præmio afficere, contra ista nihil quidquam cura, vel sollicitudo ulla potest. Id accidisse ait in Achitophelis consilio evertendo, quia decretum erat punire Absalonem. Huc pertinent verba illa Prophetæ Ier. 10. v. 23. Novi Domine, quod non est hominis via ejus, nec viri ambulantis est præparare gressum suum; Item 2. Sam. 17. v. 14. Et Dominus præceperat infringere consilium Achitophel bonum, ut induceret Dominus super Absalom malum; Item Ej. 14. v. 28. Dominus Exercituum consuluit, & quis irritabit? Item Prov. 21. v. 30. Non est sapientia, neque intelligentia, nec consilium contra Dominum. Nam decretum Dei de pœna infligenda, aut præmio aliquem adficiendo, humana cura aut industria curari non potest; Sic censuram Popularium non effugiet Iacus Orobius, quod gratiam divinam ita statuat efficacem, ut nulla humana resistere possit voluntas, uti apparet ex ipsius erudita collatione cum Limborchio pag. 83. Quia si, quamvis Deus efficaciter hominem aliquid efficere vellet, hominis voluntas ei resistere de facto posset, ut pote libera; divina frustraretur, & magis dependeret Dei voluntas ab humana quam hæc a Deo; cum tamen optioptime dixerit Magnus Augustinus de correptione & gratia cap. XIV. Magis habet Deus in manu sua voluntates hominum, quam ipsi suas: & sacra pagina: Cor regis in manu Dei. Habet Deus summum imperium in omnes creaturas; quod absolute verum non foret si hominis voluntas ab hoc imperio subtraheretur, qui voluntas Dei efficax ad hominus libitum frustrari contingeret.
units.tr: When God has decreed to punish someone, or to reward him, no care or anxiety of any kind can work against this. He says this happened in the overthrow of Ahithophel's counsel, because it had been decreed that Absalom should be punished. To this belong those words of the prophet Jeremiah, chapter 10, verse 23: I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not his own, nor is it for a man who walks to direct his own steps. Likewise 2 Samuel 17, verse 14: For the Lord had determined to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, so that the Lord might bring evil upon Absalom. Likewise Isaiah 14, verse 28 (as printed): The Lord of hosts has purposed, and who will annul it? Likewise Proverbs 21, verse 30: There is no wisdom, nor understanding, nor counsel against the Lord. For the decree of God to inflict punishment, or to bestow a reward on someone, cannot be turned aside by human care or industry. Nor will Jacob Orobio escape the censure of the common people, for holding divine grace to be so effective that no human will can resist it, as appears from his learned conference with Limborch, p. 83: For if, although God wished to bring about something in man effectively, man's will could in fact resist Him, since it is free, then the divine will would be frustrated, and God's will would depend more on man's than man's on God's. Yet Augustine the Great has rightly said, in On Correction and Grace, chapter 14: God holds the wills of men in His hand more than they hold their own. And Holy Scripture: The heart of the king is in the hand of God. God has supreme dominion over all creatures; this would not be absolutely true if the human will were withdrawn from this dominion, so that the efficacious will of God could be frustrated whenever man pleased.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Fatentur Judaei Praescientiae divinae cum libero arbitrio conciliationem, arduum ingensque esse opus, quod ipsi quoque Christiani confessi fuerint, cum valde obscurum sit, nostrumque fere superet captum, quomodo decretum Dei efficax, ejusque operatio consistere possit cum libertate humana, cumque ex una parte clare, distinctéque percipiant, omnia fieri ex decreto divino, & ab altera parte propriae libertatis sint sibi maxime conscii, nemoque unquam expertus fuerit suam cogi voluntatem, sicuti integra sectione undecima deducit Menasseh Ben Israel in Termino Vitae, quem audire necesse bene erit, sic autem loquitur pag. 223, 224. Una adhuc restat difficilis, & satis intricata quaestio, quam pro virili nostra conabimur expedire. Ea haec est, quomodo liberum hominis arbitrium, & praescientia divina conciliari possint. Haec quaestio tam est ardua, ut Cajetano inexplicabilis, Vasquezio difficillima lima visa fuerit: Hebraei eam etiam latius difficilem esse, uno ore omnes confitentur. Unde Rab Moses Aegyptius in Directorio suo Part. III. cap. 20. & tractatu de Poenitentia cap. 5. quem vertit eruditus D. Gerbrandus Ansloot, inquit, Scientia Dei, non est aliquod accidens substantiae, uti hominum scientia est: sed est ipsa Essentia Dei. Quapropter sicuti homines non possunt capere substantiam, & essentiam Dei, juxta illud Exod. 33. v. 20. Non videt me homo, & vivit: ita etiam non possunt ingenio suo indagare scientiam divinam, neque percipere modum quo ille res praescit, juxta illud Es. 55. v. 12. Quia non sunt cogitationes meae, cogitationes vestrae, neque viae meae, viae vestrae, &c. Notum est, homines, inquit Maimonides, libero arbitrio praeditos esse; ac Deum ab aeterno res omnes scire, plane extra dubium est: sed quomodo res sciat salva voluntatis libertate, illud demum est, super quo controvertitur, & adhuc sub judice lis est. Nam quaerere, quomodo res Deus cognoscat, idem est atque velle scire, quid sit Deus. Recenset praeterea Menasseh Ben Israel, quid Rabbi Abraham Bar David in Tractatu suo Asagot de hac conciliatione sentiat, cum ait pag. 225, 226. Astrologos ex constellatione & intuitu siderum, multa per conjecturam posse praedicere: non dispari etiam modo Deum posse praescire, quae hominibus eventura sunt, ex siderum cursu: nam qualem habituri sunt, ipse decrevit. At cum homo vim siderum evitare possit bene, vel male, prudenter aut imprudenter agendo: Addit, Deum etiam illum voluntatis actum, sive motum praescire, ac proinde ad quam partem se flexura sit voluntas, ut hoc aut illud agat. Qua tamen praescientia, neminem, juxta illum, necessitat aut cogit in operibus suis; Tandem Menasseh Ben Israel allegato libello non solum propriam suam aperit mentem, ostendens, qua ratione duo haec extrema bene conciliari possint, verum etiam in sententiae probationem tum ex Rabbinis in medium producit Isacum Aramam, Isacum Bar Sefat, aliosque plurimos, tum ex Christianis Justinum Martyrem, Originem, Chrysostomum, Cyrillum, Hieronymum, Augustinum, & Damascenum, cum sic allegato libello pag. 227. scribit: Deus inquit, ab aeterno disposuit totius mundi negotia, & divina sua sapientia, ac perspicacia vidit omnes effectus, qui in tempore futuri essent: qui licet pendeant (loquor enim de actionibus humanis) a libero hominis arbitrio, ut fiant aut non fiant: nihilominus tamen Deus certo & infallibiliter eos praevidit ac praescivit. Nec tamen ideo quicquam in tempore facit homo, quia Deus ea facturum praescivit: sed e contrario, quia homo in tempore hoc vel illud facit, aut operatur, ideo Deus ab aeterno illud scivit; Sic pariter Rabbi Isac Sangarus demonstrat in libro Cosri Part. V sect. 10. Praescientiam divinam neutiquam contrariari libero hominis arbitrio, sed haec facile posse
units.tr: The Jews admit that reconciling God's foreknowledge with free will is a difficult and great task, as even the Christians themselves have confessed. It is very obscure and almost beyond our grasp how God's effective decree and its operation can stand together with human freedom. They clearly and distinctly perceive, on the one hand, that everything happens by the divine decree, and on the other hand, they are most conscious of their own freedom, and no one has ever experienced his will being forced. Menasseh Ben Israel draws this out in the entire eleventh section of Termino Vitae, which it will be well worth hearing, and he speaks thus at pp. 223-224: "One difficult and rather intricate question still remains, which we will try to resolve as well as we can. It is this: how can the free choice of man and divine foreknowledge be reconciled? This question is so difficult that it seemed inexplicable to Cajetan and most difficult to Vasquez. All the Hebrews unanimously confess that it is even more difficult." Hence Rabbi Moses the Egyptian, in his Directorium, part III, chapter 20, and in the treatise on Repentance, chapter 5, which the learned Gerbrand Ansloot translated, says: "The knowledge of God is not some accident of substance, as human knowledge is; it is the very essence of God. Therefore, just as men cannot grasp the substance and essence of God, according to that saying in Exod. 33:20, 'No man shall see me and live,' so neither can they by their own wit investigate the divine knowledge, nor perceive the manner in which he foreknows things, according to Isa. 55:12, 'For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are my ways your ways,' etc." Maimonides says: "It is known that men are endowed with free choice, and that God has known all things from eternity is quite beyond doubt; but how he knows things while the freedom of the will is preserved, that is the very point in dispute, and the controversy is still before the judge. For to ask how God knows things is the same as to want to know what God is." Menasseh Ben Israel further recounts what Rabbi Abraham Bar David thinks about this reconciliation in his treatise Asagot, where he says at pp. 225-226: "Astrologers can foretell many things by conjecture from the constellation and the aspect of the stars. In a similar way God can foreknow what is going to happen to men from the course of the stars, for he himself has decreed what sort of men they will be. But since a man can well avoid the force of the stars, acting well or badly, wisely or unwisely, he adds that God also foreknows that act or movement of the will, and therefore in which direction the will is going to turn, so that it does this or that. Yet by this foreknowledge, according to him, no one is necessitated or compelled in his works." Finally, Menasseh Ben Israel, in the treatise mentioned, not only reveals his own opinion, showing by what reasoning these two extremes can be well reconciled, but also in proof of this view brings forward, from the rabbis, Isaac Arama, Isaac Bar Sefat, and very many others, and from the Christians Justin Martyr, Origen, Chrysostom, Cyril, Jerome, Augustine and Damascene, and so he writes in the treatise mentioned at p. 227: "God, he says, from eternity disposed the affairs of the whole world, and by his divine wisdom and insight he saw all the effects which would be in time. Although these depend (for I am speaking of human actions) on the free choice of man, whether they come to be or not, nevertheless God foresaw and foreknew them certainly and infallibly." Yet man does not do anything in time for this reason, that God foreknew he would do it; rather, on the contrary, because man does this or that in time, or works it, therefore God knew it from eternity. In the same way Rabbi Isaac Sangar demonstrates in the book Cosri, part V, section 10, that divine foreknowledge by no means contradicts the free choice of man, but that these can easily be reconciled, if actions are distinguished into divine, natural, accidental and free, as he declares in the following words: "Therefore he truly speaks who says that all things happen by the decree of God; truly..."

units.la: Note: the margin and footnote lines at the bottom are not legible enough to transcribe. posse conciliari, si distinguantur actiones in Divinas, Naturales, Accidentales, Liberasque, prout verbis declarat sequentibus: Itaque vere dicit, qui dicit, omnia fieri ex Decreto DEI: vere etiam dicit alter, qui asserit liberum arbitrium, & accidentia, nec quicquam derogat, vel detrahit Decreto divino. Si velis, poteris haec ista distinctione conciliare: Actiones sunt vel Divinae, vel Naturales, vel Accidentales, vel Electivae seu Liberae. Divinae, a causa divina proveniunt omnimodo, nullam aliam habentes causam praeter voluntatem divinam. Naturales, sunt a causis mediis vel secundis accomodatis illis, & perducentibus eas ad finem perfectionis sua, quamdiu nulla reliquarum trium causarum eas impediat. Accidentales, sunt etiam a causis secundis, sed accidentaliter, non naturaliter, vel ordinate, vel intentionaliter: nullam etiam habent praeparationem ad perfectionem, ad quam pertingant, & in qua subsistant: praeterea conditionantur a caeteris tribus partibus actionum. Electivarum autem causa est voluntas hominis, electionem faciens: Liberum arbitrium autem est ex censu causarum secundarum, & causas habet catenatim dependentes a causa prima, dependentia non coacta: quia possibili seu contingente existente, anima constituta est inter consilium & contrarium ejus, facere potest ex ambobus, quod vult. Et hoc liberum arbitrium vel laudandum vel vituperandum est, id quod convenit reliquis causis fecundis.
units.tr: Divine actions come from a divine cause in every way, having no other cause apart from the divine will. Natural actions are from middle or secondary causes suited to them, and leading them to the end of their perfection, as long as none of the remaining three causes hinders them. Accidental actions are also from secondary causes, but accidentally, not naturally or in an orderly or intentional way; they also have no preparation for the perfection they are to reach and in which they subsist; moreover, they are conditioned by the other three parts of actions. The cause of elective actions, however, is the will of man, making the choice. Free choice, however, belongs to the class of secondary causes, and has causes depending in a chain on the first cause, a dependence that is not compelled; for, since the possible or contingent exists, the soul is placed between a plan and its opposite, and it can do from either of the two what it wills. And this free choice is either to be praised or to be blamed, which is true of the other secondary causes.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Inter Decreta divina numerant, memorantque maximè ניין Prædestinationem divinam, singulare, excellensque illud Dei Decretum circa creaturas rationales, liberasque, hinc occupati valde in Præscientiæ Dei cum libertate voluntatis humanæ conciliatione, inculcantes passim ex adductis testimoniis, quòd non sibi invicè contrarientur, sed optimè conspirent; At, pace Judæorum, si dicendum, quod verû est, adeò tenuia & exilia omnia illa sunt, quæ de Prædestinatione proferunt, ut melius humana Prædestinatio, quàm divina appellanda esset, nec Deus Benedictus hominem prædestinet, servet, salvetque, sed homo se ipsum prius destinet, servet, salvetque, exinde quòd non solùm ex libero suo arbitrio credat, fidemque habeat præceptis Mosaicis in monte Sinai latis, sed ea propriis incipiat viribus observare, ut ita quoscunque Deus ab æterno consilio articulis Religionis Judaicæ fundamentalibus ex liberrimo arbitrio crediturōs, & Legem Mosaicam, quam in tempore tulit, servaturos præviderit, eos ad æternam vitam, lætissimamque resurrectionem elegerit, reliquos verò nec crediturōs, nec Legem Mo-sis fis observaturos ad Gehennæ ignes condem- naverit, reprobaveritque.
units.tr: Among the divine decrees they count, and especially mention, the divine predestination [ניין], that singular and excellent decree of God concerning rational and free creatures. They labour greatly over reconciling God's foreknowledge with the freedom of the human will, and they repeatedly insist, from the testimonies they cite, that these do not contradict each other but agree perfectly. Yet, with respect to the Jews, if I must say what is true, all the things they put forward about predestination are so thin and slight that it would be better to call it human predestination than divine. Blessed God does not predestine, preserve and save man; rather, man first predestines, preserves and saves himself. This happens because, by his own free will, he believes and holds the precepts given on Mount Sinai by Moses, and begins to observe them by his own strength. Thus God, by his eternal counsel, foresaw those whom he would elect to eternal life and the most joyful resurrection: those who would believe, from the most free choice, the fundamental articles of the Jewish religion, and would keep the Mosaic Law which he gave in time. The rest, who would neither believe nor keep the Law of Moses, he condemned to the fires of Gehenna and reprobated.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Profectò non mirum Judæos nostræ æta- tis sicsentire de Prædestinatione, quòd aliter ex suis Principiis loqui non possint, cùm mor- daciter liberū arbitrium in ipsis Spiritualibus defendant, viresque sufficientes tribuant ho- mini, quibus Legem Mosaicam possit observa- re, sicque vitam mereri æternam, facientes ho- minem actionum suarum salutarium artifi- cem, dominumque, affirmentque perfectio- nem operum, merita, satisfactiones tum pro- prias, tum alienas; contra verò constanter negent vim peccati originalis, hincq; Messiæ tollant liberationem spiritualem, gratiam ef- ficacem, non concedentes peccatores Deo re- conciliatos in Mediatore Messia, ejusque præ- stita satisfactione, sicuti testatur Judæus Ano- nymus Quæst. 5. cap. 7. An liberatio, quæ per Messiam fiet, solum erit corporalis ac temporaria? Omnino corporalem futuram credimus, qualis per Mosen facta est, qui populum liberavit à servitute Ægyptia. Nam spiritualis liberatio solummodo dependet ab observatione Legis, quam Deus in monte Sinai promulgavit.
units.tr: It is certainly no surprise that the Jews of our age think about predestination in this way, since they cannot speak otherwise from their own principles. For they stubbornly defend free will even in spiritual matters, and they grant man sufficient strength by which he can observe the Mosaic Law and so merit eternal life.
