They make man the author and master of his own saving actions. They affirm the perfection of works, merits, and satisfactions, both one's own and those of others. On the other hand, they constantly deny the force of original sin, and therefore they remove from the Messiah spiritual liberation and effectual grace. They do not allow that sinners are reconciled to God in the Mediator Messiah and in the satisfaction he has rendered. So testifies the anonymous Jew, Question 5, chapter 7: Will the liberation which shall be effected through the Messiah be only bodily and temporary? We believe that it will be wholly bodily, such as was effected through Moses, who freed the people from Egyptian servitude. For spiritual liberation depends only on the observance of the Law, which God promulgated on Mount Sinai.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Hinc initium boni in homine non divinæ gratiæ ferunt acceptum, continuationem, progressumque in bono adscribentes liberi arbitrii viribus, ex bono usu gratiæ à Deo in ejus principio communicatæ, quæ Pelagianorum, maximè tamen Semipelagianorum opinio fuit, sed in alia extrema abeuntes, initium boni ex se ipsis derivant, ibi tribuetes vires idoneas, sufficientesque ex libero hominis arbitrio, arcessentesque perseverantiam, inque bono continuationem ex Deo Benedicto, sicut legimus ex Manasseh Ben Israel in libello de Fragilitate Humana, quando à pag. 116. Sic pluribus loquitur de Judæis: Nam duo solum auxilij genera agnoscunt; quorum prius est, cum Deus hominem, qui opus bonum, ac pium ortus est, adjuvat, ipsiq; manum porrigit, ut inceptum absolvat. De hoc genere docte admoadum loquitur Rabbi Eliahu Haim in suo Resit hochma libro 1. cap. 4. hunc in modum: An dices, Deum homini ante appetitum ferre auxilium, ut eum vincat? idem fit hoc ac si bonorum operum merita tollas. Iterum interrogamus, utrum Deus hoc auxilium det aliquibus, an omnibus? Si omnibus, quare non omnes sunt justi? Si aliquibus, quam ob causam iflam facit distinctionem? An quia velit salvari alios, alios damnari? At respectus iste personarum in Deum non cadit. Dicimus igitur, auxilium istud, aut gratiam, præsupponere opus inceptum; haud secus, ac si homo in tollendo onere lalaboret, atq; id vires excedat, eoque alijs accedat, quiadjuvet, ac humeris imponat. Ita quoq; hominem, ubi bonum inchoavit opus, atq; in exequendo eo difficultatem experitur, a Deo adjuvari, ut opus coeptum finiat, atq; in actum deducat.
units.tr: Hence they do not attribute the beginning of good in man to the reception of divine grace. They ascribe the continuation and progress in good to the powers of free will, through the good use of the grace which God communicated at its beginning. This was the opinion of the Pelagians, but most of all of the Semipelagians. Going over to the opposite extreme, however, they derive the beginning of good from themselves. There they attribute suitable and sufficient powers to the free choice of man, and they seek perseverance from themselves, while the continuation in good they seek from blessed God. So we read in Manasseh Ben Israel, in his little book on the Frailty of Man, from page 116 onward, where he speaks thus about the Jews: For they acknowledge only two kinds of help. The first is when God helps a man who has begun a good and pious work, and stretches out his hand to him, so that he may complete what he has begun. Rabbi Eliahu Haim speaks most learnedly about this kind of help in his book Resit hochma, book 1, chapter 4, in this manner: Will you say that God brings help to man before he desires it, so that he may overcome? This is the same as taking away the merits of good works. Again we ask: does God give this help to some, or to all? If to all, why are not all just? If to some, for what reason does he make this distinction? Is it because he wishes some to be saved and others condemned? But such respect of persons does not fall upon God. We say, therefore, that this help, or grace, presupposes a work already begun, no differently than if a man labours to lift a burden which exceeds his strength, and another comes near to help him and puts it on his shoulders. So also, when a man has begun a good work and experiences difficulty in carrying it out, he is helped by God, so that he may finish the work begun and bring it into act.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Probat porro communem sententiā Menas-seh, variisq; argumentis, rationibusq; quo magis persuaderet, confirmat, cum sic a pag. 117. pergit: Si, ut nonnullis persuasum esse video, in operibus moraliter bonis, gratia Dei præcederet merita justi, non merita gratiam; sequeretur hominem agendi quidem male, non vero bene agendi potestatem habere. Contrarium docet Aristoteles Eth. lib. 3. cap. 4. ubi probat hominem esse liberum in cunctis actionibus, tam justis, quam injustis. Si nemo potest esse aliquo modo justus, sine singulari gratia Dei, sequetur, hominem, cui Deus non concessit illam gratiam, esse malum, ac proinde Deus author peccati dici posset, eoq; injuste faceret, qui peccantem puniret. Deus non est mutabilis: cui itaq; gratiam dedit, semper fuerit justus; cui vero negaverit, semper injustus: cum sine illa gratia non possit promereri.
units.tr: Furthermore, Menasseh supports the common opinion and, to persuade the more strongly, confirms it with various arguments and reasons. He goes on thus from page 117: If, as I see some are persuaded, in morally good works the grace of God preceded the merits of the just, and not the merits grace, it would follow that man has the power to act badly, but not the power to act well. Aristotle teaches the contrary, Ethics book 3, chapter 4, where he proves that man is free in all actions, both just and unjust. If no one can be in any way just without the singular grace of God, it would follow that a man to whom God has not given that grace is evil. Consequently God could be called the author of sin, and he would act unjustly who punished the sinner. God is not changeable: therefore, to the one to whom he has given grace he will always be just, and to the one to whom he has denied it he will always be unjust, since without that grace no one can merit anything.

units.la: Atqui contrarium docet experientia: quia multi boni a bono declinant; multi vero mali respiscunt.
units.tr: But experience teaches the contrary, because many good people turn away from good, and many evil people repent.

units.la: Quin & secundum multos, Angeli sunt daemones facti. S. Scriptura Gen. XVIII. 19. introducit Deum ita de Abrahamo loquentem: Quia novi eum, præcipiet filiis suis, & domi suæ, & custodient viam Domini, ut faciant justitiam & judicium. Hinc meritis gratiam Dei acquiri, non est dubitandum. Deuter. cap. X.12. Et nunc Israel, quid Dominus Deus tuus petit à te, nisi ut timeas Dominum Deum tuum, & ambules per omnes vias ejus, & diligas eum ex toto corde tuo, &c. Unde ita argumentamur, si Deus dedisset gratiam, quæ certò ac necessario opus produceret, quod à Deo imperatur, non opus fuisset, ut Deus peteret bonum illud opus ab homine: utpote qui per gratiam acceptam sine Dei petitione hoc faceret. Dicimus igitur, Deum disposuisse ita homines, ut salus ab eorum voluntate dependeat; nec agnoscere Iudaeos gratiam nisi adjuvantem, & ad hoc utilem, ut, ubi homo coeperit, Deus finiat. In hanc quoque sententiam loquuntur Antiqui in tractatu Suca cap. 5. Appetitus hominus quotidie eum vincere studet, & in ejus mortem conspirat, ואלמלא הקדוש ברוך הוא לא יכול לו, At si Deus Benedictus non adjuvet illum, non valeat adversus illum. Idem alio quoque in loco dicunt, verbis non dissimilibus: בא ליטהר מסייעין אותו Si accesserit ad purificandum, se ipsum juvat. Quid inde planius elucet, quàm primam motionem ab homine incipere: Postea Deum uti sua erga eum misericordia, auxiliando ei, quem videt bono affectu ad virtutem & opus bonum patrandum accssisse; Quibus post interjectas lineas subjungit Menasseh: nasseh: Alterum auxilii genus est, cum Deus, bonum opus facere volenti, plurimas occasiones offert. Ita cum Abraham ante fores occasionem hospitum excipiendorum expectaret, misit ipsi Deus tres Angelos.
units.tr: Indeed, according to many, the angels became demons. Holy Scripture, Genesis 18:19, introduces God speaking thus of Abraham: For I know him, that he will command his sons and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the Lord, to do justice and judgment. From this it is not to be doubted that the grace of God is acquired by merits. Deuteronomy 10:12: And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, but that you fear the Lord your God, and walk in all his ways, and love him with all your heart, etc. Hence we argue thus: if God had given a grace which would certainly and necessarily produce the work commanded by God, there would be no need for God to ask that good work from man, since he would do it through the grace received without God's asking. We say, therefore, that God has so disposed men that their salvation depends on their will; and the Jews acknowledge no grace except one that helps, and is useful for this purpose, so that, when man has begun, God may finish. The ancients also speak to this effect in the tractate Sukkah, chapter 5: The appetite of man daily strives to overcome him and conspires for his death, [ואלמלא הקדוש ברוך הוא לא יכול לו], but if blessed God did not help him, he would not be able to prevail against it. In another place they say the same thing in not dissimilar words: [בא ליטהר מסייעין אותו], if he comes to purify himself, he is helped. What is clearer from this than that the first motion begins from man, and afterwards God, by his mercy, helps the one whom he sees to have come with a good disposition to perform virtue and good work? After some lines, Menasseh adds: The second kind of help is when God, to one who wishes to do a good work, offers very many opportunities. Thus, when Abraham was waiting before the door for the opportunity of receiving guests, God sent him three angels.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Sed proderit ulterius Judaicam de Praedestinatione mentem illustrare, ut tanto clarius illam percipiamus, quapropter testem rursus producimus Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, qui in libello de Termino vitae pag. 209, 210. sic inquit: Extra controversiam est apud Hebraeos, Deum concurrere ad actiones honestas, & quidem eas adjuvando ac promovendo. Ad eas enim perficiendas homini ope & auxilio Dei indiget. Hinc docent Magistri nostri, simulatq; homo honestam aliquam actionem proponit sibi facere, mox etiam Deum ad illam actionem volitam concurrere, & sua gratia hominem adjuvare; Tandem totum Praedestinationis negotium variis illustrant exemplis, quod patet ex Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, cum in Termino vitae a pag. 212, sic loquitur: Rem exemplo illustremus. Sumamus Iosephum, & Tarquinium: hic pulchellae faeminae amore accensus turpi & foeda labe alterius torum aspersit; ille conspecta formosa, ac libidinosae mulieris forma invictus atque immotus honeste libidini restitit. Quaeritur, quid causa fit, cur in utroque tam diverfos ac contrarios motus videamus? Sine dubio causa in homine est, nempe appetitus in uno honestus; in altero depravatus & malus: nam quia in Tarquinio erat animus aftuans libidinibus, & honestatem susque deq; habens, reliquit eum Deus sibi ac pravo desiderio suo. At quia in Iofepho erat animus, nil nisi honestum appetens, & virtutem amans, Deus illuminavit mentem ejus, ob oculos ei proponendo turpitudinem facti, injuriam mariti & heri sui, poenas infernales, quibus brevis voluptas luenda effet; atque ita earum rerum consideratione juvit eum Deus, quominus tantum flagitium committeret. Hinc Rabbini solent dicere ad illa verba Sacra Scriptura, Gen. 39. 10. Et non audivit ad eam, ut concumberet secum, ut esset cum ea. Noluit dormire cum illa in hoc mundo, nepoenas daret cum illa in altero. Quia vero utrumque opus tam Iofephi, quam Tarquinij, a libero voluntatis arbitrio profectum fuit, idcirco illum manet aeterna laus & gloria, hunc vero dedecus & exitium aeternum.
units.tr: But it will be further useful to illuminate the Jewish view of predestination, so that we may grasp it all the more clearly. For this purpose we again call as witness Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, who in his book on the Term of Life, pages 209 and 210, speaks thus: It is beyond controversy among the Hebrews that God concurs with honest actions, indeed by assisting and promoting them. For a man needs the help and aid of God to carry them out. Hence our Masters teach that as soon as a man proposes to himself to perform some honest action, God at once concurs with that intended action and helps the man by his grace; Finally, they illustrate the whole matter of predestination with various examples, as appears from Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, who in the Term of Life, from page 212, speaks thus: Let us illustrate the matter by an example. Let us take Joseph and Tarquin: the latter, inflamed with love for a beautiful woman, stained another's bed with a shameful and foul disgrace; the former, having seen the beautiful form of a lustful woman, remained unconquered and unmoved and resisted the lust honorably. The question is, what is the cause that in both we see such diverse and contrary motions? Without doubt the cause lies in the man: in one the appetite is honest, in the other it is depraved and evil; for because in Tarquin the mind was seething with lusts and held honesty in no regard, God left him to his own perverse desire. But because in Joseph there was a mind desiring nothing but what is honest and loving virtue, God enlightened his mind, setting before his eyes the baseness of the deed, the injury to his master and lord, and the infernal punishments by which a brief pleasure would have to be paid for; and thus by the consideration of these things God helped him so that he did not commit so great a crime. Hence the rabbis are accustomed to say on those words of Holy Scripture, Gen. 39. 10: And he did not listen to her, to lie with her, or to be with her. He refused to sleep with her in this world, lest he be punished with her in the other. But because each deed, both of Joseph and of Tarquin, proceeded from the free choice of the will, therefore to the one remains eternal praise and glory, and to the other shame and eternal ruin.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Masculè hanc vulgatam Judaeorum sententiam deseruit Isacus Orobius, quando sic gratiam efficacem statuere nuper fuit ausus, ut effectus infallibiliter sequi debeat, quod fluat ex divina omnipotentia, infinitaque misericordia, uti loquitur in erudita collatione cum Limborchio, pag. 83. Eam (intelligit gratiam effiefficacem) Christiani Doctores pignus, quod suo pretiosò sanguine generis humani electus Christus emit, unanimes appellarunt: Nostri vero, omnipotetiæ divinæ, atque ejus infinitæ misericordiæ & amoris præcipuum effectum; Et paulò post pergit Orobius: Quando enim Deus promittit se purificaturum, se peccata omnia mundaturum, se circumcisurum cor hominis, non quamlibet excitativam gratiam promittit, sed efficacem, ad quam sequatur effectus, ut Deus vult: & tunc facit, quod homo velit eo modo, & gratiæ gradu, quo ille scit hominem liberè, sed infallibiliter voluturum. Sic explicuit Augustinus verba ex XXX. Deuteronomij à nobis allegata: Circumcidet Dominus cor tuum: dicens: Hæc autem est evidens pollicitatio gratiæ: promittit enim se esse facturum, quod solet jubere, ut fiat. Divina certè doctrina: Iubet Deus, quod eum diligamus, quod legem ejus servemus: & quando sua bonitati placet, id ipsum facit in nobis, efficace gratia fortiter suaviter ad se nostrum velle attrahens. Sic ulterius interjectis paucis lineis continuat suam disputationem cum Limborchio: Fatemur quidem, quod homo suapte natura potest liberè peccare, & efficaciæ gratiæ resistere; Sed hoc non obstanti, quando Deus vult per suam misericordiam, facit, quod agat homo, id quod ipse vult, eo modo quo vult, quin hac infallibilitas divinæ operationis aliquo modo naturalem hominis destruat libertatem, per abditos & inaccessibilas biles modos, quibus Deus hanc infallibilem sed liberam in homine mutationem operatur.
units.tr: Vigorously Isaac Orobio departed from this common opinion of the Jews, when he recently dared to hold that efficacious grace is such that its effect must infallibly follow, since it flows from divine omnipotence and infinite mercy, as he says in his learned conference with Limborch, page 83. The Christian teachers have unanimously called it (he means efficacious grace) the pledge which Christ, the chosen one, bought for the human race with his precious blood; but ours call it the chief effect of divine omnipotence and of his infinite mercy and love. And a little later Orobio goes on: For when God promises that he will purify, that he will cleanse all sins, that he will circumcise the heart of man, he promises not some merely exciting grace, but an efficacious one, to which the effect follows as God wills; and then he does what the man wills, in the way and to the degree by which he knows the man will will freely yet infallibly. Thus Augustine explained the words of Deuteronomy 30 which we have cited: The Lord will circumcise your heart, saying: this is a clear promise of grace, for he promises that he himself will do what he is accustomed to command, that it be done. This is certainly divine doctrine: God commands that we love him and keep his law, and when it pleases his goodness he does this very thing in us, drawing our will to himself strongly and sweetly by efficacious grace. Thus, after a few intervening lines, he continues his dispute with Limborch: We admit indeed that man by his own nature can freely sin and resist the efficacy of grace; but nevertheless, when God wills through his mercy, he causes man to act, which he himself wills, in the manner he wills, yet this infallibility of divine operation does not in any way destroy the natural freedom of man, through the hidden and inscrutable ways by which God works this infallible yet free change in man.

units.la: CAPUT VI. De Creatione omnium rerum.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI. On the Creation of All Things.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: POst Decreta divina considerant opera DEI externa, בראשית Opera Creationis, quae in operum divinorum numero collocant primo loco, censentes mundi creationem creditu valde necessariam, hinc inter fidei articulos referendam, quod clare apparet tum ex primo, tum ex quarto fidei articulo, in illo enim diserte affirmatur: Fundamentum primum est, credere existentiam Dei, quod is sit causa omnium prima, primumque omnium fundamentum, & quod omnia existentia tam inferna quam superna ab illo condita sint, ac in eo consistant, ut quae ex simplici sua voluntate creavit & constituit, atque pro habitu suo abolere valet; In hoc vero scribitur, ipso non dissitente Rabbi Menasleh Ben Israel in libro de Creatione, Problemate 2. Fundamentum quartum, quod ante Deum hunc unicum & corporis experexpertem nulla res extiterit, sed ille primus sit & novissimus; Quare quoque in Catechesi Judaica respondet discipulus Doctori ad Quaestionem 13. Quod creatio mundi principium magnum sit, & fundamentum totius Legis, quodque illa suppositá facile fidem inventura sint reliqua fundamenta; Sic Rabbi Isac Sangarus in Colri Part. V. pag. 362. respondet Regi Cofri, qui quaedam de fundamentis fidei Judaicae audire desiderabat, in hunc modum: Articulus primus; Confirmanda & tenenda est Novitas mundi, haecque stabilienda per destructionem ejus Antiquitatis seu Aeternitatis; Et Abarbanel in Capite Fidei cap. 22. inquit: Si quis autem seligat cum judicio articulos, in Lege divina constituendos, is non nisi unum articulum, videlicet Creationem mundi constituet: hac enim est radix ac fundamentum, cui innititur lex atque ejus capita, omniumque siforum fides, sive de narratione primae creationis, sive etiam de historiis Patriarcharum, atque operibus prodigiosis ac miraculosis, quae nullum habent locum nisi cum fide creationis. Sic etiam fidem omniscientiae, providentiae, praemii ac poenae secundum praecepta, non poterit homo perfecte credere, nisi etiam credat universalem ac voluntariam mundi creationem; Statuunt proinde, quod, qui negat mundi creationem, simul ille fundamentum fidei tollat, totamque inficietur Legem, Haereticus & Apostata fit, qui neutiquam nonomine Israelitæ sit appellandus, uti legimus apud Rabbi Moisen Gerundensem, quando in principio Commentarii sui sic loquitur: Creatio mundi est radix totius Legis: quisquis non credit illam, atque imaginatur sibi mundum esse ab æterno, certè is negat fundamentum, neque habet Legem; In hanc rem paria docet Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, cum Problemate 1. de Creatio ‑e pag. 6. inquit: Ex his omnibus igitur manifestum fit, historiam creationis esse fundamentum, cui tota Lex innititur: Proinde qui negat aliquem ex iis tredecim articulis, non aliter dicendum esse hæreticum, quàm hæreticus dici meretur us, qui mundi creationem negat. Hoc sane antiqui Sapientes senserunt, & in libro Talmude nobis tradiderunt.
units.tr: After the divine decrees, they consider the external works of God, Bereshith [בראשית], the Works of Creation, which they place first among the divine works. They judge the creation of the world to be so necessary to believe that it must be counted among the articles of faith. This clearly appears from both the first and the fourth article of faith. In the first it is plainly affirmed: The first foundation is to believe in the existence of God, that he is the first cause of all and the first foundation of all, and that all things existing, both below and above, were made by him and consist in him, since he created and established them by his simple will and is able to abolish them at his pleasure. In the fourth, with Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel not dissenting, it is written in his book on Creation, Problem 2: The fourth foundation: before God, who is one and without body, no thing existed, but he is first and last. Hence also in the Jewish Catechism the pupil answers the teacher on Question 13: That the creation of the world is a great principle and the foundation of the whole Law, and that, this being supposed, the remaining foundations will easily be found. So Rabbi Isaac Sangarus, in the Cosri, Part V, p. 362, answers King Cosri, who wished to hear something about the foundations of the Jewish faith, in this manner: The first article: the newness of the world must be affirmed and held, and this is to be established by the destruction of its antiquity or eternity. And Abarbanel, in the Chapter of Faith, ch. 22, says: If anyone chooses with judgment the articles to be laid down in the divine Law, he will establish only one article, namely the creation of the world. For this is the root and foundation on which the Law and its chapters rest, and the faith of all the figures, whether concerning the narrative of the first creation or concerning the histories of the Patriarchs and the prodigious and miraculous works, which have no place except with faith in creation. Likewise, a man cannot perfectly believe in God's omniscience, providence, and the reward and punishment according to the precepts, unless he also believes in the universal and voluntary creation of the world. They therefore hold that whoever denies the creation of the world at the same time removes the foundation of faith and corrupts the whole Law, and becomes a heretic and apostate, who by no means is to be called by the name of Israelite. So we read in Rabbi Moses of Gerona, when at the beginning of his commentary he speaks thus: The creation of the world is the root of the whole Law. Whoever does not believe it, and imagines the world to be from eternity, certainly denies the foundation and does not have the Law. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel teaches the same thing on this matter, in Problem 1 on Creation, p. 6, where he says: From all these things, therefore, it is manifest that the history of creation is the foundation on which the whole Law rests. Accordingly, whoever denies any one of those thirteen articles is to be called no less a heretic than he who denies the creation of the world deserves to be called a heretic. Certainly the ancient Sages felt this, and have handed it down to us in the book of the Talmud.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Negant מודה עולם mundi æternitatem, disputantes operosè pro omnium rerum principio, ad imitationem Abrahami, qui contra Sabæos, Arabesque, mundi asseruerat initium, teste Maimonide in More Nevochim, maximèque impugnantes Philosophos Aristoteli-cos, ducibus Maimonide in More Nevochim Part.II. Iaco Abarbanele in מעשה אלהים Operibus Dei, Isaco Ben Arama in עקדת יצחק Ligatione Isaci, aliisque bene multis, inducti non solum inde, quod fides de מודה עולם Novitate mundi sit ab omnibus recepta populis, necessa-ria, ria, fundamentalis, Mosaicaque; sed quòd mundi antiquitas sit contra omnes Legis articulos, quòd hac ratione Deus necessariò non sit independens, nec causa sit omnium caularum, quòd nulla res possit esse coæva Deo, æqualisque; si non sit infinita, quòd universa præter Deum habeant suum principium, quòd omnes res creatæ sint finitæ, quòd in tempore sint factæ, quòd nihil sui ipsius causa possit esse sufficiens; Sic loquitur Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel in libro de Creatione, Problemate 3, pag. 12. Verum enimvero omnibus, qui sequuntur Legem Mosaicam, certò & constanter credendum est, nihil Deo esse coaeternum, & non minus materiam primam, quàm cateras res omnes principium habere; Sic Rabbi Isac Sangarus in Cosri Part. V. pag. 363. probat, quòd mundus novus sit creatus, quia corpus est: Mundus est novus creatus, quia est corpus: corpus autem nequit esse sine motu & quiete: & hæc duo sunt accidentia in eo innovata, atq; sibi invicem succedentia. Quod autem alicui accidit, id suo adventu ipso novum est, & quod transit, novum est: nam si æternum esset, non privationem pateretur: itaque sic ambo sunt nova. Quod autem non potest esse sine accidentibus de novo ipsi advenientibus, illud ipsum novum est, quia non fuit ante innovationes; cùm ergo innovata sint nova, ipsum quoque novum est; Sic demonstrat Isacus Orobius in certamine.
units.tr: They deny the eternity of the world [מודה עולם], arguing laboriously that all things have a beginning. In this they follow Abraham, who, according to Maimonides in the More Nevochim, maintained the beginning of the world against the Sabians and Arabs. They attack the Aristotelian philosophers most of all, led by Maimonides (More Nevochim, Part II), Isaac Abarbanel in Of the Works of God [מעשה אלהים], Isaac Ben Arama in The Binding of Isaac [עקדת יצחק], and many others. They are moved not only by the fact that the belief in the newness of the world is received by all peoples as necessary, fundamental and Mosaic, but also because the antiquity of the world would be contrary to all the articles of the Law. On this view God would not necessarily be independent, nor would he be the cause of all causes; nothing could be coeval and equal to God unless it were infinite; all things besides God would have their own beginning; all created things would be finite and made in time; and nothing could be sufficient to its own cause. So speaks Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel in his book on the Creation, Problem 3, p. 12: Indeed, all who follow the Law of Moses must hold with certainty and constancy that nothing is coeternal with God, and that primary matter no less than all other things has a beginning. So Rabbi Isaac Sangari in the Cosri, Part V, p. 363, proves that the world was created new, because it is a body: The world was created new, because it is a body. A body, however, cannot exist without motion and rest, and these two are accidents renewed in it and succeeding one another. Whatever happens to something is new by its very coming, and what passes away is new; for if it were eternal it would not suffer privation, and so both are new. Whatever cannot exist without accidents newly arriving in it is itself new, because it did not exist before those renewals; since therefore the renewed things are new, it too is new. So Isaac Orobio demonstrates in his Certamen.

units.la: Philosophico contra os illud Diaboli, Exjudæ-um Spinosam, quod si statuatur mundum non esse creatum, sed antiquum, æternumque, per axioma illud vulgatum : Ex nihilo nihil fit, aperiatur simul Atheismo porta ingens, infe-lixque, cum sic pag. 11. scribit: Hoc axioma male intellectum, (Ex nihilo nihil fit,) Atheismo in-felicem, sed ingentem portam aperuit. Inde infe-runt, qui in hoc misero praecipitio cecidere, quod mundus non fuerit creatus, cum ex nihilo fieri non potuisset: & consequeter quod non est Deus, iste universi opifex; quod illud ab æterno, & necessario fuit, non effectus infinitæ potentiæ, quippe a nulla poten-tia potuit fieri ex nihilo.
units.tr: Against the Devil's philosophical objection, the Jew Spinoza, that if the world is held not to be created but to be ancient and eternal, then by that common axiom, Nothing comes from nothing, a vast and unhappy gate is opened at the same time to atheism. He writes thus, p. 11: This axiom, badly understood (Nothing comes from nothing), has opened a vast and unhappy gate to atheism. From it those who have fallen into this wretched precipice infer that the world was not created, since it could not have been made from nothing; and consequently that God, the maker of the universe, does not exist; that it was from eternity and by necessity, not the effect of infinite power, since it could not have been made from nothing by any power.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Afferunt Judæi mundum conditum, non ex materia præexistente, vel ex materia prima, quoniam Scriptura nullam hujus facit mentio-nem, sicuti monstrat Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel de Creatione, Problemate 4. pag. 14. At si Scriptura diserte ait, Deum cælum terramque creasse, nulla facta mentione materiæ alicujus, quæ Deo fuerit coæterna, omnino sequitur, omnia creata esse, & ex nihilo producta a Deo fuisse, eumque solum ante cælum & terram extitisse; Quod Deus Bene-dictus sit קדוש Deus æternus, quia solus est antiquus & æternus; Quod Deus sit primus & ultimus apud Esaiam cap. 44. vers. 6. Quod anteantequam mundus crearetur, solus exiterit Deus Benedictus & nomen ejus, uti loquitur Rabbi Eliefer in Pirke, cap. 3. Quòd ante Creationem nihil fuerit præter ipsum, teste Rabbi Lipmanno in Nizzachon, pag. 77. Sed uno ore confitentur omnes, quotquot credunt Legi Mosaicæ, mundum ex nihilo factum, sic Moses Maimonides in More Novochim, Part. II. cap. 13. Prima sententia est eorum, qui credunt Legi Mosis Doctoris nostri p. m. hac videlicet, mundum totum, h. e. omnia Entia præter Creatorem, post pu-ram putam privationem (h. e. postquam non velnihil fuerunt) existentia suam à Deo accepisse, & prius Deum solum fuisse, ac præter Deum nihil plane, neque Angelos, neque Cælos, neque quæ in eis continentur, extitisse, postea vero demum secundum ejus voluntatem & beneplacitum existere cœpisse, prout sunt, & quidem ex nihilo: præterea Tempus ipsum esse ex iis, quæ creata sunt, quia Tempus sequitur motum; motus autem accidens est in re mota; & res mota, cujus motum Tempus sequitur, est innovata & fa-cta, postquam non fuit; Sic in Sepher Jezira cap. 1. sect. 5. Formavit de inani solidum & ex non ente fecit ens; Sic in Tanchuma: Cùm bonus ac benignus Deus mundum condidit, fecit il-lum ex nihilo, & de potentia eduxit in actum; Sic Rabbi Jedaja Happenini in Bakkakscha, sect. 1. Existere facit existentia ex nihilo. Ostendunt, quòd, si omnia nô creata fuissent ex nihilo, miracula omnia essent rejicienda; Quòd creatio ex nihilo rationi non repugnet naturali, uti probat Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel de Creatione, Problemate 5. pag. 21. Quod enim ab agente naturali & artificiali fieri non potest, id ab agente divino fieri potest, cujus potentia est infinita; Et pag. 21. Sed id tantum signficatum volumus, agens divinum, per immensam potentiam, dedisse mundo esse, ab eoque mundum creatum esse non ex alio praexistente, sed ut ita loquamur, post privationem universalem. Quo circa non dicimus, ipsum nihilum reductum esse ad aliquid: sed mundum accepisse suum esse, cum non haberet esse, sive post non esse; Cum quo optimè conveniunt, quæ habet Isacus Orobi in Certamine Philosophico, pag. 13, 14. Sic Deus totum hoc universum, quod in infinito esse eminenter continetur, ex sua infinitate produxit. Dicitur factum ex nihilo, quia nullus concursus materia præcesserat, ex qua fieret. Non fuit ex nihilo, quasi tò nihil in id converteretur, vel etiam facto aliqua ratione inesset, seu causationem aliquam exerceret: hoc quidem foret fieri ex aliquo; fuit ex nihilo, hoc est, antea non fuit, quàm fieret. Nec oportet aliter intelligere tò nihilum, cùm non aliud significet, quàm antea non fuisse.
units.tr: The Jews assert that the world was made not out of pre-existing matter, or first matter, since Scripture makes no mention of any such thing, as Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel shows in De Creatione, Problem 4, p. 14. But if Scripture plainly says that God created heaven and earth, with no mention of any matter that was co-eternal with God, it altogether follows that all things were created and produced by God out of nothing, and that God alone existed before heaven and earth. That God, Blessed be He, is holy [קדוש], the eternal God, because he alone is ancient and eternal; that God is the first and the last, as in Isaiah 44:6; that before the world was created, God alone existed, blessed be he and his name, as Rabbi Eliezer says in Pirke, ch. 3; that before the creation there was nothing except him, as Rabbi Lipmann testifies in Nizzachon, p. 77. But all who believe in the Law of Moses confess with one voice that the world was made out of nothing. So Moses Maimonides in More Nevochim, Part II, ch. 13: The first opinion is that of those who believe in the Law of Moses our teacher, of blessed memory, namely that the whole world, that is, all beings apart from the Creator, after pure privation (that is, after they were not, or were nothing), received their existence from God; that God alone existed before, and that apart from God nothing at all existed, neither angels, nor heavens, nor what is contained in them; but that afterwards, according to his will and pleasure, they began to exist as they are, and indeed out of nothing. Moreover, time itself is among the things that were created, since time follows motion; and motion is an accident in the moved thing; and the moved thing, whose motion time follows, has been renewed and made, after it was not. So too in Sepher Jezira, ch. 1, sect. 5: He formed the solid out of the empty, and made being out of non-being. So in Tanchuma: When the good and kind God created the world, he made it out of nothing, and brought it from power into act. So Rabbi Jedaiah Happenini in Bakkakscha, sect. 1: He makes existence to exist out of nothing. They show that if all things were not created out of nothing, all miracles would have to be rejected; and that creation out of nothing does not contradict natural reason, as Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel proves in De Creatione, Problem 5, p. 21: For what cannot be done by a natural or artificial agent can be done by a divine agent, whose power is infinite. And p. 21: But we want this only to be understood: that the divine agent, by immense power, gave being to the world, and that the world was created by him not out of any pre-existing thing, but, so to speak, after universal privation. Hence we do not say that nothingness itself was reduced to something, but that the world received its being when it had no being, or after non-being. With this agree very well the words of Isaac Orobio in Certamen Philosophicum, pp. 13–14: Thus God produced this whole universe, which is eminently contained in his infinity, out of his own infinity. It is said to be made out of nothing because no matter had preceded it out of which it might be made. It was not made out of nothing as if nothing were converted into it, or as if nothing were in it in any way once made, or exercised some causality: that would indeed be to be made out of something. It was made out of nothing, that is, it was not before it was made. Nor should nothing be understood in any other way, since it means nothing more than that it did not previously exist.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Docent mundum non esse â Deo, sed à Deo in in tempore conditum, quia cum innovatus sit, necessario requirat causam innovantem, a qua innovetur, sicuti loquitur Rabbi Isacus Sangar in Cosri Part. V. sect. 18. Quod innovatum est, non potest esse sine causa innovante illud. Quod enim innovatur, nequit esse sine temporis certi assignatione; quod potuisset esse vel prius vel posterius (velcitius veltarde us.) Appropriatio autem ad suum tempus, ut nec prius sit, nec posterius, necessario requirit Appropriatorem. Ita pariter traduntur res existentes non esse ex necessitate, quod contra Aristotelem optime probavit Rabbi Moses Maimonides in More Nevochim Part. II. cap. 22. sed esse ex intentione intendentis, proinde dependere eas ex voluntate volentis Dei secundum imperveftigabilem suam sapientiam, quod rursus probatum dedit Maimonides in More citato Part. II. cap. 19. cum dicat, quod mundus hic ipse doceat, quod sit ex intentione intendentis.
units.tr: They teach that the world was not made from God, but was made by God in time, because, since it was renewed, it necessarily requires a cause renewing it, by which it is renewed, as Rabbi Isaac Sangar says in Cosri, Part V, sect. 18: What is renewed cannot be without a cause renewing it. For what is renewed cannot be without the assignment of a certain time; it could have been either before or after (or sooner or later). But its appointment to its own time, so that it is neither before nor after, necessarily requires an appointer. In the same way, existing things are taught not to exist of necessity, which Rabbi Moses Maimonides excellently proved against Aristotle in More Nevochim, Part II, ch. 22; but to exist by the intention of one who intends, and therefore to depend on the will of a willing God according to his unsearchable wisdom. Maimonides again demonstrated this in the More cited, Part II, ch. 19, where he says that this very world teaches that it exists by the intention of one who intends.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Sed objiciunt Judæis, si ante mundum conditum solus extitit Deus, quomodo passim inculcatis ante mundi principium res alias fuisse? Nonne antiqua Talmudistarum traditio extat, septem res fuisse conditas, antequam mundus crearetur? Nonne legitis in Pesachim sol. 54. col. 1. & Nedarim sol. 39. col. 2. <bl>שבעה דברים נבראו קודם שנברא העולם</bl>
units.tr: But they object to the Jews: if God alone existed before the world was made, how do you constantly insist that other things existed before the beginning of the world? Is there not an ancient tradition of the Talmudists that seven things were created before the world was created? Do you not read in Pesachim, fol. 54, col. 1, and Nedarim, fol. 39, col. 2: "Seven things were created before the world was created" [שבעה דברים נבראו קודם שנברא העולם]?

units.la: Hebrew line as printed: שבעה דברים נבראו קודם שנברא העולם משובח ועין וגהינם וכסא כנור ובית המקדש ושמו של משיח Septem res creatæ sunt prius, quam mundus conderetur, nempe hæ: Lex, Pœnitentia, Hortus Eden, Gehenna, Solium Gloriæ, Domus Sanctuarii, & Nomen Messiæ? Nonne verba Scripturæ, quibus singula superstruitis, in Rabbi Elieleris Pirke adducitis cap.3 pag.3,4. Nonne contraria, falsaque sic docetis? Ad quæ pluribus hinc inde respondent, negantes effata hæc Talmudica, Magistrorumque, receptæ, communique sententiæ de Novitate mundi contrariari, sed facile conciliari posse, cum secundum literam ex more gentis nullo modo interpretada sint, quod allegorica sint, innuentia, septem has res non ipso facto ante mundum creatas, sed extitisse in mente Dei, inque divino Decreto maxime fuerint consideratæ, ut adeo has referant ad propositum & intentionē Dei æternam, sicut hoc testatur Rabbenu Niffim, cum in Nedarim scribit: Dei intentionem fuisse creare ista, priusquam mundum conderet; Genuinum Traditionis hunc esse sensum confirmat author libri Caphtor Vaphærach, quando sol.105. col.2. ita verba explicat: Designant hæc causam finalem, quæ præcessit cogitationem Dei Benedicti in Creatione mundi; Quod egregie quoque probat Author Nizzachon sect. Berechit, par.3. Quod dixerunt Doctores nostri piæ memoriæ memoria, septem res antecesserunt mundum: idvi-detur mihi ita explicandum esse: quod nimirum ob præstantiam, & ob bona rerum illarum, res illa prævenerint, & in mentem venisse primæ omnium perhibeantur; Quibus subjungimus Rabbi Isaacum Sangarum, qui, sicuti in rebus ante mundum creatis variat, ita quoque conciliationem hoc instituit modo in libro Cosri pag. 254. Quædam denique illarum sunt, quæ primo intuitu videntur falsæ, quarum tamen sensus, si paululum diligentia & studii adhibeatur, fit manifestus, veluti cum dicunt, septem res creatæ sunt ante mundum: Hortus Edenis, Lex, Iusti, Israelitæ, Solium Gloriæ, Hierosolyma, & Messias Filius Davidis. Quod convenit cum eo, quod Philosophi dicunt: Primum in cogitatione, ultimum est in opere. Cum ergo intentio Sapientiæ (DEI) in creatione mundi fuerit Lex, quæ est corpus sapientiæ: Portantes eam (subjectum ejus) sint justi; inter hos autem sit Solium gloriæ; justi vero nulli sint nisi de peculio (populo Dei peculiari) qui sunt Israelitæ; hic nullus locus dignus sit, nisi peculium locorum (omnium præstantissimus locus) quod est Hierosolyma; nemo eos possit conjungere, nisi creaturarum omnium præstantissima, qui est Messias filius Davidis; illorumque finis sit futurus in Horto Edenis; jure merito constituuntur ista creatura in potentia, ante creatum mundum.
units.tr: The Hebrew line as printed reads: "Seven things were created before the world was created: the Law, repentance, the Garden of Eden, Gehenna, the Throne of Glory, the House of the Sanctuary, and the name of the Messiah" [שבעה דברים נבראו קודם שנברא העולם משובח ועין וגהינם וכסא כנור ובית המקדש ושמו של משיח]. Seven things were created before the world was created, namely these: the Law, repentance, the Garden of Eden, Gehenna, the Throne of Glory, the House of the Sanctuary, and the name of the Messiah? Do you not cite, against each item, words of Scripture in Rabbi Eliezer's Pirke, chapter 3, pages 3 and 4? Do you not teach these things, which are contrary and false? To these objections many answer on various grounds, denying that these Talmudic sayings conflict with the received and common opinion of the teachers concerning the newness of the world; they hold that the matter is easily reconciled, since these sayings must by no means be interpreted according to the letter, in the manner of that people, but are allegorical and indicate that these seven things were not created in fact before the world, but existed in the mind of God and were chiefly considered in the divine decree, so that they refer these things to the eternal purpose and intention of God. Rabbenu Nissim testifies to this when he writes in Nedarim: God's intention was to create these things before he founded the world; the author of the book Caphtor Vaperach confirms that this is the genuine sense of the tradition when, at fol. 105, col. 2, he explains the words thus: These designate the final cause, which preceded the thought of God the Blessed in the creation of the world; the author of Nizzachon, section Bereshit, part 3, also proves this admirably: When our teachers of blessed memory said that seven things preceded the world, it seems to me that it must be explained thus: that, namely, on account of their excellence and their goodness those things came first, and are said to have come first into mind. To these we add Rabbi Isaac Sangari, who, as he varies on the things created before the world, so also arranges the reconciliation in this way in the book Cosri, page 254. Finally, there are some of these sayings which at first sight seem false, but whose sense becomes plain if a little diligence and study are applied; for example, when they say that seven things were created before the world: the Garden of Eden, the Law, the just, Israel, the Throne of Glory, Jerusalem, and the Messiah, son of David. This agrees with what the philosophers say: the first in thought is the last in execution. Since, therefore, the intention of Wisdom (God) in the creation of the world was the Law, which is the body of wisdom; its bearers (its subject) are the just; among these is the Throne of Glory; the just are none but the peculiar people of God, who are Israel; no place is worthy of this except the peculiar place (the most excellent of all places), which is Jerusalem; no one can join them except the most excellent of all creatures, who is the Messiah, son of David; and their end is to be in the Garden of Eden; rightly, therefore, those things are constituted as creatures in potentiality before the world was created.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Comminiscuntur Judæi mundum duplicem, antiquum unum, qui plane dissolutus sit, destru-ctusque, alterum novum, præsentem nostrum, qui ex nihilo pariter sit conditus, quod fidei Judaicæ nequaquam repugnet, sed ex litera ʼ, in voce בראשית in principio, qua Lex incipit, facile demonstrari posiit, cum nota lit numeri binarii, sicCabalistæ veteres in Tikkune haffo-har loquuntur, sicque ex antiquis existimant Rabbi Abbhu & Rabbi Jehuda, uti traditum est in Berefchit Rabba, Parafchaz ; Ita quoque arbitratur Rabbi Eliefer Germanus, Caput Synagogæ in Polonia, in Maase Adonai, quod in secunda vivamus semita, id est, mundo ; sic pariter quoque è Recentioribus deliravit Isa-cus Abarbenel, quando in Mipha Lot Elohim autumavit, hunc mundum alium esse, atq; di-stinctum à veteri ; Quod ipsum etiam Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel dementavit, cùm in gra-tiam Abarbenelis in libro de Creatione, Pro-blemate 12. sic scribit : Cùm dici posset mundum hunc præsentem conditum esse ex nihilo, & ex totali privatione, mundum verò istum, qui hunc antecessit, plane dissolutum atq; destructum fuisse, quod fidei nesquaquam repugnat. Præterea cùm Cabalistæ ve-lint, mundum terrestrem quolibet anno Sabbatico, seu singulis septem millibus annorum destrui, quis nobis certò indicabit, anstemus in prima revolutione, & non in secunda aut tertia? Egregiè interim se huic sententiæ opponit Rabbi Moses Maimonides, ostenditque cum aliis Rabbinis, quod contrarietur Legi Mosaicæ fideique articulis, quòd ita ex hac opinione mundus non sit ex nihilo conditus, sed ex præexistente materia, & proinde Deo coæterna, sicuti legimus in More Nevochim Part.II.c.30. Sed ulterius progressi sunt Cabalistæ, dum leptem mundos in cerebro suo fabricarunt, volentes quolibet anno Sabbatico majori, vel singulis leptem millibus annorum veterem mundum destrui, & alium à Deo creatum, in septimo autem mundo fore perpetuum Sabbatismum, uti extat in Pirke RabbiEliezeris, cap.18. Septem mundos creavit Sanctus Benedictus, sed ex illis omnibus non selegit nisi septimum. Sex sunt ad exeundum & ingrediendum, vel mortis & nativitatis; sed unus est totus Sabbatismus & quies in vita æterna.
units.tr: The Jews invent a double world: an ancient one, which they hold was utterly dissolved and destroyed, and a new one, our present world, which was likewise created out of nothing. This is by no means inconsistent with Jewish faith, and it can easily be shown from the letter ' in the word בראשית [bereshit], in the beginning, with which the Law begins, which carries the mark of the number two. So the old Cabbalists speak in the Tikkune haffo-har, and Rabbi Abbhu and Rabbi Jehuda, as is handed down in Bereshit Rabba, Parashah, hold this view of the ancients. Rabbi Eliezer the German, head of the synagogue in Poland, likewise thinks so in Maase Adonai, where he says that we live in the second path, that is, the world. Among the more recent writers, Isaac Abarbanel also raved in Mifpa Lot Elohim, when he judged that this world is another and distinct from the old one. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel also went mad in the same way, when, to please Abarbanel, he wrote in his book On the Creation, Problem 12, as follows: Since it could be said that this present world was created out of nothing and out of total privation, but that the world which preceded it was utterly dissolved and destroyed, this is by no means inconsistent with faith. Moreover, since the Cabbalists hold that the earthly world is destroyed in every sabbatical year, or every seven thousand years, who will tell us for certain whether we stand in the first revolution and not in the second or third? Meanwhile Rabbi Moses Maimonides opposes this opinion admirably, and with other rabbis shows that it contradicts the Law of Moses and the articles of faith, since on this opinion the world would not have been created out of nothing but out of pre-existing matter, and so would be coeternal with God, as we read in More Nevochim, Part II, chapter 30. But the Cabbalists went further still, when they fabricated seven worlds in their own brains, wishing that the old world be destroyed at every greater sabbatical year, or every seven thousand years, and another be created by God; and that in the seventh world there would be perpetual Sabbath rest. This is found in Pirke Rabbi Eliezer, chapter 18: The Holy Blessed One created seven worlds, but of all of them he chose only the seventh. Six are for going out and coming in, that is, of death and birth; but the one is the whole Sabbath and rest in eternal life.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Vendicant בריה Creationem soli Deo, negantes ullam creaturam posse creare, hinc Deum Benedictum passim vocant בורא העולם Creatorem mundi, בורא שמים והארץ Creatorem cœli & terra אלהי העולם Deum mundi, עלת העולם causam causarum seu Primam, à qua condita sint existentia omnia, tam superna, quàm inferna, ex articulo fidei Judaicæ primo, hincque fatentur in culo Be-
units.tr: They claim Creation [בריה] for God alone, denying that any creature can create. Hence they everywhere call the blessed God Creator of the world [בורא העולם], Creator of heaven and earth [בורא שמים והארץ], God of the world [אלהי העולם], and cause of causes [עלת העולם], or First Cause, from which all existing things, both above and below, were made. This follows from the first article of Jewish faith. Hence they confess, in the Be-

units.la: Berefchit Rabba, Parascha prima, quòd solus Deus creaverit universa, illudque manifestum sit ex Jesaiæ verbis, cap. 44. vers. 24. Ego Dominus feci omnia, solus extendi cœlos, terramq; per me ipsum expandi. Asserunt רוּחַ Creationem opus solius Dei esse, opusque esse infinitæ divinæ potentiæ, quæ in meram non possit cadere creaturam, teste Isaço Orobio in certamine Philosophico pag. 14. Verum est, quòd creatio, enti limitatæ potentia denegetur, quod necessariò dependenter operatur: non vero infinitæ potentiæ; Excludentes proinde omnia media, instrumenta, causas instrumentales, ipsos homines, Angelosque, quod ex allegato Berefchit Rabbæ loco sic patet: Scriptum est Iefa. XLIV. 24. Quis mecum in creatione fuit? nam Ps. LXXXVI. scriptum est, tu Deus facis mirabilia solus. In humanis quidem rebus consuetudo est, ut Rex unà cum Proceribus laudem reportet administrata Reipublicæ, quia ipsi adjuvant in sustinendo onere. Verum non ita DEVS Sanctus Benedictus, sed ipse solus creavit mundum, ipse solus istam gloriam habet, ipse solus celebrandus est per mundum suum. Dixit R. Tanchuma, Tu Deus solus creasti mundum; Ostendentes pariter, quòd Creator à creatura non possit juvari, nec creatura in Creatoris admitti consortium, ut refert Rabbi Moses Maimonides in More Nevochim. Part. II. cap. 6. Horum dictorum omnium mens & sententia non est, ac si Deus loquereloqueretur, cogitaret, consilium, & considerationem aliorum peteret, vel sententia alicujus juvaretur; nam quomodo adjuvari posset Creator a Creatura sua; sic quoque Rabbi Menasse Ben Israel in libro de Creatione, Problemate 13. pag. 55. Quam ob rem affirmamus cum iis, qui melius hac de re sentiunt, mundum universum a Deo conditum esse absq; ullo medio, uti constat ex primo Genes. In principio creavit Deus caelum & terram. Unde efficitur Deum esse authorem universi, & aliud quid statuere causam universi, Scripturis repugnare. Atq; ita antiqui sapientes censuerunt; Et pag. 56. Ex quo inferunt, in vocibus his contineri admirandum hunc articulum, quod solus Deus omnia per seipsum creaverit, quasi legeretur Deum dixisse. מיהיה שותף עמי בבריתו של עולם id est, quis fuit adjunctus mihi in creatione mundi? Ex quibus verbis concludimus non esse contra rationem, ab uno DEO emanasse totam rerum multitudinem, sive unum Deum res multas creasse; Et tandem pag. 99. subjungit Menasseh: Praeterea dici potest pluribus in locis quoque per Elohim intelligendos esse Angelos: sed nimis absurdum foret, attribuere creationem, ulli alii rei, quam primae causae. Necesse nunc est, Rabbinos quandoque vel delirare, contrariaque effutire, vel improprie ac allegorice loqui, quod manifeste in doctrina de Creatione patet, cum rejecta genuina interpretatione Verborum Genes. cap. 1. vers. 26. Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram; Loco Filii, Spiritusque Sancti substituerunt creaturas, quas allocutus fuisset Deus, ad creationem se accingens, exponentes, vel quòd fabricam coeli & terrae consuluerit, vel consultaverit Deus cum opere cujusque diei, vel locutus fuerit cum causis secundis, vel elementa allocutus fuerit, quae ad corporis humani compositionem voluerit adhibere, aut consultationem invisibilem Deum cum Angelis, aut sermonem habuisse cum intelligentiis orbium Rectoribus, aut denique Deum deliberasse cum animis, quae omnes primo die fuerint creatae, sicuti operose haec deducta cernimus apud Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel in Conciliatore super Genesin, Quaestione sexta.
units.tr: Berefchit Rabba, Parashah 1, that God alone created all things, and this is plain from the words of Isaiah 44:24: "I am the Lord who made all things; I alone stretched out the heavens, and I spread out the earth by myself." They assert that creation is the work of God alone, a work of infinite divine power, which cannot belong to a mere creature. So Isaac Orobio says in his Philosophical Contest, p. 14: It is true that creation is denied to a power that is limited, since it works necessarily by dependence, but not to a power that is infinite. They therefore exclude all means, instruments, instrumental causes, and men and angels themselves. This is clear from the passage of Berefchit Rabba already cited: It is written, Isaiah 44:24, "Who was with me in creation?" For it is written in Psalm 86, "You alone, O God, do wonders." In human affairs it is the custom that the king shares the praise for the well-run commonwealth with his nobles, because they help him bear the burden. But it is not so with the Holy Blessed God; he alone created the world, he alone has this glory, he alone is to be praised through his world. Rabbi Tanchuma said: You, God alone, created the world. They likewise show that the Creator cannot be helped by a creature, nor a creature admitted to partnership with the Creator, as Rabbi Moses Maimonides reports in More Nevochim, Part II, chapter 6: The meaning and sense of all these sayings is not that God speaks as though he thought, sought counsel and consideration from others, or were assisted by someone's opinion. For how could the Creator be helped by his creature? So also Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, in his book On the Creation, Problem 13, p. 55: Therefore we affirm, with those who judge this matter better, that the whole world was made by God without any intermediary, as is clear from the first chapter of Genesis: "In the beginning God created heaven and earth." Hence it follows that God is the author of the universe, and that to assert some other cause of the universe conflicts with Scripture. So the ancient sages also judged. And on p. 56 he adds: From this they infer that this admirable article is contained in these words, that God alone created all things by himself, as if it were read that God said: מיהיה שותף עמי בבריתו של עולם, that is, "Who was my partner in the creation of the world?" From these words we conclude that it is not contrary to reason that the whole multitude of things emanated from one God, or that one God made many things. Finally, on p. 99 Menasseh adds: Moreover, it may be said that in many places Elohim should also be understood as angels; but it would be too absurd to attribute creation to any other thing than the first cause. It is now necessary that the rabbis either rave at times and talk nonsense, or speak improperly and allegorically. This is plainly seen in their doctrine of Creation, since, rejecting the genuine interpretation of the words of Genesis 1:26, "Let us make man in our image," they substituted for the Son and the Holy Spirit creatures, with whom God is supposed to have spoken as he prepared to create. They explain this in various ways: either that God took counsel about the fabric of heaven and earth, or consulted with the work of each day, or spoke with secondary causes, or addressed the elements which he wished to use in the composition of the human body; or that God consulted invisibly with the angels, or had a discourse with the intelligences, the rulers of the spheres; or finally that God deliberated with the souls, which were all created on the first day. These things are laboriously deduced, as we see in Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel's Conciliator on Genesis, Question 6.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Communis fere Judaica doctrina hodie est, mundi creationem non momentaneam, sine temporis intervallo, dierum noctiumque successione factam, sed lex dierum spatio absolutam, quod inde probant Judaei, quia Mosis narratio de Creatione est literalis & simplex, nullam sibi admixtam habens speciem Allegoriae; quòd singuli versus in Mose indicent lex distinctos dies, & fuerit vespera ac mane unoquoque die; quod si Deus singula & universa in instanti condidisset, necesse etiam fuisse, illum eodem die, quo condidisset, quievisse, sed jam ex textu manifeste apparere, Deum quievisse tantum die septimo; quòd multa absurda ex creatione, quæ facta esset in instanti, sequerentur, scilicet quòd eodem tempore tenebræ & lux extitisset, quòd eodem tempore Adam in Paradiso & extra illum fuisset, quòd eodem tempore Adam dormivisset cum Costa, & sine ea, & simul Eva facta fuisset; Sic testatur Rabbi Moses Nachmanides seu Gerundensis, dies illos, de quibus in historia Creationis, sex dies proprios fuisse, suis propriis distinctos horis, intervallis, proin secundum literam intelligendos, quando im Commentario super Genesin cap. 1. scribit: Sciendum est, Deum solum primo die creasse entia ex nihilo, & deinceps ex fundamentis illis creatis formasse ea & fecisse; Et postea quam aquis vim dedit reptificandi animam viventem; tunc verbum de illis fuisse, reptificent aquæ, fuisse etiam verbum de jumentis, producat terra. De homine autem dixit, faciamus; Sic pariter referunt Rabbini in Pirke Rabbi Eliezeris, quòd mundus decem verbis fuerit creatus, per consequens non in instanti, sicuti legimus cap. 3. Decem verbis vel effatis creatus est mundus, eaque sunt: Et dixit Deus: Fiat lux. Et dixit Deus: Fiat expansum. Et dixit Deus: Confluant aquæ. Et dixit Deus: Herbascat terra. Et dixit dixit Deus : Sunto luminaria, Et dixit Deus: Reptilia producant aquā, Et dixit Deus: Proferat terra. Et dixit Deus: Faciamus hominem. Et dixit Deus: Ecce dedi vobis. Et dixit Deus: Non est bonum hominem esse solum; Ita quoque judicant Talmudici Doctores in Capitulis Patrum, cap. 5. leƈt. 1. simulque quaerunt, quare mundus non uno verbo fuerit creatus? Decem verbis creatus est mundus. Et quae mens est doctrina? Nonne verbo uno potuit creari mundus? Quod vero mundus decem verbis sit conditus, id colligunt ex historia Creationis. Licet autem illic nonies tantum legatur : Et dixit Deus; decimum tamen includi in verbis: In principio creavit DEUS coelum & terram; quod perinde valere dicunt, ac si legas : Et dixit Deus, fiat coelum & terra; cum nihil sine verbo sit conditum; Caeterum pluribus hanc Judaeorum sententiam non solum propugnat Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel in libro de Creatione, Problemate 10. Verum quoque ostendit, quomodo cum Iaco Abarbanele idem statuerint ex Christianis Doctoribus, Hugo, Rupertus, Lombardus, Bonaventura, Dionysius, & Thomas.
units.tr: Today almost all Jewish teaching holds that the creation of the world was not instantaneous, made without any interval of time, but was accomplished through a succession of days and nights, over a space of days. The Jews prove this from the following points: Moses' account of the Creation is literal and plain, with no admixture of allegory; each verse in Moses marks off a distinct day, and "there was evening and morning" on each day; if God had created all things at once, he would have rested on the same day he created them, whereas the text clearly shows that God rested only on the seventh day; and many absurdities would follow if creation had been instantaneous, namely that light and darkness would have existed at the same time, that Adam would have been in Paradise and outside it at the same time, that Adam would have slept with his rib and without it at the same time, and that Eve would have been made at the same moment. Thus Rabbi Moses Nachmanides, also called of Gerona, testifies that the days of the creation story were six real days, each marked off by its own hours and intervals, and so to be understood according to the letter. In his commentary on Genesis, chapter 1, he writes: It must be understood that God on the first day alone created beings out of nothing, and afterwards formed and made them from those created foundations; and after he gave the waters the power to bring forth a living soul, then the word was spoken about them, "let the waters bring forth creeping things"; there was also a word about the beasts, "let the earth bring forth." But about man he said, "let us make." In the same way the rabbis, in Pirke Rabbi Eliezer, relate that the world was created by ten words, and consequently not instantaneously, as we read in chapter 3: The world was created by ten words or sayings, and they are these: "And God said, Let there be light." "And God said, Let there be a firmament." "And God said, Let the waters be gathered together." "And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass." "And God said, Let there be lights." "And God said, Let the waters bring forth creeping things." "And God said, Let the earth bring forth." "And God said, Let us make man." "And God said, Behold, I have given you." "And God said, It is not good for man to be alone." So too the Talmudic teachers judge, in the Chapters of the Fathers, chapter 5, section 1, and at the same time they ask why the world was not created by one word: The world was created by ten words. And what is the meaning of this teaching? Could not the world have been created by one word? That the world was made by ten words, they gather from the account of the Creation. Although only nine times is it read there, "And God said," they hold that the tenth is included in the words, "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth," which they say is equivalent to reading, "And God said, let heaven and earth be made," since nothing is made without a word. Moreover, this opinion of the Jews is not only defended by many, as Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel does in his book on the Creation, Problem 10; he also shows how, with Isaac Abarbanel, the same view has been held by Christian teachers: Hugh, Rupert, Lombard, Bonaventure, Dionysius and Thomas.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Communis quoque fere sententia inter modernos est Judaeos, mundum conditum esse mense Tisri, seu Septembri, explodentes Rabbi Jehosuae decantatam opinionem, quod mense Nisan, seu Martio mundus sit creatus, amplectentes Rabbi Elieseris effatum vetus, quo mundum in Septembri formatum statuit, sicuti egregie hanc doctrinam demonstravit, Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel in libro de Creatione, Problemate 9. quam ob elegantiam, eruditionemque, & quod vexatam Chronologicam quaestionem illustret, necessario adjiciendam judicamus, cum ita multis loquitur: Ratio, qua ostenditur mundum creatu esse mense Septembri, & non Martio, prima est, quia certissimum est, & ratio ipsa naturalis dictat omnia creata esse ex sententia Sapientum in בעבינו ובקומה in maturitate sua, in pulchritudine, ac statu perfecto. Itaque arbores creatae sunt cum suis fructibus: nam primiparentes Adamus & Eva simul atque oriti sunt, ex iis comederunt; at qui mense Martio non potuerunt fructus percipi: sed Septembri, vel Octobri. II. Quemadmodum potentia prior est actu, & conceptus praecedit partum: ita etiam naturaliter annus debet incipere a tempore sationis, quo universa planta terra inseruntur; non autem ab eo tempore, quo eas terra edit in lucem. Ex auctoritate Scripturarum idemconstat. I. In Levitico jubetur decimo septimi mensis die celebrari annus Jubilaeus, qui est Tisri, sive September. Et decimo quinto ejusdem mensis, cum messis colligitur in horrea, rea, jubetur celebrari festum Tabernaculorum, ex quo apparet, cum mense Tisri jubeatur coli lubilaeum, id factum idcirco esse, quia mensis iste erat anni principium. 2. Annus Sabbaticus incipit a Septembri, (quemadmodum traditur in Gemara de Rosch Haschana) ergo initium anni est. 3. Praecipitur in Deuteronomio, ut mense Septembri universus populus conveniat ad audiendam legem. At si mensis iste non fuisset mensis primus, satium fuisset addi, in Nisan, seu Martio. Enim vero quare sex mensibus Israelita lege Domini non audiissent, cujus tamen necessaria est cognitio? 4. Lex prohibet septimo anno (cui inde Semita vocabulum) ut terra neque conseratur, neque metatur. Primum vetatur terra conseri, quod fit mense Septembri, utpote initio anni, deinde messis prohibetur. 5. Quicunque, anno sexto sementem fecerat, ei non licebat metere septimo, proinde nec septimo serere. Itaque quod satum erit anno sexto, septimo non poterit colligi, atque ita biennio intermittetur agricultura, cum Dominus tantum unum annum intermitti jusserit. Unde sequitur annum incipere a Septembri, quo agros conseri lex vetat, & quo fructus, qui provenerant, metere non licebat. 6. S. Scriptura de festo Tabernaculorum inquit, & festum colleCtionis in exitu anni: atqui festum illud colebatur mense Septembri. Ergo hoc mense revolutio sive periodus anni desiit, novusque annus cœpit. 7. Versiculum 1. Regum, quo dicitur, tur, in mense Etanim, mense septimo, divinus Io- nathan Ben Uziel paraphrastice exponens ait ירחא ירחא קומאוך דעתיקיא וקין ליה ירח mensem illum antiquitus ( ante exitum ex ⌣Aegypto ) mensium primum vocabant.
units.tr: Almost equally common among the modern Jews is the opinion that the world was made in the month of Tishri, that is, September. They reject the much-repeated opinion of Rabbi Joshua, that the world was created in the month of Nisan, or March, and they embrace the old saying of Rabbi Eliezer, who held that the world was formed in September. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel has set out this doctrine admirably in his book on the Creation, Problem 9. Because of its elegance and learning, and because it illuminates the vexed chronological question, we judge it must be added here, since he speaks at length as follows: The reason by which it is shown that the world was created in September, and not in March, is first this: it is most certain, and natural reason itself dictates, that all things were created, according to the opinion of the Sages, in their maturity, in their beauty and in a perfect state. Thus trees were created with their fruits; for the first parents, Adam and Eve, as soon as they came into being, ate from them; but in March fruit could not have been gathered, only in September or October. Second: Just as potency is prior to act, and conception precedes birth, so also by nature the year ought to begin from the time of sowing, when all plants are placed in the earth, and not from the time when the earth brings them forth into the light. The same is established by the authority of the Scriptures. First, in Leviticus it is commanded that the Jubilee year be celebrated on the tenth day of the seventh month, which is Tishri, or September. And on the fifteenth day of the same month, when the harvest is gathered into the barns, the feast of Tabernacles is commanded to be kept; from this it appears that, since the Jubilee is commanded to be kept in the month of Tishri, this was done because that month was the beginning of the year. Second, the Sabbatical year begins in September, as is handed down in the Gemara on Rosh Hashanah; therefore it is the beginning of the year. Third, it is ordered in Deuteronomy that the whole people assemble in September to hear the law. But if that month were not the first month, it would have been enough to add it in Nisan, or March. For why would the Israelites not hear the law of the Lord for six months, when its knowledge is nonetheless necessary? Fourth, the law forbids, in the seventh year (from which the Sabbatical year takes its name), that the land be sown or reaped. First the sowing is forbidden, which is done in September, as the beginning of the year; then the harvest is prohibited. Fifth, whoever had sown in the sixth year was not permitted to reap in the seventh, and therefore not to sow in the seventh either. So what was sown in the sixth year could not be gathered in the seventh, and thus agriculture would be interrupted for two years, whereas the Lord commanded only one year to be left unplanted. Hence it follows that the year begins in September, when the law forbids sowing the fields and when it was not lawful to reap the fruits that had come up. Sixth, Holy Scripture says of the feast of Tabernacles, "and the feast of ingathering at the end of the year"; but that feast was kept in the month of September. Therefore in this month the revolution or cycle of the year ended, and the new year began. Seventh, Jonathan Ben Uziel, paraphrasing the verse in 1 Kings which says, "in the month Ethanim, the seventh month," explains that the month was called in ancient times (before the exodus from Egypt) the first of the months; the Hebrew reads yarach yarach qumaukh de-atiqia ve-qin leh yarach [ירחא ירחא קומאוך דעתיקיא וקין ליה ירח].

units.la: §. In Exodo legitur, Dominum novo instituto, in memoriam egressus ex ⌣Aegypto, jussisse celebrari mensem Nisan, seu ⌣Martium, proprimo anni mense. Ergo ante id tempus annus ab eo mense non incepit, ac proinde nec eodem illo mundus conditus est.
units.tr: §. In Exodus we read that the Lord, by a new institution, in memory of the going out from Egypt, ordered the month of Nisan, or March, to be kept as the first month of the year. Therefore before that time the year did not begin from that month, and consequently the world was not created in it.

units.la: §. In Gemara Aboda Zara refertur, Adamum simul atque creatus erat, vidisse dies declinare: quod non potuit fieri, nisi mense Septembri. Denique communi fere consensu omnium cum Veterum tum Recentiorum receptum est mundum hoc mense esse conditum. Quid quod idem etiam experientia probatur: nam Ægyptii, Persæ, Graeci, & omnes Orientales populi, annum à Septembri inchoant, quod procul dubio ex recepta traditione faciunt.
units.tr: §. In the Gemara on Avodah Zarah it is related that Adam, as soon as he was created, saw the days declining, which could not have happened unless it was in the month of September. Finally, by almost common agreement of all, both the ancients and the moderns, it has been received that the world was made in this month. Moreover, experience itself proves the same: for the Egyptians, Persians, Greeks and all Eastern peoples begin their year from September, which they undoubtedly do from the received tradition.

units.la: Et quemadmodum Hebraei, ita etiam Chaldaei Septembrem appellant תשרי Tisri, quæ vox deducitur à ראשית Resit, principio, & Targum loco החלותי ponit שיתי incepit: Cabalistæ verò ajunt, quod in prima voce sacræ historiæ בראשית continentur illæ literæ בא תשרי id est, in primo mensis Tisri. Hisce sententiam nostram abundè satis probatam esse arbitramur. Caeterum observan- dum est annum duplicitèr accipi, pro anno civili & sacro.
units.tr: And just as the Hebrews, so also the Chaldeans call September Tisri [תשרי], a word derived from Resit [ראשית], beginning; and the Targum renders the Hebrew hechelothi by sheythi, "began." The Cabalists, however, say that the letters be-Tishri [בתשרי], that is, "in the first of Tishri," are contained in the first word of the sacred history, Bereshit [בראשית]. We think our view has been sufficiently proved by these arguments. Moreover, it must be observed that the year is taken in two ways, as the civil year and as the sacred year.

units.la: Civilem annum cum confiderant Hebraei, &cum de civilibus negotiis agitur, eum semper ordi‑untur in calculus & supputationibus suis a mense Tishri, sive Septembri. Sacrum vero annum, cum festa & reges Israelis numerantur, semper inchoant in calculis & supputationibus suis a mense Nisan, sive Martio; ita hanc de duplici anni principio confirmat Rabbi David Kimchi 1. Regum cap. 8. vers. 2. Antequam egrederetur Israelita ex Aegypto, Tishri fuit primus mensis, quia in Tishri fuit creatus mundus. Postquam autem egressi sunt Israelitae ex Aegypto in mense Nisan, ipse factus est initium mensium, & Tishri est ab eo septimus.
units.tr: When the Hebrews consider the civil year, and when civil affairs are at issue, they always reckon their calculations and computations from the month Tishri, that is, September. When they count the sacred year, the festivals and the kings of Israel, they always begin their calculations and computations from the month Nisan, that is, March; so Rabbi David Kimchi confirms this twofold beginning of the year, on 1 Kings 8:2: Before the Israelites went out of Egypt, Tishri was the first month, because the world was created in Tishri. But after the Israelites went out of Egypt in the month Nisan, that month became the beginning of the months, and Tishri is the seventh from it.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Concedunt omnes finem Creationis fuisse Dei gloriam, quod omnis agens, qui cum intentione agit, necessario in illa re, quam efficit, propositum sibi habeat finem aliquem, propter quem illam facit, proindeque Deum Benedictum manifestare voluisse in creaturis, suas virtutes, perfectionesque, sic enim loquuntur Magistri Judaeorum in Capitulis Patrum cap. 6. §. 11. Quodcunque Deus Benedictus in mundo creavit, ad honorem suum solum creavit, sicut dicitur Iesaiae cap. 43. vers. 7. Omnem, qui vocat se de nomine meo, quem ad gloriam meam creavi, quem formavi, quem etiam feci; Et in Catechesi Judaica respondet discipulus Doctori interroganti de fine Creationis: Quod Deus omnia omnia in gloriam suam creaverit ; Ita quoque demonstrat Maimonides, quòd hæc de fine mundi creati sententia, reperiatur tradita in libris Propheticis, utiturque quam maximè argumento ex Proverb. cap. 16. verf. 4. desum-to, cùm sic inquit in More Nevochim, Part. III. cap. 17. Omnia fecit Dominus Pemaanehu, quod exponi potest, propter ipsum, & referri ad ipsum opus. Sin autem exponatur propter se, & referatur ad efficientem, exponendum est, propter subsistantiam ejus (Dei) h. e. propter voluntatem ejus, quæ nihil aliud quàm substantia vel essentia ejus est, sicut alibi in hoc libro declaratum. Ostendimus autem quoq; quòd Gloria Dei etiâ vocetur essentia ejus ; Ast digladiantur vehementer, num dici, probarique ex Scriptura possit, quòd propter hominem omnia quoque condita sint. Arbitrantur quippe plurimi, imo omnes eruditi inter Judæos homines, teste Menasseh Ben Israel de Creatione, Problemate 29. pag. 118. quòd hominis causa omnia sint facta, imo ipsi orbes cœlestes & Angeli propter homines sint creati, in specie tamen propter bonos, pios & justos, quia illi Deum timent, eumque sedulo colunt ; quòdque mundus conditus sit ad complementum & majorem hominis perfectionem ; illudque probare intendunt ex sacra Scriptura, sicenim Moses inquit Geneleos cap. 8.
units.tr: Everyone agrees that the end of creation was God's glory, because every agent who acts with intention must have some end in view in the thing he makes, for the sake of which he makes it; and so the Blessed God willed to display his virtues and perfections in creatures. For the teachers of the Jews speak thus in the Sayings of the Fathers, chapter 6, §11: Whatever the Blessed God created in the world, he created solely for his own honour, as it is said in Isaiah 43:7: Everyone who is called by my name, whom I created for my glory, whom I formed, yes, whom I made. And in the Jewish catechism the pupil, questioned by the teacher about the end of creation, answers: that God created all things for his own glory. Likewise Maimonides shows that this opinion about the end of the created world is handed down in the Prophetic books, and he makes most use of the argument drawn from Proverbs 16:4, when he says in the More Nevochim, Part III, chapter 17: The Lord made all things Pemaanehu, which can be explained as "for himself" and referred to the work itself. But if it is explained as "for its own sake" and referred to the efficient cause, it must be explained as "for his subsistence," that is, for his will, which is nothing other than his substance or essence, as is declared elsewhere in this book. We have also shown that the glory of God is called his essence. But they dispute hotly whether it can be said and proved from Scripture that all things were also created on account of man. For most, indeed all, of the learned men among the Jews, as Menasseh ben Israel testifies in his De Creatione, Problem 29, p. 118, judge that all things were made for the sake of man, and even that the heavenly spheres and the Angels were created for men, especially for the good, pious and just, because they fear God and diligently worship him; and that the world was made for the completion and greater perfection of man. They intend to prove this from Holy Scripture, for thus Moses says in Genesis 8:

units.la: cap. 8. verf. 21, 22. Non maledicam amplius terra propter hominem. Deinceps quamdiu erit terra, sementis & messis, frigus & æstus, æstas & hiems, nox & dies non cessabunt. Quod confirmant ex Propheta Jesaia cap. 45. verf. 18. Non in vanum creavit Deus terram, sed ad inhabitandum formavit illam; Ex Jeremia cap. 33. verf. 25. Ex Ecclesiastis cap. 1. Et ex aliis locis; Sicuti cœlum propter hominem esse conditum demonstrare volunt ex Genes. cap. 1. Deus fecit duo luminaria magna, posuitq; illa in expansione cæli, ut lucerent super terram; Sed pluta pro hac sententia ex citato loco Rabbi Menassis Ben Israel peti possunt, qui ex Isaco Arama, Eliesere Germano, & Mehiro Gabai ostendit, quòd propter hominem sit factum, quicquid creatum sit. Addendum interim in illustrationem hujus doctrinæ, quòd Rabbini hominem, ob præstantiam & dignitatem, cum ad imaginem Dei sit formatus, & omnia propter ipsum condita, appellent [Hebrew] Finem seu Colophonem mundi, & [Hebrew] Mundum parvum. Qui contrarium tuentur inter Judæos, negant propter unum homuncionem totum universum, vastissimumque opus illud esse factum, cum exiguam ejus partem solum videat ac capiat, maxima vero naturæ pars adhuc lateat; Sic negat Maimonides omnia propter pter hominem esse creata, quod quaelibet res propter seipsam fit facta, cum scribit in More Nevochim, Part. III. cap. 13.
