Quocirca vera & orthodoxa sententia, quae cum principiis Legalibus & Theoreticis meo judicio convenit, est; Non credendum nobis esse, quod entia omnia sint propter hominem, sed quod singula sint sui ipsius, ni alteri, alicuius causa; Sic in specie negat orbes coelestes & Angelos propter hominem esse creatos, quod pluribus exequitur, variisque Scripturae locis firmare conatur hoc allegato, & pariter capite 14.
units.tr: chapter 8, verses 21, 22: I will no more curse the ground for man's sake... While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, night and day, shall not cease. They confirm this from the Prophet Isaiah 45:18: God did not create the earth in vain; he formed it to be inhabited; from Jeremiah 33:25; from Ecclesiastes 1; and from other places. Just as they wish to demonstrate that the heaven was made for man from Genesis 1: God made two great lights, and set them in the firmament of the heaven, to give light upon the earth. But much more for this opinion can be sought from the cited passage of Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, who, following Isaac Arama, Eliezer the German and Mehir Gabai, shows that whatever has been created was made for man. Meanwhile, to illustrate this doctrine, it should be added that the rabbis, because of his excellence and dignity, since he was formed in the image of God and all things were made for his sake, call man [Hebrew] the End or Colophon of the world, and [Hebrew] the little world. Those who hold the contrary opinion among the Jews deny that the whole universe and that vast work was made on account of one little man, since he sees and grasps only a small part of it, while the greater part of nature still lies hidden. Thus Maimonides denies that all things were created for the sake of man, and that each thing was made for its own sake, when he writes in the More Nevochim, Part III, chapter 13: Therefore the true and orthodox opinion, which in my judgment agrees with the legal and theoretical principles, is this: we must not believe that all beings exist for the sake of man, but that each exists for its own sake and not for the sake of another. So in particular he denies that the heavenly spheres and the Angels were created for man, which he pursues at length, and tries to confirm with various passages of Scripture, and likewise in chapter 14.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Inter res creatas, animas collocant humanas, quas omnes simul primo die, in principio creationis formatas sentiunt, sic plerique Hebraeorum apud Rabbi Menassen Ben Israel in Conciliatore ad Genef. Quaest. 6. Quemadmodum animae jam primo die creatae erant (quod plerique Hebraeorum sentiunt.) Sic ex communi opinione omnium Hebraeorum apud eundem Menassen in libro de Creatione, Problemate 15. pag. 61. Non solum communis opinio est omnium Hebraeorum, animas humanas praecessisse corpora, sed eam opinionem etiam amplexi sunt Hermes Trismegistus, Pythagoras, Plato, & alii plures ex Gentilibus; quae certe ad illos ab Hebraeis manavit; Praedicant animas istas omnes felices, beatasque, inque glorioso vixisse statu, antequam corpus informarent humanum, ita rursus Rabbi Menaffeh Ben Israel de Resurrectione lib. II. cap. 19. Quod ad Hebraeos attinet, qui dicunt, animas omnes olim in principio rerum omnium creaturarum creatas esse; Ex eorum opinione certum est, quod quemadmodum aliquot centenis annis animae ist a felices ac beatae fuerunt in glorioso isto suo statu, antequam informarent corpus: ita etiam post mortem tales esse possint. Credunt animas omnes primo die cum luce creatas esse; sic denuo RabbiMenassfeh Ben Israel de Creatione, Problemate 16. pag. 68. Hominum animae, procul omni dubio, primo die cum luce sunt creatae; Sic testantur in Tanchuma, Parascha Pikkude, quod omnes animae ab Adamo usque ad finem mundi creatae fuerint lex diebus creationis, omnesque fuerint in horto Edenis; Probare vero contendunt opinionem suam ex diversis Scripturae dictis, quod Jesaias cap. 57. dicat: Animas ego feci: Ex quo concludunt animas omnes in ipso mundi principio fuisse formatas, cum non dicatur, facio in tempore praesenti, sed feci in praeterito; Quod Deut. cap. 29. verf. 14, 15. dicatur: Neque vobiscum solis ego pango foedus meum hoc cum adjuratione hac; sed cum eo, qui adstat hic nobiscum hodie, coram Domino Deo nostro, & cum eo, qui non est hic hic nobiscum hodie ; Ex quo sequi putant omnes animas praelentes fuisse, tam corpore vestitas, quam eas, quae nondum induerunt corpus, cum Deus foedus inire non potuerit cum iis, qui in rerum natura nondum existebant; Idem demonstrare volunt ex Jeremia cap. 1. Antequam te formassem in ventre, indidi tibi sapientiam, & antequam ex utero matris prosiliisses sanctificavi te, Prophetam gentium constituite; Quod scilicet anima Jeremiae extiterit, antequam in utero formatum esset corpus teste Isaco Abarbanele ad hunc locum : Anima hominis intelligens non est facultas vel dispositio, neq; etiam fit, quando fit corpus, nec perit, corpore pereunte, sed corpus formatur in ventre, anima vero ejus creata est in hexaemero, & est spiritus separatus, qui ex decreto creatoris sui suum ingreditur corpus. Unde dixit Dominus Ieremiae, quod antequam formaretur corpus ejus in ventre matris ejus, jam instillata fuisset in animam ejus scientia multa. Et sic explicant sapientes p.m. illud: antequam formarem te in utero. Sic statum animae felicem antequam in hunc mundum compingitur & corpore unitur, designari credunt apud Salomonem in Ecclesiaste cap. 4. ¶ 2. Laudo magis mortuos, qui sunt mortui, quam vivos qui etiamnum vivunt, & praeutrusq; eum, qui nondum natus est; Ex Jobo denique cap. 3. ¶ 11. Subsidium sententiae petunt, quando Dominus ficipsum alloquebatur : Noveris tejam tum natum fuisse ; Petetum illud intelligentes principium mundi, ita ut ab illo tempore secundum animam natus fuerit. Plura rei hujus suppeditare potest testimonia Rabbi Menasleh Ben Israel qui in libro de creatione problemate 15. nonsolum testatur opinionem hanc ab omni antiquitate esse receptam, nunquam in controversiam voca tam, omniumque sapientum consensu ac calculo comprobatam, sed pariter adducit Bereschit Rabba, ubi super illud, faciam hominem, Parascha 8. dicitur: Deum locutum esse cum animabus ; Sic Gemaram Chagigæ cap. 2. ubi refertur in cœlo Empyræo præter varia domicilia, esse etiam aliqua animarum istarum, quæ in mundum venturæ sunt. Sed satis de his, cum plura reperiantur in Medrasch Tillim, & in Jalkut ad Psalmum 139. In libro Malkiel, aliisque ; Sic apud Slevogtium in erudita disputatione de Creatione primi hominis contra Hebræos.
units.tr: Among created things they place human souls, which they hold were all formed together on the first day, at the beginning of creation. So most of the Hebrews, as Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel reports in his Conciliator on Genesis, question 6: As the souls were already created on the first day (which most of the Hebrews hold). Likewise, according to the common opinion of all Hebrews, in the same author's book on Creation, problem 15, p. 61: It is not only the common opinion of all Hebrews that human souls existed before their bodies, but Hermes Trismegistus, Pythagoras, Plato and many other Gentiles also embraced this opinion, which surely came to them from the Hebrews. They preach that all these souls were happy and blessed, and lived in a glorious state before they informed a human body. So again Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, On the Resurrection, book 2, ch. 19: As for the Hebrews, who say that all souls were created long ago at the beginning of all creatures, it is certain by their opinion that, just as for some hundreds of years those souls were happy and blessed in that glorious state of theirs before they informed a body, so after death they can likewise be such. They believe that all souls were created on the first day, together with the light. Again Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, On Creation, problem 16, p. 68: Without doubt, the souls of men were created on the first day, together with the light. So they testify in the Tanchuma, Parashah Pikkude, that all souls from Adam to the end of the world were created during the days of creation, and that all were in the garden of Eden. They try to prove their opinion from various sayings of Scripture: Isaiah ch. 57 says I made souls, from which they conclude that all souls were formed at the very beginning of the world, since it is not said "I make" in the present tense but "I made" in the past. Deut. ch. 29, vv. 14, 15 says: Neither do I make this covenant with this oath with you only, but with him who stands here with us today before the Lord our God, and with him who is not here with us today. From this they think all souls existed beforehand, both those clothed with a body and those who had not yet put on a body, since God could not make a covenant with those who did not yet exist in the nature of things. They wish to show the same from Jeremiah ch. 1: Before I formed you in the womb I put wisdom in you, and before you came forth from the mother's womb I sanctified you and appointed you a prophet to the nations. That is, the soul of Jeremiah existed before the body was formed in the womb, as Isaac Abarbanel testifies on this passage: The understanding soul of man is neither a faculty nor a disposition, nor does it come into being when the body comes into being, nor does it perish when the body perishes; but the body is formed in the womb, while its soul was created in the six days, and it is a separate spirit which, by the decree of its Creator, enters its body. Hence the Lord said to Jeremiah that before his body was formed in his mother's womb, much knowledge had already been infused into his soul. And so the wise men explain that saying, before I formed you in the womb. They believe that the happy state of the soul before it is fitted into this world and united with a body is indicated in Solomon's Ecclesiastes ch. 4, ¶ 2: I praise the dead who are already dead more than the living who are still alive, and more than both he who has not yet been born. Finally, from Job ch. 3, ¶ 11, they seek support for their view, when the Lord addressed himself: Know that you were then already born; understanding then as the beginning of the world, so that from that time he was born according to the soul. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, in his book On Creation, problem 15, can supply more testimonies to this matter. He not only attests that this opinion has been received from all antiquity, never called into controversy, and confirmed by the consensus and reckoning of all the wise, but also cites the Bereshit Rabba, where on the words let us make man, Parashah 8, it is said that God spoke with the souls. So too the Gemara of Chagigah ch. 2, where it is reported that in the Empyrean heaven, besides various dwellings, there are also some of those souls that are to come into the world. But enough of these things, since more are found in the Midrash Tillim, in the Jalkut on Psalm 139, in the book Malkiel, and elsewhere; so also in Slevogt's learned disputation on the Creation of the first man against the Hebrews.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Credunt, non omnes cum veteribus Cabalistis animas humanas in creationis principio formatas esse pares, geminas, conjugesq;, animasq; maris & fœminæ in initio fuisse conjunctas, hinc felicia, pacataque oriri conjugia, si primo juncta, in corporibus rursus conjungantur, infelicia vero infaustaque provenire matrimonia, si ab initio in prima creatione separatae, disjunctaeque, in corporibus conjungantur, sic loquitur Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, quem audire, non injucundum auribus esse puto, lib. III. de Resurrectione mortuorum c. 9. a pag. 326. Sed tamen iis occurri Potest commode, admissa opinione Cabalistarum in Zoar, quae est, omnium animas spatio sex dierum creationis pares sive conjuges conditas esse, id est, animam maris, & foeminae pariter, ac conjunctim. Deinde hominem si mereatur & dignum se praestet jungi matrimonio cum suo pari: si demereatur aut indignum se praestet, jungi alii, quae illi vice poenae, ac tormenti est, & a qua non nisi per mortem liberatur; aut si foemina ista mereatur, conjungi tandem suo pari: si id non contingat, eum semper hic a propria, ac naturali socia sejunctum ac separatum vivere. Atque hoc innuunt Psal. 68.7. Deus facit habitare unos in domo, educit vinctos in compedibus: Sed rebelles habitant in sicco, Unos inquit, id est, quorum animae unitae fuerunt in principio creationis, illos Deus jungit & copulat matrimonio, faciendo ex illis domum. Qui ob peccata veluti vinculis constricti sunt eos morte atque obitu alterius, ex carcere ipso Deus eripit, si poenitentiam factorum egerint; Sed qui sunt rebelles, & in malo pervicaces, sine liberis, sine volupta-te, te, steriles, & tristes vitam finiunt. Itaque cum anima maris, & foemina in principio creationis copulata, ac sociata fuerint, directa via unica cuique conjux propria, ac naturalis est, indirecta via aliae omnes propter peccata impropriae sunt. Hinc fit, inquiunt illi Theologi, ut illi, qui in diversis urbibus, ac regionibus habitant, hac vel illa occasione ad se mutuo accedentes, connubio jungantur. Hinc etiam fit, ut quis pacifice ac quiete vivat cum deformi conjuge, & contra cum formosa plenam contentionis & rixarum tristemque vitam transigat. Idcirco ajunt, vera, ac propria matrimonia contrahi singulari ratione, per manum Dei; reliqua vero consilio, atque industria humana; uti Talmude videre est, in quo legimus, quod percunctanti cuidam matronae, quid Deus egerit, agatque post creationem mundi, R. Iosef Bar Halpeta respondERIT, matrimonio homines jungit. Quod illa risu excipiens, inquit, idem ego etiam praestare possim ac statim connubiis junxit servos, servasque, quos domi suae alebat. Sed haud ita multo post comperit, quantum distaret opus DEI ab opere humano: Nam, quos conjuges fecerat, ii rixis & contentionibus inter se mutuo detertabant, & divellebantur a se invicem, uti in omnibus infaustis connubiis fieri solet. Paria recenset Menasseh Ben Israel in libello de Termino vitae pag. 207. Et in Tractatu de Anima lib. 2. cap. 8. quae ad majorem lucem conferri bene merentur.
units.tr: They believe, with the ancient Cabalists, that not all human souls were created in the beginning as equal pairs, twins, and spouses; that the souls of man and woman were joined together at the beginning, so that happy and peaceful marriages arise when those first joined are joined again in bodies, whereas unhappy and unlucky marriages result when those separated and disjoined from the beginning of creation are joined in bodies. So speaks Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, whom I think it is not unpleasant to hear, in Book III of On the Resurrection of the Dead, chapter 9, from page 326. Yet this can conveniently be met, granting the opinion of the Cabalists in the Zohar, which is that the souls of all were created in pairs or spouses within the six days of creation, that is, the soul of man and of woman created equally and together. Then, if a man deserves it and proves himself worthy to be joined in marriage with his equal, he is joined to her; if he does not deserve it or proves himself unworthy, he is joined to another, which is for him a punishment and torment in place of marriage, and from which he is freed only by death. Or, if that woman deserves it, she is at last joined to her equal; if this does not happen, he lives here always separated and parted from his own and natural companion. And this is what Psalm 68:7 hints at: "God setteth the solitary in families, he bringeth out those which are bound with chains; but the rebellious dwell in a dry land." "The solitary," he says, that is, those whose souls were united at the beginning of creation: God joins and couples them in marriage, making a family of them. Those who, bound as with chains on account of their sins, are set free from the prison itself by God through the death or departure of the other, if they have done penance for their deeds; but those who are rebellious and obstinate in evil end their life without children, without pleasure, barren and sad. And so, since the soul of man and of woman were coupled and joined together at the beginning of creation, the one direct way gives each one a single proper and natural spouse; by indirect ways all the others are improper because of sins. Hence it happens, those theologians say, that those who live in different cities and regions, coming to one another on this or that occasion, are joined in wedlock. Hence also it happens that one man lives peacefully and quietly with an ugly wife, and on the contrary another spends a life full of strife and quarrels and sadness with a beautiful one. Therefore they say that true and proper marriages are contracted in a singular manner, through the hand of God; the rest, however, by counsel and human industry, as may be seen in the Talmud, where we read that when a certain matron asked what God had done and was doing after the creation of the world, R. Jose Bar Halpeta answered that He joins men in marriage. She, receiving this with laughter, said that she herself could do the same, and at once joined in marriage the male and female servants whom she fed in her house. But not long afterwards she learned how far the work of God differed from the work of man: for those whom she had made spouses vexed one another with quarrels and contentions and were torn apart from each other, as usually happens in all unlucky marriages. Menasseh Ben Israel lists similar things in the little book On the Term of Life, page 207, and in the Treatise on the Soul, book 2, chapter 8, which are well worth comparing for greater light.

units.la: XIII. Sta-
units.tr: XIII. Sta-

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Statuunt Angelos non æternos, necab æterno creatos, nec ante creationem mundi factos, quod creatio consistere non n possit eum æternitate, sed cū reliquis rebus in tex illis primis diebus creatos, quoniam in Decalogo Exodi 20. dicitur, Deum sex dierum spatio fecisse cœlum & terram, omniaque quæ illis continentur, proinde quoque Angelos, cum non minimam universi faciant partem; Præterea quod Sacra Scriptura non minus de Angelorum creatione testetur, quam de creatione aliarum rerum, quando summatim comprehendendo cap. 2. Genesios, omnia ea, quæ creata sunt, dicit: Et perfecti sunt cœli, & terra, & omnis exercitus illorum; Ex quo loco deducit Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel de creatione, Problemate 24. pag. 94. Eadem plane ratione qua exercitus terræ, sunt, plantæ, pisces, aves, quadrupedia & homines: cœlorum autem exercitus esse stellas, & Angelos, uti traditur in Midras Anehelam; Probatque Angelos dici exercitus cœli ex lib. 1. Regum, cap. 22. v. 19. Vidi Dominum insidentem solio suo, & totum exercitum cœli adstantem, a dextra ejus, & a sinistra ejus; Sic Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel demonstrat ulterius Problemate 25. Angelorum in Historia Creationis fieri mentionem, refutatque Doctissimum Abenezram, Ezram, quod cum cœli expressam mentio-nem faciat Moses, implicite simul memine-rit Angelorum. Statuuntin specie Angelos bonos primo die creatos, idqueindicari ex versibus primis capitis primi Genefios, sed in-certum Judæis in quibus vocibus & qua ratio-ne, cum Rabbi MoiesGerundensis per vocem בני bonos intelligi putet Angelos, quod sæpe hac nuncupatione veniant, RabbiLevi Ben Gersom vero per אור Lucem primo die creatam indigitet Angelos, Cabbalistæ deni-que in voce שמים Cœli Angelos reperiant, Isac Abarbanel quoque in Parafcha Berefchit per בני רוח Spiritum Dei super aquas vo-lantem, significari autumet Angelos, juxta il-lud Psalmographi Ps. 104. v. 4. Qui facit Angelos suos spiritus; vocari autem eos spiritus Dei, quia propriores sunt ejus formæ & perfectioni; audiamus proinde rursus Menassen. Ben Isra-el, qui Problemate 26. de Creatione ostende-re laborat, angelos primo die esse creatos, cum sic scribit: Ex iis, quæ precedenti capite dicta sunt, facile potest colligi eos omnes, qui volunt primo versu notari creationem Angelorum, etiam statuere Angelos primo die creatos esse. Quod certissime cre-dendum est. Quoniam tam nobiles creaturas, con-veniebat existere ante alias res omnes, quemadmo-dum etiam anima humana extiterunt ante corpora. Sed observandum est, antiquos Sapientes, cum dif-quirunt de Angelis, sint ne secundo, an quinto die creati, non agere de bonis, sed malis. Confer Rabbi Menasses Ben Israel Conciliatorem, Quæstione 12. super Genesin, pag. 19, 20. ubi plu-ribus.
units.tr: They hold that the angels were not eternal, nor created from eternity, nor made before the creation of the world, since creation cannot be reconciled with eternity. Rather, they were created together with the other things in those first days. For the Decalogue in Exodus 20 says that God made heaven and earth and all that is in them in the space of six days, and therefore the angels too, since they form no small part of the universe. Moreover, Holy Scripture bears witness to the creation of the angels no less than to the creation of other things, since in summarising the whole in Genesis 2 it says: "And the heavens and the earth were finished, and all their host." From this passage Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel deduces, in De Creatione, Problem 24, p. 94: "In exactly the same way that the host of the earth consists of plants, fishes, birds, quadrupeds and men, the host of the heavens consists of the stars and the angels, as is handed down in the Midrash Anehelam." He also proves that the angels are called the host of heaven from 1 Kings 22:19: "I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him, on his right hand and on his left." So Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel further shows, in Problem 25, that mention of the angels is made in the history of creation, and he refutes the very learned Abenezra and Ezra, who say that although Moses makes express mention of the heavens, he implicitly remembers the angels at the same time. They hold that the good angels in particular were created on the first day, and that this is indicated by the first verses of the first chapter of Genesis; but the Jews are uncertain in which words, and on what ground. Rabbi Moses of Gerona thinks that by the term "sons" [בני] the good angels are meant, since they often come under this name; Rabbi Levi Ben Gershom, however, takes "light" [אור], created on the first day, to designate the angels; the Cabbalists, finally, find the angels in the word "heavens" [שמים]; and Isaac Abarbanel, in the Parashah Bereshit, holds that by "the Spirit of God" [בני רוח] moving over the waters the angels are signified, in line with the words of the psalmist, Psalm 104:4: "who makes his angels spirits." They are called spirits of God, he says, because they are closer to his form and perfection. Let us hear again Menasseh Ben Israel, who, in Problem 26 on the creation, labours to show that the angels were created on the first day. He writes thus: "From what has been said in the preceding chapter it can easily be gathered that all those who wish the creation of the angels to be noted in the first verse also hold that the angels were created on the first day. This must be believed most certainly. For since creatures so noble ought to exist before all other things, just as the human soul existed before the bodies. But it must be observed that the ancient sages, when they inquire whether the angels were created on the second or the fifth day, are not speaking of the good but of the evil." Compare Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, Conciliator, Question 12 on Genesis, pp. 19–20, where there is more to be found.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Angelos malos cum inferno secundo die creatos, multorum Judæorum, tam Veterum, quàm Recentiorum omnium est, sicut ipsos Dæmones substantias esse corporeas, aerias, igneasque, ex duobus Elementis subtilissimis conflatas, quod probare conantur ex Psalmo 104. vers. 4. Faciens Angelos suos רוחות ventos, Ministros suos אש ignem flammantem, sicut testatur, approbatque Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, de Creatione, Problemate 13. Caterum quod ad creationem eorum attinet, no abfimiliter avero dici potest, eos simul in inferno creatos esse. In Berefit Rabba probatur hoc ex Psalmista, Pfal. 104. Qui contignat aquas in aquis superiora ejus, qui ponit nubes currum suum, qui ambulat super extremitates venti, qui facit Angelos spiritus, ministros suos ignem urentem. Ex quo perspicimus eos non tantum creatos esse isto tempore, quo Deus dividebat aquas ab aquis, quod accidit die secundo: verum etiam corpora eorum compositae esse ex duobus elementis subtilissimis, aere scilicet & igne, uti ante à nobis nobis dictum est; Et de Resurrectione mortuorum lib.III. cap.6. pag.298. Hoc ipso die (loquitur Menasseh de secundo) malignos spiritus, ac daemones cum inferno creatos esse antiquitus testantur, quorum sedes est in aere, ut supplicium sumant, iubente Deo, de malis & improbis; Quod veri Judaei antiqui crediderint Infernum secundo die creatum esse, id clare videmus ex Pesach Scheni, in quo distinctione quae incipit à שפ siclo-quitur: Rabbi Iosephi dixit, Ignis quem Deus Sanctus & Benedictus creavit in secunda Sabbathi, id est, feria secunda, non extinguetur in aeternum, sicut dictum, Esaiae ultimo ‎פ. 24. Et egredientur & videbunt cadavera virorum reorum in me, quia vermis eorum non morietur, & ignis eorum non extinguetur, & erunt sicut abhorrentes vermium universa carni; Hinc Judaeorum Magistri scribunt, diem secundum caruisse benedictione, quia in eo creatus esset infernus, sicut rursus in Pesach Scheni loco citato: Traditio quoque est dixit Rabbi Benaah, cur non fuit dictum in secunda Sabbati, Genes.1. Et vidit Deus quod esset bonum! Propterea quod in ea creatus est ignis Gehennae; Hinc quoque consultum iudicarunt Rabbini, ne quis secundo die Septimanae novum adgrediatur opus. Fatendum interim, quod haec de malis angelis creatis opinio non omnibus arrisit Judaeis, tum quod mala, turpiaque non sint creata, nec possint à bono provenire Deo, teste Maimonide in More Nevochim, Part. III. cap. 10. Liquet in rei veritate, quod de Deo Optimo & Maximo non posse absolute dici, quod malum per se faciat, quod intentio ejus prima & principalis sit, facere malum. Hoc inquam nullo modo dici potest. : Nam actiones ejus omnes sunt optima; Tum quod Rabbini apud Elieserem in Pirke cap. 14. asserant, Sammaelem cum turma Angelorum praecipitatum e loco sanctitatis seu e coelo cecidisse; Praeterea quae Cabalistae referant Angelorum Hazae & Hazaelis lapsum apud Menasseh Ben Israel de Creatione, Problemate 17. ut ita communis fere videatur esse sententia, Angelos aliquos malos creatos non formaliter, quasi eorum natura seu essentia mala creata sit, sed effective, quatenus Angeli damni sint, qui ex mandato Dei puniunt, damnumque inferunt hominibus, prout pluribus demonstrabimus capite octavo de Angelis.
units.tr: That the evil angels were created on the second day together with hell is the opinion of many Jews, both ancient and modern, as is also held of the demons themselves: that they are corporeal substances, aerial and fiery, compounded of two most subtle elements. They try to prove this from Psalm 104:4: "making his angels winds [רוחות], his ministers a flaming fire [אש]," as Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel testifies and approves in De Creatione, Problem 13: "As for their creation, it can not unreasonably be said that they were created together in hell." In Bereshit Rabba this is proved from the psalmist, Psalm 104: "who lays the beams of his chambers in the waters, who makes the clouds his chariot, who walks upon the wings of the wind, who makes spirits his angels, his ministers a burning fire." From this we see that they were created not only at that time when God divided the waters from the waters, which happened on the second day, but also that their bodies are composed of two most subtle elements, namely air and fire, as we said before. And in On the Resurrection of the Dead, book 3, chapter 6, p. 298, Menasseh says (speaking of the second day): "On this very day, ancient testimony tells that the malignant spirits and demons were created together with hell, whose seat is in the air, to take punishment, at God's command, from the evil and wicked." That the true ancient Jews believed hell to have been created on the second day we see clearly from Pesach Sheni, where a discussion beginning with the letter shin says: "Rabbi Joseph said: the fire which God the Holy and Blessed created on the second day of the week, that is, on Monday, shall not be quenched for ever, as is said in Isaiah 66:24, the last chapter: 'And they shall go forth and look upon the carcasses of the men that have transgressed against me; for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they shall be an abhorring unto all flesh.'" Hence the masters of the Jews write that the second day lacked the blessing, because hell was created on it. So also in Pesach Sheni, in the passage cited: "There is also a tradition, said Rabbi Benaah: why was it not said on the second day of the week, 'And God saw that it was good' (Genesis 1)? Because the fire of Gehenna was created on it." Hence also the rabbis judged it advisable that no one should begin a new work on the second day of the week. It must be admitted, meanwhile, that this opinion, that evil angels were created, did not please all Jews, because evil and foul things were not created, nor can they come from God who is good; Maimonides attests this in Guide of the Perplexed, part 3, chapter 10: "It is clear in the truth of the matter that it cannot be said absolutely of God, the Best and Greatest, that he does evil of himself, that his first and principal intention is to do evil. This, I say, can in no way be said: for all his actions are most good." Also, the rabbis in Elieser's Pirke, chapter 14, assert that Samael fell from the place of holiness, that is from heaven, together with a troop of angels; and the Cabbalists relate the fall of the angels Haza and Hazael, according to Menasseh Ben Israel, De Creatione, Problem 17. So the view seems almost common, that some angels were created evil not formally, as if their nature or essence were created evil, but effectively, insofar as they are angels of harm, who by God's command punish and inflict injury on men; as we shall demonstrate at length in chapter 8 on the angels.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Docent Judaei coelum animatum, seu stellas rationales esse conditas, atque praedita esse intellectu voluntate, amoreque vocantes orbium coelestium animas beatas, justas, pias, sanctasque, sed distinctas tum ab animis angelicis, tum a mentibus humanis, mediumque quasi occupantes locum, quodque voluntatem Dei in infeInferioribus exequantur, obeantque functiones suas cum amore & fidelitate erga Creatorem, Deum benedictum, testanteSacraScriptura, maxime Psalmo 19. v.1. Cœli enarrant gloriam Dei! Et Nehemiæ cap.9. v.6. Et exercitus cœlorum adorant te; Et Jobi cap. 38. v.7. Cum canerent stellæ matutinæ, & jubilarent omnes filii Dei; Quod fausta, infaustaque determinentur ab astris, imo vitæ, mortisque apud homines sint moderatrices; Quod quoque plantæ & germina suis subfintsyderibus, a quibus regantur, influxumque recipiant. Sed non nova hæc opinio est, heri nudiusque tertius inter Judæos nata, verum a longa antiquitate inter ipsos recepta, cui rei testis est Philo Judæus, cum sic scribit in libro de mundi opificio: Alia res sola virtute prædita nihil omnino habent vitii, ut stellæ; Nam hæ animalia esse dicuntur, & quidem intelligentiæ, velpotius mentes singulares totæ quantæ probæ, nec ullius capaces vitii; Et in libro de Gigantibus: Cœlum, item sidera. Hæc enim in totum sunt animæ immortales divinaque & ideo moventur in orbem, qui motus mentis cognatus est. Horum enim singulorum mens est integerrima; Ita pariter plerosque hac sententia imbutos fuisse, extra omnem positum est controversiam. Eligamus primipilum Maimonidem in Constitutionibus de Fundamentis Legis cap. 3. Sect.
units.tr: The Jews teach that the heavens are animate, that is, that the stars were created as rational beings, endowed with intellect, will and love. They call the souls of the heavenly spheres blessed, just, pious and holy, but distinct both from the angelic souls and from human minds, occupying as it were a middle place. They hold that these souls carry out the will of God in lower things and perform their functions with love and faithfulness towards the Creator, blessed God, as Sacred Scripture attests, especially Psalm 19:1, The heavens declare the glory of God! and Nehemiah 9:6, and the host of heaven worships you; and Job 38:7, when the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy. They hold that fortunate and unfortunate events are determined by the stars, and indeed that the stars govern the life and death of men; that plants and seeds also are subject to their stars, by which they are ruled and from which they receive influence. But this opinion is not new, born only the other day among the Jews; it has been received among them from long antiquity. Philo the Jew is a witness to this, when he writes thus in the book On the Creation of the World: Other things endowed with virtue alone have no vice at all, such as the stars; for these are said to be living beings, indeed intelligences, or rather whole and single minds, wholly upright, and not capable of any vice; and in the book On the Giants: The heaven, likewise the stars. For these are wholly immortal and divine souls, and therefore they move in a circle, which motion is akin to mind. For the mind of each of them is most pure; That most of them were imbued with this opinion is beyond all dispute. Let us take as our leading witness Maimonides, in the Constitutions on the Foundations of the Law, chapter 3, section

units.la: 11. Sic differentem : Omnes stellae atque orbes praediti sunt anima, notitia atque sapientia; atque vitam agunt, permanentque, & cognoscunt eum, cuius dicto factus est mundus, unaquaeque pro ratione dignitatis atque excellentia sua celebrat atque glorificat formatorem suum uti Angeli: Et uti cognoscunt Deum, sic etiam intelligunt semetipsos, atque apprehendunt angelos, qui sunt supra illos; Sed cognitio stellarum & orbium est inferior notitia Angelorum, major autem cognitione hominum; Et in more Nevochim Part. II. cap. 7. Haec omnia docent te, quod apprehendant opera sua, quodque voluntatem & electionem habeant in regimen illud quod eis datum est (hoc est in ea, quorum regimen & gubernatio illis concessa est,) quemadmodum & nos voluntatem & electionem habemus in regimine illo, quod nobis datum est, illudque a momento nativitatis in potestate nostra habemus. Hac tamen cum differentia; quod nostrae actiones sunt viliores, & quod gubernationem ac operationem nostram praecedat privatio; Intelligentiae vero & Sphaerae semper faciant bonum, & quod apud eos nihil sit nisi bonum, (sicut in sequentibus capitibus explicabimus, & quicquid habent, id in perfectione & actu semper eis insit a primo eorum principio; Cui jungamus Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel libro de Creatione, Problemate 25. pag. 98. Nam caeli secundum Rabbi Moysem, & rei veritatem, habent animas proprias. prias, rationali vita praeditas, sicuti alibi a me de-monstrabitur. Caeterum de hac Judaeorum opinione bene consuli poterit Paulus Ricius, Ex-Judaeus, qui postquam Messiae Servatori nomen dedit, compendium de anima coeli composuit, illudque ex Scriptis Propheticis illustravit, quod inter arctis Cabalisticae Scriptores per Pistorium editos, reperitur.
units.tr: 11. Thus he writes: All the stars and spheres are endowed with soul, knowledge and wisdom; they live and endure, and they know him by whose word the world was made; each, according to the measure of its dignity and excellence, celebrates and glorifies its Former, like the angels. And as they know God, so they also understand themselves, and they apprehend the angels who are above them; But the knowledge of the stars and spheres is inferior to the knowledge of the angels, yet greater than the knowledge of men. And in the More Nevochim, Part II, chapter 7: All these things teach you that they apprehend their works, and that they have will and choice in that government which has been given to them (that is, in those things whose rule and direction has been granted to them), just as we too have will and choice in that government which has been given to us, and which we have in our power from the moment of our birth. With this difference, however: that our actions are baser, and that privation precedes our government and operation; but the intelligences and spheres always do good, and with them there is nothing but good (as we shall explain in the following chapters), and whatever they have, that is always in them in perfection and act from their first principle; To this let us add Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel in the book On the Creation, Problem 25, p. 98: For the heavens, according to Rabbi Moses, and in truth, have their own souls, endowed with rational life, as will be shown by me elsewhere. Moreover, concerning this opinion of the Jews, one may well consult Paulus Ricius, a former Jew, who, after he gave his name to the Messiah the Saviour, composed a compendium on the soul of the heaven and illustrated it from the Prophetic Writings. It is found among the Cabalistic writers edited by Pistorius.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Dissentiunt, diversisque stant agmini-bus Judaei circa hominis primi creationem, affirmatibus multis tum ex Veteribus, tum Recentioribus, Adamum Androgynum creatum a fronte Adamum marem referentem, a tergo Evam uxorem, proinde sicut Binis animis, ita constantem duobus corporibus ad scapulas agglutinatis, ficin Bereschit Rabba Sect. 8. Dixit Rabbi Ieremia, filius Eliefer, ea hora, qua Deus creavit primum hominem, Androgynum creavit eum, atque hoc ipsum est, quod dicitur: Masculum & foeminam creavit eos; Etin Medrasch Tillim ad Psalmum 139. Dixit Rabbi Eliefer, quod homo Androgynus fit creatus, quia scriptum est masculum & foeminam creavit eos; Pari modo Rabbi Schemuel in Medrasch citato, & Ralchi in Perusch Tituli Talmudici Berachot exponunt: Duplici vultu creavit eum in principio, quorum unus anterior ejus parte fuit, alter posterior; Ita quoque
units.tr: The Jews disagree and stand in opposing ranks concerning the creation of the first man. Many affirm, both among the ancients and the more recent writers, that Adam was created androgynous, showing the male Adam in front and the wife Eve behind, and so, like two souls, he was also joined to two bodies, fastened together at the shoulder blades. So in Bereschit Rabba, section 8: Rabbi Jeremiah, son of Eliezer, said: at the hour when God created the first man, he created him androgynous; and this is what is said: He created them male and female; And in Midrash Tillim on Psalm 139: Rabbi Eliezer said that man was created androgynous, because it is written: He created them male and female; In the same way Rabbi Shemuel in the Midrash cited, and Rashi in the commentary on the Talmudic tractate Berachot, explain: In the beginning he created him with a double face, one of which was on his front part, the other on his back; So also

units.la: A ben Esra in principio Commentarii iuiidem significat: Adam in principio creatus est duobus vultibus, & ita fuit unus pariter, atque etiam duo: In eadem quoque sententia est Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, qui nonsolum plures hujus opinionis fautores in medium producit, sed argumentis quoque variis tueri conatur, quae prolixe occurrunt in Conciliatore super Genesin, Quaestione 8. pag. 14, 15. Eo autem cum aliorum popularium redeunt, quod verba Genef. cap. 1. §. 27. Creavit Deus hominem ad imaginem suam, ad imaginem Dei creavit illum, Marem & Feminam creavit eos; Nihil aliud notent, quam quod cum DEUS in initio unum hominem creaverit, postea eum diviserit, & ex uno duos fecerit; Quod Genef. cap. 2. §. 1. Et sumsit unam ex costis ejus, vox ibidem occurrens יצלע non per costam, sed per latus debeat verti, ut ita indigitetur, Deum diffecasse illud Adami corpus, & alterum latus ab altero divisisse; Quod biforme illud corpus innuat Regius Propheta David, Psalmo 139. §. 5. Retro & ante formasti me, id est gemino, duplicique vultu creasti me, ita ut fronte fuerit Adam, retrorsum autem fuerit forma Evae; Quod Scriptura Sacra nusquam memoret Deum Evae inspirasse animam, ex quo sequatur, quod Eva in & cum Adamo fuefuerit creata animamque suam acceperit, quando Deus halitum vitæ inflavit Adam, hoc est, corpore ex mare et fœmina constanti; Quod Adamus cum crearetur, nullam habuerit costam superfluam, alias fuisset imperfectus, quod doctrinæ sapientum adversetur: Nullam etiam condita Eva ex necessariis amiserit, alias mansisset mutilus, & eodem vitio natos post se reliquisset liberos, quod contra experientiam; Qui in Negantium partibus sunt, nec numero, nec authoritate prioribus cedunt, cumprimis Rabbi Semuel, Moses Ben Maimon, Raschi, Arama, Ilac Abarbanel, Ben Sueb, Schem Tob, Alschech, inficiantes omnes, Adamum & Evam simul creatos concorporeS, biformes, humeris agglutinatos, sed Evam ex costa Adami formatam cum Scriptura asserentes, Sicuti probat Maimonides More Nevochim Part. II. cap. 30. qui cum aliis consuli potest.
units.tr: Ibn Ezra, at the beginning of his commentary on the same passage, means the same: Adam was created at first with two faces, and so he was one and likewise two. In the same opinion is Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, who not only brings forward many supporters of this opinion, but also tries to defend it with various arguments, which occur at length in the Conciliator on Genesis, Question 8, pages 14 and 15. He returns to the view of the other compatriots, that the words of Genesis 1:27: God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them, note nothing else than this: that when God had at first created one man, he afterwards divided him and made two out of one. Genesis 2:21: And he took one of his ribs: the word occurring there, yatsla [יצלע], should be rendered not by "rib" but by "side", so that it is indicated that God cut that body of Adam and separated the one side from the other. That the body was two-formed is implied by the royal prophet David in Psalm 139:5: Behind and before you have formed me, that is, you created me with a double and twofold face, so that Adam was in front, and the form of Eve was behind. Holy Scripture nowhere records that God breathed a soul into Eve, from which it follows that Eve was created in and with Adam and received her soul when God breathed the breath of life into Adam, that is, into a body consisting of male and female. Further, when Adam was created he had no superfluous rib, otherwise he would have been imperfect, which is contrary to the teaching of the wise men. Nor did Eve, when formed, lose any of the necessary parts, otherwise she would have remained maimed, and would have left children after her with the same defect, which is contrary to experience. Those who are on the side of the denial, and yield to the earlier writers neither in number nor in authority, especially Rabbi Shemuel, Moses ben Maimon, Rashi, Arama, Isaac Abarbanel, Ben Sueb, Shem Tob, and Alshech, all deny that Adam and Eve were created together, joined in one body, two-formed, fastened at the shoulders, and assert that Eve was formed from Adam's rib, as Scripture says. Maimonides proves this in the Guide of the Perplexed, Part II, chapter 30, who may be consulted together with the others.

units.la: Ornament.
units.tr: Ornament.

units.la: CAPUT VII. De Providentia Dei.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. On the Providence of God.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: ALterum Dei opus externum constituunt Providentiam Dei, quam appellant השגחה האלהיית Providentiam, Contemplationemque divinam, mutuata voce ex Psalmo 33. verf. 14, ממכון שבתו השגיח אל כל ישבי הארץ à loco parato, quo sedet, prospectat in omnes habitantes terram; quamque distinguunt in השגחה כללית Providentiam Universalem, communemve, qua omnia sine exceptione regit, gubernatque, & in השגחה פרטית Providentiam Specialem, vel particularem, quæ rationales maximè concernat creaturas, sicuti scribitur in Talmude Tractatu de Sabbato cap.14. Articulus fidei est apud nos, quod Deus Benedictus משגיח עליגו בכלל ובפרט provideat nobis non tantum in Universali, sed etiam in Particulari, id est, quod non tantum rationem habeat speciei humanæ in genere, sed quod singulos hominum etiam curet in individuo. Nam oculi ejus sunt super vias viri & omnes gressus ejus dinumerat, Iobi cap. 12. verf.4.
units.tr: The second external work of God is the Providence of God, which they call השגחה האלהיית [hashgachah ha-elohit] Providence and divine Contemplation. They borrow the phrase from Psalm 33:14, ממכון שבתו השגיח אל כל ישבי הארץ, from the place prepared where he sits he looks out upon all who dwell on the earth. They divide it into השגחה כללית Universal, or general, Providence, by which he rules and governs all things without exception, and השגחה פרטית Special, or particular, Providence, which chiefly concerns rational creatures, as is written in the Talmud, tractate Sabbath, chapter 14: It is an article of faith with us that the Blessed God משגיח עליגו בכלל ובפרט provides for us not only in general but also in particular; that is, he has regard not merely to the human species in general, but also takes care of each individual man. For his eyes are upon the ways of a man, and he counts all his steps, Job 12:4.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Docent communi voce, Providentiam Dei, maxime circa homines, Articulum esse fidei pernecessarium, fundamentalemq;, hinc decimo collocaruht loco, uti patet ex ipsorum articulorum prima inspectione. Fundamentum decimum, quod Deus נשמה videat & sciat actiones hominum, necilla aspectum ejus fugiant, unde scriptum est Ieremiae cap.32.verf.19. Magnus consilio & amplus actione, quia oculi tui aperti super omnes vias hominum; Et Amosi cap. 4. verf. 13. Et indicat homini meditationem ejus. Si vero quae meditatur homo & loquitur, cognoscit, quanto magis quid agit, sciet; Quare in Catechesi Judaica, quando interrogat Discipulus Quaestione 17. Quae scire debeat, si in utraque vita, tranquillitate, deliciisque fruendum sit? Respondetur a Doctore: Sciendum ipsi est, Deum provida nec unquam cessante cura res humanas gubernare, teste Scriptura, Psalmo 121. verf.4. Ecce non dormitabit, neque dormiet, qui custodit Israelem. Hac ipsum firmissima scientia & fiducia tenere convenit. Secundo, misericordiam Dei erga genus humanum omnium longe maximam esse, ipsius Providentiam occulta & aperta omnia penetrare agnoscat: Quod si aliorum quoque in se favorem & gratiam experiatur, id omne Deo faventi acceptum ferat, qui profuo in causas omnes secundas influxu, fluxu, corda fautorum illius eo permovit. Sic Rabbi Levi Barzelonita testatur, quòd illi, qui velint fidem profiteri orthodoxam, necessariò debeant credere Providentiam divinam circa omnes viventium occupari species, cum loquitur in suo Chinuch ad Præceptum de pollutione leprosi: Professores fidei orthodoxæ credere, Providentiam Dei extendere se ad omnes species viventium. Omnes enim species creatas in mundo semper subsistere, nec unquam aboleri omnino aut perire, cùm cuiuslibet speciei substantia in Providentia ejus reperiatur. De specie autem humana credere se, Deum Providentia sua cuiuslibet peculiarem habere rationem, singulorumque nosse actiones. Atque hoc accepimus, inquit, à magnis nostris Doctoribus, de quo etiam multa in sacra Scriptura occurrunt, quæ docent, rem ita se habere.
units.tr: By common consent they teach that the Providence of God, especially toward men, is a most necessary and fundamental article of faith, and for this reason they place it tenth in order, as is clear from a first glance at their articles. The tenth foundation is that God נשמה sees and knows the actions of men, nor do they escape his notice; hence it is written in Jeremiah 32:19, Great in counsel and mighty in work, for your eyes are open upon all the ways of men; and in Amos 4:13, And he declares to man his thought. If he knows what man thinks and says, how much more will he know what he does. Hence in the Jewish Catechism, when the disciple asks in question 17 what he ought to know, whether he is to enjoy life in tranquillity and delights, the teacher answers: He must know that God governs human affairs with a watchful care that never ceases, as Scripture witnesses, Psalm 121:4: Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep. It is fitting to hold this with the firmest knowledge and trust. Second, let him acknowledge that the mercy of God toward the human race is by far the greatest of all, and that his Providence penetrates all things, hidden and open. If he also experiences the favour and grace of others toward himself, let him ascribe all of it to God, who, by his hidden influence upon all secondary causes, moved the hearts of those who favour him. So Rabbi Levi Barzelonita testifies that those who wish to profess the orthodox faith must necessarily believe that the divine Providence is concerned with all the species of living things. He speaks thus in his Chinuch on the precept concerning the uncleanness of the leper: The professors of the orthodox faith believe that the Providence of God extends to all species of living things. For all species created in the world always subsist and are never utterly abolished or destroyed, since the substance of every species is found in his Providence. As for the human species, they believe that God has a special regard for each person in his Providence and knows the actions of each. And this, he says, we have received from our great Teachers, about which many things also occur in holy Scripture, which teach that the matter stands so.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Fatentur doctrinam de Providentia Dei in creaturas esse מלות מנה Angulum magnum legis Judaicæ, sic Rabbi Levi Barzelonita in Chinuch loco citato, sine dubio, quòd sit lapis fundamentalis, cuius multa fidei innitatur dogmata, & à quo plurimi suum habeant stabilimentum, hinc omnium maximè à longo tempore à Judæis fuit pertractata, nec solum variis rationibus probata, sed fortiter quoque tum contra Sadducæos, qui divinam inficiabantur Providentiam teste Rabbi Abrahamo Zacuto libro Juchasin pag. 139. tum contra Epicuraeos defensa, quorum posteriorum hoc videtur fuisse placitum, Deum nullam rerum habere curam, praeterquam sui ipsius, occupari vero tantum in contemplatione & occupatione sui, & in se ipsum reverti, reliqua omnia esse infra divinam majestatem, proinde fieri fortuito, vel per accidens, sicuti cernere licet ex Rabbi Maimonide de Providentia Dei, & quinque circa eam opinionibus differente, More Nevochim, Part. III. cap. 17. Prima sententia est eorum, qui existimant; Nulla plane esse in hoc mundo Providentiam, sed per accidens & fortuito omnia contingere & evenire, neque esse, qui illa regat, curet & gubernet. Atque haec est Epicuri sententia, qui Atomorum quoque est patronus & assertor, fortuito & illa commiscuit, atque ex illorum commixtione per accidens quaevis generari, asserens. Nec defuerunt ex Israelitis Haeretici quidam, qui istam sententiam arripuerunt: Tales nempe, de quibus dicitur Jerem. cap. 5. verf. 12. Negaverunt Dominum, & dixerunt, non est ipse. Hujus autem sententiae falsitatem demonstravit jam ipse Aristoteles, ostendens, non esse possibile, ut res omnes sint aut fiant per accidens, sed esse aliquem, qui illas ordinet, regat, & gubernet; & nos ipsi quoque nonnulla hac de re in praecedentibus attigimus. Hinc quoque qui Providendentiam divinam negarunt, Atheiapud Judæos appellati, uti testatur Rabbi Levi Barzelonita in Chinuch loco allegato: Alios velle, Deum Providentia sua nullas plane res in mundo hoc inferiori curare, sive homines sint, sive reliqua animantia. Esse hanc opinionem Atheorum.
units.tr: They acknowledge that the doctrine of God's Providence over creatures is the מלות מנה [mlwt mnh; great corner] of the Jewish law. So Rabbi Levi Barzelonita, in the Chinuch passage cited, says without doubt that it is the foundation stone upon which many articles of faith rest, and from which very many derive their stability. For this reason it has been treated by the Jews above all others from a long time ago, and it has been not only proved by various arguments but also vigorously defended, both against the Sadducees, who denied divine Providence (according to Rabbi Abraham Zacuto, in the book Juchasin, p. 139), and against the Epicureans. The view of the latter seems to have been that God has no care for anything except himself; that he is occupied only with contemplation and with himself, and turns back into himself; that all other things are beneath the divine majesty, and therefore happen by chance or by accident. This may be seen from Rabbi Maimonides, On the Providence of God, and from the five differing opinions about it, in the More Nevochim, Part III, chapter 17: The first opinion is of those who think that there is no Providence at all in this world, but that all things happen and come to pass by accident and by chance, and that there is no one who directs, cares for, and governs them. This is the opinion of Epicurus, who was also the patron and champion of the atoms, and who mixed them together by chance, asserting that everything is generated from their chance combination. Nor were there lacking some heretics among the Israelites who embraced this opinion, namely those of whom it is said in Jeremiah 5:12: They have denied the Lord, and said, It is not he. The falsity of this opinion was already demonstrated by Aristotle himself, who showed that it is not possible that all things exist or come about by chance, but that there is someone who orders, rules, and governs them; and we ourselves have touched upon several points on this matter in what precedes. Hence also those who denied divine Providence were called atheists among the Jews, as Rabbi Levi Barzelonita testifies in the Chinuch cited above: Others want God, by his Providence, to care for absolutely nothing in this lower world, whether men or the remaining living things. This opinion is that of the atheists.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Providentiam soli tribuunt Deo, non creaturis, cum hæ ubique esse non possint, nec ubique assistere, & providere, ita Orobius Judæus in erudita collatione cum celeberrimo Limborchio, pag. 69. Neque visibilis est Rex cœlestis; sed per fidem credibilis: quia non potest esse Rex cœlestis, nisi fuerit Deus ipse ( quidquid Socinviani contrarium somniaverint ) etenim nulla pura creatura potest ubique assistere, & providere; cum a voluntate divina omnia pedeat, dirigaturqz, sicuti rursus loquitur Judæus Orobius in Certamine Philosophico, contra Exjudæum, Exhominemque Spinosam, pag. 27. Hinc divinam Providentiam agnoscimus, per varias rerum mutationes, quæ nobis casu evenire apparent, cum a Dei voluntate omnia dirigantur. Hæc non æterna necessitate sunt, & talia qualia sunt, non ob aliam quam male fingit necessitatem, ut essent, ut Dei æternam libertatem, & providentiam oppugnet; Quod cœli sine motore Deo moveri non possint, imo ne quidem subsistere sine Conservatione divina, na, cum ipsorum esse non sit absolute esse, sicuti Dei, verum contingens sit, dependeatque ab alio, uti egregie concludit Rabbi Joleph Albo Fundamentorum libro 2, cap. 27. Vere enim tribuitur nomen entis ei, cujus esse non pendet ab alio, quam ab ipsius essentia. Ex eo enim quod ejus esse pendet ab ipsius essentia, nullo modo contingens est. Quod si dicimus de coelis, eos moveri perpetuo, id verum est, quamdiu motor est, a quo movean-tur: secus, si desinat esse motor. Sic etiam de intelligentiis separatis, si dicantur entia: verum est, quamdiu est, qui creat, atque conservat eas, sed habita praecise ipsarum ratione, earum non est absolute esse, quia pendent ab alio: nec eis debetur esse, nisi habita ratione causae ipsarum.
units.tr: They ascribe providence to God alone, not to creatures, since these cannot be everywhere, nor be present everywhere and provide for things. So the Jew Orobio, in his learned conference with the most celebrated Limborch, p. 69: Neither is the heavenly King visible, but he is to be believed through faith, because the heavenly King cannot be unless he is God himself (whatever the Socinians may have dreamed to the contrary), for no pure creature can be everywhere present and provide for things, since all things depend on and are directed by the divine will. Again, the Jew Orobio says in his Philosophical Contest against the ex-Jew and ex-man Spinoza, p. 27: Hence we recognise divine providence through the various changes of things, which appear to happen to us by chance, since all things are directed by the will of God. These things are not by eternal necessity, and they are such as they are, not for any other reason than the necessity which, falsely imagined, would attack the eternal liberty and providence of God. The heavens cannot be moved by God without a mover, nor even subsist without divine conservation, since their being is not absolutely being, as God's is, but contingent, and dependent on another. Rabbi Joseph Albo expertly concludes this in the second book of his Fundamentals, chap. 27: Truly the name of being is given to that whose existence does not depend on anything other than its own essence. For that whose existence depends on its essence is in no way contingent. If we say that the heavens are moved perpetually, that is true as long as there is a mover by which they are moved, but otherwise if the mover ceases to be. So too with separate intelligences, if they are called beings: it is true as long as there is one who creates and preserves them; but considered precisely in themselves, they do not have absolute being, because they depend on another, nor is being owed to them except in view of their cause.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Credunt Judaei divina Providentiam circa quaeque singula versari, complectique universo suo ambitu maxima, medioxyma, ipsaque minima, cum omnia contingentia sint, hinc semper ab alio dependetia, quae proinde se conservare neutiquam possunt, quod Deus Benedictus facit pro beneplacito omnem viventem, escamque suam porrecturus sit tempore suo minimis juxta ac maximis, sic in Catechesi Judaica, Quaestione & Responsione 14. Quod minima abjectaque curet animalcula, secundum Antiquorum Sapientum effatum in Tractatu Talmudico, Avo-da da Sara, cap. 1. יושב על כסא כנים ... Deus sedet & sustentat à cornibus unicornium ad ova pediculorum; Quòd Providentia Dei non minus in formica, quàm in homine sit conspicua, quòdque in pulice & musca æquè elucear, ac in ordine sphærarum, uti loquitur Rabbi Isac Sangarus in libro Cosri, Part. III. §.17. Quia Sapientia & Gubernatio ejus in creatione formicæ & vespæ non minus est conspicua, quàm in Sole, & Sphæris, seu orbibus cœlestibus; imo signa sapientiæ & gubernationis ejus in formica & vespa, vel api magis sunt subtilia & admiranda ob parvitatem illarum. Hæc secum reputabit, ne luminaria cœlestia nimis magna videantur in oculis ejus; Et Part. V. §. 20. Quòd Creator det cuique materiæ formam optimam, & convenientissimam, quam potest recipere; neque suam gratiam, sapientiam, & gubernationem subtrahat ulli rei: quòd etiam exempli gratia in pulice & in musca æquè elucear, ac in ordine Sphærarum, neque aliter differant res, quàm ratione materiæ suæ; Quòd avicula sine voluntate Dei nec capiatur, nec pereat, sic in Talmude Hierosolymitano Tractatu Scheviit capite 9. Oraculum loquebatur Rabbi Schimeoni, Ben Jochai latitanti in spelunca, videntique aucupem capientem avem: Avicula non perit sine cælo, id est, sine Dei voluntate & providentia, quanto minus homo; quod repetitur titurin Jalkut sol. 40. col. 3. Sicque concipi- tur in Berefchit Rabba, Sect. 79. Avicula si- ne voluntate cæli non capitur, quanto minus anima hominis ; Cum quo egregie convenit phrasis parallela apud Matthæum cap.10.♆.29. Nonne duo passerculi assario veneunt, & unus ex eis non cadet in terram sine patre vestro; Quod nihil per accidens fiat, sed omnia ex divina eveniant providentia, ita Rabbi David Kimchi in Com- mentario ad Psalmum 104. Nulla res fit per accidens, sed omnia fiunt ex intentione intendentis Dei ; Tandem quod omnis pius in gente Judaica teneatur credere, quod omnia sine ulla exceptione subjecta sint providentiæ divinæ, uti legitur in Tractatu Talmudico Metzia cap.1. Qui credunt omnia in hoc mundo provenire ex Providentia Dei.
units.tr: The Jews believe that divine providence is concerned with each single thing, and embraces with its whole compass the greatest, the middling, and even the least things, since all things are contingent and therefore always dependent on another, and so cannot in any way preserve themselves. This is what the Blessed God does, when he wills to give food to every living thing, and will at his time extend its food to the least as well as to the greatest. So in the Jewish Catechism, question and answer 14. That he cares for the smallest and most contemptible little creatures, according to the saying of the ancient sages in the Talmudic tractate Avoda Zara, chap. 1: "He sits upon the throne of lice ... God sits and sustains from the horns of unicorns to the eggs of lice" [יושב על כסא כנים ... ]. That the providence of God is no less conspicuous in the ant than in man, and shines out as clearly in the flea and the fly as in the order of the spheres, as Rabbi Isaac Sangari says in the book of the Kuzari, Part III, §17: For his wisdom and government are no less conspicuous in the creation of the ant and the wasp than in the Sun and the spheres, or heavenly orbs; indeed the signs of his wisdom and government are more subtle and admirable in the ant, the wasp, or the bee, on account of their smallness. He will consider these things, lest the heavenly lights seem too great in his eyes. And Part V, §20: That the Creator gives to each matter the best and most suitable form it can receive, and does not withdraw his grace, wisdom, and government from any thing; that also, for example, the flea and the fly shine out as clearly as the order of the spheres, and things differ only in respect of their matter. That a little bird is neither caught nor perishes without the will of God: so in the Jerusalem Talmud, tractate Sheviit, chap. 9, where an oracle spoke to Rabbi Simeon ben Yochai, who was hiding in a cave and saw a fowler catching a bird: A little bird does not perish without heaven, that is, without the will and providence of God; how much less man. This is repeated in Yalkut, fol. 40, col. 3, and is conceived thus in Bereshit Rabba, Sect. 79: If a little bird is not caught without the will of heaven, how much less the soul of man. With this the parallel phrase in Matthew 10.29 agrees remarkably well: Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? And one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father. That nothing happens by chance, but all things come about by divine providence, so Rabbi David Kimchi in his Commentary on Psalm 104: No thing happens by chance, but all things happen by the intention of the God who intends them. Finally, that every pious man in the Jewish nation is bound to believe that all things, without any exception, are subject to divine providence, as is read in the Talmudic tractate Metzia, chap. 1: Those who believe that all things in this world come about from the providence of God.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Maimonidem culpant immerito, non Judæi, sed Viri maximi inter Christianos, quod solus a communi sententia de Providentia omnium rerum ausus fuerit discedere, inque suo more Nevochim, Part. III. cap. 17. docere, divinam Providentiam non circa animalium individua, plantas, folia, aliaque vilia versari, quæ cæco finr relicta casui, sed occupatam unice in hominum cura, in quibus peculiare aliquod signum amoris sui elucere voluerit, rit, cum sic inquit: Credo itaque, Providentiam divinam in mundo hoc inferiori seu sublunari esse tantum in individuis speciei humanæ, & hanc speciem solam esse, cuius individuorum negotia, omniaque, sive bona, sive mala, quæ eis accidunt, secundum judicium & justitiam administrantur, sicut dicitur Deuter. cap. 32. ¶. 4. Omnes via ejus judicium. Reliqua vero animalia, plantas, & alia quod attinet, de illis amplestar sententiam Aristotelis; Minimique credo, folium illud, quod ex arbore decidit, singulari Dei Providentia cadere, vel singulari Dei decreto muscam capi ab aranea; vel a sputo quod Ruben exspuit, muscam, super quam in hoc vel illo loco cadit, ex decreto Dei interfici; vel piscem speciali voluntate Dei vermiculum natantem in superficie aquarum capere & deglutire: Sed ista omnia, mea calculo, siunt per accidens, sicut opinatus est Aristoteles; Sed reprehendunt Maimonidem sine causa, cum id nuspiam doceat, nec ex verbis allegatis sequatur, quippe bene providentiam singularem ad creaturas restringat rationales denegetque brutis, plantis, rebusque aliis in Universali Providentia complexis, proinde quod Deus non modo speciem conservet humanam, sed ipsa quoque individua intueatur, eorumque actiones & opera omnia diligentissime observet, atque adeo efficiat, ut unicuique sit pro merito, justis bene, impiis male; brutis vero in genere tantum prospiciat, quatenus eorum conservat species, individuis dispositioni causarum secundarum relictis, nec brutis praemiorum & poenarum in futuro seculo tribuat dispensationem sicuti secta Muatsali volebat, quam propterea redarguit hic, ostendens talia omnia per accidens fieri; Praeterea quod contrarium ubique docet Maimonides, sic enim scribit in Constitutionibus de Fundamentis legis cap.1. § 1. Quod nulla respicit existere nisi in Deo Benedicto. Quod omnia existentia necessario dependeant ab ipso. Et §.2. Illud Ens est Deus mundi, Dominus totius terrae, gubernans Sphaerarum potentia, quae caret fine ac termino, & virtute nunquam cessante, orbis enim indesinenter circumagitur. Fieri autem nequit, ut orbis in gyrum agatur absque circummovente: Is vero est Deus Benedictus, circumvolvens eum absque manu & corpore; Et in iisdem Fundamentis cap.2. §. 11. Omnia existentia, praeter Creatorem, a prima forma usque ad minimum reptile, quod est in umbilico terrae, omnia potentia ejus veritatis existunt. Et quia ipse cognoscit semetipsum, ac intelligit excellentiam, gloriam, atque veritatem suam, ideo cognoscit omnia, & nihil est absconditum ei. Denique nec solus Maimonides hic vapulat apud Theologos, quae hallucinatio nimii critici nuper fuit, cum Rabbi Levi Barzelonitae pariter objectum jectum sit, sicque acclamatum ab Hottingero, in Jure Hebraeorum, pag. 136. Tibi, Appella, qui ex Evangelio discere non vis, etiam capillos capitis nostri Deum in enumerato habere; Sic autem divina scribit Providentia Barzelonita in Chi-nuch ad Legem 168. Esse quosdam, qui statuant, Providentiam Dei omnia complecti in mundo, tam viventia, quam catera, adeo ut ne minima quaeque res moveatur absq; voluntate & decreto Dei Beneditti, ita ut existiment, dum folium cadit de arbore, Deum ut ita caderet decrevisse, nec citius nec tardius cadere potuisse, vel uno momento. Atque haec sententia a sensu recto longe recedit.
units.tr: It is not the Jews but certain very eminent Christians who unjustly blame Maimonides for daring alone to depart from the common opinion about the providence of all things. In his manner, in the Nevochim, Part III, chapter 17, he teaches that the divine providence does not concern the individual animals, plants, leaves, and other base things, which are left to blind chance, but is concerned solely with the care of human beings, in whom he wished some special sign of his love to shine forth. He says: I believe, therefore, that the divine providence in this lower or sublunary world extends only to the individuals of the human species, and that this species alone is one whose affairs, and all things that happen to its individuals, whether good or evil, are administered according to judgment and justice, as is said in Deuteronomy chapter 32, verse 4: All his ways are judgment. As for the remaining animals, plants, and other things, I embrace the opinion of Aristotle; and I least of all believe that a leaf falling from a tree falls by a singular providence of God, or that a fly is caught by a spider by a singular decree of God, or that a fish, by a special will of God, catches and swallows a little worm swimming on the surface of the waters, or that a fly on which Reuben's spittle falls in this or that place is killed by a decree of God. But all these things, in my judgment, happen by accident, as Aristotle thought. Yet they blame Maimonides without cause, since he nowhere teaches this, nor does it follow from the words quoted. Indeed, he restricts singular providence to rational creatures and denies it to brutes, plants, and other things comprised in universal providence. Therefore God not only preserves the human species but also watches over the individuals themselves, and most diligently observes their actions and works, and thus brings it about that each receives what is due: the just well, the impious ill. But towards brute animals in general he cares only so far as he preserves their species, leaving the individuals to the arrangement of secondary causes; nor does he assign to brutes rewards and punishments in the future age, as the sect of the Muatsali wished, which is why he here refutes it, showing that all such things happen by accident. Moreover, Maimonides everywhere teaches the contrary. For thus he writes in the Constitutiones de Fundamentis legis, chapter 1, § 1: That nothing can exist except in the Blessed God; that all existing things necessarily depend on him. And § 2: That Being is the God of the world, the Lord of the whole earth, governing the spheres by a power that has no end or limit, and by a virtue that never ceases, for the orb is ceaselessly turned around. Yet the orb cannot be turned in a circle without a mover that turns it; and that is the Blessed God, who turns it without hand or body. And in the same Fundamenta, chapter 2, § 11: All existing things, besides the Creator, from the first form down to the least reptile that is in the navel of the earth, exist by his power of truth. And because he knows himself, and understands his own excellence, glory, and truth, therefore he knows all things, and nothing is hidden from him. Finally, Maimonides is not alone in being thrashed by the theologians here. This delusion was lately that of an overly zealous critic, since the same charge was brought against Rabbi Levi of Barcelona, and Hottinger, in his Jus Hebraeorum, page 136, cried out against him thus: You, Appella, who will not learn from the Gospel, that God has even the hairs of our head numbered. The Barcelonese, moreover, writes on divine providence in the Chinuch, on the Law, 168: There are some who hold that the providence of God embraces all things in the world, living and other things alike, so that not even the smallest thing moves without the will and decree of the Blessed God; so that they think that when a leaf falls from a tree, God decreed that it should fall in just that way, and could not have fallen either sooner or later, not even by a single moment. And this opinion departs far from sound sense.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Sed stat sententia, omnium Iudaeorum calculis, ipsiusque Maimonidis firmata, Providentiam divinam naturae creatae esse perpetuam, universalemque Dei curam versari semper circa res omnes extra DEum existentes, sed specialem solis fere relictam hominibus, maxime tamen piis, quibus adhaereat, quique Deo valde sint oculis, auribus, & manibus, consentiente Apostolo Paulo in Epistola 1. ad Timotheum cap. 4. ͤ. 10. Qui est conservator omnium hominum, maxime vero fidelium; Quod nunc pluribus ex ipsis Judaeorum mo-numen-
units.tr: But the view stands, confirmed by the reckoning of all the Jews and by Maimonides himself: divine providence over created nature is perpetual, and God's universal care always extends to all things that exist outside God. Yet special providence is left almost entirely to men, and most of all to the pious, to whom it clings, and who are very dear to God's eyes, ears and hands. The Apostle Paul agrees, in 1 Timothy 4:10: "Who is the Saviour of all men, specially of those that believe." This must now be drawn out from several of the Jews' own monuments.

units.la: 1 numentis eruendum est; Et quidem de his omnibus docet Rabbi Levi Ben Gerson ad Proverbiorum cap. 15. ȣ. 3. Ecce oculi Domini sunt in omni loco. Omnes enim res promanant ex scientia ejus, & providentia ejus. Idcirco hoc recte explicatur, quod oculi ejus speculentur malos pariter & bonos, sed illos providentia generali, hos providentia speciali. Specialis enim providentia ejus adhaeret bonis; Uti quoque Rabbi Moses Bar Nachman Gerundensis ad Genef. cap. 18. ȣ. 19. Scientia Dei nihil aliud est, quam providentia ejus in hoc inferiori mundo, qua conservat universa, etiam filios hominis, qui in eo variis sunt expositi casibus, usque dum veniat tempus visitationis eorum. Quod autem attinet sanctos, eorum speciale cur am habet, ut semper eos custodiat, nec patitur sibi ex notitia & memoria prorsus excidere; Et quam maxime Rabbi Bechai in Commentario ad Genef. cap. 18. ȣ. 19. Opus est, ut intelligas, quod Providentia Dei in hoc inferiori mundo, quantum ad speciem humanam, sit tam universalis, quam particularis, sed quantum ad reliqua animantia, universalis tantum, non particularis. Nam generaliter tantum prospicit, ut conservet speciem: Particularis autem providentia, quae est circa speciem humanam divisa est in tres partes. Una earum est, quae novit in individuo singula opera hominis, etiam cognitiones ejus: Altera vero est, qua protegit hominem. minem & liberat ab accidentibus, quae contingere solent. Et providentia quidem, quae singillatim novit omnia opera hominis ea pertingit ad omnes, cum ex Israelitis, tum ex gentilibus, juxta id, quod scriptum est Psalmo 33. v. 15. Qui formavit simul cor eorum, considerans omnia opera eorum: at providentia, qua eruit hominem e contingentibus casibus, non spectat aeque ad omnes, etiamsi Israelitae sint, sed tantum adjustos, qui sunt inter eos. Nam Sanctus ille & Benedictus Deus liberat justos, si quid ipsis accidat, reliquos post habet, & unumquemvis suo arbitrio permittit. Sanctos suos non deserit, nec avertit oculum suum ab ipsis. Sed providentia ejus circa justum perfecta est, neque unquam prorsus abeo separatur.
units.tr: Rabbi Levi Ben Gerson teaches all of this on Proverbs 15:3: "The eyes of the LORD are in every place." "For all things proceed from his knowledge and his providence. Hence this is rightly explained: his eyes watch both the evil and the good alike, but the one under general providence, the other under special providence. For his special providence cleaves to the good." Rabbi Moses Bar Nachman of Gerona, on Genesis 18:19, likewise: "The knowledge of God is nothing other than his providence in this lower world, by which he preserves all things, including the sons of men, who in it are exposed to various misfortunes, until the time of their visitation comes. As for the saints, he has a special care for them, that he may always keep them and not allow them to fall utterly out of his knowledge and memory." And most of all Rabbi Bechai, in his commentary on Genesis 18:19: "You must understand that God's providence in this lower world is as universal as it is particular with respect to the human species, but with respect to the other living creatures it is only universal, not particular. For it looks out generally only so as to preserve the species." Particular providence, which concerns the human species, is divided into three parts. "One of them knows in the individual every work of man, even his thoughts. The other protects man and frees him from the accidents that are wont to befall him." Now the providence that knows each single work of man extends to all, both Israelites and Gentiles, according to what is written in Psalm 33:15: "He who fashioneth their hearts alike, who considereth all their works." But the providence that rescues a man from threatening misfortunes does not extend equally to all, even if they are Israelites, but only to the righteous among them. For that Holy and Blessed God frees the righteous if anything should befall them, and holds the rest in lower esteem, leaving each to his own choice. He does not forsake his saints, nor turn his eye from them. But his providence over the righteous is perfect, and it is never wholly separated from them.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Hinc quoque docent Dei providam curam in omni esse loco, tum in coelo, tum in terra, nihilque abscónditum illi esse, cum sit ille Deus, qui res omnes creet, & conservet, allegantes semper quae Deus de semet ipso affirmat apud Jeremiam cap. 23. verf. 23. & 24. Numquid Deus de propinquo ego sum, & non Deus de longinquo? Num occultabit se quispiam in occultis, & ego non videbo eum? Annon coelum & terram ego impleo? Ad quem locum Rabbi David Kimchi sic commentatur: Cum dicit se implere coelum & terram, nihil aliud vult dicere, quam quòd sit in omni loco, quæ locutio figurata est: Nam ipse Deus Benedictus non est corpus, quod locum impleat, & hoc vult dicere, כי השגחתו בכל מקום ובארץ בשמים quòd Providentia ejus in omni loco sit, in cælo & in terra; Et Rabbi Isac Abarbanel scribit: Ego cælum & terra impleo, vult dicere: Ego creavi eos, & providentia ac conservatione mea semper versor super eos. Convenit igitur, ut agnoscant, quòd nihil à me sit abscônditum, quandoquidem ego sum, qui res omnes creo, & conservo, earum curam ac rationem habeo. Quapropter quoque Deum Benedictum passim nominant מקום Habitaculum, & מקום Locum, sic Antiquissimi Rabbinorum in Midrasch Tillim. Quare nomen Domini, qui est Sanctus, Benedictus dicitur esse locus? quia ipse est locus mundi. Sic enim scriptum Exod. cap. 33. vers. 21. Ecce locus est apud me; Ita pariter Rabbi David Kimchi in libro Radicum ad literam y: cùm dicit, מקום Habitaculum fuisti nobis, nil aliud vult dicere, quàm מקום Locus fuisti nobis, nos scilicet portando & sustentando. Et sic accipitur vox מקום Psalmo 91. vers. 9. Quoniam dixisti, Iehova spes mea, excelsum posuisti locum tuum. Et Rabbini nostri ita Sanctum Benedictum cognominant, & appellant nomine loci, quia ipse est locus mundi, non mundus illius.
units.tr: Hence they also teach that God's provident care is in every place, both in heaven and on earth, and that nothing is hidden from him, since he is the God who creates and preserves all things. They always cite what God says of himself in Jeremiah 23:23-24: "Am I a God at hand, saith the LORD, and not a God afar off? Can any hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him? Do not I fill heaven and earth?" On this passage Rabbi David Kimchi comments thus: "When he says that he fills heaven and earth, he means nothing other than that he is in every place, which is a figurative way of speaking, for the Blessed God himself is not a body that fills a place. He means that his providence is in every place, in heaven and on earth" [כי השגחתו בכל מקום ובארץ בשמים]. Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel writes: "'I fill heaven and earth' means: I created them, and I am always present over them by my providence and preservation. It is fitting, then, that they acknowledge that nothing is hidden from me, since I am the one who creates and preserves all things, and I have care and oversight of them." For this reason they also repeatedly call the Blessed God [מקום] "Habitation" and "Place." So the most ancient of the rabbis say in the Midrash Tillim: "Why is the name of the Lord, who is Holy and Blessed, called a place?
