Because he is the place of the world, and the world is not his place." For so it is written in Exodus 33:21: "Behold, there is a place by me." Likewise Rabbi David Kimchi, in his book of roots, under the letter Yod, says: when it says "thou hast been our habitation" [מקום], it means nothing other than "thou hast been our place," that is, bearing us up and sustaining us. And the word [מקום] is taken in this sense in Psalm 91:9: "Because thou hast made the LORD, which is my refuge, even the Most High, thy habitation." Our rabbis also name and call the Holy Blessed One by the name of Place, because he is the place of the world, and not the world his place.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Referunt inter infinita Providentiæ divinæ opera, Pluviarum curam particularem, ex Leviticorum cap. 26. verf. 4. Et dabo pluvias vestras in tempore suo; Et Deuteronomii cap. 11. verf. 13. Si præcepta mea audiveritis, dabo pluviam terræ vestræ, pluviam primam & serotinam; Indicantes, Deum non minorem ostendere potentiam in pluviarum demissione & distributione, quam tum in vitæ productione vel conservatione, tum in mortuorum resurrectione, sine dubio propterea, quòd per pluviam omnia & vivere & florere incipiant, sicque eadem conspiciatur ratio; Hinc in Tractatu Talmudico Sanhedrin sol. 113. col. 1. & Tractatu Talmudico Taanit cap. 8. potentiam demittendi pluvias non Legatis, sed soli tribuunt Deo: Tres claves non sunt tradita ulli Legato, vitæ, pluviæ, & resurrectio mortuorum; Quibus quandoque quarta adjicitur clavis, sterilitatis scilicet clavis, de qua cum reliquis sic scribitur in Targum Hierosolymitano: Quatuor claves sunt in manu Domini mundi, quas non tradidit, neque ulli Angelo, neque Seraphino: clavis pluviæ, clavis justentationis, clavis sepulchrorum, clavis sterilitatis; Ita loquuntur multa de פוטנציה Potentia pluviæ, quòd non descendat nisi per Potentiam, intelligentes Deum, quòdque unum ex iis sit, in quibus divina quam maxime appareat potentia; Quod etiam bene convenit cum iis, quæ recenset Paulus in Actis Apostolorum, dicens cap. 14. verf. 17. Deum fe notificaffe, & Potentiam suam ostendisse, cum cœlitus daret pluvias ac præstituta tempora, id est, pluvias in præstitutis temporibus, sicuti me docuit Orientis, Occidetisq; Lamè, Pocockí, Delicium nostrum, in notis Miscellaneis ad Pottam Mosis Maimonidis, pag. 149. Pariter quoque in Tractatu Talmudico Bava Bathra sol. 91. col. 2, recensetur, quòd Præfectus Cisternis etiam cœlitus constituatur.
units.tr: Among the countless works of divine Providence, they count the particular care of rain, citing Leviticus 26:4, "And I will give you rain in its season," and Deuteronomy 11:13, "If you hearken to my commandments, I will give rain to your land, the early rain and the late rain." They indicate that God shows no less power in the sending down and distribution of rain than in the production or preservation of life, or in the resurrection of the dead, undoubtedly because through rain all things begin both to live and to flourish, and so the same reason is seen in each. Hence in the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin, folio 113, column 1, and in the Talmudic tractate Taanit, chapter 8, they attribute the power of sending rain to God alone and not to any legate: "Three keys have not been committed to any legate: of life, of rain, and of the resurrection of the dead." To these a fourth key is sometimes added, namely the key of barrenness, of which, together with the others, the Jerusalem Targum writes thus: "There are four keys in the hand of the Lord of the world, which he has not given to anyone, neither to any angel nor to any seraph: the key of rain, the key of sustenance, the key of graves, the key of barrenness." Thus they speak much of the "potency" [פוטנציה] of rain, that it does not descend except by power, understanding God to be the one in whom divine power above all appears. This agrees well also with what Paul recounts in the Acts of the Apostles, saying in chapter 14, verse 17, that God made himself known and showed his power when he gave rain from heaven and fixed times, that is, rain in fixed seasons, as my friend Lamy, Pococke, the delight of East and West, taught me in the Miscellaneous Notes to the Guide of Moses Maimonides, page 149. Likewise also in the Talmudic tractate Bava Bathra, folio 91, column 2, it is recorded that the overseer of cisterns too is appointed from heaven.

units.la: X. Sic mala quæque nō excludunt à divina Providentia, non quod Deus Benedictus malitiâ producat, peccatumq; creaturæ infundat rationali, cum hominem ad malum, peccatûq; nunquâ cogat, ipsūq; liberi arbitrii usu adimat; Est enim Deus benedictus nihil nisi bonitas, benignitas, & misericordia in fœculû, paraque est omni tempore & hora bonitas ejus illi, qui dignus est accipere eam, neque nutat, neque dormit custos Israelis; Sed quod peccata ordinet, antecedentia peccata puniat sequentibus, gratiam, misericordiamque suam detrahat, sicque malum non superne descen-dat, sed opus fit hominis se ipsum condemnantis, utiloquitur Rabbi Levi Barzelonita in Chinuch ad Legem 169. Scriptum item est: Non es Deus volens iniquitatem, Psalmo 5. ¶. 4. Deum neminem velle condemnare, sed Deum, qui bonus est. est, semper velle bonum. Hominem autem semet-ipsum condemnare, recedendo à recto, & removendo à se ipso dispositiones, quæ aptum illum redderent, ad recipiendum bonum. Quemadmodum qui ambu-lat in via regia, purgata à lapidibus & aliis offendi-culis; In illa autem via sepimentum est ex vepribus hinc atq; illinc concinnatum, transeatq; aliquis, & in septo se fricet, indeq; uratur; non potest utiq; de tali dici, quod Deus ejus voluerit ustionem, sed ipse causa est, quia incaute rectam semitam non trivit. Ita etiam peccatorem condemnat proprietas judicii: Neque dicendum, Deum velle condemnationem ejus; verum, dum propter peccatum ejus, arcetur ab eo bonum, reperitur in eo malum. In hunc sensum dicunt Rabbini: Nihil mali superne descendit. Summa verborum nostrorum est, quod omne accidens malum obveniens homini, opus sit in homine, productum ex abscondito vultu Dei Benedicti ab eo, cum nempe Deus illi custodiam suam subtrahit propter peccatum ipsius, usq; dum pœnas peccato debitas solverit. Concedunt omnes mala non casu accidere fortuito, sed regi, gubernarique à Deo Benedicto, imo DEum certa ratione operari illa, ita Rabbi David Kimchi in Commentario suo ad illud Esaiæ cap. 26 v. 12, Omnia opera nostra operatus es nobis Domine; scribit: Dispone nobis pacem. Nam in Manu tua est, ut possis facere, sicut quod operatus es, tu operatus es omne, & fecisti omnia opera nostra: Quicquid enim obve-nit nobis, sive bonum fuerit, sive malum, prout in hoc mundo fieri solet, ubi mala mixta bonis, omne illud tu operatus es, & nil accidit casu fortuito. Cui gemina ad eundem locum tradit Rabbi Isac Abarbanel: Da nobis pacem, idq; cum Rege Messia & redemptione, nam omnia opera nostra inde ab exilio & pressuris, quae veerut sup nos, tu es operat9, &nō obvenerunt ea nobis ex accidenti, ideo sicut perstiterunt ac rata fuerunt mala, cum viveremus in securitate tui: Sic credimus, perstituras & ratas fore promissiones de redemptione, Teq; dispositurum nobis pacem. Uti quoque Rafchi: Pone nobis pacem, nam etiam opera nostra mala, quae pro ratione peccatorum nostrorum e manu tua accepimus, tu es operatus. Nec solum operari malum dicunt Deum Benedictum, quod suaviter media disponat, quibus homo ex liberrima abutitur voluntate, sicque mala peragit; Sed quandoque etiam obdurate, excoecareque impios, non duritiem novam, & coecitatem immittendo, sed subtrahendo gratia veterem duritiem, & coecitatem relinquendo, sicuti testatur Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, cum in libello de termino vitae pag. 220. scribit, Deum induraffe Pharaonem Regem, non ei adimendo usum libertatis, sed rem ita dirigendo & disponendo, ut Regi occasio daretur per liberum voluntatis suae usum, aut potius ab usum, animum suum obdurandi. Eo ipso enim, quod videret, Magos suos eadem prodigia facere, quae faciebat Moses, parvi ea faciebat. Accedebat quod plagas facile averti posse videret: Ac proinde ius non multum commoveretur: Sed obstinato animo populum dimittere recusaret, donec tandem experrectus filii sui, & omnium primogenitorum clade, liberam abeundi potestatem faceret. Sic ostendit pag. 221. Quod eodem modo intelligendum sit, quando dicitur cor Sihon & Og Regum Basan induratum fuisse a Deo, sicuti quoque cor Rohabeami: Occasionem Deus tantum hic dedit illorum contumaciae: Non autem coegit voluntatem eorum, quo eos puniret. Similiter Deus decreverat dividere Regnum Salomonicum. Quomodo id facit? Non cogendo Rohabeamum, sed occasionem tantum ei dando, per consilia juniorum, quibus ille passus se adduci, renuit populo concedere imminutionem vectigalium. Explicat praeterea Rabbi Menasseh qua ratione Deus in puniendo malo gloriam justitiae suae manifestet, respondetque ad Proverbiorum capitis decimi sexti versum quartum, ubi impius dicitur factus ad diem mali; cum ita inquit pag. 205, & 206. Quod sequitur & etiam malum ad diem malum, id difficultatem non habet, tantundem enim est, ac si DEUS diceret, DEUM omnia propter gloriam suam creasse: Ac proinde quando punit, & casticastigat malum, etiam eo facto Deum gloriam suam manifestare, nempe gloriam justitiæ, quæ tum elucet magis impuniendo. Vel quod malim, omnia creavit Deus propter se, id est, ut sibi serviant: nam malus sæpe instar flagelli est in manu Dei, quo castigat improbos. Qualis fuit Nebucadnezar: Quo veluti virga & flagello immorigerum populum suum castigavit. Cæterum optime ex Hosea cap. 13. v. 9. monent, quod Israel sit ipsa corruptela, malitiæque fons sit in ipso homine, nec de Deo proprie dici possit, quod faciat mala, cum actiones Dei omnes sint bonæ, imo ipsa sint Dei existentia, mala vero contra omnia sint boni privationes, sicut notat Rabbi Moses Maimonides More Nevochim, Part. III. cap. 10. pag. 353. Post has itaque conclusiones liquet in rei veritate, quod de Deo Optimo Maximo non possit absolute dici, quod malum per se faciat, quod intentio ejus prima et principalis sit, facere malum. Hoc inquam nullo modo dici potest: Nam actiones ejus omnes sunt optimæ; quia ipse nihil facit præter Existentiam; Existentia autem omnis bona est. Mala vero sunt privationes, a quibus actio non dependet.
units.tr: X. So evils do not exclude a thing from divine Providence; not that God, blessed be he, produces malice or infuses sin into a rational creature, since he never compels man to evil or sin and does not take away the use of free will. For God, blessed be he, is nothing but goodness, kindness and mercy for ever, and his goodness is ready at all times and hours for him who is worthy to receive it; neither does the keeper of Israel slumber or sleep. But he orders that preceding sins be punished by subsequent ones, withdraws his grace and mercy, and so evil does not descend from above, but becomes the work of a man condemning himself, as Rabbi Levi Barzelonita says in the Chinuch on the Law, 169. "It is written likewise: You are not a God who wills iniquity" (Psalm 5:4). God does not will to condemn anyone, but God, who is good, always wills what is good. Man, however, condemns himself by turning aside from the right and removing from himself the dispositions which would make him fit to receive good. It is as with one who walks on the king's highway, cleared of stones and other obstacles; but beside that way there is a hedge of brambles put up on either side, and someone passes through it and rubs against the hedge and is burned by it. Such a man cannot be said to have been willed a burning by God; rather he himself is the cause, because he carelessly did not keep to the straight path. So too the nature of judgment condemns the sinner: nor should it be said that God wills his condemnation; rather, while on account of his sin good is withheld from him, evil is found in him. In this sense the rabbis say: "Nothing evil descends from above." The sum of our words is this: every evil accident that befalls a man is a work in the man, produced from the hidden face of God, blessed be he, when God withdraws his protection from him on account of his sin, until he has paid the penalties due to sin. All concede that evils do not befall by chance, but are ruled and governed by God, blessed be he; indeed that God works them by a certain reason. So Rabbi David Kimchi, in his commentary on that verse of Isaiah 26:12, "Lord, you have wrought all our works for us," writes: "Appoint peace for us. For it is in your hand that you are able to do, just as you have wrought: you have wrought everything and made all our works. For whatever befalls us, whether it be good or evil, as is usual in this world where evils are mixed with goods, you have wrought all that, and nothing happens by chance." Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel gives a twofold comment on the same passage: "Give us peace, and that with the Messianic King and redemption, for all our works from the exile and the oppressions that have come upon us you have wrought, and they did not befall us by accident. Therefore, just as the evils persisted and were confirmed when we lived in security under you, so we believe that the promises of redemption will persist and be confirmed, and you will appoint peace for us." Rashi too: "Appoint peace for us, for even our evil works, which we have received from your hand according to the measure of our sins, you have wrought." Nor do they say only that God, blessed be he, works evil in that he sweetly arranges the means by which man, in his most free will, abuses them and so commits evils. Sometimes they also say that he hardens and blinds the wicked, not by introducing a new hardness and blindness, but by withdrawing grace and leaving the old hardness and blindness, as Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel attests, when in his booklet On the Term of Life, page 220, he writes that God hardened Pharaoh the king, not by taking away the use of his liberty, but by so directing and disposing the matter that an occasion was given to the king, through the free use of his own will, or rather through his abuse of it, to harden his own heart. For by the very fact that he saw his magicians doing the same prodigies that Moses did, he thought little of them. Moreover he could see that the plagues could easily be averted, and so he was not much moved; but with an obstinate mind he refused to let the people go, until at last, awakened by the slaughter of his son and of all the firstborn, he granted them free leave to depart. So he shows, on page 221, that the same must be understood when it is said that the heart of Sihon and Og, kings of Bashan, was hardened by God, as also the heart of Rehoboam: "God gave only an occasion to their obstinacy; he did not force their will, so that he might punish them. Similarly God had decreed to divide the kingdom of Solomon. How did he do it? Not by compelling Rehoboam, but by giving him only an occasion, through the counsels of the young men, to whom he allowed himself to be persuaded, and he refused to grant the people a reduction of the taxes." Rabbi Menasseh further explains by what reasoning God, in punishing evil, makes manifest the glory of his justice, and he answers concerning the fourth verse of the sixteenth chapter of Proverbs, where the wicked is said to be made for the day of evil; he says on pages 205 and 206: "What follows, 'and also the evil for the day of evil', has no difficulty, for it amounts to the same as if God had said that God created all things for his own glory. Accordingly, when he punishes and chastises evil, God by that very act also manifests his glory, namely the glory of justice, which shines the more when it punishes. Or, to put it as I would prefer: God created all things for himself, that is, that they might serve him; for the wicked man is often like a whip in God's hand, with which he chastises the impious." Such was Nebuchadnezzar, by whom, as with a rod and a scourge, he chastised his stubborn people. Moreover, they rightly admonish from Hosea 13:9 that Israel is the corruption itself, and the source of malice lies in man himself, nor can it properly be said of God that he does evils, since all the actions of God are good, indeed they are God's very existence, whereas evils are on the contrary privations of good, as Rabbi Moses Maimonides notes in the Guide of the Perplexed, Part III, chapter 10, page 353. After these conclusions, therefore, it is clear in the truth of the matter that it cannot be said absolutely of God, the Best and Greatest, that he does evil in itself, or that his primary and principal intention is to do evil. This, I say, can in no way be said: for all his actions are most excellent, because he does nothing except existence; and all existence is good. Evils, however, are privations, on which action does not depend.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Negant plerique humanæ vitæ metam esse fixam, & immobilem, perque divinam Providentiam ante tempora secularia, cum omnibus suis circumstantiis determinatam, hinc necessariam, afferentes vitae terminum mobilem, mutabilemque, in ipla hominis potestate situm, diu aut breviter vivere, metamque hominis dependere & ab astris, eorumque virtute coelesti, positu, conjunctione; Et a corporis temperamento sive calido, sive humido, & a variantium saeculorum decursu, sicut illud non solum pluribus deducit RabbiMenasseh Ben Israel peculiari libello de Termino Vitae, verum ex Scripturis quoque ostendere conatur rationibus sequentibus: Quod Deus vitam polliceatur longaevam praeceptorum divinorum observatoribus, Exod.cap.20.v.12. Honora patrem tuum & matrem tuam, ut prolongentur dies tui, Deuteron.cap.4.v.40. Propterea ut prolongentur dies tui, Et cap.32.v.47. Haec reprolongabitur dies; Si vero ab aeterno dies essent decisi, vana profecto esset ejusmodi promissio, nec posset quis excedere decretum limitem. Itaque sequitur, in potestate hominis esse diu aut breviter vivere. Quia viri pii maximo desiderio quaesiverunt vitae prolongationem, inter quos Hiskia, 2. Regum cap.15 v.3. Memento Domine, quod coram te ambulaverim cum veritate & corde perfecto; Sic pessimus Cain formidans mortem ait Genes.cap.4.v.14 Quisquis me invenit, me trucidabit. Alii vero mortem postulant, larunt, uti Elias, cum inquit 1. Regum cap. 19. ¶.4. O Domine cape animam meam, non enim sum melior majoribus meis ; Jam vero inutiles suis- sent preces, si vitæ terminus absolute esset determinatus. Quia Rex Salomo potuit à Deo Benedicto petere vitam longævam, tanquam rem contingentem; Et quod Deus largiendo ipsi sapientiam, divitias, & gloriam, pollicea- tur quoque simul vitam, non absolute, sed conditionate: Si ambulaveris in viis meis, prout illud legitur 1. Regum cap 3. ¶. 2. Postquam non postulasti multos dies, nec divitias, neque animam hostium tuorum, sed tantum flagitasti sapientiam adjudicandum: Ego tibi do cor sapiens, divitias, & gloriam. Etsi ambulabis in præceptis meis, uti ambulavit pater tuus, prolongabo dies tuos. Quia nemo sibi potuisset mortem anticipare, si terminus vitæ definitus esset ab æterno; Jam vero Deum ipsum monere sæpe hominem, ut sibi caveat à periculis, & malorum occasionibus, uti patet ex Deuteron. cap. 20. ¶. 5. 6. 7. Si quis ædificavit domum novam, & nondum cæpit uti ea; Si quis plantaverit vineam, nec dum ea sacris jam soluta usus est; Si quis desponsavit uxorem, nec dum duxit eam, revertatur domum, ne moriatur in prælio ipso. Unde econsequi, vitæ terminum non esse præfinitum divina Prædestinatione absoluta. Quia in Sacris Literis nullus occurrit locus, qui asserit, Deum praefinivisse aut determinasse dies vitae, sed tantum colligatur esse vitae terminum, qui dependet a tempore, a coelo, & temperamento. Tandem sic in compendio ea proponit, quae multis in citato libello tractavit, cum loquitur pag. 232. 233.
units.tr: Many deny that the limit of human life is fixed and immovable, and that divine providence determined it beforehand, before the ages of the world, with all its circumstances, and so made it necessary. They claim that the term of life is mobile and changeable, lying in man's own power, so that he lives long or briefly. They also hold that the limit of a man's life depends on the stars, on their heavenly power, position and conjunction, on the temperament of the body, whether hot or moist, and on the passing of the changing ages. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel not only argues this in his special little book On the Term of Life, but also tries to show from Scripture the following reasons. God promises long life to those who observe his divine precepts: Exod. 20.12, Honour your father and your mother, that your days may be prolonged; Deut. 4.40, So that your days may be prolonged; and ch. 32.47, By this the days shall be prolonged. But if the days had been decided from eternity, such a promise would be empty, and no one could exceed the limit decreed. It follows, then, that it is in man's power to live long or briefly. Pious men have sought the prolonging of life with the greatest desire, among them Hezekiah, 2 Kings 15.3: Remember, Lord, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart. So the most wicked Cain, fearing death, says in Gen. 4.14: Whoever finds me will kill me. Others, however, ask for death, as Elijah does when he says in 1 Kings 19.4: O Lord, take my soul, for I am no better than my fathers. Now these prayers would be useless if the term of life were absolutely fixed. King Solomon could ask the blessed God for long life as a contingent matter; and God, in granting him wisdom, riches and glory, also promises life at the same time, not absolutely but conditionally: If you walk in my ways, as is read in 1 Kings 3.2: Since you have not asked for many days, nor riches, nor the life of your enemies, but only asked for wisdom to judge, I give you a wise and understanding heart, riches and glory. And if you walk in my precepts, as your father walked, I will prolong your days. No one could have anticipated his own death if the term of life had been defined from eternity. Indeed, God himself often warns man to take care of himself against dangers and occasions of evil, as appears from Deut. 20.5-7: If anyone has built a new house and not yet begun to use it; if anyone has planted a vineyard and not yet enjoyed it; if anyone has betrothed a wife and not yet taken her, let him return home, lest he die in the battle itself. Hence it follows that the term of life is not predetermined by absolute divine predestination. In the Sacred Letters no passage occurs that asserts God foreordained or determined the days of life; it is only gathered that the term of life depends on time, on the heavens and on the temperament. Finally, he sums up in brief the things he treated at length in the book cited, when he speaks at pp. 232, 233:

units.la: I. Ostendimus, vitae nostrae aliquem terminum esse. II. Eum considerari posse veljuxta temperamentum corporis, vel constellationem siderum, pro ut hoc vel illo modo in corpora agant; vel juxta alios in genere, ratione praesentis, & superioris seculi. III. Terminum vitae esse mobilem. IV. Vitam hominis posse abbreviari variis modis; puta providentia Dei, natura & casu. V. Vitam posse prolongari virtute, si- ve studio & meditatione legis divinae, & observatione ejusdem: Quorum unum ad mentem, & intellectum, seu Theoriam; alterum ad voluntatem seu praxim pertinet. VI. Liberè hominem posse uti remediis, & medicamentis, cum aegrotat. VII. Denique quamvis Deus praesciat futura contingentia: nihilominus tamen arbitrio cujusque relictum esse bene vel male agere.
units.tr: I. We have shown that there is some term of our life. II. This can be considered either according to the temperament of the body, or according to the constellation of the stars, as they act upon bodies in this or that way; or, according to others, in general, with respect to the present and the previous age. III. The term of life is mobile. IV. Man's life can be shortened in various ways, namely by the providence of God, by nature and by chance. V. Life can be prolonged by virtue, that is, by zeal and meditation upon the divine law and by observance of it; of which the one pertains to the mind and understanding, or theory, the other to the will, or practice. VI. Man can freely use remedies and medicines when he is sick. VII. Finally, although God foreknows future contingent things, nevertheless it is left to each person's choice to act well or badly.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Inquirunt diligenter Judaei, qua ratione Benedictus Deus per suam divinam providentiam conservet, moveat, gubernetque res omnes; mnes; Concluduntque unanimi sententia, existentia omnia extra Deum conservari, in- que suo statu conservari per yws Influentiam, seu Affluentiam, voce desumpta à fonte ingen- ti, perpetuoque, qui sicut aquas non ex uno so- lum effundit latere, sed undiquaque, inque omnes deducit partes, nec propinqua tantum loca, sed & remota irrigat, vivificatque; Sic pariter intelligentia summa, virtus est perpe- tua, maximaque, quæ non uno solum tempo- re, sed perpetuo, nec in aliquas, propinquas- que, sed in omnes, imo remotissimas influit, tum movendo, tum gubernando, sicuti hæc deducta cernere licet apud Rabbi Mosen Maimonidem More Nevochim Parte II. cap. 12. pag. 214. conferenda enim ipsius Parte I. cap. 69. pap. 126. ubi sic loquitur: Nam per ejus Existentiam omnia existunt, & ipse quoque continuat ac conservat statum ipsorum per rem quan- dam, quæ vocatur Influentia.
units.tr: The Jews inquire carefully by what method the blessed God, through his divine providence, preserves, moves and governs all things. They conclude with one voice that all existing things outside God are preserved and kept in their state through what they call shefa [שפע], that is, influence, a word taken from a great and perpetual fountain. Just as such a fountain pours out water not from one side only but on every side, and leads it into all parts, watering and enlivening not only nearby places but also remote ones, so the supreme intelligence is a perpetual and very great power, which flows not at one time only but perpetually, and not into neighbouring places only but into all, even the most remote, both in moving and in governing. These matters may be seen drawn out by Rabbi Moses Maimonides, More Nevochim, Part II, ch. 12, p. 214; they should also be compared with Part I, ch. 69, p. 126, where he speaks thus: For through his existence all things exist, and he himself also continues and preserves their state by a certain thing which is called Influence.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Conveniunt pariter Deum Sanctum confervare ac gubernare res sublunares (seu inferiores per Mundum Superiorem, seu Astrorum influentiam, nec quemquam inter Israelis Sapientes & Philosophos de hac dubitasse doctrina, sicuti ait Rabbi Moses Maimonides in Epistolis suis: Nullus est inter Sapientes Israelis & Philo-
units.tr: They likewise agree that the Holy God preserves and governs the sublunary (or lower) things through the Higher World, that is, through the influence of the stars. No one among the wise men of Israel and the philosophers has doubted this doctrine, as Rabbi Moses Maimonides says in his Epistles: There is no one among the wise men of Israel and the Philo-

units.la: Philosophos, qui de eo disceptet ; Et in More Ne- vochim, Parte II. cap.10. pag.206. Notum est, Philosophos omnes, quotiescunque loquuntur de regimine & gubernatione mundi, statuere, Mundum hunc Inferiorem generabilem & corruptibilem regi a Virtutibus & lusluentiis Spherarum cœlestium, quemadmodum aliquoties jam monuimus; Uti quoque Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel in libello de Termino Vitæ, pag.9. Hebraei autem concedunt corpora inferiora operari per virtutem cœlestium ; Quod quoque aliquali modo adstruit explicatq; Rabbi Hac Sangarus in Libro Cosri, Part. I. sect. 77. quamvis sapientiam Astris deneget : Elementa, Sol, Luna, & stellæ cætera habent equidem operationes quasdam, veluti calefaciendi, refrigerādi, humectandi, & exsiccandi, quæque ab hiis dependent; nec tamen attribuimus illis Sapientiam, sed Ministerium duntaxat; vt autem formatrix, mensuratrix, & profeminandi, ut & omnia ea, quibus Sapientia inest cum intentione certa, non attribuenda sunt nisi Sapienti & Omnipotenti : si quis illa, quæ materiam per calorem aut frigus præparant, velit Naturam appellare, non peccabit, si removeat ab illis Sapientiam, quemadmodum removetur a viro & muliere generatio infantis per ipsorum conjunctionem : suppeditant enim duntaxat materiam, quæ recipit formam humanam; forma autem est a Formatore sapiente. Ita minimam quoque terræ herbam Astrorum Influentiæ subjiciunt Hebræi, prout Sapientes eorum testantur cum Rabbi Maimonide More Nevo-chim, Part. II. cap. 10. pag. 106. In hunc sensum dicunt Sapientes nostri: Non est ulla herbabic infra, quæ non habeat בזמ Massal (h.e. Planetam, si-dus), Influentiam supra in Firmamento, qua percutit illam, eique dicit, Cresce, sicut dicitur Iobi cap. 38. vers. 33. Nunquid nosti statuta cœli? Nunquid ponès dominium ejus in terra? (Massal hoc loco vocant non solum duodecim signa Zodiaci, sed etiam Planetas, sicut videre est in Bereschit Rabba, ubi dicunt; Est Massal cursum suum absolvens spatio triginta dierum, & est Massal absolvens iter suum spatio triginta annorum.) illo enim dicto voluerunt docere, omnia Individua generabilia habere virtutes suas à syderibus vel stellis eisdem appropriatis. Et licet virtutes orbium cœlestiū diffusæ sint per omnia Entia; tamen virtutem uniuscujusq; stellæ vel Planetæ, speciei alicui propriam esse, quemadmodum se res habet in virtutibus & facultatibus corporis. Ostendit ulterius Rabbi Maimonides Part. II. c. 10. pag. 107. Globos stellatos in interiora influere corpora, illaq; motu suo movere; Ita orbem Lunæ movere aquam, cujus rei argumentum fit, quòd crescente Luna, crescant quoque maria & flumina, eademque decrescente, & illa decrescant; Orbem Solis movere ignem, quòd cum Sole calor diffundatur in omnia Entia, tia, eo vero recedente frigus dominetur: Orbem reliquorum Planetarum movere aerem, qui propter multitudinem motuum illorum hinc sæpe mutatur, variatur, coarctatur, colligatur, & diffundatur; Orbem reliquarum stellarum fixarum movere terram, unde innumeræ species germinantes oriantur. Cæterum ne sine ratione dicere videatur, mundum inferiorem regi ab orbibus cœlestibus, virtutibusque cœli, adducunt probationem ex Genesios cap. 1. verf. 18. Ut dominarentur diei ac nocti, ac dividerent lucem a tenebris; Ex quo clarissime colligatur, quòd hoc sine Gubernatione neutiquam fieri possit; Et ex Deuteron. cap. 4. verf. 19. Ne attollas oculos tuos in cælum, ut videas Solem, Lunam, & stellas, & omnem militiam cœli, & impellaris, ut incurves te eis, colasq; ea, quae distribuit Dominus Deus tuus omnibus populis sub toto cœlo; Ex quo concludunt, Astra in cœlis posita esse a divino Numine, non ut a creaturis colerentur, sed ut creaturas gubernarent; Exinde quoque ortum videmus, quod divinam Providentiam appellent Influentiam cœlestem, Astrum, Planeta, cum credant inferiora a cœlo regi, gubernarique.
units.tr: Philosophers who dispute about it. In the More Nevochim, Part II, ch. 10, p. 206: It is well known that all philosophers, whenever they speak of the rule and government of the world, hold that this lower world, which is generable and corruptible, is ruled by the powers and influences of the celestial spheres, as we have already pointed out several times. Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel also says in his booklet On the Term of Life, p. 9: The Hebrews, however, concede that lower bodies act by the power of the heavenly things. Rabbi Hac Sangarus in the Book of the Kuzari, Part I, sect. 77, affirms this in some measure and explains it, though he denies wisdom to the stars: The elements, the Sun, the Moon and the other stars indeed have certain operations, such as heating, cooling, moistening and drying, and things that depend on these. Yet we do not attribute wisdom to them, but only ministry. But the forming, measuring and begetting, and all those things in which wisdom is present with a certain intention, are to be attributed only to the Wise and Omnipotent. If anyone wishes to call those things which prepare matter by heat or cold "nature", he will not err, provided he removes wisdom from them, just as the generation of a child is removed from man and woman through their union. For they merely supply the matter which receives human form; but the form is from the wise Former. Thus the Hebrews also subject even the smallest herb of the earth to the influences of the stars, as their wise men attest, with Rabbi Maimonides, More Nevochim, Part II, ch. 10, p. 106: In this sense our wise men say: there is no herb here below that does not have its Massal [מזל] (that is, its planet or star), an influence above in the firmament, which strikes it and says to it, "Grow". As it is said in Job ch. 38 v. 33: Do you know the ordinances of heaven? Will you set its dominion on the earth? (Here they call Massal not only the twelve signs of the zodiac but also the planets, as may be seen in Bereshit Rabba, where they say: Massal is that which completes its course in a space of thirty days, and Massal is that which completes its journey in a space of thirty years.) For by that saying they meant to teach that all generable individuals have their powers from the stars or planets appropriated to them. And although the powers of the celestial spheres are diffused through all beings, yet the power of each star or planet is proper to some species, just as things stand with the powers and faculties of the body. Maimonides further shows, Part II, ch. 10, p. 107, that the starry globes flow into the inner bodies and move them by their motion. Thus the sphere of the Moon moves the water; the proof of this is that when the Moon waxes, the seas and rivers also grow, and when it wanes, they too decrease. The sphere of the Sun moves fire, because with the Sun heat is diffused into all beings, but when it recedes, cold prevails. The sphere of the other planets moves the air, which, on account of the multitude of their motions, is often changed, varied, compressed, gathered and diffused. The sphere of the other fixed stars moves the earth, whence innumerable kinds of germinating things arise. Moreover, lest they seem to speak without reason in saying that the lower world is ruled by the celestial spheres and the powers of heaven, they adduce as proof Genesis ch. 1 v. 18: That they might rule the day and the night, and divide the light from the darkness. From this it is most clearly gathered that this cannot be done in any way without government. And Deuteronomy ch. 4 v. 19: Lest you lift up your eyes to heaven, and see the Sun, the Moon and the stars, and all the host of heaven, and be driven to bow down to them and serve them, which the Lord your God has allotted to all peoples under the whole heaven. From this they conclude that the stars placed in the heavens are from the divine Power, not that they should be worshipped as creatures, but that they should govern creatures. Hence we also see the origin of their calling divine Providence "celestial influence", "star", "planet", since they believe the lower things are ruled and governed by the heavens.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Sed discordes valde, num stellarum virtutes ipsa agitent corpora humana, ipsamque hominis minis disponant, moveantque mentem? Qui affirmant, maximo sunt apud Judaeos numero, inter quos ex Veteribus Talmudistae in Moed katon sol. 28. col. 1. asserentes: Vita filii & alimentum non a pietate vel meritis hominum pendent, sed a Planeta pendet res; Et Targumistae ad Eccles. cap. 9. verl. 2. Omnia a sideribus pendent. Et ex Recentioribus Rabbi Aben Esra, Rabbi Isac Abarbanel, Rabbi Bahye, Rabbi Isac Cohen, Rabbi Levi Ben Gerson, Rabbi Meser de Leon, Rabbi Joel Ben Sueb, Rabbi Joseph Albo, Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, aliique multi, qui uno ore profitentur, expositione astrorum derivari aliquam virtutem in infantes in lucem recens editos, & disponi ordinem vitae & necis, opulentiae & paupertatis; ut adeo communis fere hodie sententia sit, astra non necessitare res humanas, sed inclinare, acregere, stellasque non tollere voluntatem hominis, ipsumque destruere liberum arbitrium, sed juvare, magisque excitare, cum non solum negent Fatum Astronomicum, seu fatalem astrorum necessitatem, quae tollat in homine omnem voluntatem accedendi aut ad virtutem, aut ad vitium, cuique nullis humanis rationibus resistere liceat. Solent autem asserentum variis probare argumentis, tum ab Experientia & ratione, tum ab auctoritate thoritate Scripturæ desumptis, quæ cum collegerit Menasseh Ben Israel in Termino Vitæ, utile erit, sequentibus his enarrare à pag. 14.
units.tr: But they strongly disagree on whether the powers of the stars actually move human bodies, shape the very constitution of man, and stir the mind. Those who affirm it are by far the greater number among the Jews. Among the older writers the Talmudists, in Moed Katan, fol. 28, col. 1, assert: The life of a son and his sustenance depend not on the piety or merits of men, but a thing depends on the Planet. The Targumists on Ecclesiastes ch. 9 v. 2 say: All things depend on the stars. Among the more recent: Rabbi Aben Ezra, Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel, Rabbi Bahye, Rabbi Isaac Cohen, Rabbi Levi ben Gerson, Rabbi Moses de Leon, Rabbi Joel ben Sueb, Rabbi Joseph Albo, Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, and many others, who with one voice profess that by the exposition of the stars some power is derived into infants newly brought into the light, and that the order of life and death, of wealth and poverty, is arranged thereby. So that the common opinion today is almost that the stars do not necessitate human affairs but incline and arouse them; that the stars do not take away the will of man nor destroy free choice, but help and rather stir it up. For they deny not only astronomical Fate, that is, the fatal necessity of the stars, which would take from man every will to approach either virtue or vice, and against which no human reason could resist. They are accustomed to prove their assertion by various arguments, both drawn from experience and reason and from the authority of Scripture, which Menasseh ben Israel collected in the Term of Life. It will be useful to recount these, from p. 14 onwards, as follows.

units.la: I. Constat Experientia, Oracula Astrologorum solere eventibus respondere, & sæpissime eos prædixisse vitā brevem aut longā, vitæque felicitate aut calamitatem. Ergo astra hæc omnia dissonunt. II. Ratio: Nemini non constat, generationem & corruptionem omnium sublunarium dependere à motu cælestium. Apparet etiam, prout aer est turbidior aut serenior, ita eum se insinuare corporibus hominum, & prout respirando attrahitur, ita etiam affici animos. Itaque non potest negari cælum potentiam aliquam in corpora humana habere.
units.tr: I. It is established by experience that the oracles of astrologers usually correspond to events, and very often have foretold a short or long life, and the happiness or calamity of life. Therefore these stars all have such an effect. II. Reason: it is known to everyone that the generation and corruption of all sublunary things depend on the motion of the heavenly bodies. It also appears that as the air is more turbid or clearer, so it insinuates itself into the bodies of men; and as it is drawn in by breathing, so the minds are also affected. Thus it cannot be denied that heaven has some power over human bodies.

units.la: III. Est ab authoritate: Scriptura enim sacra de Sole & Luna inquit Gen. 1. 14. Et posuit illa Deus in expanso cæli ad lucendum supra terram, & dominandum noctu ac interdiu. Ubi Rabbi Moseh Gerundensis quærit, quidnam per istud dominium intelligatur? Hoc est, inquit, illud dominium, quod stellæ habent in corpora humana, in quæ varias imprimunt virtutes; prout est eorum vel benevolus, vel malevolus adspectus. In libro Iudicum dicitur cap. 5. vers. 20. E cælo præliatæ sunt stellæ, è suis aggeribus pugnarunt contra Sisera. Et apud Esaiam cap. 47. vers. 13. Defetiscens multitudine consiliorum tuorum: Stent jam Astrologi, qui contemplantur stellas, qui indicant menses, & servent te ab iis, quæ superventura sunt tibi. Item Iob us ait cap. 3. verf. 2. Periisset dies, quo nasciturus eram, & nox, qua dictum est, conceptus est mas : ubi refert malafua ad horam conceptionis & nativitatis suæ. Ex his omnibus virtus istastellarum colligitur. Sed quamvis homines, humanaque omnia subjiciant astris, eorumq; operationibus, ingeminantes tritum illud Proverbium, הכל תלוי במזלות omnia pendent ab astris; non tamen omnia propterea ita tribuunt astris, quasi nihil sine astris fieret in inferioribus, cum Deum collocent supra stellas, qui disponat de rebus humanis juxta cujusque meritum, statuantque præterea Astra certis temporibus non omnes agitare homines, quare Talmudici Doctores ajunt אין מזל לישראל Non est Astrum vel Planeta Israeli, cui Israel sit subjectus; & alio loco יש מזל לישראל Est Planeta Israeli; Intelligentes & exponentes cum Rabbi Aben Esra Commentario in Exodum c. 34. Non est Israeli Planeta, omni illo tempore, quo legis sunt observatores : At si legem non observaverit, dominatur illis Planeta; Hinc quoque affirmant, quòd quicunque operam det legi, averta à se malum stellarum influentium, & qui adhæreat præceptis, sit supra Planetas, uti hæc & alia fusius explicant Rabbi Joseph Albo de Fundamentis, lib. 4. cap. 4. Rabbi Isac Abarbanel in Commentario ad Deuteronomium, mium, seft. יחמתי. Et in Commentario ad Danielem cap. 9. verf. 21. Raschba in Quæstionibus & Responsionibus, Rabbi Jedaia Happenini in Bechinat Olam cap. 17. & 18. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel de Termino vitæ, pag. 10.
units.tr: III. It is from authority. For holy Scripture says of the Sun and Moon, Gen. 1. 14: And God placed them in the expanse of heaven to give light upon the earth, and to rule by night and by day. Here Rabbi Moses of Gerona asks what is meant by this dominion? This, he says, is the dominion that the stars have over human bodies, into which they impress various powers, according as their aspect is benevolent or malevolent. In the book of Judges it is said, ch. 5 v. 20: They fought from heaven; from their courses the stars fought against Sisera. And in Isaiah ch. 47 v. 13: You are wearied by the multitude of your counsels. Let now the astrologers stand, who contemplate the stars, who announce the months, and let them save you from those things which shall come upon you. Likewise Job says, ch. 3 v. 2: Let the day perish on which I was to be born, and the night in which it was said, a male is conceived. Where he refers his misfortune to the hour of his conception and birth. From all these the power of the stars is gathered. But although men subject human affairs and all things to the stars and their operations, repeating that trite proverb, הכל תלוי במזלות [hakol talui bamazalot], all things depend on the astrological signs; yet they do not on that account attribute all things to the stars as if nothing happened in lower things without the stars. For they place God above the stars, who disposes of human affairs according to each one's merit, and they further hold that the stars at certain times do not all agitate men. Wherefore the Talmudic doctors say: אין מזל לישראל [ein mazal leyisrael], There is no star or planet for Israel, to which Israel is subject; and in another place: יש מזל לישראל [yesh mazal leyisrael], There is a planet for Israel. Understanding and explaining this with Rabbi Aben Ezra's commentary on Exodus ch. 34: There is no planet for Israel at all times when they are observers of the law; but if they do not observe the law, the planet rules over them. Hence they also affirm that whoever applies himself to the law turns away from himself the evil of the influencing stars, and whoever adheres to the precepts is above the planets. These and other things are explained more fully by Rabbi Joseph Albo, De Fundamentis, bk. 4, ch. 4; Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel in his commentary on Deuteronomy, section יחמתי [yechamti]; and in his commentary on Daniel ch. 9 v. 21; Rashba in Questions and Responsa; Rabbi Jedaiah Happenini in Bechinat Olam, ch. 17 and 18; and Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, On the Term of Life, p. 10.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Qui מעשה הכוכבים Dispositionem stellarum, vel מעשה מוה Ordinationem, Influentiam Astrorum negant, perpauci hodie sunt inter Judæos, loquentes, sentientesque cum Rabbi Mose Maimonide, qui in Epistolis suis strenue inficiatur, virtutem istam stellarum ad ipsas hominum mentes pertingere, easque vario modo afficere, tandemque ad hoc vel illud necessario disponere, sicuti videmus apud Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel in Termino vitæ à pag. 9. Rabbi Moses Ægyptius in suis Epistolis strenuè id negat, cum sic loquitur: Omnes eventus humanos quidam Philosophorum tribuunt casui, nec Providentiam admittunt; Nonnulli hos defecerunt stellarum virtuti. Alij contra omnia referunt ad fatalem aliquam astrorum necessitatem, & volunt, quod Ruben sit dives, Simeon pauper, hic felix, ille calamitosus, id omne provenire à positione & efficacia stellarum, quæ in tempus nativitatis incidit; Hanc quoque legem esse inviolabilem. Sed utraque opinio est salsissima: Quia ista, quæ casui omnia tribuunt
units.tr: Those who deny that the arrangement of the stars (מעשה הכוכבים) or their ordering (מעשה מוה) has any influence are very few among the Jews today. They speak and think with Rabbi Moses Maimonides, who in his Epistles vigorously denies that this power of the stars reaches the minds of men, affects them in various ways, and finally disposes them necessarily to this or that, as we see in Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, Termino vitæ, from p. 9. Rabbi Moses Ægyptius vigorously denies this in his Epistles, when he speaks thus: Some philosophers ascribe all human events to chance and admit no Providence; some have attributed them to the power of the stars. Others refer everything to a certain fatal necessity of the stars, and hold that Reuben is rich, Simeon poor, this man happy, that one unfortunate, and that all this arises from the position and efficacy of the stars that fell at the time of birth; and that this law is inviolable. But both opinions are utterly false, because those who attribute everything to chance

units.la: ii. it, negat Providentiam adeo decantatam in Sacris libris: Ista vero, quae tantam vim defert stellis, & sequitur Astrologiam iudiciariam, est delira. Primo, inquit, pervolvi omnes libros Arabicos, de hac scientia agentes, sed tandem deprehendi totum atq; omne istud esse meram vanitatem & vesaniam. Sed nec huic scientiae dediti fuerunt Graeci Sapientes, qui revera sapientes vocari potuerunt, neq; unquam de eo liber ullus ab iis scriptus extat. Persae quoq; eam vanam iudicarunt; Solis Casdaei, Chaldaei, Aegyptii, & Cananaei, vanitati huic fuerunt addicti; Quia in hoc eorum Religio consistebat per aliquod tempus. Postmodum accedens ad rationes magis apertas ait: Est inter articulos legis nostra, quem & omnes Philosophi admittunt, hic dari liberum arbitrium, & hominem praeditum esse absoluta potentia sequendi bonum, & discedendi a malo; uti & contra sectandi appetitum sensuum, non vero rationis dictamen? Iam vero si tanta est potentia stellarum in corpora hominum, ubi relicta est ista libertas hominum? Si homines non possunt effugere vim & impressionem stellarum, quorsum tunc sunt praecepta? Quid proderit, si quis studeat exonerare se vitiis, & accendere animum ad virtutem, cum Caelum determinaverit, quando quis nascitur, qualis futurus sit? Sic ab astris determinata est libertas humana, uti quae vana & inutilis est omnis cura & sollicitudo hominum. Ergo inquit Rabbi Moses, aequum est, ut hoc totum attriattribuamus divinæ Providentiæ: nempe quia Ruben peccavit, idcirco pauper evasit, & sic fieri potest ut novo aliquo merito suo rursus opulentus evadat. Omnes eventus prosperos, & adversos oportet tribuere cuiuslibet operibus; Quia videmus Deum promittere vitam & bona temporalia observantibus præcepta sua. Quod si videatur aliquando contrarium evenire, id est, justo mala accidere, tum oportet illud relinquere Deo; Quia ipse solus novit secreta cordium, ac scit causas, cur castiget, aut præmio afficiat.
units.tr: ii. He denies the Providence so celebrated in the sacred books. But the view that grants such great power to the stars and follows judicial astrology is mad. First, he says, I have read through all the Arabic books that treat of this science, but in the end I found that the whole of it is pure vanity and madness. Nor were the wise Greeks, who could truly be called wise, devoted to this science, and no book on it written by them exists. The Persians also judged it vain. The Chaldeans, the Egyptians and the Canaanites, the Sabians, were addicted to this vanity, because their religion consisted in it for some time. Afterwards, coming to more open arguments, he says: Among the articles of our law, which all philosophers also admit, is this: that free choice is given, and that man is endowed with an absolute power to pursue the good and to turn away from evil, and likewise to resist the appetite of the senses and not follow it, but follow the dictate of reason. Now, if the power of the stars over the bodies of men is so great, where is that freedom of men left? If men cannot escape the force and impression of the stars, what then is the point of precepts? What will it profit if someone strives to free himself from vices and kindle his soul to virtue, when heaven has determined, at the moment of a man's birth, what he will be like? Thus human freedom is determined by the stars, and every care and anxiety of men is vain and useless. Therefore, says Rabbi Moses, it is right that we attribute all this to divine Providence: namely, because Reuben sinned, he therefore became poor, and so it can happen that by some new merit of his he again becomes wealthy. All prosperous and adverse events must be ascribed to each person's works, because we see God promising life and temporal goods to those who keep his precepts. But if it sometimes seems that the contrary happens, that is, that evils befall a just man, then this must be left to God, because he alone knows the secrets of hearts and knows the causes why he chastises or rewards.

units.la: CAPUT VIII. De Angelis.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the Angels.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: SEquuntur Angeli, quos communi vocabulo מלאכים Legatos nuncupant, quod à Deo mittantur, Deique nomine quædam loquantur, faciantque. Statuunt egregie, Angelorum naturam non esse necessariam, hinc neque æternam, sed liberam, dependentem, hinc cum rebus omnibus in tempore creatam, variisque in hanc rem adducunt rationes, docentes, centes, quod Angeli ab æterno non potuerint quidem esse creati, cum Creatio non posiit cō-sistere cum æternitate; Quod Exodi cap. 20. in Decalogo dicatur, Deum sex dierum spatio fecisse cœlum & terram, & omnia quæ illis continentur, per consequens Angelos, cum non minimam partem faciant universi, (ex illis diebus creatos esse; Quod Deus solus in Scripturis appelletur Deus antiquitatis; Quod Sacra Pagina eodem modo loquatur de Creatione Angelorum, & rerum aliarum omnium, illudque maxime pateat ex verbis Psalmi 148. v. 1. Teste Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel Problemate 24. de Creatione. Credunt bonos Angelos primo die cum cœlo creatos esse, malos Angelos cum inferno secundo die formatos, uti pluribus cap. 6. de Creatione demonstratum est. Credunt insuper Angelos aliquos non creatos in iex illis primis diebus, sed post illos dies aliis temporibus productos, formatosque, statim describendos.
units.tr: Next come the angels, whom the Hebrews call by the common name מלאכים [malachim] Messengers, because they are sent by God and say and do certain things in God's name. The Hebrews rightly hold that the nature of angels is not necessary, and so is neither eternal but free and dependent, and therefore was created in time along with all other things. They bring various arguments for this, teaching that angels could not have been created from eternity, since creation cannot stand together with eternity. They point out that Exodus 20, in the Decalogue, says that God made heaven and earth and all that is in them in the space of six days, and so the angels, since they form no small part of the universe, were created in those days. They note that God alone is called the God of antiquity in the Scriptures, and that Sacred Scripture speaks of the creation of angels in the same way as of all other things, which is most evident from the words of Psalm 148:1. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, Problem 24 on Creation, is a witness to this. They believe that the good angels were created with heaven on the first day, and the evil angels formed with hell on the second day, as has been shown at greater length in chapter 6 on Creation. They further believe that some angels were not created on those first days but were produced and formed at other times after them, which will be described shortly.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Negant Judæi ullum dari Angelum increatum, ut Messiæ, Filii Dei divinitati ponant obicem, afferentes, Angelum illum, qui tam sæpe apparuit Patriarchis, imo Mosi in Rubo, Exod. cap. 3. per quem data fuit Israelitis lex, qui tentatus in deserto, qui Israelem duxit, qui Jehova totiens vocatur, qui adoratus, invocatusque, qui sibi passim divina attribuit attributa, Genes. cap. 18. 19. Exod. cap. 3. qui dicitur מלאך הברית Angelus Assertor, Redemptorque, Genes. cap. 48. In cujus medio est nomen Dei, Exod. cap. 23. Quique est מלאך הברית Angelus fœderis, Malach. cap. 3. & מלאך פני Angelus faciei DEI, Es. cap. 63. Cui auscultare debuit Israel, &c. Angelum illum non verum fuisse Jehova, Filium Dei æternum, Angelum increatum, manifestandum suo tempore in carne per nativitatem ex Virgine; Sed creaturam fuisse mere Angelicam, quæ Dei substinuerit personam, adque majorem authoritatem Dei assumserit nomen. Non intelligunt amplius moderni Judæi cum Majoribus suis per Angelum מטטרון Metatron Angelum increatum, Deum Omnipotentem, Principem facierum, Messiam; Verum nudam creaturam angelicam, quæ omnis sit expers divinitatis, indigitant, ut ita verum sit quod Optimus Wagenseilius de Rabbi Isaco Ben Abraham, ejusque Libro Chisfuk Emuna in Præfatione ejus scribit: Ipsa lectio facile cuique prodet, circa initium hujus seculi demum conceptum esse tetrum ac stygium hunc fœtum. Sed, quo recentior, eo est nequior, feriocior, & ad sucum faciendum aptior. Ita nimirum apud Iudæos quoque damnosa dities. dies multa depravat, dabuntque mox libros vitio- fiores, nisi fibulam decenter iis imponant, aut adver- sus nos grassantibus objiciant murices, illi, ad quos hoc officium pertinet. Caeterum hanc Veterum de Metatron Angelo mentem probant lucu- lenter Talmudici in Tractatu Sanhedrin, cap. 4. sol. 38. Maxime Rabbini, apud Rabbi Sche- lomo Jarchi, in Commentario Exodi, cap. 23. cum ad verba, nomen meu in medio ejus est, sic scribit: Doctores nostri dixerunt, ille est Me- tatron, cujus nomen est sicut nomen Doctorus sui, nempe Dei שדי Omnipotentis. Nam שדי Ge- matrice 314. totidem; Et apud Autho- rem libri Jalkut in hunc locum; Cum quibus conferri necessario debet Rabbi Elias Levita, qui in Thisbi ad vocem Metateron, Angelum illum praeterea vocat Principem faciem- rum, quando ita loquitur: Metatron Princeps facierum. Dicunt Rabbini Angelum esse qui semper videat faciem Regis excelsi, de quo dictum fit illud in Exodo cap. 23. Quoniam nomen meum intra ipsum est. Eo quod simile nomen habeat cum Domino suo. Metatron enim Geometrice supputatum idem valet quod שדי Schaddai; Sic Rabbi Abraham Schalom in Tractatu Neve Schalom, Metatron Angelum putat Michaelem, cum lib. 1 o. cap. 3. illa Exodi cap. 23. ו. 21. hoc modo explicat: Doctores nostri piae memoriae dixerunt runt hunc esse Metatron, cujus nomen est sicut nomen Domini sui. Hic est Michael; Sic pariter Rabbi Bechai multa in hunc commentatur locum, ostenditque quod vox Metatron duo complectatur significata, Dominum, & Legatum; Quod innuat שומר ישראל Custodem Israelis, qui Israelem custodiat, ejusque curam habeat; Quod ipse Metatron sit Dominus omnium quæ sub eo sunt, & quod omnis Exercitus superiorum & inferiorum in potestate ejus sint, & sub ejus manu; Quod Deus Benedictus ipsum Dominum posuerit domus suæ, & Dominatorem omnium suorum. Vocant ipsum alii Rabbini שר העולם Principem mundi, traduntque porro Talmudici, quod Angelo Metatron data sit potestas, ut sedeat, & conscribat meritalfraelitarum; rursus, quod ea polleat potestate, ut ipsorum possit delere merita; Ex quibus omnibus egregie judicat maximus Buxtorfius, quod hæc ad Messiam referenda sint, cum in Lexico laboriosò & doctissimo, pag. 1192. sic inquit: Hi ulterius respexisse videntur, ad Angelum nempe non creatum, (nulli enim hoc competit,) sed increatum, Messiam nempe, sive Christum.
units.tr: The Jews deny that there is any uncreated angel, lest such an angel stand in the way of the divinity of the Messiah, the Son of God. They assert that the angel who so often appeared to the patriarchs, indeed to Moses in the bush (Exod. 3), through whom the law was given to Israel, who was tempted in the wilderness, who led Israel, who is so often called Jehovah, who was worshipped and invoked, and who everywhere ascribed divine attributes to himself (Gen. 18, 19; Exod. 3), who is called מלאך הברית [malakh ha-berit] Angel the Vindicator and Redeemer (Gen. 48), in whom is the name of God (Exod. 23), who is Angel of the covenant (Mal. 3) and מלאך פני [malakh peni] Angel of the face of GOD (Isa. 63), whom Israel ought to obey, etc., was not the true Jehovah, the eternal Son of God, the uncreated Angel, who was to be manifested in the flesh in his time through birth from a Virgin. Rather, he was a purely angelic creature, which bore the person of God and assumed the name of God by greater authority. The modern Jews no longer understand, as their forefathers did, by the Angel מטטרון [Metatron] an uncreated Angel, the Almighty God, the Prince of the face, the Messiah. They designate instead a bare angelic creature, wholly devoid of divinity. Thus it is true what the most excellent Wagenseil writes of Rabbi Isaac Ben Abraham and his book Chizzuk Emuna, in its Preface: The reading itself will easily reveal to anyone that this dark and hellish brood was conceived only about the beginning of this century. But the more recent it is, the more wicked, fiercer and more fit for stirring up trouble it is. Thus indeed among the Jews also, dangerous riches deprave many days, and soon they will produce books more vicious, unless those whose office it is fasten a clasp on them properly, or throw them to the critics who attack us. Moreover, the Talmudists in tractate Sanhedrin, chapter 4, folio 38, clearly prove that this was the mind of the ancients concerning the Angel Metatron. Above all the Rabbis, Rabbi Shelomo Jarchi, in his Commentary on Exodus chapter 23, when he comes to the words my name is in the midst of him, writes thus: Our teachers have said, he is Metatron, whose name is like the name of his Master, namely the Almighty שדי [Shaddai] of God. For שדי [Shaddai], by gematria, is 314, as is Metatron. The same is found in the author of the book Jalkut on this passage. With these must necessarily be compared Rabbi Elias Levita, who in the Thisbi, under the word Metatron, also calls that Angel the Prince of the face, when he speaks thus: Metatron, Prince of the face. The Rabbis say that the Angel is one who always sees the face of the most high King, of whom it is said in Exodus 23: for my name is within him, because he has a name similar to that of his Lord. For Metatron, computed by gematria, has the same value as שדי [Shaddai]. So Rabbi Abraham Shalom, in his treatise Neve Shalom, thinks that the Angel Metatron is Michael, when in book 10, chapter 3, he explains that passage of Exodus 23:21 in this way: Our teachers of blessed memory have said that this is Metatron, whose name is like the name of his Lord. This is Michael. Likewise Rabbi Bechai comments at length on this passage and shows that the word Metatron embraces two meanings, Lord and Messenger; that it implies the שומר ישראל [shomer Yisrael] Guardian of Israel, who keeps Israel and has care of it; that Metatron himself is Lord of all that is under him, and that all the host of the higher and lower beings are in his power and under his hand; and that the blessed God placed him as Lord of his house and Ruler of all his own. Other Rabbis call him שר העולם [sar ha-olam] Prince of the world. The Talmudists further relate that power was given to the Angel Metatron to sit and record the merits of the Israelites, and again that he has power to blot out their merits. From all these things the greatest Buxtorf rightly judges that these matters are to be referred to the Messiah. In his laborious and most learned Lexicon, page 1192, he says: These seem to have looked further, namely to an Angel not created (for this applies to no creature), but uncreated, the Messiah, that is, Christ.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Scribunt Angelos maxima conditos fuisse multitudine, hinc passim memorant An-gelos gelorum exercitus, Angelorumque diversa castra, loquentes multa de מנחנ, quod turmatim concurrant Angeli ad militiam, de מחנה אלהים Castris divinis, quod castrametentur Angeli circa timentes Dominum, Psalmo 34. v. 8. probantes ex Genes. cap. 32. v. 2. Jacobum Patriarcham appellasse locum Machanaim, quod bina ibidem Angelorum comitantium castra conspexisset, castra Angelorum excubantium pro salute terrae Israelis seu Canaan, & castra Angelorum defendentium provincias extra terram Israelis, de quibus sic Author Zennorennae, qui commentarius est Hebraeo Germanicus in Legem, Genes. cap. 32. sol. 41. Es kamen die Malachim von Erez Israel, zu beleiten ihn (Jacob) in Erez Israel, Und er nennete den Ort Machanaim (zwei Heer:) dieweil er hat gesehen zwo Schaaren von Malachim: Die Malachim von außerhalb Landes / die ihn haben beleitet bis allher / und auch die Malachim von Erez Israel; Sic castrorum Angelicorum meminit quoque Rabbi Jedaia Happenini, quando in Bakkascha, seu meditatione sua, sectione secunda refert: Scintilla luminis tui ab antiquitate scaturigo diffluit, a splendore tuo effunditur, inde separantur castra intelligentiarum admirabilium, quae sunt subtiliantia purissima, intelligentes ex se ipsis; Sic Rabbi Dialman
units.tr: They write that the Angels were created in very great multitude. Hence they often speak of "the Angels' hosts" and "the diverse camps of the Angels," and they say much about מחנה [machaneh], that Angels run together in troops to serve, and about מחנה אלהים [machaneh Elohim], "the divine camps," because the Angels encamp around those who fear the Lord (Psalm 34:8). They prove from Genesis 32:2 that the Patriarch Jacob called the place Machanaim, because he had seen there two camps of Angels accompanying him: the camp of Angels keeping watch for the safety of the land of Israel or Canaan, and the camp of Angels defending the provinces outside the land of Israel. On these the author of Zennorenna, a German-Hebrew commentary on the Law, speaks thus on Genesis 32, folio 41: "The Malachim from the land of Israel came to escort him (Jacob) in the land of Israel. And he named the place Machanaim (two hosts), because he had seen two companies of Malachim: the Malachim from outside the land, who had escorted him as far as this place, and also the Malachim from the land of Israel." So too Rabbi Jedaia Happenini mentions the angelic camps, when in his Bakkascha, or meditation, section two, he writes: "The spark of your light gushes forth from the ancient fountain and is poured out from your splendour; from it are separated the camps of wondrous intelligences, which are most pure and subtle, understanding from themselves." So Rabbi Dialman,

units.la: Dfalman Backkaschæ hujus Commetator per Scaturiginem intelligit mundum Angelorum, ut ita immensam horum innuat multitudinem. Distinguunt pariter Cabbalistæ, secretiores Judæorum Theologi, exercitus Angelorum in Mizaloth, El, Ligion, Rihaton, Chirton, Giftera: Mizaloth autem dicuntur esse duodecim, juxta duodecim signa Zodiaci. El vero dicunt esse cohortes triginta pro quolibet illorum duodecim. Unde sunt in numero trecentæ sexaginta Angelorum cohortes. Ligion autem, multiplicat illum numerum trecentorum sexaginta per triginta. Unde resultat numerus decem millium, & octingentorum: Et hunc numerum ipsi Cabbalistæ multiplicant pariter per triginta: Et fit Rihaton, constans ex trecentis viginti quatuor millibus. Et hunc numerum adhuc ipsi per triginta multiplicant: & fit Chirton, constans ex nongentis millium millibus, & septuaginta duob° millib°. Et huc nuerum parimodo per triginta multiplicant: Unde resultat Giftera, constans ex ducentis, nonaginta, & uno millium millibus, & sexcentis millibus. Quorum omnium summa est, trecenta, & unum millium millia, sexcenta, & quinquaginta quinq; millia centum, & septuaginta duo. Qui omnes sunt administratorii spiritus, in minis-terium missi; Sed de his plura Archangelus à Burgo Novo in Commentario de Cabbalistarum dogmatibus, pag. 740, 741, 778. Editionis Pistoriana. IV.
units.tr: Dialman, the commentator on this Bakkascha, understands by the Fountain the world of the Angels, thereby indicating their immense multitude. Likewise the Cabbalists, the more secret theologians of the Jews, distinguish the hosts of Angels into Mizaloth, El, Ligion, Rihaton, Chirton and Giftera. The Mizaloth are said to be twelve, according to the twelve signs of the Zodiac. The El they say are thirty cohorts for each of those twelve, so there are three hundred and sixty cohorts of Angels. Ligion multiplies that number, three hundred and sixty, by thirty, which yields ten thousand eight hundred. The Cabbalists multiply this number again by thirty, and it becomes Rihaton, consisting of three hundred and twenty-four thousand. They multiply this number again by thirty, and it becomes Chirton, consisting of nine hundred thousand thousands and seventy-two thousand. Multiplying this number again by thirty in the same way yields Giftera, consisting of two hundred and ninety-one million and six hundred thousand. The sum of all of these is three hundred and one million, six hundred and fifty-five thousand, one hundred and seventy-two. All of them are "ministering spirits, sent to minister" (Hebrews 1:14). But more on these things is found in Archangelus à Burgo Novo, in his Commentary on the Doctrines of the Cabbalists, pp. 740, 741, 778, Pistorius edition. IV.

units.la: Discriminant Angelos creatos tum in bonos, מלאכי קדש Angelos sanctos, tum in malos, מלאכי חבלה Angelos damni vel perditionis, qui quoque appellantur מלאכי מות Angeli mortis, שטנים ומקקים Adversarii, Carnifices, Tortoresque; neutiquam credentes, Angelos aliquos prodiisse malos è manu Dei, seu malos à divino Numine formatos in prima rerum creatione, cum bonitati divinae maximè repugnet, sed propria libidine, ex perverso liberi arbitrii usu malos deinde factos, malosque praeterea Angelos dictos effectivè, quod adversus malos, impiosque, justitiae, iraeque divinae sint Ministri, Executoresque; Quamquam non negent Judaei Angelos formaliter malos, quos à prioribus malis distinguunt, cum illos non creatos, sed generatos censeant, prout mox pluribus. Discriminant pariter innumeras Angelorum catervas, & à diversis nominibus, functionibusque seu officiis, & à sedibus, quas inhabitant, frequentantque, hinc diversas quoque ordinant Angelorum classes. Ex communi, receptaque sententia tres gradus seu ordines maximè ximè constituunt inter Angelos, tribuuntque unicuique ordini seu classi יתר בית domum Iudicij, in qua de rebus conveniant deliberaturi, & ex his omnibus formant deinde סנהדרין Synedrium, seu Concilium illud maximum; Hinc apud Rabbinos nõ infrequens est mentio Domus Judicii, magni & parvi, sic in Midrasch Schir Hasschirim cap. 1. vers. 9. Ubicunque in sacra Scriptura dicitur יהוה Et Dominus, intelligitur de ipso, & de Domo judicij sui; Sic iisdem verbis in Bereschit Rabba; Confer Maimonidem in More Nevochim, Part. II. cap. 6.
units.tr: They distinguish created Angels both into good ones, מלאכי קדש [malachei qodesh], holy Angels, and into evil ones, מלאכי חבלה [malachei chabalah], Angels of destruction or ruin, who are also called מלאכי מות [malachei mavet], Angels of death, and שטנים ומקקים [shetanim u-mekakim], adversaries, executioners and tormentors. They by no means believe that any Angels came forth evil from the hand of God, that is, were formed evil by the divine power in the first creation of things, since this is utterly contrary to the divine goodness; rather, they became evil afterwards through their own lust, from the perverse use of free will, and they are called evil Angels also in the effective sense, because they are ministers and executors of justice and of the wrath of God against the wicked and impious. Yet the Jews do not deny that there are Angels that are evil in the formal sense, whom they distinguish from the former evil ones, since they judge these not to have been created but generated, as will be said at greater length shortly. Likewise they distinguish the innumerable troops of Angels both by their different names and functions or offices, and by the dwellings which they inhabit and frequent; hence they also arrange diverse classes of Angels. According to the common and received opinion, they establish chiefly three grades or orders among the Angels, and to each order or class they assign the יתר בית [bayit yeter], that is, the house of judgment, in which they are to meet to deliberate on affairs, and from all of these they then form the סנהדרין [sanhedrin], the Synedrium, or that greatest Council. Hence among the rabbis mention of the House of Judgment, great and small, is not infrequent; thus in Midrash Shir ha-Shirim, chapter 1, verse 9: "Wherever in sacred Scripture it says יהוה [YHWH], the LORD, it is understood of Him and of the House of His judgment." So too in the same words in Bereshit Rabba. Compare Maimonides, More Nevochim, Part II, chapter 6.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Ad primam referunt classem שרי הפנים Principes faciei divinæ, Angelos quatuor Michaelem, Gabrielem, Uriel em, & Raphaelem, qui nunquam à divina recedant facie, sed perpetuò thronū cingant divinum, ministrentq; Deo, ita ut Michael stet à dextra throni, Gabriel à sinistra, Uriel ante faciem, Raphael sit à tergo, habeantque sub se suas classes vel acies Angelorum, quas regant cum imperio, sicuti liquet ex Pirke Rabbi Elieseris, cap. 4. Quatuor autem sunt classes Angelorum Ministerij, laudes canentium coram Sancto Benedicto. Prima classis vel acies est Michaelis à dextra ejus. Secunda Gabrielis à sinistra ejus. Tertia Urielis ante ipsum ipsum. Quarta Raphaelis a tergo ejus. Majestas autem Sancti Benedicti est in medio. Ipse insidet throno excelso elevatus, atque soilium ejus sublime suspensum est sursum in aere. Figura autem gloriae ejus est sicuti color Chasmal, juxta illud, Ezechielis cap. 1. verf. 27. Et vidi quasi formam Chasmal. Corona imposita est capiti ejus, & diadema nominis Hammephorasch seu Tetragrammati circa frontem ejus, atque oculi per universum orbem discurrunt. Statuunt hos quatuor Angelos esse quam longissime remotos ab omni materia, nec ad tempus quidem aliquam induere materiam, hinc nunquam corporea specie videri, nec in terras venire, sed jugiter thronum DEI cingere, vocantes propterea illos Intelligentias a materia separatas; Quod tamen negare videtur Author Zennorennae, Commentarii in Legem, cum ad Genef. cap. 18. sol. 18. pronunciat Michaelem, Gabrielem, & Raphaelem e coelo in terram dimissos, ut Abrahamo, Lotho, Saraeque & divina annunciarent mandata, executionique mandarent; Sic autem legitur vocibus Hebraicis, Germanicisque: Da macht (Gott) drey Malachim (Engel) die kahmen zu Abraham, gleich als 3. Gäst: und die drey Malachim einer war Michael, der wolte sagen zu Sara, sie werde einen Sohn haben/und der Michael Michael hat wollen beschirmen Loth von Sodom : Der andere war Raphael, zu heilen Abraham auff sein Mila (Beschneidung:) Der dritte war der Malach Gabriel zu umbkehren die Städte Sodom und Gomorrha. Videant nunc Judæi, qua ratione hæc invicem valeant coponere; Erit sane digna materia, quæ alterum aliquem Menasseh Ben Israel exercere posset, si quis Judæorum contrarias sæpe sententias conciliare vellet. Sed hæc animorum diversitas nota est insignis Theologiæ Judaicæ.
units.tr: To the first class they refer the שרי הפנים [sarei ha-panim], the Princes of the divine Face: four Angels, Michael, Gabriel, Uriel and Raphael, who never depart from the divine face but ever surround the divine throne and minister to God, so that Michael stands at the right of the throne, Gabriel at the left, Uriel before the face, and Raphael behind; and they have under them their own classes or battalions of Angels, which they rule with authority, as is clear from Pirke Rabbi Eliezer, chapter 4: "There are four classes of Angels of the Ministry, who sing praises before the Holy One, blessed be He. The first class or battalion is that of Michael, at His right hand. The second is that of Gabriel, at His left. The third is that of Uriel, before Him. The fourth is that of Raphael, behind Him. The majesty of the Holy One, blessed be He, is in the middle. He Himself sits upon a lofty throne, raised up, and His seat is suspended on high in the air. The figure of His glory is like the colour of chashmal, according to that of Ezekiel 1:27: 'And I saw as it were the form of chashmal.' A crown is placed on His head, and the diadem of the Name Hammephorash, that is the Tetragrammaton, is about His forehead, and His eyes run through the whole world." They hold that these four Angels are as far removed as possible from all matter, and never put on any matter even for a time, and hence are never seen in a bodily form, nor come down to the earth, but constantly surround the throne of God; for this reason they call them "Intelligences separated from matter." Yet the author of Zennorenna, a commentary on the Law, seems to deny this, when on Genesis 18, folio 18, he states that Michael, Gabriel and Raphael were sent down from heaven to earth, to announce the divine commands to Abraham, Lot and Sarah, and to carry out the execution of them. It is read thus in Hebrew and German words: "God made three Malachim (Angels) who came to Abraham, just like three guests. And of the three Malachim, one was Michael, who was to tell Sarah that she would have a son, and Michael wished to protect Lot from Sodom. The other was Raphael, to heal Abraham on his Mila (circumcision). The third was the Malach Gabriel, to overturn the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah." Let the Jews now see by what reasoning these things can be reconciled with one another. It would surely be a worthy subject to exercise some other Menasseh Ben Israel, if any Jew wished to reconcile their often contrary opinions. But this diversity of minds is a well-known mark of Jewish theology.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Secundam classem occupant Angeli boni, מלאכי קדש Angeli sancti, qui quandoque assumunt corpora, interque mortales versantur, maximeque piorum hominum usibus inservientes, Prophetis apparent, vaticinia communicantes, qui mundum regunt simul inferiorem, Cœlorum Orbes gubernant, supra cœlorum orbes habitantes, hinc vocati Cœlorum Exercitus, & Angeli ministerii, מלאכי השרת, qui cum sanctimoniæ & pietati operam dent continuam, puri sunt ab omni malo, nec peccare unquam possunt, sed liberè semper bonum expetunt, sicuti egregiè describuntur à Rabbi Joleph Albo Authore Fudamentorum Parte II. cap. 28. Scito, cum sint Angeli expertes materia, neque sint capaces accidentium materialium, verbi gratia invidia, odij, & ira; Sunt enim puri ab omni malo, neque in iis reperiatur superbia, neque libertas admalum, & peccatum ullo modo, sed libertas eorum semper sit circa bonum, & id quod rectum est in oculis Dei; ideo licet illis, cum mittuntur ad homines, loqui nomine ejus, qui mittit eos; quemadmodum id compertum habemus ex multis Scripturae locis: Ubi Angelus apparens loquitur nomine Dei, a quo mittitur. Sic Genes. cap. 16. verf. 9. Dixitque ei (Hagar) Angelus Domini, revertere ad Dominam tuam, & humiliare sub manuillius.
units.tr: The second class consists of the good angels, [מלאכי קדש] holy angels, who sometimes take on bodies and move among mortals, serving especially the uses of pious people. They appear to the Prophets and communicate prophecies. Some rule the lower world, others govern the orbs of the heavens, dwelling above the orbs of the heavens; hence they are called the Host of Heaven and the ministering angels, [מלאכי השרת], who, as they devote continual effort to holiness and piety, are pure from all evil and can never sin, but always freely desire the good. This is well described by Rabbi Joseph Albo, author of the Fundamentals, Part II, chapter 28: Know that, since angels are free of matter and are not capable of material accidents, such as envy, hatred and anger, they are pure from all evil. Pride is not found in them, nor is there freedom to evil, nor sin in any way; their freedom is always directed to the good and to what is right in the eyes of God. Therefore, when they are sent to men, they may speak in the name of him who sends them, as we know from many places of Scripture, where an angel appearing speaks in the name of God by whom he is sent. So in Genesis 16:9: "And the angel of the Lord said to her (Hagar), return to your mistress, and submit yourself under her hand."

units.la: Dispescuntur Angeli boni, quisecunda classe continentur, cum Angeli primae classis quoque valde boni sint, in decem classes, seu ordines minores, discretos a se invicem tum sapientia, tum dignitate & potestate, quorum supremi infra solium divinae sint Majestatis, infimi vero cum hominibus conversentur, & iiscum aliquando loquantur; Quorumque omnium sequens sit nomenclatura, ex Ezechiele cap. 1. desumta: Animalia sanctitatis, Ophanim, Oralim, Chasmalim, Seraphim, Angeli, Dii, Filii Dei, Cherubim, & Ischim, teste Rabbi Mose Maimonide, qui sic decem hos minores ordines classis describit secundae, in Constitutionibus de Fundamentis Legis cap.2. §.8. Varietas nominum Angelorum est pro ratione graduum ipsorum, & propterea vocantur Animalia sanctitatis, quae omnium sunt suprema, & Ophanim, Oralim, Chasmalim, Seraphim, Angeli, Dii, Filii DEI, Cherubim, & Ischim; Decem horum graduum quoque meminit Berelchit Rabba; Item Rabbi Meir Aldabi in Schevile Emunah lib. 1. Sic horum ordinum aliqui recensentur in Tractatu Talmudico Chagiga cap.2. Disposuisti ibi (in expanso) Ophanim, Seraphim, Animalia sanctitatis, atque Angelos minimi erit, sicut dicitur Psalmo 68. vers. 5. Ex tollite qui inequitat amoenitatibus. Sed de his plura Viri Celeberrimi Wilhelmus Vorstius, & Martinus Geierus, qui egregiam, doctamque horum decem nominum exhibent explicationem; Ille in Notis ad Maimoni, dis allegatam Constitutionem de Fundamentis, pag. 18, 19. Hic ex Rabbi Joseph Karo Hispano, Maimonidis commentatore inclyto, in Conformitate Judaeo Papistica, pag. 580. 581. Editionis novissimae.
units.tr: The good angels, who are contained in the second class, are divided into ten lesser classes or orders, distinguished from one another by wisdom, dignity and power, though the angels of the first class are also very good. The highest of them stand beneath the throne of the divine Majesty, while the lowest converse with men and sometimes speak with them.
