The whole of them has the following nomenclature, taken from Ezekiel chapter 1: Living creatures of holiness, Ophanim, Oralim, Chasmalim, Seraphim, Angels, Gods, Sons of God, Cherubim and Ischim. So Rabbi Moses Maimonides, in the Constitutions on the Foundations of the Law, chapter 2, §8, describes these ten lesser orders of the second class: The variety of the names of the angels corresponds to the rank of each, and therefore they are called Living creatures of holiness, which are the highest of all, and Ophanim, Oralim, Chasmalim, Seraphim, Angels, Gods, Sons of God, Cherubim and Ischim. Berechit Rabba also mentions these ten grades, and likewise Rabbi Meir Aldabi in Shevile Emunah, book 1. Some of these orders are also listed in the Talmudic tractate Chagiga, chapter 2: You have arranged there (in the expanse) Ophanim, Seraphim, living creatures of holiness, and the least of the angels, as is said in Psalm 68:5: "Extol him who rides through the heavens." But more on these matters is given by the most celebrated men Wilhelm Vorstius and Martin Geier, who offer an excellent and learned explanation of these ten names: the former in his notes to the above-mentioned Maimonides' Constitution on the Foundations, pp. 18–19, the latter from Rabbi Joseph Karo of Spain, the famous commentator on Maimonides, in Conformitas Judaeo-Papistica, pp. 580–581 of the newest edition.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Attribuunt Angelis bonis ingentem Dei, rerumque aliarum noticiam, quæ humanam valde superet, cū quidam faciem Dei semper intueantur, quidam infra thronum sint divinum, & èlonginquo Deum videant, cum vaticinia, voluntatemq; divinam communicent mortalibus, sicque nomine Dei loquantur; neutiquam tamen summè perfectam, infinitamque, quod non simplici intuitu omnia intelligant,sed plurima ex revelatione discant, necita cognoscantCreatorem suum,uti ipse se ipsum cognoscit, prout loquitur Rabbi Moses Maimonides in Constitutionibus de Fundamentis Legis,cap.2.§.10. Omnes autem istæ forme viventes cognoscunt Creatorem, atq; valde excellenti notitia eum nescunt, unaquæque forma pro ratione gradus sui, non pro ratione excellentiæ suæ; ac idcirco gradus primus non poterit comprehendere veritatem Conditoris, sicuti in se est, siquidem intellectus ejus contractior est, quam ut assequatur & cognoscat eum: attamen magis apprehendit atque cognoscit, quam adsequitur ac intelligit forma inferior illa. Et ita unusquisque gradus usque ad gradum decimum cognoscit Creatorem notitia, quali homines, compositi ex materia & forma, Deum non possunt adsequi aut cognoscere. Nulli autem cognoscunt Creatorem, uti ipse cognoscit se ipsum; Sic AnAngelorum sapientiam maximam & præstantissimam deprædicat Rabbi Jedaia Happenini, cum sic in Bakkascha, seu meditatione sua, Sectione secunda inquit: Sunt Substantiæ purissimæ, intelligentes ex se ipsis, stolidi præ illis alii. Negant pariter sicut stellarum animatarum, ita Angelorum Potentiam, virtutemque esse infinitam, absolutamque, afferentes stellas, Angelosque non necessario, plenaque operari libertate, sed libertate dependente, proinde finitam, determinatamque possidere potentiam, quod testatur Rabbi Josephalbo de Fundamentis lib. 4. cap. 16. Patet autem eos in hoc errare, quia virtus potestatum superiorum finit a est & determinata, nullaque earum potest aliud facere, quam quod natura ejus fert, & secundum dispositionem subjecti tantum, nullo modo vero ex libero arbitrio.
units.tr: They ascribe to the good angels a vast knowledge of God and of other things, far beyond human knowledge. Some of them always gaze upon the face of God, and some are below the divine throne and see God from afar. They communicate prophecies and the divine will to mortals, and so speak in the name of God. Yet they are by no means supremely perfect or infinite, since they do not understand all things by a single intuition but learn many things through revelation, and they do not know their Creator as he knows himself. So speaks Rabbi Moses Maimonides in the Constitutions on the Foundations of the Law, chapter 2, §10: Now all these living forms know the Creator, and they know him with a very excellent knowledge, each form according to the measure of its own degree and not according to the measure of his excellence. Therefore the first degree cannot grasp the truth of the Maker as it is in itself, since its intellect is too limited to attain and know him. Yet it apprehends and knows him more than the lower form attains and understands. And so each degree, up to the tenth, knows the Creator with a knowledge such as men, composed of matter and form, cannot attain or know God. Yet none knows the Creator as he knows himself. In the same way Rabbi Jedaia Happenini extols the very great and most excellent wisdom of the angels, for he says in the Bakkascha, that is, his Meditation, section two: They are most pure substances, understanding of themselves, and others are foolish in comparison with them. Likewise they deny that the power and strength of the angels, as of the animated stars, is infinite and absolute. They assert that the stars and angels act not by necessity and with full freedom, but with a dependent freedom, and therefore possess a finite and determined power. Rabbi Josephalbo testifies to this in On the Foundations, book 4, chapter 16: It is clear that they are wrong in this, because the power of the higher powers is finite and determined, and none of them can do anything other than what its nature brings, and according to the disposition of the subject only, and in no way by free choice.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: In tertia Angelica classe maxima sunt Angeli Corrumpentes, מלאכי חבלה Angeli damni, perditionisve appellati, quod noxam, damnumque ex sententia divina inferant mortalibus, & מלאכי מות Angeli mortis, quod mortem adducant, procurentque, hinc משטנים ומוקים Tortores & Carnifices, quod ut divinæ iræ ac justitiæ in terris ministri, homines puniant, castigentque, omnia judicia in malos quam maxime, ob com-
units.tr: In the third angelic class the most prominent are the Corrupting Angels, called Angels of damage or destruction [מלאכי חבלה], because they inflict harm and loss on mortals by the sentence of God, and the Angels of death [מלאכי מות], because they bring about and procure death. Hence they are called Tormentors and Executioners [משטנים ומוקים], because, as ministers of the divine wrath and justice on earth, they punish and chastise men and carry out every judgment upon the wicked as far as possible, on account of the com-

units.la: commissa peccata, exerceant, habentes sedem ordinariam tum in sublunaribus, tum in infernalibus, de quibus tritum Rabbinorum occurrit verbum, quoties scilicet aliquis moritur fame, peste, gladio, aut captivitate: Angelus mortis percussit ipsum. Horum malorum Angelorum, qui de male factis instituunt supplicia, & assidue inquirunt in hominum peccata, ingens a Talmudistis traditur numerus, quando in tractatu Schabbath in distinctione, Amar Rabbi Akiba sic referunt: Exposuit Rabbi Simai; In hora qua promiserunt Israel, faciemus & audiemus, sicut dictum est Exod. cap. 24. v. 7. Et dixerunt, omnia qua Dominus locutus est faciemus & audiemus, descenderunt sexcenta millia Angelorum ministerii, & unumquemque Israelitarum coronaverunt duabus coronis; unam imposuerunt ei propter faciemus; alteram propter audiemus. Cum autem peccaverunt Israel in vitulo, descenderunt sexcenta millia super sexcenta millia, id est, bis sexcenta millia Angelorum tormenti, id est, daemonum, & diripuerunt eas coronas, sicut dictum est Exod. cap. 33. v. 6. Et privati fuerunt Israel ornamento suo a monte Oreb. Idem recensetur in Libro Caphtor Vaperach, qui per duas illas coronas intelligit, perfectionem contemplationis Legis, & perfectionem operationis Legis. Scribunt praeterea Angelos malos secundo do die cum inferno creatos, quod patet & ex dictis cap. 6. & ex Tanchuma seu Jelammede- nu, qui commentarius est in quinque libros Moßs, sectione משה רבנו פ, forte intelli- gentes Angelos non creatos secundo die, sed lapsos, & ita ex bonis malos factos, inprimis cum Angelos aliquos vocent malos, non quod eorum intima natura sit mala à Deo creata, sed mali propria culpa facti sint, & quod ad mala hominibus immittenda à DEO sint ordina- ti.
units.tr: mitted sins. They have their ordinary seat both in the sublunary world and in the infernal regions. The common saying of the rabbis refers to them, whenever someone dies of hunger, plague, the sword, or captivity: "The Angel of death struck him." The Talmudists record a great number of these evil angels, who devise punishments for wicked deeds and constantly investigate the sins of men. In the tractate Shabbath, in the section beginning "Rabbi Akiba said," they report the following: Rabbi Simai expounded: At the hour when Israel promised, "We will do and we will hear," as is said in Exodus chapter 24, verse 7, "And they said, All that the Lord has spoken we will do and we will hear," six hundred thousand ministering angels descended and crowned every Israelite with two crowns: one they placed on him for "we will do," and the other for "we will hear." But when Israel sinned with the calf, six hundred thousand upon six hundred thousand descended, that is, twice six hundred thousand angels of torment, that is, demons, and they tore away those crowns, as is said in Exodus chapter 33, verse 6, "And the children of Israel were stripped of their ornaments from Mount Horeb." The same is recounted in the book Caphtor Vaperach, which understands by those two crowns the perfection of contemplation of the Law and the perfection of its practice. Moreover, they write that the evil angels were created on the second day together with hell, which is clear also from what was said in chapter 6, and from the Tanchuma, or Jelammedenu, a commentary on the five books of Moses, in the section Moshe Rabbenu. Perhaps they understand that the angels were not created on the second day but fell, and so from good became evil. This is especially so since they call some angels evil, not because their inner nature was created evil by God, but because they became evil through their own fault, and because they were appointed by God to bring evils upon men.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Lubet nunc, cum operæ dignum sit prætium, ex ipsis percipere Judæis triplicem hanc Angelorum classem, ut ita appareat, quomodo figmenta hæc Authoribus Judæis in lucem protrusa, ipsam quoque Theologiam Christianam occupaverint, infestaverintque; Cum verò id nemo melius Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel explicaverit, restat, ut ea, quæ accurate suo more consignavit, licet prolixiora describamus ex libro de Creatione, Problemate 22.
units.tr: Since it is worth the effort, it is now pleasing to learn from the Jews themselves this threefold class of angels, so that it may appear how these fictions, brought to light by Jewish authors, have also taken hold of and troubled Christian theology itself. Since no one has explained this better than Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, it remains that we describe at greater length those things which he has set down accurately in his own manner, from his book on the Creation, Problem 22.

units.la: Nonnulli Theologi statuunt tres gradus dari entium spiritualium: quorum est primus intelligentiarum à materia separatarum; quales esse statuunt quatuor illos Michaelem, Gabrielem, Raphaelem, & Uriel- lem; qui omnes, uti in Pirque à Rabbi Eliefer traditur, circumsistunt thronum divinæ Majestatis.
units.tr: Some theologians hold that there are three degrees of spiritual beings. The first is that of intelligences separated from matter, such as the four whom they name Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, and Uriel, all of whom, as Rabbi Eliezer relates in the Pirke, surround the throne of the divine Majesty.

units.la: Illi autem, qui sunt ex hoc ordine, non possunt comprehendi corporeis sensibus, sed solum in Prophetica visione. Sic Angelus apparuit Abrahamo, cum filium vellet immolare: sic apparuit Jacobo pascenti oves Labanis, & in visione scalarum: sic etiam Moysi in rubo, Jehosuae in Jerichunte, & Jezechieli & Zachariae visus est. Nullus istorum Angelorum unquam visus est Prophetis: sed tantummodo ab iis, quando in apparitionibus istis intellectus eorum elevabatur ad spiritualem contemplationem, vox Angelorum audita est; Sicuti etiam a Mose ingrediente tabernaculum, tantum audita vox fuit ex interioribus partibus sacrarii. Secundus gradus Angelorum est, מלאכי השרת Angelorum ministerii. Hi sunt legati & ministri, quos condidit Deus ad regendum mundum, id est, eos qui sanctimonia & pietati operam dant: Idcirco a Psalmista dicitur Ps. 91. v. 11. Angelis suis praecipiet de te, ut te custodiant in omni via. Tales nonnunquam visibiles formas assumere, & apparuerunt Prophetis. Ex hoc ordine illi fuerunt, quos Abrahamus hospitio excepit, & ille qui luctatus est cum Jacobo, quique visus est Agar, Gideoni, Manoacho, & famulo Prophetae Elisaei. Cum Abrahamus diceret servo suo Gen. 24. 7. Deus emittet coram te Angelum suum, intellexit aliquem ex his Angelus: Similiter etiam Daniel, Deus meus misit Angelum suum, qui occlusit os Leonis, Daniel cap. 6. Ex hoc ordine etiam fuerunt illi, qui Jacobo obviifiebant in via sive itinere. Hi vero, qui habitant supra orbes, vocantur exercitus coelorum. Denique Tertius gradus est Spirituum sublunarium, qui sunt ministri & executores divinae irae, ac justitiae. Hos appellarunt antiqui מלאכי חבלה Angelos damni, & alio nomine מלאכי מורים Angelos mortis, uti etiam שטנים ומזיקים id est, tortores & carnifices: Nam illi sumunt de malis supplicia, & assiduo inquirunt in hominum peccata. Hujus ordinis Angelus ille fuit, qui maxima clade concidit castra Regis Assyriorum. Ex hac classe fuit, quem vidit David tenentem strictum mucronem adversus Hierosolyma. Ex his fuit ille qui tanto damno lobum affecit, eumque adeo graviter afflixit: uti etiam ille, qui visus fuit asina Bileami, & illi sex viri armati, quos vidit Iehasquel.
units.tr: Those who belong to this order cannot be perceived by the bodily senses, but only in prophetic vision. Thus an angel appeared to Abraham when he was about to sacrifice his son; thus he appeared to Jacob tending Laban's sheep and in the vision of the ladder; thus too he was seen by Moses in the bush, by Joshua at Jericho, and by Ezekiel and Zechariah. None of these angels was ever seen by the Prophets; only their voice was heard by them, when in those appearances their understanding was raised to spiritual contemplation, just as the voice was heard by Moses when he entered the tabernacle, coming from the inner parts of the sanctuary. The second degree of angels is that of the ministering angels [מלאכי השרת], that is, of ministry. These are the messengers and servants whom God established to govern the world, that is, those who labour for holiness and piety. Therefore the Psalmist says, Psalm 91, verse 11: "He shall give his angels charge over you, to keep you in all your ways." Such angels sometimes assume visible forms and have appeared to the Prophets. Of this order were those whom Abraham received in hospitality, and he who wrestled with Jacob, and he who appeared to Hagar, to Gideon, to Manoah, and to the servant of the Prophet Elisha. When Abraham said to his servant, Genesis 24, verse 7, "God will send his angel before you," he understood one of these angels. Likewise Daniel: "My God has sent his angel, who shut the lions' mouths," Daniel chapter 6. Of this order also were those who met Jacob on the way or journey. Those who dwell above the spheres are called the hosts of heaven. Finally, the third degree is that of the sublunary spirits, who are the ministers and executors of the divine wrath and justice. The ancients named them the Angels of damage [מלאכי חבלה], and by another name the Angels of death [מלאכי מורים], and likewise the Tormentors and Executioners [שטנים ומזיקים], for they take vengeance on the wicked and constantly investigate the sins of men. Of this order was that angel who struck down the camp of the king of the Assyrians with a great slaughter. Of this class was the one whom David saw holding a drawn sword against Jerusalem. Of these was the one who inflicted such loss on Job and so grievously afflicted him, as well as the one who appeared to Balaam's donkey, and those six armed men whom Jehasquel saw.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Agnoscunt moderni Judæi Angelorum multorum lapsum, confitenturque unamines, Angelos quosdam Creatori suo inobedientes fuisse, sicque malos redditos, testibus Rabbinis plurimis, sæpe coram, & per literas consultis. Credunt non pauci cum Veteribus, Angelos e coelo decidisse, imo rebellionis capita, principesque habuisse. Qui ex Judæis, numerum augent, duos comminiscuntur nominibus descriptos, Schamchazai & Uzielem, de quibus Jonathan Paraphrastes Chaldæus, Gen. cap. 6. cap. 6. ¥. 4. ad vocem םימש: Schamchazai & Vziel, qui cadebant ex cælis, erant in terra, in diebus illis; Et Perusch Targum in hunc locum: Gigantes Schamchosai & Afael; explicatio: Duo Angeli sunt, qui ceciderunt e loco sanctitatis suæ e cælo, ceu memoratur in Jomafol.3.col.2; Sic Rashi ad Numer. cap.13. ¥.34. Gigantes Enakim sunt de filiis Schamchafai & Afael, qui e cælo ceciderunt tempore Enosch; Ita Autor Hebræus Baal Hatturim scribit Reges Sichon & Oghum ex Schamchosai natos,cum dicit: Sighon & Oghsii Schamchafai & Afael, ceciderunt ex cælo tempore diluvii propterea scribitur hic: Gigantes fuerunt in terra. Nec aliud dicunt ex Judæis, qui nomina duorum appellant Asa & Afael; necabludit Autor Juchasin, qui voce Machasaelutitur. At reliqui Judæi unum ponunt Principem, Sammaelem, qui cum turma sua e cælo sit dejectus, de quo Rabbi Elieser in Pirke cap. 14. Sammaelem vero & turmam ejus præcipitavit e loco sanctitatis suæ ceu cælis, quique multas Israeli intulerit calamitates; Hinc Sammaelem nominant Principem cæli maximum, in Sohar sol. 28, col.2. Omnium omnino diabolorum nequissimum, in Devarim Rabba Sect. ult. qui serpenti inequitans seduxerit Evam. Elias Levita in suo Thisbi Sammaelem cum Asmodæo eundem dicit, quando scribit ad vocem םושש: Atque mihi videtur Asmedai, & alio nomine Samael appelappellatum fuisse, sicut declarabo in Radice sua. Vocant pariter Sammaelem Angelum mortis, de quo, ejusque seductione, ac depulsione e coelo egregie Rabbi Bechai in Commentario ad Legem cap. 3. cum ait: Vim illam quae serpenti se conjunxerat, seu Satanam & Angelum mortis in poenam seductionis dignitate sua ejectum, & a consortio Trinitatis ac superni domicilii communione exclusum fuisse; unde inimicitiae ortae sint inter Diabolum & Hominem. Affirmant porro Judaei, Angelos e coelo lapsos matrimonia in terris iniisse cum Caini filiabus, unde natos perhibent Daemones & Gigantes, nixi Genes. cap. 6. vers. 2. Et viderunt filii Dei filias hominum, quod pulchrae ipsae, & acceperunt sibi uxores, ex omnibus quas elegerunt; Per filios Dei Angelos intelligentes, uti illud videmus ex Rabbi Eliezeris Pircke, cap. 22. Rabbi inquit: (Meir) viderunt Angeli qui exciderant e coelo loco suo sancto, filios Caini ambulantes in nuditate carnis, & fucantes oculos suos instar scortorum, atque vagati sunt post illos, atque sumpserunt ex iis mulieres veluxores, prout dicitur Genes. cap. 6. vers. 2. Viderunt filii Dei filias hominum. Rabbi Josua filius Karcha ait: Angeli sunt ignis flammarum, juxta illud Psalmo 104. vers. 4. Qui facit ministros suos ignem flammantem. Venit autem ex coitu ignis in carnem & sanguinem, neque combussit corpus: sed tempore illo, quo ceciderunt e coelo loco sanctitatis suae, robur atque statura eorum facta est instar hominum, & vestimentum illorum fuit ramentum pulveris, sicut dicitur Jobi cap. 7. v. 5. Induit caro mea vermes, & ramenta pulveris. Probabant quoque Judæi Angelos esse lapsos, quod appellati essent Nephilim, ex cecidit, lapsus est, ratione pœnæ, exilii, vel ejectionis e cœlo. Quod nam vero Angelorum primum fuerit peccatum, unanimi mente non determinant. Aliqui in Angelis superbiam & fastum accusant. Alii invidiam causam putant, quam erga Hominem habuerint. Rursus alii Angelos ob luxuriam e felicitate sua excidisse volunt. Denique alii Angelos cœlo exclusos scribunt, quod primos nostros seduxerint Parentes.
units.tr: The modern Jews acknowledge the fall of many angels, and they unanimously confess that some angels were disobedient to their Creator and so became evil. Many rabbis bear witness to this, consulted often in person and by letter. Not a few of them believe, with the ancients, that angels fell from heaven, and that they had leaders and heads of rebellion. Those Jews who increase the number invent two, named Shamchazai and Uziel. Of these, Jonathan the Chaldee paraphrast, on Gen. 6. 4, at the word "heavens," says: Shamchazai and Uziel, who were falling from the heavens, were on the earth in those days. The Perusch Targum on this place says: The giants Shamchosai and Afael. Explanation: they are two angels who fell from the place of their holiness in heaven, as is recorded in Jomafol 3, col. 2. So Rashi on Num. 13. 34: The giants Enakim are of the sons of Shamchafai and Afael, who fell from heaven in the time of Enosh. So too the Hebrew author Baal Hatturim writes that the kings Sihon and Og were born of Shamchosai, when he says: Sihon and Og were of Shamchafai and Afael; they fell from heaven at the time of the flood. Therefore it is written here: there were giants in the earth. Nor do other Jews say anything different when they name the two as Asa and Afael; nor does the author Juchasin differ, who uses the word Machasael. But the rest of the Jews posit one prince, Sammael, who was cast down from heaven together with his host. Of him Rabbi Eliezer, in Pirke, chapter 14: But Sammael and his host he hurled down from the place of their holiness as from the heavens; and he brought many calamities upon Israel. Hence they call Sammael the greatest prince of heaven (Sohar, fol. 28, col. 2), the most wicked of all devils (Devarim Rabba, last section), who, riding on the serpent, seduced Eve. Elias Levita in his Thisbi says that Sammael is the same as Asmodeus, when he writes at the word Asmedai: And it seems to me that Asmedai, also called by another name Samael, was so named, as I will explain in its root. They likewise call Sammael the Angel of death. Of him, and of his seduction and expulsion from heaven, Rabbi Bechai writes admirably in his commentary on the Law, chapter 3: That power which had joined itself to the serpent, namely Satan and the Angel of death, was cast out of its dignity as a punishment for the seduction, and was excluded from the fellowship of the Trinity and from communion with the heavenly dwelling; whence enmity arose between the Devil and Man. Moreover the Jews affirm that the angels who fell from heaven contracted marriages on earth with the daughters of Cain, from whom they say demons and giants were born, relying on Gen. 6. 2: And the sons of God saw the daughters of men, that they were fair, and they took wives for themselves from all whom they chose. They understand the sons of God as angels, as we see from Rabbi Eliezer's Pirke, chapter 22. Rabbi (Meir) says: The angels who had fallen from heaven, from their holy place, saw the sons of Cain walking in the nakedness of the flesh, and painting their eyes like harlots; and they went after them and took from them women for wives, as it is said in Gen. 6. 2: The sons of God saw the daughters of men. Rabbi Joshua son of Karcha says: Angels are the fire of flames, according to that in Psalm 104. 4: He makes his ministers a flaming fire. But the fire came, by intercourse, into flesh and blood, and did not burn the body; but at that time, when they fell from heaven from their holy place, their strength and stature became like those of men, and their clothing was a fragment of dust, as it is said in Job 7. 5: My flesh is clothed with worms and fragments of dust. The Jews also prove that the angels fell because they were called Nephilim, from cecidit (he fell), by reason of punishment, exile, or ejection from heaven. Yet as to what was the first sin of the angels, they do not agree. Some accuse the angels of pride and arrogance. Others think envy of man was the cause. Again others want the angels to have fallen from their happiness because of lust. Finally others write that the angels were shut out of heaven because they seduced our first parents.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Formant Judæi præter has tres Angelorum distinctas classes, quartam denique, quæ composita fit ex Angelis natura malis, non creatis a Divino Numine in prima creatione, sed generatis postmodum ex Adami nuptiis cum Spiritu fœmineo Lilith, vel ex coitu Evæ cum Angelis e cœlo delapsis, postquam a viro, ut dicunt, f. parata, vel ex congressu Angelorum cum filiis hominum; quæ tamen subsit tertiæ classis Angelis malis, ab illisque originem trahat, hinc quoque regatur ab Asmodæo, Dæmone principe, uti hæc pridem observavit Antonius. tonius Hulsius, in perdoƺta sua Theologia Judaica, quae tota fere Messiam describit, pag. 72. Interim negare non possunt Judæi præter ipsos מלאכי הבלה dari etiam spiritus formaliter & moraliter malos, ipsos autem neque ad tres illas classes referunt, nec à Deo creatos, nec per lapsum à Deo defecisse volunt, sed per impuram & carnalem cum hominibus commixtionem esse genitos; Quod annotatum quoque videmus à Johanne Sauberto, cum in Palæstra Theologico Philologica sic loquitur pag. 44. Primi igitur Angeli cum mundo creati, erunt illi gradus potissimum primi & secundi: Licet & tertii ordinis spiritus sive dæmones conditos die II. creationis, quo sc. infernus creatus, antiquorum ferat judicium, testante Menasse Benisrael de Resurr. mortt. III. 6. Veruntamen postliminio plurimi numero horum generati quoque ab angelis, dæmonibus & hominibus perhibentur. Appellant hos Angelos שדים Dæmones, à שדה Agro, quod plerumque agant in locis desertis, uti vult Menasseh Problemate 22. cum tamen rectius deducantur à שוד vastavit, perdidit, quod ad vastandum, perdendumque sint nati; Et שעירים Hircos, vel Hirsutos, quod saepe appareant in figura hircorum, imo tanquam hirsuta & pilosa conspiciantur animalia; Et קליפות Putamina, desumta voce à nuce; quod sicuti dantur nucis interiora, quae sunt fructus, ita dentur etiam exteriora, quæ sint putamina, observante Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel de Creatione, Problemate 23. Statuunt Dæmones hos esse aerios & igneos, sexu discretos, edentes, bibentes, Venere utentes, tandemque hominum instar morientes. Probant operose horum Dæmonum existentiam, adscribuntq; ipsis exorcismos & incantationes, uti patet ex Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, qui sic Problemate 22. de Creatione loquitur: Quamvis autem nonnulli reperiantur, qui negant ejusmodi spiritus esse, quos vulgo vocamus dæmones: certissimum tamen est, tales revera dari. Nam antiqui Sapientes, uti videre est opere Talmudico, nomina eorum recensent: scilicet Hasmeday, Higueret bat Mahalat, & Nahama: & apud Jesaiam cap. 34. verf. 14. ubi prænuntiatur excidium Edomitarum, dicitur: אך שם הרגיעה לילית certe illic requievit Lilith; quod est nomen feminei spiritus, quem quidam volunt fuisse primam Adami conjugem, antequam Evam in uxorem a Deo acceperat. Hæc confirmantur in tractatu Meguila cap. 1. in quo dicitur eos non temere nec in vanum efferre seu pronunciare nomen Domini. Et multi sane reperiuntur, qui dæmonas istos adjurationibus advocant, & Necromantias ope mira admodum multa patrant. Quin & libris quibusdam Cabalistarum, quales sunt Pirque Ehalot, Raziel & aliorum, rum, recensentur eorum nomina, exorcismi, & incantationes. Sed & quis negare potest id, quod sensibus ipsis percipitur verissimum esse? De hoc generere angelorum antiqui varia narrant Haguigac.2. nimirum eos cibis vesci, generare, & mori instar hominum, alis praditos esse, & ex una parte mundi volare in aliam, quin & sapius etiam audire quae futura sunt. Et alibi ajunt, eos cum apparent uni tantum homini, noxios esse & damnum inferre: cum duobus apparent, innoxios esse: tribus autem simul hominibus nunquam apparere. In admirabili autem libro Zoar varia dicuntur de illis, & in specie quidem, quod alii sint spiritus aeris, alii ignis; idque probant ex Psalmista, Psalm. 104. Fecit angelos suos spiritus, & ministros suos flammam ignis. Sed & volunt nonnullos eorum esse astutos & calidos, nonnullos stolidos & fatuos. Rabenu Ay, & R. Moises Gerundensis hanc de spiritibus opinionem confirmant. Denique veritas hujus opinionis liquet ex variis scriptura locis.
units.tr: The Jews form, besides these three distinct classes of angels, a fourth, which is composed of angels that are evil by nature, not created by the Divine Power in the first creation, but generated afterwards from the marriage of Adam with the female spirit Lilith, or from the intercourse of Eve with angels fallen from heaven, after she had been, as they say, prepared by the man; or from the mingling of angels with the sons of men. Yet this class is subordinate to the third class of evil angels, and derives its origin from them, and is therefore ruled by Asmodeus, the prince of demons, as Antonius Hulsius observed some time ago in his much-esteemed Theologia Judaica, which describes almost the whole of the Messiah, p. 72: Meanwhile the Jews cannot deny that, besides themselves, there are also spirits formally and morally evil, malachei habalah [מלאכי הבלה]; but they do not refer them to those three classes, nor do they want them created by God, nor fallen away from God through a fall; they hold that they were begotten through impure and carnal mixing with men. We see this also noted by Johann Sauberti, when in his Palaestra Theologico-Philologica he speaks thus, p. 44: The first angels, then, created with the world, will be chiefly those of the first and second orders. Although the spirits or demons of the third order, created on the second day of creation, when hell was made, bear the judgment of the ancients, as Menasseh ben Israel testifies in De resurrectione mortuorum III. 6. Nevertheless, many of them are said to have been generated afterwards also from angels, demons and men. These angels they call shedim [שדים], demons, from sadeh, a field, because they mostly act in desert places, as Menasseh wishes in Problem 22; although more correctly they are derived from shud, he laid waste, destroyed, because they were born to lay waste and destroy. And they call them se'irim [שעירים], goats or hairy ones, because they often appear in the figure of goats, or are seen as hairy and shaggy creatures. And they call them qelipot [קליפות], husks, a word taken from a nut: just as there is the kernel of a nut, which is the fruit, so there are also the outer parts, which are the husks, as Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel notes in De creatione, Problem 23. They hold that these demons are airy and fiery, distinguished by sex, eating, drinking, given to sexual intercourse, and at last dying like men. They laboriously prove the existence of these demons, and ascribe to them exorcisms and incantations, as appears from Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, who speaks thus in Problem 22 on Creation: Although some are found who deny that those spirits which we commonly call demons exist, it is nevertheless most certain that such really exist. For the ancient sages, as can be seen in the Talmudic work, list their names: namely Hasmeday, Higueret bat Mahalat, and Nahama; and in Isaiah 34. 14, where the destruction of the Edomites is foretold, it is said: [אך שם הרגיעה לילית] Surely there Lilith rested; which is the name of a female spirit, whom some hold to have been Adam's first wife, before he had received Eve from God as his wife. These things are confirmed in the tractate Megillah, chapter 1, where it is said that they do not utter the name of the Lord rashly or in vain. And indeed many are found who summon these demons by adjurations, and accomplish many marvellous things by necromancy. Moreover, in certain books of the Cabbalists, such as Pirque Ehalot, Raziel and others, their names, exorcisms and incantations are recorded. But who can deny what is perceived by the senses to be most true? Concerning this kind of angel the ancients tell various things in Chagigah 2: namely that they eat food, beget children, and die like men; that they are furnished with wings, and fly from one part of the world to another; and moreover that they often hear what is to come. And elsewhere they say that when they appear to only one man, they are harmful and inflict loss; when they appear to two, they are harmless; but they never appear to three men at once. In the admirable book Zohar, various things are said about them, and in particular that some are spirits of the air and others of fire; and they prove this from the Psalmist, Psalm 104: He made his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire. They also hold that some of them are cunning and shrewd, and some stupid and foolish. Rabbenu Ay and Rabbi Moses of Gerona confirm this opinion about spirits. Finally, the truth of this opinion is clear from various passages of Scripture.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Fingunt, calumniantur que Judaei, & hodie, & olim, Adamum, cum ab uxore Eva separatus, & per centum & triginta annos propter peccatum excommunicatus esset, procreasse ex daemonibus juniores daemones, spiritusque immundos; Pariterque Evam excommunicatam eodem illo tempore concubuisse cum An-
units.tr: The Jews, both today and in former times, invent and slander that Adam, when he had been separated from his wife Eve and excommunicated for a hundred and thirty years on account of sin, begot younger demons and unclean spirits from demons. Likewise Eve, excommunicated at the same time, lay with the evil angels and brought forth harmful spirits into the light, Lamiae and Lemures, as the Talmudists attest in tractate Erubhin, chapter Gnofin, passim.

units.la: Angelis malis, inque lucem protulisse spiritus noxios, Lamias, Lemuresque, sicuti testantur Talmudistæ in Tractatu Erubhin, cap. Gnofin Passim: Ait Rabbi Jeremia, Ben Eliezer: omnibus illis annis quibus Adam Protoplastus fuit in Anathemate excommunicationis, genuit spiritus, dæmones & spectra nocturna, sicut dicitur Genef. cap. 5. verf. 3. Et vixit Adam triginta & centum annos, & genuit in similitudine sua, in imagine sua. Id docet, quod ad hoc usque tempus non genuerat in similitudine sua; Et Magistri in Berefchit Rabba super illud Genef. cap. 5. verf. 20. Et vocavit Adam uxorem suam Chavva, quia ipsa fuit mater omnis viventis: Dixit Rabbi Simon, mater omnis viventis, id est, mater omnium viventium: in omnibus enim centum & triginta annus, in quibus separavit se Adam ab uxore sua, concepit, & peperit Eva spiritus masculos, & Adam spiritus fœmineos; & hoc est quod scribitur 2. Samuelis cap. 7. verf. 14. Quem, cum depravatus fuerit, arguam in virga hominum, & in plagis filiorum Adam; filiorum Adam antiquorum; Ad quem locum notandum venit, quod in Editione Cracoviensi Berefchit Rabba, verba aliter legantur, & sequentem sensum faciant, uti observavit Voysinius in Notis ad Raymundi Martini Pugionem Fidei, pag. 578. Spiritus masculi incalescebant ab ea, & ipsa peperit ex eis. Spiritus vero fœminæ incalescebant ab Adamo, & ex eo pepererunt: Sic Rafchi ad 2. Sam. cap. 7. verf. 14. Et in plagis filiorum Adam, hoc est Asmodæorum, qui pepulerunt ipsum è regno suo. Nam filii Adam Protoplasti fuere dæmones, quoniam omnibus centum & triginta annis, quibus separatus erat Adam Protoplastus ab uxore sua propter mortem Abelis, spiritus fœmellæ commixtæ sunt cum eo, & inde pepererunt: Conferatur Rabbi Schimeonis Jalkut ad l. c. Nugantur denique multa de Lilit, Adami conjuge prima, fœmina valde furiosa, litigiosaque, quæ mater quoque fit Dæmonum, hinc in Medrafchim Hebræorum appellata אם השדים והרוחות Mater dæmonum, spirituumque malignorum; Puerperis quoque maxime infesta, de qua Rabbi Elias Levita in Thisbi ad vocem Lilit sic inquit: Lilith, Jel. cap. 34. verf. 14. Quin & Lamia ibi quiescet. Rabbi Schelemo dicit esse nomen dæmonis, atque Jonathan transtulit לילין in plurali numero. Sic quoque & in isto versu. In diebus illis cum sederet Rex &c. Tharg. Hierosoly. שדין ולילין dæmones & lamias. Inventur porro scriptum quod in centum & viginti annis quibus Adam continuit se ab uxore sua Havah, venerint ad eum dæmones & conceperint ab eo, sicque genuerit dæmones & spiritus, lamias, & lemures. Et in alio loco inveni: Quatuor esse matres tres daemonum, Lilith, Naema, Ogereth, & Ma-chalath. In libro quoque Ben Sira quaestione 60. legitur, quod Nebucadnezar interrogaverit eum hunc in modum. Quam ob causam pueri octo dierum moriuntur? Cui respondit ille. Eo quod Lilith occidit eos, qua de re ibidem multa prolixe tractat, quae huc adscribere mihi fastidio fuit quandoquidem illis nullam adhibeo fidem. Verumtamen mos inolevit inter Judaeos praesertim Germanos, quod faciunt circulum per circuitum in parietibus cubiculi in quo jacet puerpera cum creta, aut carbone, scribuntque in singulis parietibus, Adam, Havah, Chutz, Lilith. Atque in ostio cubiculi interiori scribunt nomina trium angelorum, qui sunt Senoi, Sanfenoi, & Sanmangeloph, quemadmodum tradidit illis ipsa Lilith ea hora qua voluerunt eam suffocare in mari. Totum istud bene explicatum habetur in libro Ben Sira, quem ipsum videre potest qui huic rei fidem habet. Caeterum pluribus hoc praestitit ex Ben Sira Celeberrimus Buxtorfius, qui in accurata sua Judaeorum Synagoga consuli potest, cap. 4. Laudandus proinde quoque Rabbi Isac Abarbanel, cum pertaesus nugarum popularium, minime secundum literam haec omnia intelligere vult, sed allegorice de filiis, filiabusque malis exponit, in Commentario ad Pentateuchum sol. 38. col. 4. VeVerum vocant daemones & spiritus & spectra, filios & filias, quas Adam genuit ante Sethum; quoniam Cain fuit daemon respectu impietatis suæ & operum suorum: Abel autem spiritum sanctitatis est, scilicet gloriolam, & desiderium, atq; imperium.
units.tr: Rabbi Jeremiah ben Eliezer says: in all those years in which Adam the first-formed was under the anathema of excommunication, he begot spirits, demons and nocturnal phantoms, as is said in Genesis chapter 5, verse 3. And Adam lived a hundred and thirty years, and begot in his own likeness, in his own image. This teaches that until that time he had not begotten in his own likeness. The masters in Bereshit Rabba, on that verse of Genesis chapter 5, verse 20, And Adam called his wife Chavvah, because she was the mother of all living, say: Rabbi Simon said, "mother of all living," that is, mother of all living beings. For in all the hundred and thirty years in which Adam separated himself from his wife, Eve conceived and bore male spirits, and Adam female spirits; and this is what is written in 2 Samuel chapter 7, verse 14: When he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the sons of Adam; of the ancient sons of Adam. On this passage it must be noted that in the Cracow edition of Bereshit Rabba the words are read differently and make the following sense, as Voisin observed in his notes to Raymund Martini's Pugio Fidei, p. 578: The male spirits grew hot with her, and she bore from them. But the female spirits grew hot with Adam, and bore from him. So Rashi on 2 Samuel chapter 7, verse 14: And with the stripes of the sons of Adam, that is, of the Asmodaei, who drove him from his kingdom. For the sons of Adam the first-formed were demons, since in all the hundred and thirty years in which Adam the first-formed was separated from his wife because of the death of Abel, female spirits mingled with him and bore from him. Let Rabbi Shimon's Yalkut on the same passage be consulted. Finally, many things are fabled about Lilith, the first wife of Adam, a woman very furious and quarrelsome, who also becomes the mother of demons, and is therefore called in the Midrashim of the Hebrews אם השדים והרוחות [em hashedim veharuchot] Mother of demons and of evil spirits. She is also especially hostile to women in childbirth, concerning whom Rabbi Elias Levita in the Tishbi, under the word Lilith, says thus: Lilith, Isaiah chapter 34, verse 14: Yea, Lamia shall rest there. Rabbi Solomon says it is the name of a demon, and Jonathan rendered לילין [lilin] in the plural. So also in this verse: In those days, when the King sat, etc., the Targum of Jerusalem has שדין ולילין [shedin velilin], demons and lamiae. It is further found written that during the hundred and twenty years in which Adam kept himself from his wife Havah, demons came to him and conceived from him, and so he begot demons and spirits, lamiae and lemures. And in another place I have found: There are four mothers of three demons: Lilith, Naema, Ogereth, and Machalath. In the book of Ben Sira, question 60, it is read that Nebuchadnezzar asked him in this manner: For what reason do boys die on the eighth day? To which he answered: Because Lilith kills them. On this matter he treats many things at length there, which I have thought tedious to set down here, since I give them no credence at all. Nevertheless a custom has grown up among the Jews, especially the German ones, that they draw a circle round the walls of the room in which the woman in childbirth lies, with chalk or charcoal, and write on each wall: Adam, Havah, Chutz, Lilith. And on the inner door of the room they write the names of three angels, who are Senoi, Sanfenoi, and Sanmangeloph, as Lilith herself handed them down to them, at the hour when they wished to suffocate her in the sea. All this is well explained in the book of Ben Sira, which anyone who gives credence to this matter may see for himself. Moreover, the most celebrated Buxtorf has done more on this matter from Ben Sira, and may be consulted in his accurate Synagogue of the Jews, chapter 4. Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel is therefore also to be praised, since, weary of popular trifles, he does not wish to understand all these things literally, but expounds them allegorically as evil sons and daughters, in his Commentary on the Pentateuch, folio 38, column 4: Truly they call demons, spirits and phantoms the sons and daughters whom Adam begot before Seth; because Cain was a demon in respect of his impiety and his works; but Abel is of the spirit of holiness, that is, of vainglory, desire, and dominion.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Credit imperitum vulgus Judaicum, plumbeus, carnalisque ille in rebus divinis populus, cum non paucis Religionis suæ Magistris, Angelos non esse substantias simplices, puras, spirituales, seu intellectuales, quarum consistat essentia in cogitatione, sed esse corporeos & materiales, non quidem crassos, palbabilesque, sed subtilissimos, qui vel ex Elementis subtilioribus sint compositi, sicuti non de omnibus Angelis, sed de certis quibusdam pronunciat Rabbi Isac Sangarus, cum sic in libro Cosri Part. 4. §. 3. loquitur: Tales Angeli vel Legati, vel sunt pro certo tempore creati ex corporibus subtilibus elementaribus, vel sunt Angeli perpetui; Vel sint aerii, maxime vero ignei, ex aere, vel igne facti; Quod sub forma ignis undique fere in Veteri Testamento apparuerint; Quod statim post rerum omnium initium flammam gladii vibraverint, ut viam custodirent ad Arborem Vitæ; Genef. cap. 3. verf. 24. Quod ab igne nomina quædam fuerint sortiti, hinc Seraphim appellati; Quod Psalmo dicatur 104. verf. 4. Qui facit Angelos suos ventos, Ministros suos ignem flammantem; Quod magna Doctorum Rabbinorum pars credi-derit, Angelos malos secundo Creationis die cum Inferno formatos esse. Accedebat, quod audiret per lucem primo die creatam, vel per cœlum, Angelos pariter intelligen-dos esse; Præterea quod in corporibus sæpe fuerint visi, comederint, biberint, aliaque corporalia peregerint; Quod Angeli tertiæ classis, eorumque dæmones juniores sobo-lem producant, morianturque; Quod ex Angelorum tum cum Evæ congressu, tum cum filiabus hominum, uti quoque ex coi-tu Adami cum spiritibus impuris fœminei sexus nati sint dæmones, Lemures, & La-miæ. Sed licet hæc communis Popelli Ju-daici sit opinio, imo quorundam quoque Magistrorum, contrariam tamen longeque meliorem de Angelorum natura mentem habuerunt, qui cordatiores semper extite-runt, asserentes Angelos naturam possidere incorporeanam, immaterialemque, in appa-ritionibus & functionibus junctam sæpe cor-pori, hincque factam conspicuam, tum in Visionibus Propheticis & in Imaginatione, tum absque imaginatione, uti docet Rabbi Moses Maimonides in Constitutionibus de Fundamentis Legis cap. 2. §. 4. Quædam creatura habent formam absque ulla omnino materia, videlicet Angeli, quia non sunt corpora, sed forma distincta à se invicem; Et in More Nevochim Part. 1. cap. 49. Angeli quoque non habent corpora, sed sunt Intelligentiæ abstractæ à materia: attamen facti sunt, & à Deo creati, quemadmodum explicabitur. Hinc dixerunt in Berefchit Rabba Sapientes nostri: Locus ille Genes. cap. 3. verf. 24. Lahat flammam gladij versatilis, vel vertentis se, intelligendus est juxta illud; Ministros suos ignem lohet flammantem (h.e. per Lahat ibi intelligitur Angelus, qui est instar flammæ) hammithappechet gladij versatilis, (h. e. Versatilis ille Angelus appellatur,) quia Angeli instar Prothei in varias formas se convertunt; quandoque enim Virorum, quandoque Mulierum, quandoque Ventorum, quandoque Legatorum forma & specie vestiti apparent. Quibus verbis aperte testantur, Angelos non esse materiales, neque certam & constantem aliquam habere formam vel figuram corporalem extra intellectum, sed omnia tantum fieri in Visionibus Propheticis, & in Imaginatione, quemadmodum explicabitur, quando agemus de Prophetia; Sic Rabbi Joseph Albo de Fundamentis lib. 2.
units.tr: The ignorant Jewish crowd, that leaden and carnal people in matters of religion, believes, together with not a few teachers of its own religion, that angels are not simple, pure, spiritual or intellectual substances whose essence consists in thought, but are corporeal and material. They are not gross or palpable, but very subtle, being composed either of more subtle elements. Rabbi Isaac Sangarus pronounces this not of all angels but of certain ones, when he speaks thus in the book Cosri, Part 4, §. 3: Such angels or messengers are either created for a certain time out of subtle elementary bodies, or they are perpetual angels. They are either airy, or especially fiery, made of air or of fire. They appeared almost everywhere in the Old Testament under the form of fire. Immediately after the beginning of all things they brandished a flaming sword to guard the way to the Tree of Life (Gen. 3:24). Some of them received their names from fire, and hence are called Seraphim. Psalm 104:4 says: "Who makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flaming fire." A great part of the Rabbinic teachers believed that evil angels were formed with Hell on the second day of Creation. To this was added that they heard that angels are to be understood also through the light created on the first day, or through heaven. Moreover, they were often seen in bodies, ate, drank, and performed other bodily functions. The angels of the third class and their younger demons produce offspring and die. From the intercourse of angels with Eve, and also with the daughters of men, and likewise from the coupling of Adam with impure spirits of the female sex, demons, Lemures and Lamiae were born. But although this is the common opinion of the Jewish people, and indeed of some teachers too, others have held a contrary and far better view of the nature of angels. These have always been the more judicious, asserting that angels possess an incorporeal and immaterial nature, often joined to a body in their appearances and functions, and therefore made visible, both in prophetic visions and in imagination, and also apart from imagination. So teaches Rabbi Moses Maimonides in the Constitutions on the Foundations of the Law, chap. 2, §. 4: Some creatures have a form without any matter at all, namely the angels, because they are not bodies but distinct forms, separate from one another. And in the More Nevochim, Part 1, chap. 49: The angels also do not have bodies, but are intelligences abstracted from matter; yet they have been made and created by God, as will be explained. Hence our wise men said in Bereshit Rabba, on that passage of Genesis 3:24, "lahat, the flame of the sword that turns," that it is to be understood according to the verse, "his ministers a flaming fire": that is, by lahat is understood there an angel who is like a flame; hammithappechet, the sword that turns, (that is, that turning angel is called so), because the angels turn themselves into various forms like Proteus; for sometimes they appear clothed in the form and appearance of men, sometimes of women, sometimes of winds, sometimes of messengers. By these words they plainly testify that angels are not material, nor have any fixed and constant bodily form or figure outside the intellect, but that all these things happen only in prophetic visions and in imagination, as will be explained when we treat of prophecy. So Rabbi Joseph Albo, On the Foundations, book 2,

units.la: cap. 28. Scito cum sint Angeli expertes materia, neque sint capaces accidentium materialium ; Sic quoque Rabbi Ilac Abarbanel in Commentario in Pentateuchum sol. 38. col. 2. Angeli enim spirituales sunt, jeparati plane ab omni materia, ita ut ne inclinent ad corporeitatem, nec possibile sit eos peccare: Quare igitur, quatenus sunt Intelligentia separata mutarent naturam suam ; Pariter Rabbi Jedaia Happenini in Bakkascha, seu Meditatione, Sect. 2. A scintilla luminis tui ab antiquitate scaturigo diffluit, a splendore tuo effunditur, inde separantur castra Intelligentiarum admirabilium, quae sunt substantia purissima, Intelligentes ex se ipsis, stolidi pra illis alij, invisibiles, incorporea, exhibentes se splendore tuo absque tegumento ; Et Rabbi Moseh Ben Jacob in Praefatione Praeceptorum Affirmativorum : Hominem creatum esse participem de utrisque, intelligentiam & scientiam communem habere cum Angelis, materialitatem vero & pugnam contrariarum qualitatum cum brutis.
units.tr: chap. 28: Know that since angels are free of matter, they are not capable of material accidents. So too Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel in his Commentary on the Pentateuch, fol. 38, col. 2: For spiritual angels are wholly separated from all matter, so that they do not incline to corporeality, nor is it possible for them to sin. Why then, insofar as they are separate intelligences, would they change their nature? Likewise Rabbi Jedaiah Happenini in the Bakkascha, or Meditation, Sect. 2: From the spark of your light a fountain flows out from antiquity, from your splendour it is poured forth; thence are separated the hosts of wonderful intelligences, which are the purest substance, intelligent from themselves, others foolish beside them, invisible, incorporeal, presenting themselves in your splendour without covering. And Rabbi Moses ben Jacob in the Preface to the Affirmative Precepts: Man was created a participant in both: he has intelligence and knowledge in common with the angels, but materiality and the conflict of contrary qualities with the brutes.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: De Angelorum ministerio insulsa multa comminiscuntur Rabbini, singulis distincta sua adsignantes munia, officiaque, adeo ut quod unus efficere poterit, alter non possit, tribuentesque cuilibet Angelo peculiarem rem legationis suæ provinciam, siccquenegan-tes duobus aut pluribus Angelis unam ean-demque demandari legationem, hocnixi fundamento Veterum, quod ipsi posuerunt, שאין מלאך אחד עושה שתי שליחיות Angelum unum unafolummodo legatione fungi,non duabus. Hinc tritum illud Magistrorum quod occur-rit in Berefchit Rabba cap. 20. Et in Pesa-chim, cap. 10. Traditio est, nunquam unus An-gelus duas obit legationes, neque unquam duo An-geli obeunt legationem unam; Sic etiam sensit Paraphraftes Hierosolymitanus, qui ad ver-sum secundum cap. 18. Genes. ita habet. Tres Angeli missi sunt ad Patrem nostrum Abraham, tresque illi missi sunt ad tria, quia non potest uni Angelorum Excelsi nisi una res delegari; Ad quem pariter locum sic inquit Rabbi Moles Gerundensis: Unus venit, qui nunciaret Sarae; unus, qui Abrahamum (e dolore scilicet recentis circumcisionis laborantem) curaret; Tertius qui Sodomam everteret. Et Raphael qui-dem, postquam Abrahamum curasset, abiit quo Lothum servaret: quia neque duæ (simul) legatio-nes fuerunt, quæ diversis locis ac mandatis per-actæ sunt; aut si duæ fuerunt, utraque salutis fuit. Rabbi Bechai hic annotat Angelos illos fuisse Michaelem, Raphaelem, Gabrielem, ac Mi-chaelem fuisse, qui venerit nunciatum Sarae &c
units.tr: The rabbis invent many foolish things about the ministry of the angels. They assign to each angel its own distinct duties and offices, so that what one can perform another cannot. They give each angel a particular province of its mission, and deny that two or more angels are ever given one and the same commission. They rest this on a principle the ancients laid down: שאין מלאך אחד עושה שתי שליחיות [one angel does not perform two missions]. Hence the familiar saying of the masters, found in Bereshit Rabba ch. 20 and in Pesachim ch. 10: It is a tradition that one angel never performs two missions, nor do two angels ever perform one mission. The Jerusalem Paraphrast also understood it so. On verse 2 of Genesis ch. 18 he says: Three angels were sent to our father Abraham, and those three were sent for three things, because one of the angels of the Most High cannot be assigned more than one thing. On the same passage Rabbi Moses of Gerona says: One came to announce to Sarah; one to heal Abraham (who was then suffering from the pain of his recent circumcision); a third to overthrow Sodom. Raphael, indeed, after he had healed Abraham, went away to save Lot, because there were not two missions (at the same time) carried out in different places and for different orders; or if there were two, both were for salvation. Rabbi Bechai notes here that those angels were Michael, Raphael and Gabriel, and that Michael was the one who came to announce to Sarah etc.

units.la: S Lothum servaverit, quæ sunt duæ legationes misericordiæ & miserationum; Raphaelem vero fuise, qui venerit curatum Abrahamum; Gabriel̄ denique venïsse eversum Sodomam; Quod ex Zennorenna quoque supra partim observavimus, partimque confirmamus, cum ad citatum locum fol. 20. b. sic inquit: Da fragt man eine Kaschja (schwere Frage:) und hätte doch können ein Malach (Engel) das alles thun? Der Tiruz (Antwort) ist: Ein Malach der kan nicht thun gutes und böses/ dann ein Malach thut gutes/und ist eitel Chesed und Rachamim. (Gnad und Barmherzigkeit) und ist ein ander Malach, der thut eitel böses / und eitel die (Straffen/) und darumb auch Michael gesetzet ist auff eitel Chesed und Rachamim; der hat gesagt gutes zu Sara / und hat beschirmet Loth. Da fragt man noch ein Kaschja, und warumb hat Michael nicht auch geheilet Abraham? aber der Tiruz ist: Raphael ist gesetzt auff die Rephuoth (Heilung) da darff ihn kein Malach massig gesul thun (das ist / keiner darff ihm ins Gehäg fallen;) Darumb hat müssen kommen Raphael zu heilen Abraham. Cum itaque Rabbini judicant, duas Legationes non obire unum Angelum, in-telli-
units.tr: and that he saved Lot, which are two embassies of mercy and compassion; that it was Raphael who came to heal Abraham; and finally that Gabriel came to overthrow Sodom. We have observed this partly above from Zennorenna, and we confirm it now, since at the place cited, fol. 20 b, he says: Da fragt man eine Kaschja (a hard question): could an Malach (angel) not have done all this? The Tiruz (answer) is: a Malach cannot do both good and evil, for one Malach does good and is pure Chesed and Rachamim (grace and mercy), and another Malach does nothing but evil and nothing but punishments. That is why Michael is set over pure Chesed and Rachamim: he spoke good things to Sarah and protected Lot. Then one asks another Kaschja: why did Michael not also heal Abraham? The Tiruz is this: Raphael is set over the Rephuoth (healing), and no other Malach may meddle with him in any way (that is, no one may fall into his province). Therefore Raphael had to come to heal Abraham.

units.la: telligunt hoc de oppositis&contrariis legatio- nibus, cum una alteri adversatur; siquidem minimè fit rationi consentaneum, Angelum miserationibus præpositum exercere judici- um, quod cum ea re pugnat, sicut nec Ange- lum præpositum judicio exercere miseratio- nes: verum quando duæ legationes inter fe conveniunt, suntque judicii aut miseratio- num, tunc duas pluresve unum Angelum ob- ire posse.
units.tr: Since, then, the rabbis judge that one angel cannot perform two embassies, they understand this of opposed and contrary embassies, when one is at odds with the other. For it is by no means reasonable that an angel set over mercies should exercise judgment, since that clashes with his office, just as an angel set over judgment should not exercise mercies. But when two embassies agree with each other, and both belong to judgment or both to mercy, then one angel may perform two or more of them.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Singulis populis, regionibusque' An- gelos Præfectos, Rectoresque apponunt, exi- ftimantes totumOrbemAngelis,Orbibusque cœlestibus subjectum, inprimisque omnes nationes per Angelos, Stellasque regi, qui- bus Deus istam commiserit curam, hinc fe- ptuaginta Angelos in confusione linguarum apud Babelem præpositos fuisse septuaginta populis ac nationibus, uti cum contribulibus loquitur Rabbi Don Joseph Jachiades in Commentario ad Danielem cap. 10. verf. 13. Septuaginta populis respondent in cœlo septuaginta Principes, atque sic Israelita habent Principem unum, scilicet Michaelem. Sed licet Michae- lem gentis suæ Princeps extollant valde, mox Israelis Ducem, exercitusque Israelita- rum Præfectum passim ex Danielis cap. 10. appellent, moxque cum Targumiftis Princi-pem Hierololymarum nominent, & Præce-ptorem Israelitarum, qui sapientiæ præfectus sit, interim tamen Michaelis Regimen toto distinguunt cœlo ab aliorum Angelorum do-minio, quod in gentes exercent reliquas, do-centes se, qui unius Dei sint hæreditas, qui sponsa & corculum Dei sint, divino magis subesse imperio, Michaelem esse Principem subalternum & vicaria sub Deo pollere po-testate, cujus mandata solum accipiat & exe-quatur, cum cæteri sive Angeli sive Astra cæ-teras gubernent gentes cum absoluto impe-rio, teste Rabbi Jachiade, loco citato: Diffe-rentia est inter Principem Israelis in gubernatione populi sui à gubernatione Principum aliorum in suos populos. Principes enim aliorum populorum sunt etiam Dii ipsorum, & instar Deorum in eos operan-tur, nec reguntur quàm à Principibus suis. Sed Israel regitur à Providentia Dei, & licet Michael ipsis dominetur, fit tamen hoc juxta præscriptum sui Creatoris, absque cujus permissu rem nec parvam nec magnam unquam tentat; Cum quo conferri bene meretur Rabbi Isac Abarbanel in Com-mentario ad Danielem cap. 10. & in Libello de Capite Fidei, cap. 12. Firmant vero sua hæc de Angelorum præsidio dogmata, tum ex Deuter. cap. 32. vers. 8. Cum hæreditatem di-stridistribueret Altissimus gentibus, cum divideret filios hominis, statuebat terminos populorum juxta numerum filiorum Israel; Cum praesertim ex Danielis cap. 10. verf. 13. Et Princeps Regni Persarum stabat adversum me unum & viginti dies, & ecce Michael, unus Principum primorum, venit ad juvandum me, & ego superfui ibi apud Reges Persarum.
units.tr: They assign to each people and region an angel as prefect and ruler, thinking that the whole world, and the heavenly spheres too, is subject to angels, and above all that all nations are governed by angels and stars, to whom God has committed this care. Hence they hold that the seventy angels who were set over the seventy peoples and nations at the confusion of tongues at Babel correspond to them, as Rabbi Don Joseph Jachiades says with his fellow-countrymen in his commentary on Daniel, chapter 10, verse 13: To the seventy peoples there correspond in heaven seventy princes, and so the Israelites have one prince, namely Michael. But although they greatly exalt Michael as the prince of their own nation, and everywhere, from Daniel chapter 10, call him the leader of Israel and the prefect of the Israelite army, and although with the Targumists they name him the Prince of Jerusalem and the teacher of the Israelites, who is set over wisdom, nevertheless they distinguish the rule of Michael from the dominion of the other angels by a wide gulf in heaven. The others exercise dominion over the remaining nations, while they teach that Israel, being the inheritance of the one God, the bride and darling of God, is subject more directly to the divine rule; that Michael is a subordinate prince, possessing a vicarious power under God, whose commands alone he receives and carries out; whereas the others, whether angels or stars, govern the other nations with absolute power. So says Rabbi Jachiades in the place cited: There is a difference between the Prince of Israel in governing his people and the governance of the princes of other peoples over their peoples. For the princes of other peoples are also their gods, and they act upon them as gods, and are governed only by their own princes. But Israel is governed by the providence of God, and although Michael rules over them, he does so according to the decree of his Creator, without whose permission he never undertakes any matter, great or small. With him should well be compared Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel, in his commentary on Daniel chapter 10, and in his little book on the Articles of Faith, chapter 12. They confirm these doctrines of the protection of angels both from Deuteronomy chapter 32, verse 8: When the Most High divided their inheritance to the nations, when he separated the sons of men, he set the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel; and especially from Daniel chapter 10, verse 13: But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me one and twenty days, and behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me, and I remained there with the kings of Persia.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Assignant pariter singulis gentis suae hominibus certum genium, qui Angelus Custos sit, apud hominem jugiter degens, ipsumque custodiens, parumper vero, si peccet, abeo recedens. De hoc Angelo Tutelari pleni sunt modernorum Hebraeorum libri, ne de Antiquorum nunc verba faciamus. Sic Angelos apud mortales constituunt Doctores, qui cura Praeceptorum fungantur. Razielem Angelum Adami Informatorem vocant. Semo tribuunt Praeceptorem, Angelum Jophielem appellatum. Abrahamo in studiis Moderatorem tribuunt Angelum Sedkielem. Jacobi Magistrum Angelum Pelielem fuisse volunt. De Gabriele memorant, quod septuaginta linguas tradiderit Josepho, cum ad Aegypti gubernacula esset admotus. Viatorum Angelum, qui hominum dux, & itineris protector sit, ex Cabbala nuncupant Juhadh. Ad sanan-dum dum hóminem mittitur Raphael. Dæmon Schibta infantum nervos exsiccat & contrahit. Angelus Duma mortuis præfectus est, illorumque tenet rationem, de quo referunt, quod totus oculis plenus sit. Sic Angelos quoque præficiunt rebus inanimis, Elementis, mundi plagis, planetis, mensibus, anni quatuor partibus, singulis hebdomadis diebus, & quibus non aliis. Haniel Angelus curam habet Januarii. Gabriel præpositus est Februario. Romiel princeps custodiæ est in mense Martio. Uriel mensis Aprilis Dominus dicitur. Zaphniel Majo præest. Amriel Junium regit. Haniel Julium, Barkiel Augustum. Qui Septembrem gubernat, hactenus mihi incognitus. Tzuriel est Octobris Angelus. Bafcariel Novembrem moderatur. Adoniel præpositus est Decembri. Septem Angelos præficiunt septem hebdomadis diebus, ita ut quilibet suum distinctum habeat diem. Recenseant Angelos diei noctisque, hujusque quatuor constituunt, quod quatuor sint noctis excubiæ, quarum singulas peculiaris gubernet Angelus. Narrant certum Angelum præpositum esse lapidibus, certum ferro. Igni non solum præfectum esse Gabrielem, verum etiam fructibus, ut ad maturitatem perducantur. Azariel aquarum habere regimen, ne transeant terterminum suum & operiant terram. Iorkemi grandini praeesse. Duma ventos regere. Nekid Principem esse cibi, qui custodiae panis praefectus sit. Radja pluvias & irrigationes curare. Lilam Angelum conceptui praeesse.
units.tr: They likewise assign to each man of their nation a particular genius, who is his guardian angel, dwelling with him continually, watching over him, though if he sins he withdraws from him for a while. Modern Hebrew books are full of this guardian angel, not to mention the ancients. Thus the Doctors appoint angels over mortals to act as tutors. They call Raziel the angel who instructed Adam. To Seth they assign a teacher, an angel called Jophiel. For Abraham in his studies they assign as guide the angel Sedkiel. They hold that Peliel was Jacob's teacher. Of Gabriel they relate that he taught Joseph seventy languages when he was raised to the government of Egypt. The angel of travellers, who is the leader of men and the protector of the journey, they name from the Cabbala Juhadh. To heal a man, Raphael is sent. The demon Schibta dries up and contracts the sinews of infants. The angel Duma is set over the dead and keeps their account; of him they report that he is wholly full of eyes. Thus they also set angels over inanimate things, the elements, the regions of the world, the planets, the months, the four parts of the year, each day of the week, and whatever else there is. Haniel has charge of January. Gabriel presides over February. Romiel is the prince of the watch in the month of March. Uriel is called lord of April. Zaphniel presides over May. Amriel rules June. Haniel rules July, Barkiel August. Who governs September is so far unknown to me. Tzuriel is the angel of October. Bafcariel governs November. Adoniel presides over December. They set seven angels over the seven days of the week, so that each has his own distinct day. They enumerate angels of the day and of the night, and make four of them, because there are four night watches, each of which a particular angel governs. They relate that a certain angel is set over stones, and a certain one over iron. That Gabriel is set not only over fire but also over fruits, so that they are brought to ripeness. Azariel has the governance of the waters, lest they pass their boundary and cover the earth. Iorkemi presides over hail. Duma rules the winds. Nekid is the prince of food, set over the keeping of bread. Radja takes care of rains and irrigation. Lilam presides over conception.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Magnifica profecto sunt quae moderni Iudaei praedicant de Angelis, ut mirum non sit, quod Angelos maximi faciant, venerentur, imitentur, offensosque saepe timeant, non tamen interim censent adorandos vel invocandos esse Angelos, neque festis, neque templis, neque ulla cultus religiosi specie volunt prosequendos, gravibus persuasi rationibus, quod Exodi cap. 20. prohibeatur expresso praecepto; Non habebis Deos alienos coram me; Sicuti illud patet ex Rabbi Joseph Albo de Fundamentis lib. 2. cap. 28. Sed orare Angelum, aut adorare eum propter se, aut propter potestatem illi propriam, & propter id quod nomine ejus exprimitur, hoc demum prohibetur illo praecepto, Exodi 20. Non habebis Deos alienos coram me. Et haec est doctrina Rabbi Mosis filii Nachmanis. Hinc patet error eorum qui in orationibus suis proferunt nomina Angelorum: nomina enim Angelorum illis conveniunt propter propriam ipsorum virtutem. Id vetitum est Exodi 20. Non habebis Deos alienos, &c. ut diximus. Causam erroris præbuit illis quod repererunt in quibusdam precibus peculiaribus veterum referri nomina quædam propria: & ideo putaverunt licitum esse uti quibuscumque nominibus in precibus. Non ita res est: Nefas est enim ullum proferre nomen in precibus, præter nomina Dei propria, & ideo vocatur hæc scientia Cabala, quia eâ uti non licet, nisi ex traditione. Alioqui periculum esset erroris; posset que alius Deus coli præter Deum verum. Et ut id pateat attendenti, hujus rei exemplum afferam. Reperitur in precibus Veterum nomen Mitspats, quod lector existimare posset nomen esse alicujus Angeli: non est tamen; sed est nomen יהוה Tetragrammaton facta literarum permutatione per Atbasch; Quod Deus Benedictus ex beneplacito & summa operetur libertate, idcirco ei soli competat cultus divinus, Angeli vero reliquaque omnia à Deo ad sua sint ordinata opera, uti egregie ratiocinatur Rabbi Isac Abarbanel in Libello de Capite fidei cap. 12. Ad dubium secundum. Quare constituat Rab in classe articulorum quintum articulum, quod non oporteat ponere mediatores inter Deum Benedictum ac hominem: Respondeo ac ajo, quod jam commemoraverim in propositione quinta, sub hoc articulo comprehendi sublimia fidei dogmata. Primum est, Deum operari libere, non autem sicuti reliqua existentia, vel Angeli, vel orbes, aut astra, aut elementa, vel quicquid ex iis compositipositum est; quia omnia ista ordinata sunt ad sua opera, neque inest iis delectus aut voluntas ad operandum, quod agunt: Sed Deus Benedictus operatur ex beneplacito, atque libertate; idcirco etiam ei convenit cultus, cantio, laus atque celebratio; Quod Deus solus sit misericors, qui gratiam possit infundere, & a quo omnes species misericordiae emanent & deriventur, proinde solus sit invocandus, uti rursus loquitur Rabbi Joseph Albo de Fundamentis lib. 4. cap. 17. Nemo praeter Deum potest facere misericordiam, quia ipse solus est fons misericordiarum, & bonorum omnium, juxta illud Psalmo 130. vers 7. Quia cum Domino misericordia est: id est, & non cum alio. Ideoque ipsum orare decet, & non alium. Quomodo enim oraret aliquis eum a quo non posset consequi quod petit? Quod potentia Dei sola sit absoluta & infinita, Angelorum virtus sit finita, atque ex ordinatione divina determinata, indice Rabbi Isaco Abarbanele in Capite Fidei, cap. 12. Fides secunda est, quod praeditus sit potentia infinita, atque hoc ipsum innuit, cum ait: quia omnia ista ordinata sunt ad sua opera, hoc est, opera atque potentia eorum limitata atque determinata sunt ex ordinatione, ac virtus eorum finita est, nec transcendit ordinem inter eos constitutum, sed Deus Benedictus facit quicquid vult, prout ait Psalmista Psalmo 135. vers 6. Quicquid vult Deus, facit in caelis lis ac in terra, atque idcirco convenit ei cultus Jerem. cap. 18. verf. 6. Omnia enim in manu ejus, tanquam lutum in manu figuli, neque est qui dicat ei: Quare hoc fecisti? Consentiente pariter Rabbi Joseph Albo de Fundamentis lib. 4. cap. 16.
units.tr: What the modern Jews preach about the angels is indeed magnificent, so it is no wonder that they esteem and revere the angels greatly, imitate them, and often fear them when they are offended. Nevertheless, they do not think the angels should be adored or invoked, and they will not have them honoured with festivals, temples, or any form of religious worship. They are persuaded by weighty reasons, because Exodus 20 forbids it by express precept: "You shall have no other gods before me." This is plain from Rabbi Joseph Albo, On the Fundamentals, book 2, chapter 28: But to pray to an angel, or to adore him, either for his own sake or on account of the power proper to him, and on account of what is expressed by his name, this is what that precept of Exodus 20 forbids: "You shall have no other gods before me." This is also the teaching of Rabbi Moses son of Nachman. Hence the error of those is plain who in their prayers utter the names of angels: for the names of the angels belong to them on account of their own virtue. This is forbidden in Exodus 20, "You shall have no other gods," etc., as we have said. The cause of their error was that they found in certain prayers of the ancients that certain proper names are cited, and therefore they thought it lawful to use any names whatever in prayers. It is not so: for it is wicked to utter any name in prayers except the proper names of God. That is why this science is called Cabbala, because it is not lawful to use it except by tradition. Otherwise there would be danger of error, and another god besides the true God could be worshipped. To make this plain to the attentive reader, I will offer an example of this matter. In the prayers of the ancients there is found the name Mitspats, which a reader might suppose to be the name of some angel. It is not, but it is the name יהוה, the Tetragrammaton, with the letters changed by the Atbash method. Since God, blessed be he, works by his good pleasure and supreme freedom, divine worship belongs to him alone, while the angels and all other things are ordered by God to their own works, as Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel reasons admirably in his little book On the Chapter of Faith, chapter 12. To the second question. Why does Rab place in the list of articles the fifth article, that it is not fitting to posit mediators between God, blessed be he, and man? I answer and say that, as I have already mentioned in the fifth proposition, the sublime dogmas of the faith are comprehended under this article. The first is that God works freely, not as the other existing things do, whether the angels, or the spheres, or the stars, or the elements, or whatever is composed of these; for all those things are ordered to their own works, and there is in them no choice or will to do what they do. But God, blessed be he, works by good pleasure and freedom; therefore worship, song, praise and celebration are also fitting for him. That God alone is merciful, who can pour in grace, and from whom all kinds of mercy flow and are derived, and therefore he alone is to be invoked, as Rabbi Joseph Albo again says in On the Fundamentals, book 4, chapter 17: No one but God can show mercy, because he alone is the fountain of mercies and of all good things, according to that verse of Psalm 130:7, "For with the LORD there is mercy": that is, and not with another. Therefore it is fitting to pray to him and not to another. For how would anyone pray to one from whom he could not obtain what he asks? That the power of God alone is absolute and infinite, while the virtue of the angels is finite and determined by divine ordinance, as Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel indicates in On the Chapter of Faith, chapter 12. The second faith is that he is endowed with infinite power, and this he himself hints at when he says: "because all those things are ordered to their own works," that is, their works and power are limited and determined by ordinance, and their virtue is finite, nor does it transcend the order established among them; but God, blessed be he, does whatever he wills, as the Psalmist says in Psalm 135:6: "Whatever the LORD pleases, he does in heaven and on earth," and therefore worship is fitting for him, Jeremiah 18:6: "For as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand; nor is there anyone who says to him, 'Why have you done this?'" Rabbi Joseph Albo likewise agrees, in On the Fundamentals, book 4, chapter 16.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Quare solius Dei invocationem non solum valde urgent Judæi passimque auditoribus suis commendant, imoque ipsis inserunt articulis fidei fundamentalibus, verum contra cultum Angelicum graviter damnant, Ecclesiamque Romanam Idololatricam propterea appellant, uti abunde perspicitur ex articulo Fidei Judaicæ quinto, apud Maimonidem in Commentario super tractatum Talmudicum Sanhedrin. cap. 11. Fundamentum quintum est, quod oportet solum Deum Sanctum Benedictum colere, magnificare, celebrare, atque extollere voce laudis, neque tale quid præstandum esse ulli existenti, præter illum, sive Angelis, sive stellis, vel orbibus, aut elementis, aut cuiquam ex iis conflato: quia omnia ista ordinata sunt propter operationes suas, neque inest iis potentia, aut voluntas, nisi amor Dei: neque decet constituere Mediatores inter Deum Sanctum Benedictum & homines; Sed omnes cogitationes in eum dirigere & segregare ab alio extra illum. Hoc vero fundamentum discimus ex præcepto nobis lato, ne videlicet serviamus Idolis, atque atque plurima sunt de hoc negotio dicta legis: Et ex eodem Maimonide in libro de idololatria c.2. Fundamentum praecepti de idololatria est, non serviendum esse ulli creaturae, nec Angelo, nec Sphaerae, nec stellae, nec ulli ex quatuor elementis, aut cuiquam quod ex illis compositum est. Quamquam autem is, qui ea colit, sciat non esse Deum, & coluerit creaturam quandam eo modo, quo Enoschi & sui temporis homines idola coluerunt, tamen idololatra est; Quod quoque patet ex Rabbi Isaco Abarbanele de Capite Fidei, cap 12. Non est autem dubium, quin hic sit surculus idololatrarum, qui Deo super biam tribuunt, ideoque ad Mediatores preces suas direxerunt. Haec vero sententia superstes permansit inter homines, & etiamnum hodie manifeste fovetur in fide Christianorum. Nos vero non sic judicamus, sed preces ad Deum Dominum nostrum dirigimus, semper eum invocamus.
units.tr: Hence the Jews not only press the invocation of God alone very strongly and commend it everywhere to their hearers, indeed they insert it among the fundamental articles of faith themselves, but they also condemn the worship of angels severely, and for that reason they call the Church of Rome idolatrous, as is abundantly clear from the fifth article of the Jewish faith in Maimonides' commentary on the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin, chapter 11. The fifth fundamental is that one must worship, magnify, celebrate and extol with the voice of praise the one God, the Holy and Blessed, and that no such honour is to be given to any existing thing besides him, whether to angels, or to stars, or spheres, or elements, or to anything compounded of these; because all these things have been ordained for their own operations, and they have no power or will except the love of God; nor is it fitting to appoint mediators between the Holy and Blessed God and men; but all thoughts are to be directed to him and separated from anything outside him. We learn this fundamental from the precept given to us, namely that we should not serve idols, and there are very many sayings of the law about this matter. And from the same Maimonides in the book on idolatry, chapter 2: The fundamental principle of the precept concerning idolatry is that one must not serve any creature, neither an angel, nor a sphere, nor a star, nor any of the four elements, or anything compounded of them. Although he who worships these knows that there is no God, and has worshipped some creature in the way that the men of Enosh's time and his own worshipped idols, nevertheless he is an idolater. This also appears from Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel on the Articles of Faith, chapter 12: There is no doubt that this is the offshoot of idolaters, who ascribe [divinity] to God over and above, and therefore direct their prayers to mediators. This opinion has survived among men and even today is plainly cherished in the faith of the Christians. We, however, do not judge so, but direct our prayers to God our Lord, and always invoke him.

units.la: Sic in Catechismo Judaico Anathema pronunciant in eos, qui cultum divinum exhibuerint Angelo: Fundamentum quintum, quod soli huic Deo aeterno, Creatori, & unico competat cultus & magnificatio, non aliis, quia omnes alii sunt creati, is vero Creator. Neque etiam licet quicquam petere ab ulla creatura ejus, nisi ab illo, quia omnia potest, nec quoquam eget. Si autem quis sacrificando, aut serviendo, aut quicquam petendo,ulli alii principi, vel Angelo, vel dominationi sive caelesti, cœlesti, sive terrestri cultum divinum exhibuerit, anathema sit.
