units.tr: Thus in the Jewish Catechism they pronounce an anathema upon those who have offered divine worship to an angel: The fifth fundamental is that worship and magnification belong to this one eternal God, the Creator and only one, and not to others, since all others are created, but he is the Creator. Nor is it lawful to ask anything of any of his creatures, but only of him, since he can do all things and needs nothing. If anyone, by sacrificing, or serving, or asking anything of any other prince, or angel, or heavenly or earthly dominion, shall have offered divine worship, let him be anathema.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Ostendunt præterea nullum præter Deum invocandum esse, quod ille solus sit redemptor & liberator ab omni angustia; non Sanctos, non Angelos, neque in specie Michaelem aut Gabrielem, principes illos Angelos adorandos, sicuti egregie docet Rabbi Kimchius in Commentario ad Esaiam cap. 63. v. 16. Licet Abraham pater noster sit, tamen ante multa secula mortuus est. Atqui pater carnis & sanguinis non novit filium suum, aut nepotem, nisi dum in vivis est: Tu vero pater noster vivis & permanes a seculo ad seculum, nec ullum alium præter te invocare debemus, & in omnibus seculis sive præteritis sive futuris pater noster tu es, & redemptor noster ab omni angustia, & a seculo super nos nomen tuum. Confirmaturque in Talmude Hierosolymitano Tractatu Berachot, Cap. 9. Et in En Jacob pag. 49. col. 4. his sequentibus: Rabbi Jodan proprio nomine suo ait, unicuique homini Patronum suum esse, & si calamitate quadam obruatur, eum non e vestigio intrare ad illum, sed ante fores ejus praestolari, servumque aut filium prius advocare, qui ante omnia quærant, num admittendus sit, nec ne: Deum autem non sic comparatum esse, & si calamitas quadam oboriatur, non Michaelem, lem aut Gabrielem: Sed Deum ipsum invocandum esse, qui è vestigio respondsurus sit, juxta illud: Qui nomen Dei invocabit, liberabitur; Cum quibusnecessario offerri debet Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel, qui praeterea tum ad objectiones, tum ad morem Judaeorum modernum, quo se super mortuorum expandunt sepulchra, respondet, cum in libello de Capite fidei, cap. 12. Sic inquit: Sed ait Rab, ex hoc articulo illud praeceptum deduci, quasi diceret, ex articulo, quem commemoravi, oportet hominem non constituere Mediatores inter se ac Creatorem suum, juxta id, quod Propheta Jeremias ait cap. 4. v. 1. Si reverteris es Israel, dictum Domini, ad me revertere; quasi diceret, & non ad Mediatorem. Hoc etiam modo commentati sunt sapientes piae memoriae super versum: Quia Dominus Deus noster apud omnem, qui invocat eum: ad eum tu clamabis, non ad Michaelem, vel Gabrielem, &c. Non autem oportet difficultatem in eo movere, quod Iacob adoraverit Angelum, cum ait Gen. cap. 48. v. 16. Angelus qui liberavit me: est enim precatio ad Deum, quemadmodum cum dicit: Patres mei ambulaverunt coram Deo, qui gubernat me; & Angelus missus erat ex providentia ad liberandum eum; atque ideo ait: Angelus liberavit me ex omni malo. Opera enim Dei in rebus fortuitis necessario fiunt per manus Mediatoris, etiamsi Dei actio providentia influat in istud opus: atque hoc modo expofui istudin tractatu peculiari Etheret Sekanim. Et huic convenit, quod invenimus de Abrahamo, cum dicit: Dominus Deus cæli, qui sumsit me è domo patris mei, &c. Iste mittet Angelum suum coram te. Ubicunque autem reperitur invocatio ad Angelum, ibi intenditur precatio ad Deum, qui misit Angelum suum legatum, ad expediendum istud negotium. Et jam illud ipsum exposuerunt sapientes laudata memoria pro sua scientia in sectione: Ecce ego mitto Angelum meum coram te, dixerunt: Ne muter cum illo, non mutabis me cum eo: quasi diceret, non exhibendus ei cultus est, quia cultus convenit Deo, neque alteri existenti præter illum. Quod autem legimus Iojuam se incurvasse coram Angelo, possumus dicere, quod incurvaverit se coram Deo: quia commemorat benignitatem ac fidelitatem ejus erga Dominum Israelis in mittendo Angelum suum coram eo, ut possideret terram: vel prostravisse se ipsum coram Angelo, ad exequendum ejus mandatum, per modum inferioris, ut coram eo humiliaret se, quia major erat illo. Et sane videtur ex hac sententia Rabbinorum laudata memoria esse, quod etiamnum hodie inter nos moris sit, expandere se super sepulchra mortuorum, ut pro nobis misericordiam effagitent; & juxta hoc ait Propheta Ieremias cap. 31. Rachel flet super filios suos, &c. Certè hoc fit ex una duarum caularum; vel ut deprimamus animos nostros coram Deo excelso, velut tanquam mortui coram eo censeacenseamur. Atque hæc est mens sapientis, dicentis in responsione ad quæstionem: Quare tempore angustiæ eximus ad sepulchra? respondet: ad indicandum, nos esse tanquam mortuos, atque hoc fit propter humiliationem. Ipsud etiam responderunt ad negotium de indumento sacci, nos videlicet esse instar bestiarum. Velut preces effundamus ad Deum, ut nostri memor esse velit propter illorum innocentiam ac justitiam, quæ semper permansura est. Atque hoc intendit alius Sapiens, cum ait in responsione ad commemoratam quæstionem: Ut efflagitent mortui commiserationem pro nobis. Plura hujus rei testimonia adduci possent ex Bereschit Rabba Sect. 79. Ex Rabbi Alschech in Torat Mosche, p. 140. col. 4. Ex aliis innumeris, nisi properandum ad alia esset.
units.tr: Moreover, they show that no one but God is to be invoked, since he alone is the redeemer and deliverer from every distress; not the saints, not the angels, nor in particular Michael or Gabriel, those chief angels, are to be worshipped. Rabbi Kimchi teaches this admirably in his commentary on Isaiah 63:16. Although Abraham is our father, he died many ages ago. But a father of flesh and blood does not know his son or grandson unless he is still alive. "You, however, are our father; you live and endure from age to age. We ought to invoke no one besides you. In all ages, past or future, you are our father and our redeemer from every distress, and your name is upon us from of old." This is confirmed in the Jerusalem Talmud, tractate Berachot, chapter 9, and in En Jacob, p. 49, col. 4, in these words: Rabbi Jodan says in his own name that every man has his own patron; if some calamity overwhelms him, he should not go straight in to him but wait before his door and first send a servant or son to ask whether he may be admitted or not. But God is not so constituted: if some calamity arises, one should not invoke Michael or Gabriel, but God himself, who will answer at once, according to that saying: Whoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be delivered; with whom must be set Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel, who in addition answers both the objections and the modern custom of the Jews, by which they spread themselves over the graves of the dead. In his book on the Articles of Faith, chapter 12, he says: But Rab says that from this article a precept is derived, as if he said: from the article I have mentioned, a man ought not to set up mediators between himself and his Creator, according to what the prophet Jeremiah says in chapter 4, verse 1: "If you return, O Israel, says the Lord, return to me"; as if he said, and not to a mediator. The wise men of blessed memory have also commented in this way on the verse: "For the Lord our God is near to all who call upon him; to him you shall cry, not to Michael or Gabriel," etc. Nor ought we to be troubled by the fact that Jacob worshipped an angel, when he says in Genesis 48:16: "The angel who delivered me." For this is a prayer to God, just as when he says: "My fathers walked before God, who has fed me"; and the angel had been sent by providence to deliver him, and therefore he says: "The angel delivered me from all evil." For the works of God in matters of chance necessarily come about through the hands of a mediator, even if the action of God flows by providence into that work; and I have explained this in a separate treatise, Etheret Sekanim. To this agrees what we find about Abraham, when he says: "The Lord God of heaven, who took me from the house of my father," etc. "He will send his angel before you." Wherever, however, an invocation of an angel is found, there the prayer is directed to God, who sent his angel as an envoy to carry out that business. Indeed the wise men of blessed memory, in their wisdom, have already explained this same point in the section: "Behold, I send my angel before you"; they said: "Do not be changed toward him; you shall not be changed toward him"; as if to say, worship is not to be rendered to him, because worship belongs to God, and to no other existing beside him. As for what we read, that Joshua prostrated himself before the angel, we may say that he prostrated himself before God, because the passage recalls God's goodness and faithfulness toward the Lord of Israel in sending his angel before him to take possession of the land; or that he prostrated himself before the angel, in carrying out his command, in the manner of an inferior, so as to humble himself before him, because the angel was greater than he. And indeed it seems that from this opinion of the rabbis of blessed memory comes the custom that still today prevails among us, of spreading ourselves over the graves of the dead, so that they may obtain mercy for us; and in accordance with this the prophet Jeremiah says in chapter 31: "Rachel weeps for her sons," etc. Certainly this is done for one of two reasons: either to bring low our spirits before the most high God, as if we were counted dead before him. This is the mind of the sage who, answering the question, "Why do we go out to the graves in a time of distress?", replies: to show that we are as dead, and this is done for the sake of humiliation. They gave the same answer about the matter of wearing sackcloth: that we are, namely, like beasts. It is as if we were pouring out prayers to God, that he would be mindful of us for the sake of those men's innocence and justice, which will always remain. Another sage intends this same thing when, answering the question mentioned, he says: that the dead may implore mercy for us. Many more testimonies on this matter could be adduced from Bereshit Rabba, section 79; from Rabbi Alschech in Torat Moshe, p. 140, col. 4; and from innumerable others, were we not hastening on to other matters.

units.la: CAPUT IX. De Homine in statu integro, & ad divinam imaginem formato.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. Of Man in the State of Integrity, and Formed to the Divine Image.

units.la: 1. Constantissima gentis Judaicæ semper sententia fuit, Adamum inter homines extiextitisse primum, qui omnes ex hoc uno eandem ducant originem, appellans hinc Adamum אדם הראשון Adamum primum, & Chaldaice אדםקדמון, nec ullus unquam inter Judaeos repertus, qui omnium hanc seculorum veritatem aulus fuit in controversiam vocare, nec enim contradicit Rabbi Ilac Sangarus, cum de Adami Praeceptore Janbuschare loquens, non Judaeorum exprimat mentem, sed Indorum, Barbarorumque populorum, uti patet ex libro Cofri part. I. §. 61, 62. mentionem faciunt nominum, Ianbuschari, Zagrithi, & Roani, dicuntque quod fuerint ante Adamum, quod Ianbuschar Praeceptor fuerit Adami primi; Neque refragatur Maimonides, cum sermonem instituat non de Judaeis, sed populis Sabaeis, qui in More Nevochim part. III. cap. 29. Existimarunt, Adamum primum fuisse virum ex viro & foemina, sicut reliqui homines, progenitum; quare quoque suos monet contribules, dehortaturque, ne animum ad has applicent fabulas, quando eodem capite sic inquit: Id vero, quod narrant de Adamo primo, de serpente, de arbore scientiae boni & mali, de vestimentis, quod antea non in usu fuerint, cave, ne intellectum tuum abripiat, & existimes, illa vere Adamo, vel alii contigisse. Illa enim omnino nunquam fuerunt in rerum natura. Verum si leviter tantum & superficialiter rem consideres, deprehendes, quod falsa sint ea omnia, quæ in hac fabula narrantur, & conficta ab illis, postea- quam Lex nostra Gentibus innotuit, & historiam Operis Creationis audiverunt; Ut necesse nunc sit, Peyrerium, Præadamitarum Patronum no- vissimum, insignem commisisse errorem, dum parte prima Systematis Theologici lib. 3. cap. 3. pag. 120. Sic ob Judæorum gloriatur consensum: Quin & Rabbi Moses Ben Maymon re- fert libros antecessorum suorum, qui mentionem fa- ciunt Præceptoris ipsius Adami, quem dicunt fuisse nomine Somboscer. Et quamvis parum credam Rabbinorum fabulis: nihil tamen adeo fabulosum est, quod non antiquam redoleat veritatem.
units.tr: 1. The most constant opinion of the Jewish nation has always been that Adam was the first man among humans, and that all of them trace their origin to him alone. Hence they call him Adam [אדם הראשון], the first Adam, and in Chaldee [אדםקדמון]. No Jew has ever been found who called this truth of all the ages into question. Nor does Rabbi Isaac Sangari contradict it: when he speaks of Adam's teacher Janbuschar, he expresses not the mind of the Jews but that of the Indians and other barbarian peoples, as is clear from the book Cosri, part I, §§ 61, 62. They mention the names Janbuschar, Zagrithi and Roani, and say that they existed before Adam, and that Janbuschar was the teacher of the first Adam. Nor does Maimonides gainsay this, since he is speaking not of the Jews but of the Sabaean peoples, who, in More Nevochim part III, ch. 29, thought that Adam the first was born of a man and a woman, like the other men. Hence he also warns his fellow countrymen and dissuades them from giving their minds to these fables, since in the same chapter he says: As for what they relate about the first Adam, about the serpent, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and about garments, which were not in use before, beware lest it carry off your understanding and you think those things truly happened to Adam or to anyone else. For they never existed at all in the nature of things. But if you consider the matter lightly and superficially, you will discover that all the things related in this fable are false, and were invented by them after our Law became known to the Gentiles and they heard the history of the Work of Creation. Hence it is now necessary to say that Peyrerius, the latest patron of the Pre-Adamites, made a notable error when, in part I of his Theological System, book 3, ch. 3, p. 120, he boasts thus of the consensus of the Jews: Moreover Rabbi Moses ben Maimon reports the books of his predecessors, which mention the teacher of Adam himself, whom they say was named Somboscer. And although I little believe the fables of the Rabbis, nothing is so fabulous that it does not smell of ancient truth.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Depræicant Judæi in Tractatu Talmu- dico Sanhedrin, inque Glossa Talmudica ad Sanhedrin c. 11. Adamum primum ab uno mundi fine ad alterum usque mundi finem creatum, post lapsum minorem factum, referuntque Sapien- tes Hebræorum apud Rabbi Schem Tof in Sepher Haemunoth sol. 68. Adami primi sta- turam a terra usq; ad cælum exporrectam fuisse; Et in Berefchit Rabba, Sectione 7. Adami primi magnitudinem ab una terræ extremitate ad alte- ram usq; fuisse; Innuentes his locutionibus hy- perbolicis familiaribus, excellentem Adami integri tum naturam, tum scientiam, persectiones, atque virtutes, quod omnes mundi intellexerit res, naturasque, quodque eminentissima fuerit in terris creatura, caput & principium humani generis, multiplici praeditum perfectione, in quo integritas certaverit cum universali fere rerum divinarum, humanarumque scientia, quae maxime apparuerit in nominibus, quae cunctis imposuerit animantibus, quodque honore & gloria à Deo Benedicto fuerit mactatus, indice Psalmo 8. Et honore & gloria coronasti eum.
units.tr: The Jews proclaim in the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin, and in the Talmudic gloss on Sanhedrin ch. 11, that Adam the first was created from one end of the world to the other end of the world, and that he was made smaller after the fall. The wise men of the Hebrews report, in Rabbi Schem Tof in Sepher Haemunoth, fol. 68, that the stature of the first Adam stretched from the earth up to heaven; and in Bereschit Rabba, section 7, that the greatness of the first Adam reached from one extremity of the earth to the other. By these familiar hyperbolic expressions they signify the excellent nature, knowledge, perfections and virtues of Adam in his integrity: that he understood all the things and natures of the world, that he was the most eminent creature on earth, the head and beginning of the human race, endowed with manifold perfection, in whom integrity vied with an almost universal knowledge of divine and human things, which was most evident in the names he gave to all living creatures; and that he was honoured and glorified by the Blessed God, as Psalm 8 shows: And thou hast crowned him with honour and glory.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Nominant hinc Adamum. אדם Sapientem magnum, conferuntque cum Mose & Salomone, testibus Rabbi Schem Tofin Sepher Haemunoth sol. 68. Adamus primus statim a sua nativitate fuit sapiens magnus, & ingressus est in vias prophetiae, locutusque est Deus cum Deo; Et Rabbi Gedalja in Schalscheleth Hakkabala ab initio: Non est dubium, Adamum primum, qui fuit plasma manuum Dei benedicti, penitus fuisse imbutum omnibus sapientiis naturalibus, & divinis, comprehensis Lege Mosis, quae ipsam mundi creationem antecedit, quemadmodum id explicant Magistri nostri ad locum; Et ero ipsi nutritius, Proverb. cap. 8. v. 30. Afferre igitur possumus, eum fuisse affectum gradum Mosis Magistri nostri, & Salomonis, quo adsequi potuit. Hinc pa-
units.tr: Hence they call Adam [אדם] a great sage, and compare him with Moses and Solomon, as witnessed by Rabbi Schem Tof in Sepher Haemunoth, fol. 68: Adam the first, from the moment of his birth, was a great sage, and entered the ways of prophecy, and God spoke with God. And Rabbi Gedalja, in Schalscheleth Hakkabala, at the beginning: There is no doubt that Adam the first, who was the handiwork of the Blessed God, was thoroughly imbued with all natural and divine wisdom, including the Law of Moses, which precedes the creation of the world itself, as our Masters explain the passage "and I was beside him as a nursling," Proverb. 8. 30. We may therefore affirm that he attained the degree of our Master Moses and of Solomon, as far as he could reach. Hence in like manner

units.la: pariter appellant Adamum perfectissimam creaturam, tum ratione corporis, quod ex manibus prodierit divinis, quibus nullum obtigerit obstaculum, tum inprimis ratione animæ, quæ maximam innatam sine ulla institutione habuerit notitiam, concreatamque scientiam, sicuti illud cum innumeris, quos adducere possemus, Judæis demonstrat Rabbi Isac Sangarus in libro Cosri part. 1. §. 95. Adamus enim perfectissimus fuit sine ulla conditione & exceptione: quia nullus exceptioni vel objectioni locus est circa perfectionem operis immediate facti ab Opifice Sapientissimo & Omnipotenti, & ex materia quam ipse elegit pro forma quam ei indere voluit, in quo etiam nihil impedimenti intervenire potuit, vel a temperamento seminis paterni, vel sanguinis materni, vel a ciborum & nutrimenti qualitate, vel a diæta & regimine in annis educationis & pueritiæ, vel a mutatione aeris, aquæ, & terræ. Creatus enim fuit Adamus, tanquam perfectè affectus ætatem juvenilem ratione membrorum & qualitatum: Idem accepit animam in integritate perfectissima, & Intellectum in summo, qui in hominem competere potest, gradu; Facultatem insuper, post Intellectum, divinam, hoc est gradum quo Deo & rebus spiritualibus adhæsit, & rerum veram notitiam habuit sine institutione, cogitatione sola: unde vocatur a nobis Filius Dei; Confirmatque Rabbi
units.tr: they likewise call Adam the most perfect creature, both in respect of his body, which came forth from the divine hands, to which no obstacle could be opposed, and especially in respect of his soul, which had the greatest innate knowledge, without any instruction, and infused science. This is shown to the Jews by Rabbi Isaac Sangari in the book Cosri, part I, §95, together with countless others whom we could adduce: For Adam was most perfect without any condition or exception, since there is no room for exception or objection concerning the perfection of a work made immediately by the most wise and omnipotent Maker, out of the matter which he himself chose for the form he willed to impart to it, in which nothing of impediment could intervene, whether from the temperament of the paternal seed, or of the maternal blood, or from the quality of food and nourishment, or from the regimen and diet in the years of upbringing and boyhood, or from change of air, water and land. For Adam was created as one fully endowed, in his limbs and qualities, with the age of youth. He received a soul in most perfect integrity, and an intellect in the highest degree that can belong to man; moreover, after the intellect, a divine faculty, that is, the degree by which he clung to God and spiritual things, and had a true knowledge of things without instruction, by thought alone. Whence we call him the Son of God. This is confirmed by Rabbi

units.la: Schem Tof, cum in Sepher Haemunoth sol. 68. Sic loquitur: Quando creatus fuit Adamus, non creatus fuit secundum formam & dispositionem ordinariam corporum humanorum, sed creatura subtilissima & purissima, proxime accedens ad corpus spirituale: accedebant etiam scientia in perfectione sua, scivitque & intellexit omnes mundos; Neque dissentit Rabbi Jsac Abarbanel, cum in Commentario suo in Legem ad Genef. 2. ד. 19. sol. 27. col. 4. testatur: Et cum creasset hominem in imagine sua, ecce sicut infudit ei scientias vel notitias veras, divinas, absque studio, disquisitione, vel industria ulla. Hinc est etiam, quod Rabbini passim referant, corporis Adami lucem, pulchritudinem, ac perfectionem, peccato peracto statim fuisse immutatam, deperditamque.
units.tr: Shem Tof, who in Sepher Haemunoth, fol. 68, speaks thus: When Adam was created, he was not created according to the ordinary form and disposition of human bodies, but as a most subtle and pure creature, drawing very near to a spiritual body. Knowledge also came to him in its perfection, and he knew and understood all worlds. Nor does Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel dissent, when in his commentary on the Law, on Gen. 2. 19, fol. 27, col. 4, he testifies: And when he had created man in his own image, behold, he infused into him sciences or true knowledge, divine, without study, inquiry or any industry. Hence it is also that the Rabbis frequently report that the light, beauty and perfection of Adam's body were changed and lost immediately once sin had been committed.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Consentit Rabbi Bechai, ostendens insuper, quo modo Adamus primus, totus intellectualis, perfectissimus, pulcherrimus, ipsaque praeditus Justitia Originali, post commissum peccatum, vitam amiserit spiritualem, totusque carnalis factus fuerit, quando scribit sol. 152. col. 3. Homo primus antequam peccaret, & inordinate concupisceret, erat Angelus Dei exercituum, totus intellectualis, perfectissimus, pulcherrimus, vitium nullum erat in ipso. Proinde aequum etiam erat erat ipsum vivere in aeternum Ministrorum superiorum instar. Impositus erat Paradiso terrae omnium praestantissimae. Postquam autem peccavit, & inordinate concupivit, exutus fuit spiritualitate, & induta carnalitate, & ex Paradiso expulsus,
units.tr: Rabbi Bechai agrees, and further shows how the first Adam, wholly intellectual, most perfect, most beautiful, and endowed with original justice, lost his spiritual life after he committed sin and became wholly carnal. He writes, at p. 152, col. 3: Man, before he sinned and lusted inordinately, was an angel of the Lord of hosts, wholly intellectual, most perfect, most beautiful, with no vice in him. Therefore it was also fitting that he should live forever, like the higher ministers. He was placed in the Paradise of the earth, the most excellent of all. But after he sinned and lusted inordinately, he was stripped of spirituality, clothed with carnality, and expelled from Paradise.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Credunt Adamum primum non infantem creatum, sed in justa statura virum, quasi viginti annorum filium, uti legitur in Bereschit Rabba, Sectione 14. Dixit Rabbi Jochanan, Adam & Eva, quasi filii viginti annorum creati sunt; variis persuasi argumentis, quod Judice Rabbi Isaco Sangaro, in libro Cosri, Part. 1. citato articulo 95. genitus non sit ex femine paterno, sanguineque materno, sed ab ipso Deo formatus, hincque juvenilem aetatem ratione membrorum, qualitatumque perfecte assecutus fuerit; Quod hac ratione opus habuisset nutrice, quae ipsum lactasset, sicuti inquit Rabbi Schem Tob in Sepher Haemunoth sol. 68. Quod creatus sit perfectus in intellectu suo, non vero instar parvuli infantis. Hac ratione enim opus habuisset nutrice, quae ipsum lactasset & educasset, Praeceptore item, qui ipsum informasset; Quia omnia opera Creationis facta fuerunt in statura sua, in scientia sua, & in decore suo, testante ex Tractatu Talmudico Rosch Hashchana, sol. 11. Rabbi Maimonide in More Nevochim Part. II. cap. 30 Scitu for-ro tibi necessarium in hoc negotio est illud quoque, quod Rabbini nostri inquiunt, omnia opera Creatio-nus creata sunt בקיומן instatura sua, creata sunt בעתן inscientia sua, creata sunt בצביונם in de-core suo: quo innuere volunt, quod universa & sin-gula, quæ Deus creavit, in perfectissima sua quantitate, in perfectissima sua forma, & in elegantissimis suis accidentibus creata sint; hoc enim sibi volunt, quando ajunt בצביונם in decore suo creata sunt, ex illo Ezech. cap. 20. s. 6. צבי Decor vel ornamentum est omnibus terris. Diligen-ter itaque & hoc retine, quia non exiguum quoque est fundamentum; Quia in duodecim diei ho-ris Adamus primus & creatus, & uxoratus, & liberis ornatus, & lapsus, & Paradiso denique ejectus dicitur apud Rabbi Eliezerem in Pir-cke cap. 11. Duodecim sunt horæ diei: Prima con-gessit pulverem hominis: Secunda determinavit e-um: Tertia artificiose efformavit: Quarta insper-sit ei animam: Quinta constituit eum super pedes: Sexta vocavit nomina: Septima in uxorem illi da-ta fuit Eva: Octava præcepta data sunt de fructibus arboris: Nona ascenderunt duo in lectum & quatuor descenderunt: Decima introduxit eum in hortum Eden, atq; transgressus est præceptum: Undecima judicatus, seu sententiam accepit: Duodecima ex-pulsus fuit horto.
units.tr: They believe that the first Adam was created not as an infant but as a grown man, about twenty years old, as is read in Bereshit Rabba, section 14: Rabbi Jochanan said, Adam and Eve were created as if they were sons of twenty years. They are persuaded by various arguments that, according to Rabbi Isaac Sangari, in the book Cosri, part 1, article 95 cited there, he was not begotten of a paternal seed and maternal blood, but was formed by God himself, and so he attained the age of youth in the form and qualities of his limbs perfectly. For in that case he would not have needed a nurse to suckle him, as Rabbi Shem Tob says in Sepher Haemunoth, p. 68: He was created perfect in his understanding, not like a little infant. For in that case he would have needed a nurse to suckle and rear him, and a tutor too, to instruct him. For all the works of creation were made in their stature, in their knowledge, and in their beauty, as the Talmudic tractate Rosch Hashanah, p. 11, testifies. Rabbi Maimonides, in More Nevochim, part II, chap. 30, writes: It is also necessary for you to know in this matter what our rabbis say, that all the works of creation were created in their existence [בקיומן], created in their knowledge [בעתן], created in their beauty [בצביונם]; by which they wish to signify that all and each of the things God created were created in their most perfect quantity, in their most perfect form, and in their most elegant accidents. For this is what they mean when they say "created in their beauty", from that passage of Ezekiel 20:6, beauty [צבי]: "the glory of all lands." Therefore hold this carefully, for it is no small foundation. For among the rabbis, in Pirke, chap. 11, Rabbi Eliezer says that in the twelve hours of the day the first Adam was created, married, blessed with children, fell, and was finally expelled from the garden: There are twelve hours of the day. In the first, he gathered the dust of man; in the second, he determined him; in the third, he formed him skilfully; in the fourth, he breathed a soul into him; in the fifth, he set him upon his feet; in the sixth, he gave names; in the seventh, Eve was given to him as wife; in the eighth, commandments were given concerning the fruit of the tree; in the ninth, the two went up into the bed and four came down; in the tenth, he brought him into the garden of Eden, and he transgressed the commandment; in the eleventh, he was judged, or received his sentence; in the twelfth, he was expelled from the garden.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Credunt Adami primi corpus immortale extitisse in statu integro, non ex se, suaque natura, quod ea corporis e materia sit ratio, ut singulis dissolvi possit momentis, sicque mori, sed ex ordinatione divina, si non peccasset, quare per peccatum morti subjectum, utita mors corporis non ex naturae dependeat conditione, sed a peccato oriatur Adami, uti egregie probavit Rabbi Bechai contra Philosophos, quorum hoc dogma erat, quod licet Adam non peccasset, tamen morte obiisset naturali, quia omne compositum tandem dissolvitur & naturaliter moritur, idque secundum necessariam naturae conditionem, qua omne compositum ad sua redit principia, cum in Commentario sol. 1 3. sic scribit: Putant vero isti se rationibus quibusdam niti, quarum unam vel alteram afferrem, nisi sententia eorum contra fundamentum fidei esset. Sapientum vero nostrorum beata memoria sententia, a qua nos recedere non decet, utpote ex ore Prophetarum derivata, hoc est, quod si homo non peccasset, in aeternum vixisset; Quare certatim corruptionem corporis, mortemque Adami adscribunt peccato, nullo modo sentientes cum Socinianis, Judaeorum consensum perperam allegantibus, sicuti patet ex Sohar in Genesin, col. 218. Adamus primus rebellavit Domino suo, & causatus est morte mundo; Ex Ir Gibborim,sol.79.col 3. Homo corruptionis reus est propter peccata qua perpetravit; Ex Jalkut Chaddafch, pag.77. col.2. Adamus causatus est mortem omni mundo; Ex Rabbi Schem Tof in Sepher Haemunoth, sol.68. col. 2. Dicunt Rabbini in Commentariis; Si Adam & Eva non peccassent, tum generationes ipsorum fuissent sine ulla mala concupiscentia, & copulatio ipsorum fuisset convenientissima, qualis scilicet est conjunctio formarum superiorum, ut maledictiones arguere videntur, & vivi ac stabiles perpetuo manssissent in mundo; Et Ex sol.69. Si fuisses usus illo corpore, in quo creatus es, sicut conveniens erat, vi ac virtute loci illius fuisses aeternus in perpetuum: quandoquidem autem peccasti, & conversus es in virum alium, pertinges & vades ad corruptionem; Idem quoque apparet ex Rabbi Mosfe Gerundensi, cum in Commentario ad Genesin sol.6. refert: Verum juxta sententiam Rabbinorum nostrorum, si Adam non peccasset, non fuisset mortuus in seculum. Anima quippe superna dedisset ipsi vitam in perpetuum, & voluntas seu beneplacitum Dei, quod in ipso fuit in principio Creationis ejus, jugiter ei adhaesisset, & in perpetuum ipsum conservasset, ut supra exposui, &c. Et scito, quod compositio non necessario corruptionem inferat, nisi apud Aristotelem, &c. & perpetuitas illa fuisset in ipso, quamdiu beneplacitum illud lud durasset: atque hæc pura puta est veritas; Et ex Rabbi Lipmanno in Nizzachon, num. 8. Ne obvertas mihi id quod dixerunt Sapientes nostri, beata memoria, per Adamum mortem super totum mundum introivisse. Nam ex esu frućtus arboris corpus naturam solubilitatis elementorum accepit. Ista vero natura cum semine toti posteritati communicata est. Ante esum istum autem natura humana animantium naturam longe superabat, it aut perennare posset: Siquidem perennante anima pura, etiam corpus quod organum ejus est, in æternum superesse potest; Et ex Rabbi Joseph Albo Fundamentorum lib. 4. cap. 41. Antequam de arbore scientiæ ederat, virtus naturalis in eo æqualem ejus quod digerebatur permutationem reddebat, ita ut digestio non excederet permutationem cibi, qui extrinsecus corpus ingrediebatur, atque hac ratione corpus semper hunc tenorem servasset. Postquam autem de arbore scientiæ gustaverat, digestio permutationi prædominari cæpit, perinde ac hodie fit, unde mors necessario insequitur.
units.tr: They believe that the body of the first Adam was immortal in the state of integrity, not from itself and by its own nature, as though the material of the body were such that it could be dissolved at any moment and so die; but by the divine ordinance, had he not sinned. Therefore, since he became subject to death through sin, the death of the body does not depend on the condition of nature but arises from the sin of Adam. Rabbi Bechai proved this admirably against the philosophers, whose doctrine was that even if Adam had not sinned, he would still have died a natural death, because every compound is at last dissolved and dies naturally, by the necessary condition of nature, by which every compound returns to its principles. In his commentary, p. 13, he writes thus: Those men think they rest on certain arguments, one or other of which I would set forth, were not their opinion contrary to the foundation of faith. But the opinion of our wise men, of blessed memory, from which we ought not to depart, being derived from the mouth of the prophets, is that if man had not sinned, he would have lived forever. Therefore they ascribe the corruption of the body and the death of Adam to sin, in no way agreeing with the Socinians, who wrongly appeal to the consent of the Jews, as is plain from the Sohar on Genesis, col. 218: Adam the first rebelled against his Lord, and by his fault brought death to the world. From Ir Gibborim, p. 79, col. 3: Man is liable to corruption on account of the sins he committed. From Jalkut Chaddash, p. 77, col. 2: Adam brought death upon the whole world. From Rabbi Shem Tob in Sepher Haemunoth, p. 68, col. 2: The rabbis say in their commentaries: If Adam and Eve had not sinned, then their generations would have been without any evil lust, and their union would have been most fitting, namely such as the conjunction of the higher forms is, as the curses seem to show, and they would have remained living and stable forever in the world. And from p. 69: If you had used that body in which you were created, as was fitting, by the power and virtue of that place you would have been eternal forever; but since you sinned and were turned into another man, you tend and go toward corruption. The same appears from Rabbi Moses of Gerona, who in his commentary on Genesis, p. 6, reports: But according to the opinion of our rabbis, if Adam had not sinned, he would not have died for ever. For the superior soul would have given him life forever, and the will or good pleasure of God, which was in him from the beginning of his creation, would have clung to him continually and preserved him forever, as I explained above, etc. And know that composition does not necessarily bring corruption, except according to Aristotle, etc. And that perpetuity would have been in him as long as that good pleasure lasted; and this is the pure and certain truth. And from Rabbi Lipmann in Nizzachon, no. 8: Do not object to me what our wise men, of blessed memory, said, that through Adam death entered the whole world. For from eating the fruit of the tree the body received the nature of the dissolubility of the elements. But this nature has been communicated to the whole posterity along with the seed. Before that eating, human nature far surpassed the nature of the animals, and it could last forever; for if the pure soul endures, the body too, which is its organ, can remain forever. And from Rabbi Joseph Albo, Fundamentorum book 4, chap. 41: Before he ate from the tree of knowledge, his natural power produced an exchange equal to what was being digested, so that digestion did not exceed the replacement of the food which entered the body from outside; and in this way the body would always have kept this condition. But after he tasted from the tree of knowledge, digestion began to prevail over replacement, just as happens today, and hence death necessarily follows.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Hanc Judæorum communem fere sententiam, non modo convenire cum scriptis Mosis, ipsorumque Antiquorum Magistrorum, sed ratione, imo ipsa experientia niti, demonstravit nuper Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, quando libro III. de Resurrectione mortuorum, cap. 11. Sic loquitur: Ut quæstionem hanc hanc solvamus, inquiramus oportet, an Adamus, si non peccasset, moriturus fuisset, an vero immortalis semper vixisset? Cabalistæ, R. Moses Gerundensis, & R. Meyr Gabay, aliique plures statuunt, Adamum si non peccasset, semper victurum fuisse, etiamsi ea corpora e materia composita conditione essent, ut mori posset; per lapsum vero sive peccatum morti necessariæ subjectum fuisse. Hæc sententia mihi videtur convenire non modo cum authoritate Sacræ Scripturæ, & antiquorum: Sed etiam cum ratione & experientia. Quod ad Sacram Scripturam attinet, manifestum hoc est ex præcepto Dei, Adamo dato, Genes. cap. 2. De arbore scientiæ boni & mali non comedes; nam in die, quo ederis ex illa, morte morieris. Hic certe constat pœnam Adamo peccaturo interminatam, fuisse mortem corporalem. Atque hinc erat, quod Dominus Adamum Paradiso directurus (ejecturus) angelos alloqueretur in hunc modum, Genes. cap. 3. v. 22. Ecce homo sicut unus ex nobis, ad sciendum bonum & malum; Et nunc ne forte mittet manum suam, & sumat etiam de arbore vitæ, & comedat, & vivat in sæculum. Et emisit eum Dominus Deus de horto Hedenis. Quasi diceret, nihil obstabit quo minus Adamus, quando solam cognitionem boni tantum habebat in statu innocentiæ, in æternum in terra viveret, quia anima ejus ibi hic felix ac beata erat futura: Sed nunc, quoniam per lapsum comparavit sibi cognitionem boni simul & mali, non est æquum ut in æternum vivat. Eandem Antiquorum Rabbinorum sententiam fuisse probat Rabbi Menasseh ex Rabbi Hanæ Bar Haninæ celebri dicto in Bereschit Rabba, Parascha 9. Dignus erat primus Adam, qui non gustaret saporem mortis; Ex Parascha 16.21. Ex Rabbi Jehuda & Rabbi Nehemia in Vajickra Rabba, Parascha 22. Ex Elia exemplo constat, Adamum, si non peccasset, perpetuo victurum fuisse. Ex Schemot Rabba, Parascha 15. Quoniam præceptum tuum nihili fecit, ideo induxisti super illum mortem. Ex Sohare: Et vidit (Enoch sublatus in sublime) locum Adami in Paradiso, in quo, si Adamus observasset præceptum illud, vixisset perpetuo, & in æternum mansisset. Ostendit pariter Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel ipsam immortalitatem corporis Adami cum ratione convenire, cum loco citato sic pergit: Ratio quoque idipsum docet, quia mortis causa est, vel interior, id est alimentum per os assumptum; vel exterior, id est aer, calor, frigus, & id genus alia. At ab his Adamus metuere opus non habebat: nam fructus & arbor vitæ, ex qua vescebatur, gratissimi saporis erant, & non modo non debilem atque infirmum hominem reddebant: Sed & longævam & perpetuam vitam ei sufficiebant. Et cum viveret in Paradiso, loco amœnissimo, in aere temperatissimo & gratissimo, ubi sine ulla alteratione tione jaluberrimum semper aevum ducebat, quis du-bitat sublata mortis causa non etiam effectum ejus sublatum fuisse? Videmus etiam posteros Adami aliquamdiu valde longaevos fuisse, & paulatim magis magisque aevum hominis declinasse & imminuitue esse, usque dum in septuaginta, vel praeter propter annis terminus ejus stare coepit. Quod profecto non caret ratione. Nam Adamus natus erat immortalis, & quamquam peccato mortalem se reddiderat: non propterea tamen omnem statim corporis vigorem, ac robur primigenium perdidit. Tandem in rei probationem adducit Experientiam, scribens: Accedat huc experientia, qua edoctifumus, Hanochum & Eliam non esse mortuos; Mosen vero contra mortuum esse. Si quis hujus rei causam scire velit, dicendum omnino est, hunc peccasse, illos autem neutiquam vitiis sese polluisse. Nam uti antiqui ajunt אין מיתה בלא חטא non est mors absque peccato. Itaque si Adamus non peccasset, non fuisset mortuus. Sed plura de hac sententia Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel in libello de fragilitate humana, pag. 37.
units.tr: Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel has recently shown that this opinion, which is almost the common view of the Jews, agrees not only with the writings of Moses and of their own ancient masters, but also rests on reason and even on experience. He says so in book III, chapter 11, of his work on the resurrection of the dead: To solve this question we must inquire whether Adam, had he not sinned, would have died, or would have lived forever without dying. The Kabbalists, R. Moses of Gerona, R. Meyr Gabay, and many others, hold that Adam, had he not sinned, would always have lived, even though his body was composed of matter in such a condition that it could die; but through the fall, or sin, he became subject to necessary death. This opinion seems to me to agree not only with the authority of Holy Scripture and of the ancients, but also with reason and experience. As for Holy Scripture, it is plain from God's command given to Adam in Genesis 2: You shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for on the day you eat of it you shall surely die. Here it is certain that the penalty threatened to Adam, should he sin, was bodily death. Hence also the Lord, about to send Adam out of Paradise, spoke to the angels in this manner, Genesis 3:22: Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil; and now lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever. And the Lord God sent him forth from the garden of Eden. As if He had said: nothing would stand in the way of Adam, who in the state of innocence had only the knowledge of good, living forever on earth, since his soul would there be happy and blessed; but now, since through the fall he has acquired for himself the knowledge of good and evil together, it is not fitting that he should live forever. Rabbi Menasseh proves that the ancient rabbis held the same opinion from the well-known saying of Rabbi Hanina Bar Hanina in Bereshit Rabba, Parashah 9: The first Adam was worthy not to taste the flavour of death; from Parashah 16 and 21; from Rabbi Judah and Rabbi Nehemiah in Vayikra Rabba, Parashah 22: From the example of Elijah it is clear that Adam, had he not sinned, would have lived in perpetuity; from Shemot Rabba, Parashah 15: Because he made your command of no account, therefore you brought death upon him. From the Zohar: And he saw (Enoch, taken up on high) the place of Adam in Paradise, where, if Adam had kept that command, he would have lived in perpetuity and remained for ever. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel likewise shows that the very immortality of Adam's body agrees with reason, for he continues in the place cited: Reason also teaches the same, since death has a cause, either internal, namely food taken in by the mouth, or external, namely air, heat, cold, and other such things. But Adam had no need to fear these: for the fruit and the tree of life, of which he ate, were of most pleasant taste, and not only did not make a man weak and feeble, but also sufficed for him a long and perpetual life. And since he lived in Paradise, a most pleasant place, in the most temperate and agreeable air, where he spent his age always in the most wholesome condition without any change, who doubts that, the cause of death being removed, its effect was also removed? We see also that the posterity of Adam were for some time very long-lived, and that by degrees the life of man declined and was diminished, until its limit began to stand at about seventy years. This certainly is not without reason. For Adam was born immortal, and although by sin he had made himself mortal, yet he did not at once lose all the vigour of his body and his original strength. Finally, to prove the matter he adduces experience, writing: Let experience be added here, by which we are taught that Enoch and Elijah are not dead, while Moses on the contrary is dead. If anyone wishes to know the cause of this, it must be said that the latter sinned, while the former by no means defiled themselves with vices. For as the ancients say, [אין מיתה בלא חטא] there is no death without sin. Therefore, if Adam had not sinned, he would not have died. But Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel discusses this opinion at greater length in his little book on human frailty, p. 37.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Non inficiantur moderni Judaei Adamum primum ad divinam formatum fuisse imaginem, sicuti perperam plurimis instillavit Raymundus Martini in Pugione Fidei adversos Mauros & Judaeos, Part. III. Dist. II. cap. I.
units.tr: The modern Jews do not deny that the first Adam was formed in the divine image, as Raymundus Martini wrongly instilled into most people in his Pugio Fidei against the Moors and Jews, Part III, Dist. II, cap. I.

units.la: Sed dissentiunt valde de imaginis divinae natura, hocipso ostendentes, ledivinaadhuc dum imagine privatos esse,licet interim fatendum sit ingenue, multos sequioris nostrique ævi cum Veteribus Judæis, non absona omnia de divina tradere imagine, quod clarissime evincitur ex Rabbi Maimonidis Constitutionibus de Fundamentis Legis, in quibus imago nonlolum collocatur in mentis scientia & intellectu, verum quoque omnis rejicitur corporis figura, quæ oculis potest cognosci, uti ex verbis subsequis cap. 4. §. 14. patet: Anima cuiuslibet carnis est forma ejus, quam dedit ei Deus, intellectus vero insuper existens in anima hominis, est forma hominis perfecti cum suo intellectu. Et de hac forma dicitur in Lege, Genes. 1. 26. Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram, juxta similitudinem nostram, quasi diceret, erit ei forma, qua intelligit atque cognoscit Intelligentias, non habentes materiam, sicut Angeli, adeo ut sit futurus similis illis: neque loquitur de forma ejusmodi, quae cognoscitur oculis, uti est bucca, nasi, atque maxillae, aliave corporis figura, nam ipsius forma nomen est Thoar. Neque ista anima existit in omni vivente, qua comedit, bibit, generat, sentit atque imaginatur; sed intellectus est forma anima. Ac de ea forma anima loquitur Scriptura: ad Imaginem, ad similitudinem nostram; idem pariter liquet ex Rab-
units.tr: But they disagree greatly about the nature of the divine image, thereby showing that they are as yet deprived of the divine image; yet it must be frankly admitted that many of our own later age, together with the ancient Jews, deliver nothing absurd about the divine image. This is most clearly shown from the Constitutions of Rabbi Maimonides on the Foundations of the Law, in which the image is placed not only in the knowledge and understanding of the mind, but also every bodily figure which can be known by the eyes is rejected, as appears from the following words, ch. 4, §14: The soul of every creature of flesh is its form, which God gave to it; but the intellect existing above in the soul of man is the form of the perfect man with his intellect. And of this form it is said in the Law, Gen. 1:26: Let us make man in our image, after our likeness, as if to say: there shall be given to him the form by which he understands and knows the intelligences that have no matter, like the angels, so that he will be like them. Nor does it speak of a form of that kind which is known by the eyes, such as the mouth, nose and jaws, or any other bodily figure; for the name of that form is Thoar. Nor does that soul which eats, drinks, generates, feels and imagines exist in every living thing; rather the intellect is the form of the soul. And Scripture speaks of this form of the soul: in the image, in our likeness; the same is equally clear from Rab-

units.la: Rabbi Maimonidis Mor Nevochim, in quo Part.1. cap.1. sic inquit: At vero id quod dicitur Genes.1. v.26. Faciamus hominem in imaginem nostra, intelligitur de forma specifica interna, quae est apprehensio Intellectiva, nequaquam vero de forma & figura externa; Et mox eodem capite: Quandoquidem igitur homo proprietatem aliquam in se habet, quae ipsi soli convenit, neque in ulla alia creatura sub sphaera lunae reperitur, facultatem nempe, sive apprehensionem intellectivam, quae nullo sensu vel opera corporis utitur, ut manu, pede, &c. Ideo assimilat eam Scriptura Intellectui Creatoris, qui itidem non existit in instrumento vel membro aliquo corporeo. Etsi autem similitudo non sit vera, sicut omnis similitudo claudicat, sed tantum secundum apparentiam externam, tamen de homine propter istam rem, intellectum inquam divinum, qui ipsi inest, dicitur, quod sit ad imaginem & Similitudinem Dei: non autem ideo, quod Deus habeat corpus & figuram externam.
units.tr: Rabbi Maimonides' More Nevochim, where in Part I, ch. 1, he says thus: But that which is said in Gen. 1:26, Let us make man in our image, is understood of the inner specific form, which is intellectual apprehension, and by no means of the outer form and figure. And soon after in the same chapter: Since therefore man has a certain property in himself, which belongs to him alone, and is found in no other creature under the sphere of the moon, namely the faculty, or intellectual apprehension, which uses no sense or bodily organ, such as hand, foot, etc., therefore Scripture likens it to the Intellect of the Creator, who likewise does not exist in any instrument or bodily member. Although, however, the likeness is not true, as every likeness limps, but only according to outward appearance, yet concerning man, on account of this thing, namely the divine intellect which is in him, it is said that he is in the image and likeness of God; not, however, because God has a body and outward figure.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Sic Rabbi David Kimchi in libro Radicum, Imaginem Dei ponit in mentis humanae praestantia & dignitate, quae propterea Similitudinem habuerit cum mente divina, quando loquitur: Zelem significat similitudinem, & interdum corpoream & sensibilem, interdum vero incorpoream & insensibilem, quae mente & cogitatio. tatione tantum percipitur, hoc est, æstimationem & similitudinem, qua aliquid alicui in præstantia & dignitate simile est, significat. Et hoc quidem hoc in loco, Faciamus hominem in imagine nostra, juxta similitudinem nostram; Sic quoque Rabbi Isac Abarbanel in perdocto, raroque Commentario ad Legem exponit multis, quomodo triplici ratione imago Dei potuerit primo tribui homini, & Primo quidem, quod perfectiones divinæ in homine fuerint conspicuæ tanquam imagine vel umbra, ipseque homo has aliquo modo possederit perfectiones, sicut apparebit, si hæc Abarbanelis verba, quæ pag.20.col.1.2. occurrunt, attento lustremus oculo: Neque perfectiones illæ in Deo benedicto, modo particulari, aut definito, prout est in Entibus finitis, sed reperiuntur in Deo benedicto ratione & ordine universali Effectoris, Productoris & Creatoris eorum; inveniunturque in creaturis cum discrimine suo & substantia, prout formæ extant in suis subjectis, & forma eorum, in accipientibus ea. Ecce, sic ita sit, reperiuntur perfectiones illæ omnes in Idea & scientia Dei benedicti, unde eas ille format, eædemque reperiuntur in homine, qui suscipit ea receptione corporea, neque tamen in ullo homine perfectiones illæ congregatæ exstant, ad formam Ideæ divinæ, proinde dicitur de eo; quod secundum imaginem divinam, quia continentur sub eo omnes perfectiosectiones existentes in Idea Dei Benedicti, dum eam creaturis suis suppeditat. Et sic forte vox ביה erit significatus צל umbra, quod, quemadmodum exprimitur & figuratur are, quae ex opposito objecta ad eam refertur, cum omnibus suis partibus; Sic homo expressus est & figuratus a figura divina, quam communicat suis creaturis. Et quemadmodum umbra proficiscitur ex adverso illuminantis, e regione nempe ejus, sic convenit homini, ut sequatur Dominum in viis ejus: Secundo ait Abarbanel praedicari de homine, quod imaginem Dei gerat, quatenus est מעפ עולם mundus parvus, in se complectens omnium rerum creatarum compendium, deque omnibus rebus aliqua ratione participans, sicuti ex his ipsius dictis clare videbitur: Ratio secunda, ob quam homo dicitur creatus ad imaginem Dei, est, quod in eo comprehendatur species quaedam sive figura mundi, tam secundum totum, quam secundum ejus partes, quae suppeditata ei sunt ordinatione & creatione divina: id quod declaratur tum respectu facultatum, tum etiam memborum ejus. Ecce enim reperitur in homine facultas intelligens, caeteraque facultates affluentiam largientes, cujus respectu est caput, pars nempe superior hominis ad pectus ejus, quod respondet mundo intelligenti, in quo reperitur facultas vitalis cum motu & sensu, estque sedes ejus, in medio corporis, cor, quod perpetuo movetur, supp- pedipeditans vitam & motum omnibus corporis membris. Hæc autem pars, ratione facultatum & membrorum, respondet regioni mundi intermedii, mundi sphærarum, quæ perpetuo moventur, & movent omnes motus. Reperitur etiam in homine facultas naturalis in nutrimento & accretione, & generatione univoca; Sedes ejus est in jecore, stomacho & reliquis membris quæ interiora occupant corporis: ubi etiam producuntur quatuor humores. Hujus autem partis respectu, e facultatibus & membris, est mundus inferior, in quo sunt quatuor elementa: ibidemque generatio & corruptio, nutritio & accretio, generatio. Et quemadmodum partes mundi omnes uniuntur cum forma superiori Dei benedicti, quæ custodit & colligat ea: ita in homine anima rationalis custodit & colligat membra & facultates ejus omnes; adeo ut eo respectu homo vocetur mundus parvus, & mundus homo magnus, ex sententia veterum & traditione Autoris More. Ecce tibi, quomodo homo, hac ratione, imago & effigies Dei Benedicti, eo quod impressi ei sunt concepti us & opera ejus, modo valde mirabili.
units.tr: Thus Rabbi David Kimchi in the book of Roots places the image of God in the excellence and dignity of the human mind, which therefore had a likeness with the divine mind, when he speaks: Zelem signifies likeness, sometimes bodily and sensible, sometimes however incorporeal and insensible, which is perceived by the mind and thought alone; that is, it signifies esteem and likeness, by which something is like another in excellence and dignity. And indeed in this place, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. So also Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel in his very learned and rare Commentary on the Law explains in many ways how the image of God could be attributed to man in a threefold manner. And first, indeed, that the divine perfections were visible in man as in an image or shadow, and man himself possessed these perfections in some way, as will appear if we examine with attentive eye these words of Abarbanel, which occur on p. 20, col. 1, 2: Those perfections are not in the blessed God in a particular or definite mode, as they are in finite beings, but they are found in the blessed God in the universal manner and order of their Effector, Producer and Creator; and they are found in creatures with their own difference and substance, as forms exist in their subjects, and their form in those who receive them. Behold, thus it is: all those perfections are found in the Idea and knowledge of the blessed God, whence He forms them, and the same are found in man, who receives them by a bodily reception; yet in no man are those perfections gathered together so as to correspond to the form of the divine Idea. Therefore he is said to be according to the divine image, because all the perfections existing in the Idea of the blessed God are contained under him, while He supplies them to His creatures. And so perhaps the word tselem will have the meaning of tsel, shadow: just as the air is expressed and shaped, which is referred to it from the opposite object, with all its parts, so man is expressed and shaped from the divine figure, which He imparts to His creatures. And just as the shadow proceeds from the opposite side of the one shining, namely from its region, so it suits man to follow the Lord in His ways. Secondly, Abarbanel says that it is predicated of man that he bears the image of God, inasmuch as he is a microcosm, a little world, comprehending in himself a summary of all created things and participating in all things in some way, as will be clearly seen from his own words: The second reason why man is said to be created in the image of God is that in him is comprehended a certain species or figure of the world, both according to its whole and according to its parts, which were supplied to him by divine ordering and creation; which is declared both with respect to his faculties and also to his members. For behold, in man there is found the intelligent faculty, and the other faculties dispensing influx, with respect to which the head is the upper part of man down to his breast, which corresponds to the intelligent world, in which is found the vital faculty with motion and sense, and whose seat, in the middle of the body, is the heart, which is perpetually moved, supplying life and motion to all the members of the body. This part, in respect of faculties and members, corresponds to the region of the intermediate world, the world of the spheres, which are perpetually moved and move all motions. There is also found in man the natural faculty in nutrition and growth, and univocal generation; its seat is in the liver, stomach and the other members that occupy the interior of the body, where also the four humours are produced. Of this part, with respect to faculties and members, there is the lower world, in which are the four elements, and there generation and corruption, nutrition and growth, generation. And just as all parts of the world are united with the superior form of the blessed God, which guards and gathers them, so in man the rational soul guards and gathers all his members and faculties; so that in this respect man is called a little world, and man a great world, according to the opinion of the ancients and the tradition of the Author of More. Behold how man, in this way, is the image and effigy of the blessed God, in that His concepts and works are impressed upon him, in a very wonderful manner.

units.la: Tertio vult Abarbanel hominem ad imaginem Dei dici conditum esse, ratione Intellectus actualis sapientiæque, qua præditus fuit, sicuti illud rursus exprimimus verbis Autoris: Ratio tertia vult sic dici ratione Intellectus actualis. Ecce enim homo primus conditus est sapiens, gradu excellencellentiori, pro conditione Regis, qui creavit illum, & anima ejus, quam suppeditavit ei fuit de natura separatorum, non potentia & dispositio, prout putavit Autor More, sed forma actu separata. Ac propterea, propter naturam animae ejus, & pro natura gradus receptivitatis & intellectus ejus dicitur: ad imaginem nostram, secundum similitudinem nostram. Homo enim, quatenus scientia pollet superiori, fere est in imagine Dei.
units.tr: Thirdly, Abarbanel wishes that man is said to have been created in the image of God by reason of the actual intellect and wisdom with which he was endowed, as we again express that in the author's words: The third reason wishes it to be said thus by reason of the actual intellect. For behold, the first man was created wise, in a more excellent degree, according to the condition of the King who created him; and the soul which He supplied to him was of the nature of the separate beings, not a potency and disposition, as the author of More thought, but a form actually separate. And therefore, on account of the nature of his soul, and according to the nature of the degree of his receptivity and intellect, he is said to be in our image, according to our likeness. For man, inasmuch as he excels in knowledge of a higher kind, is almost in the image of God.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Egregie quoque Imaginem divinam exprimit Rabbi Raphael, cum in Orach Chajim sol. 2. sic scribit: Deus ex gratia sua creavit hominem ad imaginem suam; Habuitque ille facultatem creatorem suum cognoscendi, inque viis ejus perfecte ambulandi, ad finem intentionis creationis suae assequendum. Elegit autem libere malum. Optime tamen divinam in homine delineavit imaginem Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, dum paucis ostendit, hominem ob impressam sibi imaginem de divina participare natura, licet supremi creatoris forma immensa & infinita, hominis creati vero sit finita ac determinata, in Conciliatore, Quaest. 7. in Genes. pag. 25. Pingitur divina quaedam species Creatoris in forma creata, quomodo formosa aliqua figura in speculo: nec tamen aequalis fit imago divina illi natura, quae repraesentatur, sed ejus duntaxat simulachrum est, & & similitudo. Deus igitur his verbis offendere vult, quantum divina natura homo participet. Ita ut cum creatum esse ait ad imaginem & similitudinem suam, tantundem sit, ac si diceret, sui simulachrum. Deducit pariter Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel in libello de Termino vitæ, quomodo homo dicatur quoque ad imaginem Dei factus respectu liberi arbitrii, quo quam maxime præditus fuit, uti ex verbis sequentibus, pag. 196. liquet: Sed hoc ipsum attestatur Sacra Scriptura, quia in ea legimus, Adamum libero arbitrio in creatione hujus universi præditum fuisse; eaque facultate cæteras omnes creaturas superare: nam sol necessario & semper lucet, ignis calefacit, aqua humectat, & sic de aliis: homo vero liber est in opere suo. Hujus etiam respectu, homo dicitur factus ad imaginem Dei. Neque solet quippiam cuiquam homini præscribi, quod in ipsius potestate non facere, aut omittere. Idcirco enim necesse fuit Adamo libero arbitrio prædictus (præditus) esset, quando ei vetabat Deus edere de arbore scientia boni & mali.
units.tr: Rabbi Raphael also expresses the divine image admirably. In Orach Chajim, fol. 2, he writes thus: God, out of his grace, created man in his own image. He gave him the ability to know his Creator and to walk perfectly in his ways, so as to attain the end intended by his creation. Man, however, freely chose evil. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, however, has best portrayed the divine image in man. He shows briefly that, because of the image impressed upon him, man shares in the divine nature, although the form of the supreme Creator is immense and infinite, while that of created man is finite and determinate. In the Conciliator, Quaest. 7 on Genesis, p. 25, he says: A certain divine likeness of the Creator is pictured in a created form, as a beautiful figure is in a mirror. Yet the divine image is not equal to that nature which is represented, but is only its likeness and resemblance. Therefore by these words God wishes to indicate how far man participates in the divine nature. So when he says that man was created in his image and likeness, it is the same as if he said: his image. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel also shows, in the booklet On the Term of Life, how man is said to have been made in the image of God with respect to free will, with which he was most richly endowed. This is clear from the following words, p. 196: But Sacred Scripture itself attests this, for we read there that Adam was endowed with free will at the creation of this universe, and that by this faculty he surpassed all other creatures. For the sun shines necessarily and always, fire heats, water moistens, and so on for the others; but man is free in his work. Man is also said to have been made in the image of God with respect to this. Nor is anything usually prescribed to a man which is not within his power to do or to omit. For this reason it was necessary that Adam be endowed with free will, when God forbade him to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Sed licet hæc multorum de Imagine divina sint placita, credunt nihilominus ex modernis plurimi, Imaginem divinam vel in animæ humanæ positam fuisse immortalitate, vel in solo mentis libero arbitrio, ajentes, quod cum nulla esset creatura habens libertatem, voluerit Deus benedictus producere creaturam, quae liberum habeat arbitrium faciendi, quod velit, quomodo Deus ipse habeat libertatem, quod vult, faciendi, qua Angeli vero careant, cum ex mera necessitate semper bonum agere debeant; Sic nec desunt inter hodiernos Judaeos, qui Imaginem divinam ad solum restringunt dominium in creaturas concessum; Sic alios imaginem ad Dei referre unitatem, scribentes, quod sicut Deus unus sit in coelo, ita unum fecerit in terra hominem; Rursus nonnullos ad effigiei similitudinem recurrere, ut sicut Deus nullum sibi similem habet, ita hominem condiderit, ut inter tot mille ne unus quidem inveniatur, qui alterum effigie habituque corporis exprimat; Non paucos denique cum Jarchio & Lipmanno afferere, Deum hominem creasse ad imaginem suam, id est, ad typum qui fuerat in Deo ante creationem, seu ad ideam aut formam, quam ante conceperat, in mente sua divina, secundum formam corporis externam, quam in mente sua ante hominis creationem delineaverat, proinde queimaginem in figura corporis externa consistere; Tandem non defuerunt, qui per imaginem, non divinam intellexerunt imaginem, sed humanam, adducentes tes verba illa, ad imaginem nostram, non Dei esse verba, sed Mosis, sicuti legimus apud Rabbi Aben Esram, qui jure meritoque hanc interpretationem, hominis fatui vocat explicationem.
units.tr: But although many hold these opinions about the divine image, nevertheless many of the moderns believe that the divine image was placed either in the immortality of the human soul, or in free will alone. They say that since no creature had freedom, God, blessed be he, willed to produce a creature which has free will to do what it wills, just as God himself has the freedom to do what he wills, while the angels lack this, since by mere necessity they must always do good. Thus there are also among the Jews of today some who restrict the divine image solely to the dominion granted over creatures. Others refer the image to the unity of God, writing that just as God is one in heaven, so he made one man on earth. Again, some resort to the likeness of form, arguing that just as God has no one like himself, so he made man such that among so many thousands not even one can be found who resembles another in form and bodily appearance. Not a few, finally, with Jarchi and Lipmann, assert that God made man in his image, that is, according to the type which existed in God before creation, or according to the idea or form which he had conceived beforehand in his divine mind, in accordance with the external bodily form which he had outlined in his mind before the creation of man. Therefore they hold that the image consists in the external figure of the body. Finally, there have not been lacking those who understood by "image" not the divine image but the human image, adducing those words "in our image" as not words of God but of Moses. Such an interpretation, as we read in Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra, he rightly and justly calls the explanation of a foolish man.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Evam omnis vitae matrem primam, negant ad Imaginem divinam formatam, quod non in pari perfectionis gradu cum Adamo fuerit creata, nec abscondita viderit sapientiæ, sed ut viro esset adjutorium, & ad conservationem speciei, ex Genes. cap 1. v. 27. Et creavit Deus Adamum ad imaginem suam, ad imaginem Dei creavit eum, intelligentes per ארם Adamum non humanam speciem, in duobus individuis consistentem, sed unum singulare individuum, sicut patet ex Rabbi Isaco Abarbanele in Commentario ad Legem, sol. 20. col. 3. Causa cur Scriptura Genes. 1. verf. 27. bis dicit, בצלם אלהים Ad imaginem suam creavit Deus hominem, ad imaginem inquam Dei creavit illum, hæc mihi videtur esse, quod voluerit indicare, quam vis Deus creaverit hominem marem & feminam, tamen ambos non creatos esse in eodem perfectionis gradu: neque de ambobus æqualiter dicitur. Et creavit Deus hominem: quamvis enim ejusdem fuerint speciei, tamen non ex æquo fuerant ad imaginem Dei. Ideo dicitur: In imagine Dei creavit eum: masculum & fœminam creavit illos; vult quippe indicare, Adamum solum creatum fuisse in imagine Dei : Illa enim fuit intentio & finis primarius in creatione, quamvis propter conservationem speciei masculum & fœminam illos crearit. Virilitas autem & Fœmineitas, non sunt de imagine Dei, sed pertinent ad conservationem & propagationem sui similis. Et in hoc conveniunt cum cæteris animantibus, non in imagine Dei. Hinc cognoscere potes, quare non dicatur de Adamo, secundum speciem suam; Sed: masculum & fœminam creavit eos: quia longe alia fuit ratio Adami, quam cæterorum animalium, in quibus fœmina in eodem gradu est quo mas, & æqualis ipsi in natura & existentia; hinc de illa dicitur, secundum speciem suam, sine ulla prærogativa viro supra fœminam concessa. In homine vero primaria creationis ratio fuit in viro, qui solus dicitur creatus in imagine Dei, sicut in singulari numero dicitur: In imagine Dei creavit eum; quia nimirum ille est, qui videt abscondita sapientiæ, non fœmina, quæ non habet sapientiam nisi in colo. Mulier enim creata duntaxat est propter finem secundarium, ut viro esset adjutorium, & ad conservationem speciei, prout postea scriptura explicat in modo Creationis ejus. Summa: Adam solus a principio creatus est in perfectione sua: mulier postea facta est, tanquam instrumentum ejus; Et ex Rabbi Abrahamo Seba in Tzeror Hammor, Commentario tario in Legem, Sect. Berefchit: Hinc mulieres manserunt imperfectiores, unde & Rabbini nostri ajunt, mulierum scientia est exigua. Quare contemtim abjecteque de Sexu lentiunt foeminino, loquentes in Tractatu Talmudico, Bava Batra, sol. 16. Impossibile est orbem tam sine maribus, quam sine foeminis subsistere: At, vae illis, quorum liberi foemellae, & o beatos, quorum sunt mares; Ut mirum proinde non sit, mares Judaeos quotidie in Synagogis suis, Deo agere gratias, quod viri creati sint, non vero foeminae, quasi illae naturae essent abortus, naturaeque monstra horrenda ac informia, quibus divinae imaginis lumen sit ademtum; sicut ex eadem causa obligatae sunt foeminae quotidie in precibus Numini divino gratias reddere, quod secundum Dei voluntatem sint formatae, uti ex ordinariis precum libellis quam clare liquet.
units.tr: They deny that Eve, the first mother of all life, was formed in the divine image, because she was not created in the same degree of perfection as Adam, and did not see the hidden things of wisdom, but was made to be a help to the man and for the preservation of the species, from Genesis 1:27: And God created Adam in his own image, in the image of God created he him. They understand by אדם [Adam] not the human species, consisting of two individuals, but one singular individual, as is evident from Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel in his Commentary on the Law, fol. 20, col. 3: The reason why Scripture says twice in Genesis 1:27, "in his own image God created man, in the image, I say, of God created he him" [בצלם אלהים], seems to me to be this: that although God created man male and female, nevertheless the two were not created in the same degree of perfection, and it is not said of both equally: "And God created man." For although they were of the same species, they were not equal in the image of God. Therefore it is said: "In the image of God created he him." He created them male and female; he wishes to indicate, of course, that Adam alone was created in the image of God. For that was the primary intention and purpose in creation, although he created them male and female for the preservation of the species. Maleness and femaleness, however, are not of the image of God, but pertain to the preservation and propagation of their like, and in this they agree with the other living creatures, not in the image of God. From this you may learn why it is not said of Adam, according to his species, "male and female he created them." For the reason for Adam was far different from that of the other animals, in which the female is on the same level as the male and equal to him in nature and existence. Hence of her it is said "according to her species," without any pre-eminence granted to the man over the woman. But in the human being the primary reason of creation was in the man, who alone is said to have been created in the image of God, as is said in the singular number: "In the image of God created he him." For he is the one who sees the hidden things of wisdom, not the woman, who has no wisdom except at the distaff. For the woman was created only for a secondary end, to be a help to the man and for the preservation of the species, as Scripture afterwards explains in the manner of her creation. In sum: Adam alone was created from the beginning in his perfection; the woman was made afterwards as his instrument. And from Rabbi Abraham Seba in the Tzeror Hammor, a commentary on the Law, section Bereshit: Hence women have remained more imperfect, and so our rabbis say: the knowledge of women is small. Therefore they feel contemptuously and disdainfully about the feminine sex, speaking in the Talmudic tractate Bava Batra, fol. 16: It is impossible for the world to subsist without males as well as without females. But woe to those whose children are girls, and blessed are those whose children are boys. So it is no wonder that Jewish men thank God every day in their synagogues that they were created men and not women, as if women were abortions of nature, horrible and misshapen monsters, from whom the light of the divine image has been taken away. For the same reason women are also obliged every day in their prayers to give thanks to the divine Majesty that they were formed according to the will of God, as is clearly evident from the ordinary prayer books.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Inter arbores creatas extollunt valde Arborem vitae Paradisiacam, עץ החיים, nolentes Arborem vitae signum, sacramentum vitae, exitiale aeternae, hincque appellationem fortitudinis, sed quod arbor vivifica fuisset, quae virtute & vi physica, hominis primi, si perstitisset, vitam perduum, eiusmque confervallet & propagasset, illudque indicari in verbis Genesis. cap.ȝ.ꝟ. 22, 23. Nunc igitur ne extendens manum suam accipiat de fructu arboris vitæ, & edat, & vivat in æternum. Et exterminavit eum Dominus Deus ex horto Eden ; Quod licet Adam peccasset, nihilominus vivere potuisset, modo permansisset in Paradiso, atque edisset de arbore vitæ ; sicut cum Rabbi Maimonide, Rabbi Isaco Abarbanele, Rabbi Leone Hebræo, aliisque multis nuper probare voluit Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel in libello de Fragilitate humana, pag. 38. Hi statuunt, arborem vitæ, quæ in Paradiso erat, illa fuisse facultate præditam, ut cum nativus calor consumsisset humorem radicalem, quo lampas vitæ semper ardet, ex esu illius arboris fructus, usque adeo potuisse restitui, ut prorsus rediret natura vigor, tam integer, vegetus, ac sanus, ac si tunc primum fuisset creatus. Ideoque vocatur Arbor vitæ, nomine ab effectu impositio. Idem etiam sentit Augustinus lib. XIII. de Civit. Dei cap. XX. Huc etiam conferebat situs loci, ubi aer erat purissimus, & saluberrime temperatus, ut redderet Paradisum idoneum omnibus fructibus producendis, quos humana natura desiderare posset, ad vitam conservandam ; Et libro III. de Resurrectione Mortuorum cap. II. Quod si relinquamus eum in Paradiso, forte quia libero arbitrio præditus est, extendet manum suam, & comedet de arbore vitæ, atque ita vi fructus ipsius, qua tantum restituitur, quan-
units.tr: Among the trees that were created, the Jews greatly extol the Tree of Paradisiacal life, [עץ החיים], refusing to take the Tree of life as a sign or sacrament of life, a token of eternal life, and therefore a name of strength. They hold instead that it was a life-giving tree, which by its physical power and force would have kept the first man alive forever, if he had persisted, and would have preserved and propagated his life. They claim this is indicated in the words of Genesis 3. v. 22, 23: "Now therefore, lest he put forth his hand and take also of the fruit of the tree of life, and eat, and live forever. Therefore the Lord God sent him forth from the garden of Eden." Although Adam sinned, they say, he could nevertheless have lived, provided he had remained in Paradise and eaten of the tree of life. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel recently wished to prove this, following Rabbi Maimonides, Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel, Rabbi Leo Hebraeus and many others, in his book On the Frailty of Man, p. 38: They hold that the tree of life which was in Paradise had such a power that, when the native heat had consumed the radical moisture, by which the lamp of life always burns, the vigour of nature could be so fully restored from eating its fruit that it would return entirely, vigorous, sound and healthy, as if it had just then been created. Therefore it is called the Tree of life, a name taken from its effect. Augustine also holds the same view in Book XIII of The City of God, ch. 20, where the situation of the place also contributed: the air was most pure and most healthily tempered, so that Paradise was suited to producing all the fruits that human nature could desire for preserving life. And in Book III of On the Resurrection of the Dead, ch. 2: "But if we leave him in Paradise, perhaps because he is endowed with free will, he will stretch out his hand and eat of the tree of life, and so by the power of its fruit, which restores only as much as has been consumed of the radical moisture, he would live forever."

units.la: {} quantum de humido radicali consumptum est, semper vivat. Quare consentaneum est, ut ejiciatur foras, & morte ista corporali afficiatur, cujus se reum reddidit. Itaque si non peccasset, ejus arboris subsidio, ac beneficio indesinenter, ac perpetuo vixisset; Et in libello de Termino vitæ, pag. 85. Nam uti arbor vitæ, quæ in Paradiso erat, eam vim habebat, ut degustati ex ea fructus, quicquid humidi radicalis consumptum esset, statim instaurarent, & pristinum vigorem redderent, integritatemque corporis conservarent in debita quantitate & qualitate. Extollunt valde Arboris vitæ magnitudinem, quod iter sit quingentorum annorum, indigitantes arboris perfectionem maximam, sicuti liquet ex Rabbi Maimonide in More Nevochim, Part. II. cap. 30. Caeterum & hoc notatu dignum, quod ajunt: Arboris vitæ iter est quingentorum annorum, & omnes aquæ creationis dividuntur sub illa. Et mox: Atque hæc Metaphora vel Allegoria quoque ab ipsis ad perfectionem rei alicujus explicationem allata est. Caeterum referunt Arborem vitæ, statim post Adami peccatum, abconditam fuisse, neque ulli mortali amplius visam, ita cum pluribus statuit Rabbi Maimonides loco citato: Porro, sicco pede neque hoc pratereundum, quod ajunt: Arborem vitæ non revelavit Deus ulli homini, neque etiam unquam revelabit; id quod est verissimum. Natura enim hujus universitatis hoc exigit. Sed cur Chanocho ergo Arborem vitae monstravit? Objici poflet. Sine dubio tibi responde-bunt, quod mihi factum: Chanochus non fuit mortalis, quia non peccavit. Deinde non vidit Arborem vitae in terra, sed sublatus in sublime, ex testimonio Soharis.
units.tr: As much as has been consumed of the radical moisture, so he would always live. Therefore it is fitting that he be cast out and afflicted with that bodily death of which he made himself guilty. And so, had he not sinned, he would have lived without ceasing and forever by the help and benefit of that tree.
