In his book On the Term of Life, p. 85: "For just as the tree of life which was in Paradise had the power that, once its fruits were tasted, whatever radical moisture had been consumed would immediately be restored, and the former vigour given back, and the integrity of the body preserved in due quantity and quality." They greatly extol the size of the tree of life, saying that its circuit is five hundred years, pointing to the tree's very great perfection, as is clear from Rabbi Maimonides in More Nevochim, Part II, ch. 30. Moreover, what they say is also worth noting: the circuit of the tree of life is five hundred years, and all the waters of creation are divided under it. And soon after: this metaphor or allegory has also been brought forward by them to explain the perfection of something. They also report that the tree of life was hidden immediately after Adam's sin and was never seen again by any mortal. Rabbi Maimonides, in the place cited, agrees with many others: "Further, we must not pass over in silence what they say: God did not reveal the tree of life to any man, nor will He ever reveal it, which is most true. For the nature of this universe requires it." But why then, it may be objected, did He show the tree of life to Enoch? They will doubtless answer me as I answer them: Enoch was not mortal, because he did not sin. Moreover, he did not see the tree of life on earth, but was taken up on high, according to the testimony of the Zohar.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Arborem cognitionis boni & mali Adamo Evaeque severe sub comminatione mortis interdictam fuisse, credunt ex Mose, Genef. cap. 2. v. 17. Defructu vero Arboris scientiae boni & mali, de isto ne comedas: nam quo die comederis, de eo, utique moriturus es; Affirmantes pariter, Arborem hanc, non propterea, ץ״ן ׳ןנ?ן ״ן Arborem cognitionis boni & mali appellatam, quod comesti arboris fructus intellectum & voluntatem ingenerarent, vel mirificam producerent, augerentque sapientiam, sicut a multis viris doctis traditum est, hanc Judaeorum communem esse sententiam, cum contrarium moderni statuant, sentientes hominem a reliquis semper distinctum fuisse animantibus, semperque intellectu praeditum, nec Adamum in ignorantia & simplicitate instar infantis sine ulu rationis conditum, sed divina corruscalle imagine, imo ipsam experientiam Adamum, posterosque aliter longe docudocuisse, uti egregie demonstrat Rabbi Maimonides, cum ad objectionem sibi factam, in More Nevochim, Part. 1. cap. 2. sic respondet: Objectionem ipsam quoque proponam. Dixit Opponens: Videtur ex simplici sensu Scriptura, Intentionem primam in Hominis creatione fuisse, ut esset similis reliquis animantibus, sine Intellectu & cogitatione, nescien discernere inter bonum & malum: quando autem rebellavit, tum demum rebellionem ipsius, magnam istam perfectionem in illo produxisse, quae propria ipsi est; Cognitionem scilicet vel discretionem istam existentem in nobis, quae omnibus aliis rebus, quae nobis insunt, est nobilior, & per quam ipsam subsistimus, & sumus id quod sumus. Atque hoc admirandum est, quod poena inobedientiae ejus perfectionem ipsi dederit, quam antea carebat, nempe intellectum. Perinde enim est, ac si quis diceret, quidam homo peccavit & gravissimum aliquod commisit flagitium, ideo mutarunt ipsius creationem in melius, & constitutus est tanquam stella aliqua in firmamento. Haec est summa & sensus objectionis illius. Nunc audi quoque responsionem nostram; Quam paucis interjectis, ad rem nostram nihil facientibus, sic continuat Rabbi Maimonides: Intellectus, quem Creator Adamo primo infudit, (qui est perfectio ipsius postrema,) collatus ipsi fuit jam ante rebellionem ejus. Propter illum enim dictum est de de homine, quod creatus fit ad Imaginem & similitudinem Dei: propter illum etiam locutus dicitur Deus cum eo, & praecepta ei dedisse, sicut dicitur Genes. 2. v. 16. Et praecepit Dominus Deus Adamo. Praeceptum etenim non datur brutis, & intellectu ac ratione carentibus. Per Intellectum autem potest homo discernere inter verum & falsum, & hic inditus fuit ipsi ad perfectionem & absolutionem ejus; Et ita mox pergit: Quando autem homo adhuc extitit in integritate & perfectione sua, mentis inprimis & intellectus, cujus respectu dictum est de eo, Psalmo 8. v. 6. Et minorem fecisti eum paululum ab Angelis: tum nulla plane erat in eo facultas utendi sensibilibus, vel ea apprehendendi. Id enim, quod inter ea, quae manifeste in sensus incurrunt, maxime turpe est, revelatio nempe nuditatis, ab ipso nullo modo turpe habebatur, suamque propriam turpitudinem ipsemet non cognovit. Deficiente vero ipso, & ad vanas concupiscentias, sensuumque corporalium libidines inclinante, sicut dicitur Genes. 3. v. 6. Vidit igitur mulier, quod bona arbor ad vescendum, quodque desiderabilis oculis, punitus est merito, quia abnegavit apprehensionem illam Intellectivam. Et quia peccavit contra praeceptum illud, quod ratione Intellectus ei datum erat, ideo in locum hujus successit apprehensio sensibilium, sicque praecipitatus est in turpes & libidinosos affectus. Tunc demum agnovit pretium & aestimatiomationem ejus quod perdiderat, & quo spoliatus erat, quamque miserum in statum prolapsus fuerit. Idem testatur Rabbi Isac Abarbanel in Commentario super Legem sol. 27. col. 3. Non fuit ille arboris hujus usus, ut ejus hominem perfectiorem redderet in apprehensionibus aut scientiis suis, sive speculativis, sive practicis, siquidem homo cum perfectione actuum intellectus sui creatus erat.
units.tr: That the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was forbidden to Adam and Eve under severe threat of death, they believe from Moses, Genesis 2. v. 17: "But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it; for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die." They also maintain that this tree was not so called because the fruit eaten would generate understanding and will, or produce wonderful wisdom and increase it, as many learned men have reported. They say this is the common opinion of the Jews, whereas the moderns hold the contrary. They think man has always been distinct from the other animals and always endowed with understanding, and that Adam was not created in ignorance and simplicity like an infant without the use of reason, but shone with the divine image. Indeed, experience itself taught Adam and his posterity quite otherwise, as Rabbi Maimonides shows admirably. When an objection was raised against him, in More Nevochim, Part I, ch. 2, he answers thus: I will also state the objection itself. The opponent said: It seems from the plain sense of Scripture that the primary intention in the creation of man was that he should be like the other animals, without understanding or thought, not knowing how to distinguish between good and evil. But when he rebelled, then at last his rebellion produced in him that great perfection which is proper to him, namely that cognition or discernment which exists in us, which is more noble than all the other things that are in us, and through which we subsist and are what we are. And it is remarkable that the punishment of his disobedience gave him a perfection which he previously lacked, namely the intellect. For it is just as if someone were to say: a certain man sinned and committed some very grave crime, therefore his creation was changed for the better, and he was set up like a star in the firmament. This is the sum and sense of that objection. Now hear also our answer. After a few intervening remarks that have nothing to do with our matter, Rabbi Maimonides continues thus: The intellect which the Creator infused into the first Adam, which is his final perfection, was bestowed upon him even before his rebellion. For because of it it was said of man that he was created in the image and likeness of God. Because of it also God is said to have spoken with him and given him commands, as it is said in Genesis 2. v. 16: "And the Lord God commanded Adam." For a command is not given to brutes, which lack intellect and reason. Through the intellect man can distinguish between true and false, and this was implanted in him for his perfection and completion. And then he goes on: When man still existed in his integrity and perfection, of his mind and intellect, with respect to which it is said of him, Psalm 8. v. 6: "And thou hast made him a little lower than the angels," then he had absolutely no faculty of using the senses or of grasping sensible things. For that which is most shameful among those things that obviously fall under the senses, namely the uncovering of nakedness, was in no way regarded by him as shameful, and he did not himself know his own shame. But when he was deficient and inclined to vain desires and the lusts of the bodily senses, as it is said in Genesis 3. v. 6: "The woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes," he was deservedly punished, because he had rejected that intellectual apprehension. And because he sinned against that command, which had been given to him by the reason of the intellect, therefore the apprehension of sensible things came in its place, and so he was cast down into shameful and lustful affections. Only then did he recognise the worth and estimation of what he had lost, and of what he had been stripped, and how miserable a state he had fallen into. Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel also testifies to the same in his Commentary on the Law, fol. 27, col. 3: The use of this tree was not such as to make man more perfect in his apprehensions or sciences, whether speculative or practical, since man was created with the perfection of the acts of his intellect.

units.la: Addit Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, quare arbor cognitionis boni & mali sic vocata fuerit, cum lib. III. de Resurrectione mortuorum cap. 11. ad verba Genes. cap. 3. v. 22. ita scribit: Quasi diceret, Nihil obstabit quo minus Adamus, quando solam cognitionem boni tantum habebat in statu innocentia, in aeternum in terra viveret, quia anima ejus ist hic felix ac beata erat futura: Sed nunc, quoniam per lapsum comparavit sibi cognitionem boni simul & mali, non est aequum ut in aeternum vivat; Et in libello de Fragilitate humana, pag. 40. Verum quia ista felicitas non poterat satis percipi nisi sub specie alicujus meriti, eo sic Deo visum fuit mandatum dare Adamo. Cumque in Paradiso inter aliquas arbores quaedam foret, cujus proprietas ista erat, ut qui comedisset ex illa, aequali inclinatione ferretur in bonum & malum, concessit illi de omnibus arboribus edere, excepta arbore scientia boni, & mali. Nam voluit, ut, postea quam illum creavisset libero arbitrio praeditum, ditum, effet duntaxat pronus in virtutem, & bo-num.
units.tr: Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel adds why the tree was so called, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. In book III of his work on the Resurrection of the dead, chapter 11, on the words of Genesis 3:22, he writes: As if he were saying, nothing would have prevented Adam, while he had only the knowledge of good in the state of innocence, from living forever on earth, since his soul was going to be happy and blessed here. But now, since through the fall he has acquired for himself the knowledge of good and evil together, it is not fitting that he should live forever. And in his little book on human frailty, page 40: But because that happiness could not be sufficiently grasped except under the appearance of some merit, it therefore seemed good to God to give Adam a command. And since in Paradise there was among the other trees one whose property was this, that whoever ate from it would be carried with an equal inclination toward good and evil, he granted him to eat from all the trees except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. For he wished that, after he had created him endowed with free will, he should be inclined only toward virtue and good.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Inter divinas Leges Adamo, posterisque mandatas, commendant mirum in modum Præceptum affirmativum de Conjugio, inculcantes omnibus illud ב‮ו ‮פרו Fructificate & multiplicamini, ex Genes. cap. I. v. 28. Et benedixit ius Deus, & dixit, fructificate, & multiplicamini, & implete terram; Quod præceptum hoc fundamentum sit, ob quod reliqua omnia tradi potuerint, sicuti loquitur Rabbi Levi Barzelonita in Chinuch, Sect. 1. Est hoc præceptum magnum, cujus causa constituta sunt omnia præcepta mundi, utpote quæ hominibus tradita sunt, non vero Angelis ministerii; Quod mundus alias habitabilis non esset futurus, uti idem Rabbi Levi loco citato inquit: Ex fundamentus hujus præcepti est, ut mundus sit habitabilis; idenim Deus Benedictus fieri voluit. Neminem ab hujus præcepti observatione excipiunt, judicantes hoc mandato omnes teneri, cujuscunque sint ordinis, conditionisque, modo per naturam & ætatem sint apti, quod omnibus sine discrimine id mandatum fit; Quare, loquor cum Buxtorfio in Dissertatione de Sponsalibus pag. 8. nulla apud Judæos cælibatus & virginitatis leguntur vota, nulla encomia, nulla illi adscripta merita, nulla proposita præmia: Sed matrimonio: Nullum hic illi agnoscunt discrimen inter personas sacras & politicas, sed illas æque ac has nonsolum esse idoneas, sed & de hoc præcepto teneri. Quod si vero quis propter Legis Dei studium, ut à curis multis corporalibus immunis, tanto liberius & expeditius ei vacare queat, velit, & simul per continentiæ donum possit, cœlibem vitam ad tempus agere, is potest id facere sine peccato, sed libere, & hac lege, ut si concupiscentiæ stimulis urgeri se sentiat, non tantum possit, sed & debeat ad sponsalia progredi, & nuptiarum remedio uti, sicut refertur à Rabbi Levi, cum sermonem suum de hoc præcepto continuat: Obtinet omni loco & tempore, ita ut teneatur ei homo dare operam primum atque aptus, consecutus fuerit terminum, quem præfixerunt Magistri nostri ducendæ uxori. Hoc autem præceptum mulieribus non est impositum. Transgressor violat affirmativum, quem proinde magna manet pœna, quod complere noluerit voluntatem Dei ad habitabilem faciendum mundum ejus; Pluribusque describitur in Schulchan Aruch, Part. IV. Num 1. §1, Omnis homo tenetur de ducenda uxore, ut fœtificet, & multiplicet: & quicunque hoc non observat, perinde facit, ac si effunderet sanguinem; Et §. 3. Præceptum est cuivis homini ducere ducere uxorem, qui est 18. annorum: quod si vero quis hoc tempus antevertat, & decimo tertio anno ducat, us longe praestantius facit, sed ante 13. annum non licet. Nullo autem prorsus modo excedet vige-simum annum sine uxore: quod si autem quis id fe-cerit, nec ducere uxorem velit, domus judicii eum cogit, ut huic praecepto satis faciat. Nihilominus, si operam dederit Legi, & assidue in ea occupetur, metuat que ducere uxorem, ne in alimentis comparandis laborare cogatur, & sic a studio legis avocetur, is potest diutius exspectare; cujus animus jugiter delectatur versari in Lege, & in ea studere, ut Ben Assai, eique omnibus diebus suis adhaerere, atque ea propter non ducit uxorem, in ejus manu nulla est iniquitas; puta, si concupiscentia ipsius non praevaleat ei, sed, si praevaleat, obstrictus est ut ducat uxorem, etiam si jam liberos habeat, idque ne incidat in pravas cogitationes.
units.tr: Among the divine laws given to Adam and his posterity, they commend in a remarkable way the affirmative precept concerning marriage, impressing on everyone the words "Be fruitful and multiply" [פרו ורבו] from Genesis 1:28: And God blessed them, and said, Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the earth. This precept, as Rabbi Levi Barzelonita says in the Chinuch, section 1, is the foundation on which all the other precepts could be given: This is a great precept, for the sake of which all the precepts of the world were established, since they were given to men and not to the angels of ministry. Without it the world would not have been habitable, as the same Rabbi Levi says in the place cited: The foundation of this precept is that the world should be habitable, for God, blessed be he, wished it to be so. They except no one from the observance of this precept, judging that all are bound by this command, of whatever order or condition they may be, provided that by nature and age they are fit; the command is given to all without distinction. Hence, I agree with Buxtorf in his Dissertation on Betrothals, page 8, that among the Jews no vows of celibacy or virginity are read, no praises, no merits ascribed to them, no rewards proposed; but matrimony. They recognise no distinction here between sacred and secular persons, but hold that both alike are not only fit but also bound by this precept. But if anyone, out of zeal for the Law of God, wishing to be free of many bodily cares so that he may devote himself to it more freely and readily, and at the same time has the gift of continence, chooses to live a celibate life for a time, he may do so without sin, but freely, and on this condition, that if he feels himself urged by the goads of concupiscence, he may not only be permitted but must proceed to betrothal and use the remedy of marriage. This is related by Rabbi Levi when he continues his discourse on this precept: It holds in every place and time, so that a man who is first and fit is bound to take pains to marry a wife once he has reached the age that our Masters have fixed. This precept, however, is not imposed on women. The transgressor violates an affirmative command, for which a great penalty remains, because he was unwilling to fulfil the will of God to make his world habitable. It is described more fully in the Shulchan Aruch, Part IV, number 1, §1: Every man is bound to marry a wife, so that he may be fruitful and multiply; and whoever does not observe this acts as if he shed blood. And §3: It is a precept for every man to marry a wife when he is eighteen years old; but if anyone anticipates this time and marries in his thirteenth year, he does a far more excellent thing, though before the thirteenth year it is not lawful. In no way, however, may he go beyond his twentieth year without a wife; and if anyone has done so and is unwilling to marry, the court compels him to satisfy this precept. Nevertheless, if he has devoted himself to the Law and is constantly occupied with it, and fears to marry lest he be forced to labour to get his living and so be drawn away from the study of the Law, he may wait longer; his mind delights continually in dwelling on the Law and studying it, like Ben Assai, and clinging to it all his days, and for this reason he does not marry; in his hand there is no iniquity, that is, if his concupiscence does not prevail over him; but if it does prevail, he is obliged to marry a wife, even if he already has children, lest he fall into wicked thoughts.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Negant Judaei concupiscentiam Adamo primo innatam, quod rectus fuerit conditus, Solum modo vide, hoc inveni, Deum ipsum hominem fecisse rectum; Quod summa gavisus fuerit tranquillitate, cum omnes affectus subjecti essent rationi, illique proni morem gererent, sicut loquitur Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel in libello de Fragilitate humana, pag. 38. Cum autem supra omnia, mnia necessaria sit justitia ad Reipublicæ administrationem; Deus animæ Adami, ut Domina esset Reipublicæ interioris, contulit justitiam, quæ ad hunc finem erat necessaria, & dedit rectitudinem, quæ subjiceret appetitum rationi, & corpus animæ; Quod ex mente Psalmistæ tanquam Angelus in terra vixerit; Quod Adamus in statu integro solam cognitionem boni habuerit, post lapsum vero cognitionem mali simul acquisiverit, uti rursus inquit Rabbi Menasseh lib. III. de Resurrectione mortuorum, pag. 333. Nihil obstabit quo minus Adamus, quando solam cognitionem boni tantum habebat in statu innocentiæ, in æternum in terra viveret, quia anima ejus isthic felix ac beata erat futura: Sed nunc, quoniam per lapsum comparavit sibi cognitionem boni simul & mali, non est æquum ut in æternum vivat; Et in libello citato de Fragilitate, pag. 40. Nam voluit, ut, postquam illum creavisset libero arbitrio præditum, esset duntaxat pronus in virtutem, & bonum; Quod facultas concupiscens in statu integritatis per donum justitiæ Originalis ita compressa fuerit, ut nihil in se pudendum adverterent, cum teste Rabbi Abarbanel Comment. in Leg. sol. 27. col. 2. Genitalia membra apud ipsos essent instar manuum, pedum, & reliquorum membrorum adussum necessariorum; Quod figmentum malum demum post peccatum catum occupaverit Adamum, ex testimonio Ralchi in Comment. adGenef. cap. 2. ¶. 25. Idem tradit Rabbi Bechai in Comment. ad Genef.cap. 3.¶.6. Sensus est quod concupiscentia prava in eo nondum formata erat. Fuit enim totus Intellectualis, sine concupiscentia prava, per quam demum mediante Eva persuasus, deceptusque est; Quod serpens inquinamentum suum in Evam projecerit, uti referunt Rabbini in Berefchit Rabba: Quo tempore venit serpens ad Evam, inquinamentu suu in ea projecit; Quod ex peccato Adami multa mala scaturire inceperint, uti quiritatur Rabbi Lipmannus in libro Nizzachon, num. 10. Væ nobis! quod peccavit. Ex eo tempore enim vitam nostram abbreviamus cupiditatibus figmenti mali, immodico veneris usu & reliquis jucunditatibus dies nostros consumimus, ut Deo nostro serviendi, & legi operam dandi nullum sit nobis otium; Quod concupiscentia interna sive connata peccatum sit, hinc ab Adamo integro removenda, uti pluribus demonstrat Rabbi Bechai allegato Commentario, sol. 99.143. Non ergo duplex credunt figmentum in homine primo Figmentum bonum, & Figmentum malum, sicuti plurimis ex Christianis visum fuit, exinde decepti, quod antiqui quidam Judæi, illud probare voluerint ex voce Et formavit, Genef. cap. 2. ¥. 7. quasi duplex insertum Jod duplex denotaret figmentum; cum tamen hæ veterum quorundam Cabbalistarum sint ludicræ conjecturæ; quarum complures ad hunc locum enarravit Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel de Resurrectione mortuorum lib. 1. pag. 2,3. non vero fidei Judaicæ sint articuli.
units.tr: The Jews deny that concupiscence was innate in the first Adam, on the ground that he was created upright. "Only look," they say, "I have found this: that God himself made man upright, and that he rejoiced in the greatest tranquillity, since all the affections were subject to reason and readily obeyed it," as Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel says in his booklet On the Frailty of Man, p. 38. Since above all things justice is necessary for the administration of a commonwealth, God gave to the soul of Adam justice, which was necessary for this purpose, so that it might be mistress of the inner commonwealth, and he gave uprightness, which would subject appetite to reason and the body to the soul. Following the mind of the Psalmist, Adam lived on earth as an angel. Adam, in the state of integrity, had only the knowledge of good; but after the fall he acquired the knowledge of evil along with it, as Rabbi Menasseh says again in Book III of On the Resurrection of the Dead, p. 333. Nothing would have prevented Adam, while he had only the knowledge of good in the state of innocence, from living on earth for ever, since his soul was to be happy and blessed there. But now, since by the fall he has acquired for himself the knowledge of good and evil together, it is not right that he should live for ever. And in the booklet on Frailty already cited, p. 40: for God willed that, having created him endowed with free will, he should be only inclined towards virtue and good. The concupiscent faculty in the state of integrity was so restrained by the gift of original justice that they noticed nothing shameful in themselves; as Rabbi Abarbanel attests in his Commentary on the Law, sol. 27, col. 2, the genitals among them were like the hands, feet and other members needed for action. The evil figment only took possession of Adam after sin, according to the testimony of Ralchi in his Commentary on Genesis, chap. 2, ¶ 25. Rabbi Bechai gives the same account in his Commentary on Genesis, chap. 3, ¶ 6: The meaning is that depraved concupiscence was not yet formed in him. For he was wholly intellectual, without depraved concupiscence, by which he was at last persuaded and deceived, through the mediation of Eve. Also, the rabbis in Bereshit Rabba report that the serpent cast its pollution into Eve: At the time when the serpent came to Eve, it cast its pollution into her. Rabbi Lipmann complains in the book Nizzachon, no. 10, that many evils began to spring from the sin of Adam: Woe to us, because he sinned! For from that time we shorten our lives by the desires of the evil figment, we spend our days in immoderate use of sex and other pleasures, so that there is no leisure left for us to serve our God and to apply ourselves to the Law. Rabbi Bechai, in the Commentary already cited, sol. 99, 143, shows at length that innate or inborn concupiscence is sin and must therefore be removed from Adam in his integrity. Therefore they do not believe that there were two figments in the first man, a good figment and an evil figment, as many Christians have thought, deceived by the fact that some ancient Jews wanted to prove this from the word And he formed, Genesis chap. 2, ¶ 7, as if the doubled inserted yod denoted a double figment. Yet these are the playful conjectures of certain ancient Cabbalists, many of which Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel recounts on this passage in On the Resurrection of the Dead, book I, pp. 2, 3; they are not articles of Jewish faith.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Credunt Adamum primum non diu in integro vixisse statu, audacter insuper ex tripode definientes, Adamum non ultra aliquot horas perstitisse in felicitate, diei & noctis residuum in mœrore transegisse & pœnitentia, proximo vero mane in gratiam rursus receptum, ex Psalmo 49. ¥. 13. Adam in gloria non pernoctabit, uti patet in Midrasch Tillim ad Psalm. 92, in quo de hominis creatione, lapsu & ejectione è Paradiso hæc habentur: In vespera Sabbathi creatus est primus homo. Hora prima Deus de opere cogitavit; Secunda consultavit cum Angelis Ministratoriis; Tertia collegit pulverem ejus; Quarta terminavit eum pulverem; Quinta facit eum embryonem; Sexta ei formam & figuram dedit; Septima insufflavit ei animam; Octava constituit eum super pedes suos; Nona mandatum ei dedit; Decima peccavit; Undecima judicatus est, Et duodecima expulsus è Paradiso; Deinde mox sequitur: Et Angeli ministratorii ei clamabant, homo homo in honore non pernoctavit, sed similis factus est beatus: amborum perierunt; Sicin Berefchit Rabba §. 12, Rabbi Jofes dixit: traditur: Gloria primi hominis cum eo non pernoctavit; Idem refertur in Capitulis Rabbi Elieferis, c. 11. licet alio ordine duodecim horarum opera recensean-tur. Alii felicitatem metiuntur sex horis, alii octo horis, rursus alii ex Judaeis quadraginta diebus. Alii denique, Cabbalistae praesertim felicitatem primaevam aestimant annis viginti, somniantes Adamum a creatione vicesimo ex Paradiso expulsum fuisse. Profecto dum curiosis atque vanis hujusmodi hariolationibus humanum indulget ingenium, facile ja-cturam veritatis facit necessarie. Quamdiu autem Adamus Deo familiaris, vitae integer, scelerisque purus fuerit, non liquet ex sacris literis. Videtur tamen illud tempus nimis breve definiendum non esse, nec horis aliquot circumscribendum, cum opera Dei augusta tam angustè coartari non debeant.
units.tr: They believe that the first Adam did not live long in the state of integrity. They boldly add, moreover, from a tripod, that Adam did not continue in happiness for more than a few hours, and spent the rest of the day and night in sorrow and repentance, and that on the next morning he was received back into favour, from Psalm 49, ¶ 13: Adam in glory will not spend the night. This is evident in the Midrash Tillim on Psalm 92, where the following is found about the creation, fall and expulsion of man from Paradise: On the eve of the Sabbath the first man was created. In the first hour God thought about the work; in the second he consulted the ministering Angels; in the third he gathered its dust; in the fourth he finished the dust; in the fifth he made him an embryo; in the sixth he gave him form and shape; in the seventh he breathed a soul into him; in the eighth he set him upon his feet; in the ninth he gave him a commandment; in the tenth he sinned; in the eleventh he was judged; and in the twelfth he was expelled from Paradise. Then immediately follows: And the ministering Angels cried out to him, "Man, man, you did not spend the night in honour, but have become like the beasts;" both have perished. So too in Bereshit Rabba §12, Rabbi Jose said: it is handed down that the glory of the first man did not spend the night with him. The same is related in the Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer, chap. 11, though the works of the twelve hours are listed in a different order. Others measure that happiness by six hours, others by eight hours, and still others among the Jews by forty days. Finally, others, especially the Cabbalists, reckon the primeval happiness at twenty years, dreaming that Adam was expelled from Paradise in the twentieth year after his creation. Indeed, while the human mind indulges in curious and vain guesses of this kind, it easily and necessarily loses the truth. How long Adam remained familiar with God, whole in life and pure of sin, is not clear from the sacred letters. It seems, however, that this time should not be defined as too brief, nor confined within a few hours, since the majestic works of God ought not to be so narrowly restricted.

units.la: CAPUT
units.tr: CHAPTER

units.la: CAPUT X. De Homine per Peccatum destituto.
units.tr: CHAPTER X. Of Man Deprived through Sin.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: CRedit imperitum vulgus Judaicum, nec displicet Rabbinis quibusdam, primos nostros parentes, non per Diabolum, serpentem antiquum fuisse seduCtos, sed per nudam bestiam, existimantibus sicut nihil praeter corporalem serpentem, ita nihil nisi externum odium & infestationem hic cogitantibus, quae hominibus cum serpentibus intercedat, uti satis superque liquet, tum ex plebis promiscua confessione, tum ex Rabbinorum scriptis, quorum nonnulla adducemus testimonia; Sic enim Rabbi Aben Esra in Commentario in Genes. cap 3. Dicunt, quod fuerit Satan, & non inspiciunt sectionis finem. Ecquomodo enim Satanas eat super ventre, & quomodo vescatur pulvere? Et quis tandem sensus erit maledictionis? Ille conteret tibi caput; Sic quoque
units.tr: The ignorant Jewish crowd believes, and some rabbis are not displeased, that our first parents were seduced not by the Devil, the ancient serpent, but by a mere beast. They think that just as there is nothing but a bodily serpent, so there is nothing to consider here except the outward hatred and hostility that exists between humans and serpents. This is plain enough, both from the common confession of the people and from the writings of the rabbis, some of whose testimonies we shall cite. Thus Rabbi Aben Ezra, in his Commentary on Genesis chapter 3: They say it was Satan, and they do not look at the end of the section. For how could Satan go upon his belly, and how would he eat dust? And what then will be the sense of the curse? He shall bruise your head; So also

units.la: Rabbi Isac Abarbanel, qui hoc novum praeterea addidit commentum, refert nihil omnino verborum inter Evam & serpentem commutatum esse, neque spiritui alicui loquenti hic locum fuisse, sed Evam aemulatam fuisse serpentem in arborem illam ascendentem, & ex fructu absque noxa comedentem, exemploque duntaxat seductam fuisse, cum in Commentario in Genes. ad cap. 3. narrat: Ideo ut meam opinionem in hac narratione intelligas, tibi hic indicabo fundamentum, in quo veritas sectionis hujus consistit. Nempe quod serpens nihil quicquam locutus sit ad foeminam, neque haec ad illum. Minime enim loqui potest, & idcirco Scriptura non ait in hoc negotio: & aperuit Dominus os serpentis, veluti dixit de asina Bileami, quia ibi eo, quod asina loqueretur, ut litera habet, & quidem miraculose, dictum est: & aperuit Dominus os asinae; Sed de serpente non dixit, quod Dominus os ejus aperuerit, quia nihil omnino est locutus neque naturaliter, neque supernaturaliter. Sed res ita habet; illa foemina vidit serpentem ascendentem in arborem vitae, & subinde de fructibus ejus comedentem, neque tamen inde mortem contrahentem vel damnum, & ipsa igitur foemina hoc secum volvit & invest igavit, tanquam cum serpente loqueretur, & hoc in arborem ascendente, diceret ad se ipsam, non moriemini, & sic ad sua verba respondet cogitatiotionibus suis, eum in modum, quo dicitur Iob. cap. 35. ¶. 11. Docες nos ex jumentis terra & de volatili cœli reddes nos sapientes. Illa enim ex serpente sapere & investigare cœpit, & isthæc verba Scriptura ad illum serpentem refert; Pergitque mox citato loco Rabbi Abarbanel: Sententia illorum, qui perhibent, serpentem loquentem fuisse Satanam, qui homini apparuerit in forma serpentis, veluti scripsit Haggaon Rabbi Saadia, & alii cum eo, revera nihil aliud continet, quam vanissimas cogitationes, quibus nihil inest solidi; Ita Rabbi Isac Bar Abraham, argutis rationibus ostendere conatur, per serpentem non intelligendum Satanam, cum in Munimine Fidei, lib. 1. c. 12. ad locum Genes. cap. 3. ¶. 15. Sic argumentatur: Vtuntur Nazareni hoc dicto ad specicm conciliandam religioni suae, ajunt que per verba, hoc conteret tibi caput, Iesum significari, qui sit occisurus Satanam, Scriptura Serpentem appellatum. Responsio. Hoc argumentum vim nullam habet. Nam, si verum esset quod prædicant, atque, hoc conteret tibi caput, id de Iesu diceret, occisurum eum Satanam, hoc est, sublaturum e medio causam peccatorum, tum nulla penitus commissuri erant peccata, quotquot in eum credunt. Cum vero ipsi in hanc usque diem peccent, vacillat eorundem hypothesis, quin & ipsum hoc Scriptura dictum hypothesin eorundem profiternit. Nempe additur postea: tu autem tem conteres ei calcaneum; at, quomodo conterere possfet serpens, si fuit peremtus? Adde, quod si Satanas, ceu fert illorum opinio, homines Iudaeos Paganosque pellexit, ut ipsum ejusque discipulos & Apostolos trucidarent, tum utique non occidit is Satanam, sed potius Satanas necis eis, necisque discipulorum ipsius causa extitit. Reperimus quoque Paulum Apostolum dogma illud evertere, quoniam in sua ad Romanos Epistola cap. 16. v. 20. scribit: Deus autem pacis conteret Satanam sub pedes vestros cito. Idemque in priore ad Thessalonicenses epistola cap. 2. v. 18. his utitur verbis: Ideo voluimus venire ad vos, ego quidem Paulus semel atque iterum, sed impedivit nos Satanas. Ecce ex iis testimoniis elucescit, Satanam, adeo post mortem etiam Iesu, Pauli temporibus, adhuc fuisse superstitem, & in credentes in ipsum exercuisse imperium; Refert pariter Rabbi Lusitanus in Colloquio Mittelburgensi, sol. 148. necessario nudum animal intelligi debere, quod deceperit Evam, cum astutum valde & calliditate omnes agri bestias superans per Mosen, Genesis cap. 3. v. 1. describatur, quod opus nullo fuisset modo, si Diabolus per serpentem locutus fuisset; Respondet quin etiam Rabbi Aben Esra ad motam difficultatem, quod serpens corporalis nec loqui, nec ratiocinari, multo magis blandiloquentia versutissima decipere primos potuerit homines, nes, ostendens serpentem hunc & sermone & intelligentia à Deo fuisse instructum, cum loco allegato sic scribit: Mihi verba illa fecundum sensum literalem intelligenda videntur. Serpens nempe loquebatur, erecta incessit forma, & qui scientiam posuit in homine, is & in illo posuit. Ecce vero scriptum testimonium huic perhibet. Fuit enim serpens callidior omnibus animalibus agri, sed non ut homo.
units.tr: Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel, who moreover added this new fiction, reports that nothing at all of the words was exchanged between Eve and the serpent, and that no speaking spirit had any place here. Rather, Eve imitated the serpent that climbed the tree and ate of its fruit without harm, and she was seduced only by example. He says this in his Commentary on Genesis chapter 3: So that you may understand my opinion on this narrative, I will here point out to you the foundation on which the truth of this section rests. Namely, that the serpent said nothing at all to the woman, nor she to him. For it cannot speak, and therefore Scripture does not say in this matter, "And the Lord opened the mouth of the serpent," as it said of Balaam's donkey, because there, that the donkey spoke, as the letter has it, and indeed miraculously, is stated: "And the Lord opened the mouth of the donkey." But of the serpent it did not say that the Lord opened its mouth, because it spoke nothing at all, neither naturally nor supernaturally. But the matter stands thus: that woman saw the serpent climbing into the tree of life and from time to time eating of its fruit, and yet not incurring death or harm from it. So the woman turned this over and investigated it in her own mind, as if the serpent were speaking with her, and, as the serpent climbed the tree, she said to herself, "You will not die." Thus she answered her own thoughts with her own words, in the manner of what is said in Job chapter 35 v. 11: "Who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth, and makes us wiser than the birds of heaven." For she began to become wise and to investigate from the serpent, and Scripture refers these words to that serpent. Rabbi Abarbanel continues in the cited passage: The opinion of those who maintain that the serpent that spoke was Satan, who appeared to man in the form of a serpent, as Rabbi Saadia wrote in Haggaon, and others with him, really contains nothing but the emptiest fancies, with nothing solid in them. Likewise Rabbi Isaac Bar Abraham tries, by subtle arguments, to show that by the serpent Satan is not to be understood. In his Munimen Fidei, book 1 chapter 12, on the passage Genesis 3 v. 15, he argues thus: The Nazarenes use this saying to win favour for their religion, and they say that by the words, "He shall bruise your head," Jesus is signified, who was to kill Satan, and Scripture called him the serpent. Reply: This argument has no force. For if what they preach were true, and if "He shall bruise your head" said that Jesus would kill Satan, that is, remove the cause of sins from the midst, then all who believe in him would commit no sins at all. But since they, to this very day, do sin, their hypothesis wavers, and this very saying of Scripture refutes their hypothesis. For it is added afterwards: "And you shall bruise his heel." But how could a serpent bruise anyone if it had been killed? Add that if Satan, as their opinion holds, enticed the Jewish and pagan peoples to slaughter him and his disciples and apostles, then he did not kill Satan at all, but rather Satan became the cause of their slaughter and of the slaughter of his disciples. We find also that the Apostle Paul overturns that doctrine, since in his Epistle to the Romans chapter 16 v. 20 he writes: And the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly. And in his first Epistle to the Thessalonians chapter 2 v. 18 he uses these words: Therefore we wanted to come to you, I, Paul, once and again, but Satan hindered us. From these testimonies it is clear that Satan, even after the death of Jesus, was still alive in the times of Paul, and exercised dominion over those who believed in him. Rabbi Lusitanus likewise reports, in the Colloquy of Middelburg, page 148, that the bare animal must necessarily be understood as the one that deceived Eve, since Moses, Genesis chapter 3 v. 1, describes it as more crafty and cunning than all the beasts of the field. This would not have been needed in any way if the Devil had spoken through the serpent. Rabbi Aben Ezra, moreover, answers the difficulty raised: that a bodily serpent could neither speak nor reason, much less deceive the first humans by the most cunning flattery. He shows that this serpent was instructed by God both in speech and in understanding, and in the passage cited he writes thus: Those words seem to me to be understood according to the literal sense. The serpent, indeed, was speaking, and it walked with an upright form; and he who placed knowledge in man, placed it also in that creature. Behold, Scripture bears witness to this. For the serpent was more crafty than all the animals of the field, but not as man is.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Non desunt interim, nec defuerunt unquam innumeri insignes Hebraei, omnes planissime agnoscentes, Diabolum misere circumvenisse hominem adhibito serpente, callidissimo animalculo, nequitiae suae instrumento accommodo, proinde apud Mosen Genef.cap 3. v. 1. non nudum intelligendum serpentem, qui Evam fuerat aggressus, sed Diabolum per Serpentem tanquam organum operatum fuisse, quare passim Diabolum appellarunt נחש הקדמוני Serpentem primaevum, vel antiquum, phrasi parallela obvia in Apocalypsi Johannis, cap. 12. v. 9. & cap. 20. v. 2. uti patet ex Rabbi Jehuda in Celi Jakar sol. 6. super Genef cap 3. v. 15. Plurimi interpretes dicunt, quod figmentum malum suam vim trahat a serpente antiquo; Hinc pariter Diabolum ipsam malam concupiscentiam vocarunt fine dubio quod ipse causa figmenti mali in homine extiterit, illudque etiam conspicitur ex Rabbi Ephrajimi Ir Gibborim, qui satis clare peccatum à Satana distinguit sol. 10. c. 1. Concupiscentia prava est robur Sammaelis; Et sol.55.c. 4. Concupiscentia prava trahit robur à Sammaele. Et Angelum mortis, fine dubio quoque, quod mortales fecisset homines, sicuti liquet ex Rabbi Maimonide in More Nevochim, Part.III. cap.22. pag. 398. Tale est quod in Talmud ajunt; Dixit Rabbi Schimeon Ben Lakisch: Ipse est Satan, hoc est, Adversarius; Ipse est figmentum malum; ipse est Angelus mortis; Ex Rabbi Bechai in Commentario super Genesin, cap.3:v.5. Porro jam ante nosti, quod serpens est Satan, & figmentum malum, & Angelus mortis; Et ex Rabbi Mose Alschech in Commentario super Legem, sol.13. Constat Satanam esse figmentum malum, Sammaelem, Angelum mortis. Ecce vero, si homo non peccaffet, in aeternum victurus fuisset, illo Satana in ate rnum absorpto. Idcirco omnibus modis pro viribus studuit eum in peccatum adducere. Non enim hoc in se prævalere potuit, quia sanctus erat Dei & adhæsit Creatori suo. Materia ejus erat pura, & facile contaminari nequibat. Ecquid vero ille fecit? Mulierem adiit, deceptu faciliorem viro, ut post seductionem illa adjutrix esset in seducendo marito, donec & ille seduceretur. retur. Atque hoc est quod Doctores l.m. dixerunt: Maritum, cum serpens loqueretur cum illa, non fuisse præsentem. Iverat enim in locis commodis terram habitabilem definiturus, ut perhibent ad comma (Ier. 11. 6.) non terram transfuit ibi vir neque habitavit ibi homo. Quid, quod mulier etiam illa non fuit ut fæmella cujusvis temporis. Extitit enim illa opus manuum Dei Benedicti, neque facile cogitationibus seduci potuit, ut quivis homo, cui a concupiscentia mala cogitationes suggeruntur ad malefaciendum. Idcirco artifice perito opus habebat sibi, qui proxeneta esset, quo se induceret, figmento malo scilicet, quod Satan est, & Samael, & oretenus cum illa locutus est, ut cogitationibus & verbis ageret. Adeo perito artifice opus habuit, quo proxeneta sive mediatoris vice uteretur, nempe serpente. Hic enim oris loco ei fuit, omnia verba vero promanabant e Samaele, qui indutus erat eo. Et quicquid serpens agebat, id ille peregit. Et quam concinna sunt verba in Pirche Rabbi Eliezeris, dum ait: Insedit Samael serpenti veluti eques equo; Hinc quoque Diabolum nomine usitatissimo vocarunt Samaelem, qui equitans super serpentem seduxerit Evam, apud Rabbi Maimonidem, sensum literalem in Allegoricum sive Mysticum convertentem, in More Nevochim Part. II. c. 30. At nec hoc prætereundum, quod in Medrasch adducunt Sapientes nostri, Serpentem
units.tr: Nor are there lacking, nor have there ever been lacking, countless distinguished Hebrews who plainly acknowledge that the Devil wretchedly deceived man by means of the serpent, a very crafty little creature, fitted as an instrument of his wickedness. Therefore, in Moses (Gen. 3:1), the serpent that attacked Eve is not to be understood as a mere serpent, but the Devil acted through the serpent as through an instrument. For this reason they commonly called the Devil נחש הקדמוני [the primeval serpent], or ancient serpent, a parallel phrase found in the Apocalypse of John, ch. 12:9 and ch. 20:2, as is clear from Rabbi Jehuda in Celi Jakar, fol. 6, on Gen. 3:15. Most interpreters say that the evil figment draws its power from the ancient serpent. Hence likewise they called the Devil the evil concupiscence itself, doubtless because he was the cause of the evil figment in man. This is also seen from Rabbi Ephraim in Ir Gibborim, who distinguishes sin from Satan quite clearly, fol. 10, ch. 1: Evil concupiscence is the strength of Samael; and fol. 55, ch. 4: Evil concupiscence draws its strength from Samael. And they call him the Angel of death, doubtless also because he made men mortal, as is plain from Rabbi Maimonides in More Nevochim, Part III, ch. 22, p. 398. Such is what they say in the Talmud: Rabbi Simeon ben Lakish said: He is Satan, that is, the Adversary; he is the evil figment; he is the Angel of death. From Rabbi Bechai in his commentary on Genesis, ch. 3:5: Furthermore, you already know that the serpent is Satan, and the evil figment, and the Angel of death. And from Rabbi Moses Alschech in his commentary on the Law, fol. 13: It is established that Satan is the evil figment, Samael, the Angel of death. Now indeed, if man had not sinned, he would have lived forever, Satan having been swallowed up for eternity. Therefore he strove by every means, as far as he could, to lead him into sin. For he could not prevail in himself, because he was holy to God and clung to his Creator. His substance was pure and could not easily be defiled. What then did he do? He approached the woman, more easily deceived than the man, so that after the seduction she might be a helper in seducing her husband, until he too was seduced. Hence also the learned teachers of blessed memory said that the husband was not present when the serpent spoke with her. For he had gone off to choose in suitable places a habitable land, as they relate on the verse (Jer. 11:6): "no man has passed through that land, nor has any man dwelt there." Moreover, that woman was not like an ordinary female of any age. For she was the work of the hands of God, blessed be he, and could not easily be seduced by thoughts, as any man is, to whom evil thoughts are suggested by the evil concupiscence for doing wrong. Therefore she needed a skilled craftsman as a go-between to lead her on, namely the evil figment, which is Satan and Samael, and he spoke with her by word of mouth so that he might act through her thoughts and words. So skilled a craftsman was needed to serve as a go-between or mediator, namely the serpent. For it served him as a mouth, and all the words came forth from Samael, who was clothed in it. And whatever the serpent did, he accomplished. And how elegant are the words in the Pirke of Rabbi Eliezer, when he says: Samael sat upon the serpent as a horseman upon a horse. Hence also they commonly called the Devil by the name Samael, who, riding upon the serpent, seduced Eve, according to Rabbi Maimonides, who turns the literal sense into an allegorical or mystical one, in More Nevochim, Part II, ch. 30. But this must not be passed over either: that our wise men, in the Midrash, bring in the serpent as ridden,

units.la: (Ier. 11. 6.) pentem equitatum fuisse, quantitatem ejus instar cameli, & sessorem ejus fuisse illum, qui decepit E-vam huncque sessorem fuisse Sammaelem, quod nomen absolute usurpant de Satana ; Et paulo post: Sic itaque apparet, quod Sammael sit ipse Satan, & quod per illud nomen, certi & occulti aliquid significetur, sicut per nomen Nachasch, hoc est, serpens. Dicunt etiam ; cum veniret serpens ad decipiendam Evam, fuit Sammael equitans super illum, & Deus irridebat camelum & sessorem ejus ; Sic Rabbi Eliezer in Capitulis narrat multis cap. 1;. quomodo Sammael descenderit e cœlis visurus creaturas Dei Benedicti, non invenerit astutiorem ad malefaciendum quam serpentem, qui figuram habuerit cameli, & cui inequitaverit, quomodo præterea serpens ex suggestu Sammaelis cum homine egerit, verbaque miscuerit, uti ex his patet: Sic etiam serpens quacunque opera patrabat & verba loquebatur, ea nonnisi ex suggestu Sammaelis egit; Caeterum pluribus Sammaelem describunt, referentes cum Targumistis ex Genef. 3. ¶. 6. & Job cap. 28. ¶ 7. quod Sammael fuerit Angelus mortis, quod Princeps fuerit aëris, quod per aërem volaverit, quod mortem toti mundo fuerit causatus, quod Princeps Esavi fuerit, uti loquitur Rabbi Isac Abarbanel in Commentario ad Danielem, pag. 30. col. 2. Quod SamSammael (it Princeps Esavi, & quod ipse, uti me-morant Sapientes felicis memoriæ, insederit serpen-ti, qui decepit Evam, quique adhuc sit Israeli Basi-liscus.
units.tr: (Gen. 3:1) (the serpent) was ridden, its size like that of a camel, and its rider was he who deceived Eve; and this rider was Samael, a name they use absolutely of Satan; and a little later: Thus it appears that Samael is Satan himself, and that by that name something certain and hidden is signified, just as by the name Nachash, that is, serpent. They also say; when the serpent came to deceive Eve, Samael was riding upon it, and God mocked the camel and its rider; so Rabbi Eliezer relates in the Chapters, ch. 1, how Samael came down from heaven to see the creatures of God, blessed be he, and found no craftier creature for doing evil than the serpent, which had the shape of a camel and which he rode upon; moreover, how the serpent, from the vantage of Samael, acted with the man and mingled words, as is clear from these: Thus also the serpent, in whatever deeds it performed and whatever words it spoke, acted only from the vantage of Samael. Otherwise they describe Samael in many ways, reporting with the Targumists, from Gen. 3:6 and Job ch. 28:7, that Samael was the Angel of death, that he was the Prince of the air, that he flew through the air, that he caused death for the whole world, that he was the Prince of Esau, as Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel says in his commentary on Daniel, p. 30, col. 2: That Samael is the Prince of Esau; and that he himself, as our wise men of blessed memory report, sat upon the serpent that deceived Eve, and that he is still the basilisk of Israel.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Sed nunc alia adducamus Hebræorum testimonia, ut ita planum fiat, nequaquam serpentem hunc nudam fuisse bestiam, sed Angelum malum in Serpente latitasse, sicque per illum locutum fuisse, sicut patet ex Rabbi Saadia Haggaon apud Rabbi Abraham Aben Esram in Commentario, loco citato: Dixit Rabbi Saadia Gaon, quandoquidem explora-tum est nobis quod non sit sermo scientiæ nisi in homine solo, cogimur dicere quod serpens, sicut & asi-na Bileami, non locuti sunt, sed Angelus quispiam locutus est per eos; Ex Rabbi Bechai in Com-mentario super Genes. ad cap. 3. v. 15. Non sunt nobis inimicitiæ cum serpente magis, quam cum cæteris reptilibus. Quamobrem Scriptura hæc mystice innuit eum qui in serpente occultabatur. Corpus enim serpentis callidi erat instrumentum aptum ad recipiendum virtutem conjunctam cum eo. Et ille est qui Evam peccare fecit, unde mors intravit in omnem progeniem ejus. Et hæc est inimicitia inter serpentem & inter semen mulieris. Et hoc est mysterium linguæ sanctæ, quod serpens alibi appellatur Saraph, juxta nomen quo Angelus etiam etiam appellatur Saraph; Et ex Commentario ad cap. 3. v. 14. praecedentem; Jehova igitur dum dejecit erectam staturam ejus, (serpentis) dejecit simul etiam virtutem illam quae se ei uni-verat, quam dejecit & praecipitavit deorsum, e gradibus caelestibus, qui sunt Trestrium in Deo. Nam non es Deus volens iniquitatem, non manebit tecum malus. Propterea ille ejectus est de omnibus illis tribus mansionibus supernis, planeficut leprosi solebant ejici e tribus mansionibus in terris. Et jam nosti quod virtus illa coeperat linguam tollere adversus Creatorem suum, ac ob id lepra spirituali percussa est, & praecipitata est de excellentia & dignitate sua; Illud pariter liquet ex Rabbi Samuel Sirfain Mekor Chajim, cum sol. 23. sic inquit: Qui recte vult intelligere verba Genes. cap. 3. v. 15. ita intelligat, Diabolus plenarias inimicitias gerit adversus omnes qui Deo inservire studdesignt, & operam omnem eo convertit, ut eos ad errorum praecipitia seducat; Et ex libro Caphtor, sol. 125. Fingmentum malum provenit ab antiquo serpente, qui venenum suum in Evam inspuit, & omnes homines seduxit, juxta testimonium Genes. cap. 3. v. 15; Egregie quoque Rabbi Maimonides in More Nevochim, Part. II. cap. 30. Ex quo serpens venit ad Evam, humorem vel sordes projecit in Evam: Israelitis, qui steterunt in monte Sinai, sordes illae abstergantur: Gentibus quae non steterunt in mon-te
units.tr: But let us now bring forward other Hebrew testimonies, so that it becomes plain that this serpent was by no means a bare beast, but that an evil angel lay hidden in the serpent and spoke through it. This is evident from Rabbi Saadia Gaon, cited by Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra in his commentary (passage cited above): Rabbi Saadia Gaon said: since we know for certain that speech belongs to man alone, we are compelled to say that the serpent did not speak, any more than Balaam's ass did, but that some angel spoke through them. From Rabbi Bechai in his commentary on Genesis, on chapter 3, verse 15: We have no enmity with the serpent more than with the other reptiles. Therefore Scripture hints mystically at him who was hidden in the serpent. For the body of the crafty serpent was a fitting instrument for receiving the power joined with it. And it is he who made Eve sin, whence death entered into all her offspring. This is the enmity between the serpent and the seed of the woman. And this is the mystery of the holy tongue, that the serpent is elsewhere called Saraph [שָׂרָף], according to the name by which the angel also is called Saraph. And from the commentary on the preceding verse, chapter 3, verse 14: Therefore when Jehovah cast down the serpent's upright stature, he at the same time cast down that power which had attached itself to it alone, and he hurled it down from the heavenly steps, which are the three dwelling places in God. For you are not a God who wills iniquity; the evil one shall not remain with you. Hence he was cast out from all three of those supernal dwelling places, just as lepers used to be cast out from the three dwelling places on earth. And you already know that this power had begun to lift its tongue against its Creator, and for this reason it was struck with spiritual leprosy and thrown down from its excellence and dignity. That is equally clear from Rabbi Samuel Sirfain in Mekor Chajim, where on folio 23 he says: Whoever wishes to understand rightly the words of Genesis 3:15 should understand them thus: the Devil wages complete enmity against all who strive to serve God, and turns all his effort toward leading them astray into the precipices of error. And from the book Caphtor, folio 125: The evil fabrication arose from the ancient serpent, who spat his poison into Eve and seduced all men, according to the testimony of Genesis 3:15. Rabbi Maimonides also, excellently, in More Nevochim, part II, chapter 30: Since the serpent came to Eve, it cast a humour or filth into Eve. Let those filths be wiped away from the Israelites who stood on Mount Sinai; but from the Gentiles who did not stand on Mount

units.la: Note: the printed text is partly illegible in the scan; some words above are uncertain. te Sinai, sordes illa non absterguntur. Animum igitur intende & ad istud; Sic Autor Jalkut Chadasch pag. 12. col. 1. bene duplicem distinguit serpentem: Intentio serpentis & sessoris ejus erat, ad defectionem quoque concitare hominem, ideoque dixerunt: Eritis sicut Elohim, quasi voluissent dicere sicut ille sessor, qui est Sammael; Eritis similes rebellando Deo; Calculum apponit Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, quando in libello de Fragilitate humana, pag. 40. & 41. sic inquit: Hæc fuit causa lapsus Adami. Nam tanta gloria invidens Dæmon, assumsit serpentis speciem tanquam instrumentum malitiæ suæ conveniens, cum issit astutissimus inter omnes animantes, itaque sub falsa quadam, & apparente ratione, eritis velut Deus, & cognoscetis bonum & malum, seducit partem magis debilem, puta Evam, quæ deinde imposuit marito, cumq; eo decidit in omnis generis miserias & calamitates. Quippe Deus spoliavit ambos omnibus prærogativis illorum, quæ dederat, ac eliminavit ex horto Edem, aut delectationis, in quo solo vita erat vitalis; Cæterum Diabolum per serpentem intelligendum esse, probat mos circumcisionis hodiernus, quo præputium hanc quoque ob causam in arenam projiciunt, ut hoc pabulo se reficiat serpens antiquus; Imo sententiam hanc Cabbalistica quadam ratione firmare laborant ex vocibus Hebraicis braicis ℥ Satan, & ⅼⅼⅼ Serpens, quod cum in numeris conveniant, necesse quoque sit, ut eadem sit significatio, ita Rabbi Bechai loco saepe citato: Tantum numerorum continet vox Satan, quantum habet serpens, nisi quod una littera superflua sit in Satan.
units.tr: te Sinai, the filth is not wiped away. Look therefore with attention also at this. Thus the author of Jalkut Chadasch, page 12, column 1, rightly distinguishes a double serpent: The intention of the serpent and of its rider was to stir up man also to rebellion; therefore they said: You shall be like Elohim, as if they had wished to say, like that rider who is Sammael; you shall be alike in rebelling against God. Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel adds his own reckoning in his little book on the frailty of man, pages 40 and 41, where he says: This was the cause of Adam's fall. For the Demon, envious of so great a glory, took on the form of the serpent as an instrument suited to his malice, since it was the most crafty of all animals; and so, under a certain false and plausible pretext, "you shall be as God, knowing good and evil," he seduced the weaker part, namely Eve, who then imposed it on her husband, and together with him fell into miseries and calamities of every kind. Indeed God stripped both of all the privileges which he had given them, and expelled them from the garden of Eden, that is, of delight, in which alone there was vital life. Moreover, that the Devil is to be understood through the serpent is proved by the present custom of circumcision, by which the foreskin is thrown into the sand for this reason, so that the ancient serpent may feed on this food. Indeed they labour to confirm this opinion by a certain Cabbalistic reasoning from the Hebrew words Satan [שָׂטָן] and Serpent [נָחָשׁ], which, since they agree in their numerical values, must also have the same meaning. So Rabbi Bechai, cited often above: The word Satan contains just as many numbers as the serpent has, except that there is one letter too many in Satan.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Non opus nunc operosius, altiusque ex Judaeis inquirere Magistris, quae causa lapsus in primo exiterit homine, cum illa fuerit hominis voluntas mutabilis, indifferensque, cum libero condita arbitrio, quaesive impulsu nudi serpentis, sive instinctu Diaboli Sammaelis Legem de non comedendo exarbore cognitionis boni & mali violavit, sicque rea facta, uti patet ex Rabbi Raphaele in Orach Chajim, sol. 2. Deus ex gratia sua creavit hominem ad imaginem suam. Habuit quoque ille facultatem creatorem suum cognoscendi, inque viis ejus perfecte ambulandi, ad finem intentionis creationis suae assequendum. Elegit autem libere malum; Et ex Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel infinitis locis, quorum unum solum ex libro III. de Resurrectione Mortuorum, pag. 329.330. adducemus: Quia Adamus liber creatus est, & cum in hortu Edenis ageret, libero arbitrio praeditus fuit. Sed Samael, sive satanas invidens homini eam gloriam, commutavit se in serpentem, & et eo perduxit Adamum, ut in peccatum labere-tur.
units.tr: There is no need now to inquire more laboriously and deeply of the Jewish masters what caused the fall of the first man. His will was changeable and indifferent, created with free choice. Whether he was moved by the naked serpent or instigated by the devil Samael, he violated the law not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and so became guilty. This is clear from Rabbi Raphael in Orach Chajim, fol. 2: God in his grace created man in his own image. He also had the ability to know his Creator and to walk perfectly in his ways, so as to attain the end for which he was created. But he freely chose evil; and from Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, in countless places, of which we will adduce only one from book III of his De Resurrectione Mortuorum, pp. 329-330: Because Adam was created free, and while he was in the garden of Eden he was endowed with free will. But Samael, or Satan, envying man that glory, changed himself into a serpent, and led Adam by this means into falling into sin.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Docent Rabbini, Lapsus effecta describentes, imaginemque deperditam deplorantes, corpus primi hominis, quod lucidum, perfectum, proceraque admodum staturae volebant, per peccatum fuisse obscuratum, imminutum, ac deperditum, ex Psalmo 139. ¥. 5. Et posuisti supra me manum tuam; Quod per lapsum pulchritudinem amiserit & splendorem, quo corpus totum circumdatum fuerat, ex Bereschit Rabba cap. 12. suffulti verbis Jobi cap. 14. Mutasti faciem ejus, & eliminasti eum, ex Paradiso scilicet; Hinc se videns nudum, timuerit, cum lux post peccatum discesserit, ut loquitur Rabbi Elia Hajin in Reschit Chochma lib. 1. cap. 15. Quod post commestos fructus ex arbore scientiae boni & mali, debilem & labefactatam acquisiverit naturam, quae pari proclivitate ferebatur in vitium & virtutem, sicque multa excogitasse ratiocinia, ex Ecclesiastis cap. 7. ¥. 29, teste Rabbi Mose Gerundensi cum aliis Hebraeorum Sapientibus; Quod nube gloriae, qua rectus fuerat homo integer, orbatus fuerit post lapsum, sicuti refert Rabbi Eliefer in Pirke cap. 14. Quale fuit vestimentum primi hominis? Pel-
units.tr: The rabbis, describing the effects of the fall and lamenting the lost image, teach that the body of the first man, which they held to be bright, perfect and very tall, was through sin darkened, diminished and lost. This is supported by Psalm 139:5: And you laid your hand upon me. Through the fall he lost the beauty and splendour with which his whole body had been surrounded, as Bereshit Rabba ch. 12 says, supported by the words of Job ch. 14: You changed his face and cast him out, namely from Paradise. Hence, seeing himself naked, he was afraid, since the light departed after the sin, as Rabbi Elijah Hajin says in Reshit Chochma book 1 ch. 15. After eating the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, he acquired a weak and enfeebled nature, which was carried with equal inclination toward vice and virtue, and so devised many arguments (Ecclesiastes 7:29), as Rabbi Moses of Gerona testifies along with other Hebrew sages. After the fall he was deprived of the cloud of glory that had enveloped upright and whole man, as Rabbi Eliezer relates in Pirke ch. 14: What was the garment of the first man? Skin-

units.la: Y lis ex onycha ; & nubes gloriæ obumbrabat eum. Postquam autem comederat ex fructu arboris exu-tus fuit pelle onychæ, & conspexit fe nudum, atq; re-motafuit ab eo nubes gloriæ, sicut dicitur Genef. cap. 3. Et dixit quis indicavit tibi, quod nudus effes? Nonne de arbore, quam præceperam tibi, &c. Quod per peccatum insignem scientiæ par-tem amiserit, occupatusque maxime in rebus fuerit temporalibus, uti ostendit Rabbi Me-nafseh Ben Israel in libello de Fragilitate hu-mana, pag. 41. Perdidit Adam primo magnam doctrinæ partem. Nam cum effet ingenium ejus, & intellectus fpeculativus, & in rebus spiritualibus semper occupatus, redditus est intellectus prac-ticus, districtus magis in rebus temporalibus, ac cum scientia illa infusa, ac supernaturali, qua lata-batur, eum paulatim amisit. Hinc Rabbi Eliah Hain in Refit Hochma lib. 11. cap. vi. dicit, Adamum per materiam & tenebras, in quibus morabatur corpus ejus, attraxisse impossibilitatem perfectam attendendi studiis Theologicis, aut rebus, quarum objectum prorsus sit spirituale; Sic Rabbi Bechai in Commentario sæpe citato ad hunc locum pluribus describit, quomodo homo concu-piscentias induerit peccando, & apprehende-rit defectum possessionis eximiæ, quam initio habuerit; Sic Rabbi Moses Maimonides in More Nevochim Part. III. cap. 12. postquam expoexposuisset Figmentum malum esse ipsum Satanam, quod à Satana in homine excitatum fuerit,enarrat quomodo figmentum malum majus dominium in homine exerceat, quam figmentum bonum: Ideo dicunt vocari Figmentum malum, Regem magnum; Figmentum autem bonum,puerum pauperem & sapientem, Hanc Imaginis divinæ violationem, peccatique hæc effecta videntur expressisse Talmudici in Tractatu Sota, sol. 5. quando scripserunt Adamum אדם his tribus constare literis, quod fuerit מות, דם, אפר, Cinis, sanguis, atque Fel.
units.tr: of onyx; and a cloud of glory overshadowed him. But after he had eaten from the fruit of the tree, he was stripped of the skin of onyx and saw himself naked, and the cloud of glory was removed from him, as it is said in Genesis ch. 3: And he said, who told you that you were naked? Have you not eaten from the tree which I commanded you?, etc. Through sin he lost a remarkable part of knowledge and became occupied chiefly with temporal things, as Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel shows in his little book De Fragilitate Humana, p. 41: Adam first lost a great part of doctrine. For since his mind was speculative and always occupied with spiritual things, his practical intellect became more bound up with temporal things, and he gradually lost that infused and supernatural knowledge in which he had rejoiced. Hence Rabbi Elijah Hajin, in Reshit Chochma book 2 ch. 6, says that Adam, through matter and the darkness in which his body dwelt, drew upon himself a complete incapacity to attend to theological studies, or to things whose object is wholly spiritual. So too Rabbi Bechai, in the commentary often cited, describes at length on this passage how man, by sinning, took on concupiscences and grasped the loss of the outstanding possession he had at first. So Rabbi Moses Maimonides, in More Nevochim part III ch. 12, after explaining that the evil inclination is Satan himself, who was stirred up in man by Satan, relates how the evil inclination exercises a greater dominion over man than the good inclination: Therefore they say that the evil inclination is called a great king, but the good inclination a poor and wise boy. The Talmudists, in tractate Sota fol. 5, seem to have expressed this violation of the divine image and these effects of sin when they wrote that the name Adam [אדם] consists of three letters, which are [מות] death, [דם] blood and [אפר] ash: ash, blood, and gall.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Confitentur Judæi corporis mortem peccati primi fuisse effectum, hominemque ob lapsum immortalitate corporis fuisse privatum, hinc ab arbore vitæ separatum, & è Paradiso ejectum, vocantes mortem pœnam, stipendiumque peccati, quod necessario illud debeat sequi, unde sapientum Hebræorum apud Rabbi Maimonidem dictum in More Nevochim Part.III.cap.17. בלא חטא אין מות Non est mors absque peccato, neque castigationes sine peccato; negantes constanter mortem naturæ sequelam esse, seu hominem naturali quadam necessitate mori aliquando debuisse, quod opinio hæc à nullo fit vel acceptata, vel proprobata, pugnet cum authoritate sacrarum literarum, neque Veterum Sapientum consensu nitatur, uti loquitur Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel lib. III. de Resurrectione Mortuorum, pag. 340. demonstratumque pluribus ex mente Hebraeorum, cap. 9 §. 6, 7. Theologiae nostrae Judaicae; Quibus solum addimus quae habet Rabbi Eliezer in Pirke cap. 14. Foeminae autem impertiit novem maledictiones & mortem, quae sunt: afflictio sanguinis menstruati: sanguinis virginitatis ejus: afflictio conceptionis in utero: dolor partus: molestia educationis liberorum: caput velatum instar lugentis: neque radat illud nisi ob fornicationem: perforavit etiam aurem ejus veluti mancipium aeternum: ut tanquam ancilla serviat marito suo: quod non fidelis seu idonea sit ad testimonium: atque post haec cuncta mors. Eduxit Adamum, & decrevit contra illum novem maledictiones & mortem: succidit robur ejus, cum immunditiae fluxus feminis, breviorem reddidit statuam, cum forditie coitus; ut seminaret triticum; meteret spinas vel urticas, & cibus ejus esset herba terrae veluti bestia: panis ejus esset cum sollicitudine; esca ejus cum sudore; & post haec omnia mors.
units.tr: The Jews confess that death was the effect of the first sin, and that man, because of the fall, was deprived of the immortality of the body. Hence he was separated from the tree of life and cast out of Paradise. They call death a punishment and the wages of sin, which must necessarily follow it. Hence the saying of the Hebrew sages in Maimonides, More Nevochim part III ch. 17: [בלא חטא אין מות] There is no death without sin, nor chastisements without sin. They constantly deny that death is a consequence of nature, or that man had at some time to die by natural necessity. No one has accepted or approved this opinion; it conflicts with the authority of the sacred letters and does not rest on the consensus of the ancient sages, as Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel says in book III of De Resurrectione Mortuorum, p. 340, and as is demonstrated by many arguments from the mind of the Hebrews in our Jewish Theology, ch. 9, §§ 6, 7. To this we only add what Rabbi Eliezer has in Pirke ch. 14: But upon the woman he bestowed nine curses and death, which are: the affliction of menstrual blood; the blood of her virginity; the affliction of conception in the womb; the pain of childbirth; the trouble of raising children; the head veiled like one mourning, and not to be shaved except for fornication; her ear pierced like a perpetual slave, so that she serves her husband as a maidservant; that she is not faithful or fit to bear witness; and after all these, death. He brought Adam out and decreed against him nine curses and death: he cut down his strength with the flux of uncleanness for women; he made his stature shorter with the pains of intercourse; that he should sow wheat and reap thorns or nettles, and his food should be the herb of the field like a beast; his bread should be eaten with anxiety and his food with sweat; and after all these, death.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Sed licet Judaei peccati sequelas multis describant, ipsamque mortem corporalem inter peccati effecta numerent, imo Adami peccapeccatum (spirituale quandoque vocent, asse-rentes cum Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, de Fragilitate humana, pag. 44. Quod per peccatum perdiderit justitiam & rectitudinem, in qua fuerat creatus; Et cum Rabbi Bechai in Commentario ad Legem, sol. 15. col. 1. 2. Quod peccando justitiam amiserit concreatam, & originariam; negant tamen omnes fere quotquot vivunt, non sine ingenti animi contentione, homini per lapsum ademptum esse liberum ad bonum arbitrium, voluntatem humanam servam factam esse peccatorum, tantumque ad mala inclinare, affirmantes, hominem post lapsum quin etiam liberrimo gaudere ad bonum arbitrio, nec solum bene uti voluntate in naturalibus, verum quoque in ipsis spiritualibus, adeo ut fortunae, infortuniique sui ipse maneat faber; Negant quoque omnes, per mortem, quam ex peccato traxit, spiritualem, aeternamque intelligendam esse mortem, sed solam mortem corporalem, sicuti hoc non solum ex illorum fluit Religionis principiis, quae hominem Legi Mosaicae credentem, secundumque hanc operantem, vitae & aeternae mortis constituunt Dominum. Sed satis clare quoque docetur a Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel lib. III. de Resurrectione Mortuorum, pag. 333. Hic certe con-flat stat pœnam Adamo peccaturo interminatam, fuisse mortem corporalem; Et pag. 334. Consentaneum est ut ejiciatur foràs, & morte ista corporali afficiatur, cujus se reum reddidit; Respondet quoque ibidem Rabbi Menasseh ad verba Genel. cap. 2. ŷ. 17. Moriendo morieris; Quod quidem la-tissimo sensu accipienda sint, adducens testi-monium Rabbi Hanæ Bar Haninæ ex Bere-schit Rabba: Moriendo morieris, mortuus est Adam, mortua est Eva : defuncti us est ille, defuncti sunt posteri ejus; Non vero omnes mortis spe-cies, quæ in Scripturis veniunt, sint intelligen-dæ; Sic quoque Judæus Anonymus apud Coccejum in Consideratione Responsionis Judaicæ pronunciat verbis expressis Quæ-stione 23, quod pœnæ peccati Adamo debitæ omnes fuerint corporales; Pari modo Rabbi Isac Bar Abraham in Munimine fidei Part. 1. cap. 11. putat mortem corporalem Adami pœ-nam fuisse gravissimam, cum ita loquitur: Et quia mors corporalis pœnarum est gravissima, ac reliquas pœnas corporales superat, ideo sub ejus nomine comprehenduntur cætera mala quibus humanum genus fuit affectum; Scribitque quomodo voces, moriendo morieris, non solam respiciant mortem, sed simul quoque reliquas pœnas corporales, quæ Adamo post peccatum irrogatæ sunt, & de quibus est sermo Gen. c. 3. Madledi. ledicta esto terra propter te, cum dolore commedes proventum ejus, omnibus diebus vitæ tuæ. Et spinam & carduum proferet tibi &c. In sudore vultus tui vescéris pane, &c. Refert præterea quomodo verba, morte morieris ad mortem corporalem tantum attineant, cum in pulverem nil reverti possit, nisi id quod pulvis fuerat; interim non negat quoque, quod simul mors animæ inclusa intelligatur, quatenus divina transgreditur præcepta.
units.tr: But although the Jews describe many consequences of sin, and count bodily death itself among the effects of sin, indeed they call Adam's sin sometimes a spiritual sin, asserting with Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel (De Fragilitate humana, p. 44) that through sin he lost the righteousness and uprightness in which he had been created, and with Rabbi Bechai (in his Commentary on the Law, fol. 15, col. 1, 2) that by sinning he lost the original righteousness created with him; nevertheless almost all who are alive today deny, and with no small vehemence, that free choice toward the good was taken from man by the fall, that the human will was made a slave of sins and inclined only to evil. They affirm instead that after the fall man enjoys a most free choice toward the good, and uses his will well not only in natural matters but also in spiritual ones, so that he himself remains the maker of his own fortune and misfortune. They also deny that the death which he drew from sin is to be understood as spiritual and eternal death, but only bodily death. This follows not only from the principles of their religion, which make the man who believes in the Mosaic Law and acts according to it the master of life and of eternal death. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel also teaches this quite clearly in Book III of De Resurrectione Mortuorum (p. 333): Here it is certain that the penalty threatened to Adam had he sinned was bodily death; and (p. 334): It is fitting that he be cast out and afflicted with that bodily death, of which he made himself guilty. In the same place Rabbi Menasseh also answers the words of Genesis 2:17, In dying you shall die, saying that they must be taken in the widest sense, citing the testimony of Rabbi Hanina Bar Hanina from Bereshit Rabba: In dying you shall die: Adam died, Eve died; he died, and his posterity died. Yet not all the kinds of death that occur in the Scriptures are to be understood in this way. Likewise the anonymous Jew cited by Coccejus in his Consideratio Responsionis Judaicae states in express words, in Question 23, that all the penalties owed to Adam for sin were bodily. In the same way Rabbi Isaac Bar Abraham in the Munimen fidei, Part 1, chapter 11, thinks that Adam's bodily death was the most grievous penalty, when he speaks thus: And because bodily death is the most grievous of punishments, and surpasses the other bodily punishments, therefore under its name are included the other evils with which the human race was afflicted. He writes too how the words in dying you shall die refer not only to death but at the same time to the other bodily penalties imposed on Adam after the sin, and of which the text of Genesis 3 speaks: Cursed is the ground for your sake; in toil you shall eat of it all the days of your life. It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, etc. In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, etc. He further explains how the words you shall surely die pertain only to bodily death, since nothing can return to dust except what was dust; meanwhile he does not deny that the death of the soul is also included, insofar as the divine precepts are transgressed.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Imo quamvis Judæi moderni, cum Veribus tateantur, mortem temporalem pœnam esse peccati, mortemque corporalem propter Adami peccatum transiisse & pervenisse in omnes homines, inculcantes ex Paraphrasi Chaldaica in Ecclesiastem, cap. 7. ℣. 29. quod Adam & Eva arcessiverint sibi mortem, & omnibus, qui morantur super terram; Et referentes ex codice Talmudico Schabbat cap. 5. quod licet quatuor hi, Benjamin filius Patriarchæ Jacobi, Amram Pater Mosis, Isai pater Davidis, & Chilhab filius Davidis, ob proprium peccatum non fuerint morte condemnati, mortui tamen fuerint ex solo illo consilio serpentis, Et licet Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel per totum libellum de Fragilitate humana, nihil aliud videatur agere, quam Adami posteros poenarum corporalium haeredes declarare, interim tamen liquet, Judaeos recentiores & sibi & nobis facum facere insignem, vel intelligentes mortem temporalem, quam ipsi subeunt, non poenam esse peccati Adami, sed proprii, quod ipsi commiserunt, quaque remissionem peccatorum obtinere se sperant; vel communem istam legem moriendi propter peccatum primum impositam nimis restringentes, extenuantesque, quod scilicet ex elementis corporeis simus compositi, nec arboris vitae copia relicta nobis sit, postquam illa ob peccatum Adami ex oculis hominum fuit remota, uti legimus apud Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel de Fragilitate humana, pag. 112. Nempe mors inde provenit, quod ex quatuor elementis simus compositi, nec arboris vitae copia nobis esse potuit. Videmus enim, Adamum, postquam peccasset, si ex arbore vitae ista comedisset, immortalem se potuisset reddere. Hoc enim verba ista indicant in divinis literis: Ne fit, ut extendat manum suam, & edat, ac vivat semper: qua de causa quoque ex Paradiso fuit ejectus.
units.tr: Indeed, although modern Jews, when they truly acknowledge the Scriptures, admit that temporal death is the punishment of sin, and that bodily death passed through Adam's sin and came upon all men, inculcating from the Chaldee Paraphrase on Ecclesiastes 7:29 that Adam and Eve brought death upon themselves and upon all who dwell on the earth, and relating from the Talmudic tractate Shabbat, chapter 5, that although these four, Benjamin son of the patriarch Jacob, Amram father of Moses, Jesse father of David, and Chileab son of David, were not condemned to death for their own sin, they nevertheless died solely from that counsel of the serpent; and although Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, throughout his little book De Fragilitate humana, seems to do nothing else than declare the posterity of Adam heirs of bodily punishments, it is nonetheless clear that the more recent Jews play a remarkable trick both on themselves and on us.
