Either they understand the temporal death which they undergo not as the penalty of Adam's sin but of their own, which they committed, and by which they hope to obtain forgiveness of sins; or they restrict and weaken too much the common law of dying imposed on account of the first sin, namely that we are composed of bodily elements, and that no abundance of the tree of life was left to us after it was removed from the eyes of men on account of Adam's sin, as we read in Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, De Fragilitate humana, p. 112: Death indeed arises from this, that we are composed of the four elements, and an abundance of the tree of life could not be ours. For we see that Adam, if after he had sinned he had eaten from that tree of life, could have made himself immortal. For these words in the divine letters indicate this: lest he stretch out his hand, and eat, and live forever; for which reason also he was cast out of Paradise.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Ihficiantur ex moderna Synagoga omnes, peccatum Adami singulis imputari hominibus, reatumque ex peccato contractum ad universos transmittri posteros, mortemque animarum aeternam ob peccatum Adami totum occupasse genus humanum, hincque omnes necessario tantum nasci malos, miserosque ipsaque divina imagine destitutos, ne teneantur, tum propriam fateri turpitudinem & impotentiam, tum ne cogantur ad Messiam, animarum ducem spiritualem recurrere, reatum gravissimum, qui propriis expungi non poterat viribus, in ipsum transferre, siccque per imputationem mortis ejus salvari, & ab aeterna morte liberari; Quare non mirum quod peccatum Adami extenuent, occisionem Abelis a Caino factam gravius nominantes peccatum, quod mille partibus majus quam illud, nec tanta tamen illi annectatur poena; Quod animae posterorum non potuerint peccare, quia non erant ex Adamo, sed ex Deo Creatore; Quod non ejus fuerit naturae, ut aeternam posset mereri damnationem, non solum Adami, verum etiam posterorum ejus; Quod contra Dei misericordiam esse videatur, tam severe peccatum punire in Auctoribus & posteris; Quod Adam non persona publica, sed privata fuerit; Quod mille repugnet Scripturae locis; sicuti haec & alia non ipsis solum verbis Judaeorum exprimemus, sed simul mox ostendemus, quomodo quo recentiores, eo pejores facti sint Judæi, nec consentientem secum habeant veteris Synagogæ doctrinam; Sit itaque primo hujus rei testis luculentus, Judæus Anonymus, apud Coccejum, Quæstione 23. sic inquiens: An Iudeia gnoscant peccatum cum quo omnes nascimur, etsi negent, quæ negationis causæ? Iudei peccatum originale negant idque gravissimus de causis. Nam locus peccati in animo solum consistit, omnesque animæ originem suam ducunt non ex Adamo, sed ex Deo Creatore, unde sequitur animas posterorum Adami non potuisse peccare. Peccatum in anima consistere patet, est enim illud vitium seu delictum per animam vel intellectum perpetratum. Et Scriptura aperte dicit, anima ista exscindetur & peccatum ejus in ea. Hinc jam perspici potest peccatum in anima consistere. Animas similiter a Deo creari absque ullo medio, testatur Esaias: spiritus a me illigatur, & animas ego feci. Idem Ezechiel confirmat dicens: omnes animæ meæ sunt, tam anima patris quam filii, meæ sunt. Anima quæ peccavit, morietur. Hinc ergo consequentia certa est ac evidens: animas posterorum Adami in ipso non potuisse peccare, omne genus humanum nasci obnoxium pœnis peccato Adami debitis, quæ cum omnes corporales exstant, ad omnes etiam liberos ejus secundum corpus attinent, quatenus corporales ejus liberi sunt. Quemadmodum si quis in servitutem tutem mancipetur, omnes illius liberi servi fiunt, utpote ex patre servo prognati. Atque hoc durabit usque ad illud tempus, quo Deus promisit mundum in pristinam suam perfectionem restituere, dicens per Iesaiam Prophetam cap.25. ¶. 10. Mors in æternum absorbebitur, Deusq; lachrymas ab omnium faciebus abstergèt, & auferet opprobrium populi sui in universa terra. Nam Dominus dixit: In illo tempore dicetur: Ecce hic est Deus noster in quem exspectavimus & ipse servabit nos. Hic est Dominus quem exspectamus. Gaudebimus & exultabimus in salute ipsius &c.
units.tr: They maintain, all of the modern Synagogue, that the sin of Adam is imputed to each individual person, that the guilt contracted through sin is passed on to all his descendants, and that the eternal death of souls, owing to the sin of Adam, has seized the whole human race. Hence all are necessarily born only wicked and wretched, and stripped of the divine image itself. They do this so that they need not confess their own baseness and impotence, and so that they need not be compelled to take refuge in the Messiah, the spiritual leader of souls. They wish to transfer the most grievous guilt, which could not be wiped away by their own strength, onto him, and so be saved through the imputation of his death and be freed from eternal death. It is therefore no wonder that they minimise Adam's sin, calling the slaying of Abel by Cain a greater sin, one a thousand times greater than that, and yet no such great punishment is attached to it. They say that the souls of his posterity could not have sinned, because they were not from Adam but from God the Creator. They say that it was not of the nature of Adam's sin, or of his posterity's, to deserve eternal damnation. They say that it seems contrary to God's mercy to punish sin so severely in the authors and in their descendants. They say that Adam was not a public but a private person. They say that it contradicts a thousand passages of Scripture. We will set out these and other points not only in the Jews' own words, but will also soon show how the more recent Jews have become worse the later they came, and how they do not hold to the doctrine of the older Synagogue. Let the first witness of this matter be the clear one: an anonymous Jew, cited by Coccejus, Question 23, who speaks thus: "Do the Jews acknowledge the sin with which we are all born, even though they deny it? What is the cause of their denial? The Jews deny original sin, and that for very serious reasons. For the seat of sin lies only in the mind, and all souls derive their origin not from Adam but from God the Creator; hence it follows that the souls of Adam's posterity could not have sinned." That sin resides in the soul is plain, for it is a vice or offence committed by the soul or the intellect. And Scripture plainly says that "that soul shall be cut off, and its sin is in it." From this it can now be seen that sin resides in the soul. Isaiah bears witness that souls are likewise created by God without any intermediary: "The spirit goes forth from me, and I made the souls." Ezekiel confirms the same, saying: "All souls are mine, the soul of the father as well as the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins shall die." From this, then, the consequence is certain and evident: the souls of Adam's posterity could not have sinned in him, yet the whole human race is born liable to the punishments owed to Adam's sin. Since these punishments are all bodily, they also reach all his children according to the body, insofar as his children are bodily. "Just as if someone is handed over into slavery, all his children become slaves, as being born of a slave father." And this will last until that time when God promised to restore the world to its original perfection, saying through the prophet Isaiah, chapter 25, verse 10: "Death shall be swallowed up for ever, and the Lord God shall wipe away tears from all faces, and shall take away the reproach of his people from all the earth." For the Lord said: "In that day it shall be said: Behold, this is our God, for whom we have waited, and he will save us. This is the Lord whom we have waited for. We will rejoice and be glad in his salvation, etc."

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Patet hæc sententia quam maxime ex Judæo, Auctore Nizzachon, apud Munsterum, in Evangelio Matthæi, pag. 125. qui varias præterea adfert rationes, quare imputationem peccati primi rejiciant, insuperque negent mortem æternam non transfivisse ad omnes posteros, cum sic loquitur: Interroga Hæreticum (Christianum indigitat) nunquid vos creditis, quod Dominus impertit misericordias omnibus creaturis suis, & omnes proprietates ejus sunt pietas & veritas erga creaturas suas? In fiducia harum proprietatum accedimus quotidie ante conspectum ejus, quem admodum ait David: Miserere mei Deus secundum pietatem tuam: secundum multitudinem miserationum tuarum dele iniquitates tates meas. Praterea dicit Dominus : quoniam non defidero mortem morientis, sed ut convertatur a viis suis & vivat: & vos quoque creditis quod in magnitudine miserationum suarum sit extensa manus ejus ut suscipiat poenitentes. Idsi ita est, quomodo ascendit super corvestrum, quod venerit Dominus cum tanta severitate contra primum hominem, ut illum vinctum teneret propter rem exiguam, nempe propter morsum pomi unius, illum perderet in hoc seculo atq; in futuro, & non ipsum tantum, sed & omnes posteros ejus: qui tamen errans hoc fecit, cum non fuerit adhuc in eo cognitio, sicut dicitur: Et aperti sunt oculi amborum & cognoverunt quod nudi essent. Hæc autem apertio fuit in oculo sapientiæ. Quin in occisione Habel, fuit transgressio illa mille partibus major quam ista, & tamen non annectitur illi poena tanta; Sic Rabbi Isac, Bar Abraham subsannat, refutatque Nazarenos, quod perhibeant Adamum cum filiis, posterisque, imo ipsos Sanctos Patriarchas, Prophetasque morte animarum aeterna, ob unicum facinus in arbore cognitionis commissum, fuisse affectos, inque infernum detrusos, Messiam vero Deum nostrum morte sua has animas a perditione liberasse; Absit enim, scribit Rabbi in Munimine fidei, Part. I. cap. II. Deo Servatore, ut concedat sanctis suis videre corruptionem, ut spernat eos qui gratiogratiosi apud illum fuerant, & ut aversetur quos dilexerat. Praecipue vero quia dilexerat ipsos Deus amore magno mirandoque, & ab omni malo tuitus fuerat, cum adhuc animae illorum imbecillum ac vile corpus inhabitarent eique adhaererent, ecquomodo credemus ipsum in die quo animae eorundem purissimae a corporibus separantur, in hostem immutari, ut eos in infima inferni detrudat, ac pari forte justus cum impio perfruatur; Et mox pergit: Quomodo enim fieri potest ut peccatum unum, commestio nimirum Adami protoplasti ex arbore scientiae, per aliud eodem longe gravius, hoc est peremtione corporis, quod Deus ipsorum habebat, expietur? Porro conatur Rabbi imputationem peccati primi evertere ex Ezechielis cap.18. Anima quae peccat, ipsa morietur, filius non feret propter iniquitatem patris, & pater non feret propter iniquitatem filii; Quasi anima non subitura sit mortem, nisi ob causam peccati proprii, minime vero ob peccatum alienum; Caeterum quod Exod. cap. 20. legimus: Visitans iniquitatem patrum in filios; Id tantum in eos attinere vult, qui suis tenent manibus instituta parentum; Pari modo Rabbi Iiac Abarbanel in Commentario ad Esaiam cap. 54. tueri laborat, peccatum Adami, nec per naturam, nec per imputationem transire posse ad posteros, cum sic loquitur: Quid fecerunt quo infernalis poena pœna rei essent? Siquidem ipsi non peccarunt, nec anima filii portabit iniquitatem patris sui, nam ecce homo ratione corporis sui duntaxat patris sui filius est, anima autem ab ipso generata non est, quod itaque anima Adami improbe egit, e contra vero anima Abrahami Deo adhæsit, & non fecit sicut Adam, anjustitia Dei puniet utramque pariter, eritq; ipsi justus & improbus perinde? siquidem utraque cum generaretur innocens erat, & munda ab omni spuma; Sic quoque nuper Isacus Orobius contra Limborchium demonstrare voluit, quod non constet ex scripturis ira illa Dei contra genus humanum, neque æterna illa maledictio, quæ peccatum primum fuerit secuta, quando pag. 55. Amicæ collationis ita inquit: Respondemus, quod non constat ex toto sacro textu illa ira Dei contra genus humanum, neque illa aeterna maledictio: neque meminii in quatuor Evangeliis me legisse hoc secretum a Christo fuisse detectum: quare putamus id postea inventum ut aliis dogmatibus fundamentum substerneretur. Id vero clare ex divinis scriptis liquet, quod Henoch & Elias vivi ad Deum fuerunt assumpti: quod Patriarchæ, Moses & David, caeterique divini Prophetæ, & ex popularibus pii, erant Deo Benedicti, Dilecti, & in hominum oculis sanctificati; quod Dominus jubet Aaroni, & femini ejus, populo benedicere; Et ponam benedictionem meam super eis, & erunt benedicti: nedicti: Eritis sancti coram me in die expiationis: Et, sancti estote, quia sanctus est Dominus Deus vester: Dixitque Bilhamo: Ne maledicas populo, quia benedictus est ille. Qua omnia aeterna maledictioni adeo contrariantur, ut neque Deus ipse posset ea componere; quia maledictio Dei, & benedictio Dei eodem tempore circa idem subjectum, suapte natura sunt incompatibiles, sicuti Deum hominem amare, eumque simul odio habere. Iam video Theologos Christianos hic plurima congerere de crimine laesae majestatis infinitae, ideoque ad mensuram peccati infinita malitia, justitia divina aequam satisfactionem exigente, quam homo ob sui limitationem, & corruptionem praestare nequit, & catera quae ex iis consequuntur: Sed haec & similia pro Christianis necessaria sunt, aliter non essent Christiani: Israel vero has Theologias, sine fundamento in divina lege non admittere tenetur, sed constantissime eam servare, Deo ipso admonitus ne ab hominibus scientiam aliam discere audeat. Haec est vestra sapientia, hic est vester Intellectus.
units.tr: This opinion is most clearly set out by the Jew Nizzachon, the author cited by Munster, in his commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, page 125. Besides this, he brings forward various reasons why they reject the imputation of the first sin, and he further denies that eternal death passed to all posterity. He speaks thus: "Ask the heretic (he means the Christian) whether you believe that the Lord bestows mercies on all his creatures, and that all his attributes are piety and truth towards his creatures. Trusting in these attributes we draw near every day before his face, as David says: 'Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy loving-kindness; according to the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions.' Furthermore, the Lord says: 'I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth, but that he turn from his ways and live.' And you too believe that in the greatness of his mercies his hand is stretched out to receive the penitent. If it is so, how has it come about that the Lord came with such severity against the first man, that he held him bound for a trifling matter, namely for the biting of one apple, and destroyed him in this world and in the world to come, and not him only but all his posterity? He did this in error, since there was not yet in him any knowledge, as it is said: 'And the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked.' But this opening was in the eye of wisdom. Moreover, in the killing of Abel there was a transgression a thousand times greater than that one, and yet no such great punishment is attached to it. So Rabbi Isaac Bar Abraham mocks and refutes the Nazarenes, because they assert that Adam with his sons and posterity, indeed the holy patriarchs and prophets themselves, were struck with eternal death of souls for the single deed committed at the tree of knowledge, and were thrust down into hell, while the Messiah, our God, by his death freed these souls from perdition. Far be it, writes the Rabbi in the Munimen fidei, part 1, chapter 2, that God the Saviour should allow his holy ones to see corruption, should despise those who had been in favour with him, and should turn away from those whom he had loved. Above all, since God had loved them with a great and wonderful love, and had guarded them from all evil, while their souls still dwelt in and clung to the feeble and base body, how shall we believe that on the day when their most pure souls are separated from their bodies he is changed into an enemy, so as to thrust them down into the depths of hell, and the righteous man fares the same as the wicked? And presently he goes on: 'For how can it be that one sin, namely the eating of the first man Adam from the tree of knowledge, is expiated by another far more grievous, that is, by the destruction of the body which God had given them?'" Further, the Rabbi tries to overturn the imputation of the first sin from Ezekiel, chapter 18: "The soul that sins, it shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father bear the iniquity of the son." As if the soul were not to undergo death except on account of its own sin, and not at all on account of another's sin. Moreover, what we read in Exodus, chapter 20: "visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children," he wishes to apply only to those who hold in their own hands the institutions of their parents. In the same way Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel, in his commentary on Isaiah chapter 54, labours to maintain that the sin of Adam cannot pass to posterity either by nature or by imputation. He speaks thus: "What had they done that they should be liable to the punishment of hell? For they did not sin, nor shall the soul of a son bear the iniquity of his father. For behold, a man is the son of his father only in respect of his body; but the soul is not begotten by him. Therefore, if the soul of Adam acted wickedly, and on the contrary the soul of Abraham cleaved to God and did not act as Adam did, will the justice of God punish both alike, and will the one be just and the other wicked in the same way? For each, when it was born, was innocent and clean of all dross." So too recently Isaac Orobio wished to show, against Limborch, that it is not established from Scripture that wrath of God against the human race, nor that eternal curse which followed the first sin. In his Friendly Conference, page 55, he says: "We answer that it is not established from the whole sacred text that there is such a wrath of God against the human race, nor that eternal curse. Nor do I recall having read in the four Gospels that this secret was revealed by Christ. We therefore think it was invented later, so that a foundation might be laid for other dogmas. But it is clear from the divine writings that Enoch and Elijah were taken up alive to God; that the patriarchs, Moses and David, and the other divine prophets, and among the common people the pious, were blessed by God, beloved, and sanctified in the eyes of men; that the Lord bids Aaron and his seed bless the people: 'And I will put my blessing upon them, and they shall be blessed'; 'You shall be holy before me on the day of atonement'; 'And be holy, for the Lord your God is holy'; and Balaam said: 'Do not curse the people, for they are blessed.' All these things are so contrary to eternal curse that God himself could not reconcile them, since the curse of God and the blessing of God at the same time, concerning the same subject, are by their very nature incompatible, just as to love a man and at the same time to hate him. I see that Christian theologians here heap up many arguments about the crime of infinite majesty offended, and therefore about the infinite malice of sin in proportion, which divine justice demands an equal satisfaction for, a satisfaction that man cannot render because of his limitation and corruption, and other things which follow from these. But these and similar things are necessary for Christians; otherwise they would not be Christians. Israel, however, is bound not to admit these theologies, which have no foundation in the divine law, but to keep constantly to that law, since God himself has warned it not to dare to learn any other wisdom from men. This is your wisdom; this is your understanding."

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Docuit Synagoga vetus Judaica, peccati primi imputationem omnibus factam fuisse hominibus, quod in Adamo species humana peccaverit, ipsoque Adamo peccante, totus peccaverit mundus sic enim patet ex Sohar in Genes. col. 218. Adamus primus rebellavit DomiDomino suo, & causatus est mortem mundo; Ex Jalkut Chaddasch, pag. 77. col. 2. Adamus causatus est mortem omni mundo; Sic loquuntur Sapientes Veterum Hebraeorum apud Rabbi Lipmannum in Nizzachon, num 8. Neobvertas mihi id quod dixerunt Sapientes nostri beata memoria, per Adamum mortem super totum mundum introivisse; Sic omnis homo a Rabbi Kimchio dicitur naturaliter immersus peccato cum scribit in Esaiam cap. 43. v. 27. Ecce pater tuus primus peccavit, & is est primus Adam. Nam hominus natura infixum est peccatum, eo quod figmentum cordis ejus malum est ab infantia: Sic Josephus Voysinius ad Raymundi Pugionem Fidei, pag. 590, 591. quaedam veterum communicavit loca, quae ut in rei allegemus probationem, institutum jubet nostrum; Primo autem ex recentiori Rabbi Josepho Albo, Fundamentorum lib. 1. cap. 11. monstrat, quod poenae omnes ad posteros transierint: Poenae omnes, quae de Adamo & Eva referuntur, communes sunt totius speciei; Et Fundamentorum lib. 4 cap. 41: refert ad Genef. cap. 2. v. 17. In die quo comederis ex ea, morte morieris: Haec geminatio mortis in Scriptura designat mortem corporis & animae; Sic infantes nasci filios irae, privatos gratia Dei, ideoque futuri seculi gloria indignos docet Talmud Tract. Sanhedrin. cap.II. Quaeritur, quando Infans particeps esse possit futuri seculi &c- Rabbi Nachman filius Isaaci respondet: statim atque circumcisus est, juxta illud Psalmi 88. v.16. afflictus ego sum, & moribundus ab adolescentia mea, portavi terrores tuos: Timebo. Et cum peccatum sit privatio gratia, posteri Adami nascentes privati gratia, peccatores etiam nascuntur; Uti quoque docet Rabbi Menachem Rakanatensis Sect. Bereschit ex Midrasch Tehilim: Non est mirum cur peccatum Adami, & Evae exaratum sit, & sit signatum annulo regus ad generationes sequentes propagandum: quia quo die creatus est Adam, absoluta sunt omnia, ita ut ipse extiterit perfectio, & complementum totius mundani opificii; sic quando ille peccavit, totus mundus peccavit, cujus peccatum nos portamus, & patimur. Quod non ita se habet in peccatis posteritatis ejus; Et in Talmude Tract. Berachot cap. 1. Finis hominis est ad mortem. Causa quoque est, quia peccavit species humana, id est, natura, ex qua quisque constat: sive peccatum Adami & Evae; Sic in libro Neve Schalom, lib.10.cap.9. Observatione praeceptorum sanctificatur homo ab immunditia sua, & mundatur ab inquinamento serpentis antiqui; Hactenus cum Voysinio.
units.tr: The ancient Jewish Synagogue taught that the imputation of the first sin was made to all men, because in Adam the human species sinned, and with Adam sinning the whole world sinned. So it appears from the Sohar on Genesis, col. 218: Adam the first rebelled against his Lord, and caused death to the world. From Jalkut Chaddasch, p. 77, col. 2: Adam caused death to every world. So speak the wise men of the ancient Hebrews, according to Rabbi Lipmann in Nizzachon, num. 8: You overturn for me what our wise men of blessed memory said, that through Adam death entered upon the whole world. So every man is said by Rabbi Kimchi to be naturally immersed in sin, when he writes on Isaiah ch. 43, v. 27: Behold, your father first sinned, and he is the first Adam. For sin is fixed in human nature, because the imagination of his heart is evil from childhood. So Josephus Voysinius, on Raymund's Pugio Fidei, pp. 590, 591, has brought together certain passages of the ancients, which our plan requires us to cite as proof of the matter. First, however, from the more recent Rabbi Joseph Albo, Fundamentals, book 1, ch. 11, he shows that all the punishments passed on to posterity: All the punishments which are related of Adam and Eve are common to the whole species. And in Fundamentals, book 4, ch. 41, he refers to Gen. 2, v. 17, "In the day you eat of it, you shall surely die": This doubling of death in Scripture designates death of body and soul. So the Talmud, Tract. Sanhedrin, ch. 2, teaches that infants are born sons of wrath, deprived of the grace of God, and therefore unworthy of the glory of the future age: "The question is, when can an infant be a partaker of the future age, etc." Rabbi Nachman son of Isaac answers: as soon as he is circumcised, according to that of Psalm 88, v. 16, I am afflicted and dying from my youth; I have borne your terrors: I shall fear. And since sin is the privation of grace, the posterity of Adam, being born deprived of grace, are also born sinners. Rabbi Menachem Rakanatensis also teaches this, in Sect. Bereschit, from Midrash Tehilim: It is no wonder why the sin of Adam and Eve was written down and sealed with the king's signet to be propagated to the following generations: because on the day Adam was created, all things were finished, so that he himself was the perfection and completion of the whole worldly work; thus when he sinned, the whole world sinned, and we bear and suffer its sin. It is not so with the sins of his posterity. And in the Talmud, Tract. Berachot, ch. 1: The end of man is death. The cause also is that the human species, that is, the nature from which each one consists, sinned, namely the sin of Adam and Eve. So in the book Neve Schalom, book 10, ch. 9: By observance of the precepts man is sanctified from his uncleanness, and is cleansed from the defilement of the ancient serpent. Thus far with Voysinius.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Constat eadem haec veterum Hebraeorum sententia ex Talkut, in quo refertur justos,cum moriuntur,pervenire in alium mun-dum ad Adamum, & in hunc modum gravi-ter apud illum conqueri: Tu fuisti nostri da-mni causa. Quibus illum respondere: unum ego solum commisi peccatum, nullus autem vestrum huc venit,qui ad minimum non qua-tuor commiserit peccata. Eximius in hanc rem locus occurrit in Siphre, libro antiquissi-mo, seculi ut putatur, tertii, Venetiis impres-so, in quo scribitur multas mortes nonsolum obvenisse Adamo, verum omnibus quoque generationibus ejus ; usque ad finem omni-um generationum, sicut ex his quæ sequun-tur, patet: Dixit Rabbi Iose Galilæus: egredere, & disce meritum Regis Messiæ, & præmium justorum pro Adamo antiquo cui unum solum præceptum ne-gativum fuit mandatum, & transgressus est illud. Vide quot mortibus punitus fuerit ille, & generatio-nes ejus, & generationes generationum ejus usque ad finem generationum omnium. Porro quæ men-sura præponderat, mensura boni, aut mensura vin-dictæ seu pœnarum. Dic mensuram boni præponde-rare: mensuram vero vindictæ seu pœnarum minui: Rex enim Messias afflictus dolore, pœnisque affectus propeccatoribus, sicuti legitur Iesa. cap. 53. v. 5. Et ipse propter iniquitates nostras vulneratus est, &c. quanto magis justificabit omnes omnino generatio-nes? Hoc est quod dicitur ibidem v. 6. Dominus ob-viare viare fecit in eo peccata omnium nostrum; In Midrasch Tillim super Eccles. cap. 7. s. 29. scribunt interminationem factam Adamo, si peccaret, sore eum causam mortis Messiæ Redemptoris; Videtur quoque, si conjecturare licet, ipsos Cabalistas, hanc peccati primi imputationem agnovisse, & simul ad Messiam, qui solus peccata omnia expiare deberet respexisse, dum nominis אדם tres literas ajunt designasse has tres voces אדם דוד משיח Adam, David, Messias, putantes animam Adami secreta revolutione migrasse in Davidem, hincque in Messiam, qui ob peccata Judæorum adhuc dum lateat.
units.tr: This same opinion of the ancient Hebrews appears from the Talkut, in which it is related that the righteous, when they die, come into another world to Adam, and there complain bitterly to him: "You were the cause of our loss." To whom he answers: "I committed only one sin, yet none of you has come here who has not committed at least four sins." A notable passage on this matter occurs in the Siphre, a very ancient book, printed at Venice, thought to date from the third century, in which it is written that many deaths befell not only Adam but also all his generations, even to the end of all generations, as appears from what follows: "Rabbi Jose the Galilean said: Go out and learn the merit of the King Messiah and the reward of the righteous for ancient Adam, to whom only one negative precept was commanded, and he transgressed it. See by how many deaths he was punished, and his generations, and the generations of his generations, even to the end of all generations." Moreover, which measure predominates: the measure of good, or the measure of vengeance or punishments? "Say that the measure of good predominates; the measure of vengeance or punishments is diminished. For the King Messiah, afflicted with pain and affected with punishments for sinners, as is read in Isaiah ch. 53, v. 5, 'And he was wounded for our iniquities,' etc., how much more will he justify all generations altogether?" This is what is said there at v. 6: "The Lord caused to meet in him the sins of us all." In Midrash Tillim on Ecclesiastes ch. 7, s. 29, they write that a threat was made to Adam, that if he sinned, he would be the cause of the death of the Messiah the Redeemer. It also seems, if one may conjecture, that the Cabalists themselves acknowledged this imputation of the first sin, and at the same time looked to the Messiah, who alone ought to expiate all sins. For they say that the three letters of the name אדם designate these three words, Adam, David, Messiah [אדם דוד משיח], thinking that the soul of Adam by a secret revolution migrated into David, and hence into the Messiah, who on account of the sins of the Jews still lies hidden.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Non negant peccatum Originale, concupiscentiamque connatam, asserentes per carnalem generationem labem propagari originalem, appetitumque malum hominí inesse ab utero, sicuti liquet ex Catechési Judaica, in qua ad Genef. cap. 8. s. 21. Figmentum cordis humani malum est à pueritia ejus, respondet discipulus, Quæstione 25. hoc modo: Et unus quisque à prima ætate stimulante conscientia facile à pravitate mentis adsestandas mundi illecebras abripitur, nec res illicitas à licitis discernit, modo bellicina anima desiderja impleat; Et clare patet ex Rabbi Menasseh Ben Itrael, qui in libello de Fragilitate humana, pag. 2. peccatum scribit esse quasi naturale & inseparabile in hac vita, quando ad verba Psalmi 51. ‡. 7. En in iniquitate formatus sum, & in peccato concepit me mater mea, ita loquitur: Sive autem hoc intelligatur de matre communi, quae fuit Eva, sive de sua solum David hoc dixerit; significare voluit, esse peccatum quasi naturale, & inseparabile in hac vita. Ideo & post commissum delictum Eva concepit, & quot quot postea geniti sunt, non juxta regulam, rectae rationi conformem, sex affectus perturbatos, & libidinosos produxisse sunt; Et ex Rabbi Menasseh Praefatione ad libellum citatum, pag. 9. Haec vero vitiositas ex primorum parentum profecta crimine, contagio, invasit utramque animae rationalis facultatem, intellectum, quo apprehendimus, & voluntatem, qua appetimus; Sic pariter Rabbi Aben Esra ad Psalmum 51. ‡. 7. Ecce propter concupiscentiam innatam cordi humano dicitur, in iniquitate genitus sum, atque iensus est, quod a nativitate implantatum sit cordi humano figmentum malum; Et ad Jobi cap. 14. ‡. 4. Quis dabit mundum de immundo? neminem quidem: Sensus est sicuti ejus, in iniquitate genitus sum, quia homo fit ex re immunda; Uti quoque Rabbi Schelomo Jarchi ad Psalmi verba allegata: Quomodo non peccem? Origo mea corrupta est, atque hinc ea peccata. Aliter, Origo mea mea est a viro & fœmina, qui iniquitate pleni sunt; Ita Rabbi Isac, Bar Abraham scribit in Munimine Fidei Part. 1. cap. 11. Circumcisionis ritum propterea quoque Judæis impositum fuisse, ut concupiscentiam imminueret; Sic Rabbi Levi, Ben Gersom observat ad Prov. cap.22.v.15. Quod in principio jam ipsa stultitia puero quasi adnata sit; In Bereschit Rabba ad Genes. cap.21.v.22. sequentia de figmento malo traduntur: Figmentum malum crescit in homine, vel nutritur a pueritia ejus usque adsenectutem; Et in Midrasch Tillim ad Psalmum 34.v.23. Figmentum malum natum est cum homine, & crevit cum eo omnibus diebus ejus; Sic referunt Sapientes Judæorum & nostri ævi & præteritorum, quod יצר הרע Figmentum malum occupet maxime hominem usque ad annum ætatis decimum tertium, יצר הטוב Figmentum bonum vero ab anno decimo tertio ingrediatur hominem, quando incipit fieri filius præcepti, & ad præceptorum observationem obligatur; Sic Rabbi Kimchi ad Esaiæ cap.43.v.26. Ecce pater tuus primus peccavit, & is est primus Adam. Nam hominis natura infixum est peccatum, eo quod Figmentum cordis ejus malum est ab infantia; Et memorant Antiquii in Tractatu Berachot cap.1. Rabbi Alexandrum in more habuisse, finita sua oratione, illa sem-per per verba dicere: Totius universi Domine, manifestum est tibi, & notum, quod mea voluntas sit, facere voluntatem tuam: at quis impedit istud, nisi massæ fermentum; Cæterum quomodo è femine, readeo impura, immundaque, non purus, mundusque prodire possit, multis probavit Rabbi Menasleh Ben Israel, adductis testimoniis Mosis Gerundensis, Abrahami Perisolii, Simeonis Bar Semæ, Obadiæ Sphormionis, Meiri Aramæ, aliorumq;, quæ in libello de Fragilitate humana cap. 1. conferri bene possunt.
units.tr: They do not deny original sin or the concupiscence born with us. They teach that original corruption is passed on by carnal generation, and that an evil appetite is in man from the womb. This is clear from the Jewish Catechism, where, on Genesis 8:21, "the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth," the disciple answers in Question 25 as follows: "Each one, from his earliest age, is easily swept away by the stinging of conscience and by the depravity of his mind toward worldly allurements, and he does not distinguish unlawful things from lawful, provided only that his unbridled soul fulfils its desires." It is also plain from Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, who in his little book on human frailty, p. 2, writes that sin is almost natural and inseparable in this life. When he comes to the words of Psalm 51:7, "Behold, I was formed in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me," he speaks thus: "Whether this is understood of the common mother, who was Eve, or whether David said it only of his own mother, he meant that sin is almost natural and inseparable in this life. Therefore, even after the offence was committed, Eve conceived, and all who were afterwards born brought forth disturbed and lustful passions, not according to the rule that conforms to right reason." And from Rabbi Menasseh's preface to the book cited, p. 9: "This wickedness, arising from the crime of our first parents, as a contagion invaded both faculties of the rational soul, the intellect, by which we apprehend, and the will, by which we desire." So too Rabbi Abenezra on Psalm 51:7: "It is said of the human heart, because of the innate concupiscence, 'I was born in iniquity,' and it is understood that the evil imagination has been implanted in the human heart from birth." And on Job 14:4, "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? Not one": "The sense is as follows: 'I was born in iniquity,' because man is made from an unclean thing." Rabbi Solomon Jarchi likewise, on the words of the Psalm cited: "How should I not sin? My origin is corrupt, and hence these sins. Otherwise: my origin is from a man and a woman who are full of iniquity." So too Rabbi Isaac Bar Abraham writes in the Munimen Fidei, Part 1, ch. 11, that the rite of circumcision was therefore also imposed on the Jews so as to diminish concupiscence. Rabbi Levi ben Gershom likewise observes on Proverbs 22:15 that folly is, from the beginning, as it were, grown into the child. In Bereshit Rabba on Genesis 21:22 the following is said of the evil imagination: "The evil imagination grows in a man, or is nourished from his childhood until old age." And in the Midrash Tillim on Psalm 34:23: "The evil imagination is born with a man, and grows with him all his days." Thus the wise men of the Jews, both of our own age and of past ages, report that the evil inclination [יצר הרע] chiefly occupies a man until his thirteenth year, while the good inclination [יצר הטוב] enters a man from his thirteenth year, when he begins to become a son of the precept and is bound to observe the precepts. So Rabbi Kimchi on Isaiah 43:26: "Behold, your father sinned first, and he is the first Adam. For sin is fixed in the nature of man, because the imagination of his heart is evil from infancy." And the ancients, in the tractate Berachot, ch. 1, record that Rabbi Alexander had the habit, when he had finished his prayer, of always saying these words: "Lord of the whole universe, it is manifest and known to you that my will is to do your will; but what hinders this, except the leaven in the lump?" Moreover, how a clean and pure thing can come forth from seed that is unclean and impure, Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel has shown at length, citing the testimonies of Moses of Gerona, Abraham Perisol, Simeon bar Sema, Obadiah Sphormio, Meiri of Aram, and others, which may well be compared in his little book on human frailty, ch. 1.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Hinc disputarunt Judæi in Tractatu Talmudico Sanhedrin sol. 91. a quo tempore figmentum malum in hominem obtineat dominium? An a tempore nativitatis, an a tempore formationis hominis in utero? Et responsum est a Rabbi Jehuda Hakkadosch, a tempore formationis. Describserunt quoque figmentum illud malum multis diversisque nominibus, vocaruntillud mox infixum implantatumque peccatum naturali quasi inclinatione ex Aben Esra in Psalmum 51. ¶. 7. Et Kimchio in Esaiæ cap. 43. ¶. 26. mox יצר Inquinamentum serpentis, quod Evam Adamumque invasit, ex Tract. Talmud. Joma sol. 28. & Neve Schalom lib. 10. cap. 9. mox עיכרה העיכר Massam malam, quæ totum genus corruperit humanum, ex Talmudistis & Catechesi Judaica, Resposione ad quæstionem 25. mox פגימה Maculam seu labem animæ. Præterea Talmudici in Tractatu Succa sol. 52. Appetitum illum innatum septem appellarunt nominibus, quæ sunt hæc sequentia.
units.tr: Hence the Jews disputed in the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin, fol. 91, from what time the evil imagination gains dominion over a man: from the time of birth, or from the time of his formation in the womb? And the answer given by Rabbi Jehudah Hakkadosch was: from the time of formation. They also described that evil imagination by many and various names. They called it, at one time, sin implanted and fixed in us as a kind of natural inclination, following Abenezra on Psalm 51:7 and Kimchi on Isaiah 43:26; at another time, the pollution of the serpent [יצר], which invaded Eve and Adam, following Tractate Talmud Joma, fol. 28, and Neve Shalom, bk. 10, ch. 9; at another time, the evil mass [עיכרה] which corrupted the whole human race, following the Talmudists and the Jewish Catechism, answer to question 25; at another time, the stain or blemish of the soul [פגימה]. Moreover, the Talmudists in the tractate Succa, fol. 52, called that innate appetite by seven names, which are the following.

units.la: (1) Deus appellavit illum ערלה malum, Genes. c. 8. v. 21. (2) Moses appellavit illum ערלה præputium, Deuteron. cap. 10. v. 16. (3) David vocavit illum טמא Immundum, Psalmo 51. v. 12. (4) Salomo nominavit illum שנאה Oforem, Proverb. cap. 25. v. 21. (5) Jesaias vocavit illum משכול Offendiculum, Jesa. cap. 57. v. 14. (6) Ezechiel nominavit illum אבן Lapidem, Ezech. cap. 36. v. 26. (7) Joel vocavit illum אבשלום Absconditum, Joel cap. 2. v. 20.
units.tr: (1) God called it evil [ערלה], Genesis 8:21. (2) Moses called it foreskin [ערלה], Deuteronomy 10:16. (3) David called it unclean [טמא], Psalm 51:12. (4) Solomon named it offender [שנאה], Proverbs 25:21. (5) Isaiah called it stumbling-block [משכול], Isaiah 57:14. (6) Ezekiel named it stone [אבן], Ezekiel 36:26. (7) Joel called it the Hidden One [צפוני], Joel 2:20.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Distinguunt quin etiam peccatum Originale ab Actuali, quod hoc ex eo ceu fonte fluat: quod pluribus exequitur Menasseh, dum in libello de Fragilitate humana, peculiari describit capite, quod fomes sit reliquorum peccatorum, quod ex re impura purus non possit prodire, quod ex femine, ex re immunda mundus non possit prodire, proinde omnem hominem actu peccare; quod impossibile sit hominem consequi posse perfectionem.
units.tr: They even distinguish original sin from actual sin, holding that the latter flows from the former as from a source. Menasseh pursues this at length in his little book on human frailty, where he devotes a special chapter to showing that the inclination (fomes) is the source of the other sins; that what is pure cannot come from what is impure, nor what is clean from unclean seed; and that therefore every man sins in act, and it is impossible for a man to attain perfection.

An Iudaei agnoscant peccatum, cum quo omnes nascimur, & si negent, quae negationis causa? Iudaei peccatum Originale negant, idque gravissimis de causis; Verum quoque peccatum Originale credant esse fontem plurimorum errorem, proinde primum subvertendum, uti loquitur pariter Anonymus in Manuscripto, quod Venetiis apud Orientalium Judaeorum Archisynagogum aliquando pervolvit Doctissimus Wulferus.
units.tr: ...their souls to be saved, as the Nazarenes devise from their own wit, as Rabbi Isaac Bar Abraham says in the Munimen fidei, Part I, chapter 11. And it is clear enough from this that they not only deny original sin in so many words, as we see in the anonymous Jew cited by Coccejus, Question 23, "Do the Jews acknowledge the sin with which we are all born, and if they deny it, what is the reason for the denial?" The Jews deny original sin, and for very weighty reasons. Yet they also believe that original sin is the source of very many errors, and therefore that it must first be overthrown, as the same anonymous author says in a manuscript which the most learned Wulferus once looked through at Venice, at the chief synagogue of the Oriental Jews.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Sicuti Actualium peccatorum numerum statuunt immensum, ita pariter horum varietatem atque diversitatem judicant maximam, tam in gradibus, quam in poenis, distinguentes ea praeterea ratione subjecti, in carnis seu corporis, & animae; vocantes alia peccata simplicia, alia mixta; alia ignorantiae & infirmitatis peccata, alia malitiae; Quaedam gravia, quaedam levia, quorum remissionem a divino petunt Numine, clamantes ex quotinem, ob materiam, quae ipsum semper peccare facit; probatque illud diversis Rabbinorum testimoniis, inter quae elucet Rabbi Perisolii, quod tale est: Nosti Dominë structuram hominis, sicut impossibile esse, hunc perfectionem consequi, ob materiam, quia ipsum peccare facit: & quare hunc semper affligis? potest aliquis prodire purus aut mundus, ex re aliqua immunda? certe non est ex hac classe aliquis, quoniam non est homo justus, qui non peccet. Bene hoc quoque expressit Paraphrasis Chaldaica, quando ad Psalmum 104. ¶. 14. scribit: Quia ille novit nostrum appetitum malum, quo in peccatum illicimur; Enarrat praeterea cap. 1. ex mente omnium Hebraeorum, quomodo nullus mortalium sit, qui non peccet, sic loquens: Quare judicamus neminem naturâ ductu ad sanctitatem pervenire, adeo omnis vitii expertem, ut non incurrerit in peccatum vel sponte vel errore. Demonstrat veritatem cum reliquis popularibus ex Davidis Psalmo 51. ¶. 7. En in iniquitate formatus sum, & in peccato concepit me mater mea. Psalmo 143. ¶. 2. Ne congrediaris judicio cum servo tuo: nam non se justificabit coram te ullus vivens. Ex Eccles. cap. 7. ¶. 20. Quia homo non justus in terra, qui faciat bonum & non peccet. Ex Proverb. cap. 20. ¶. 9. Quis dicere possit, purificavi animum meum, mundus sum à peccato meo. Ex Job. cap. 14. ¶. 4. Quis edat edat mundum ex immundo? ne unus quidem. Et Jobi cap. 15. v. 15. Quid homo, quod mundus sit? Et quod justificet se natus muliere? Roborant quoque hanc veritatem Rabbini suis quae le- quuntur, testimoniis: Obadias Sphormio ad Psalm. 143. v. 2: explicat: quia non est homo sine peccato. Aben Efra ad Eccles. cap. 7. v. 26. non potest fieri, quin peccet homo nonnunquam vel mente, vel verbis, vel factis. Rabbi Bechai sol. 158. Caro & sanguis debilis est propter peccatum, neque quisquam hominum a necessitate peccandi est exemptus, ne justissimi quidem: Scriptura enim dicit Eccles. 6. v. 22. Nullus homo justus est in terra, qui faciat bonum & non peccet. Moses Alchech in R. Peninim: quod nemo sit, qui non cogitationibus peccet, aut per ignorantiam. Rabbi Simeon Bar Semah in Oeb Mispat: Impossibile est ut non peccet homo. Rabbi Levi Ben Gerson ad Job. cap. 15. v. 15. Quomodo putas, quod esses innocens, & justus, & quod non tibi accidere deberet aliqua afflictio? Certe impossibile est, ut homo per suam imperfectionem sit innocens & justus. Nam si Angeli, & coeli non puri sunt in oculis Domini, quomodo homo poterit pervenire ad istam fortunam. Imo dicunt Hebraei, ex clasife contradictoria esse, hominem esse, & nihilominus innocentem, ac sine peccato, ut adeo impossibile sit, non incidere in peccatum vel spon-te, te, vel per errorem, hincque inter ןיינם illud referunt, & verum esse veterum illud confir-mant; Humanum est peccare.
units.tr: Just as they reckon the number of actual sins to be immense, so they judge their variety and diversity to be very great, both in degrees and in punishments. They further distinguish them by the subject in which they lie, the flesh or body and the soul; they call some sins simple and others mixed; some are sins of ignorance and weakness, others of malice; some are grave, some light, and for the forgiveness of these they seek help from the divine Majesty, crying out on account of the evil inclination, which by its nature always makes man sin. They prove this by various testimonies of the rabbis, among which Rabbi Perisol stands out, and it runs thus: "You know the structure of man, that it is impossible for him to attain perfection, because of the matter which makes him sin. And why do you always afflict him? Can anyone come forth pure or clean out of some unclean thing? Surely there is none of this class, for there is no righteous man who does not sin." The Chaldee paraphrase also expresses this well, when on Psalm 104:14 it writes: "For he knows our evil appetite, by which we are enticed into sin." Moreover, in chapter 1 he sets out, in the mind of all the Hebrews, how there is no mortal who does not sin, speaking thus: "Therefore we judge that no one by nature attains to holiness, so free from all vice as not to fall into sin either willingly or by error." He demonstrates the truth along with the other countrymen from David's Psalm 51:7, "Behold, I was formed in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me"; from Psalm 143:2, "Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living man will be justified before you"; from Ecclesiastes 7:20, "For there is not a righteous man upon earth who does good and does not sin"; from Proverbs 20:9, "Who can say, I have cleansed my heart, I am clean from my sin?"; from Job 14:4, "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? Not one"; and Job 15:14–15, "What is man, that he should be clean, and that he who is born of a woman should be justified?" The rabbis too strengthen this truth by their own testimonies. Obadiah Sphormio, on Psalm 143:2, explains it: "because there is no man without sin." Aben Ezra, on Ecclesiastes 7:26: "It cannot be but that a man sins sometimes, in mind, or in words, or in deeds." Rabbi Bechai, fol. 158: "Flesh and blood is weak because of sin, and no one among men is exempt from the necessity of sinning, not even the most righteous; for Scripture says, Ecclesiastes 6:22 [7:20], There is no righteous man upon earth who does good and does not sin." Moses Alshech, on Rabbi Peninim: "that there is no one who does not sin in thought, or through ignorance." Rabbi Simeon Bar Semah, in Oeb Mispat: "It is impossible that a man should not sin." Rabbi Levi Ben Gershom, on Job 15:15: "How do you think that you could be innocent and righteous, and that no affliction should befall you? Surely it is impossible that a man, by reason of his imperfection, should be innocent and righteous. For if the Angels and the heavens are not pure in the eyes of the Lord, how can man come to that good fortune?" Indeed the Hebrews say that it is a contradictory combination to be a man and yet innocent and without sin, so that it is impossible not to fall into sin either willingly or through error; and therefore they count this among their proverbs, and they confirm the old saying which is true: "To sin is human."

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Sed quamvis tot sententiis magnificis peccatum describant Originale, totiesque malam accusent concupiscentiam, imo licet figmentum illud malum, quod ab utero statim hominem occupat, indesinenter exaggerent, ingentisque peccati nomine insigniant, & omnibus, quotquot sunt, hominibus tribuant, revera tamen labem originalem negant, praeter vocem, exilemque effectum nihil amplius praedicantes, cum omnem fere ejus vim & potentiam nonsolum extenuent, diminuantque, verum quoque tollant; Inficiantur quippe Judaei omnes recentiores, quod abunde quoque ex tota eorum patet Theologia, concupiscentiam connatam tollere hominis ad bonum liberum arbitrium, hominemque per hanc concupiscentiam soli vivere Diabolo, sub ejusque jacere potestate, sed, non obstante illa, manere hominem semper suarum actionum Dominum, ipsumque esse & vitae & mortis aeternae primum auctorem, proinde pios, sanctosque homines salutem consequi aeternam tum misericordia Dei, tum propriis meritis, nec opus habere alieno merito ad animas nimas suas salvandas, ceu Nazareni ex suo ingenio commi- nisceantur, prout loquitur Rabbi Isac, Bar Abraham in Munimine fidei, Part. I. cap. 11. Et patet assertum exinde abunde, quod non solum expressis verbis saepe negent peccatum Originale, sicuti videmus in Judaeo Anonymo apud Coccejum, Quaestione 23. An Judaei agnoscant peccatum, cum quo omnes nascimur, & si negent, quae negationis causa? Judaei peccatum Originale negant, idque gravissimis de causis; Verum quoque peccatum Originale credant esse fontem plurimorum errorem, proinde primum subvertendum, uti loquitur pariter Anonymus in Manuscripto, quod Venetiis apud Orientalium Judaeorum Archisynagogum aliquando pervolvit Doctissimus Wulferus.
units.tr: But although they describe original sin in so many splendid phrases, and so often accuse concupiscence, and even tirelessly magnify that evil figment which occupies a man from the womb, and mark it with the name of great sin, and attribute it to all men without exception, they nevertheless in truth deny original stain. Beyond the word itself they assert little more than a slight effect, since they weaken and diminish almost all its force and power, and indeed take it away altogether. For all the more recent Jews deny, as is abundantly clear from their whole theology, that innate concupiscence removes man's free choice to good, and that through this concupiscence man lives only for the Devil and lies under his power. Rather, notwithstanding it, man remains always the lord of his actions and is himself the first author both of life and of eternal death. Therefore pious and holy men attain eternal salvation both by the mercy of God and by their own merits, and have no need of another's merit to save their souls. The Nazarenes invent this from their own wit, as Rabbi Isaac Bar Abraham says in the Munimen fidei, Part I, chap. 11. And it is abundantly evident from this that they not only often deny original sin in express words, as we see in the anonymous Jew cited by Cocceius, Question 23: Do the Jews acknowledge the sin with which we are all born, and if they deny it, what is the reason for the denial? The Jews deny original sin, and that for the most serious reasons; but they also believe that original sin is the source of very many errors, and therefore must first be overthrown, as the same anonymous writer says in a manuscript which the most learned Wulferus once went through at Venice, at the archsynagogue of the Eastern Jews.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Sicuti Actualium peccatorum numerum statuunt immensum, ita pariter horum varietatem atque diversitatem judicant maximam, tam in gradibus, quam in poenis, distinguentes ea praeterea ratione subjecti, in carnis seu corporis, & animae; vocantes alia peccata simplicia, alia mixta; alia ignorantiae & infirmitatis peccata, alia malitiae; Quaedam gravia, quaedam levia, quorum remissionem a divino petunt Numine, clamantes ex quotidiadianarum precum vulgatis libellis: Propitius esto super leve & grave seu ob peccata levia & gravia;Ex quibus hæc nominant עבירות חמורות Transgressiones graves, sub pœna mortis interdictas, hincque mortem, excisionemque merentes, appellata pariter peccata mortalia, quod morte hominis sint expianda, cujus ultima in agone vox soleat esse: Sit mors mea propitiatio pro peccatis meis; Illa vocant עבירות קלות Transgressiones leves, quæ absque morte in hac vita possint expiari & peccatorum confessione, pœnitentia, afflictionibus, flagellationibus, & aliis denique bonis operibus, venialia propterea quoque appellata; Ut ita ex his quam clare appareat, Judæorum doctrinam non esse, omnia peccata ex se & sua natura esse mortalia, vel mortem mereri damnationemque, sed quædam esse levia, venialiaque, non solum ex Dei misericordia, quam absolutam nimis, & absque reali satisfactione, & absque intuitu in Messiam concipiunt, verum quoque ex natura rei talia, quæ non adeo Deus Benedictus curet, cum parva sint, exiliaque, subitoque motu ac subreptione facta sint, sicuti videre est ex Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel in libello de Fragilitate humana, pag. 105.
units.tr: Just as they judge the number of actual sins to be immense, so too they judge their variety and diversity very great, both in degrees and in punishments. They also distinguish them by the nature of the subject, into sins of the flesh or body and sins of the soul. They call some sins simple and others mixed; some sins of ignorance and weakness, others of malice; some grave and some light. For the forgiveness of these they seek the divine Majesty, crying out in the common little books of daily prayers: "Be propitious concerning the light and the grave," that is, for light and grave sins. Among these they name the grave transgressions [עבירות חמורות], forbidden under pain of death, which therefore deserve death and excision, and which are likewise called mortal sins, because they must be expiated by the death of the man. The last word of such a man in his agony is usually: "Let my death be an atonement for my sins." The light transgressions [עבירות קלות] they call those which can be expiated in this life without death, by confession of sin, repentance, afflictions, scourgings, and finally other good works; for this reason they are also called venial. From this it clearly appears that the doctrine of the Jews is not that all sins are by their own nature mortal, or deserve death and damnation, but that some are light and venial. This is not only from God's mercy, which they conceive as altogether absolute, without real satisfaction and without regard to the Messiah; it is also from the nature of the thing, since such sins are of a kind that the blessed God does not much care about, being small and slight, and committed by a sudden movement and surprise. This may be seen from Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel in his little book On the Frailty of Man, p. 105.

units.la: Quando vero Rabbi Nehamia in Vaikra Rabba cap. XXVII. dicit, Eliam non oppetiisse mortem, ideo, quod quod non peccaverit, necessario id, non de peccato mortali, quod obligat ad mortem, sed veniali est intelligendum, quomodo & ipsum hoc intellexisse arbitramur; Et ex pag.108. Non tamen ut hoc credamus, inde potest colligi, non peccasse Henochum, etiamsi de nullo ejus peccato fiat mentio, potuit enim deliquisse in re adeo exiguo momenti, ut non videatur mortem ob id fuisse commeritus; Et denique pergit Rabbi Menasseh ex Rabbi Samuele Arcovolte, pag.III. Quippe dicere voluit, quatuor istos mortuos esse, non propter peccatum mortale, quod morti eos addiceret; Sed per legem aliquam universalem, & communem, quam consilium illud serpentis in mundum introduxit.
units.tr: When Rabbi Nehemiah in Vayikra Rabba chap. 27 says that Elijah did not die because he had not sinned, this must necessarily be understood not of a mortal sin, which obliges to death, but of a venial one; and we judge that he too understood it so. And from p. 108: Yet, not that we should believe this, it may be inferred from it that Enoch did not sin, even though no mention is made of any sin of his; for he could have offended in a matter of such small importance that he does not seem to have deserved death on that account. And finally Rabbi Menasseh goes on, from Rabbi Samuel Arcovolte, p. 111: For he meant to say that these four died not on account of a mortal sin, which would have condemned them to death, but through some universal and common law, which the serpent's counsel introduced into the world.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Credunt internam concupiscentiam, seu cogitationes pravas, etiamsi crimen propositum ad executionem non destinetur, inque actum abeat externum, vitiosas esse, peccaminosasque, testibus Judaeis in Tractatu Talmudico, Bava Bafra, sol.134.col.2. Et 164. col.2. Tres sunt transgressiones, a quibus homo nullo die immunis esse, aut sibi cavere potest; Cogitationes malae, aberratio attentionis in oratione, & Lingua mala; Neque is tantum committit inter Judaeos adulterium, qui actu ipso alienam violat uxorem, sed & qui icorratrices volvit cogicogitationes, juxta doctrinam Talmudicam Antiquæ Pharisaicæ contrariam, in Tractatu Challa, ab initio: Quicunque aspicit mulierem cum intentione, perinde est, ac si rem habuisset cum ea; Christianæ vero conformem, apud Matth. in Evangelio cap. 5. v. 27. & 28. Audistis dictum fuisse a Veteribus: Non mœchaberis. Ego vero dico vobis, quicunque aspicit mulierem ut eam concupiscat, jam adulteravit eam in corde suo; Ad horum Talmudistarum dictum respexit quoque Rabbi Bechai, cum sol. 153. col. 1. simili modo loquitur: Dictum Veterum est, qui aspicit mulierem, transgreditur præceptum: Ne respicias ad idola. Est enim prohibitum de aliena uxore cogitare; Sic Idem Rabbi Bechai demonstrat, quod non is tantum suum defraudet proximum, qui rem suam ipsi invito aufert, sed & qui alienas opes inordinate concupiscit, cum sol. 99. col. 2. inquit: Defraudatio proximi magnum peccatum est, plerisque omnibus familiare. Tanto gravius est, quia est principium naturā notum, non secus ac quintum, sextum, septimum & octavum præceptum. Quia autem concupiscentia prava subordinatur, cum nemo quidquam alieni adsepertrahat, nisi prius concupiscat, secundum illud Micha cap. 2. v. 2. Qui concupiscunt agros quos rapiant: Propterea non opus erat hujus peccati expresse mentionem facere, sed comprehendit eam ScriScriptura sub praecepto Negativo, non concupiscες. Accedit quod Deus ipsam etiam vult concupiscentiam prohibere, quae est motus cordis omni tempore ac hora operosus, nec tantum opus externum, ut ita homo discat, sine interna quidem concupiscentia sit licita, quanto minus externum opus licitum esse possit; Hinc est, quod dehortentur suos quam vehementer a concupiscentiae peccato, referentes cum Berefchit Rabba, quod principio sit peregrinus, deinde hospes, tandem fiat paterfamilias, herusque domesticus: Quod in Succah Talmudis sol. 52. col. 1. Concupiscentia mala in initio similis sit filo aranearum, in fine vero densó funi plaustri; Quod ex Vajikra Rabba, sect. 17. Concupiscentia initium dulce est, finis vero amarus; Hinc quoque adhortantur pios, ut per omnem vitam decertent cum concupiscentia, sicuti patet ex Berefchit Rabba, Sect. 9. Quamdiu pii vivunt, tamdiu pugnandum ipsis cum concupiscentia sua; Imo, quod magis est, credunt Judaei ipsas malas cogitationes peccati graviores esse peccato perpetrato, juxta effatum illud Talmudicum, in Joma, sol. 29. Cogitationes peccati graviores sunt ipso peccato; Et in Rabbi Ephrajimi Ir Gibborim, sol. 79. Dicunt Veteres: Cogitatum peccatum gravius est perpetrato. Rationem hanc dat Rabbi Moses Maimonides, quia sic homo peccat praestantissima animae suae parte. te, quæ est facultas rationalis; Hinc pravas cogitationes non potuisse expiari nisi holocausto, quod sacrificium erat nobilissimum, sicut refert Rabbi Bechai sol.137. col.1. Holocaustum non offerebatur pro peccato externo, sed tantum pro peccaminosis cogitationibus & animi motibus, à quibus nemo hominum liber est.
units.tr: They believe that inner concupiscence, or evil thoughts, are vicious and sinful, even if the crime is not directed to execution and does not pass into external act; the Jews bear witness to this in the Talmudic tractate Bava Bathra, fol. 134, col. 2, and 164, col. 2: There are three transgressions from which a man can never be free or guard himself on any day: evil thoughts, wandering of attention in prayer, and an evil tongue. Nor among the Jews does only he commit adultery who actually violates another's wife, but also he who rolls lustful thoughts in his mind, according to the Talmudic doctrine, contrary to the old Pharisaic one, in the tractate Challah, at the beginning: Whoever looks at a woman with intent is just as if he had had to do with her. The Christian doctrine, however, agrees with this in Matthew, chap. 5, vv. 27 and 28: You have heard that it was said by the ancients: You shall not commit adultery. But I say to you, whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. Rabbi Bechai also had regard to the saying of these Talmudists, speaking in the same way at fol. 153, col. 1: It is a saying of the ancients: whoever looks at a woman transgresses the precept, "Do not turn to idols." For it is forbidden even to think of another's wife. So the same Rabbi Bechai shows that he defrauds his neighbour not only who takes his property from him against his will, but also he who inordinately covets another's goods. At fol. 99, col. 2, he says: Defrauding a neighbour is a great sin, and very common among almost everyone. It is all the more grave because it is a principle known by nature, no less than the fifth, sixth, seventh and eighth precepts. But because an evil desire comes first, since no one drags anything of another's toward himself unless he has first desired it, according to that saying of Micah, chap. 2, v. 2: "They covet fields and seize them," there was therefore no need to mention this sin expressly, but Scripture comprehends it under the negative precept, "You shall not covet." Add to this that God wills also to forbid concupiscence itself, which is a motion of the heart working at every time and hour, and not only the external act; so that man may learn that, if without inner concupiscence something may be lawful, how much less can an external act be lawful. Hence they warn their people how vehemently to avoid the sin of concupiscence, citing the Bereshit Rabba, that it is at first a stranger, then a guest, and at last becomes the master of the house and lord of the household. In the Talmudic Sukkah, fol. 52, col. 1: Evil concupiscence at the beginning is like a spider's thread, but at the end like a thick cart-rope. From Vayikra Rabba, sect. 17: The beginning of concupiscence is sweet, but its end is bitter. Hence they also exhort the pious to struggle with concupiscence throughout their whole life, as is clear from Bereshit Rabba, sect. 9: As long as the pious live, so long must they fight with their concupiscence. Indeed, and what is more, the Jews believe that evil thoughts themselves are graver than a sin actually committed, according to that Talmudic saying in Yoma, fol. 29: Sinful thoughts are graver than the sin itself. And in Rabbi Ephraim's Ir Gibborim, fol. 79: The ancients say: a sin thought of is graver than one committed. Rabbi Moses Maimonides gives this reason: because in this way a man sins with the most excellent part of his soul, which is the rational faculty. Hence evil thoughts could not be expiated except by a burnt offering, which was the most noble sacrifice, as Rabbi Bechai reports at fol. 137, col. 1: A burnt offering was not offered for an external sin, but only for sinful thoughts and motions of the mind, from which no man is free.

units.la: CAPUT XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: De libero Arbitrio Hominis Peccatoris.
units.tr: On the Free Will of Sinful Man.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Judæos Recentiores omnes Religionis, Salutisque suæ principium constituere, tum in promissionibus, absolutaque divina Misericordia, absque peccatorum satisfactione per alium præstita, tum in ipso homine, ejusque יהוה Electione, absolutisque liberi arbitrii viribus, extra omnem positum est controversiam, cū nonsolum illud quotidie in familiaribus testentur colloquiis, valdeque urgeant, si nobiscum disputent, verum abunde etiam pateat, patear ex scriptis ubique obviis, teste luculento Rabbi Ilac, Bar Abraham, cum in munimine Fidei, sic inquit Part. I. cap. ii. Ecce, vides ex omnibus iis rationibus, quod homines pii, sancti Patriarchae, non detrusi fuerint in infernum, nec ob peccatum protaplasti passi sint poenas animarum. Abjit ut tale quid iis evenerit, nec enim ceu ipse adversus Dei os rebellaverant, sed invenere gratiam in oculis Domini, salutem, aeternam consecuti sunt propriis meritis, nec opus habebant alieno merito ad salvandas animas suas, ceu Nazareni ex suo ingenio comminiscuntur; Assentiente Rabbi Lipmanno in Carmine Memoriali, pag. iii. Editionis Wagenseilianae: Sed, sciendum, omnes mortales, quaeque ipsi possident, in Dei esse manibus, ita ut de his ex arbitrio disponat: Tantum excipitur Religio, sive Pietas erga Numen, quae a cujusque voluntate pendet, nec a Deo tribuitur, cum liberum sit homini, tam virtutibus se mancipare, quam contrarius vitiis: Nec enim aliter supremo Domino constare posset de iis qui se amant, nisi plenam boni malique optionem haberent; Suffragantibus pari modo Talmudistis, in Tractatibus Berachot, f. 33. col. 2, & Nidda, f. 16 col. 2 quorum sequens erat placitum: omnia sunt in manibus caeli, (Dei) excepto timore caeli. (Dei.) Credunt quippe, quod quicquid homini accidat, a Deo procedat Benedicto,
units.tr: All modern Jews, beyond any dispute, base the beginning of their religion and their salvation both on the promises and on God's absolute mercy, apart from any satisfaction for sins made by another, and on man himself and his election by Jehovah [יהוה], and on the absolute powers of free will. They do not merely say this every day in familiar conversation and press it hard when they argue with us; it is also abundantly clear from writings found everywhere, as the distinguished Rabbi Isaac ben Abraham bears witness in the Hizzuk Emunah, Part I, chap. ii, where he says: "Behold, you see from all these reasons that pious men, the holy patriarchs, were not cast down into hell, nor suffered punishment of souls because of the sin of the first parent. Far be it that such a thing should happen to them. For they had not rebelled against the mouth of God like him, but found grace in the eyes of the Lord, and obtained eternal salvation by their own merits. Nor did they need another's merit to save their souls, as the Nazarenes invent out of their own wit." Rabbi Lipmann agrees in the Carmen Memoriale, p. iii of the Wagenseil edition: "But it must be known that all mortals and all that they possess are in the hands of God, so that he disposes of these at his will. Only religion, or piety toward the Deity, is excepted; this depends on each person's own will and is not bestowed by God, since it is free for a man to devote himself to virtues as much as to their opposites. For otherwise the Supreme Lord could not be sure of those who love him, unless they had a full option between good and evil." The Talmudists agree in the same way, in the tractates Berachot, f. 33, col. 2, and Nidda, f. 16, col. 2, whose settled view was: "All things are in the hands of heaven (God), except the fear of heaven (God)." For they believe that whatever happens to a man proceeds from the blessed God,

units.la: Aa veveluti quod fit procerus, brevis, albus, ater, sapiens, stultus, dives, pauper, at vero quod fit justus aut injustus, pius aut impius, id non fit a Deo, sed in manu hominis a Deo sit positum.
units.tr: just as it is that one becomes tall, short, white, black, wise, foolish, rich, or poor; but that one becomes just or unjust, pious or impious, that is not done by God, but is placed by God in the hand of man.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Credunt hominis salutem ex libero dependere arbitrio, ita loquitur Rabbi Menalfeh Ben Israel de Fragilitate Humana, pag. 118. Dicimus igitur, Deum disposuisse ita homines, ut salus ab eorum voluntate dependeat; Hominem q; a poenis liberari, tam spiritualibus, quam corporalibus, quod liberi arbitrii a summo Numine constitutus sit Dominus, uti scribit Rabbi Levi in Commentario, 1. Reg. 17. 1. Deus non cogit hominem ut peccet, sed posuit eum תוירה יבא Dominum Electionis, seu liberi arbitrii, ut liberaretur a panis spiritualibus & corporalibus.
units.tr: They believe that a man's salvation depends on free choice. So speaks Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel in De Fragilitate Humana, p. 118: We say, therefore, that God has so disposed men that their salvation depends on their will. And that man is freed from punishments, both spiritual and bodily, because the Supreme Deity has appointed him lord of free choice, as Rabbi Levi writes in his Commentary on 1 Kings 17:1: God does not compel man to sin, but has placed him as lord of election, that is, of free will [בחירה], so that he might be freed from spiritual and bodily punishments.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Credunt, quotquot sunt, hanc liberi arbitrii doctrinam, non tantum in Lege Moisis firmiter radicatam, verum Legis ipsum esse fundamentum, cui a nullo ex gente Judaica unquam sit contradictum, proinde cui maxima animi contentione semper sit inhaerendum, uti loquitur Rabbi Maimonides in More Nevochim, Part. III cap. 17. Dico ergo: Fundamentum Legis Moysis Doctorum nostri, omniumque eorum, qui illi adhaerent, est, quod homo habeat absolutissimam mam potestatem, hoc est, quod homo per naturam, arbitrium & voluntatem suam facit, quicquid homo facere potest, sine ulla re alia in ipso creata & innovata. Omnia pariter animalia irrationalia moventur voluntate sua. Et sic voluit Deus Optimus, & Maximus, hoc est, voluntas ejus æterna fuit, ut omne animal moveatur per voluntatem suam, & ut homo habeat potestatem ejus, quod vult vel eligit, in iis, quæ cadunt sub ipsius potentiam. Huic fundamento unquam ab aliquo in Gente nostra contradictum fuisse, non est auditum.
units.tr: All of them, whoever they are, believe that this doctrine of free will is not only firmly rooted in the Law of Moses, but is the very foundation of the Law, which no one of the Jewish nation has ever contradicted, and to which therefore one must always cling with the greatest effort of mind. So speaks Rabbi Maimonides in More Nevochim, Part III, chap. 17: I say, therefore: the foundation of the Law of Moses, of our teachers and of all who adhere to it, is that man has the most absolute power, that is, that man by nature makes his own choice and will, whatever he can do, without any other thing being created or renewed in him. In the same way all irrational animals move by their own will. And thus God, the Best and Greatest, willed, that is, his eternal will was, that every animal should move by its own will, and that man should have power over what he wills or chooses, among those things which fall under his power. It has never been heard that anyone in our nation contradicted this foundation.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Negant hinc Adami lapsu homini adem-ptam arbitrii ad bonum libertatem, sublatasq; ad conversionem sufficientes vires, ingemi-nantes, quot possunt modis, Adami Posteros omnes, eodem, quo præditus in prima Crea-tione fuerat arbitrio, excultos hodie, exorna-tosque esse, referente Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel in Libello de Termino Vitæ, pag. 198.
units.tr: From this they deny that free will to do good was taken from man by the fall of Adam, and that sufficient strength for conversion was removed. They repeat in as many ways as they can that all Adam's posterity are today endowed and adorned with the same free will with which Adam was endowed at the first creation, as reported by Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel in the book De Termino Vitae, p. 198.

units.la: Aben Ezra inquit, nominibus proprius in Sacra Scriptura non præfigi הא הדיעי He Demonstrati-vum, quod tamen in voce Adam sit: ratio est quia in Adamo, notantur omnes ejus posteri, & universa species humana designatur: quia si Adam in crea-tione rerum libero arbitrio præditus fuit, eodem etiam libero arbitrio, omnes homines ejus posteri præditi sunt; Insiciantur hinc strenue, liberum arbiarbitrium miserrimam esse peccatorum servitutem, libertatemque voluntatis humanae solum vitiis, injustitiaeque esse deditam, ac mancipatam, ita ut non tantum non possit ad Spiritualia. Deique terium allurgere amorem, sed ut potius necessitate quadam quasi feratur in malum, & quae Deo sunt contraria, atque ea propter tam ipsam conversionem, quam prima ejus initia omnia, solius Dei gratiae speciale esse munus. Pernegant hinc quoque maliciam voluntati nostrae connatam, impotentiam naturae inesse maximam, sicuti patebit ex iis, quae Capite XIII. De Justificatione & Conversione hominis, plenius erunt adducenda. Licet quandoque concedant, docentque, Naturam humanam per primi hominis peccatum debilitatam fuisse, labefactamque, ipsumque perdidisse hominem justitiam & rectitudinem, simulque varias contraxisse poenas, prout testatur Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, cum in Libello de Fragilitate Humana, pag. 44. sic loquitur: Ultimo, Adam peccati causa perdidit justitiam, & rectitudinem, in qua fuerat creatus: & quemadmodum supra diximus, cum antea solum naturaliter ad virtutem inclinaret, postea quam de arbore scientiae boni & mali comedisset, (sicut bene advertit R. Moseh Gerundensis) debilis, & labefacta natura, pari proclivitate, in vitium, & & virtutem ferebatur. Ac velut dicit Selomoh in Ecclesiastes cap. VII,29: Creavit Deus Adam rectum; verum illi (puta Adam, & Eva) cogitaverunt rationicinia multa, ut introducerent peccatum: & hoc ipso, (ut in eundem locum notavit Nar aphrasis Chaldaica) גרמו לאסתקפא עלוהי ולכל דיירי ארעא מכתא arcessiverunt sibi mortem, & omnibus, qui morantur super terram.
units.tr: Aben Ezra says that the demonstrative He [הא הידיעה] is not prefixed to proper names in Holy Scripture, although it is in the word Adam. The reason is that in Adam all his posterity are noted, and the whole human species is designated. For if Adam was endowed with free will at the creation of things, then by the same free will all men, his posterity, are endowed. From this they vigorously deny that free will is the most wretched slavery of sins, and that the freedom of the human will is given over and enslaved only to vices and injustice, so that it not only cannot aspire to spiritual things and to God's love, but is rather carried toward evil by a certain necessity, as it were, and toward what is contrary to God. For this reason, both conversion itself and all its first beginnings are a special gift of God's grace alone. They likewise deny that malice is innate in our will, or that the greatest impotence inheres in our nature, as will be made plain from those things which will be set forth more fully in Chapter XIII, On the Justification and Conversion of Man. Although at times they concede and teach that human nature was weakened and undermined by the sin of the first man, and that man lost justice and rectitude and at the same time contracted various punishments, as Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel testifies in De Fragilitate Humana, p. 44, where he speaks thus: Lastly, Adam by his sin lost the justice and rectitude in which he had been created; and as we said above, since before he inclined naturally only toward virtue, but afterward, when he had eaten from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (as Rabbi Moses of Gerona rightly notes), his nature, weakened and undermined, was carried with equal proneness toward vice and toward virtue. And as Solomon says in Ecclesiastes 7:29: "God made man upright, but they (namely Adam and Eve) sought out many inventions," so that by this (as the Chaldee paraphrast also noted on the same passage) they brought upon themselves and upon all the inhabitants of the earth a plague [gramu le-'astaqpa 'alohi ul-khol dayyire arga makhta].

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Probant fidei Pharisaicæ Palladium ex innumeris Sacræ Scripturæ dictis, confirmantque multis tam rationibus, quam authoritatibus, ipsaque magistra experientia; Et ex sacra pagina adducunt verba Genes. cap. 3. vers. 22. Dixitque Dominus Deus, ecce homo est, sicut unus ex nobis, sciendo bonum & malum, itaque ne extendat manum suam, sumat de arbore vita, comedatque, & æternum vivat. Emisit igitur eum Dominus Deus ex horto Edenis; Concludentes, si non quod volebat poterat, quid intererat expelli eum Paradiso, quando etiam illic agitans, comedere non posset; Proinde ex his constare, conditum cum libero arbitrio hominem, atque illud tanquam proprium naturæ humanæ, retinuisse; Adducunt pariter Exod. cap. 13. vers. 17. ut cum egrediente ex Ægypto Israele dicitur: Non duxit eos Deus via regionis Philistæorum, quod propinqua esset: dicebat enim Deus, ne pœniteat hunc popupopulum, cum viderint bellum, & revertantur in Ægyptum; Et Deuteron. cap. 5. verf. 29. Quis dabit hunc illis animum, ut timeant me, & observent præcepta mea omnibus diebus; Ex quibus colligunt, quod actus ille humanus non sit absolute in manu Dei, seu quod non pendeat a Deo, tanquam necessarius effectus, a causa suprema manans, sed sit tanquam affectus liber a causa libera, seu voluntate hominis libere agente producendus, vel opus fuerit, ut homo ipse vellet, qui velle poterat & nolle, uti ratiocinatur Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel in Conciliatore ad Exodum, Quæst. 6. Et in Libello de Termino Vitæ, pag. 198. 199. Utuntur præterea in causæ demonstrationem, verbis Dei apud Mosen, Deuteron. cap. 30. verf. 15. in quibus non inst ar cogentis, sed suadentis ait: Ecce proposui tibi hodie vitam & bonum, item mortem & malum: id quod ego tibi præcipio hodie, est, ut ames Dominum Deum tuum; Quasi diceret, proposui tibi quidem bonum & malum, sed præcipio tibi ut me ames; Illudque fluere ex versu sequenti 19. Contestor hodie contra vos cælum & terram, me vitam ac mortem proposuisse tibi, benedictionem & maledictionem: & elige vitam; Ex quibus judicant, si vitam Deus elegi suadet, sequitur libertatem iis ad utrumque relictam esse, cum consilium supervacue detur, si ele-ctio étio sit sublata; Sic quoque ex Jeremiæ Lamentationibus cap. 3. ℣. 38, argumentantur: Ex ore Excelsi non prodeunt mala, & bonum; Quasi diceret: Si bona & mala non egrediuntur ex ore Excelsi, ergo exeunt ex ore & voluntate hominis; Idcirco quoque Jeremiam verf. 40. progredi in oratione: Perscrutemur vias nostras & pervestigemus, & revertamur usq; ad Deum; Hisque incitari homines, ut, tanquam liberi in actionibus suis, videant quid agant, redeantque ad Deum, & peccatorum pœnitentia ducantur; Frustra autem illud urgeri à Prophéta, si homines libero carerent arbitrio; Unde quoque Esaiam citant, apud quem Dominus cap. 66. verf. 3, 4. loquatur: Illi eligunt vias suas, & ego eligam in damnis eorum.
