units.tr: They defend the Pharisaic faith's Palladium from countless sayings of Holy Scripture, and they confirm it with many arguments and authorities, and with experience itself, the teacher of all things. From the sacred page they cite the words of Genesis 3:22: "And the Lord God said, Behold, the man is become as one of us, knowing good and evil; and now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever." Therefore the Lord God sent him forth from the garden of Eden. They reason: if man could not do what he wished, what would it matter that he was expelled from Paradise, when even there, though moving about, he could not eat? Therefore it is clear from these things that man was created with free will, and has kept it as something proper to human nature. They likewise adduce Exodus 13:17, where it is said of Israel going out of Egypt: "God did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, although it was near; for God said, lest the people repent when they see war, and return into Egypt." And Deuteronomy 5:29: "Oh that there were such an heart in them, that they would fear me, and keep all my commandments always." From these they gather that the human act is not absolutely in the hand of God, or that it does not depend on God as a necessary effect flowing from a supreme cause, but is like a free affection, to be produced by a free cause, that is, by the will of man acting freely; or, as it was necessary, that man himself should will, since he was able both to will and not to will. So Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel reasons in his Conciliator on Exodus, Question 6, and in the little book On the Term of Life, pp. 198, 199. They also use, to demonstrate their cause, the words of God to Moses in Deuteronomy 30:15, in which he speaks not as one compelling but as one persuading: "Behold, I have set before thee this day life and good, and death and evil; that which I command thee this day is, that thou love the Lord thy God." As if he said: I have indeed set before you good and evil, but I command you that you love me. And this follows from the next verse, 19: "I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life." From these they judge that if God persuades us to choose life, it follows that freedom is left to them with respect to either, since counsel would be given in vain if choice were taken away. Likewise they argue from Lamentations 3:38: "Out of the mouth of the Most High proceedeth not evil and good"; as if he said: if good and evil do not proceed from the mouth of the Most High, then they proceed from the mouth and will of man. For this reason also Jeremiah, in verse 40, goes on in his prayer: "Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the Lord"; and by these words men are stirred, as free in their actions, to see what they are doing, and to return to God, and be led to repentance for their sins. But it would be pointless for the prophet to urge this if men lacked free will. Hence they also cite Isaiah, in whom the Lord speaks in chapter 66, verses 3 and 4: "They choose their own ways, and I will choose their delusions."

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Instant rationibus multis, ut liberum arbitrium, voluntatisque libertatem demonstrent ac defendant, ratiocinantes sæpe ex ipsis primæ Philosophiæ principiis, ipsisque hominis interioribus, uti patet ex Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, cum in Conciliatore ad Exodum, Quæst. 6. pag. 108. sic Philosophatur: Etenim videmus nonnulla sine intellectu agere, ut lapidem deorsum cadentem, aliuque id genus, quibus judicium non est. Nonnullis scientia naturalis est, sed determinata ad unam solam rem, neque libera, ut mutus animantibus. Etenim ovis lupum sentiens, scit fugiendum sibi, sed hoc fit naturali intellectu, & non libere, quia natura instinctu id necessario faciunt. Atque hujusmodi judicium omnibus animalibus est: sed homini judicium liberum est, quia per intellectum judicat necessario alia sibi vitanda, alia sequenda: adeo ut judicium hoc in singulis actionibus non a natura, sed ratione proficiscatur, qua cum libera sit, velle & nolle, agere & non agere possit. Cum igitur hominum actiones sint contingentes, neque judicium uni adstrictum sit, sequitur esse ei liberum arbitrium.
units.tr: They press many arguments to demonstrate and defend free will and the liberty of the will, often reasoning from the very principles of first philosophy and from the inner workings of man himself, as appears from Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, who in his Conciliator on Exodus, Question 6, p. 108, philosophizes thus: "For we see some things act without intellect, as a stone falling downward, and others of that kind, which have no judgment. Some have natural knowledge, but determined to one thing only, and not free, as dumb animals. For a sheep, sensing a wolf, knows that it must flee, but this happens by natural intellect and not freely, because by instinct they do these things necessarily by nature. Such judgment belongs to all animals; but to man judgment is free, because through the intellect he judges necessarily that some things are to be avoided and others to be pursued, so that this judgment in individual actions proceeds not from nature but from reason, which, since it is free, can will and not will, act and not act. Since therefore the actions of men are contingent, and judgment is not bound to one thing, it follows that free will belongs to him."

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Ajunt Liberi Arbitrii veritatem satis superque apparere ex ipse, metuque hominum, qui si certo persuasum haberent, quae praedestinata sunt, necessario eventura, neque arma ad defensionem sui, aut noxam alteri tollerent, neque munimenta excitarent; imo frustra malum vitari, & bonum quaeri, si libertatis voluntatis nullus esset religuus locus; sublato libero arbitrio, omnia cessare opera, consilia, admonitionesque, quippe quod supervacanea forent ad consequenda destinata, monente Rabbi Maimonide in Dissertationibus suis praefixis commentariis in varias Mischnajoth, Edit. Procockianae pag. 234. Quod si homo actiones suas coactus ederet, cessarent jam praecepta & & prohibitiones legales: effentque ea omnia penitus frustanea, cum nulla superesset homini in eo quod agit electio; Hominem denique non posse laudari, vel vituperari, si in actionibus suis nullo modo liber esset, uti conspicitur ex Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, in libello de termino vitæ, pag. 204. Videmus etiam hominem solum prorationE & modo agendi, prosine quem propositum sibi habet, & medius quibus utitur, vel laudari, vel vituperari: & merito. Neque enim infans, aut dormiens, ne dicam stolidus, aut satuus, si forte damnum alicui inferat, culpari idcirco a nobis solet, cum tamen si ex eventu judicandum est, non minus reprehendi mereatur, propter damnum illatum, quam alii homines: sed vero nemo tam demens est, ut tales accuset: unde sequitur, persuasum omnibus esse, nec laudandum, nec arguendum quenquam, nisi qui libero arbitrio, & consulto bene agit, aut delinquit. Adeo ut nullus suasioni, consiliis, redargutioni, præmio, aut pœnæ locus sit, si homo non est liber in actionibus suis.
units.tr: They claim that the truth of free will is plain enough and more than enough from experience itself, and they fear that if men were firmly persuaded that what has been predestined must necessarily come to pass, they would neither take up arms to defend themselves or to harm another, nor build fortifications. Indeed, it would be pointless to avoid evil and seek good if there were no remaining place for freedom of the will. With free will removed, all work, counsel and admonition would cease, since they would be superfluous for attaining what has been decreed, as Rabbi Maimonides notes in the Dissertations prefixed to his commentaries on the various Mishnayoth, Procockian edition, p. 234. And if man performed his actions under compulsion, the legal precepts and prohibitions would now cease, and all of them would be utterly futile, since no choice would remain to man in what he does. Finally, man could not be praised or blamed if he were in no way free in his actions, as is seen from Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel in his little book on the term of life, p. 204. We also see that a man is praised or blamed only for his reason and manner of acting, for the purpose he has set before himself and the means he uses. And rightly so. For if a child, or a sleeping man, not to say a fool or a madman, happens to inflict some harm on someone, we are not accustomed to blame him for it, though if judgment were to be made by the outcome, he would deserve no less reproach for the harm done than other men. But no one is so mad as to accuse such people. Hence it follows that it is agreed by all that no one should be praised or rebuked unless he acts well or does wrong by free will and deliberately. So that there is no place for persuasion, counsel, rebuke, reward or punishment if a man is not free in his actions.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Tandem prostant infinita Judæorum testimonia, quæ congesta cernere licet apud Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, in Conciliatore ad Exodum, Quæst. 6. Respondent quoque ad argumenta, quæ objiciuntur, contraria, stantes pro libero arbitrio, tanquam pro aris & focis, cis, demonstrantes simul, Præscientiam divinam nihil arbitrii derogare libertati; Sic pariter audacter calumniantur, nos liberum tollere arbitrium, dum vitam æternam supremæ causæ singulare esse beneficium prædicamus, conversionemque nostram divinæ attribuimus gratiæ; Sed de his aliquando pluribus.
units.tr: Finally, there are endless testimonies of the Jews, which one may see gathered together in Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, in the Conciliator on Exodus, Question 6. They also answer the contrary arguments that are objected, standing up for free will as for their altars and hearths, while at the same time showing that divine foreknowledge takes nothing away from liberty. In the same way they boldly slander us as abolishing free will, while we proclaim eternal life to be the singular benefit of the supreme cause and attribute our conversion to divine grace. But of these things, at some other time, at greater length.

units.la: CAPUT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: De Homine per Gratiam restituto, sive de Peccatoris Reconciliatione cum Deo per Messiam.
units.tr: Of Man Restored by Grace, or of the Reconciliation of the Sinner with God through the Messiah.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Quam diversa, distinctaque facies sit Judaismi, tum moderni, tum antiqui, facile deprehendi potest, si utriusque accurata institutuatur collatio; Quippe Veteres, quamquam operum aliqua turgerent fiducia, Pharisaica inflati justitia, saepe tamen multum Messiae, Gratiaeque tribuebant divinae; Hinc de Messiae aeterna, divinaque natura, gloria, miraculis, variisque pro humano genere, quod per peccatum destitutum erat, exantlandis officiis, quibus illud restituat, reconciliet, justificet, glorificet, tot, tantaque innumera extant testimonia, in unam pridem summam collecta, ut illa amplius velle negare, sit in meridiana coecutire luce; Imo ipsam saepe erga nos divinam praedicabant gratiam, ad operum non attendentes bonitatem, uti liquet ex ruderibus Theologiae antiquae, reliduisetiam in ipsa Catechesi Judaica, Responsione ad Quaestionem 14. Fiducia est donum nostris a Deo inditum animis, quo mediante certam animat is nostris pollicemur felicitatem, idque non ob nostrorum operum bonitatem, sed ob divinam erga nos gratiam; Cum, quotquot sunt hodie Recentiores, a veritatis antiquae tramite longe discedant, inque contraria omnia nunc abeant, pervicaciter exististimantes, peccatoris cum Deo restitutionem, reconciliationemque, non patere per Messiam Mediatorem, ejusque, quotquot sunt beneficia, sed per opera, meritaque sua humana, sive illa sint propria, sive aliena; ut ita miseranda Ecclesiae Judaicae sit facies, dum tota hodierna Religio ita modis omnibus e-lumbata est, utinane fpeftaculum facta, absq; omni divina fit spe, ac consolatione.
units.tr: How different and distinct the face of Judaism is, both modern and ancient, can easily be seen if a careful comparison of the two is made. The Ancients, though some of them swelled with confidence in their works and were puffed up with Pharisaic righteousness, often nevertheless ascribed much to the Messiah and to the divine grace. Hence there remain so many great and countless testimonies about the eternal and divine nature, the glory, the miracles of the Messiah, and the various offices he was to perform for the human race, which had been cast down by sin: to restore it, reconcile it, justify it, and glorify it. These testimonies were long ago gathered into one sum, so that to wish to deny them would be to grow blind in the noonday light. Indeed, they often proclaimed the divine grace toward us, not looking to the goodness of works, as is clear from the remnants of ancient theology and from the Jewish Catechism itself, in the answer to Question 14: Confidence is a gift implanted in our souls by God, through which we promise ourselves certain happiness in our hearts, and this not on account of the goodness of our works but on account of the divine grace toward us. But all the modern writers, however many there are today, have wandered far from the path of ancient truth and now go over to the opposite in everything. They stubbornly think that the restoration and reconciliation of the sinner with God does not come through the Messiah the Mediator and all his benefits, but through their own works and merits, whether these are their own or another's. Thus the face of the Jewish Church is pitiable, since the whole present religion has been so weakened in every way that it has become, I wish it were not so, a spectacle without any divine hope or consolation.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Et quæso an alia Judæis nostris his temporibus mens esse potest? Nonne ex male jacto fundamento ultro sequitur? Si enim homo suarum cogitationum est proprius Dominus, salutisque & damnationis suæ architectus audit; Si Pietas erga Deum a cujusque libero dependet arbitrio; Si Meffias homo purus putus futurus, non vero Deus simul in una Persona; Si populi Judaici extiturus ductor, qui externam aboliturus fit corporalemq; servitutem, non vero animarum ad vitam æternam dux, medicusque, quia poenis spiritualibus, servituteque diaboli fit liberaturus ac erepturus, necessario Meffiæ officium vel nullum in salutis negotio, vel saltem exile valde esse oportet.
units.tr: And I ask, can our Jews in these times have any other mind? Does this not follow of its own accord from a badly laid foundation? For if man is the proper lord of his own thoughts and the architect of his own salvation and damnation; if piety toward God depends on each person's free choice; if the Messiah is to be a mere man and not also God in one Person; if he is to be the leader of the Jewish people who will abolish external and bodily servitude, and not the leader and physician of souls to eternal life, since he is to free and rescue them from spiritual punishments and the servitude of the devil, then the office of the Messiah in the business of salvation must necessarily be either nothing or, at the least, very slight.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Hinc credunt Meffiam certo venturum, & licet adventum differat, maxima tamen animi contentione expectandum, ut tandem ab externa hostium vexatione immunes facti, Meffiæ auspiciis patrios repetant lares, Rempublicam instaurent Judaicam, Hierosolymasque cum templo reædificent, confitentibus illud
units.tr: Hence they believe that the Messiah will certainly come, and although he delays his coming, he is to be awaited with the greatest eagerness of mind, so that at last, freed from the external harassment of enemies, under the auspices of the Messiah they may recover their ancestral home, restore the Jewish commonwealth, and rebuild Jerusalem with the temple, confessing that in the creed of their religion,

units.la: in Symbolo suæ Religionis, articulo duodeci-mo, apud Rabbi Maimonidem, in Commen-tario ad Sanhedrin, cap. II. Fundamentum duo-decimum מנוח המשיח Dies Messiæ, quod oporteat credere, illum certissimo venturum, neque moratu-rum, & si cunctatus fuerit, expecta eum, Habac. cap. 2. verf. 3. Non decet autem aliquem supputare tem-pus, aut curiose elicere ex Scripturis, ut cognoscatur tempus adventus ejus, quemadmodum dixerunt Sapientes cel. mem. in cap. Chelek: Rumpatur ani-mus supputantium terminos. Porro credendum, quod ejus Excellentia, Majestas, & gloria supra omnes Reges, qui unquam a sæculo fuerunt, sicuti de eo vaticinati sunt Prophetæ omnes inde a Mose Magistro nostro, qui in pace quiescat, usque ad Malachiam beatæ memoriæ. Quisquis vero de eo dubi-taverit, aut saltem apud semet ipsum persuaserit Majestatem ejus, is legem abnegat, utpote quæ eum apertissime promisit in Parascha Bileam & Nizzabhim. Tandem ad hunc articulum pertinet, ut credamus, quod non sit Rex Israeli, nisi de domo Davidis, & ex femine quidem Salomonis tantum. Quisquis ergo se huic familiæ opposuerit, is apostata est, & Deum pariter, atque verba Prophetarum abnegat; Et in Catechesi Judaica, Responsione ad Quæstionem 10. Fundamentum duodecimum, quod Deus missurus sit Messiam Redemptorem populi sui. Quem licet cunctatus fuerit, expectapectabimus tamen. Prodibit autem Messias ille ex femine Davidis, virga Isai, Bethlehemo. Vir quoque ille statuet in justitia terram, judicabit populos multos, justitia cingulum lumborum ejus erit, videbit semen, & prolongabit dies super regnum suum, neque ullam seculo huic innovationem asse-ret, nisi quod tum restituetur Israelitis regnum pri-stinum, ipsi vero terram illorum repetent, aedifica-turi domum Sanctuarii, eaque quae ad cultum ejus oblationesque pertinent sua quaque loco restauratu-ri, Sacerdotibus servitiis suis, Levitis autem can-tionibus suis redditis; Patetque illud ex Rabbi Matthiae Manuscripto, apud Schickardum in Jure Regio Hebraeorum, cap. 6. Credimus nos, qui sumus de coetu Judaeorum, instare nostram redemptionem, qua recolliget Deus Optimus Maximus dispulsos, & mittet nobis Messiam nostrum. Is instaurabit cultum sacrum in adyto domus suae, & admovebit nos servitio ejus. Tunc recreabit populum suum e diebus afflictionis, quando restituet cultum pristino vigori. Utinam celeriter illo tempore nos dignaretur? etiamsi moretur diu, num tamen propterea non expectabimus; Nec e diametro repugnat Rabbi Joseph Albo, in contrarium fere semper citatus, Part. 1. Libri de Articulis; Cum adventum Regis Messiae non neget Albo, sed solum inficietur, quod unus ex tribus sit fundamentalibus, libens bens concedens, quod articuli fundamenta-lis iti ramus propullulans, perconsequens fide amplectendus, sicuti aliquando pluribus de-monstrabimus.
units.tr: in the twelfth article, according to Rabbi Maimonides, in his Commentary on Sanhedrin, chapter 11: The twelfth foundation, the Days of the Messiah [מנוח המשיח], is that one must believe he will certainly come and will not delay; and if he tarries, wait for him (Habakkuk 2:3). It is not fitting, however, for anyone to calculate the time or to deduce curiously from the Scriptures when his coming will be known, as the wise men of blessed memory said in the chapter Chelek: "Let the soul of those who calculate the ends be broken." Furthermore, one must believe that his excellence, majesty, and glory are above all the kings who have ever been from the age, just as all the prophets prophesied about him, from Moses our Teacher, may he rest in peace, down to Malachi of blessed memory. Whoever doubts this, or at least persuades himself that his majesty is otherwise, denies the Law, since it promised him most plainly in the parashah of Balaam and Nizzavim. Finally, this article pertains to the belief that there is no king of Israel except from the house of David, and from the seed of Solomon only. Whoever therefore sets himself against this family is an apostate and denies God as well as the words of the prophets. And in the Jewish Catechism, in the answer to Question 10: The twelfth foundation is that God will send the Messiah, the Redeemer of his people. Though he delays, we shall nonetheless wait for him. That Messiah will come forth from the seed of David, the rod of Jesse, from Bethlehem. That man will also establish the earth in justice, he will judge many peoples, justice will be the girdle of his loins, he will see his seed and prolong his days over his kingdom; and he will assert no novelty to this age, except that then the former kingdom will be restored to the Israelites, and they will recover their land, rebuilding the house of the sanctuary and restoring those things that pertain to its worship and offerings, each in its place, with the priests in their service and the Levites rendered in their songs. This is also clear from the manuscript of Rabbi Matthias, as cited by Schickard in Jus Regium Hebraeorum, chapter 6: We believe that we, who are of the assembly of the Jews, are about to have our redemption, by which God, the Best and Greatest, will gather together those who have been scattered, and will send us our Messiah. He will restore the sacred worship in the inner sanctuary of his house and will bring us near to his service. Then he will refresh his people from the days of affliction, when he restores worship to its former vigor. Would that he might deign to do so quickly in that time! Even if he delays long, shall we not therefore wait? Nor does Rabbi Joseph Albo, who is almost always cited to the contrary, stand diametrically opposed, in Part 1 of his book On the Articles. For Albo does not deny the coming of the King Messiah, but only denies that it is one of the three fundamental articles. Willingly granting that this is a shoot springing from the root of the fundamental article, and consequently to be embraced by faith, as we shall at some time show more fully.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Confitentur Judæi immensam Messiæ gloriam, majestatem, honores infinitos, felicitatem summam, doctrinam eximiam, Regnum illustre, hinc virtutibus quoque esse divinum, Deumque & Filium Dei appellari concedunt, sed eo tantum sensu, quo Moses Deus Aaronis, Exod. cap. 4. vers. 16. Et Pharaonis, Exod. cap. 7. vers. 1. Judicesque Dei, Exod. cap. 21. vers. 6. Israelitæ primogenitus Dei filius, Exod. cap. 4. vers. 22. Omnesque pii filii Excelsi, Psal. 82. vers. 6. vocati, Ast inficiantur manibus, pedibusque, Messiam naturalem esse Dei Filium, ab æterno ex substantia Patris genitum, eandemque cum ipso possidentem divinam essentiam, naturamque, nihilque de Messia prædicantes nisi humanam naturam, humanaque omnia; Inficiantur Oracula sancta Messiam passim appellare Jehova, Germenque Jehovæ, Jes. cap. 4. Jehova Justitiam, Jerem. cap. 23. Filium Dei, Psal. 2. Cujus nomen ante solem fit filiarum, Psalm. 72. Genitum, acquisitumque ante secula, Proverb. c. 8. Mich. cap. 5. Hæredem omnium, Psalm. 2.
units.tr: The Jews confess the immense glory, majesty, infinite honours, supreme happiness and outstanding teaching of the Messiah, and his illustrious kingdom. Hence they also concede that he is divine in virtue, and that he is called God and Son of God, but only in the sense in which Moses is called God of Aaron (Exod. 4:16) and God of Pharaoh (Exod. 7:1), judges are called God's (Exod. 21:6), Israel is God's firstborn son (Exod. 4:22), and all pious sons of the Most High are called such (Ps. 82:6). But they deny with hands and feet that the Messiah is by nature the Son of God, begotten from eternity from the substance of the Father, and possessing the same divine essence and nature as he does. They affirm of the Messiah nothing but human nature and all things human. They deny that the holy oracles everywhere call the Messiah Jehovah, the Branch of Jehovah (Isa. 4), Jehovah our righteousness (Jer. 23), the Son of God (Ps. 2), one whose name endures before the sun (Ps. 72), begotten and acquired before the ages (Prov. 8), (Mic. 5), and heir of all things (Ps. 2).

units.la: Deum fortem, Patrem æternitatis, Jesai.c.9. Dominum Davidis, Psalm.110. Dominum templi sui, Malach. cap.3. Negant Messiam Immanuelem, Jesai.cap.7. Simul in una Persona verum Deum & hominem, Dominum & servum, æternum & natum, Principem vitæ & Filium mortis, sublimiorem Angelis & inferiorem paulo factum, Filium Dei & Filium hominis, Davidis Dominum & Germen; Negant animarum beatitudinem à Messia dependere, felicemque vitæ æternæ statum Messiæ donum esse, uti liquet ex Catechesi Judaica, in qua ad Quæstionem 11. Num vero etiamnum antequam venerit Redemptor ille, animæ perfectionem earum & felicem vitæ æternæ statum attingere possint? Respondetur: Non dubium est, quin tam ante quam post adventum Redemptoris homo probus Legisque & præceptorum sedulus observator perfectionem & beatitudinem animæ suæ comparare queat. Veruntamen, siquidem angustiæ undiquaque premunt, & quam plurima Legis præcepta exsequi non possumus nisi in terra Israelis, cum domus sancta station fuerit, quo spectant sacrificia, ministeria, oblationes, decimæ, & reliqua: Idcirco, ut eo facilius homo perfectionem assequatur, Deus è domicilio suo sancto respiciens habitaculi sui miserebitur, ac mittet Sioni Redemptorem, atque tum salvabitur Juda, omnes tam. tam pusilli, quam magni Deum cogniturí sunt, per-reuntibus, qui cohibent & retardant, quibuscunque.
units.tr: God the mighty, Father of eternity (Isa. 9), the Lord of David (Ps. 110), the Lord of his temple (Mal. 3). They deny that the Messiah is Immanuel (Isa. 7), or that in one Person he is at once true God and man, Lord and servant, eternal and born, Prince of life and Son of death, made higher than the angels and a little lower than them, Son of God and Son of man, Lord and Root of David. They deny that the blessedness of souls depends on the Messiah, and that the happy state of eternal life is a gift of the Messiah. This is clear from the Jewish Catechism, in which, to question 11, Whether indeed, even before that Redeemer comes, souls can attain their perfection and the happy state of eternal life? the answer is given: There is no doubt that, both before and after the coming of the Redeemer, an upright man and a diligent observer of the Law and its precepts can obtain perfection and blessedness for his soul. Nevertheless, since distresses press on us on every side, and we cannot carry out very many of the precepts of the Law except in the land of Israel, while the holy house stands, to which the sacrifices, ministries, offerings, tithes and the rest pertain, therefore, so that a man may attain perfection more easily, God, looking down from his holy dwelling, will have mercy on his habitation and will send a Redeemer to Zion, and then Judah will be saved. All, both small and great, shall come to know God, when those who hinder and delay are removed, whoever they may be.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Negant Redemptionis beneficia hominibus conferenda per Messiam, sed à Deo Omnipotenti, qui cum Judæos dispersérit, illos pariter sit restiturus, illisque Messiam, Regem suum sanctissimum præpositurus, qui populum ad terram Canaan venientem, ut bonus Pastor sit receptúrus, gubernaturus, suaque doctrina & exemplo ad vitam integerrimam provocatur, testimonium perhibente Judæo Iaco Orobio, in Collatione de Veritate Religionis Christianæ cum Limborchio, pag 73. Fatemur multa & magnifica de Messia Rege divinitus prædicta, non tamen quæ ejus humanam naturam excesserint, sed quod perfectissimus erit præcæteris filius hominum. Talem debebat perfectionem habere, qui tunc temporis, regnum Davidis desolatum restitueret, & omnes gentes terræ ad veri Dei cultum perduceret, ejusque nomini inimicos, potentissime subjiceret, & de medio tolleret; qui suo exemplo, & sapientia omnes sectas destrueret, & Israelem, & gentes suavissimo, sed invincibili jugo ad amorem Dei, & ejus puram adorationem cogeret. Et pag. 13. Profecto redemptionis beneficia non à Messia conferentur, sed à Deo Omnipotenti: Ego disperi, ego restituam. Anne Messias totas orbis orbis terras percurret, ut Israelitas ex captivitate liberet, & secum adducat? Non certe: sed à Deo miraculose admonitus veniet populus ex omnibus locis suae dispersionis ad quaerendum Dominum, & Davidem Regem suum. Ideo Dominus in omnibus locis, & pro uno, vel altero Israelita, prodigia efficiet, quae Aegypti miracula excedant, ut inde liberetur, & erit profama, & honore in terra captivitatis suae, & cantabunt gentes Domino canticum novum, quia fecit veritatem, quam promiserat filiis Israel. Messias erit, utpote Rex Sanctissimus, omnium redemptorum caput, in quo etiam sensu Redemptoris munus exercebit: quia populum venientem, ut bonus Pastor recipiet, gubernabit, rectissime judicabit, & sua doctrina, & exemplo ad sanctissimam vitam provocabit: Sedebit in trono Davidis patris sui, ex gentibus, & ex Israele iniquos dispergedet: Cui omnes reges, & populi amantissime parebunt: non quod mundanum imperium exerceat, ut Alexander, vel Julius Caesar; sed quod divina virtute à Deo ipsi concessa, omnes gentes in Dei amore, & filiali timore continebit: Ita ut non ultra bellum, sed pax perpetua usque ad fines terrae, non aemulatio, non contentio, non sectarum diversitas: quia talis est Dei voluntas & in ejus manu prosperabitur, & erit Adonai unus, & nomen ejus unum: & totus Israel jam sanctificatus, Regnum Sacerdotum omnibus populis: Tunc Deus Israelis solus regnabit in suo mundo, quem creavit, & generis humani hoc modo miserebitur, ne amplius sit diabolo in prædam: Non quod vim libero hominum arbitrio sit illaturus; sed quod ex affluentia gratiæ in bonum fere semper dirigetur, ut jam peccato finis imponatur. Hæc sunt beneficia, quæ Israelis miram redemptionem comitabuntur & insequentur, à solo Deo Jacob manu forti, suo tempore efficienda, quorum omnes pii, vel ex gentibus, vel Israele, erunt participes, ipse erit nobis, & omnibus in Deum, & servus suus David Pastor in medio nostri, cui si aliquis obedire noluit, si insanus non fuerit, crimen læsæ majestatis committet, ut qui tempore Davidis ei subjici noluerit. Sed quid hoc cum side in mediatorem, in qua generis humani salus consistat?
units.tr: They deny that the benefits of redemption are to be conferred on men through the Messiah, but by Almighty God, who, having scattered the Jews, will likewise restore them, and will set over them the Messiah, their most holy King, who will receive the people coming to the land of Canaan as a good Shepherd, will govern them, and will summon them by his teaching and example to the most upright life. The Jew Jacob Orobio bears witness to this in his Collation on the Truth of the Christian Religion with Limborch, p. 73: We admit that many great things have been foretold by God about the Messiah the King, but not those which exceed his human nature; rather that he will be the most perfect of the sons of men. He had to have such perfection who, at that time, would restore the desolate kingdom of David, bring all the nations of the earth to the worship of the true God, most powerfully subdue and remove those who are enemies of his name, who by his example and wisdom would destroy all sects, and would compel Israel and the nations, by a most sweet but invincible yoke, to the love of God and his pure worship. And on p. 13: Certainly the benefits of redemption are not conferred by the Messiah, but by Almighty God: I scattered, I will restore. Will the Messiah travel through all the lands of the world to free the Israelites from captivity and bring them back with him? Certainly not. Rather, the people, divinely admonished, will come from all the places of their dispersion to seek the Lord and David their King. Therefore the Lord will work, in all places and for one or another Israelite, wonders that exceed the miracles of Egypt, so that he may be freed from there, and he will be honoured and held in esteem in the land of his captivity, and the nations will sing a new song to the Lord, because he has fulfilled the truth which he had promised to the sons of Israel. The Messiah will be, as the most holy King, the head of all the redeemed, and in this sense he will exercise the office of Redeemer, because he will receive the people coming to him as a good Shepherd, will govern them, will judge most justly, and will summon them by his teaching and example to the most holy life. He will sit on the throne of David his father, and will scatter the wicked, both from the nations and from Israel. All kings and peoples will obey him most lovingly. Not that he will exercise worldly empire, as Alexander or Julius Caesar did, but that, by divine virtue granted to him by God, he will hold all nations in the love of God and filial fear, so that there will be no more war, but perpetual peace to the ends of the earth, no rivalry, no strife, no diversity of sects, because such is the will of God, and in his hand it will prosper; and Adonai will be one, and his name one. All Israel, now sanctified, will be a kingdom of priests to all peoples. Then the God of Israel alone will reign in his world, which he created, and he will in this way have mercy on the human race, so that it is no longer a prey to the devil. Not that he will do violence to the free will of men, but that from the abundance of grace it will almost always be directed to good, so that an end may now be put to sin. These are the benefits which will accompany and follow the wonderful redemption of Israel, to be accomplished by God alone, with a strong hand of Jacob, in his time, and of which all the pious, whether from the nations or from Israel, will be partakers. He himself will be to us and to all a God, and his servant David will be a shepherd in our midst; if anyone is unwilling to obey him, and is not insane, he will commit the crime of treason, as one who in David's time was unwilling to be subject to him. But what has this to do with faith in the Mediator, in which the salvation of the human race consists?

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Negant Messiæ Regnum æternum, divinum, cœleste, spirituale, internum, ad peccatores e potestate Satanæ eripiendos, cum Deo reconciliandos, hinc tranquillandos, refocillandosque, gerendum Messiæ potenti divino verbo, spiritu, virgaque oris efficaci, omnian-tes Imperium humanum, mundanum, carnale, externum, temporarium, post bellum contra Gog & Magog feliciter transactum, debellatos Gentium Reges, Rempublicam instauratam Judaicam, ex Psalm. 72. Jesai. c. 2, 11, 60, 65, 66. Ezech. cap. 28, 39. 40. Zachar. cap 9.
units.tr: They deny that the Messiah's kingdom is eternal, divine, heavenly, spiritual and internal, that it is to be exercised by the Messiah through his mighty divine word, his Spirit and the effective rod of his mouth, to snatch sinners from the power of Satan, to reconcile them to God and so to give them peace and refreshment. Instead they imagine a human, worldly, carnal, external and temporal empire, which will follow the successful end of the war against Gog and Magog, when the kings of the nations have been overthrown and the Jewish commonwealth restored. They cite Psalm 72, Isaiah chapters 2, 11, 60, 65 and 66, Ezekiel chapters 28, 39 and 40, and Zechariah chapter 9.

units.la: Non diffitentes interim Meffiæ sanctitatem, sapientiam, Spiritum Sanctum, aliaque dona eximia, quibus populum sit ad vitam æternam gubernaturus, & ad vitam sanctissimam provocaturus, omneque malum sublaturus; Laudantes pariter Chiliastas, quintæ Monarchiæ defensores, quod una credant, Messiam in terram reversurum, regnumque terrenum Judæis restituturum, uti loquitur Judæus Isacus Orobius in Collatione cum Limborchio, pag. 57. Hanc veritatem ex antiquis, & pluribus nostri seculi Christiani Doctores agnoscentes Christum in mundum rediturum credunt, regnumque Israeli terrenum restituturum, & omnia quæ Prophetæ prædixere, realiter, & ad litteram adimpleturum, & satis diserte probant, nullam ex Prophetiis quæ ad Judæorum futuram felicitatem spectant in Christo suum complementum habuisse: iisdem Chiliastæ seu quintæ monarchiæ propugnatores, neque pauci, neque indocti, neque Christo infideles; Apocalypsis prophetia valde innixi.
units.tr: Meanwhile they do not deny the Messiah's holiness, wisdom, the Holy Spirit and his other outstanding gifts, by which he will govern his people unto eternal life, call them to a most holy life, and remove all evil. They likewise praise the Chiliasts, the defenders of the Fifth Monarchy, in that they believe that the Messiah will return to the earth and restore an earthly kingdom to the Jews, as the Jew Isaac Orobio speaks in his Conference with Limborch, p. 57. Acknowledging this truth from the ancient writers and from many Christian teachers of our own age, they believe that Christ will return into the world and restore an earthly kingdom to Israel, and will fulfil really and literally all that the prophets foretold; and they sufficiently clearly prove that none of the prophecies which concern the future happiness of the Jews has found its complement in Christ. The defenders of this Chiliasm, or Fifth Monarchy, are not few, nor unlearned, nor unbelievers in Christ, and they lean heavily on the prophecy of the Apocalypse.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Deprædicant maximam Regni Messiani felicitatem, aureumque Messiæ seculum, nil nisi beata sibi imaginantes tempora, sine fame, bello, & invidia, in quibus cum profunda perpetuaque pace ad fines usque terræ, concipica futura sit rerum omnium abundantia, in quibus de præsentibus malis nil præter nomina sint cognituri, in quibus abstrusissima aperienda sint mysteria, ut summi numinis perfectam acquirant notitiam, uti patet tum ex Orobii citatis verbis, §. 5. Tum ex Rabbi Maimonide in Commentario ad Sanhedrin, sol.120. col.1. Dies Messiæ sunt tempus illud, quo Regnum Israelitis restituetur, omnesq; in terram Israeliticam redibunt, ubi Messias Rex magnus valde futurus, suamq; regiam in Zione habiturus est. Crescet nomen ejus, & fama pervagabitur gentes magis quam Regis Salomonis, pacemq; cum eo colent omnes populi, omnesq; terræ ei propter summam ejus justitiam & miracula manu ipsius patranda servient. Quicunque vero se ei opposuerit, illum Supremum Numen perdet, in ipsiusmet manus traditum. De hac ejus simulque nostra felicitate omnes Scripturæ textus testimonium perhibent. Cæterum quoad substantiam nihil quicquam de eo, quod nunc est, immutabitur, nisi quod regnum Israelitis restituendum sit, & hoc sibi vult illud Sapientum, quo nihil differre hoc præsens sæculum a futuris Messiæ diebus afferunt, nisi quod non amplius regnus cæteris servituri sint. Divites & pauperes, fortes & imbelles juxta se illo tempore erunt, sed facile tamen fuerit admodum cuivis hominum, habere unde vivat, quippe exiguo labore, quem quis tulerit, magnum sibi paraturus commodum. Et hoc est, quod dicere solent, terram Israeliticam placentas vestesque, sericas producturam, siquidem ita communiter de eo, quirem aliquam jam paratam facile invenerit, dicere solent: invenit bucellam panis pi-stam & cibum coctum, id quod confirmatur ex eo, quod Iesai cap.61, vers.5. dicitur: Et erunt alienigenae agricolae vestri & vinitores vestri, quo indicatur, sementem & messem tunc ibi paratam fore. Et in Tractatu de Regibus cap. 12. Illo tempore procul aberunt fames, bellum, & invidia: bonitas vero effundetur abundantissime, omnisque generis voluptates praesto erunt instar pulveris. Nemo tamen occupabitur alia re, quam cognitione Dei. Tunc Israelitae sapientissimi cluent, quibus etiam profundissima mysteria omnino aperientur.
units.tr: They proclaim the greatest happiness of the Messianic kingdom and the golden age of the Messiah, imagining nothing but blessed times for themselves, without famine, war or envy, in which, with deep and lasting peace to the ends of the earth, an abundance of all things is to be conceived; in which they will know nothing of present evils except by name; in which the most hidden mysteries are to be opened, so that they may acquire a perfect knowledge of the highest Deity. This is clear both from the words of Orobio already cited, §5, and from Rabbi Maimonides in his Commentary on Sanhedrin, fol. 120, col. 1. The days of the Messiah are that time in which the kingdom will be restored to the Israelites, and all will return to the land of Israel, where the Messiah will be a great king indeed, and will have his royal seat in Zion. His name will grow, and his fame will spread among the nations more than that of King Solomon; all peoples will keep peace with him, and all lands will serve him, on account of his great justice and the miracles to be wrought by his hand. But whoever opposes him, the Supreme Deity will destroy, delivering him into his hand. All the texts of Scripture bear witness to this happiness of his and ours. Moreover, in substance nothing of what now exists will be changed, except that the kingdom is to be restored to Israel. This is what the saying of the Sages means, by which they assert that the present age differs from the future days of the Messiah only in that the nations will no longer be in servitude to others. Rich and poor, strong and weak, will be alongside one another in that time; yet it will be quite easy for any man to have something to live on, since by a small labour, which a man undertakes, he will procure a great advantage for himself. And this is what they are wont to say: that the land of Israel will produce cakes and silken garments; for thus they commonly speak of a man who finds some bread already prepared: "He has found a morsel of fine bread and cooked food." This is confirmed by Isaiah 61:5, where it is said: "And strangers shall be your ploughmen and your vinedressers," which indicates that the seed and the harvest will then be ready there. And in the Treatise on Kings, chapter 12: In that time famine, war and envy will be far away; goodness will be poured out most abundantly, and every kind of pleasure will be at hand like dust. Yet no one will be occupied with anything but the knowledge of God. Then the Israelites will be renowned for their wisdom, and to them the most profound mysteries will be wholly opened.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Collaudant Messiae convivium Regium, tum a vini Messiani potione, quod in Paradiso plantatum, inque Adami cella vinaria hactenus fuit reservatum, ex Psalm 75. vers. 9. Calix in manu Domini, & vinum quod in eo rubet, plenum est mixtione, effunditque ex illo; Ex Esai. c. 17. ¶. 2. In die illa vini commendatissimi vinea cantabitur, Ego Dominus servo illud; Et ex c 64. ¶. 4. Oculus non vidit praeter te; Tum ab esu Barjuchne, avis inusitatae magnitudinis, cujus unum ovum e nido aliquando delapsum, trecentas proceras cedros contudit, & liquore suo elisofexasexaginta inundavit pagos, uti scribitur in Talmude, Tractatu Bechorot, sol. 57. Cum aliquando ovum e nido decidisset, trecentas proceras cedros casu suo profstravisse ac perfregisse, tandem elisum, sexaginta pagos inundasse; Et confirmatur ab Elia Levita in Thisbi ad vocem Juchne: Invenitur in Agadah avem esse magnam, quae vocatur Bar Juchne, cujus ovum mirae magnitudinis esse dicunt in Maffechet Bechorot. Etiam audivi quod Deus Sanctus Benedictus paraturus sit ex ea justis convivium, una cum Leviathan & Bove, quem vocant Pehor Habbar; Tum a fruitione mactandi bovis sylvestris, mirae magnitudinis, & roboris, Behemot appellati, de quo mentio apud Jobum, cap. 40. vers. 10. Ecce Behemot, quem feci juxta te: gramen ceu bos comedit; Referuntque praeterea, quod olim creatus, singulis diebus mille depascat montes, ex Psalm. 50. vers. 10. Mea est omnis bestia sylvae, & Behemot in montibus mille; Tum a Leviathane, magno illo pisce, ex Jobo, cap. 40. vers. 20. An trahes Leviathan hamo, aut fune demerges linguam ejus? Cujus foemella, ne fastidissimum animal se multiplicaret, jam olim necata, & in futurum convivium salita fuit; Tum a magna pompa, inefabiliq; gaudio, quo convivas suos Judaeos ad mensam auream excipiet Rex Messias.
units.tr: They praise the royal banquet of the Messiah: first, from the drinking of the Messianic wine, which was planted in Paradise and has until now been kept in the wine cellar of Adam, from Psalm 75:9, The cup is in the hand of the Lord, and the wine in it is red, full of mixture, and he pours out of it; from Isaiah 17:2 (sic: 65:8 in the Hebrew sense), In that day the most excellent vineyard of wine will be sung of: I the Lord keep it; and from Isaiah 64:4, The eye has not seen besides you. Then from the eating of the Bar Juchne, a bird of unusual size, one egg of which once fell from its nest and crushed three hundred tall cedars, and, broken by its fall, flooded sixty villages with its liquid, as is written in the Talmud, Tractate Bechorot, fol. 57: When once an egg fell from its nest, its fall flattened and broke three hundred tall cedars, and at last, when it was broken, it flooded sixty villages. And this is confirmed by Elijah Levita in the Tishbi, under the word Juchne: It is found in the Aggadah that there is a great bird called Bar Juchne, whose egg they say is of wondrous size, in Massechet Bechorot. I have also heard that the Holy Blessed God is going to prepare for the righteous a banquet from it, together with the Leviathan and the ox which they call Pehor Habbar. Then from the enjoyment of slaughtering the wild ox, of marvellous size and strength, called Behemoth, of which mention is made in Job 40:10, Behold Behemoth, which I made beside you; he eats grass like an ox. They report moreover that, once created, he will graze on a thousand mountains each day, from Psalm 50:10, Every beast of the forest is mine, and Behemoth on a thousand mountains. Then from the Leviathan, that great fish, from Job 40:20, Will you draw out Leviathan with a hook, or press down his tongue with a cord? Its female, lest that most loathsome creature multiply, was long ago killed and salted for the future banquet. Then from the great pomp and unspeakable joy with which King Messiah will receive his Jewish guests at the golden table.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Sed licet Messianum illud epulum miris extollant modis, imo, quotquot sunt ex plebe cum multis Doctoribus, secundum externam literam illud intelligant, explicentque, diffitendum tamen interim non est, plurimos nostro tempore inveniri gentis Judaicæ Magistros, qui sensu repudiato historico seu literali, epuli omnia parabolice, mysticeque exponunt, ut ita somnia & fabulas majorum suorum excusare ac palliare, pudoremque declinare valeant, prout factum a nupero Judæorum Doctore, Rabbi Menalsseh Ben Israel de Resurrectione mortuorum, lib. II. c. 19. p. 225. Atque hæc intelligentia, intimaq; ac perfectissima rerum omnium cognitio, est epulum illud, de pisce Leviathan, de quo legitur in tractatu Baba Batra, quod Deus isto tempore præparabit illis, qui optime, ac sanctissime in terris vixere. Hæc eadem est fragrantissimum vinum illud conservatum in uvis sex dierum Berefit sive creationis, cujus mentio fit in Berachot. Quæ omnia non sunt proprie, sed metaphorice intelligenda, uti recte monemur in libro Zoar, Parasat Toldot. Et quemadmodum probe observatum est a R. Gabay, in libro Abodat Hacodes; per ista, ac similia, significatur spiritualis animarum oblectatio, voluptas, ac gaudium, quo in illo statu potientur: sicuti enim vinum hic hominum animos mos oblectare, & exhilarare solet: sic etiam statu ille spiritualis resuscitatos omni ac perpetuo gaudio perfundet. Sed de his Rabbinorum, & Talmudis allegoriis alias, ac seorsum singulari tractatu agere, mihi propositum est.
units.tr: Although they extol that messianic feast in wonderful terms, and although all the common people, with many of their teachers, understand and explain it according to the outward letter, it must nonetheless be admitted that in our time there are found among the Jewish nation teachers who, rejecting the historical or literal sense, expound everything about the feast allegorically and mystically. They do this so that they can excuse and cover up the dreams and fables of their forefathers and avoid the shame. This is what the recent Jewish teacher Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel did in his book on the resurrection of the dead, book II, chapter 19, page 225. And this understanding, and the intimate and most perfect knowledge of all things, is that feast, the feast of the fish Leviathan, of which we read in the tractate Baba Batra, which God will prepare at that time for those who lived best and most holily on earth. This is the same as the most fragrant wine kept in the grapes from the six days of Bereshit, that is, of creation, which is mentioned in Berachot. All these things are not to be understood properly but metaphorically, as we are rightly warned in the book Zohar, Parashat Toldot. And as R. Gabay has well observed in the book Avodat Hakodesh, by these and similar things is signified the spiritual delight, pleasure and joy of souls which they will enjoy in that state. For just as wine is wont to cheer and gladden men's minds here, so that spiritual state will steep the revived in continual and perpetual joy. But it is my intention to treat these allegories of the Rabbis and the Talmud elsewhere, in a separate and special tractate.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Negant Messiam in oraculis divinis, utrumnum tantum ratione personae delineatum, sed duplicem designatum credunt, ad evitanda eloquia, quae de duplici Messiae statu, cum humili, tum glorioso agunt, statuentes egenum, vilemque alterum, משיח בן יוסף Messiam filium Josephi, ex Genes. cap. 49. vers. 26. ex tribu Ephraim, hinc quoque Ben Ephraim, & Nehemiam filium Hufiel appellatum, qui cum vir strenuus, reique bellicae peritissimus, alterius que Messiae praecursor futurus, in praelio contra Gogum & Magogum est occubiturus, postea tamen a Successore ad vitam reducendus, vicariaq; dignitate sub ipso fruiturus; alterum statuentes gloriosum, felicem, perpetuum victorem. משיח בן דוד Messiam filium David & Messiam Ben Jehuda, Regia majestate conspicuum, qui Messiam Ben Joseph resuscitatur, Israelem redemptur in antiqua regiam dignitatem restituturus, sacrificia instauraturus, & rerum omnium abundantiam est adducturus, testimoniis passim obviis apud R. Josephum Coecum, in
units.tr: They deny that the Messiah is depicted in the divine oracles as one person only; they believe he is designated as twofold, in order to avoid the sayings which speak of a twofold state of the Messiah, both humble and glorious. They hold that one is needy and abject, Messiah the son of Joseph [משיח בן יוסף], from Genesis 49, verse 26, of the tribe of Ephraim, and hence also called Ben Ephraim, and Nehemiah the son of Hushiel; he, though a vigorous man and most skilled in warfare, and destined to be the forerunner of the other Messiah, is to fall in battle against Gog and Magog, but afterwards is to be brought back to life by his successor and to enjoy a vicarious dignity under him. They hold that the other is glorious, happy, and a perpetual victor: Messiah the son of David [משיח בן דוד], and Messiah Ben Jehuda, conspicuous in royal majesty, who, when Messiah Ben Joseph has been raised up, is to redeem Israel, restore it to its ancient royal dignity, restore the sacrifices, and bring in an abundance of all things. This is found in numerous passages everywhere, in R. Joseph Caecus, in

units.la: Paraphrasi Chaldaica ad Cantic. cap. 4. verf 5. Duo Salvatores tui, qui te salvaturi sunt, similes sunt Mosi & Aaron filiis Jocabed; Apud Rabbi Schelomo in Comment. ad Jesai. cap. 14. verf. 18. Qui se liberaverit a gladio Messiae Ben Joseph, incidet in gladium Messiae Ben David & qui inde se proripuerit, in bello Gogi illaqueatus peribit; Apud Rabbi Machir, in Athkat Rochel, quod Clarissimus Hulsius versione latina, notisque exornavit. lib. 1. part. 1. signo nono: Clanget Michael clangorem magnum quo sepulchra mortuorum aperientur Hierosolymis, eosque Deus Benedictus vitae restituet. Messias etiam Ben David, & cum ipso Elias Propheta e mortuis suscitabunt Messiam Ben Joseph, qui sub portis Hierosolymae asservabatur. Deinde mittent Messiam Ben David ad colligendas Judaeorum reliquias in omnibus terris dispersas. Et confestim omnes gentium reges totius orbis Israelitas humeris suis impositos ad Deum deducent; Apud Rabbi Isacum Abarbanelem in Commentario ad Danielem: Tradiderunt Rabbini nostri; Primo revelabitur Messias Ben Ephraim, & bella gesturus est cum gentibus, venientibus contra Hierosolymam, sed in bello occumbet. Post ipsum autem surget Messias Ben David, & caedet inimicos, & armillum, Principem sive Ducem copiarum Christianarum; sicut Gog Dux erit exercituum Ismaelitarum; Apud Rabbi Davidem KimKimchi, Aben Elram, Bechai, aliosque sine numero.
units.tr: the Chaldee paraphrase on Canticles, chapter 4, verse 5: Your two saviours, who are to save you, are like the sons of Jochebed, Moses and Aaron; in Rabbi Shelomo's commentary on Isaiah, chapter 14, verse 18: Whoever escapes the sword of Messiah Ben Joseph will fall into the sword of Messiah Ben David, and whoever escapes from that will perish, caught in the war of Gog; in Rabbi Machir, in Athkat Rochel, which the most distinguished Hulsius adorned with a Latin version and notes, book 1, part 1, sign nine: Michael will sound a great trumpet, by which the graves of the dead will be opened in Jerusalem, and the blessed God will restore them to life. Messiah Ben David, and with him the prophet Elijah, will raise from the dead Messiah Ben Joseph, who was kept under the gates of Jerusalem. Then they will send Messiah Ben David to gather the remnants of the Jews scattered in all lands. And at once all the kings of the nations of the whole world will carry the Israelites on their shoulders and lead them to God; in Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel's commentary on Daniel: Our Rabbis have handed down: first Messiah Ben Ephraim will be revealed, and he is to wage war against the nations who come against Jerusalem, but he will fall in the battle. After him, however, Messiah Ben David will rise, and will slay the enemies, and Armilus, the leader or commander of the Christian forces, just as Gog will be the leader of the armies of the Ishmaelites; in Rabbi David Kimchi, Aben Ezra, Bechai, and countless others.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Sic de duplici Judæorum Messia, Ben Ephraim, & Ben David, multis agit Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel in spe Israelis, libello in varias nuper linguas translato, pag. 78. Tempore illo X Tribus venient Hierosolymam sub ductu Principis, quem Rabbini nonnulli in Talmud & Paraphrasi Chaldæa aliquot in locis, vocant Messiam filium Joseph, & alibi Messiam filium Ephraim, qui casus in ultimo bello Gog & Magog offendit, se non esse Messiam filium David, qui erit, ut dicunt Oseas & Ezechiel, princeps æternus omnium XII Tribuum, Messiæ ipsius filii Ephraimi mentionem faciunt multis in locis sapientes, maxime vero in Talmud Babylonico, in Tractatu Succah cap. 5. ubi moriturum eum ajunt in ultimo bello Gog & Magog, & ita explicant cap. 13. Prophetæ Zachariæ: & adspiciente ad me, quem confixerunt, plangentq; super eo, ut solet super unigenito filio. Adaunt etiam, quod quatuor duces, de quibus Propheta idem loquitur cap. 2. sunt Messias filius Joseph, Messias filius David, Propheta Elias, & summus Sacerdos, quæ quatuor ista dignitates sunt, quæ in isto seculo beato offendent potentiam suam. Advertite autem quod aliquando vocent Messiam filium Ephraimi, aliquando Josephi: Prodibit enim ex Tribu Ephraim, & & erit Dux omnium X Tribuum, nomen Ephraimo dantium, propterea quod primus eorum Rex Jeroboam ex ista tribu fuit. Non sine ratione vocant ipsum filium Josephi; ipse enim erat verus typus domui Israelis propter incarcerationem suam, ac subsequentem felicitatem.
units.tr: So Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel treats at length of the twofold Messiah of the Jews, Ben Ephraim and Ben David, in his Hope of Israel, a book recently translated into several modern languages, p. 78. At that time the ten tribes will come up to Jerusalem under the leadership of a prince whom some rabbis in the Talmud, and in several places in the Chaldee paraphrase, call the Messiah son of Joseph, and elsewhere the Messiah son of Ephraim. This prince meets his fate in the last war of Gog and Magog, and he is not the Messiah son of David, who will be, as Hosea and Ezekiel say, the eternal prince of all twelve tribes. The wise men mention the Messiah son of Ephraim in many places, most of all in the Babylonian Talmud, in the tractate Succah, chapter 5, where they say he will die in the last war of Gog and Magog. They explain in this way chapter 13 of the prophet Zechariah: "they will look on me whom they have pierced, and mourn for him, as one mourns for an only son." They add also that the four leaders of whom the same prophet speaks in chapter 2 are the Messiah son of Joseph, the Messiah son of David, the prophet Elijah, and the high priest; these four dignities will display their power in that blessed age. Note, however, that they sometimes call him the Messiah son of Ephraim and sometimes son of Joseph: for he will come forth from the tribe of Ephraim, and will be the leader of all ten tribes, which take their name from Ephraim, because their first king, Jeroboam, was of that tribe. They call him son of Joseph not without reason, for he was a true type of the house of Israel, because of his imprisonment and the happiness that followed it.

units.la: Adde, quod tam diu fratres sui latuerit, ut plane iis ignoraretur; prorsus ut hodie decem Tribus, qua, utut captivas se dicant, postmodum tamen ad summum felicitatis fastigium adscendent eodem ac Joseph modo. Iste Messias Josephi morietur in prælio Gog & Magog, & postea resurget, ut fungatur dignitate sua, non sceptro quidem Regis, sed munere tantum Vice Regis, ut Josephus in Ægypto; eo quod imperium domus Israelis, quod cecidit sub regno Ofeæ filii Elæ, ut ait Propheta Amos cap. 5. v. 2. Non restaurabitur igitur regnum decem Tribuum, ut monet Ezechiel c. 37. sub imperio Messiæ filii Davidis, qui erit æternus, & per mortem Messiæ filii Josephi agnoscent X Tribus, Deum nolle, ut plures habeant, præter unum, Principes.
units.tr: Add to this that he was so long hidden from his brothers that he was altogether unknown to them, just as the ten tribes are today; although they call themselves captives, they will afterwards rise to the highest summit of happiness in the same way as Joseph. This Messiah of Joseph will die in the battle of Gog and Magog, and afterwards will rise again to exercise his office, not indeed with the sceptre of a king but only with the function of a viceroy, as Joseph was in Egypt; because the rule of the house of Israel, which fell under the reign of Hoshea son of Elah, as the prophet Amos says in chapter 5, verse 2, will not be restored. Therefore the kingdom of the ten tribes will not be restored under the rule of the Messiah son of David, who will be eternal, as Ezekiel warns in chapter 37; and through the death of the Messiah son of Joseph the ten tribes will acknowledge that God does not wish them to have more than one prince.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Credunt Regnum Messiæ non æternum, sed temporarium, continuandum vel annis, juxta quosdam Gentis Doctores, 7000, vel juxta alios 400, rursus ex mente certorum 365, aliorum 300, denique secundum alios 70, tandemque ex sententia quorundam 40; Regem gem Messiam vero uxorem Reginam ductu- rum pulcherrimam ex filiabus Israelis, quae continuo latus ipsius dextrum fit clausura, uxores reliquas habituram ex filiabus Regum Gentilium, aflervantis in Gynæceo, ex Psalm. 45. verf. 10. Filiæ Regum in honore tuo: stetit conjux in dextra tua in diademate ophir; Sicuti testatur Rabbi David Kimchi in Commentario ad hæc Psalmi verba; Regem Messiam procreaturum liberos, nepotesque, regni successores, ex Isaia cap. 53. verf. 10. Videbit semen, quod prolongabit dies, & voluntas Jehovæ in manu ejus prosperabitur; Hoc est, prout Rabbi Moses Bar Nochman scribit: Messias quidem tempore sat longo vivet, postremo vero morietur, & ipse in splendore magno, & filius ejus regnabit post eum, & hoc vita functo, regnum obtinebunt ejus posteri post eum; Tandem Regem Messiam moritu- rum, uti refert Rabbi Moses Maimonides in Commentario ad Sanhedrin, sol. 110. Caeterum Messias morietur, & regnabit post ipsum filius ejus, hinc isto quoque demortuo nepos, & sic porro secuturi posteri. Jam pridem vero mortalitatem ejus expositurus Propheta Isaias, cap. 42: verf. 4. Non caligabit, nec frangetur, donec ponat in terra judicium. Ipsum autem regnum ejus temporibus longe plurimis durabit, similiter vita hominum erit longæva, siquidem cum mærores animi & molestia remoremoventur, dies hominis prolongari solent; Licet aliqui cum vulgo, illud intelligant de Messia Ben Ephraim, non vero de Messia Ben David.
units.tr: They believe that the kingdom of the Messiah is not eternal but temporary, to last, according to some teachers of the nation, 7000 years, or according to others 400, again in the opinion of certain men 365, of others 300, finally according to others 70, and at last in the view of some 40 years. They hold that the Messiah king will take as wife a most beautiful queen from the daughters of Israel, who will always stand at his right side, and that he will have other wives from the daughters of the Gentile kings, kept in the harem, from Psalm 45, verse 10: The daughters of kings are among your honourable women; the queen stands at your right hand in gold of Ophir. So Rabbi David Kimchi testifies in his commentary on these words of the Psalm. The Messiah king will beget children and grandchildren, successors to the kingdom, from Isaiah 53, verse 10: He shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days, and the will of Jehovah shall prosper in his hand. That is, as Rabbi Moses Bar Nochman writes: The Messiah will live a fairly long time, but at last he will die, and he himself in great splendour, and his son will reign after him; and when he has passed from life, his posterity will obtain the kingdom after him. Finally, the Messiah king will die, as Rabbi Moses Maimonides reports in his commentary on Sanhedrin, fol. 110: Moreover, the Messiah will die, and his son will reign after him, and then his grandson after that son's death, and so on, with posterity following. Long ago the prophet Isaiah, to explain his mortality, said in chapter 42, verse 4: He shall not grow dim nor be broken, until he has set judgment in the earth. His kingdom, however, will last for very many ages; likewise the life of men will be long, since when grief of mind and trouble are removed, the days of man are usually prolonged. Although some, with the common people, understand this of the Messiah son of Ephraim and not of the Messiah son of David.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Negant audacter Messiam Regem cum gloria & majestate regia apparuisse, quod Elias, Regni Messiani Praecursor hactenus nondum venerit, ex Malach. cap. 4. vers. 5. 6. Ecce ego mittam vobis Eliam Prophetam, antequam veniat dies Jehova maximus & reverendus, ut convertat cor patrum ad filios, & cor filiorum ad patres ipsorum, ne veniens percutiam terram anathemate. Hinc calidis exoptant votis Messiae Regis adventum, Eliaeque Prophetae dulcissimam apparitionem, clamantes jugiter: Veniat Elias Propheta, Elias Propheta, Elias Propheta, repente ad nos veniat, cum Messia filio Davidis; Ingeminantes in precibus quotidianis: Mitte nobis Germen Davidis servi tui; Et illud vulgare: Quando, quamdiu, quam longe moretur; Repetentes saepe, ut cito & in diebus suis veniat, ut adventum maturet, ut Sanctuarium aedificet, ut commiserationum suarum habeat memoriam; Instituentes quoque jejunia, seq; ad poenitentiam componentes feriam; Non inficiantibus interim plurimis Doctoribus, Messiam ipsum pridem venisse, sed nondum cum
units.tr: They boldly deny that the Messiah King has appeared with glory and royal majesty, because Elijah, the forerunner of the Messianic kingdom, has not yet come, according to Malachi 4:5-6: Behold, I will send you Elijah the Prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of Jehovah, that he may turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers, lest I come and smite the earth with a curse. Hence they long with ardent prayers for the coming of the Messiah King and the most welcome appearance of the prophet Elijah, crying out continually: Let Elijah the Prophet come, Elijah the Prophet, Elijah the Prophet, let him come to us at once, together with the Messiah the son of David. In their daily prayers they repeat: Cause the Branch of David your servant to spring up. They also use the common saying: "When, how long, how far off is he?" They often repeat the wish that he may come quickly and in their days, that he may hasten his coming, build his Sanctuary, and remember his mercies. They also appoint fasts and set aside the day of the week for repentance. Meanwhile, many teachers do not deny that the Messiah came long ago, but say that he has not yet appeared with title and majesty.

units.la: Hebrew phrase in the text ("Quando, quamdiu...") printed with Hebrew characters; rendered approximately.
units.tr: The Hebrew phrase in the text ("When, how long...") is printed with Hebrew characters; rendered approximately.

units.la: cum titulo & majestate apparuisse; Proinde Messiam ad portam urbis Romæ inter pauperes sedere, sicut testatur Rabbi Iosua Ben Levi, qui Messiam ipsum sub porta vidit, allocutusque est, in Tractatu Talmudico Sanhedrin, cap. 11. Rabbi Jehosua filius Levi reperit Eliam stantem ad ostium spelunca Rabbi Simeonis Ben Jochai. Quasivit ex eo, perveniamne in seculum futurum? Respondit, si voluerit ipse Dominus. Aderat enim ipsis sancta divinitas. Regessit Iosua: binos tantum vidi, sed vocem trium audivi. Quando autem veniet Messias? Respondit, abi, roga ipsummet. Ubinam ergo est? Sedet ad portam Romæ. Et quodnam ejus signum? Sedet inter pauperes oneratos morbis; Cæteri omnes solvunt & ligant universas simul, ipse vero unam post alteram sigillatim, dicens fortasse post ulabor, nec immora ero. Abiit igitur ad Messiam salutans illum: pax super te! mi Magister, mi Doctor. Respondit, pax quoque super te, o fili Levi. Quasivit autem, quando veniet Dominus meus? Respondit, hodie; Vel alibi Messiam latitare, aut dissimulato oris habitu in mundo agere, calamitatemque populi sui deflere; Vel in Schytia ultra mare Caspium delitescere; vel inter Angelos vivere; imo afferentibus multis extraditione antiqua, Messiam non cognitum iri suis, adeoque occultatum iri, quod partim impletum, pletum, partimque adhuc implendum in novissimo Impostore, Sabethai Zevi aliqui credunt; Non enim ipsum abjurata Religione Judaica Turcicis Sacris initiatum sibi imaginantur, sed latitare solum, & ad certum tempus incognitum manere Judæis, ut ita majori gloria populum e gentium servitute liberet, uti nuper testatus est in concione apud nostros Judæos publica, Rabbi Chanoch Mokiach, de quo mox pluribus in Historia de Pfeudo Meffiis.
units.tr: Accordingly, they say the Messiah sits at the gate of the city of Rome among the poor, as Rabbi Joshua ben Levi testifies, who saw the Messiah at the gate and spoke with him, in the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin, chapter 11: Rabbi Joshua son of Levi found Elijah standing at the entrance of the cave of Rabbi Simeon ben Yochai. He asked him whether he would reach the world to come. He answered: if the Lord himself wills it. For the holy divinity was present with them. Joshua replied: I have seen only two, but I have heard the voice of three. "When will the Messiah come?" He answered: "Go and ask him yourself." "Where then is he?" "He sits at the gate of Rome." "And what is his sign?" "He sits among the poor who are burdened with diseases. All the others loose and bind all their bandages together, but he does so one after another, separately, saying: perhaps I shall be summoned later, and I shall not delay." So he went to the Messiah and greeted him: "Peace be upon you, my Master, my Teacher." He answered: "Peace be upon you also, son of Levi." He asked, however: "When will my Lord come?" He answered: "Today." Others hold that the Messiah lies hidden elsewhere, or that he acts in the world with his outward appearance concealed and mourns the calamity of his people; or that he lives hidden in Scythia beyond the Caspian Sea, or lives among the angels. Indeed, many, relying on ancient tradition, affirm that the Messiah will not be recognized by his own people and will remain hidden, which has in part been fulfilled and is still to be fulfilled in the most recent impostor, Sabbatai Zevi. For they do not imagine that he has been initiated into Turkish rites after renouncing the Jewish religion, but that he only lies hidden and remains unknown to the Jews for a set time, so that he may free the people from the servitude of the nations with greater glory. This was recently affirmed in a public sermon among our Jews by Rabbi Hanoch Mokiach, about whom more will be said shortly in the History of the Pseudo-Messiahs.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Credunt Regis Meffiæ adventum hactenus differri, vel ob peccatum vituli, a majoribus perpetratum, quod hodie adhuc luant, juxta effatum magistrorum: Non est tibi Israel ultio, in qua non fit uncia de iniquitate vituli; vel ob ingentia populi peccata, de quibus Rabbi Menaffeh Ben Israel de Resurrectione mortuorum Lib. III. cap. 3. pag. 268. Et profecto verissimum est, fi Israelita ferio factorum suorum pœnitentiam egissent, Meffiæ adventus non fuisset procrastinatus: at nunc quia profunde immersi jacent harentes, defixi in vitiis & peccatis suis, hinc est quod differatur beatitudo illa usque ad finem dierum; Imo sunt, qui Meffiæ adventum differunt, rejiciuntque, vel ad mundi ferme finem, vel ad mortuorum resurrectionem, quod varius riis delusi fuerint Pseudo-Messiis, quodq; Redemptionis dies à diversis designatus Doctoribus praeterierit, frustraque desideratus fuerit; Inter hos est Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, de Resurrectione Mortuorum Lib. III. cap. 2. pag. 251, 252. Non tantum ex libris Mosaicis, verum etiam Propheticis constat, Resurrectionem mortuorum conjunctam & annexam fore adventui Messiae: solum in controversia relinquitur utrum is primus, & unus, an secundus Messiae adventus futurus sit. Hanc disputationem nunc non ingredior: sed simpliciter dico, tum venturum & fore Resurrectionem mortuorum. Et post aliqua interjecta pergit Rabbi Menasseh: Itaque eodem fere tempore & die, Messias veniet, & mortui resurgent.
units.tr: Some hold that the coming of the King Messiah has so far been delayed either on account of the sin of the calf, committed by their forefathers, which they still expiate today, according to the saying of the teachers: "There is no vengeance for you, Israel, in which there is not an ounce of the iniquity of the calf"; or on account of the great sins of the people, concerning which Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, in On the Resurrection of the Dead, Book III, chapter 3, page 268, says: "And indeed it is most true that, if the Israelites had repented of their deeds with their whole heart, the coming of the Messiah would not have been put off." But now, because they lie deeply immersed, stuck fast and fixed in their vices and sins, that blessedness is deferred until the end of days. Indeed there are some who postpone and reject the coming of the Messiah, either to nearly the end of the world or to the resurrection of the dead, because they have been deceived by various false Messiahs, and because the day of redemption fixed by various teachers has passed and been longed for in vain. Among these is Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, in On the Resurrection of the Dead, Book III, chapter 2, pages 251 and 252: "It is clear not only from the books of Moses but also from the Prophets that the resurrection of the dead will be joined and attached to the coming of the Messiah. The only question in dispute is whether there will be one first and single coming of the Messiah or a second one. I do not enter upon that debate now, but I simply say that both will come, and the resurrection of the dead as well." And after some intervening remarks Rabbi Menasseh goes on: "So at almost the same time and on the same day, the Messiah will come and the dead will rise."

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Docent decem illustria miracula, portentave Messiae Regis praecessura adventum, quibus gens Judaica sit admonenda, excitandaque, ut Messiam advenientem sancta possit ampleCti obedientia, inter quae Primum cum Rabbi Machir in Abhkat Rochel constituunt, quod Deus excitaturus sit tres Reges Apostatas, qui multos homines sint seducturi, imo plurimos quoque Israelitas; Secundum dicunt, quod ex calore solis intensissimo, multa hominum millia, tum ex Ethnicis, tum eximpiis piis Israelitis, quotidie sint peritura; Tertium, quod sanguineum rorem, quem Deus in terram stillabit, potaturi sint mundi populi cum impiis Judæi, hinc morituri; Quartum; Quod Deus rorem salubrem sit demissurus, quiæ-grotantes pios sit sanaturus; Quintum, Quod sol per triginta dies sit obscurandus; Sextum, quod Deus Imperio Romano totius orbis regimen sit concessurus, quo plurimi Judæi delendi, deinceps vero excitaturus sit Messiam filium Joseph, qui imperium cum Imperatore Romano sit destructurus; Septimum, Quod Armillus in proelio sit prostraturus Messiam filium Joseph, seu Nehemiam; Octavum, quod ad clangorem tubæ Angeli Michaelis, Messias Ben David, cum Elia Propheta sit appariturus, qui cum dispersis Judæis Hierosolymam sit ingressurus; Nonum, quod ad sonitum Michaelis sepulchra Hierosolymis sint experienda, omnesque mortui vitæ restituendi, imo ipse Messias Ben Joseph e mortuis suscitandus; Decimum tandem, quod ad sonum tubæ Michaelis Deus congregaturus sit Judæos, & in Paradisum deducturus.
units.tr: They teach that ten famous miracles or portents will precede the coming of the King Messiah, by which the Jewish nation is to be admonished and roused, so that it may embrace the Messiah when he comes with holy obedience. Among these, (1) first, with Rabbi Machir in Abhkat Rochel, they set down that God will raise up three apostate kings who will lead many men astray, indeed very many Israelites as well; (2) second, they say that from the most intense heat of the sun many thousands of men, both Gentiles and pious Israelites, will perish daily; (3) third, that the wicked among the nations, together with the impious Jews, will drink the bloody dew which God will drip upon the earth, and so will die; (4) fourth, that God will send down a healing dew, by which he will cure the sick among the pious; (5) fifth, that the sun will be darkened for thirty days; (6) sixth, that God will grant rule over the whole world to the Roman Empire, by which many Jews will be destroyed, but afterwards God will raise up the Messiah the son of Joseph, who will overthrow the empire together with the Roman Emperor; (7) seventh, that Armillus will strike down in battle the Messiah the son of Joseph, or Nehemiah; (8) eighth, that at the blast of the trumpet of the angel Michael, the Messiah the son of David will appear with the prophet Elijah, and will enter Jerusalem with the scattered Jews; (9) ninth, that at the sound of Michael the sepulchres at Jerusalem are to be opened, and all the dead are to be restored to life, indeed the Messiah the son of Joseph himself is to be raised from the dead; (10) tenth and last, that at the sound of Michael's trumpet God will gather the Jews and lead them into Paradise.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Negant Jesum Nazarenum Messiæ Regis titulo maclandum, quod Messias in fine dierum venire debeat, sed Jesus Nazarenus ante milmille & fexcentos vixerit annos; Quod pet Messiam montis templi elevatio super alios omnes montes futura sit, ita ut Tabor,Sinai,& Carmel ad montem Sion conveniant ex Je- sai. cap.2. verf.2. Illa autem a Nazareno prae- ftita non fit; Quod Messia regnante pacis felicia tempora futura sint, ferarumque & armentorum mira concordia late conspici debeat, cum tamen contraria omnia Nazarenum insecuta fuerint; Quod Messiae non ultima laus futura sit, ex toto congregare orbe Judaeos, Hierosolymas restaurare, templum reaedificare, sacrificia de novo instituere, contraria rursus post Iesum Nazarenum accciderint, dispersi in omnes terrae partes Judaei, destructae fuerint Hierosolymae, templum crematum, ipsaque sacrificia abolita; Quod ad Messiam Regem omnes gentes, Judaeique confluere debeant, cum Iesum Nazarenum & Judaei & gentes pariter rejecerint; Quod Messias Rex gloriosus futurus esset, Iesus vero Nazarenus vilis & humilis fuerit, imo suspensus in cruce; Quod Rex Messias in justitia & aequitate totum debeat judicare mundum, Nazarenus vero paucos habuerit allectas, non de primoribus populi, sed ex obscura plebe; Quod Messias Legem Mosaicam debuerit confirmare, Nazarenus vero Legi contraria ria docuerit, hinc populo displicuerit Judaico, sicuti loquitur Judæus Isac Orobius in Collatione cum Limborchio, pag. 150. Respondeo: quod quare Patres tunc temporis viventes Christo & Apostolis sidem non dederint, non est cognitu nobis difficile. Primo, non credidere, quia non sufficiens sundamentum eis apparuit, ut crederent: quia si invenirent, non esset ratio aliqua, qua eum negarent, & rejicerent: & non modo docti, & seniores, sed etiam populus Hierosolymitanus, admitterent. Secundo: quia Regem terrenum non viderunt, qui ut talis fuerat promissus, & ab Israële per totsecula ab eodem Deo edoĉto, expectatus. Doctrina magis displicuit, ut divina Legi contraria, qua majorem ejus partem, ut vanam, & inutilem, neq; Deo amplius gratam, prædicabat. Non cognoverunt esse Messiam, quia docebat se Deo æqualem, imo ipsum Deum, quem antea incorporeum, immortalem, impatibilem esse, crediderant: nec putabant esse modum aliquem quo Deus per suam omnipotentiam posset se contrario modo facere: sicuti nunc putamus esse impossibile, quod Deus fiat panis, aut panis sit Deus, neq; per transmutationem, neq; per suam naturæ assumptionem. Tali doctrina erant Judæi à Deo imbuti: post vero corporeus, patibilis, mortalis proponebatur adorandus; duarum naturarum hypostatica unione non adhuc excogitata, neq; à Christo, neq; ab Apostolis aliquando prædicta: quæ quamvis praprædicaretur, minime admitteretur à Iudæis, utpote impossibilis, & suo divino dogmati contraria.
units.tr: They deny that Jesus of Nazareth should bear the title of the King Messiah, because the Messiah ought to come at the end of days, whereas Jesus of Nazareth lived one thousand six hundred years ago. They say that by the Messiah the elevation of the mountain of the temple will be raised above all other mountains, so that Tabor, Sinai and Carmel will come to Mount Zion (Isaiah 2:2), but this has not been brought about by the Nazarene. They say that under the reign of the Messiah happy times of peace will come, and a wonderful harmony of wild beasts and cattle ought to be seen far and wide, yet all the opposite has followed the Nazarene. They say that it will be no small praise of the Messiah to gather the Jews from the whole world, to restore Jerusalem, to rebuild the temple, and to institute sacrifices anew; but the opposite has happened since Jesus of Nazareth: the Jews have been scattered into all parts of the earth, Jerusalem has been destroyed, the temple burned, and the sacrifices themselves abolished. They say that all nations and Jews ought to flow together to the King Messiah, yet both Jews and Gentiles alike have rejected Jesus of Nazareth. They say that the King Messiah would be glorious, whereas Jesus of Nazareth was base and lowly, indeed hanged on a cross.
