Lavite aqua, ut eluerem sanguinem tuum a te, & unxi te unguento. Dicunt Infideles, isti is innui aquas impuras illorum, & oleum quo frontem inungunt, quodq; Confirmationem vocant; Convitiantes denique, formulam baptismi, in nomine Patris, Filii, & Spiritus Sancti, aequipollere sententiae: Esto sacrificium Satanae, uti patet ex Nizzachon Veteri, libro virulentissimo in Christianam Religionem, pag. 148. Cum proluunt infectà sua (Infantes dicere vult) aquas immundas, ajunt iidem conceptis verbis: In nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus Sancti: Amen. Quod nostro sermone valet, Esto sacrificium Satanae: Argumentantes tes tandem, quod per nefandum baptismum neutiquam a gehenna possint liberari, ex eodem Nizzachon Veteri, pag. 191;192: Nefando baptismo suo, de quo in Lege ipsorum scriptum est, non liberari quem a Gehenna, nisi fuerit aquis baptizatus, argumentum & confirmationem petunt in illo Esai. cap. 36. verf. 25. Et aspergam vos aquis mundis, ut mundemini. Sed respondendum. An non inter vos minime aspersio recepta est? verum in aquas immittimini, quod Scriptura vestra dictis adversatur. Porro, quale peccatum aut immunditiem tollit nefandus ille baptismus? quod peccatum aut impuritas inest infantibus recens natis, quos vos baptismo initiatis? Si ob olim contrahendum id sit peccatum, non opus est; porro illos monere, ut pietati studeant, & vitia procul habeant, nam ex vestra sententia sufficit iste baptismus.
units.tr: They also mock and scoff at the divine sacraments of our Christian Church, and most of all at those of the Papists. In the greatest blasphemy they call the waters of Baptism מים טמאים [mayim temeim], foul and putrid waters, and מים זורמים [mayim zorerim], proud waters, citing Rabbi Bechai in Kad Hakkemach, p. 61. David calls the kingdom of Edom מים הזדונים [mayim hazedonim] proud waters, because it is an article of faith among them that people are baptized with water; this is from Rabbi Moses Israel Demercato in his Commentary on the Psalms, p. 104. And against this long exile he says: Then the proud waters would have passed over our soul, etc., because this kingdom, that is, of the Christians, is called מלכות זדון [malkhut zadon] the proud kingdom. They also cite Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel in the Preface to the book Sebach Pesach, and the Old Nizzachon, p. 150. They call the waters of Baptism מים טמאים [mayim temeim] unclean waters, which are the seats and receptacles of unclean spirits. Rabbi Solomon Zevi does not deny this, but he gives a milder opinion in words, when he puts on a show for us in the Jewish Theriac, chap. 2, §25. Since therefore the Papists, without any distinction, sprinkle men with water, as once tombs and whatever else were, and baptize even infants themselves, whom original sin contaminates, to be cleansed, they say, not unjustly [they are called] דמא ןד [the Hebrew as printed], that is: water of the unclean, with which they themselves used to wash. Yet the water itself is not unclean, since by the same right our water in the Tabernacle and the Sanctuary would have been unclean. They call our Baptism nefandum, unspeakable, in the Old Nizzachon, p. 70, on Jeremiah chap. 31, verse 31: At this place the unbelievers abuse the text and say that the Prophet prophesies about Jesus, that when he is born he will give them a new Law, and will introduce an unspeakable baptism in place of the covenant of circumcision, and the observance of the first day of the week, or the Day of the Sun, in place of the worship of the Sabbath. They call the waters of Baptism impure waters, from the same Old Nizzachon, p. 74, on Ezekiel chap. 16, verse 9: Wash with water, that I may cleanse your blood from you, and I anointed you with ointment. The unbelievers say that by this are meant their impure waters, and the oil with which they anoint the forehead, which they call Confirmation. Finally, they revile the formula of baptism, In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, as equivalent to this sentence: Be a sacrifice to Satan, as is clear from the Old Nizzachon, a most venomous book against the Christian Religion, p. 148. When they wash their infected ones (he means infants) in unclean waters, they say the same words: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit: Amen. Which in our language means, Be a sacrifice to Satan. Lastly, they argue that through their unspeakable baptism one can by no means be freed from Gehenna, from the same Old Nizzachon, pp. 191–192: Concerning their unspeakable baptism, of which it is written in their Law that no one is freed from Gehenna unless he has been baptized with water, they seek an argument and confirmation in that passage of Isaiah chap. 36, verse 25: "And I will sprinkle you with clean water, that you may be clean." But it must be answered: Is sprinkling not, among you, by no means accepted? Rather you are immersed in water, which your Scripture contradicts. Furthermore, what sin or uncleanness does that unspeakable baptism take away? What sin or impurity is in newborn infants, whom you initiate by baptism? If that sin is to be contracted later, there is no need for it; and it is enough to advise them to seek piety and keep far from vices, for by your own judgment that baptism suffices.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Rident, subsannantque pariter Sacram Coenam, alterum Ecclesiae Christianae Sacramentum, impugnantes tum Symbola externa, tum rem significatam internam, appellantes ore maledico Sacram Coenam מעוּדַת שמה Coenam impuram, nominantes Sacrae Coenae panem לחם שמה Panem immundum, לחם מגואל Panem pollutum, לחם קרבן עצביהם Panem sacrificy idoli sui, ex Rabbi Josepho Jachiade in Commentar. ad Psalm. 127. Comedentes panem nem Sacrificij Idoli fui; Convitiantes, quod licet de Christianis fateantur, ipsos in Sacra Coena comedere Suspensum, nullam tamen inde calumniæ impingant ignominiam, uti refert Judæus Salomon Zevi, in Theriaca Judaica, cap.2.§.30. Etsi vero Judæus diceret, Christianum, in Sacra Cœna, Talui commediffe, ut Apostata scribit, nulla tamen id effet ignominia, siquidem aliud nihil diceret Judæus, quam, Christianum, Jesum Nazarenum edijfe; Sic vinum sacræ Cœnæ, magis tamen Missæ Pontificiæ, omnibus exfibilant modis, appellantes vinum illud ꞏ Vinum libaminis, vinum Idolis libatum, hinc quoque à vinis abstinentes sæpe, quæ à Sacerdote Pontificio Missa præleêta, quotannis solent benedici, non diffitentibus Judæis, imo ut videtur, approbante Rabbi Elia Levita in suo Thisbi, ad vocem Nefeçh: Omne vinum quod libatur Idolis, vocatur ꞏ, & qui bibit illud, dignus est juxta Legem ut vapulet, secundum illud, quod dicitur Deuteron cap.23. Quorum adipem comederunt, & quorum libamina biberunt. Hoc autem tempore prohibuerunt Rabbini in universum non esse bibendum vinum cum gentibus, eo quod dubium sit num libatum fuerit Idolis nec ne? Et licet dicant gentes, quod hoc tempore non servi-ant Idolis, nihilominus tamen prohibitum est, eo quod res est, quæ prohibita fuit per certum numerum rum Rabbinorum. Unde necesse est alium adesse numerum ubi solvendum est, quod priores illi statuerunt. Hinc prohibitum est vinum Nefech, & omnia reliqua ad ipsum pertinentia, sicut explicatum est apud authores, (quos Hebraei םיפנכ a determinando denominant.) Neque mihi licet hac de re prolixius agere.
units.tr: Likewise they mock and scoff at the Holy Supper, the other sacrament of the Christian Church, attacking both the external signs and the inward thing signified. With a cursing mouth they call the Holy Supper מעודת שמה [edat shemah], an unclean supper, and they name the bread of the Holy Supper לחם שמה [lechem shemah], unclean bread, לחם מגואל [lechem megu'al], polluted bread, and לחם קרבן עצביהם [lechem korban atzvehem], bread sacrificed to their idol, citing Rabbi Joseph Jachiade in his Commentary on Psalm 127. Eating bread of the sacrifice to their idol. They revile the Christians, because although they admit that Christians eat the Suspended in the Holy Supper, they nevertheless do not hurl any slander of shame from it, as the Jew Solomon Zevi reports in the Jewish Theriac, chap. 2, §30. Yet even if a Jew were to say that a Christian has eaten the Taluy in the Holy Supper, as the Apostate writes, it would be no disgrace at all, since the Jew would say nothing else than that the Christian has eaten Jesus of Nazareth. In the same way they hiss at the wine of the Holy Supper, and even more at the Mass of the Papists, in every way, calling that wine wine of libation, wine poured out to idols. Hence they also often abstain from wines which have been blessed each year by the Papist priest after the Mass, the Jews not denying this, and indeed, as it seems, Rabbi Elijah Levita approving it in his Tishbi, under the word Nefesh: Every wine that is poured out to idols is called [yayin nesech], and whoever drinks it deserves, according to the Law, to be beaten, according to what is said in Deuteronomy chap. 23: "Who ate the fat of their sacrifices and drank the wine of their libations." But in this time the Rabbis have forbidden, in general, that one drink wine with the Gentiles, because it is doubtful whether it was poured out to idols or not. And although the Gentiles say that in this time they do not serve idols, nevertheless it is forbidden, because it is a matter that was prohibited by a certain number of Rabbis. Therefore there must be another number present, where what those earlier ones decreed must be loosed. Hence the wine of Nefech is forbidden, and all the other things pertaining to it, as has been explained by the authors (whom the Hebrews name from determining, [םיפנכ]). Nor is it permitted to me to treat this matter at greater length.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Exagitant valde corporis Christi tum oralem manducationem cumque hostia commixtionem, tum ipsam Transsubstantiationem, afferentes Pontificiorum Transsubstantiationem, monstrum esse horrendum, vanissimumque commentum, quod intellectus humanus nullo possit concipere modo, ipsis primis repugnet rectæ rationis principiis, ipsaque sensuum refutetur experientia, ex Rahbi Albo de Fudamentis, Part. III. cap. 25. Quod insuper de sacrificio panis & vini dicunt, quod id sacrificium sit, vanissimum est, siquidem panis iste & vinum Deo ipsorum non offeruntur, sed juxta ea, quae ipsi dicunt, corpus Dei ipsorum est. Dicunt enim corpus Jesu, quod in cœlo est, mensura vastissimum esse, ita ut magnitudo ejus ad altape pertinegat, ibi pane & vino veluti veste induatur, finita mussitatione sacrificuli, qualiscunque ille sit, sive bonus sive malus, fiat vero totum corpus unum cum corpore Messiæ, quod è cœlo absq; ulla temporis successione. ceßione citissime descendit, post autem finita comestione & potatione in cœlum ad locum suum iterum ascendat: Atq; hoc in omnibus altaribus fieri. Ita eorum de sacrificio hoc sententia habet. Sunt vero in hac doctrina absurda, quæ intellectus humanus nullo modo concipere aut amplecti potest, quippe quæ ipsis primis principiis repugnant. Primum enim à sensibus alienum est, credi debere, motum fieri absq; temporis intervallo e distantia tanta, quæ est inter cœlos cœlorum superiorum, sive è throno gloriæ usq; ad terram, item, corpus unum in duobus aut pluribus locis diversis reperiri, siquidem corpus Messiæ in multis diversis altaribus simul adsit, item corpus Christi ascendere & descendere, absq; scissione cœlorum, qui rupturam non patiantur, item, quod dicunt carnem & sanguinem hoc momento ex hoc pane & vino in hunc usum finitis & circumscriptis confecta, esse idem corpus Messiæ, quod olim fuit, absq; ulla quantitatis additione vel diminutione: Quod ad credendum penetrationem corporum deducit. Hæc, inquam, omnia præter quam quod principiis primis repugnant, ipsam sensuum experientiam redarguunt. Dicunt enim panem & vinum, quæ oculis videntur, cibum non esse, nec animali aut homini edenti nutrimentum præbere, quamvis palam sit, panem istum & vinum, si debita mensura sumerentur, edenti alimento futura, & membris æque ac alium panem & vinum pro-
units.tr: They vehemently attack both the oral eating of Christ's body and its mingling with the host, and also Transubstantiation itself. They call the Papists' Transubstantiation a dreadful monster and a most vain invention, which the human intellect cannot conceive in any way, which is opposed to the very first principles of right reason, and which is refuted by the experience of the senses. (From Rabbi Albo, De Fundamentis, Part III, ch. 25.) As for what they say about the sacrifice of bread and wine, that it is a sacrifice, that is most vain, since this bread and wine are not offered to their God, but, according to what they themselves say, they are the body of their God. For they say that the body of Jesus, which is in heaven, is of immense size, so that its magnitude reaches to the altar; that there it is clothed in bread and wine as in a garment, once the mumbling of the little priest, whoever he may be, good or bad, is finished; and that the whole body then becomes one with the body of the Messiah, which very swiftly descends from heaven without any succession of time, and after the eating and drinking is finished, ascends again into heaven to its place. And they say this happens at all altars. Such is their opinion about this sacrifice. Now there are absurdities in this doctrine which the human intellect cannot in any way conceive or embrace, since they are opposed to the very first principles. For, first, it is contrary to the senses to believe that a motion occurs without any interval of time over so great a distance as that between the highest heavens, or from the throne of glory down to the earth; likewise, that one body is found in two or more different places at once, since the body of the Messiah is present at many different altars simultaneously; likewise, that the body of Christ ascends and descends without a splitting of the heavens, which do not admit of a rupture; likewise, that they say the flesh and blood, made in this way at this moment from this bread and wine, which are finite and circumscribed for this purpose, are the same body of the Messiah that it once was, without any addition or diminution of quantity, which leads to belief in the penetration of bodies. All these things, I say, besides being opposed to the first principles, refute the very experience of the senses. For they say that the bread and wine, which are seen by the eyes, are not food, nor do they provide nourishment to an animal or a man who eats them, although it is plain that this bread and wine, if taken in due measure, would be food for the one eating and would benefit the limbs as much as other bread and wine would.

units.la: Hæc, inquam, omnia præter quam quod principiis primis repugnant, ipsam sensuum experientiam redarguunt. profutura esse. Deinde dicunt panem & vinum ipsum converti in corpus Messiæ, & remanere accidentia per se subsistentia sine subjecto, saporem enim, colorem, odorem, tactum, gravitatem, levitatem, mollitiem & duritiem, quæ in pane sentiuntur, non esse in pane, cujus corpus in corpus Messiæ migraverit. Hæc omnia talia sunt, quæ nec intellectus capere, nec os eloqui, nec auris auditu percipere potest: Ideoq; fide hæc & similia, utpote intellectui & sensibus contraria, apprehendi nequeunt.
units.tr: Hæc, inquam, omnia præter quam quod principiis primis repugnant, ipsam sensuum experientiam redarguunt. Then they say that the bread and wine themselves are converted into the body of the Messiah, and that the accidents remain subsisting on their own without a subject. For the taste, colour, smell, touch, weight, lightness, softness and hardness which are perceived in bread are not in the bread, whose body has migrated into the body of the Messiah. All these things are such that the intellect cannot grasp them, the mouth cannot utter them, nor the ear perceive them by hearing. Therefore these things and the like, as contrary both to the intellect and to the senses, cannot be apprehended by faith.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Exagitant Transubstantiationem valde, quod sit ex rebus istis, quæ nunquam fieri possint, imo omnem superet rationem, manducare Deum suum, ex Judæo Anonymo sæpe citato, Quæst. 46: Qui fit ut Christiani omnia fidei sua fundamenta superstruant rebus impossibilibus, captum omnem excuperantibus, & rationi adversis, uti sunt unus & tres, Deus & homo, virgo & puerpera, panis & caro, vinum & anguis, unum corpus in multis diversis locis uno eodemq; temporis articulo; Ex Judæo Isaco Orobio in Collatione cum Limborchio, pag. 130. Sicuti nunc putamus esse impossibile, quod Deus fiat panis, aut panis fit Deus, neq; per transmutationem, neq; per suam naturam assumptionem; Ex Rabbi Lipmanno in Nizzachon ad Psalm. 34. versf. 9. Gustate quam suavis Dominus. Hic loquuntur Christiani verba, quæ qua audire nefas est. Exponunt enim verbum gu-state, significatione manducandi, dicentes se man-ducare Deum suum, quod est contra omnem ratio-nem; Et ex eodem Lipmanni Nizzachon ad Psalm.90: Quidam tamen illorum ajunt: Nazarenum per mortem ab ipsis esse reparatum. At tu oppone: annon dicunt, quod ad ipsos singulis diebus veniat, appareat eis in ipsorum pane? Sic Sacrae Coenae panem vocant abominabilem, qui perTranslubstantiationem tantum fit corpus & sanguis, ex Nizzachon Veteri, pag.148. Congregationibus Edomitarum, (quales audiunt Christiani,) ne inest quidem tantillum sanae fidei, quod granum sinapis aquet. Cum profanant & inquinant abominabilem panem, inquiunt verbis conceptis: Hoc est enim corpus meum. Quod verbis Hebraicis idem valet ac: Ego tantum corpus sum & sanguis.
units.tr: They vehemently attack Transubstantiation, because it is made of things that can never happen, indeed things that surpass all reason: that one eats his God. (From the anonymous Jew often cited, Quaestio 46.) How does it come about that Christians build all the foundations of their faith on impossible things, which exceed every grasp and are contrary to reason, such as: one and three, God and man, virgin and mother, bread and flesh, wine and serpent, one body in many different places at one and the same moment? (From the Jew Isaac Orobio, in his Collatio with Limborch, p. 130.) Just as we now judge it impossible that God should become bread, or that bread should become God, neither by transmutation nor by assumption of its nature. (From Rabbi Lipmann, in the Nizzachon, on Psalm 34:9, Taste and see that the Lord is good.) Here the Christians speak words which it is impious even to hear. For they explain the word taste in the sense of eating, saying that they eat their God, which is against all reason. And from the same Lipmann's Nizzachon, on Psalm 90: Some of them, however, say that the Nazarene was restored to them by death. But you object: do they not say that he comes to them every day and appears to them in their bread? Thus they call the Lord's Supper the abominable bread, which by Transubstantiation alone becomes body and blood. (From the Old Nizzachon, p. 148.) In the congregations of the Edomites (such as Christians are), there is not even as much sound faith as equals a grain of mustard seed. When they profane and defile the abominable bread, they say in set words: This is my body. Which in Hebrew words amounts to the same as: I am only body and blood.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Accusant valde Sacrificulos Romanos, quod ex pane & vino suum formént factorem, Creatorem ive, uti liquido patet ex Nizzachon Veteri, pag 149: Quod sequitur, mussitant in omnibus missis secretis, nec tradunt id nisi sacerdotio initiatis; sic inquam clanculum murmurant in templis, verbis Latinis: Offerimus tibi Domine calicem salutarem, secundum ordinem Melchisedek, & secundum ordinem Mosis & Aaronis & SacerSacerdotibus ejus, & Samuel inter eos qui invocant nomen Domini. Ecquomodo dici potest id Deum esse, quod ipse Sacrificulus tantum Sacrificium prædicat? Tu vero, mi homo, ipse parasti vinum, & excoxisti panem, qua igitur ratione affirmare audes esse ipsa factorem tuum creatoremq; tuum? Cum panem deglutit, hæc verba Latina profert: Calicem salutis accipiam, & nomen Domini invocabo. Postea haurit vinum cui canis nares admovit; Accusant Pontificios Sacerdotes, quod Jesus, quem manibus tenent, sit opus manuum humanarum, ex Nizzachon Veteri, pag. 252: Infideles dicunt Sacrificulum tenere suis manibus corpus, ipsumq; adeo Jesum, quantus quantus in flamine & subtemine pendebat. Sic illis respondet: Id quod Sacrificulus manibus tenet, est opus manuum humanarum; at, de re ejusmodi pronunciat Propheta Hoseas, cap. 14. verf. 4. Non dicemus amplius, o Deus noster, operi manuum nostrarum, nec incurvabimus nos amplius operi manuum nostrarum. Jeremias quoq; cap. 16. verf. 20. graviter ait: Anfacturus esset sibi homo Deos, qui non sunt Dii? &c.
units.tr: They bitterly accuse the Roman sacrificers of making their Maker and Creator out of bread and wine, as is plain from the Nizzachon Vetus, p. 149: What follows, they mutter in all the secret prayers of the mass, and they do not hand it on except to those initiated into the priesthood. Thus, I say, they murmur secretly in the temples, in Latin words: We offer to you, Lord, the saving cup, according to the order of Melchizedek, and according to the order of Moses and Aaron and his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon the name of the Lord. How can that be called God which the sacrificer himself merely proclaims to be a sacrifice? But you, my good man, yourself prepared the wine and baked the bread; by what reasoning, then, do you dare to affirm that it is your maker and your creator? When he swallows the bread, he utters these Latin words: I will take the cup of salvation, and will call upon the name of the Lord. Afterwards he drinks the wine, to which he has brought the nostrils of a dog. They accuse the Papist priests that Jesus, whom they hold in their hands, is a work of human hands, from the Nizzachon Vetus, p. 252: Unbelievers say that the sacrificer holds in his hands the body, and indeed Jesus himself, however much he hung in warp and woof. To this they reply thus: What the sacrificer holds in his hands is a work of human hands. But the prophet Hosea pronounces on such a thing, ch. 14, verse 4: We will say no more, O our God, to the work of our hands, nor will we bow ourselves any more to the work of our hands. Jeremiah too, ch. 16, verse 20, says sharply: Will a man make for himself gods, which are not gods? etc.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Impugnant, destruuntque Transubstantiationem, quod hostia, quam pro Deo venditant, non tantum ab Angelo pedibus fuerit conculcata, sed sæpe situ obducta corrumpatur, imo a gliribus & muribus quandoque devore-
units.tr: They attack and destroy transubstantiation, because the host, which they peddle as God, is not only trampled underfoot by an angel but often corrupted by mould, and sometimes devoured by dormice and mice-

units.la: voretur, ex Judæo Anonymo, Quæst. 42: Siarcam Dei in qua solum posita erant tabula Legis attrectans Aza veritus ne caderet, statim examinatus concidit, qui ergo fit ut hostia quam Christiani pro ipsomet Deo offerant, semel coram Pontifice & alio rursus tempore rege Hispaniæ attrectata sit & pedibus conculcata ab Angelo, nec divina vindicta eum apprehendit. Tum si hostia Deus est, cur sitû obducta corrumpitur, cur à gliribus & muribus corroditur; Quod concipi non posset, qua ratione suis discipulis dederit suum corpus, ut illud manducarent, ut ita necesse omnino sit, vel quod membrum ex corpore suo dilaceratum, ipsis porrexerit, vel corpus in panem mutatum fuerit, uti argumentatur Judæus in Nizzachon Veteri, pag. 211: Apud Marcum scriptum tenent. In vespera Paschatos cum accumberent mensæ, accepit Jesus panem, illumque divisit, & benedixit, deditque discipulis suis, inquiens iis: Accipite hunc panem, quoniam est corpus meum. Amplius, accepit quoque calicem, & benedixit, deditque omnibus: atque biberunt ex eo omnes. Ait vero illis: Hic est sanguis meus, in Testamentum novum. Qua ratione dedit ipsis corpus suum, ut illo vescerentur? Discinditne membrum e corpore, illudque ius porrexit? Aut, conversumne est prius corpus in panem & vinum, atque dedit is eis quod erat residuum? Insuper illud corpus quod comederunt & biberunt, quorsum abibat descenditq; ? Petebatne viam propriam? Aut anne in ventriculo cum cibis reliquis commiscebatur?
units.tr: —so an anonymous Jew writes, Question 42: Aza, touching the ark of God in which only the tablets of the Law were placed, feared that it would fall, and at once, having been examined, fell down dead. How is it, then, that a host which Christians offer as God himself was once handled by the Pope and at another time by the king of Spain, and trampled underfoot by an angel, and yet divine vengeance did not seize him? Then, if the host is God, why is it corrupted by mould, why is it gnawed by dormice and mice? It could not be conceived by what means he gave his body to his disciples to eat, unless it was necessary either that he held out to them a limb torn from his body, or that the body was changed into bread, as the Jew argues in the Nizzachon Vetus, p. 211: They hold that it is written in Mark: On the evening of the Passover, when they were reclining at the table, Jesus took bread, broke it, blessed it, and gave it to his disciples, saying to them: Take this bread, for it is my body. Moreover, he also took the cup, blessed it, and gave it to all, and they all drank from it. But he said to them: This is my blood of the New Testament. In what way did he give them his body that they might feed on it? Did he tear a member from his body and hold out that limb? Or was the body first changed into bread and wine, and did he give them what was left over? Moreover, that body which they ate and drank, where did it go and descend? Did it seek its own path? Or was it mixed in the stomach with the rest of the food?

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Destruunt pariter Transsubstantiationis, Missæque fundamenta, respondentes ad verba Genes. cap. 14. vers. 18. Malchizedek autem protulit panem & vinum: atque ipse erat Sacerdos Dei altissimi, ex Nizzachon Veteri, pag. 10: Dicunt Hæretici, ista Jesum respicere, & panem quidem, notare corpus illius, vinum autem sanguinem effusum: atq; corpus manducari, & afflictionibus fuisse subjectum. Hinc quærunt: Quid indicare volebat Malchizedek Abrahamo, cum panem & vinum illi offerret? Respondere licet, indicasse hunc, filios ipsius sacrificaturos libamina & panes similagineos; Non mirum hinc, quod Sacræ Cœnæ usum non solum graviter fastidiant, verum oculos quoque procul avertant, clamantes Væ illa videnti! Væ illa credenti! Uti patet ex Schevet Jehuda, editionis & versionis Gentianæ pag. 347: Ego accepi, Hebræum quendam, qui ad Religionem Christianam coactus erat, sacram ædem frequentantem, Servatoris nostri mystico corpore, dum res divina perageretur, in altum sublato, pectore manu percussò, dixisse: Væ hæc videnti! Væ hæc credenti!
units.tr: They likewise destroy the foundations of transubstantiation and of the Mass, answering the words of Genesis 14:18: And Melchizedek brought forth bread and wine, and he was the priest of God Most High, from the Nizzachon Vetus, p. 10: The heretics say that these things look to Jesus, and that the bread indeed signifies his body, but the wine his shed blood, and that the body is eaten and was subjected to afflictions. From this they ask: What did Melchizedek wish to indicate to Abraham when he offered him bread and wine? One may answer that he indicated that his sons would offer libations and loaves of fine flour. Hence it is no wonder that they not only loathe the use of the Holy Supper bitterly, but also turn their eyes far away, crying: Woe to him who sees that! Woe to him who believes that! As is plain from the Schevet Jehuda, in the edition and translation of Gentius, p. 347: I heard of a certain Hebrew who had been forced into the Christian religion, and who attended the sacred temple; when the divine service was being performed, and the mystical body of our Saviour was lifted high, he struck his breast with his hand and said: Woe to him who sees this! Woe to him who believes this!

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Credunt Reformatorum de Sacra Cœna sententiam, cum aliis collatam, sibi videri probabilissimam, repudiantes maxime Pontificiorum de hoc capite doctrinam, imo ipsos Augustanæ Confessionis Socios redarguentes, uti mihi constat, non ex unius tantum alterius ve Judæi, sed ex Celeberrimi Wulferi quoque testimonio, cum ex ore plurimorum Judæorum, in Animadversionibus ad Salomonis ZeviTheriacam Judaicam, pag. 117. sic scribit:
units.tr: The Jews believe that the Reformed opinion on the Holy Supper, when compared with the others, seems to them most probable. They especially reject the doctrine of the Papists on this point, and even refute the fellow members of the Augsburg Confession. This is clear to me not only from the testimony of one Jew or another, but also from that of the most celebrated Wülfer, who, drawing on the mouths of many Jews, writes thus in his Animadversions on Salomon Zevi's Jewish Theriaca, page 117:

units.la: Imo vero expertus loquor, ipsos, quos vocant, Reformatos, majores quando apud Judæos fieri, quam vel Pontificios, vel Lutheranos. Inter Christianos enim minime omnium Reformatos desipere, videri sibi affirmabat quondam Judæus Venetus, qui & Transsubstantiationem vehementer riserat, & in Eucharistia, sub pane, corpus Christi realiter adesse, ratione nullus afferri poterat, Reformatorum sententiam probabilissimam sibi videri fassus, a quo, bene novi, alieni non sunt Judæorum plurimi.
units.tr: Indeed I speak from experience: the so-called Reformed are held in greater favour among the Jews than either the Papists or the Lutherans. For among Christians a Venetian Jew once affirmed that the Reformed seemed to him the least foolish of all. He both greatly laughed at transubstantiation and confessed that the Reformed opinion seemed to him most probable, since no reason could be given why the body of Christ should be really present in the Eucharist under the bread. I know well that many Jews are not averse to this view.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Ex his patet omnibus, graviter errare Pontificios, cum Transsubstantiationis præsidium in ipsis Hebræorum quærunt monumentis, gloriantes in opinionis concordia, uti tentatum, sed inani successu a Jofepho Voysio, dum, cum Raymundo suo in notis ad Pro-
units.tr: From all this it is plain that the Papists go badly wrong when they look for support for transubstantiation in the very monuments of the Hebrews. They boast of agreement of opinion, as Joseph Voisin tried to do, though without success, when in his notes to the

units.la: Prooemium Pugionis Fidei, sol. 151. ita loquitur: Quod dam in figura Manna משנה לחם, id est, Panem Transsubstantiatum, dici Exod. 16. v. 22. ne ipsi quidem Judaei negant, teste R. Abarbanele in Exod. Sect. ולחם משנה משנה לחם, id est, Panis Mischneh, Exod. 16. Panis Transsubstantiatus. Non enim Abarbanelis mens est in Comment. ad Exod. sol. 162. col 3. Panem quoad substantiam mutatum fuisse, cum manserit idem Manna, sapore & odore solum mutatis; Praeterea non interpretatur לחם משנה Panem Mischneh per panem transubstantiatum, sed per לחם יום יום duplam panis portionem, pro biduo sufficientem; imo tandem vocat panem immutatum, non ratione Essentiae, sed pro ratione edentium, infantum, puerorum, & senum; Neque sententiae suae praesidium melius reperiet Voysinius in Rabbi Davide Kimchio ad Hoseae cap. 14. verf. 8. cujus verba subdole citat, malitiose truncat, & male denique sic vertit: Quidam exponunt, vivent tritico, quod futura fit mutatio naturae, sive Transsubstantiatio in tritico adventu Messiae; Cum Kimchiana hoc velint: Quidam exponunt vivificabunt frumentum, quod futura fit mutatio naturae in frumento, cum venerit Redemtor, nempe quod illud vivificabunt (crescere facient) instar vitis, & non necesse habebunt frumentum ferre nisi semel tantum, perinde ac cum vitę sit; Quibus verbis innuitur, Messiæ temporibus, frumentum semel satum crescere debere instar vitis, nec iterata satione opus esse; An frumentum mutatur in vitem? An non frumentum manet frumentum? Sed de his pluribus consuli potest Odhelius in Synagoga Bifronte, pag. 108,109.
units.tr: Prooemium of Raymund's Pugio Fidei, fol. 151, he speaks thus: "That in the figure of the manna [משנה לחם], that is, 'transubstantiated bread,' is mentioned in Exod. 16:22, not even the Jews themselves deny, as witnessed by R. Abarbanel on Exodus, section [ולחם משנה], that is, 'Mishneh bread,' Exod. 16, 'transubstantiated bread.'" For Abarbanel's meaning in his Commentary on Exodus, fol. 162, col. 3, is not that the bread was changed in substance, since the manna remained the same, only its taste and smell being altered. Moreover, he does not render לחם משנה [lechem mishneh] as "transubstantiated bread" but as a double portion of bread, enough for two days [לחם יום יום]. Indeed, he finally calls it bread changed not in its essence but in relation to those who eat it: infants, boys and old men. Nor will Voisin find better support for his view in Rabbi David Kimchi on Hosea 14:8, whose words he cites deceitfully, truncates maliciously, and finally translates badly. Kimchi's words are these: "Some explain, 'they will make the grain live,' that there will be a future change of nature, or transubstantiation, in the grain when the Messiah comes, namely that they will make it live (grow) like a vine, and will not need to sow the grain more than once." By these words it is implied that in the days of the Messiah grain sown once should grow like a vine, and that no repeated sowing would be needed. Does grain turn into a vine? Does grain not remain grain? More on these matters can be consulted in Odhelius, Synagoga Bifrons, pp. 108, 109.

units.la: CAPUT XVII. De Statu Hominis ultimo, deque animarum post hanc vitam conditione.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII. On the Final State of Man and the Condition of Souls after This Life.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: CRedunt, Animas hominum esse immortales, non dissolvi cum suis corporibus in particulas minutissimas, sed post mortem superstites, in futuro semper vivere seculo, demonstrantes operose contra Sadducæos, Atheosque, quod de animarum immortalitate doctrina, non solum fundamentum fidei sit Judaicæ, cui omnia Legis Mosaicæ dogmata sint superædificata, sed semper quoque à Veteribus Judæis sit æstimata tanti, ut negantem illam ex Israelitarum expungerent numero, uti patet ex perdocta Epistola Dedicatoria, quam Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel tribus suis libris de Resurrectione mortuorum præfixit:
units.tr: They believe that the souls of men are immortal, that they are not dissolved with their bodies into the smallest particles, but survive after death and live forever in the future age. They argue at length against the Sadducees and atheists that the doctrine of the immortality of the soul is not only the foundation of the Jewish faith, on which all the doctrines of the Mosaic Law are built, but has always been held in such high esteem by the ancient Jews that they struck from the number of Israelites anyone who denied it. This is clear from the learned dedicatory epistle that Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel prefixed to his three books on the Resurrection of the Dead:

units.la: Tanti semper ab antiquis æstimatum est dogma de immortalitate animarum, & resurrectione mortuorum, ut illud negantem, ex numero Israelitarum expungerent, neq; crederent partem habituram esse in futuro seculo, sive mundo animarum: utcunq; is aliis in rebus, pietatis quam maxime studiosus, & præceptorum divinorum fuisset observantissimus.
units.tr: The doctrine of the immortality of the soul and the resurrection of the dead has always been held in such esteem by the ancients that they struck from the number of Israelites anyone who denied it, and did not believe that such a person would have a part in the future age, or the world of souls, however devoted he might be in other matters to piety and most observant of the divine precepts.

units.la: Quod non sine ratione, quantum mihi videtur, ab illis factitatum est. Etenim si quis animum diligenter advertat, comperiet præcipua Legis dogmata fundata esse in articulo de immortalitate animarum. Quippe qui credit in homine aliquid divini esse, animamq; ejus esse immortalem, is extra controversiam etiam ponit, aliquem excellentiorem esse spiritum, qui hoc universum imperio ac majestate sua gubernet. Quod qui ingenue profiteatur, idem credat necesse est, primum fidei articulum, Deum esse: alterum item, Deum esse unicum. Nam quemadmodum in homine unica anima rationalis multa officia obit, ad individuum, ac speciem humanam conservandam: ita etiam unicus Deus multa facit, ac præstat ad continuationem & conservationem universi mundi. Præterea etiam ex eo liquet veritas tertij articuli, Deum scilicet esse incorporeum. Nam si tanta dignitas, atq; excellentia convenit animæ, quæ à Deo creata est: quanto magis Creatori totius mundi conveniet. Similiter quartum fidei articulum de æternitate Dei, inde probaveris. Si enim anima habens principium caret fine, sane aliqua parte præcellat necesse est auctor ac creator illius. Eminentia autem illa hæc est, quod careat Deus non principio minus, quam fine. Pari jure inde evincitur veritas quinti articuli, de invocatione atque adoratione solius Dei. Cum enim Deus sit Ens per se, ac suam essentiam, & non per participationem, neq; ab aliqua causa efficiente dependeat: solum consequitur invocari oportere. Solus siquidem pro arbitrio suo bona, vel mala immittere hominibus potest. Ab eodem forte promanat sextus articulus, de revelatione Prophetica, per quam Deus mentem suam hominibus aperit. Nec enim fieri potest, ut Deus solis se corporeis, ac materialibus substantiis communicet, nisi etiam aliquid spirituale atq; divinum habeant. Quippe quatenus homo corporeus est, neutiquam aliis præstat animantibus, sed in omnibus suis actionibus illis similis est.
units.tr: This, as it seems to me, was not done without reason. For if anyone attends carefully, he will find that the chief doctrines of the Law are founded on the article concerning the immortality of the soul. Indeed, whoever believes that there is something divine in man, and that his soul is immortal, also holds beyond dispute that some more excellent spirit governs this whole universe by his power and majesty. Whoever professes this sincerely must also necessarily believe the first article of faith, that God exists, and likewise the second, that God is one. For just as in man the single rational soul performs many offices for preserving the individual and the human species, so also the one God does many things and provides for the continuation and preservation of the whole world. Moreover, the truth of the third article, that God is incorporeal, is also clear from this. For if such dignity and excellence belongs to the soul, which was created by God, how much more will it belong to the Creator of the whole world. Likewise you may prove from this the fourth article of faith, concerning the eternity of God. For if the soul, having a beginning, lacks an end, its author and creator must certainly surpass it in some respect. That eminence is this: God lacks a beginning no less than an end. By the same right the truth of the fifth article is proved, concerning the invocation and worship of God alone. For since God is a being in himself, whose essence is his own and not by participation, and who depends on no efficient cause, it follows only that he must be invoked. He alone can at his pleasure send good or evil upon men. Perhaps from the same source comes the sixth article, concerning prophetic revelation, through which God opens his mind to men. For it cannot happen that God communicates himself only to corporeal and material substances unless they also have something spiritual and divine. Indeed, insofar as man is corporeal, he is in no way superior to other animals, but in all his actions is like them.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Demonstrant animam esse immortalem, quod sit substantia cogitans, hinc incorruptibilis. bilis, toto coelo à substantia distincta corporea, quæ tres complectitur dimensiones, longitudinem, latitudinem & profunditatem, partesque habet extra partes, quæ omnem causantur corruptionem. Quodque operationes mentis nullo modo possint tribui substantiæ corporeæ, cum neque manibus palpari, neque pedibus calcari queant, aut in oculos, auresque incurrant, uti egregie ratiocinatur Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel lib. 1. de Resurrectione Mortuorum, pag. 55, 56: Sed venia-mus ad demonstrationes, quibus evincemus animam non mortalem, sed immortalem esse. Earum prima esto R. Joseph Albi. Is hunc in modum argumentatur; Anima est substantia spiritualis, ergo incorruptibilis. Consequentia patet. Constat enim consensu omnium Philosophorum, & ex ipsis Philosophia primis principiis, corruptionem omnem e materia sive corpore manere, nihilque nisi corporeum esse corruptibile, quia corpus per luctam & pugnam primarum quatuor qualitatum, calidi & frigidi, humidi & sicci, disponitur ad corruptionem. Animam vero esse substantiam, ex eo probatur, quia exercet actiones quasdam spirituales, quæ non dependent a corpore, uti sunt ratiocinatio, sapientia, variarum rerum scientia. Animam etiam spiritualem esse ex eo recte concluditur, nam omnis actus & operatio fluit a potentia, potentia a substantia tia, haud aliter quam fructus fluit ex arbore; ergo si actiones sunt spirituales, substantia quoque erit talis, a qua operationes ista emanant. Accedat huc quod accidentia spiritualia non cadant in subjectum, corporeamve rem. Negare vero sapientiam esse spirituale quid, nimis est absurdum. Nam ejus unius beneficio tractamus e rebus spiritualibus de Deo ac angelis, multa subtiliter differimus, judicamus futura, cognoscimus praeterita, nec tantum res dun-taxat singulares, sed etiam universales ejus ope apprehendimus; quae omnia cum in oculos non incurrant, nec manibus palpari, nec pedibus calcari, auribus percipi queant, necesse utique est, ut dicamus dari aliquam animae operationem, quae a corpore abstracta est, ac proinde animam non esse formam materialem, qualis est brutorum, quae idcirco tota a corpore dependet. Atque haec etiam ratio Aristoteli placuit;
units.tr: They demonstrate that the soul is immortal because it is a thinking substance, and hence incorruptible, being entirely distinct from a corporeal substance, which has three dimensions, length, breadth and depth, and has parts outside of parts, and which is subject to every corruption. And because the operations of the mind can in no way be attributed to a corporeal substance, since they cannot be handled by hands, trodden by feet, or fall under the eyes or ears. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel reasons well on this in his first book on the Resurrection of the Dead, pp. 55, 56: But let us come to the demonstrations by which we will prove that the soul is not mortal but immortal. The first of them is that of R. Joseph Albo. He argues in this way: The soul is a spiritual substance, therefore it is incorruptible. The consequence is plain. For it is agreed by the consensus of all philosophers, and from the very first principles of philosophy, that all corruption remains in matter or body, and that nothing but what is corporeal is corruptible, because the body is disposed to corruption by the struggle and conflict of the four primary qualities, hot and cold, moist and dry. That the soul is a substance is proved from the fact that it exercises certain spiritual actions which do not depend on the body, such as reasoning, wisdom, and knowledge of various things. It is also rightly concluded that the soul is spiritual, for every act and operation flows from a power, and a power from a substance, just as fruit flows from a tree; therefore if the actions are spiritual, the substance from which these operations emanate will also be such. Add to this that spiritual accidents do not inhere in a subject or a corporeal thing. To deny that wisdom is something spiritual is far too absurd. For by its help alone we treat of God and the angels, spiritual things, we discuss many matters subtly, we judge future things, we know past things, and we grasp not only singular things but also universals by its power. Since none of these fall under the eyes, can be handled by hands, trodden by feet, or perceived by ears, we must necessarily say that there is some operation of the soul which is abstracted from the body, and therefore that the soul is not a material form such as that of the brutes, which for that reason depends entirely on the body. This reasoning also pleased Aristotle.

units.la: Optime quoque Rabbi Abenn Tybbon observat, quod non solum realis sit differentia inter Substantiam Cogitantem, & Substantiam Extensam, verum quod quicquid sit in mundo ad has duas debeat referri substantias, & non ad plures, cum scribit in Ruah Hachen, cap. 1. Ea omnia quae sunt, in duas formas vel species dividuntur. Aut enim nec sunt corpus, nec affectio corpori insita, ut Deus benedictus, & intelligentia separata. Vel sunt corpora. Corpus autem est, quicquid tres dimensiones comcomplectitur, longitudinem, latitudinem, & altitudinem.
units.tr: Rabbi Abenn Tybbon also observes well that there is not only a real difference between a thinking substance and an extended substance, but that whatever exists in the world must be referred to these two substances and not to more, as he writes in Ruah Hachen, chapter 1: All things that exist are divided into two forms or species. For either they are neither a body nor an affection inherent in a body, like God, blessed be he, and a separate intelligence; or they are bodies. A body, however, is whatever embraces three dimensions, length, breadth and height.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Probant animam immortalem, quod sit substantia libera, actuosa, voluntate praedita, cujus tota natura in continuo consistat actu, hinc distincta a substantia corporea, quae tota passiva est, hinc determinata, imo quae nec moveri quidem posset, nisi moveretur ab alio, uti non sine ratione concludit contra Sadducaeos R. Menasseh Ben Israel, lib. 1. de Resurrect. mort. pag. 56, 57: Idem hoc probari potest, ex parte voluntatis. Ecquis enim negare potest voluntatem hominis liberam esse in operationibus suis? ita ut objectum suum amare vel odisse, fugere vel prosequi possit? Libertas illa non potest esse in potentia corporali, tanquam in subjecto. Appetitus enim sensitivus in nullo animali bruto istius libertatis est particeps, quia sequitur cognitionem & ductum phantasiae, quae non minus est corporalis. Quid, quod voluntas hominis multa saepe appetat & probet, quae appetitus sensitivus improbat, & aversatur, & vice versa, phantasia amet ea, quae voluntas repudiat? Quod certe manifestum judicium est animam esse spiritualem. Nisi enim talis esset, non fugeret homo stimulatus virtutis amore, delicias & voluptates corporis: nam animalia muta nihil praeterquam, quod delectabile & sensibus gratum est, sequuntur.
units.tr: They prove that the soul is immortal, because it is a free, active substance endowed with will, whose whole nature consists in continual act. Hence it is distinct from corporeal substance, which is wholly passive, and therefore determinate, indeed one that could not even be moved unless it were moved by another. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel reasons this not without cause against the Sadducees, in his book On the Resurrection of the Dead, book 1, pages 56 and 57: The same can be proved from the side of the will. For who can deny that the human will is free in its operations, so that it can love or hate its object, flee from it or pursue it? That freedom cannot reside in a bodily power as its subject. The sensitive appetite of no brute animal shares in this freedom, because it follows knowledge and the guidance of the imagination, which is no less bodily. Moreover, the human will often desires and approves many things that the sensitive appetite disapproves and shuns, and conversely the imagination loves things that the will rejects. This is certainly a clear sign that the soul is spiritual. For if it were not, a man stirred by love of virtue would not flee the delights and pleasures of the body; mute animals follow nothing but what is pleasant and agreeable to the senses.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Adstruunt animarum immortalitatem, ex Justitia Dei naturali, quæ, cum sæpe in hoc fe- culo non exerceatur, sed differatur, necefle in sæculo futuro administrari debet, per conle- quens, animæ debent esse immortales, ut pro merito, vel bono afficiantur, vel puniantur, uti rursus argumentatur Rabbi Menasseh, l b cit. pag. 57, 58: Accedat huc, quod concedo Deum esse, necessario quoq; concedendum sit, dari providentiam: si providentia datur, ergo etiam justitia detur necesse est: si justitia datur, necessario sequitur animam esse immortalem. Ratio est, quia actus justitiæ aliquando non exercetur in hac vita. Ergo si in alia exercebitur, necesse sane est, ut anima cum corpore non occidat. Res manifesta est: Videmus in hac vita sæpe malis bene, & bonis, ac probis viris male esse: necesse ergo est, ut post hanc vitam alia sit, in qua pios & probos præmium, improbos pœna maneat. Idcirco dicunt Philosophi quidam, quum olim homines viderent, optimum atq; innocentissimum Abelum esse interfectum, parricidam vero Cainum supervixisse, atq; urbes ædificare, devenerunt, ut crederent, vanum & inane esse, servire Deo. Ut autem rursus in animis hominum Deus generaret, atq; imprimeret sidem providentiæ suæ, sustulit Hanochum, eumq; a morte præservavit. Exinde homines ab impietate illa animum revocavere, ocuoculos q; conjecere in alterum ac futurum seculum, & cogitare cœperunt de æternitate vitæ sequentis, in qua inæqualitas ea, quæ in hac vita inter bonos & malos est, tolletur.
units.tr: They maintain the immortality of souls from the natural justice of God. Since this justice is often not exercised in this age but deferred, it must necessarily be administered in the age to come. Consequently souls must be immortal, so that they may be rewarded or punished according to their merit. Rabbi Menasseh argues in the same way, in the place cited, pages 57 and 58: Let this be added: since I grant that God exists, it must necessarily also be granted that providence exists. If providence exists, then justice must also necessarily exist. If justice exists, it necessarily follows that the soul is immortal. The reason is that the act of justice is not always exercised in this life. Therefore, if it is to be exercised in another, it is certainly necessary that the soul not perish with the body. The matter is plain: we see in this life that it often goes well for the wicked and ill for the good and upright. It is necessary, then, that after this life there be another in which the pious and upright receive their reward and the wicked their punishment. For this reason certain philosophers say that when men once saw that the best and most innocent Abel had been slain, while the murderer Cain survived and built cities, they came to believe that it was vain and empty to serve God. But in order that God might again beget and imprint the faith of his providence in the minds of men, he took up Enoch and preserved him from death. From then on men called their minds back from that impiety, turned their eyes to the other and future age, and began to think about the eternity of the life to come, in which the inequality that exists between good and bad men in this life will be removed.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Asserunt animarum immortalitatem, quod communis sit notitia, omnibus impressa hominibus, imo quam ipsi Barbari non ignoraverint, animam esse immortalem, teste Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, lib. 1. de Resurrect. mort. pag. 61, 62: Denique immortalitas animæ ab ipsis Barbaris & gentilibus credita fuit. Hinc in descriptione Guineæ legitur: Affirmabant aliam esse rationem hominum, aliam pecudum. De Ægyptiis refert Diodorus Siculus hunc in modum, Parentes & majores suos ad æternam habitationem translatos autumant. De Chinensibus testatur Joannes Hugo Linschotanus, eos credere in altero mundo vitam immortalem esse, idque repetit in Historia sua de China. De Peruanis populis scribit Josephus Acosta eos credere, animas hominum immortales esse, ac pios vitam æternam, impios autem æternam damnationem manere. Idem etiam de Mexicanis refert, addit eos ea propter secum sepelire quæcunque habent pretiosissima. Similiter de Insulis Virginiæ testatur Thomas Hariot Anglus. Ex his apparet omnibus tanquam communem notitiam impressam esse, Animam esse immortalem.
units.tr: They assert the immortality of souls because it is a common notion, impressed on all men; indeed the barbarians themselves have not been ignorant that the soul is immortal. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel testifies to this in his book On the Resurrection of the Dead, book 1, pages 61 and 62: Finally, the immortality of the soul was believed even by the barbarians and gentiles. Hence in the description of Guinea we read: they affirmed that the race of men is one thing and that of beasts another. Diodorus Siculus reports this of the Egyptians: they hold that their parents and ancestors have been transferred to an eternal dwelling. Of the Chinese, John Hugo Linschoten testifies that they believe life in another world is immortal, and he repeats this in his History of China. Of the Peruvian peoples, Joseph Acosta writes that they believe the souls of men are immortal, and that the pious remain in eternal life while the impious remain in eternal damnation. He reports the same of the Mexicans, adding that for this reason they bury with themselves whatever they have that is most precious. Similarly, Thomas Hariot, an Englishman, testifies concerning the islands of Virginia. From all these it appears that the notion that the soul is immortal has been impressed as a common notion on all.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Probant pariter animarum immortalitatem sacrarum literarum authoritate, adducentes Henochi, Eliæque exempla, hinc ex Genef. cap. 5. verf. 24. concludentes: Si Henoch, qui ambulavit cum Deo, non amplius inter homines apparuit in terra, quia tulerat eum Deus, ergo, cum anima & corpore in aliam sit translatus vitam, necessario animam possidet immortalem; Probant animarum immortalitatem ex verbis Patriarchæ Jacobi fere ultimis, Genef. cap. 47. verf. 30. Dormiam cum Patribus meis; Quibus innuisset Resurrectionem: nam qui dormit naturaliter expergiscitur; Et cum patribus meis; Quibus ostendisset animam esse immortalem; Probant ex Exod. cap. 3. verf. 6. Ego sum Deus patrum tuorum, Deus Abrahami, Deus Ifaci, Deus Jacobi; Intererentes inde: Atqui Deus non est Deus mortuorum, quia mortui non sunt, sed vivorum, quia vivi existunt. Itaque Patriarchas etiamnum, respectu animæ vivere ex eo recte infertur, uti loquitur Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, lib. 1. de Resurr. mort. pag. 68. Adducunt quin etiam Exod. cap. 33. verf. 22. Non videt me homo, & vivit: Quasi diceret Deus Mosi, petenti ab eo, ut gloriosam faciem suam ostenderet: quamdiu vivit, & cum materia conjunctus est homo, me videre nequit: sed ubi e vivis excef- ferit, me intueri poterit; Itaque hinc liquere, animam post mortem esse superstitem; Ad- duntquoque Deuteron. cap.14.verf.1. In sen- tentiae probationem: Ne incidete vos, neque inducite calvitium inter oculos vestros, propter mortuum: quia populus sanctus es Domino Deo tuo, & te elegit Dominus, ut sit ei in populum thesauri, prae omnibus populis, qui sunt in superficie terrae; Ratiocinantes: Nolite eum in modum lugere ac plangere mortem eorum, qui in vita sua vobis cari fuere, quasi plane interiissent, uti vas aliquod figulinum, quod confractum, redintegrari non potest. Non ita vobiscum comparatum est: estis enim populus sanctus, quem elegit Dominus Deus: similes estis vasis aureis & argenteis, quae in partes soluta, instaurari queunt. Quare post mortem non plane cum corpore interitis atque in nihilum abitis: sed copulati, & conjuncti estis, cum illo, quicum vobis est affinitas, & similitudo quaedam sanctitatis. Ex hoc itaque concluditur, animas esse immortales. Certe argumentum hoc maxime movere debet Israelitas, ne in plangendis mortuis suis modum excedant, quia certum est omnes Israelitas vitam hanc cum meliore commutare, juxta veterum illud: Omnibus Israelitis pars est in futuro munmundo; Affirmant denique ex Deuteron. cap. 18. verf. 11. Ubi Deus vetuit requirere a mortuis, seu mortuos excitare & consulere; Quod Deus prohibere non potuisset, si non animae polt mortem fuissent superstites.
units.tr: They likewise prove the immortality of souls by the authority of Holy Scripture, citing the examples of Enoch and Elijah, and from Genesis 5:24 they conclude: If Enoch, who walked with God, no longer appeared among men on earth, because God had taken him, then, since he was translated with soul and body into another life, he necessarily possesses an immortal soul. They prove the immortality of souls from the nearly last words of the patriarch Jacob, Genesis 47:30: I will sleep with my fathers. By these words he would have hinted at the resurrection, for one who sleeps naturally wakes up; and with my fathers would have shown that the soul is immortal. They prove it from Exodus 3:6: I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob; and they infer from this: but God is not the God of the dead, because the dead do not exist, but of the living, because the living exist. Thus it is rightly inferred that the patriarchs still live, with respect to the soul, as Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel says in book 1 of On the Resurrection of the Dead, page 68. They also adduce Exodus 33:20 (verse 22 in the text as printed): No man sees me and lives. As if God were saying to Moses, who asked him to show his glorious face: as long as man lives and is joined to matter, he cannot see me; but when he has departed from the living, he will be able to behold me. Hence it is clear that the soul survives after death. They also add Deuteronomy 14:1 in support of this opinion: You shall not cut yourselves, nor make baldness between your eyes for the dead, for you are a holy people to the Lord your God, and the Lord has chosen you to be his own treasured people above all peoples that are upon the face of the earth. They reason: do not mourn and lament the death of those who were dear to you in their life, as if they had utterly perished, like a potter's vessel that, once broken, cannot be made whole again. It is not so with you, for you are a holy people whom the Lord God has chosen: you are like golden and silver vessels, which, though taken apart, can be restored. Therefore after death you do not utterly perish with the body and pass into nothing; rather you are joined and united with him to whom you are related and who shares a certain likeness of holiness. From this it is concluded that souls are immortal. Surely this argument ought especially to move the Israelites not to exceed the bounds in mourning their dead, since it is certain that all Israelites exchange this life for a better, according to the old saying: All Israelites have a share in the world to come. Finally, they affirm from Deuteronomy 18:11, where God forbade seeking the dead, that is, raising and consulting the dead, that God could not have forbidden this if souls were not surviving after death.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Confirmat animarum immortalitatem Rabbi Menasseh, ex verbis Abigalis, prudentissimae foeminae, ad Davidem, 1. Sam. cap. 25. verf. 29: Et erit anima Domini mei colligata in fasciculo viventium, cum Domino Deo tuo, & animam inimicorum tuorum funda jaciet, in medio curvaturae fundae; Quibus verbis significetur, non tantum animam immortalem esse, sed post hanc vitam quoque praemii & poenae esse spem; Sic stabilire vult Menasseh excura & sollicitudine Achitophelis, quam postremo vitae luae tempore habuit, 2. Sam. c. 17. Ex gratulatione Batsebae, venientis ad Davidem, & dicentis: Vivat Rex David in aeternum, 1. Reg. cap. 1. Quod Deus homines non in aeternum velit castigare, ex Jesa. c. 57. verl. 17. Quod Deus misurus sit Eliam ante diem judicii, ex Malach. cap. 4. Quod Lex Domini sit perfecta, reducens animam, ad eum scilicet locum, ex quo exivit, ex Psalm. 19. Quod tempore mortis spiritum nostrum in manu Dei commendemus, ex Psalm. 31. quod anima afflicta redeat ad requiem suam, ex Ps. 116. Quod Justus in morte sua speret, ex Proverb. cap. 11. verf. 7. Quod magis laudandi mortui, quam vivi, ex Eccles. cap. 4. verf. 2. Quod melior sit dies mortis, quam dies natalis, & melius sit ire ad domum luctus quam ire ad domum convivii, ex Eccles. cap. 7. verf. 2. Quod Deus hominem sit adducturus in judicium, ex Eccl. cap. 12. verf. 1. Quod pulvis redeat ad terram, anima vero ad Dominum, qui illam dedit, ex Eccles. c. 12. v. 9.
units.tr: Rabbi Menasseh confirms the immortality of souls from the words of Abigail, that most prudent woman, to David, 1 Sam. 25:29: "And the soul of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of life with the LORD thy God; and the souls of thine enemies, them shall he sling out, as out of the middle of a sling." By these words, he says, is signified not only that the soul is immortal, but that there is also hope of reward and punishment after this life. Menasseh wishes to establish this also from the anxious care and concern of Ahithophel, which he had at the last period of his life, 2 Sam. 17. He draws it from the greeting of Bathsheba, coming to David and saying: "Let King David live for ever," 1 Kings 1. That God does not wish to chastise men for ever, from Isa. 57:17. That God will send Elijah before the day of judgment, from Mal. 4. That the law of the Lord is perfect, restoring the soul, that is, to that place from which it went out, from Ps. 19. That at the time of death we commend our spirit into the hand of God, from Ps. 31. That the afflicted soul returns to its rest, from Ps. 116. That the just hopes in his death, from Prov. 11:7. That the dead are to be praised more than the living, from Eccl. 4:2. That the day of death is better than the day of birth, and that it is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting, from Eccl. 7:2. That God will bring man into judgment, from Eccl. 12:1. That the dust returns to the earth, but the soul to the Lord who gave it, from Eccl. 12:9.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Tandem in precibus, quas fundunt mulieres, parvuli, imo ipsi, qui inter Hebraeos nostros exstiterunt Sapientes, fidem de immortalitate animarum testantur, cum apud Rabbi Isacum Sangarum in libro Cosri, Part. 1. n. 115. sic divinum alloquuntur Numen: Deus mi, Animam, quam indidisti mihi mundam, illam tu creasti, finxisti & insufflasti mihi, eam custodis in medio mei, & iterum a me resumturus es, & mihi in futuro seculo restituturus. Quamdiu in me est anima, confiteor coram te, Domine Deus mi, quod tu es Dominus omnium actionum. Benedictus sit, qui cadaveribus mortuis animas restituit.
units.tr: Finally, in the prayers which women and children offer, and indeed even those who have been among our Hebrew sages, they bear witness to their faith in the immortality of souls. In Rabbi Isaac Sangari's book Cosri, Part 1, n. 115, they address the divine Majesty thus: My God, the soul which thou hast put into me pure, thou didst create it, form it and breathe it into me; thou dost keep it in the midst of me, and thou wilt take it back from me again, and restore it to me in the future age. As long as the soul is in me, I confess before thee, O Lord my God, that thou art the Lord of all actions. Blessed be he who restores souls to dead bodies.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Credunt animam, post mortem superstitem, non protinus coelestia subire gaudia, sed anni unius spatio in hoc oberrare mundo, maxime circa iuum versari cadaver, quod visitet, quandoque ingrediatur, nequiens ita cito vetus amicum quae oblivisci contubernium, hinc a daemonibus in aere versantibus inquietari valde, variis vexari modis, multaque pati, usque dum in caelum veniat, ibidemque quiescat, testantibus Rabbinis in Taanith, sol. 23. Animam non illico caelum, unde orta est, repetere, sed in hoc mundo per duodecim menses errare, iterum in sepulchrum redire, multa in purgatorio interim pati, et demum post duodecim menses in caelum venire, ibique quiescere. In Scheveth Jehuda: Animam in caelum non venire, donec corpus sepultum, et in pulverem denuo redactum fuerit, ac proinde diu adhuc in terris manere, et omnia quae hic fiunt rescire. Apud Rabbi Eliam Levitam in suo Thisbi, ad vocem Scribitur in Midrasch Rabbi Isaac, filij Sarnach: Interrogaverunt discipuli ipsum Rabbi Eliezer, quomodo se habet ritus percussionis sepulchri? Respondit eis: Postquam separatus est homo ab hoc saeculo, venit Angelus mortis, et sedet super sepulchrum ejus, statim intrat anima ejus in corpus ejus, et facit illum stare super pedes suos, etc. Donec dixit Rabbi Jehoschua filius Levi. Et in manu ejus est (inquit) catena, cujus media pars est ferrea, et altera ignea, qua verberat ipsum hominem. Et prima vice dissolvuntur. tur membra ejus: altera vice offa ejus dissipantur, tum veniunt Angeli & colligunt ea. Quod ubi tertia vice ipsum percusserit, redigitur in pulverem & cinerem; Et apud Rabbi Menaslen Ben Israel de Resurrectione Mortuorum, lib. II. cap. 6. pag. 171: Idcirco certo statuendum esse dicunt, dari spiritus quosdam quorum tanta potestas in animas hominum defunctorum sit, ut eas sibi subjectas habeant, & quo ipsis videtur corpore induant. Sed necesse est ut id faciant intra spatium XII mensium, post excessum hominis: Nam per id tempus sepe numero (uti in Gemara Sabat legitur) anima ascendit & descendit ad corpus. Et ratio est, anno integro anima non omnino abest a corpore suo, neque amorem domicilii sui plane abjicit, hinc quamdiu annus ille absolutus non est, remigrare ac retrahi potest a spiritibus in corpus suum quippe qui in aere habitant; Hinc quoque filii tenentur apud Judaeos per integros undecim menses, singulis diebus recitare precatiunculam, quae קדיש Kaddisch nominatur, opinantes patrem hoc pacto ex purgatorio liberari, ex Rabbi Leone Mutinensi in Opusculo de Ceremoniis & Consuetudinibus Judaeorum, Part. V. cap. 9: Filius parentibus orbatus, indies mane & vesperi in Synagoga parentum gratia preces recitat, quae dicuntur Kaddisch, in quo pietatis officio pergit, & ferme totus est per undecim menses. Quidam dam quolibet anno, isto quidem die, quo unus vel alter parentum diem obiit supremum, inedia se macerare solent.
units.tr: They believe that the soul, surviving after death, does not at once enter into heavenly joys, but wanders in this world for the space of one year, and especially hovers about its own corpse, which it visits and sometimes enters, being unable so quickly to forget its old companionship. Hence it is greatly disturbed by demons who move in the air, is harassed in various ways, and suffers much until it comes to heaven and rests there. The rabbis bear witness to this in Taanith, fol. 23: The soul does not at once return to heaven, whence it came, but wanders in this world for twelve months, again goes back to the sepulchre, suffers much in purgatory meanwhile, and at last after twelve months comes into heaven and rests there. In Scheveth Jehuda: The soul does not come into heaven until the body has been buried and reduced again to dust, and therefore it remains for a long time on earth and learns everything that happens here. In Rabbi Elias Levita's Thisbi, under the word It is written in the Midrash of Rabbi Isaac, son of Sarnach: The disciples asked Rabbi Eliezer himself, how is the rite of the striking of the sepulchre? He answered them: After a man has departed from this age, the Angel of Death comes and sits upon his sepulchre; at once his soul enters his body and makes him stand upon his feet, etc. Until Rabbi Joshua son of Levi said: And in his hand (he says) is a chain, the middle part of which is iron, and the other fiery, with which he strikes the man himself. At the first blow his limbs are dissolved; at the second his bones are scattered, then Angels come and gather them together. When he has struck him a third time, he is reduced to dust and ashes. And in Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel's On the Resurrection of the Dead, book II, ch. 6, p. 171: They say therefore that it must certainly be held that there are certain spirits who have such power over the souls of the dead that they hold them subject to themselves, and clothe them with a body as seems good to them. But they must do this within the space of twelve months after the man's departure; for during that time, as often as is read in the Gemara Sabat, the soul ascends and descends to the body. The reason is that for a whole year the soul is not wholly absent from its body, nor entirely casts off the love of its dwelling; hence, as long as that year is not complete, it can be sent back and drawn back into its body by the spirits who dwell in the air. Hence also among the Jews the sons are bound, for a full eleven months, to recite each day a little prayer called Kaddisch [קדיש], believing that in this way the father is freed from purgatory; so Rabbi Leo of Modena, in his little work On the Ceremonies and Customs of the Jews, Part V, ch. 9: A son bereaved of his parents recites prayers every morning and evening in the synagogue for the sake of his parents, which are called Kaddisch, and he continues in this duty of piety almost the whole of eleven months. Some every year, on that very day on which one or other of their parents died, are accustomed to starve themselves.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Putant sententiam suam de animarum mora circa sua sepulchra non destitui sacrarum literarum authoritate, adducentes Eccles. cap. 12. verf. 7. Revertatur pulvis in terram suam unde erat, & spiritus redeat ad Deum, qui dedit illum; Sicque ratiocinantes: Si spiritus tum redit ad Deum, quando corpus in pulverem redactum est, sequitur necessario, quod spiritus non eo ipso, quo per mortem separatus est a suo corpore, revertatur ad Deum, sed moras nectat, usque dum corpus sepultum sensim atque sensim in pulverem redigitur; Adducentes pariter, Samuelis animam arte magica in suum fuisse revocatum corpus, uti vult Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, lib. II. de Resurrect. Mort. cap. 6. pag. 171. 172:
units.tr: They think their view, that souls linger about their graves, lacks no authority of Sacred Letters, citing Eccles. 12:7: "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was, and the spirit shall return to God who gave it." And they reason thus: if the spirit returns to God only when the body has been reduced to dust, it follows necessarily that the spirit does not return to God at the very moment it is separated from its body by death, but delays until the buried body is gradually reduced to dust. They also cite that the soul of Samuel was recalled by magic art into his body, as Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel maintains, Book II, On the Resurrection of the Dead, ch. 6, pp. 171–172:

units.la: Dicendum proinde est Samuel animam arte magica pythonissa in corpus suum revocatam, potuisse Saulem alloqui eique futura prædixisse. Quemadmodum etiam a R. Meyr Gabay in libro Avodat a Kodes observatum est. Item ab antiquis in Jalkut ditum legitur כל הנביאים כלם נבאו בחייהן אבל לא Reliqui Prophetæ omnes, præter Samuelem במותם חוץ משמואל שנבא אף לאחר מותו שנאמר מחר אתה ובניך עמי muelem vaticinati sunt, dum viverent: ille autem non tantum in vita, sed etiam post eam prophetavit, quoniam dixit Sauli, cras tu & filij tui mecum erunt. Sed, ut ad propositum nostrum revertamur, cum Deus velit honestatis & verecundiæ ergo, ut qui post mortem apparent vivi veste tecti appareant; Samuelem idcirco eodem amictu pallio aparuisse quo in vita usus, & quo cum sepultus fuerat.
units.tr: We must therefore say that Samuel's soul, recalled into his body by the magic art of the medium, was able to speak to Saul and foretell the future to him. This is also noted by R. Meyr Gabay in the book Avodat a Kodes. Likewise it is read in the Jalkut by the ancients (Hebrew: כל הנביאים כלם נבאו בחייהן אבל לא במותם חוץ משמואל שנבא אף לאחר מותו שנאמר מחר אתה ובניך עמי) that all the other prophets prophesied while they were alive, but Samuel prophesied not only in life but also after it, since he said to Saul: "Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me." But, to return to our purpose, since God wishes that those who appear after death should appear clothed, for the sake of decency and modesty, Samuel therefore appeared in the same garment and mantle in which he had been used to dress in life, and in which he had been buried.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Crediderunt plurimi inter Judæos, animas per mortem à corporibus suis separatas, in alia transmigrare corpora, fuitque hæc sententia olim vulgatissima, quam non solum amplexi fuerunt Pharisæi, uti testatur Josephus, Hebraeorum Historicorum accuratissimus, lib. 2. de bello Judaico, cap. 7. Pharisæi dogma habent, animam quidem omnem incorruptam esse, transire vero in alia corpora solas bonorum, improborum vero interminabili supplicio cruciari; Sed in populo quoque floruit Judaico, uti aliquo modo patet ex Matth. cap. 16, verf. 14. ubi Christus rogabat, quem me esse dicunt homines? Respondebant discipuli, alios exstimare ipsum esse Johannem, alios Eliam, alios vero Jeremiam, vel alium aliquem ex Prophetis. Quasi dicerent, quidam ajunt animam Johannis, vel Eliæ, vel Jeremiæ, remiæ, vel etiam alicujus ex Prophetis in corpus tuum migrasse; imo, videtur, quod hæc de animarum revolutione opinio, ipsis quoq; Apostolorum inhæserit animis, sicuti ejus rei indicia extant Johan. cap 9. verf. 2. Cum enim de cæco, quem a nativitate cognoverant fuisse cæcum, quæstionem instituerent, cur hac pœna esset multatus, an ob sua propria peccata hoc factum esset, an propter parentum delicta? Num potuerit cæcus peccare, priusquam nasceretur? Per consequens putabant, quod anima illius cæci in alio peccaverit corpore, ob quod in hoc puniatur.
units.tr: Many among the Jews believed that souls, separated from their bodies by death, pass into other bodies. This opinion was once very widespread, and it was embraced not only by the Pharisees, as Josephus, the most accurate of the Hebrew historians, attests, Book 2 of The Jewish War, ch. 7: "The Pharisees hold the doctrine that every soul is incorruptible, but that only the souls of good men pass into other bodies, while the souls of the wicked suffer everlasting punishment." It also flourished among the Jewish people, as is clear in some measure from Matt. 16:14, where Christ asked, "Who do men say that I am?" The disciples answered that some thought him to be John, others Elijah, others Jeremiah or one of the prophets. As if they said: some say that the soul of John, or of Elijah, or of Jeremiah, or of some other prophet, has migrated into your body. Indeed, it seems that this opinion about the revolution of souls clung also to the minds of the Apostles themselves, as evidence of this matter exists in John 9:2. For when they asked about the blind man whom they had known to have been blind from birth, why he had been afflicted with this punishment, whether it was on account of his own sins or those of his parents, and, "Could he have sinned before he was born?" they consequently supposed that the soul of that blind man had sinned in another body, on account of which it is punished in this one.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Amplexati pariter sunt hanc sententiam de שובתבי Animarum revolutione Hebræorum nonnulli Philosophi, Scrutationis Sapientes appellati, de quibus id testatur Rabbi David Kimchi ad Psalm. 104. verf. 30: Dixerunt quidam ex Sapientibus Scrutationis, omne vivens, postquam mortuum est, resurrecturum propterea, quod futurum sit, ut anima circumvolvantur, & redeant in mundum: Attamen non redeunt ad materiam primam, sicut ipsa materia in se est. Et hoc juge futurum est, & fiet per aliquot mille annos; Sed Philosophi & maximi quidem ex illis, dicunt, quod anima in æternum non redeat in corpus; Maxime tamen celebris & decantata fuit apud Judæos Judæorum Theologos Cabalistas, uti probat ex libro Sohare Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, libro II. de Resurrectione Mortuorum, c.18. pag.214,215: Celebris, ac decantata illa opinio Cabalistarum, de transmigratione animarum fundamentum suum juxta eos habet in gratia, ac misericordia divina. Addunt vero iidem, quod sicut operationes animæ, plerumq; sequuntur temperamentum corporis; ita animæ etiam aliquo modo apud Deum conquerantur de eo, quod in meliora, & aptius disposita corpora ab eo non fuerint missæ ac compactæ, cum tota differentia, quæ inter homines est, ratio, à corporum temperamento vario dependeat. Hinc cholericus forte dicat, in corpore meo prædominatur bilis; ignavus, ac segnis, in corpore meo phlegma, seu pituita redundat; libidinosus, in meo sanguis bullit, atq; ita in reliquis. Ob hanc rem Dominus Deus, ne habeant animæ quod conquerantur aut prætexant, eas in alia nova corpora transmigrare facit; & quidem triplici de causa; vel ut perfectionem istam acquirant, quam ob malam prioris corporis temperiem consequi non potuerant, vel ut perfectiores multo, imo omnibus virtutum numeris absolutæ fiant in hoc mundo, qui virtuti exercendæ destinatus est, uti futurus mundus præmio ac remunerationi; vel deniq; ut castigentur, & à peccatis, ac vitiis istis purgentur, quæ in priore corpore commiserant, ut ita purgatæ, ac liberatæ à pecpeccatis in hoc mundo, in mundo animarum bonis quibusdam frui possint; atq; ita transmigratio haec tota cedat bono ac commodo anima. Hanc transmigrationem dicunt ter fieri voluntate ac per miss su Dei, juxta illud Jobi, Cap.33.verf.29. Ecce omnia ista operabitur Deus vicibus tribus cum homine.
units.tr: Some Hebrew philosophers, called "Sages of Inquiry," likewise embraced this doctrine of the revolution of souls (the Hebrew term is garbled in the scan, but it denotes transmigration). Rabbi David Kimchi testifies to this on Psalm 104:30: "Certain of the Sages of Inquiry have said that every living thing, after it has died, will rise again, because it is to be that the souls will revolve and return into the world. Yet they do not return to primal matter as matter is in itself. And this will go on continually, and will happen for some thousands of years. But the philosophers, and the greatest of them, say that the soul does not return into a body for ever." Yet this opinion, of the Cabalists among the Jewish theologians, was by far the most celebrated and most sung of all among the Jews, as Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel proves from the book Sohar, Book II, On the Resurrection of the Dead, ch. 18, pp. 214–215: The famous and much-celebrated opinion of the Cabalists concerning the transmigration of souls has, according to them, its foundation in the grace and mercy of God. The same writers add that, just as the operations of the soul generally follow the temperament of the body, so souls also in some way complain before God that they were not sent and fitted into better and more suitably disposed bodies. For the whole difference that exists among men depends on the varying temperament of the bodies. Hence the choleric man perhaps says: "In my body bile predominates"; the lazy and sluggish man: "In mine phlegm or pituita overflows"; the lustful: "In mine the blood boils"; and so on with the rest.
