For this reason the Lord God, so that souls may have nothing to complain of or to pretend, makes them migrate into other new bodies, and indeed for a threefold reason: either that they may acquire that perfection which they could not attain because of the bad temperament of their former body, or that they may become far more perfect, indeed absolute in all the measures of virtue, in this world, which is destined for the exercise of virtue, as the future world is for reward and recompense; or finally that they may be chastised and purged of the sins and vices they committed in the former body, so that, cleansed and freed from sins in this world, they may enjoy certain goods in the world of souls; and thus this whole transmigration turns to the good and advantage of the soul. They say that this transmigration takes place three times, by the will and mission of God, according to the saying of Job 33:29: "Behold, all these things God works twice, or three times, with man."

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Stat quoque pro animarum revolutione Rabbi Beachai, cum in Paraicha הנשמה verba illa: Vivet Ruben, & non morietur; juxta viam Cabalae, quam ipse sequitur, sic interpretanda putat: Juxta viam Cabalae illud, vivet Ruben & non morietur, sic est interpretandum, ut vox vivet, de vita seculi futuri, non morietur vero, ita accipiatur, quod non fit rediturus inde in corpus, & moriturus morte secunda, sicut expositi Onkelos in Targum: & morte secunda non morietur: Quo ipso nobis revelavit, quod anima revolvantur, & redeant in corpus, postea quam acceperunt mercedem suam, & etiam multam vel in horto Eden, vel in Gehenna. Et hoc cognitum ac per traditionem acceptum est, quod, sicut intermissiones mundi redeunt atq; revolvuntur: sic anima, postquam accepit vel mercedem in horto Eden, vel multam in Gehenna, ipsa etiam post aliquod tempus redeat in corpus, ut accipiat, quod ipsi conveniens est, mensuram pro mensura. Et haec revolutio illa est, quae apud Rabbinos nostros vocatur revivificatio mortuorum; Stat pariter pro animarum transmigratione Rabbi MenaffehBen Israel,multis ostendens, quod opinio hæc non tantum in sacris fit fundata literis, pateat ex historia Judæ & Thamaris, & ex præcepto de fratri suscitando femine colligatur, verum approbata fit à Paraphrafte Chaldæo apud Efaiam cap. 22. v.14. confirmata in Sohare, imo denique ab ipsis antiquis credita Philosophis & Poetis Gentilibus, uti liquet ex lib. 11. de Resurrectione Mortuorum, cap. 18. pag. 216: Ac licet à R. Sedhadya Agaon, & R. Josephus Albo negetur hujusmodi transmigratio animarum: nihilominus tamen ea in Zoar, non exiguæ autoritatis libro, comprobatur ac confirmatur. Quam veram etiam hæc sit opinio, patet ex historia Judæ, & Thamaris, & ex præcepto de suscitando fratri femine, si improlis diceffrit. Multi præterea ex antiquis Philosophis agnoverunt transmigrationem animarum; uti ex Platone in Phædro conflat, qui refert ultima Socratis verba hac de refuiffe, cum Athenis ad mortem damnatus venenum bibere est coactus. Similiter Pythagoras, & Virgilius hac de re multa sensere: & fortassis hanc opinionem hausere vel à Prophetis, vel à superioribus seculis. Eandem quoq; opinionem fequutus esse videtur Chaldæus Paraphrastes apud Efaiam cap. XXII. XIV. Si expiabitur iniquitas hæc vobis, donec moriamini. Ubi addit הנשמה מתה (morte secunda) id est, donec in aliud corpus anima transmigret, & fecunda morte ab eo separetur; Et ex Conciliatore in Genesin, Quaestione 43. pag. 65, 66. Septimo, atque ultimo, divini Cabalistae in μετεμψύχωσιν, seu animarum transmigrationem credunt, multi quoque Gentilium traditam, & in his Orpheo, Mercurio Trismegisto in Poemandro, Pythagora, Platoni in Phaedro, Timaeo, & Menone, ac Virgilio, qui sexto Aeneid. ait:
units.tr: Rabbi Bechai also supports the revolution of souls. On the words in Parashah Ha-Naso, "Reuben shall live and not die," he thinks the passage must be interpreted in line with the Cabalistic method he follows: By the way of the Cabala, the words "Reuben shall live and not die" must be interpreted so that the word "shall live" refers to the life of the future age, and "shall not die" is understood to mean that he will not return from there into a body and die a second death, as Onkelos explained in the Targum: "and shall not die the second death." By this he has revealed to us that souls revolve and return into bodies after they have received their reward, and indeed many times, either in the garden of Eden or in Gehenna. And this is known and received by tradition: just as the ages of the world return and revolve, so the soul, after it has received either its reward in the garden of Eden or its punishment in Gehenna, will return again into a body after some time, so that it may receive what is fitting for it, measure for measure. This revolution is what among our rabbis is called the revivification of the dead. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel likewise supports the transmigration of souls, showing by many arguments that this opinion is founded not only on the sacred letters. It is evident from the history of Judah and Tamar, and it is gathered from the precept concerning raising up seed for a brother. Moreover, it is approved by the Chaldee paraphrast in Isaiah 22:14, confirmed in the Zohar, and indeed was believed by the ancient philosophers and pagan poets themselves, as is clear from book 11 on the Resurrection of the Dead, chapter 18, page 216. Although R. Saadia Gaon and R. Joseph Albo deny this kind of transmigration of souls, nevertheless it is supported and confirmed in the Zohar, a book of no small authority. That this opinion is true is also shown by the history of Judah and Tamar, and by the precept concerning raising up seed for a brother, if he dies without children. Moreover, many of the ancient philosophers acknowledged the transmigration of souls, as is plain from Plato in the Phaedrus, who reports that Socrates' last words, spoken when he was condemned to death at Athens and forced to drink poison, were to this effect. Pythagoras and Virgil also thought many things on this subject, and perhaps they drew this opinion either from the Prophets or from earlier ages. The Chaldee paraphrast also seems to have followed the same opinion in Isaiah 22:14: "If this iniquity be purged from you until you die," where he adds "second death" [הנשמה מתה], that is, until the soul passes over into another body and is separated from it by a second death. And from the Conciliator on Genesis, Question 43, pages 65–66: Seventhly and lastly, the divine Cabalists believe in metempsychosis [μετεμψύχωσιν], or the transmigration of souls, which many of the Gentiles also taught, and among these Orpheus, Mercurius Trismegistus in the Poemander, Pythagoras, Plato in the Phaedrus, the Timaeus and the Meno, and Virgil, who says in the sixth book of the Aeneid:

units.la: Has omnes, ubi mille rotam volvere per annos, Lethaeum ad fluvium Deus evocat agmine magno: Scilicet immemores supera ut convexa revisant, Rursus & incipiant in corpora velle reverti.
units.tr: All these, when they have turned the wheel for a thousand years, God calls in a great throng to the river Lethe: clearly so that, forgetful, they may revisit the upper vaults, and then begin again to desire to return into bodies.

units.la: Itaque possit quoque bonus improsperus uti rebus, ob delicta quae non in ipso, sed alio corpore anima commisit.
units.tr: So also a good man who is unprosperous may use the things of this world, on account of the faults which the soul committed not in himself but in another body.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Adducunt in patrocinium sententiae de animarum transmigratione, Rabbi Isaacum Abarbanelem, referentes, quod in Commentariis suis ad Legem divinam, non tantum contra Aristotelem animarum defenderit revolutionem, motasque diluerit difficultates, sed simul ad sequentem respondERIT quaestionem, uti patet ex Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel Lib. II. de Resurrectione Mortuorum, cap. 18.
units.tr: They bring forward in support of the opinion about the transmigration of souls Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel, reporting that in his Commentaries on the divine Law he not only defended the revolution of souls against Aristotle and resolved the difficulties raised, but also answered the following question. This is clear from Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, book II on the Resurrection of the Dead, chapter 18,

units.la: pag. 216, 217: Hinc itaque quaeritur, cum unica tantum sit anima informans corpus, eaque in duo, vel tria corpora transmigret; in quod istorum trium revertatur die resurrectionis, quoniam unica anima non potest in pluribus simul corporibus esse? Respondemus, quamquam verum est sapientissimum Ambonit in Epistola ista quam ad Arisbam scripsit, ista ratione adductum negasse animarum transmigrationem: nihilominus tamen doctissimus vir Ifac Abravanel istam quaestionem erudite solvit in commentariis suis ad legem divinam: & refutat insuper ea, quae ab Ariftotele adversus istam de gilgul, five transanimatione opinionem obji-ciuntur. Ac primo quidem ad quaestionem istam in specie respondens probabile esse ait, in resurrectione mortuorum, animas quas reversuras in prima quae informarunt corpora, ut in iis, & cum iis praemio, aut poena afficiantur. Quod attinet ad alia corpora, in quae postea migrarunt, ut in illis virtuti operam darent, vel castigarentur, ac punirentur, in istis a Deo tempore extremi judicij non judicabuntur: quoniam instrumenta tantum fuere voluntatis divinae; Sunt tamen inter Judaeos, qui in responsione ad formatam quaestionem, in contraria omnia abeunt, judicantes, non primum refurrectu-rum corpus, sed postremum, quod ab anima fuit informatum, uti ex Zoare refert Rabbi Me-
units.tr: pages 216–217: Hence the question arises: since there is only one soul informing the body, and that soul transmigrates into two or three bodies, into which of these three will it return on the day of resurrection, since one soul cannot be in several bodies at once? We reply: although it is true that the most wise Ambonit, in the letter he wrote to Arisba, denied the transmigration of souls on the ground of this argument, nevertheless the most learned man Isaac Abravanel solved this question skilfully in his commentaries on the divine law, and moreover refutes those objections which Aristotle raised against this opinion of gilgul, or transanimation. And first, answering this question in particular, he says it is probable that at the resurrection of the dead, souls will return to the first bodies which they informed, so that they may be rewarded or punished in them and with them. As for the other bodies into which they afterwards migrated, in order to labour in virtue in them or to be chastised and punished, these will not be judged in them at the time of the last judgment by God, since they were only instruments of the divine will. Yet there are among the Jews some who, in answering the question as posed, go to the opposite extreme, judging that the body which will rise first is not the first but the last that was informed by the soul, as Rabbi Me-

units.la: Menasseh Ben Israel, citato lib. II. pag. 218: R. Husquiha inquit, si mihi dicas, quod omnia corpora expergisicentur, ac resurgent, quid ergo, quaero ego, futurum est illis corporibus, quae informata fuerunt ab una anima? Respondit R. Joseph, quod attinet ad corpora illa, quae nihil meruerunt, neque quicquam boni praestiterunt: certe cum illis agetur, ac si nunquam in rerum natura fuissent; & quia non aliter quam arbor sicca fuerunt in hoc mundo, non aliter etiam erunt in futuro. Postremum tamen quod informatum ab ea fuit corpus resurget: quoniam fuit plantatum, & fructus protulit, radices egit, uti oportet. Idcirco etiam scriptum est, Psalmo 1: Et erit instar arboris consitae juxta aquas: quippe fructus dedit, & radices extendit. Quod ad primum corpus attinet, de eo fiet, uti scriptum legitur Jerem. cap. 17, verf. 6. Et erit tanquam juniperus in planicie, & non videbit cum venerit bonum: bonum, scilicet, resurrectionis mortuorum. Facile liquet ex verbis ipsis, quae fuerit veterum opinio. Ratio etiam pro hac opinione est: aequum, enim ac par est, ut corpus consequatur illud bonum, quod promeruit vel bene agendo, vel ob delicta, & peccata sua poenas ferendo; Tandem quoque responsum tuli a diversis Rabbinis, quos super hanc consului difficultatem, quod, licet anima ingrediatur aliud corpus, illud propterea non destitutum sit sua propria anima. ma, sed alteram praeterea accipiat animam, per consequens unumquodque corpus cum sua propria relurgat anima.
units.tr: Menasseh Ben Israel, cited book II, page 218: R. Huskiha says: if you tell me that all bodies will be awakened and rise, what then, I ask, will become of those bodies which were informed by one soul? R. Joseph replied: as for those bodies which merited nothing and did no good, certainly they will be dealt with as if they had never been in the nature of things; and since in this world they were no different from a dry tree, so in the future they will be no different. The last body, however, which was informed by the soul will rise, since it was planted, bore fruit, and put forth roots, as it ought. For this reason it is also written, Psalm 1: And he shall be like a tree planted by the waters, for it gave fruit and extended its roots. As for the first body, it will happen to it as written in Jeremiah 17:6: And he shall be like a juniper in the wilderness, and shall not see when good comes: the good, namely, of the resurrection of the dead. From the words themselves it is easy to see what the opinion of the ancients was. There is also a reason for this opinion: it is fair and proper that the body should share in that good which it has earned, either by acting well, or by bearing punishment for its faults and sins. Finally, I have also received an answer from various rabbis whom I consulted on this difficulty: although the soul enters another body, that body is not for this reason left without its own soul, but receives another soul besides; consequently each body rises with its own soul.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Credunt pariter plerique inter Judaeos hodiernos, Animas Justorum tribus saltem vicibus in humana migrare corpora, tum ut ex meliori novorum corporum temperamento existant perfectiores; seu ut quod virtutum defuit, in novo acquirant corpore, easdemq; in hoc adhuc seculo exerceant; tum i tcafti-gentur ob vitia & delicta in priori commissa corpore, atque ita in hac purgentur vita; Im-proborum vero animas migrare in bruta cor-pora pro ratione peccatorum, uti adulterorum in corpus Cameli, libidinosorum, rapacium, in animantia paribus obnoxia affectibus; imo ipsas impiorum animas migrare in pisces, avesque, uti mihi constat non ex pluribus tantum Judaeorum testimoniis, sed clare quoque liquet ex Rabbi Elia Levita in Thisbi ad vocem Gilgul: Autores Cabalistici differunt de revolutione animarum: quorum opinio est, unamquamque animam tribus vicibus creari: volunt dicere, quod ea volvat se per corpora trium filiorum hominis. Et locus scripturae unde probationem accipiunt, est iste: Ecce omnia ista operatur Deus cum homine tribus vicibus, Jobi cap. 33. verf. 29;
units.tr: Likewise, most of the Jews today believe that the souls of the righteous pass into human bodies at least three times: partly so that they may exist as more perfect beings from a better temperament of the new bodies, or so that they may acquire in the new body what virtue they lacked and exercise it again in this age; and partly so that they may be chastised for the vices and sins committed in the earlier body, and so be purged in this life. The souls of the wicked, however, they say, pass into brute bodies according to the nature of their sins: adulterers into the body of a camel, the lustful and rapacious into animals that share their passions. Indeed, they hold that the souls of the impious pass even into fish and birds. This is clear to me not only from the testimony of many Jews, but also plainly from Rabbi Elijah Levita in the Thisbi, under the word Gilgul: The Cabbalistic authors differ about the revolution of souls. The opinion of one group is that each soul is created three times; they mean that it turns itself through the bodies of three sons of man. The passage of Scripture from which they take their proof is this: "Behold, God does all these things three times with man," Job, chap. 33, verse 29.

units.la: Unde sic dicunt, quod anima primi hominis voluta- verit se in corpus Davidis Regis, & ex Davide vol- vet se in corpus Messiæ; idq; significari per literas, quæ sunt in voce יהוה, quarum unaquæq; integram dictionem constituat, ש Adam, ד David, ם Messias. Sic quoq; dixerunt, quod animæ hominum prævaricatorum migrent in corpora animalium, uniuscujusq; animasecundum id, quod peccavit. Exempli gratia, qui rem habuit cum masculo, anima ejus migrat in leporem; quia is silicet in coitu modo marem agit, modo fæmellam. Qui vero rem habuerit cum alterius uxore, anima ejus in camelum migrat; Hinc est, quod David dicit Psal. 13: Cantabo Domino חסד כי hoc est, cantabo tibi, & confitebor tibi, quod abstulisti peccatum meum, & liberasti animam meam de camelo; Sicuti autem fabulantur Adami animam in Davidem revolutam, & ex inde in Messiam devolvendam esse, ita eodem modo fingunt animam Habelis in Sethum, & ex Setho in Molen translatam, quod trium nominum primores literæ nomen משה efficiant; Commentanturque similiter animam Labanis in Bileamum, & hinc in Nabalem migrasse, quod primæ literæ trium horum nominum itidem nomen נבל faciant.
units.tr: Hence they say that the soul of the first man turned itself into the body of King David, and from David will turn itself into the body of the Messiah. They say this is signified by the letters of the word יהוה [YHWH], each of which makes up a whole word: the letter shin [ש] for Adam, daleth [ד] for David, and mem [ם] for Messiah. They also say that the souls of sinners pass into the bodies of animals, each according to the sin he committed. For example, one who had intercourse with a male has his soul pass into a hare, because in intercourse he acts sometimes as the male and sometimes as the female. One who has had intercourse with another man's wife has his soul pass into a camel. Hence David says in Psalm 13: "I will sing to the LORD [חסד]," that is, "I will sing to you and confess to you, because you have taken away my sin and delivered my soul from the camel." But just as they fable that the soul of Adam turned into David and is to pass from him into the Messiah, so in the same way they imagine that the soul of Abel passed into Seth and from Seth into Moses, because the first letters of the three names make up the name Moses [משה]. Likewise they comment that the soul of Laban passed into Balaam, and from him into Nabal, because the first letters of these three names likewise make up the name Nabal [נבל].

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: qui inter Judaeos animarum transmigratio- nem negant, vocantes sententiam hanc ftoli- dam, uti liquet ex Rabbi Benjamin Tudelenfi, qui postquam Dogzeos, homines gentiles, Tfidoniis finitimos descripsisset, sic subjungit pag. 54. Itineratii fui, editionis L'Empereu- riae: Animam, cum ex alicujus probi corpore mi- grat, occupare tradunt corpus cujusdam pueruli, qui eo momento, quo anima e corpore suo migrat, nascitur; sin ex improbo discedat, occupare canis aut jumenti corpus. Hujusmodi cum fit via istorum, stoliditatem suam produnt; Sic Rabbi Saadia Gaon, & Rabbi Jofeph Albo a partibus negantium steterunt, uti testatur Rabbi Menasseh Benifrael, Revolutionis animarum propugnator acerrimus, lib. II. de Resurrectione mortuorum, pag. 216: Ac licet a R. Sehadya Agaon, & R. Jofeph Albo negetur hujusmodi transmigratio animarum: nihilominus tamen ea in Zoar, non exigua autoritatis libro, comprobatur ac confirmatur; Imo inter negantes fuit Ambonit, in Epistola, quam ad Arisbam exaravit, teste Rabbi Menasseh libr. cit. p. 217: Respondemus, quamquam verum est sapientissimum Ambonit in Epistola ista quam ad Arisbam scripsit, ista ratione adductum negasse animarum transmigrationem: nihilominus tamen doctissimo vir Ifac Abravanel istam quastionem erudite sol-vit. vit in commentariis suis ad legem divinam: & refutat insuper ea, quae ab Aristotele adversus istam de gilgul, sive transanimatione opinionem objiciuntur; Pariter doctrinam de gilgul Revolutione animarum impugnat Rabbi Happenini à Judæis plerumque Badrefchi appellatus; Tandem testatur Rabbi Leo Mutinensis, quod multi opinionem hanc suo non approbent calculo, cum ait in Opusculo de Ceremoniis & Consuetudinibus Judæorum, Part. V. c. 11. Opinionem singularem, (Pythagorica alias dicitur,) Judæorum nonnulli fovent, quae tradit migrare animas ex uno corpore in aliud. Dicunt hoc ipsum gilgul, sustinentes hanc migrationem probare ex multis scripturæ locis, potissimum ex Ecclesiaste & Jobo depromtis: multi tamen eam suo haud approbant calculo. Sed quicquid demum sit, utraque sententia tolerari potest: neque quis alterutram amplectens, ideo statim ad classem Haereticorum relegandus est.
units.tr: Among the Jews there are some who deny the transmigration of souls, calling this opinion foolish, as is clear from Rabbi Benjamin of Tudela, who, after describing the Dogzeos, heathen people neighbouring the Sidonians, adds this on page 54 of his Itinerary, in the L'Empereur edition: They say that when the soul migrates from the body of a good man, it occupies the body of a little child who is born at the very moment the soul leaves its body; but if it departs from a wicked man, it occupies the body of a dog or a beast of burden. Since such is the way of these people, they reveal their foolishness; Thus Rabbi Saadia Gaon and Rabbi Joseph Albo stood on the side of those who deny it, as Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, the most fierce champion of the revolution of souls, attests in book II of his work on the resurrection of the dead, page 216: Although this kind of transmigration of souls is denied by R. Saadia Gaon and R. Joseph Albo, nevertheless it is proved and confirmed in the Zohar, a book of no small authority; Indeed, Ambonit was among the deniers, in the letter he wrote to Arisba, as Rabbi Menasseh attests in the book cited, page 217: We reply that, although it is true that the most wise Ambonit, moved by that reasoning, denied the transmigration of souls in the letter he wrote to Arisba, nevertheless the most learned man Isaac Abravanel solved this question skilfully in his commentaries on the divine law, and moreover he refutes those objections which Aristotle raised against this opinion of gilgul, that is, transanimation. Likewise Rabbi Happenini, whom the Jews commonly call Badrefchi, attacks the doctrine of gilgul, the revolution of souls. Finally, Rabbi Leo of Modena bears witness that many do not give their approval to this opinion, when he says in his little work on the ceremonies and customs of the Jews, Part V, chapter 11: Some of the Jews favour a singular opinion (otherwise called Pythagorean), which teaches that souls migrate from one body into another. They say this is the very gilgul, and they maintain that this migration is proved from many passages of Scripture, chiefly taken from Ecclesiastes and Job; yet many do not approve of it. But whatever the case, either opinion may be tolerated, and whoever embraces either one is not for that reason to be at once relegated to the class of heretics.

units.la: CAPUT XVIII. De Resurrectione Mortuorum.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII. On the Resurrection of the Dead.

units.la: CRedunt Resurrectionem Mortuorum, fidei articulum esse fundamentalem, proproinde negantem resurrectionem ex albo Israelitarum expungendum, uti liquet ex Rabbi Maimonidis articulo decimo tertio, Theologiæ Judaicæ cap. 1. Et in Catechesi Judaica, ad Quæst. 12. Fundamentum decimum tertium est, ut credamus fixum esse tempus, sólique Deo notum, quo reviviscent mortui; quod si quis non credat, is religione caret, & quam longissime abest à fide judaica. Scriptum est namque, Esai. cap. 26. vers. 19. Vivent mortui tui & cadavere resurgent; Et iterum ibid: Expergiscite & laudate cubantes in pulvere; Et rursus Daniel. cap. 12. v. 2. Et multi qui dormiunt in terra pulveris, evigilabunt. Id autem justis contingeret, utinam in numero illorum essemus, Hosea cap. 6. vers. 2. Vivificet nos post duos dies, surgamus & vivamus coram eo; Et ex Rabbi Mosche de Trana in Beth Elohim, sol. 103. col. 4. Scripsit Raf (innuit Maimonidem) pia memoria, articulus fundamentalis decimus tertius agit de resurrectione, cujus rationem & fundamenta jam expositimus. Quod si homo crediderit fundamenta illa omnia, seque illa credere declaraverit, ingreditur ecclesiam Israelis, & jubemur diligere illum, & misericordiam illi exhibere, & conversari cum illo juxta omnia, quæ præcepit Deus benedictus cuilibet erga proximum facienda. Si quis autem vilipenderit hoc fundamentum excellentium fundamentorum, ecce exit ille ex ecclesia, fia, quippe qui abnegat articulum fidei, & vocatur impius ac Epicurus, amputat q; plantas, quem odio habere & perdere jubemur; Patetque idem illud abunde ex Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, qui tres libros de Resurrectione Mortuorum consignavit, cum lib.1. cap.1. de Rabbi Maimonidis articulo fidei decimo tertio, ficloquitur pag.1,2. R. Moses Aegyptius, vir singulari prudentia, ac multarum rerum cognitione longe instructissimus, inter XIII articulos fidei etiam hunc articulum ultimo loco refert: Quod omnibus Israelitis credenda sit Resurrectio mortuorum; id est, mortuos, vitaque defunctos, quorum corpora discessu anima in pulverem, ac cineres resoluta fuerunt, infusa rursus illis eadem anima, redituros esse in lucem, ut secundo vita corporali in hoc mundo fruantur. Quia vero Rabbi Moses, cui adstipulantur omnes Hebraeorum Magistri, albo expunctos vult, quotquot Articulum hunc, ex Israelitarum, tanquam essentialem fidei articulum negant, operae pretium putavi, ad hanc rem comprobandam, primum ea loca adducere, ex quibus antiqui sapientes illum articulum, seu probabili, seu apodictica ratione collegerunt. Deinde subjicere rationes ex ipsa natura petitas, ac denique ipsa experientia confirmare.
units.tr: They hold that the resurrection of the dead is a fundamental article of faith, and so whoever denies the resurrection must be struck off the roll of the Israelites. This is clear from Rabbi Maimonides' thirteenth article, in the Jewish Theology, chap. 1, and in the Jewish Catechism, Question 12: The thirteenth fundamental is that we believe there is a fixed time, known to God alone, at which the dead will be revived; and if anyone does not believe this, he lacks religion and is very far from the Jewish faith. For it is written, Isaiah 26:19: Thy dead shall live, together with my dead body shall they arise; and again in the same place: Awake and sing, you who lie in the dust; and again Daniel 12:2: And many of those who sleep in the land of dust shall awake. This would befall the righteous; would that we were among their number, Hosea 6:2: He will revive us after two days; we shall rise and live before him. And from Rabbi Moses of Trani in the Beth Elohim, fol. 103, col. 4: Raf (he means Maimonides), of pious memory, wrote that the thirteenth fundamental article deals with the resurrection, the reason and foundations of which we have already set out. But if a man believes all those foundations and has declared that he believes them, he enters the congregation of Israel, and we are commanded to love him, to show him mercy, and to deal with him in accordance with all that the blessed God has commanded to be done toward a neighbour. But if anyone despises this foundation among the excellent foundations, behold, he goes out of the congregation, since he denies an article of faith, and he is called "impious and an Epicurean", and he is one who cuts down the plants, whom we are commanded to hate and destroy. The same is abundantly clear from Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, who wrote three books on the Resurrection of the Dead. In book 1, chap. 1, he speaks of Rabbi Maimonides' thirteenth article of faith, pp. 1, 2: R. Moses the Egyptian, a man of singular prudence and by far the most learned in many matters, among the thirteen articles of faith also places this article last: that the resurrection of the dead is to be believed by all Israelites; that is, the dead, who have departed this life, whose bodies have been dissolved into dust and ashes after the soul has left them, will return to the light, the same soul being poured back into them, so that they may enjoy a second corporeal life in this world. Since Rabbi Moses, whom all the Hebrew masters support, wishes that all who deny this article, as an essential article of the Israelites' faith, be struck off, I thought it worth while, to confirm this matter, first to adduce those passages from which the ancient sages drew that article, whether by probable or by demonstrative reasoning. Then to set out the arguments drawn from nature itself, and finally to confirm it by experience.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Credunt Resurrectionem mortuorum fundamentum fidei esse magnum, quod venerari firmifirmiter debeant omnes Judæi, tam magni, quam parvi, quodque apud omnes populos maxime fuerit æstimatum perconsequens quod, quiResurrectionem inficiatur, non tantum neget Legem, Prophetas, & Hagiographa, sed simul Deum neget, aliaque omnia quæ reliquis comprehenduntur fidei articulis, uti liquet ex Rabbi Leone Mutinensi in Opusculo de Ceremoniis & Consuetudinibus Judæorum, Part. V. cap. 11. Exanimatos in fine mundi iterum suscitatum iri firmiter credunt, uti etiam inter tredecim articulos fidei sua hunc ipsum de resurrectione numerare solent; Ex Rabbi Isaco Abarbanele in Capite Fidei, cap. 15. En expositum est, hanc fidem extare in Lege, Prophetis, & Hagiographis; Atque idcirco credendum de Resurrectione factum est generale, & est articulus atque fundamentum magnum. Qui autem negat hoc, idem est, ac si negaret Legem, Prophetas, & Hagiographa; Ex Rabbi Machir in Abhkat Rochel, Part. IV. lin. 5: Omnino omnes Judæi, tam magni, quam parvi credere debent Deum Benedictum mortuos vivificaturum, & resuscitaturum, & excitaturum illos ex pulvere illorum, & spiritum illis inditurum, ut antea fuerat; Ex Rabbi Salomo de domo Levi in Chelek Harischon Miscepher Difre Schelomo, sol. 94. col. 4: Ecce autem contrarium invenimus, & videmus, scilicet quod quod hæc fides de resurrectione mortuorum habea-tur pro vera & firma apud omnes populos, & me-moretur creberrime a Prophetis, numeretur inter articulos legis & fundamenta ejus, quam qui ne-gat, perinde facit ac si negaret esse Deum, legem esse e cœlo, & quod in aliis ipsis articulis tractatur; hinc quoque in quotidianis precibus fidem suam de mortuorum resurrectione testantur, acclamantes ad Deum Benedictum : Tu potens in seculum Domine, tu mortuos vivificas, & magnus es ad servandum, uti patet ex libro precum editionis Amstelodamensis, pag. 25.
units.tr: They hold that the resurrection of the dead is a great foundation of faith, which all Jews, great and small alike, ought to revere firmly, and which has been esteemed above all among all peoples. Consequently, whoever denies the resurrection denies not only the Law, the Prophets and the Hagiographa, but also God, and all the other things that are contained in the remaining articles of faith. This is clear from Rabbi Leo of Modena, in his little work on the Ceremonies and Customs of the Jews, Part V, chap. 11: They firmly believe that the dead will be raised again at the end of the world, and therefore they are accustomed to count this very article on the resurrection among the thirteen articles of faith. From Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel, in the Chapter of Faith, chap. 15: It has been set out that this faith is found in the Law, the Prophets and the Hagiographa; and therefore belief in the resurrection has been made a general matter, and it is an article and a great foundation. Whoever denies this is the same as one who would deny the Law, the Prophets and the Hagiographa. From Rabbi Machir in Abhkat Rochel, Part IV, line 5: All Jews, great and small, altogether must believe that the blessed God will make the dead live, and will raise them up and rouse them from their dust, and will breathe into them the spirit as before. From Rabbi Solomon of the house of Levi in Chelek Harischon, Miscepher Difre Schelomo, fol. 94, col. 4: Behold, however, we find and see the contrary, namely that this faith concerning the resurrection of the dead is held to be true and firm among all peoples, is very often recalled by the Prophets, and is numbered among the articles of the Law and its foundations; whoever denies it acts just as if he denied that there is a God, that the Law is from heaven, and the other articles themselves, which are treated there. Hence also in their daily prayers they bear witness to their faith in the resurrection of the dead, crying out to the blessed God: Thou art mighty for ever, O Lord; thou quickenest the dead, and art great to save, as appears from the book of prayers of the Amsterdam edition, p. 25.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Probant Resurrectionem mortuorum auctoritate librorum Mosaicorum, allegantes sæpe illa Legis testimonia, non quod debebant, evincentia; Et primo quidem argumentantur ex Genes. cap. 2. v. 7. Et formavit Dominus Deus; Ubi in vocabula duplex observatur jod, ajentes inter alia duas significari formationes, unam hujus vitæ, alteram sequentis post resurrectionem, uti loquitur Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, lib. I. de Resurr. Mortuorum, cap. 1. pag. 3: Denique ajunt eo designari duas formationes, quæ homini propriæ sunt, unam quam habet in hac vita; alteram quam in sequenti, id est, in resurrectione mortuorum sortietur; Probant המתים תחיית Resurrectionem mortuorum,ex Genef. cap. 3. verf. 19. In sudore narium tuarum comedes panem, donec ad terram revertaris de qua defumtus es: pulvis enim es, in eumq; reverteris; Concludentes, quia scriptum ואל עפר תשוב Et ad pulverem redibis, non vero תהלך ibis, quod manifesta hic in Lege mentio sit de resurrectione mortuorum, uti Rabbi Schimeon Ben Jochai inquit apud Rabbi Ifacum Abarbanelem in Capite Fidei, cap. 15. Atq; in Bereschit Rabba: Pulvis es & in pulverem reverteris, ait Rabbi Simeon filius Jochai: Hinc liquet, de resurrectione mortuorum extare in Lege: In pulverem ibis, non scriptum hic est, sed in pulverem redibis; Quod pariter confirmat Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, cum in Resurrect. Mort. ex Rabbi Schimeone Ben Jochai, ita ratiocinatur lib. I. cap. 1. pag. 4: Verum hoc loco resurrectio mortuorum indicatur: tantundem enim est, ac si legeretur dictum, pulvis nunc es, o Adam, illoq; pulverem iterum induëris, tempore resuscitationis mortuorum: quod necessarium non fuisset, si Adam non peccasset: quia tum aut non fuisset moriturus; aut cum corpore simul atque anima transferendus, uti Hanoch & Elias; Probant Resurrectionem mortuorum, ex Genef. cap. 37. verf. 10. An ego & mater, & fratres tui venturi, te adoratum ; Quasi diceret Jacob Josepho: Rachel jam obiit, Genef. cap. 35. verl. 19. Et tu ais, ego & mater tua? Credens tempus resurrectionis mortuorum jam esse præ foribus, atque idcirco etiam Rachelem, etiamsi in vivis jam esse defiiflet, resuscitatam revertendam, uti ex Jalkut ad hæc verba Jacobi refert RabbiMenasleh lib. 1. de Refur. mort. cap. 1. pag. 5: Pater nostER Jacobus arbitrabatur, jam tum suo tempore resurrectionem mortuorum futuram, ideoque dixit: An ego & mater tua veniemus? Rachel jam obiit, & tu ais, ego & mater tua; Adducunt quin etiam in probationem Resurrectionis mortuorum, Exod. cap. 6. verf. 3: Etiam sta- bilivi fœdus meum cum illis, (scilicet Patriarchis, non autem dici cum vobis; Colligentes, exinde bene patere Patriarchas debere resurgere, quia terra Canaan illis fuerat promissa, ut ibi sepelirentur, & resurgerent; non autem resurrexisse ibi tum temporis, cum terra Canaan Israelitis traderetur; Ergo Patriarchas resurrecturos ibi in posterum, sicuti ex Rabbi Simai probat RabbiMenasleh Ben Israel lib. 1. de Refurrect. Mort. c. 1. p. 6,7: R. Simai in Perek Helek, evidentissime demonstrat fore resurrectionem mortuorum, ex verbis Exodi 6. 3. quibus Deus (Mosem alloquens, ait: Apparui AbraAbrahamo, Isaca, & Jacobo, in Deo omnipotente, sed nomen meum. A. non feci illis notum: niholominus tamen interposito fœdere promisi, me daturum illis terram Canaan, in qua peregrini fuere. Dicit ad hæc verba Auctor לאת לכם לא נאמר אלא להם מכאן לתחית המתים מן התורה (Non dicitur in textu ut dem vobis, sed ut dem illis; unde ex Lege manifesta fit resurrectio mortuorum) Probatio lu-culenta hæc est, quia Dominus Deus non dicit Mosi se jurasse futurum ut stabiliret pactum suum cum Patriarchis initum, dando terram promissam possi-dendam Patriarcharum filiis, sed dando eam ipsis Patriarchis: uti ex 17. Cap. Gen. videre est, ubi Deus cum Abrahamo loquens ait, dabo tibi, & semini tuo post te, terram peregrinationis tuæ. Atqui constat Abrahamum, & reliquos Patriarchas eam terram non possedisse: necesse ergo est, ut resuscitentur, quo bonis promissis fruantur; alioqui promissa Dei irrita & falsa forent. Hinc itaque non tantum animæ immortalitas probatur; sed etiam essentiale fundamentum legis, Resurrectio scilicet mortuorum; Adducunt Exod. cap. 15. verf. 1. אז ישיר משה Tunc canet Mose; Non autem dici cecinit in præterito, cum non solum adsit futurum, sed particula quoque אז futurum respiciat tempus; Sensum ergo esse, cantaturum illum impofterum, sicut cecinit tunc. Sed tunc canebat canticum de salute & liberatione populi Ifraelitici; Ergo & in Resurrectione hujusmodi canticum canet, sicuti testatur Rabbi Mehir apud Rabbi MenassenBen Israel, lib.1. de refurrect. mort, cap.1. pag.7: R. Mehir idem quoque astruit ex cantico (Mosis) quod cecinit, cum mare Erythræum transisset: משה ישיר אז Ad quæ verba annotavit שיר לא נאמר אלא ישיר מבאן לתחית המתים מן התורה Non dicit cantavit, sed cantabit deinceps, scil. ex hoc loco legis apparet sore resurrectionem mortuorum.
units.tr: They prove the resurrection of the dead from the authority of the books of Moses, often citing those passages of the Law which do not prove it as they ought. First, they argue from Genesis 2:7, And the Lord God formed, where they note a double yod in the word. They say this signifies, among other things, two formations: one of this life, and another of the life to come after the resurrection, as Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel says in book I, On the Resurrection of the Dead, chapter 1, page 3: Finally, they say that two formations are thereby designated, which belong to man: one which he has in this life; the other which he will receive in the next, that is, in the resurrection of the dead. They prove the resurrection of the dead [תחיית המתים] from Genesis 3:19, In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, until you return to the ground from which you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return. They conclude that since it is written, And to dust you shall return [ואל עפר תשוב], and not you shall go [תהלך], there is here in the Law a plain mention of the resurrection of the dead, as Rabbi Simeon ben Yochai says, quoted by Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel in the Book of Principles, chapter 15: And in Bereshit Rabbah, Rabbi Simeon son of Yochai says: Dust you are, and to dust you shall return. Hence it is clear that the resurrection of the dead is found in the Law: "you shall go to dust" is not written here, but "you shall return to dust." Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel likewise confirms this, reasoning from Rabbi Simeon ben Yochai in his work On the Resurrection of the Dead, book I, chapter 1, page 4: But in this place the resurrection of the dead is indicated; for it amounts to the same as if it were said: "Dust you now are, O Adam, and into dust you will be turned again at the time of the resurrection of the dead." This would not have been necessary had Adam not sinned; for then either he would not have been destined to die, or he would have been translated with body and soul together, as Enoch and Elijah were. They prove the resurrection of the dead from Genesis 37:10, Shall I and your mother and your brothers come to bow down to you? As if Jacob were saying to Joseph: "Rachel has already died (Genesis 35:19), and do you say, I and your mother?" Believing that the time of the resurrection of the dead was already at the doors, and that therefore Rachel too, although she had ceased to be among the living, would be restored and return; as Rabbi Menasseh reports from the Jalkut on these words of Jacob, in book I, On the Resurrection of the Dead, chapter 1, page 5: "Our father Jacob thought that the resurrection of the dead would come in his own time, and therefore said: Shall I and your mother come? Rachel has already died, and you say, I and your mother." They also adduce, in proof of the resurrection of the dead, Exodus 6:3: And I also established my covenant with them (that is, with the patriarchs, not said with you). They gather from this that it is plainly evident that the patriarchs must rise again, because the land of Canaan had been promised to them, that they might be buried there and rise there; and that they did not rise there at that time, when the land of Canaan was delivered to the Israelites. Therefore the patriarchs will rise there in the future, as Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel proves from Rabbi Simai in book I, On the Resurrection of the Dead, chapter 1, pages 6–7: "Rabbi Simai, in Perek Helek, most clearly demonstrates that there will be a resurrection of the dead from the words of Exodus 6:3, in which God, addressing Moses, says: I appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as God Almighty, but my name Jehovah I did not make known to them; nevertheless, by an interposed covenant I promised to give them the land of Canaan, in which they were sojourners." The author adds on these words: לאת לכם לא נאמר אלא להם מכאן לתחית המתים מן התורה (It is not said in the text, "that I may give it to you," but "that I may give it to them"; hence from the Law the resurrection of the dead becomes plain). This proof is an excellent one, because the Lord God does not tell Moses that he had sworn to fulfil his covenant made with the patriarchs by giving the promised land to be possessed by the sons of the patriarchs, but by giving it to the patriarchs themselves; as can be seen from Genesis chapter 17, where God, speaking with Abraham, says: I will give to you and to your seed after you the land of your sojourning. But it is certain that Abraham and the other patriarchs did not possess that land; it is therefore necessary that they be raised, so that they may enjoy the good things promised; otherwise the promises of God would be void and false. Hence not only the immortality of the soul is proved, but also the essential foundation of the Law, namely the resurrection of the dead. They also adduce Exodus 15:1: אז ישיר משה Then Moses will sing; not, it is said, sang in the past tense, since the future is not only present but the particle אז also refers to future time. The sense, therefore, is that he will sing in future, just as he sang then. But then he sang a song about the salvation and deliverance of the Israelite people; therefore in the resurrection he will sing a song of this kind as well, as Rabbi Mehir attests, cited by Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel in book I, On the Resurrection of the Dead, chapter 1, page 7: Rabbi Mehir also asserts the same from the song (of Moses) which he sang when he had crossed the Red Sea: משה ישיר אז. On these words he annotated: שיר לא נאמר אלא ישיר מבאן לתחית המתים מן התורה. It is not said "he sang," but "he will sing" henceforth; that is, from this passage of the Law it appears that there will be a resurrection of the dead.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Probant Resurrectionem Mortuorum ex reliquis Legis Mosaicæ testimoniis, allegantes Levit. cap.25. vers.10: Jubilæus vobis erit, & singulí ad possessiones vestras redibitis, & unusquisque ad cognationem revertetur; Quibus significetur verbis, cum in hoc seculo non detur reditus ad familiam, quod illud necesse in altero debeat fieri seculo, uti ex Rabbi Josua Ben Levi infert Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, lib.1. de Resurrect. Mort. cap.1. pag.8: Ubiper Jubilæum indicari ait, resurrectionem mortuorum: tum enim unusquisque redibit ad cognationem, & cognoscet genus & stirpem suam; Sic probant ulterius ex Numeror.cap.18. vers.28. Dabitis portionem Domini Sacerdoti Aaroni, non vero dabitis decimas vestras Sacerdotibus, autse-mini mini Aaronis ; Ex quo concludunt, quod, cum Aaron non perpetuo vixerit, ita ut Israelitæ decimas illi offerre potuerint, eo ipso quam clare innuatur, Aaronem revicturum, sicuti cum Rabbi Jochannan deducit Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, lib. cit. cap. 1. pag. 9: At expressis verbis dicit, dabitis Aaroni. Ex quo consequitur venturum esse tempus aliquod, in quo tota Lex, & hoc etiam, quo ipsi Aaroni decimæ offerantur, adimpleatur: at illud erit, cum mortui resuscitabuntur; Ita ex Deuteron. cap. 4. verf. 4: Et vos adhærentes in Domino Deo vestro, vivitis vos omnes hodie; Ex quo inferatur, cum sermo non tantum sit de illis, qui tum vivebant, nihil enim opus fuisset dicere quod viverent, sed de omnibus universis, ex quibus jam multi obierant, quod in leculo victuri sint futuro, uti cum R. Gamliel concludit Rabbi Menasseh, loc. cit. pag. 10: Et quamquam multi ex iis diem suum obierant: nihilominus tamen vivebant; quia anima ipsæ remanebat futurum uti aliquando iterum idem numero corpus informaret; Ex Deuteron. cap. 6. verf. 24: Ut bene sit nobis omnibus diebus, ut nos vivificet sicut hodie, apud Rabbi Machir in Abhkat Rochel, part. iv. lin. 7. Ex Deuteron. cap. 11. verf. 9. Nam multiplicabuntur dies vestri, & filiorum supra terram, quam juravit Dominus patribus se daturum illis; Ex quibus sequatur tur, quod, cum dicatur illis, non vobis, mortuorum indigitent relurrectionem, ex Rabbi Gamliel apud Rabbi Menaflen loc. cit. p. 10. Sic quoque ex Deuteron. cap 32. verf. 39: Videte quod ego, ego ipse, & non Deus mecum, ego occido, & ego vita restituo, ego percutio, & ego sano; Ex quibus demonstrat Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, libr. cit. pag. 12: Ex eo igitur, quod Deus dicat se primo occidere, & deinde vitam restituere; & primo vulnus infligere, & deinde mederi; patet dari resurrectionem mortuorum; De hac resurrectionis probatione affirmat Rabbi Hac Abarbanel, quod illa validissima in Lege sit Mosaica, uti patet ex Capite Fidei, cap. 15. Et quod probabilior sit longe reliquis omnibus, ex Rabbi Menasseh libr. cit. pag. 11; Tandem ex Lege adducunt Deuteron. cap. 33. verf. 6. Vivet Ruben, & non morietur; De quo sic Rabbi Menasseh, libr. cit. pag. 11: Quod non est de hac vita intelligendum, quia Ruben ex ea discesserit: sed de futura. Cum enim Rubenem peccatorum poenituisset, anima ejus non perpetuo exilio multanda erat, sed die resurrectionis revocanda ad uniendum sibi corpus: idcirco dicitur מִכָּאן לְחַיִּית הַמֵּתִים מִן הַתּוֹרָה Liquet igitur ex lege fore resurrectionem mortuorum.
units.tr: They prove the resurrection of the dead from other testimonies of the Law of Moses, citing Lev. 25.10: It shall be a jubilee to you, and each of you shall return to his possession, and each shall return to his kindred. By these words, they say, it is signified that since there is no return to one's family in this age, this must happen in another age. So Rabbi Joshua ben Levi infers, as cited by Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, book 1 On the Resurrection of the Dead, ch. 1, p. 8: Where he says that the Jubilee indicates the resurrection of the dead: for then each will return to his kindred, and will know his family and stock. They prove it further from Num. 18.28: You shall give the Lord's portion to Aaron the priest, not indeed give your tithes to the priests, but to the seed of Aaron. From this they conclude that, since Aaron did not live forever, so that the Israelites could offer him tithes, it is clearly hinted that Aaron will live again. So Rabbi Johanan draws it, as cited by Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, loc. cit., ch. 1, p. 9: But he says in express words, you shall give to Aaron. From this it follows that there will be some time in which the whole Law, and this very thing, that tithes are offered to Aaron himself, is fulfilled; and that will be when the dead are raised. Likewise from Deut. 4.4: And you who cleave to the Lord your God are alive, all of you, today. From this it is inferred that since the speech is not only about those who were then living (for there would have been no need to say that they were alive), but about all of them, many of whom had already died, they will live in a future age. So Rabbi Gamliel concludes, as Rabbi Menasseh cites, loc. cit., p. 10: And although many of them had finished their day, nevertheless they were still living, because the souls remained, so that at some time the same body in number would again take shape. From Deut. 6.24: That it may be well with us all days, that he may keep us alive, as at this day, as cited from Rabbi Machir in Abhkat Rochel, part 4, line 7. From Deut. 11.9: For your days shall be multiplied, and the days of your children, upon the land which the Lord swore to your fathers that he would give them. From these it follows that, since it is said to them, and not to you, they point to the resurrection of the dead, according to Rabbi Gamliel, as cited by Rabbi Menasseh, loc. cit., p. 10. Likewise from Deut. 32.39: See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god with me: I kill, and I make alive; I wound, and I heal. From these Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel demonstrates, in the book cited, p. 12: From the fact, then, that God says he first kills and then restores life, and first inflicts a wound and then heals, it is evident that there is a resurrection of the dead. Concerning this proof of the resurrection, Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel affirms that it is most powerful in the Mosaic Law, as is clear from the Chapter of Faith, ch. 15; and that it is far more probable than all the rest, according to Rabbi Menasseh, book cited, p. 11. Finally from the Law they cite Deut. 33.6: Let Reuben live, and not die. Of this Rabbi Menasseh says, book cited, p. 11: This is not to be understood of this life, as if Reuben had departed from it; but of the future. For since Reuben had repented of his sins, his soul was not to be punished with perpetual exile, but was to be recalled on the day of resurrection to be joined again to his body; therefore it is said [מִכָּאן לְחַיִּית הַמֵּתִים מִן הַתּוֹרָה]. It is clear, therefore, that the resurrection of the dead will come from the Law.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Demonstrant Resurrectionem mortuorum rum ex vaticiniis Prophetarum Veteris Testamenti, allegantes Iof. cap. 8. verf. 30: Tunc exstruet Iofua altare; Ex quo inferunt cum non dicatur exstruxit, sed in futuro, exstruet, necessario sequatur, Iosuam etiam impositerum altare exstructurum esse, ieu, Israelem impositerum Iosuae adhaesurum ita esse, sicut adhaerebat ei, cum exstrueret altare; Adducentes Prophetiliae, & sapientissimae mulieris Channae verba, quae leguntur in Cantico, 1. Samuel. cap. 2. verf. 6. Iehova morte afficit, & in vitam reducit; demittit in sepulchrum, & educit; De quibus sic pronunciat R. Menasseh Ben Israel libr. 1. de Resurr. Mort. cap. 2. pag. 14. Quibus verbis haud obscure innuit prudens femina resurrectionem mortuorum; Sicingens hoc miraculum probant ex Esai. cap. 26. verf. 19. Reviviscent mortui tui, cadavera mea resurgent: expergiscimini, & cantate, qui habitatis in pulvere, quia ros lucis, ros tuus, & terra eiiciet mortuos, Utipatet post Rabbi Iacum Abarbanelem in Capite Fidei, cap. 15. Ex Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel libr. 1. de Resurrect. Mort. cap. 2. pag. 15, 16. Cum admiratione quaerit (Propheta) annon mortui resuscitabuntur? cum colliget Dominus captivos, annon videbunt ejus salutem? Huic respondetur, annon credis Prophetam illud eventurum, quod ante dixisti, nimirum mortuos resurrecturos esse, id est, eos ex populo meo qui naturali morte defuncti sunt; quodsq; cadavera mea resuscitabuntur, id est, illi qui pro gloria nominis mei & mea religionis ergo perempti sunt: nam idcirco additur emphatice pronomen mea cadavera. Cum autem ait, expergiscimi, & cantate inhabitantes pulverem, mortuos designat, qui morte tanquam somno quodam opprimebantur, quando Dominum Deum Servatorem suum hymnis celebrabant. Cum vero dicit, ros lucis, ros tuus, & terra ejiciet defunctos, innuere vult Propheta, quod tempore resurrectionis e coelo ros decidet, qui instar feminis virilis, immisscentis sese mulieris sanguini menstruo, commisscebit sese pulveri terrae, apte & idonee praeparato, & deinde ea e sinu suo producet (uti in Creatione Adami accidit) corpora defunctorum; Probant ex eodem Esaia, cap.26. vers.8. Vocem Speculatores tui attollent, pariter cantabunt; Quasi diceret Propheta: Omnes expergefacti & resuscitati de terra, voce una Deo canticum sunt dicturi, parati sunt omnes Prophetae ut in diebus Messiae unanimi canant voce, uti liquet ex Rabbi Molche de Trana, in Beth Elohim, sol. 108. col. 1: Postquam conjuncti & conniti fuerunt Prophetae in praecepto, puta in increpandis impiis, conveniens est, ut uniantur etiam in futurum, & canant simul, quod evenerint, quae praedixerant; Et ex Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, libr.1. de Resurr. furr. Mort. cap. 2. pag. 18: Pariter cantabunt, tempore futuro, non autem praeterito. Itaque appâret ex lege futuram aliquando resurrectionem mortuorum; Deniq; demonstrat Resurrectionem Mortuorum ex Ezech. cap. 37. Ecce ego aperiens vestra sepulchra, educam vos e vestris sepulchris populem meum, & reducam vos in terram Israelis, ut sciatis me Dominum esse, aperiente me sepulchra vestra, & educente vos, populemi, ex vestris sepulchris. Et indam spiritum meum vobis ut reviviscatis, & collocabo vos in terra vestra, ut cognoscatis me Dominum dicere, & facere, dictum Domini; Ex quibus sic concludit Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, libr. 1. de Resurr. Mort. cap. 2. p. 18. Textus hic expressus & omni exceptione major est pro resurrectione mortuorum; Tandem ex Malach. cap. 4. verf 1. 5. 6: Nam ecce dies ille adveniet ardens, tanquam fornax &c. Ecce ego mittam vobis Eliam Prophetam antequam veniat magnus ac tremendus dies Domini, ut convertat cor patrum ad filios, & cor filiorum ad patres ipsorum; Inferentes inde Prophetam loqui de die resurrectionis & judicii, tum resurrectionem per Eliam futuram, & in resurrectione patres filiis, & contra enarraturos quicquid obvenerit in separatione animae, uti testatur Rabbi Isac Abarbanel in Capite Fidei, cap. 15: Quia nimirum resuscitatio fiet per manus Eliae, qui cor corpore ac anima vivit. Quia autem in resurrectione patres filiis, ac filii patribus indicabunt, quidnam illis in separatione animae eorum a corpore acciderit, hinc ait: Ut convertat corda patrum ad filios.
units.tr: They demonstrate the resurrection of the dead from the prophecies of the Old Testament, citing Josh. 8.30: Then Joshua shall build an altar. From this they infer that, since it is not said he built, but in the future, he shall build, it necessarily follows that Joshua will also build an altar in the future; that is, that Israel will in future cleave to Joshua just as it cleaved to him when he built the altar. They adduce also the words of the prophetess and most wise woman Hannah, read in the Song, 1 Sam. 2.6: The Lord kills and makes alive; he brings down to the grave and brings up. Of these words Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel says, book 1 On the Resurrection of the Dead, ch. 2, p. 14: In these words the wise woman hints, not obscurely, at the resurrection of the dead. Likewise they prove this miracle from Isa. 26.19: Your dead shall live, my dead bodies shall rise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust, for your dew is the dew of light, and the earth shall cast out the dead. So it is shown, after Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel, in the Chapter of Faith, ch. 15; from Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, book 1 On the Resurrection of the Dead, ch. 2, pp. 15, 16: The prophet asks with wonder: will the dead be raised? When the Lord shall gather the captives, will they not see his salvation? To this it is answered: do you not believe that the prophet will bring about what you said before, namely that the dead will rise, that is, those of my people who have died a natural death; and that my dead bodies will be raised, that is, those who have been slain for the glory of my name and my religion; for that is why the pronoun "my dead bodies" is added emphatically. But when he says, Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust, he designates the dead, who were overcome by death as by a kind of sleep, when they celebrated the Lord God their Saviour with hymns. And when he says, your dew is the dew of light, and the earth shall cast out the dead, the prophet wishes to indicate that at the time of the resurrection a dew will fall from heaven, which, like the male seed mingling with the menstrual blood of a woman, will mix itself with the dust of the earth, fittingly and suitably prepared, and then will bring forth from its bosom the bodies of the dead (as happened in the creation of Adam). They prove it from the same Isaiah, ch. 26, v. 8: Your watchmen shall lift up their voice, together they shall sing. As if the prophet said: all, awakened and raised from the earth, are about to sing a song to God with one voice; all the prophets are ready to sing with one accord in the days of the Messiah, as is clear from Rabbi Moses de Trani, in Beth Elohim, fol. 108, col. 1: After the prophets have been joined and united in a command, namely in rebuking the wicked, it is fitting that they be united also in the future and sing together that what they foretold has come to pass. And from Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, book 1 On the Resurrection of the Dead, ch. 2, p. 18: They shall sing together in the future time, not in the past. Therefore it appears from the Law that there will at some time be a resurrection of the dead. Lastly they demonstrate the resurrection of the dead from Ezek. 37: Behold, I will open your graves, and bring you up out of your graves, O my people, and bring you into the land of Israel; that you may know that I am the Lord, when I open your graves and bring you up out of your graves, O my people. And I will put my spirit in you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land; and you shall know that I the Lord have spoken and done it, says the Lord. From these words Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel concludes thus, book 1 On the Resurrection of the Dead, ch. 2, p. 18: This text, plainly stated, and greater than any exception, is for the resurrection of the dead. Finally from Mal. 4.1, 5, 6: For behold, the day comes, burning like a furnace, etc. Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and dreadful day of the Lord comes, that he may turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers. From this they infer that the prophet speaks of the day of resurrection and judgment, and that the resurrection will come through Elijah; and that in the resurrection fathers will tell their children, and children their fathers, whatever befell them in the separation of the soul, as Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel attests in the Chapter of Faith, ch. 15: Because the resurrection will surely be effected by the hands of Elijah, who lives in heart, body and soul. And because in the resurrection fathers will show their children, and children their fathers, what happened to them in the separation of their souls from the body, therefore he says: to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Comprobant Articulum de Resurrectione Mortuorum ex Hagiographis Veteris Testamenti, maxime ex Psalmo 72, verl. 16. Florebunt de civitate, sicut herba terrae; Uti patet ex Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, libr. 1. de Resurrect. Mortuor. cap. 3. pag. 20: Qua phrasi fieri non potest, ut intelligantur alii quam resuscitati a mortuis, qui instar herbae ex terrae gremio efflorescent; Ex Psalm. 104. verl. 29,30. Colliges spiritum eorum; exspirabunt, & in pulverem suum revertentur. Emittes spiritum tuum, creabuntur, & innovabis faciem terrae; Ex quibus ita Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, libr. 1. de Resurrect. Mort. cap. 3. pag. 21: Si igitur postquam spiritus collectus est a Deo, & corpus in pulverem redactum, altera vice spiritus rediturus est in corpus, & facies terrae nova futura: quis non videt hoc in resurrectione mortuorum eventurum esse? Sic ex Danielis cap. 12, verl. 2. Tandemque multi ex dormientibus in pulverulenta terra expergiscentur, hi ad vitam aeternam, illi ad opprobria & contemtum aeternum; Uti rursus liquet ex Rabbi Menasseh libr. cit.
units.tr: They confirm the article on the resurrection of the dead from the Hagiographa of the Old Testament, chiefly from Psalm 72:16: They shall flourish out of the city like the grass of the earth. As is clear from Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, De Resurrectione Mortuorum, book 1, chapter 3, page 20: By such a phrase it cannot be understood otherwise than of those raised from the dead, who sprout like grass from the bosom of the earth. From Psalm 104:29-30: Thou takest away their breath, they die, and return to their dust. Thou sendest forth thy Spirit, they are created, and thou renewest the face of the earth. On which Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, book 1, De Resurrectione Mortuorum, chapter 3, page 21, says: If, therefore, after the spirit has been gathered by God and the body reduced to dust, the spirit is to return to the body a second time and the face of the earth is to be made new, who does not see that this will happen in the resurrection of the dead? Likewise from Daniel 12:2: And many of those who sleep in the dusty earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, others to everlasting shame and contempt. As again appears from Rabbi Menasseh, the book cited,

units.la: pag. 22: Satis perspicue hinc constat, omnes, qui mortui sunt, resurrecturos esse, alii, ut praemium & gloriam consequantur, alii, ut perpetuo puniantur.
units.tr: page 22: It is quite plainly established from this that all who have died will rise again, some to obtain reward and glory, others to be punished forever.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Probant Articulum de Resurrectione mortuorum ex ipsa ratione, quod amice cum ratione conspiret, eique sit consentanea, non involvat ullam contradictionem, aut repugnantiam, uti testatur Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, libr. 1. de resurrect. Mort. cap. 4. pag. 26: Cum enim qui secum cogitat Deum esse Autorem, Dominumque naturae, ac proinde eum pro arbitrio suo posse naturam intendere, extendere, contrahere, ac mutare; facile is etiam credet, quod Deus aliquem sine cibo vivum conservare, & mortuum in vita revocare possit; Ratiocinantes cum Rabbi Gebia, Ben Pesissa: Si illud quod non fuit, existit, quanto magis id restituetur quod aliquando fuit; Sic illustrant resurrectionem mortuorum, petitis similitudinibus a figulo, vitro, Rege palatium exstruente, mure, limace, ex Tractatu Talmudico Sanhedrin, cap. 11. sol. 91. Et apud Rabbi Menassen Ben Israel, libr. cit. cap. 4. Tandem demonstrant resurrectionem mortuorum ipsa experientia, referentes de Elia, quod resuscitaverit filium foeminae Sareptanae; De Elisaeo, qui Sunamitica filium in vitam revocaverit; Et de Ezechiele, quod mortuos istius vallis vitæ restituerit; Imo probant ex exemplo Jonæ, quod multis facit Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, libr. 1. de resurrect. mort. cap. 5. notans interalia, quod hæc divinorum Cabaliftarum sit mens, cum pag. 34. sic loquitur: Sed addamus huic, quo- modo divini Cabalistæ, ex historia Jonæ, sensu alle- gorico probent resurrectionem mortuorum.
units.tr: They prove the article on the resurrection of the dead from reason itself, since it agrees well with reason, is consistent with it, and involves no contradiction or repugnance. So Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel testifies, De Resurrectione Mortuorum, book 1, chapter 4, page 26: For whoever considers that God is the Author and Lord of nature, and so can at his pleasure extend, contract and change nature, will easily believe also that God can keep someone alive without food and recall the dead to life. Reasoning with Rabbi Gebia ben Pesissa: if that which was not comes into being, how much more will that be restored which once was. So they illustrate the resurrection of the dead by similitudes taken from the potter, the glass-maker, the king building a palace, the mouse, and the snail, from the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin, chapter 11, folio 91, and in Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, the book cited, chapter 4. Finally, they demonstrate the resurrection of the dead by experience itself, relating that Elijah raised the son of the widow of Zarephath; that Elisha recalled to life the son of the Shunammite woman; and that Ezekiel restored to life the dead of that valley. Indeed they prove it from the example of Jonah, which Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel does at length, book 1, De Resurrectione Mortuorum, chapter 5, noting among other things that this is the mind of the divine Cabalists, when on page 34 he speaks thus: But let us add to this how the divine Cabalists, from the history of Jonah, prove the resurrection of the dead by an allegorical sense.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Tribuunt resurrectionem mortuorum soli Deo Benedicto, qui unicus potens sit opus hoc maximum perficere, quod non solum patet ex Judæorum precibus quotidianis, in quibus sic loquuntur: Tu potens in seculum Domine, tu mortuos vivificas, & magnus es ad servandum; Et ex Catechesi Judaica, Quæst. 12. Quod tempus illud resurrectionis mortuorum sit fixum, solique Deo notum; Verum illud quoque clarum sit ex innumeris Scripturæ locis, uti probat Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, libr. II. de resurrect. mort. cap. 1. p. 139: Cæterum miraculi hujus, de quo agimus, non alia causa efficiens erit, quam supremum Numen: uti dif- ferte illud innuit Moses in Deut. 32. 39. Videte nunc, quod ego, ego sum, & non sunt dij mecum. Quasi diceret, videte nunc, quod ego, ego sum ille, qui illa facio sine alterius alicujus Numinis, aut causa natu- ralis adminiculo, ego morifacio, & ad vitam revoco; scilicet in resurrectione mortuorum: verba enim haec ultima ad resurrectionem pertinent, uti superiore libro diximus. Hanna in eandem quoque sententiam dicit, 1.Sam.2.6. Dominus mortificat, & vivificat, descendere facit ad inferos, & ascendere facit. Ezechiel 37.13. Et scietis quod ego Dominus, cum aperuero sepulchro vestra, & eduxero vos e tumulis vestris populus mi; Imo patet ex Tractatu Talmudico Sanhedrin, sol.113. Ex Tractatu Talmud. Taanith cap.8. Quod inter solius Dei reservata sit resuscitare mortuos, cum dicunt: Tres claves sunt in manu Dei Benedicti, quae non sunt traditae ulli legato, scilicet vitae, pluviae & resurrectionis mortuorum; Cui egregie adstipulatur Rabbi Ifac Abarbanel, quando in Praefatione ad Esaiam, rad.3. sic inquit: Ecce Propheta Esaias Dei arcanis admissus, explicat resurrectionem se habituram valde mirabiliter, & causam efficientem ejus fore Deum Benedictum, non vero sidera, dum ait in prophetia 20 (cap.24.verf.22.) Et erit tempore illo, animadvertet Jehova in exercitum excelsum &c. ut colligantur colletti &c. (ibid. verf.22.) Et pudebit ipsam lunam, & erubescet sol, cum regnabit Jehova exercituum in monte Tzionis & Hierosolymis. Propterea vocatur tempus resurrectionis mortuorum dies Domini, quia illa fiet per miraculum; Respondent quin etiam ad notam objectionem, quod Elias & Elisaeus mormortuos resuscitaverint, per conlequens re-surrectio mortuorum foli Deo non fit propria; Referentes, quod licet Elias & Elifæus excita-verint mortuos, non tamen propterea existi-mandum fit, eos tanti miraculi fuisse autho-res, cum Deus Benedictus ad illorum effusas preces, ipsam patraverit mortuorum refurre-ctionem, uti de Elia & Elifæo testatur Rabbi Menasseh Benlsrael lib. II. de refurrect. mort. cap. I. pag. 142: Nam etiamsi alia miracula, absq; prævius precibus edere facile possint: nibilominus tamen ad resuscitandum mortuos, sese impotentes esse videbant: ideo precibus confugiebant ad Deum, qui solus tanti miraculi est autor & causa efficiens. Et ratio in promptu est.
units.tr: They ascribe the resurrection of the dead to God alone, the Blessed One, who alone is able to accomplish this greatest work. This is clear not only from the daily prayers of the Jews, in which they speak thus: Thou art mighty forever, O Lord; thou quickenest the dead, and art great to save; and from the Jewish Catechism, question 12, that the time of the resurrection of the dead is fixed and known to God alone. But this is also plain from countless places of Scripture, as Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel proves, De Resurrectione Mortuorum, book 2, chapter 1, page 139: Moreover, the efficient cause of this miracle of which we speak will be no other than the supreme Deity, as Moses hints in Deuteronomy 32:39 when he says so pointedly: See now that I, I am he, and there are no gods with me. As if he said: see now that I, I am he who does these things without the aid of any other deity or natural cause; I kill, and I make alive; namely, in the resurrection of the dead, for these last words pertain to the resurrection, as we said in the previous book. Hannah, too, says to the same effect, 1 Samuel 2:6: The Lord kills and makes alive, brings down to the grave and brings up. Ezekiel 37:13: And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I have opened your graves and brought you up from your tombs, my people. Indeed it is evident from the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin, folio 113, and from the Talmudic tractate Taanith, chapter 8, that among the things reserved to God alone is raising the dead, when they say: There are three keys in the hand of the Blessed God which have not been entrusted to any messenger: the keys of life, of rain, and of the resurrection of the dead. Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel agrees with this admirably, when in his preface to Isaiah, root 3, he says: Behold, the prophet Isaiah, admitted to God's secrets, explains that the resurrection will come about most wonderfully, and that its efficient cause will be the Blessed God and not the stars, when he says in the prophecy at 20 (chapter 24, verse 22): And it shall be in that time that Jehovah will visit the high host... that they may be gathered together, etc. (ibid., verse 22): And the moon shall be ashamed, and the sun confounded, when Jehovah of hosts shall reign in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem. For this reason the time of the resurrection of the dead is called the day of the Lord, because it will be done by miracle. They also answer the familiar objection, that Elijah and Elisha raised the dead, and consequently the resurrection of the dead is not proper to God alone, by saying that although Elijah and Elisha raised the dead, it is not therefore to be thought that they were the authors of so great a miracle, since the Blessed God himself, in response to their outpoured prayers, brought about the resurrection of the dead. So Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel testifies of Elijah and Elisha, book 2, De Resurrectione Mortuorum, chapter 1, page 142: For although they could easily perform other miracles without prior prayers, nevertheless, when it came to raising the dead, they saw themselves as powerless; therefore they fled to prayer, to God, who alone is the author and efficient cause of so great a miracle. And the reason is at hand.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Credunt communi fere mente, idem numero corpus, quod in hac habuerunt vita, re-surrecturum, negantes novum reproducen-dum corpus, vel ex materia cœlesti, vel ex materia alia aëria, subtilique, quod eadem quantitate, qualitate, ac temperie prædituin, prioriique forma atque figura parsit, uti testatur Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, libr. II. de resurr. mortuor. cap. 15. pag. 198: Varia sunt opiniones de corporibus, quibus inducentur resuscitati: multi enim arbitrantur ea longe alia, atq; à prioribus diversa fore, scilicet aëria, subtilia, & agilia, aliquantum. tant ea similia futura coelestibus & angelicis corporibus: verum meo judicio opiniones illæ non sunt assis faciendæ, neque admittendæ: nam resurrectio nihil aliud est, quam ejusdem corporis cum eadem anima conjunctio, in eadem forma ac figura, ac proinde vocatur (תחיית) id est, nova vita, quia hæc resurrectioni propria est. Quare ex communi Hebræorum dicimus resurrectionem fore, quoad idem numero corpus easdemque numero qualitates; Abunde quoque patet illud ex R. Meir Ben Gabbay in Afodat Haccodefch, sol.52. col.4. Quod Deus Benedictus vivificaturus sit mortuos, & excitaturus eos ex pulvere illorum, ita ut illud ipsum corpus, quod fuerat mortuum, surgat, & pateat manifeste esse revera vivificationem mortuorum, non novam creationem, ut fuerat creatio prima; Et ex Rabbi Chaja apud eundem Rabbi Meir in Afodat Haccodefch, sol.53.col.1. Non aliud, sed illud ipsum corpus, quod fuit, resurget, sic ut scriptum est: mortui tui vivent (Esai. cap.26. verf.19.) non scriptum est: creabuntur, ut essent sensus illos creatum iri; sed יחיו vituros esse; Et ex Rabbi Machir in Abhkat Rochel, part.iv. cum contrariam refellit sententiam: Ecce ille non erit ipse, qui moriebatur, sed alium conderet Deus Benedictus ad exemplar prioris demortui, & hæc nova structura esset, quam produceret; Noli cogitare, quod alius sit homo ita fabricatus, sed illum ipsum ipsum resuscitabit & exstruet ex priori materia; Sic pariter Rabbi Ioseph Albo, Fundamentorum libr. iv. sol. 146. contra Rabbi Aaronem hanc tuetur sententiam, afferens, si Deus Benedictus tempore resurrectionis de novo fabricaret aliud corpus, quod tum non futura fit resurrectio mortuorum, sed potius dicenda nova foret creatio; imo non in contraria opinione est Rabbi Saadia Gaon, uti clare liquet ex testimonio Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, libr. II. de resurr. mortuorum, cap. 15. pag. 201: R. Sehadya Gaon conatus huic difficultati occurrere, hac ratione, quod corporis humani natura, vel casu extincti, elementa non mutentur, neque misceantur aliis corporibus seu universalibus elementis: sed quod signata, ac distincta maneant ad uniendum se, & componendum rursus idem numero corpus: corpora vero humana de novo partibus elementaribus semper fiant. Illæ autem partes servantur eo fine, ut in resurrectione mortuorum, idem corpus constituant; & quamvis separatæ, longe à se mutuo sejunctæ sint: nihilominus tamen potentia divina facile conjungi ac copulari iterum possunt. Idem sentit quoque R. Samuel Japhe.
units.tr: Almost everyone holds, by common consent, that the same body in number which they had in this life will rise again. They deny that a new body is to be produced, either from heavenly matter or from some other airy, subtle matter, endowed with the same quantity, quality and temperament and given a different form and figure. So Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel testifies, book II, On the Resurrection of the Dead, ch. 15, p. 198: There are various opinions about the bodies with which the raised will be clothed. For many think they will be quite different from the former ones, namely airy, subtle and somewhat agile, and so like heavenly and angelic bodies. But in my judgment those opinions are not to be taken seriously or admitted. For resurrection is nothing other than the reunion of the same body with the same soul, in the same form and figure, and for this reason it is called (tehiyat) [תחיית], that is, new life, since this belongs properly to resurrection. Hence, following the common view of the Hebrews, we say that the resurrection will be of the same body in number and with the same qualities in number. This is also abundantly clear from R. Meir Ben Gabbay in Afodat Haccodesh, fol. 52, col. 4: that the Blessed God will quicken the dead and raise them from their dust, so that that very body which had died rises again; and it is plainly evident that this is truly a quickening of the dead, not a new creation such as the first creation was. And from Rabbi Chaja, cited by the same R. Meir in Afodat Haccodesh, fol. 53, col. 1: Not another, but that very body which was will rise again, as it is written, "Your dead shall live" (Isa. 26:19). It is not written "they shall be created," as though they would be made into new senseless beings; but that they shall live [יחיו]. And from Rabbi Machir in Abhkat Rochel, part iv, where he refutes the contrary opinion: Behold, it will not be the same man who died; rather the Blessed God will form another, after the pattern of the one who died, and this would be a new structure which he would produce. Do not think that another man is so fashioned, but He will raise up that very same one and build him again from the former matter. Likewise Rabbi Joseph Albo, Fundamentorum book iv, fol. 146, defends this view against Rabbi Aaron, asserting that if the Blessed God at the time of resurrection were to fashion anew a different body, then it would not be a resurrection of the dead but rather ought to be called a new creation. Indeed Rabbi Saadia Gaon is not of the contrary opinion, as is clear from the testimony of Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, book II, On the Resurrection of the Dead, ch. 15, p. 201: Saadia Gaon tried to meet this difficulty by reasoning that the elements of the human body, even when a person has died by accident, are not changed or mixed with other bodies or with the universal elements; rather they remain marked and distinct, so as to unite and again compose the same body in number. Human bodies are always made anew from elemental parts, and those parts are kept for the purpose that, at the resurrection of the dead, they may constitute the same body. And although they are separated and far apart from one another, nevertheless by divine power they can easily be joined and fitted together again. Rabbi Samuel Japhe also holds the same view.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Probant variis argumentis ex Scripturis Veteris Testamenti depromtis, idem numero resurrecturum corpus, quod ipsa divina effla-gitet gitet justitia, illud debere puniri vel glorificari corpus, quod Deum offendit vel glorificavit, uti recte observavit Rabbi Menasleh Ben Israel, quando libro II. de resurrectione mortuorum, cap. 15. pag. 201: sic inquit: Adde cum finis resurrectionis sit, ut idem corpus animae iunctum, praemio aut poena factorum afficiatur, quis non videt hoc fieri non posse, si novum atq; aliud numero corpus sit? Quod teste Esaia cadaver meum, non alienum, non novum in resurrectione sit ad vitam revocandum; Quod resuscitati per Eliam, Elisaeumq;, non diversis, sed propriis corporibus fuerint vestiti; Quod teste Ezechiele, ossa, quae inter se commixta jacebant, in ordinem compagemq; humanam fuerint restituta, non nova vero ossa creata; Quod sicut vulnus & vulneris sanatio in uno eodemq; fiant corpore, ita pariter cum morte vita in eodem sit futura corpore, uti egregie haec aliaque ulterius deducit Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, libr. II. de resurrect. mort. c. 15. pag. 205, 206: Hoc saltem dico, luce meridiana clarius hinc liquere, quod idem numero corpus aliquando resurget. Idcirco ait Esaias: Mortui tui vivent, cadaver meum expergiscetur; Id est, idem numero cadaver, seu corpus mortuum. Hujus rei etiam manifestum exemplum sumere licet ab infantibus, quos Elias, atq; Elisaeus suscitarunt: sicuti enim enim hi iisdem corporibus vestiti fuerunt, ita etiam idem quid accidet reliquis corporibus omnibus in resurrectione mortuorum. Non minus illustris locus est apud Ezechielem ad idem comprobandum. Verba haec sunt cap. 37. 7. Et fuit tempestas, & acceperunt offa, os ad os suum, id est, cum offa diversi-mode inter se commixta jacerent, facta est commotio, qua offa vehementer agitata conturbataq; fuerunt, ita ut unumquodq; illi se jungeret, cui jungi debebat; id est, caput pedibus, crura brachiis, ac ita porro in reliquis.
