Viri Synagoga magna in fine quarundam precum idem quoq; innuerunt juxta illud בּרוּך אתה י״י המחזיר נשמות לפגרים מתים (Benedictus tu sis Domine, faciens redire animas in corpora emortua.) Et in Midras R. Simhon Ben Johay, inquit R. Hya הוא גופא דהוא יקום ממש דכתיב יחיו מתיך ולא כתיב יבראו (Idem illud corpus, quod ante fuit, resurget; quoniam scriptum est, revivi scent mortui tui: non autem, creabuntur.) Sanhedrin cap. 11. Similiter antiqui ajunt אני אמית ואחיה מחצתי ואני ארפא מה מחיצה ורפואה באחד אף מיתה וחיים באחד Ego occido, & vita revivuo, percutio & medicor. Quemadmodum vulnus & sanatio in eodem corpore recipiuntur: ita mors & vita in eodem corpore erunt.) Nimirum hoc erit in resurrectione mortuorum: id enim postulat verborum sensus. Praeterea alibi legitur, עומדין במומן ומתרפאין (Expergiscentur cum suis vitiis, & mox sanabuntur.) tur.) Atque haec quidem omnia ostendunt, eadem omnino fore corpora, quae homines induent, cum suscitabuntur.
units.tr: By various arguments drawn from the Scriptures of the Old Testament, they prove that the body which rises again must be the same in number as the body which offended or glorified God, since divine justice itself demands that the body which sinned or served be punished or glorified. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel rightly observed this, in book II, On the Resurrection of the Dead, ch. 15, p. 201, where he says: Add that, since the purpose of the resurrection is that the same body, joined to the soul, should receive reward or punishment for its deeds, who does not see that this cannot happen if the body is new and different in number? That, as Isaiah testifies, my corpse, not a strange one nor a new one, is to be called back to life in the resurrection; that those raised by Elijah and Elisha were clothed not in different but in their own bodies; that, as Ezekiel testifies, the bones which lay mixed together were restored to order and to human frame, and no new bones were created; and that, just as a wound and its healing take place in one and the same body, so likewise life after death will be in the same body. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, book II, On the Resurrection of the Dead, ch. 15, pp. 205-206, excellently develops these and other points further: I say only this, that it is clearer than midday light that the same body in number will rise again. Hence Isaiah says: "Your dead shall live; my corpse shall awake" (Isa. 26:19); that is, the same corpse in number, or the dead body. We may also take a clear example of this from the infants whom Elijah and Elisha raised: for just as these were clothed with the same bodies, so the same thing will happen to all the other bodies in the resurrection of the dead. Ezekiel also offers a no less illustrious passage to prove the same. The words are in ch. 37:7: "And there was a noise, and the bones came together, bone to its bone." That is, while the bones lay mixed together in various ways, there was a shaking, by which the bones were violently moved and disturbed, so that each joined itself to that to which it had to be joined: the head to the feet, the legs to the arms, and so on with the rest. The men of the Great Synagogue also indicate the same at the end of certain prayers, according to that saying: [בּרוּך אתה י״י המחזיר נשמות לפגרים מתים] (Blessed art thou, O Lord, who restorest souls to dead bodies.) And in the Midrash of R. Simeon Ben Yochai, R. Chaja says: [הוא גופא דהוא יקום ממש דכתיב יחיו מתיך ולא כתיב יבראו] (That very body which was before will rise again; for it is written, "Your dead shall live," not "they shall be created.") Sanhedrin, ch. 11. Similarly the ancients say: [אני אמית ואחיה מחצתי ואני ארפא מה מחיצה ורפואה באחד אף מיתה וחיים באחד] (I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal. Just as wound and healing are received in the same body, so death and life will be in the same body.) Certainly this will be in the resurrection of the dead, for the sense of the words requires it. Moreover, it is read elsewhere: [עומדין במומן ומתרפאין] (They will rise with their blemishes, and will soon be healed.) Indeed all these things show that the bodies which men put on when they are raised will be altogether the same.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Non diffitentur interim perdifficile esse, concipere qua ratione eadem resurgant corpora, quae in infinitas resoluta sint particulas, quarumque plurimae in substantiam alterius viventis sint mutatae, uti lubens concedit Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel libr. II. de resurrectione mortuorum, cap. 15. pag. 198,199: Caeterum non ignorandum est, hanc opinionem suis difficultatibus non carere, & quidem hac imprimis, quod tale quid propemodum fieri non posse videtur. In confesso est, ac certo constat, corpus humanum ex quatuor elementis compositum esse, idemque post mortem destrui, & partem ejus quamlibet in sua elementa resolvi, ex quibus postea alia, atque alia, in infinitum fere fiant juxta corpora. Id si ita est, quomodo in resurrectione mortuorum idem numero corpus cum omnibus membris ac partibus suis revertetur ad constituendum & integrandum eundem numero hominem? quippe fieri potest, ut dilaniato corpore a feris, partes ejus in substantiam alterius viventis mutatae sint: quomodo igitur restituentur eadem partes in resurrectione? ponamus partem unam in leonis, alteram in formica, tertiam in piscis substantiam esse commutatam: ac forte dicemus cemus animalia illa destructum & in partes resolu-tum sri, ut ea iterum ingrediantur compositionem hominis? Profecto hoc tantumdem foret, ac si quis guttulam aquæ, quam in medium mare effuderat, inde recolligere vellet. Posito etiam casu, quod ex unius hominis elementis fiat ac componatur alius homo, & uterque meritus sit, ut resurgat: qua ratione fieri potest ut eadem portiones eidem jungantur ac copulentur corpori? Quod quod de eadem portione oculi non potest fieri alius, idemq; numero oculus? Et sic in reliquis. Ex quo consicitur, fieri non posse, ut idem numero corpus, eisdemq; qualitatibus, quibus ante præditum fuit, resurgat; Concedunt quin etiam, ex Judæis quosdam, cum difficultatem hanc solvere non possent, in eam proclaplos fuisse opinionem, eosdem quidem homines esse resurrecturos, non ratione corporis, quod novum, atque numero aliud futurum sit, sed respectu animæ, quia illa præcipua ac potissima pars est, quæ hominem constituat; Et in hac sententia non tantum fuit R. Chasdai, apud Rabbi Menassen Ben Israel, libr. II. de resurrect. mort. cap. 15. pag. 200; Sed ipse Abarbanel, quando in Præfatione ad Esaiam, rad. 4 suadet simile priori corpus producendum: Magis autem conveniens & solidum est, ut dicatur: Deum de novo creaturum tempore resurrectionis corpora e pulvere terræ, & rore cœlesti, si, quem in illa immissurus sit, sicut in corpus primi hominis tempore creationis, & illa corpora se habitura priorum instar, sine defectu, vel excessu, ejusdem fore temperamenti. Quia autem mores & qualitates sequuntur temperamentum, sequitur easdem illis in hæsuras instar priorum, sine ulla mutatione. Itaque cum materia prorsus instar priorum constent, eademque anima quæ in priori fuerat; vere affirmabitur eosdem numero mortuos resurgere: imo ipse Rabbi David Kimchi ad Malach cap. 4. Etiamsi ego vos admoneo legis Mosaicæ singulis seculis: nihilo tamen minus in bonum vestrum mittam vobis Eliam Prophetam. Sensus est: quod immissurus sit denuo animam ejus, quæ abierat in cælum, in corpus creatum ad instar corporis prioris, quandoquidem corpus primum reddit in terram, cum ille ascenderet, quodlibet elementum ad suum elementum. Postquam autem illum in corpore vivificaverit, mittet illum ad Israelem, ante diem judicii, qui est dies Domini magnus & terribilis.
units.tr: They do not deny, meanwhile, that it is extremely difficult to conceive how the same bodies will rise again when they have been dissolved into infinitely many particles, most of which have been changed into the substance of other living things. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel gladly concedes this in De resurrectione mortuorum, book II, chapter 15, pages 198–199: Yet it must not be overlooked that this opinion is not free from its difficulties, and chiefly this, that such a thing seems almost impossible. It is agreed and certainly established that the human body is composed of the four elements, that after death it is destroyed, and that any part of it is resolved into its elements, from which afterwards other and other bodies are made, almost without end. If this is so, how in the resurrection of the dead will the same body in number, with all its members and parts, return to constitute and complete the same man in number? For it can happen that, when the body has been torn to pieces by wild beasts, its parts have been changed into the substance of other living things. How, then, will the same parts be restored in the resurrection? Suppose that one part has been changed into the substance of a lion, another into that of an ant, a third into that of a fish. Will we perhaps say that those animals were destroyed and resolved into parts, so that these may enter again into the composition of a man? Certainly this would be no different from someone wishing to gather back a little drop of water that he had poured into the middle of the sea. Suppose further the case that from the elements of one man another man is made and put together, and that both have deserved to rise: by what means can the same portions be joined and united again to the same body? What if, from the same portion of an eye, another eye can be made, identical in number? And so with the rest. From this it follows that it cannot happen that the same body in number, with the same qualities it had before, should rise. Indeed, they also concede that some of the Jews, when they could not solve this difficulty, fell into the opinion that the same men will indeed rise, not with respect to the body, which will be new and different in number, but with respect to the soul, because that is the chief and principal part which constitutes the man. In this view was not only R. Chasdai, cited by Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, book II, De resurrectione mortuorum, chapter 15, page 200; but also Abarbanel himself, when in his preface to Isaiah, root 4, he argues that a body similar to the former is to be produced: "It is more fitting and solid to say that God will create anew at the time of the resurrection bodies from the dust of the earth and the heavenly dew, into which he will send the soul, just as into the body of the first man at the time of creation; and those bodies will be like the earlier ones, without defect or excess, of the same temperament. Since morals and qualities follow the temperament, it follows that they will cling to them just as the earlier ones did, without any change. Therefore, since they consist of matter altogether like the earlier, and the same soul which was in the earlier one, it will truly be affirmed that the same dead in number rise again." Indeed Rabbi David Kimchi himself, on Malachi chapter 4: Although I admonish you by the Mosaic law in every age, nevertheless I will send to you for your good Elijah the Prophet. The sense is this: that he will send again his soul, which had gone to heaven, into a body created like the earlier body, since when he ascended, the first body returned to the earth, each element to its own element. But after he has quickened him in the body, he will send him to Israel before the day of judgment, which is the great and terrible day of the Lord.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Credunt pariter communi fere calculo, mortuorum resurrectionem instituendam à summo Numine, ex ossiculo, לוז Luz appellato, quod unicum in corpore humano remaneat incorruptibile, & ex quo idem prodeat corpus, per priorum particularum dissipata-rum rum reductionem, restaurationemque, uti hoc non tantum Veterum Judaeorum probantte stimoniis, verum ex sacris quoque firmant Pandectis, alferentes Davidem Prophetam de hoc spinae dorsi ossiculo facere mentionem, cum dicit Psalmo 34. verf. 21: Custodiens offa ejus, unum ex iis non consumptum est; uti liquet ex Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, libr. II. de resurrectione mortuorum, cap. 15. pag. 201, 203, ex Berefchit Rabba, Parascha 28: Adrianus (cujus offa comminuantur) quaesivit ex R. Jeofuah filio Hanina, unde Deus benedictus germinare faciet hominem in futuro saeculo? respondit ille, ex luz seu ossiculo spinae. Rursus alter, unde nosti hoc? da mihi illud, inquit ille, ossiculum, et te docebo: contudit illud in mola, sed non tusum est; conjecit in ignem et non conflagravit; conjecit in aquam, et non attritum est; imposuit incudi, malleoque cecidit, sed ne hilum comminutum est. Imperator Romanus, sive quod rideret resurrectionem mortuorum, sive quod audiverat aliquod incorruptibile ossiculum esse in corpore humano, cupiditate ejus sciendi; vel quia, uti verisimilius est, haesitabat ob difficultates eas, quas jam recensuimus, quaesivit ex R. Jeofua filio Hanina, unde, vel quomodo restituentur mortui, quorum membra tam longe, lateque dispersa essent ac dissipata? Respondit illi R. Jeofua, ex ossiculo spinae dorsi, appellato luz, quod incorruptibi ptibile est; Qui cum non posset facile adhibere fi-dem, experimento ei ostendit ita esse. Haec opinio, si quid antiquus credimus, non improbabilis est. Illud enim ossiculum tale est, ut nequeat interire, quamvis hodie nullus sit, qui illud noverit. Sunt qui arbitrentur, Davidem hujus ossiculi mentio-nem facere, cum ait Psal. 34.21, Custodiens ossa ejus, unum ex iis non consumptum est; Liquetque ex eodem cap. 15. pag. 203, 204, apud Rabbi Me-nassen Ben Israel, cum in Toldot Noah, & Toldot Ilac ex Zoar sic loquitur: Omnibus de-functis, qui inveniuntur procul in peregrina terra, creabit Deus benedictus corpus suum quale convenit: nam unicum ossiculum hominis manet sub ter-ra, quo corpus illud formabitur, tanquam ex massa fermenti, id est, quamvis multorum corpora deper-ditis multis partibus integra restituinon possunt; non idcirco tamen destituentur in resurrectione: nam semper remanet aliquod ossiculum, quod instar fer-menti per massam totam se diffundit, vel quod ita excrescit, uti granum tritici, ex quo nascitur arista. Et ex Rabbi Chaja apud citatum Rabbi Me-nassen pag. 204: Est enim ossiculum, quod sub ter-ra manet incorruptibile, neque senescit unquam aut in pulverem abit. Isto tempore Deus benedictus emolliet illud, & turgidum reddet sicuti massam fermenti, & allevabit, atque extendet in quatuor partes; atque hinc corpus, ejus membra fient, tum Deus
units.tr: Almost by common consensus they likewise believe that the resurrection of the dead will be brought about by the Supreme Power from a little bone called luz [לוז], which alone remains incorruptible in the human body, and from which the same body will come forth through the reassembling and restoring of the former scattered particles. The Jews not only confirm this by the testimonies of the ancient writers but also affirm it from the sacred Scriptures, asserting that David the Prophet makes mention of this little bone of the spine when he says in Psalm 34, verse 21: He keeps all his bones; not one of them is broken. This is clear from Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, book II, De resurrectione mortuorum, chapter 15, pages 201, 203, and from Bereshit Rabba, Parashah 28: Hadrian (whose bones are crushed) asked Rabbi Jehoshua son of Hananiah, "From where will God blessed be he make man sprout in the future age?" He replied, "From the luz, that is, the little bone of the spine." Again another said, "How do you know this? Give me that little bone," he said, "and I will teach you." He crushed it in a mill, but it was not ground up; he cast it into the fire, and it was not burned; he cast it into water, and it was not dissolved; he placed it on an anvil and struck it with a hammer, but not even a bit of it was broken. The Roman emperor, whether because he laughed at the resurrection of the dead, or because he had heard that there is some incorruptible little bone in the human body, desired to know it; or, as is more likely, because he hesitated over those difficulties which we have already set out, asked Rabbi Jehoshua son of Hananiah how, or by what means, the dead would be restored whose limbs were so widely and far scattered and dissipated? Rabbi Jehoshua replied to him: from the little bone of the spine, called luz, which is incorruptible. When he could not easily give assent, he showed him by experiment that it was so. This opinion, if we believe the ancients, is not improbable. For that little bone is such that it cannot perish, although today there is no one who knows it. There are those who think David makes mention of this little bone when he says in Psalm 34:21, "He keeps all his bones; not one of them is broken." And it is clear from the same chapter 15, pages 203–204, in Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, when in Toldot Noah and Toldot Isaac from the Zohar he speaks thus: "To all the dead who are found far off in a foreign land, God blessed be he will create a body such as is fitting; for one little bone of man remains under the earth, from which that body will be formed, as from a lump of leaven. That is, although the bodies of many, with many parts lost, cannot be restored whole, yet they will not therefore be left out in the resurrection; for some little bone always remains, which, like leaven, spreads through the whole mass, or which grows as a grain of wheat, from which the ear is born." And from Rabbi Chaja, cited by the same Rabbi Menasseh, page 204: "For there is a little bone which remains incorruptible under the earth, and never grows old or turns to dust. At that time God blessed be he will soften it and make it swell like a lump of leaven, and will raise it up and spread it out into four parts; and from this the body, its members, will come to be; then God

units.la: Hebrew note: not legible in this page scan; see running text. Deus Benedictus infundet illi animam. Ita est, inquit R. Elhazar. At ossiculum istud quo pacto emolietur? rore; sic scriptum est Esai. cap. 26. quia ros olerum ros tuus; Confirmat idem illud de ossiculo luz Rabbi Ifac Abarbanel in Nachalath Abhoth, sol.140: Praeterea tradunt Sapientes nostri pia memoria, esse os aliquod in cranio hominis loco medulla spinae dorsi, quod nullo tempore putrescat & corrumpatur, idque esse subjectum velfundamentum resurrectionis, ut aequale corpus prodeat, quo ad compositionem, temperamentum, atque partes suas; Similia tradit Rabbi Machir in Abhkath Rochel, part. iv. Dicunt esse durissimum os, instar mallei dissipantis petram. Et referunt de homine aliquo, qui probaturus ejus duritiem, percussit illud malleo, sed malleus frangebatur, in illo nullo apparente percussionis vestigio; Atque ex hoc osse fabricabit Deus structuram corporis, illudque instaurabit in structuram suam priorem; Eadem repetuntur in Rabbi Eliezeris Pirke, cap. 34: Rabbi Simeon inquit: Omnia corpora resolvuntur in pulverem terrae, adeo ut non superstes maneat, nisi plenum cochlear putredinis, quod non permixtum sit pulvere terrae, veluti fermentum mixtum cum massa rinacea. In futuro autem seculo, cum clamabit Sanctus benedictus ad terram, ut reddat depositum omnium corporum, tum miscebitur cum pulvere terrae, sicut fermentum miscetur cum pasta.
units.tr: blessed be he will infuse the soul into it. So it is," says R. Elazar. "But by what means will that little bone be softened?" By dew; so it is written in Isaiah chapter 26: for your dew is a dew of herbs. Isaac Abarbanel confirms the same thing about the bone luz in Nachalath Abhoth, page 140: Moreover, our wise men of pious memory teach that there is a bone in the skull, in the place of the marrow of the spine, which never rots or decays, and that this is the subject or foundation of the resurrection, so that an equal body may come forth as to its composition, temperament, and parts. Rabbi Machir teaches similar things in Abhkath Rochel, part iv: They say it is a very hard bone, like a hammer that shatters a rock. And they report of a certain man who, to test its hardness, struck it with a hammer, but the hammer was broken, and no trace of the blow appeared on it. And from this bone God will fashion the structure of the body and restore it to its earlier structure. The same things are repeated in Rabbi Eliezer's Pirke, chapter 34: Rabbi Simeon says: All bodies are resolved into the dust of the earth, so that nothing remains except a full spoonful of corruption, which is not mixed with the dust of the earth, like leaven mixed with a mass of dough. But in the future age, when the Holy One blessed be he calls to the earth to give back the deposit of all bodies, then it will be mixed with the dust of the earth, just as leaven is mixed into the dough.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Statuunt Judæi, Deum in mortuorum resurrectione naturæ ulurum adminiculo, ministerioque, aflerentes, ossiculum illud Luz rore cœlesti emolliendum, & ad instar fermenti extendendum, quod apte informet terram, corporaque reproducat priora, uti illud non tantum probare conantur ex Esai. cap.26.verf.19. Quia ros olerum, ros tuus; Sed quia quoque resurrectio mortuorum est nova recreatio, non distincta multum ab Adami creatione; Cum itaque vapor irrigaret superficiem terræ, cum primus formaretur homo, necesse est, ut rursus ros terram fœcundet, cum nova recreatio in mortuorum resurrectione sit futura; Teste Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, libr. II. de resurrectione mortuorum, cap.14. pag.196,197: Ac proinde ex opinione vetrum certissimum est, quod resurrectio mortuorum futura sit, ope & auxilio roris cœlitus missi, qui vim plasticam habiturus est, uti in Talmude Hierosolymitano, & Jalkude perscriptum est מנין שאין המתים חיים אלא בטללים שנאמר כי טל אורת טליך Unde probas, quod mortui non resurgent nisi mediante rore? quia legitur Esaiæ cap.26.verf.19. Vivent mortui tui, cadaver meum resurget; expergiscimini, & cantate habitatores terræ, quia ros olerum, ros tuus. Ad hæc R. Joseph Albo inquit, quod ros ille prapraeditus fit futurus vi plastica ad modum feminis virilis, ad informandam terram apte & convenienter disposuitam, quae vice materiae est instar feminis mulieris. Idem etiam a nobis supra observatum est, in citatione quorundam textuum ex libro Zohar. Hucsepecilarunt quoque viri Synagogae magnae, in oratione illa, qua ajunt: אתה גבור לעולם ... מחיה מתים אתה רב להושיע מוריד הטל " Tu potens es perpetuo Domine, resuscitans mortuos, tu magnus ad servandum, facis descendere rorem. Nota quod miraculosa resurrectioni mortuorum nox adjungant rorem, non alio fine, quam ut indicent eam mediante rore futuram esse. Erit tum reformatio aut recreatio nova non dissimilis creationi & formationi Adami: nam quando ille creabatur, tum ut inquit S. S. ascendit vapor ex terra, & irrigavit superficiem terrae, & fecit Dominus Deus hominem. Id est, juxta Ishak Arama, vapor, qui nihil aliud est quam humidus aer, qui vi caloris solaris sursum sublatus, descendit super terram, eamque humectans, praeparavit maßam illam, ex qua factus est homo. Eodem modo se res habebit in resurrectione: tum enim ros ille coelestis idem efficiet; Sic de hoc rore coelesti agit Rabbi Machir in Abhkath Rochel, Part. iv: Dicunt Rabbini nostri pia memoria, Deum benedictum demissurum rorem ex luce superna, qui sit immeaturus in pulverem, & perventur ad illud os, & humectaturus instar massae, ut illud os in
units.tr: The Jews hold that God, in raising the dead, uses the help and ministry of nature, asserting that the little bone called Luz is to be softened by heavenly dew and spread out like leaven, so that it may aptly shape the earth and reproduce the former bodies. They try to prove this not only from Isaiah 26:19, "For your dew is a dew of herbs," but also because the resurrection of the dead is a new re-creation, not much different from the creation of Adam. Just as a vapour watered the surface of the earth when man was first formed, so the earth must again be made fruitful by dew, since the resurrection of the dead is to be a new re-creation. So Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, in book II of his work on the resurrection of the dead, chapter 14, pages 196–197: From the opinion of the ancients it is therefore quite certain that the resurrection of the dead will come about by the help and aid of dew sent from heaven, which will have a plastic power, as is written in the Jerusalem Talmud and the Jalkut [How do you know that the dead will live only by dews? Because it is said: For your dew is a dew of lights.] How do you prove that the dead will rise only through dew? Because it is read in Isaiah 26:19: Your dead shall live, my body shall rise; awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust, for your dew is a dew of herbs. Here R. Joseph Albo says that this dew will be endowed with a plastic power, like the male seed, to shape the earth, which has been suitably and fittingly disposed and which takes the place of matter, as the female seed does. We have also noted this above, in citing certain texts from the book Zohar. The men of the Great Synagogue also hinted at this in that prayer which they say: You are mighty forever, Lord, who raise the dead, you are great to save, you make the dew descend. [אתה גבור לעולם ... מחיה מתים אתה רב להושיע מוריד הטל] Note that they join the dew to the miraculous resurrection of the dead for no other purpose than to show that it will come about through the dew. The reformation or new re-creation will then be not unlike the creation and formation of Adam: for when he was created, as Holy Scripture says, a vapour rose from the earth and watered the surface of the ground, and the Lord God made man. That is, according to Isaac Arama, the vapour, which is nothing other than moist air, lifted up by the power of the sun's heat, descends upon the earth and moistens it, and prepares that mass from which man was made. In the same way it will be in the resurrection: for then that heavenly dew will do the same. So Rabbi Machir speaks of this heavenly dew in Abhkath Rochel, part 4: Our rabbis of blessed memory say that God, blessed be he, will send down a dew from the supernal light, which will penetrate into the dust, and will reach that bone, and will moisten it like a mass,

units.la: Nota quod: marginal mark "Nota" printed beside the line "rore" (note not separately legible). in pulvere sit instar fermenti in massa, quod hinc inde diffunditur; Sic pariter Rabbi Meir, Ben Gabbay in Afodath Haccodesch, sol. 53: Ros hic se diffundit in pulverem, donec pertingat ad os illud, ut fiat instar massae in pulvere, extendaturque quaquaversum. Exinde expanduntur omnia membra, nervi, caro, & pellis superinducitur; Sic in libello Hebraico, Adam Sichli, qui tredecim fidei Judaicae articulos complectitur, non solum fit mentio ossis Luz, quod credunt esse incorruptibile, sed simul referunt, quomodo rore coelesti irrigatum, animae suae restituet totum corpus, illudque vivificabit, uti patet ex articulo ultimo de resurrectione: Est autem radix hujus ossis ex ipso caelo, & humectatur rore, quo Deus aliquando in vitam revocaturus est mortuos, tanquam fermento, quod est in massa farinae; Caeterum de hoc rore plura suppeditabit R. Hac Abarbanel, qui in Nachalath Abhoth consuli poterit.
units.tr: so that the bone in the dust is like leaven in the dough, which spreads on every side. Likewise Rabbi Meir ben Gabbay, in Afodath Haccodesch, folio 53: This dew spreads into the dust until it reaches that bone, so that it becomes like a mass in the dust and is extended on all sides. Then all the limbs, sinews and flesh are stretched out, and skin is laid over them. Likewise in the Hebrew booklet Adam Sichli, which contains the thirteen articles of Jewish faith, mention is made not only of the bone Luz, which they believe to be incorruptible, but they also relate how, watered by heavenly dew, it will restore the whole body to its soul and will make it live, as is clear from the last article on the resurrection: The root of this bone is from heaven itself, and it is moistened by the dew with which God will one day call the dead back to life, like the leaven that is in a mass of flour. Moreover, Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel will supply more on this dew, and he may be consulted in Nachalath Abhoth.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Negant Resurrectionem hominum generalem, omnium quotquot a condito fuerunt aevo, eruntque imposterum, quod terra hos capere neutiquam possit, & ex Daniele clarum sit, quod multi sint resurrecturi, non omnes, uti liquet ex Rabbi Isaco Abarbanele in Praefatione ad Elaiam, rad. 6: Radix sexta agit de de materia resurrectionis, seu de illis, qui resurgent; an nimirum omnes homines, qui conditi fuerunt inde a diebus creationis usque ad illud tempus resurrectionis? quod foret impossibile, cum terra illos non caperet; Et ex Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, libr. II. de resurrectione mortuorum, cap. 8. p. 180: Quare ex mente, ac opinione omnium antiquorum, concludimus, resurrectionem mortuorum non fore generalem, ac communem omnibus hominibus; uti etiam ex loco Danielis constat, multi ex dormientibus in pulvere terrae expergiscentur. Nota quod dicat multos, non vero omnes; Sic longe non tantum a Majoribus multum melioribus recedentes, qui universalem mortuorum statuentes resurrectionem, sicut omnes nascuntur & moriuntur, ita pariter resurrecturos omnes docebant, uti liquet ex Tractatu Talmudico aureo, Pirke Abhot, cap. 4. Qui nati sunt morientur, qui mortui sunt revivescent, qui revivescent, judicabuntur. Scient qui adhuc nascentur, scient qui modo nati sunt, scient qui ex mortuis resurgent, quod ipse Deus est formator & creator. Ipse est qui animadvertit omnia. Ipse judex est. Ipse testis est. Ipse est qui accusat in judicio. Ipse est qui in futurum judicabit, Benedictus sit ipse, quoniam non est coram ipso, neque oblivio, neque acceptio personarum, neque acceptatio muneris: omnia enim sua sunt. Noveris insuper quod omnia juxta subductam Nothing further. duƐam rationem transsigentur. Neques curum te faciat malus genius tuus, quasi sepulchrum futurum sit refugium tuum. Tesiquidem nolente formatus es, te vel nolente vivis, te vel nolente moriens. Tandem q futurum est, ut stes judicio, reddituras rationem coram rege omnium regum: qui scil.est Deus sanctus, benedictus sit ipse; Sed justo pariter Dei Judicio de Resurgentium numero altercantes, inque partes abeuntes diversissimas, satentibus aliis Judæorum Doctoribus, omnes resurrecturos Israelitas, sive pios, sive impios, ita ut tantum excipiantur aliqui; Negantibus aliis impios resurrecturos, quod beneficium solum sit piorum ex Israele; Aliis denique concedentibus, pios ex gentibus, impiosque innumeros resurrectionis quoque fore participes.
units.tr: They deny that there will be a general resurrection of all men, of all who have been from the beginning of the age and will be hereafter, since the earth could by no means hold them; and it is clear from Daniel that many, not all, will rise, as appears from Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel in his preface to Isaiah, root 6: The sixth root deals with the matter of the resurrection, or with those who will rise: namely, whether all men who have been created from the days of creation until that time of the resurrection? This would be impossible, since the earth would not hold them. And from Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, book II on the resurrection of the dead, chapter 8, page 180: Therefore, from the mind and opinion of all the ancients, we conclude that the resurrection of the dead will not be general and common to all men; as also appears from the passage in Daniel, many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake. Note that it says many, not all; Thus they depart far from the much better elders, who, holding that there is a universal resurrection of the dead, taught that as all are born and die, so all will likewise rise, as is clear from the golden Talmudic treatise Pirke Abhot, chapter 4: Those who are born will die, those who are dead will be revived, those who are revived will be judged. Let those who are yet to be born know, let those who have just been born know, let those who rise from the dead know, that God himself is the former and creator. He himself is the one who observes all things. He himself is the judge. He himself is the witness. He himself is the one who accuses in judgment. He himself is the one who will judge hereafter. Blessed be he, for with him there is neither forgetfulness, nor respect of persons, nor taking of bribes: for all things are his. Know moreover that all things are carried out according to the reckoning. Let not your evil impulse persuade you that the grave will be your refuge. For against your will you were formed, against your will you live, against your will you die; and in the end you must stand in judgment, and give an account before the King of kings, who is the Holy God, blessed be he. But the Jewish doctors, disputing in the same way about the number of those who will rise, went off into very diverse parties: some, the other doctors of the Jews, holding that all the Israelites will rise, whether pious or impious, so that only certain persons are excepted; others denying that the impious will rise, since the benefit belongs only to the pious of Israel; others finally conceding that the pious of the nations and countless impious will also share in the resurrection.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Qui inter Judæos impiorum negant resurrectionem, solorum justorum tantummodo statuentes, nituntur tum authoritate veterum, maxime Talmudicorum, tum multitudine Rabbinorum, tum variis hinc inde, mox ex Scriptura Sacra, mox ex Doctorum scriptis, conquisitis rationibus; Hinc tritum illud Antiquorum in ore volvunt perpetuo: Virtus pluviarum communis est probis & improbis, sed Resurrectio mortuorum pertinet ad solos Iolos probos; allegantque continuo ex Tra-ctatibus Talmudicis Sanhedrin & Taanith, quod vivificatio mortuorum pertineat adju-ftos,non vero ad impios,uti patet ex R.David Kimchi, cum in Commentario ad Pialm.104. verl.30,& in Efaiam cap.26.verf. 19.sic loqui-tur: An futura fit resurrectio mortuorum omnium hominum, controvertitur inter Sapientes nostros: at stylus seu cursus Talmudicus huc inclinat, quod resurrectio mortuorum futura fit tantum justorum, non vero improborum; Nec solum refert Rabbi David Kimchi,hanc de resurrectione Talmudiftarum esse mentem, verum eam quoque ambabus ampleCtitur manibus,quod & liquet ex ipsius verbis in Commentario ad Psalmum 1. verf. 5. Impius non erit resurrectio; sed peribit anima ipsorum cum corpore ipsorum in die mortis; Et magis patebit ex reliquis Kim-chianis di&is apud Efaiam Propheram, c. 30. v.ult. cap. 38. verf. 18. cap. 65. verf. 11. quae in-defeflo studio eruit eduxitque Clarissimus Daffovius in erudita sua diatribe de Refurre-ctione mortuorum, cap.4 pag.34,35,36; Nec inficiatur illud de Rabbi Davide Kimchi, R. Menasseh Ben Israel, quando libr. II: de Re-furrectione mortuorum, cap.8. pag.176,177. dicit: Accedentibus nobis ad tertiam causam, nempe materia, prima quaestio fit, an resurrectio futura tura fit universalis? Super eo varie sunt Rabbinorum opiniones; R. Sehadia Gaon, & R. Moses Gerundensis, & R. David Kimchi ad Psal. 2. existimant resurrectionem mortuorum ad solos justos pertinere: quod confirmant antiquorum testimonio, quod hunc in modum sonat גבורות גשמים לצדיקים ולרשעים אבל תחית המתים לצדיקים בלבד Pluvia beneficium commune est probis, & improbis: sed resurrectio mortuorum duntaxat eorum bonum est, qui pie ac probe vixerunt; Sic proborum hominum resurrectionem defendit Rabbi Saadia Gaon in Sepher Emunah, sol. 36. col. 2. Prima quaestio: si quis quaesiverit, quinam sint e populo revicturi tempore salutis? Respondeo & dico: omnis justus, & qui agit poenitentiam; Defendit Resurrectionem Justorum Rabbi Joseph Albo de Fundamentis, sol. 28. De resurrectione sunt inter Rabbinos nostros, qui dicunt, quod ad solos perfecte justos pertineat. Quae cum sit gradus mercedis non promissus hominibus universim, cum impossibile sit, ut omnes sint perfecte justi: erit, qui illam resurrectionem negaverit, quasi neget unum ex magnus miraculis in justis exhibendis; Ita R. Moses Maimonides articulo fidei Judaicae decimo tertio, resurrectionem solis tribuit justis, uti constat ex Theologiae nostrae Judaicae cap. 1. §. 17. Et hoc cap. 18. §. 1. Confirmatq; de Maimonide, aliosque sententiae patronos simul adducens, Rabbi Isac Abarbanel in Nachalath Abhoth, sol. 148: Hoc est quod censuerunt quidam ex Sapientibus nostris, non esse resurrecturos, nisi justos ex Israelitis. Hac est sententia Rambam in Epistola de resurrectione, & Gaon in libro Emunath, & Ramban in Sohaar Haggamul, & Rabbi Chasdai cum suis discipulis; Quibus paria adducunt Raschi, & Rabbi Aben Elra, in Comment. ad Esai. cap. 26 vers. 19. Alique plurimi, alio citandi tempore.
units.tr: Among the Jews, those who deny the resurrection of the wicked, holding that only the righteous rise, rely on the authority of the ancients, especially the Talmudists, on the great number of the rabbis, and on various arguments gathered from here and there, sometimes from Holy Scripture and sometimes from the writings of the teachers. Hence they constantly repeat that old saying: "The virtue of rains is common to the good and the bad, but the resurrection of the dead belongs only to the upright." They also continually cite from the Talmudic tractates Sanhedrin and Taanith that the quickening of the dead pertains to the just, not to the wicked. This is evident from R. David Kimchi, who, in his commentary on Psalm 104:30 and on Isaiah 26:19, speaks thus: Whether there will be a resurrection of the dead of all men is disputed among our wise men; but the style and course of the Talmud inclines to this, that the resurrection of the dead will be only of the just, and not of the wicked; Nor does Rabbi David Kimchi merely report that this is the mind of the Talmudists; he embraces it with both hands, as is clear from his own words in his commentary on Psalm 1:5: There will be no resurrection for the wicked; but their soul will perish together with their body on the day of death; And it will be more plainly evident from the other sayings of Kimchi on Isaiah 30 (last verse), 38:18, and 65:11, which the most distinguished Dassovius has with tireless zeal dug out and brought forth in his learned treatise on the resurrection of the dead, chapter 4, pages 34, 35, 36. Nor does R. Menasseh Ben Israel deny that this is the view of Rabbi David Kimchi, when in book II of his work on the resurrection of the dead, chapter 8, pages 176 and 177, he says: As we come to the third cause, namely the matter, the first question is whether the future resurrection will be universal? On this the opinions of the rabbis vary; R. Saadia Gaon, R. Moses of Gerona, and R. David Kimchi on Psalm 2 hold that the resurrection of the dead pertains to the just alone; which they confirm by the testimony of the ancients, which sounds in this manner [גבורות גשמים לצדיקים ולרשעים אבל תחית המתים לצדיקים בלבד]: "The mighty rains are a common benefit to the righteous and the wicked, but the resurrection of the dead is only for the righteous." Thus Rabbi Saadia Gaon defends the resurrection of the upright in his Sepher Emunah, page 36, column 2: First question: if anyone should ask who of the people will revive at the time of salvation? I answer and say: every just man, and whoever does repentance; Rabbi Joseph Albo defends the resurrection of the just in his Fundamentals, page 28: Concerning the resurrection there are among our rabbis those who say that it pertains to the perfectly just alone. Since this is a degree of reward not promised to men in general, and since it is impossible that all should be perfectly just, whoever denies that resurrection will be as one who denies one of the great miracles to be shown in the just; So also Rabbi Moses Maimonides, in the thirteenth article of the Jewish faith, assigns the resurrection to the just alone, as appears from our Jewish Theology, chapter 1, §17, and this chapter 18, §1. Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel, in Nachalath Abhoth, page 148, confirms this concerning Maimonides and other patrons of the opinion, bringing them forward together: This is what some of our wise men held, that only the Israelites who are just will rise. This is the view of the Rambam in his Epistle on the resurrection, and of the Gaon in the book Emunath, and of the Ramban in Sohaar Haggamul, and of Rabbi Chasdai with his disciples; To these they add similar authorities, Rashi and Rabbi Aben Ezra, on Isaiah 26:19. Many others, to be cited at another time.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Probant hi omnes suam de Justorum resurrectione sententiam, ex diversis Sacrae Scripturae dictis, quod Deuteron. cap. 32. vers. 39. dicatur: Ego interficiam & vivificabo; In praecedentibus autem mentio fit de populo Dei seu de Justis, quos Deus esset judicaturus; Quod Esai. cap. 26. vers. 19. per mortuos tuos, qui reviviscent, & per cadavera mea, quae resurgent, intelligendi sint justi, qui sponte se obtulerunt, ut caderent propter Dominum; Quod Deus apud Ezechielem c. 37. vers. 12, velit suum populum, id est, justos educere ex sepulchris; Quod ex Daniele cap. 12. vers. 2. multi justi ex dormientibus in pulvere terrae sint suscitandi; Sic firmant sententiam suam multis rationibus; Quod justi corpus obimpressionem in ipso relictam per spiritum divinum, num, aptius sine dubio futurum sit, ad spiritum illum divinum secundo recipiendum, quam primo fuerat, ex Rabbi Josepho Albo de Fundamentis, sol. 151; Quod justi & sancti in cultu Dei Benedicti, ob meritum necessario ex morte sint revocandi, ex Rabbi Molche de Trana in Beth Elohim, sol. 104. col. 1; Superstunt aliæ, quas Daffovius pariter in perdocta sua Diatribe suppeditabit.
units.tr: All of these prove their opinion about the resurrection of the just from various sayings of Holy Scripture. Deuteronomy 32:39 says: "I will kill and I will make alive"; but in the preceding verses mention is made of the people of God, or of the just, whom God is about to judge. Isaiah 26:19, "Your dead shall live, and my dead bodies shall rise," is to be understood of the just, who offered themselves willingly to fall for the Lord. In Ezekiel 37:12 God wishes to bring up his people, that is, the just, out of their graves. From Daniel 12:2 many of the just who sleep in the dust of the earth are to be raised. Thus they support their opinion with many arguments: that the body of the just, since the impression left in it by the divine Spirit remains, will without doubt be more fit to receive that divine Spirit a second time than it was the first time, from Rabbi Joseph Albo, Fundamentals, page 151; that the just and the saints who serve the Blessed God must of necessity be recalled from death on account of their merit, from Rabbi Moses of Trani in Beth Elohim, page 104, column 1. Other arguments remain, which Dassovius likewise will supply in his very learned Treatise.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Sic qui inter Gentis Judaicæ Doctores contrariam priori fovent, defenduntque sententiam, statuentes non pios tantum quam maxime ex Israelitis resurrecturos, sed improbos quoque populi Judaici, licet non omnes, cum sint inter illos, qui resurrectione sint orbandi, nituntur non modo ipsius intellectus lumine naturali, authoritateque antiquorum Magistrorum, verum etiam sacræ scripturæ testimoniis, uti videre est apud Rabbi Menassen Ben Israel, libr. II. de resurrectione mortuorum, cap. 8. pag. 177, 178: Cæterum si illud ad rationis obrussam exigamus, rectè rem, uti sapientum est, examinemus, comperiemus non minus improbos, quam probos resurrecturos esse; uti liquet non modo ex lumine intellectus; Sed etiam authoritate sacrarum literarum, veterumq; sapientum. Ex lumine intellectus, seu vi rationis inquam, quia si finis resurrectionis est, ut corpus conjunctum animæ, præmio aut pœna factorum afficiatur (uti ante ostendimus) ergo etiam improbi suscitabuntur, ut crucientur ac puniantur. Ex sacris literis, quia apud Danielem dicitur cap. 12. verf. 2: Multi ex dormientibus in pulvere terræ suscitabuntur. Quod si illi multi, soli justi forent, pauci profecto essent: nam tales haud ita multi inveniuntur. Quid quod statim addatur, alii in vitam æternam, alii in opprobrium, ut videant semper: Quod equidem de malis & impiis dicitur. Accedat huc testimonium veterum, quorum hujuscemodi verba sunt in Perek Heleq: Omnis Israel particeps erit futuri sæculi. Cæterum ex omnibus istis tria genera tantum excipiunt, primo, eos qui non credunt resurrectionem mortuorum, deinde, qui negant legem esse divinam, deniq; Epicureos. Item in Midras Soher tob legitur: דור המבול אין להם חלק לעולם הבא Generatio diluvij non erit particeps futuri sæculi. Idem quoq; confirmatur in Sanhedrin, & Berefit Raba. Quod si antiqui Sapientes credidissent malos non resurrecturos, quorsum istos particulatim excepissent? Sed ex hoc apparet eos ex malorum qui resurrecturi sunt ordine istos tantum exclusisse, quos diximus. Item si alibi antiqui negent omnes & singulos malos atq; impios resurrecturos esse, quare excipiunt solam generationem diluvij? Et cap. 22. Libr. II. de Reiurr. Mort. pag. 241: Nempe tum probi omnes ac pij, qui multis miseriis hic affli- cti fuerint, digni certe meliore fortuna, omnis gaudij & deliciarum fient compotes: improbi vero & mali, qui delicate ac molliter hic ævum suum transegerunt, cruciabuntur ac gravissime punientur; Patetque illud abunde ex Rabbi Moseh Alschech in Thorath Molche, sol. 323. col. 4. in Deuteron. cap 32: Quæ etiam est una ex rationibus, quare Deus benedictus omnes mortuos Israelitas vivificaturus sit cum vitiis corporum, ut ea ipsa plaga, quam quisq; habet, surrecturus sit & visurus, quanam plaga obventura sit percussori suo, qui illum percussit, & ultionem sumpturus, & postea quam lætabitur justus, quod viderit ultionem, Deus Benedictus eum sit sanaturus; Sic Rabbi Chasdai Crescas docet, pios cum impiis resurrecturos, non vero intermedios, apud Rabbi Menaffen Ben Israel, libr. II. de Resurrectione mortuorum, cap. 8. pag. 179: R. Hasday Crescas in libro suo Or a jem motus autoritate quorundam locorum, quæ jam citavimus, statuit; resurrectionem mortuorum solum pertinere ad eos, qui vel rectissime, vel pessime vixerunt: non autem ad illos, qui inter utrumq; medij fuere; Ita quoque fatentur in Rabbi Elieseris Pirke, quod omnes mortui resurrecturi sint, tam pii per consequens, quam impii, præter generationem diluvii, Gigantes, gentilesque, uti liquet ex cap. 34: R. Jonathan nathan inquit: omnes mortui resurgent prater generationem diluvii, sicuti dicitur Efai. c.26. v.14. Mortui non reviviscent. Mortui non vivent: isti sunt gentiles, qui sunt veluti cadaver bestiae. Surgent quidem ad diem judicij, sed non revivi-scent. Generatio autem diluvij etiam non resurget die judicij; Hinc dicitur: Gigantes non resurgent. Omnes autem eorum animae factae sunt spiritus noxij vel tacodaemones hominis, atque eos in futuro seculo disperdet Sanctus benedictus e mundo, ne amplius noceant Israelitis, juxta illud: Idcirco visitabit, & exterminabit eos, atque perdes omnem memoriam illorum; Sic Rabbi Bechai Resurrectionem mortuorum de solis praedicat Israelitis, quod unum ex quatuor sit privilegiis, quibus destituantur Gentiles, uti loquitur in Kad Hakkemach, sol. 8. Quatuor sunt speciales Israelis dignitates, quas in reliquis gentibus reperire non est, ut sunt Terra Canaan, Lex, Prophetia, & mortuorum Resurrectio.
units.tr: Those among the Jewish teachers who hold the opposite view to the former, and defend the opinion that not only the pious of Israel but also the wicked of the Jewish people will rise again (though not all of them, since some among them are to be deprived of resurrection), rely not only on the natural light of reason and the authority of the ancient masters, but also on testimonies of Holy Scripture. See Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, On the Resurrection of the Dead, book II, chapter 8, pages 177 and 178: Moreover, if we test this by the touchstone of reason and examine the matter properly, as wise men do, we shall find that the wicked will rise no less than the good. This is clear not only from the light of the intellect, but also from the authority of the sacred writings and of the wise men of old. From the light of the intellect, or the power of reason, I say, because if the purpose of the resurrection is that the body, joined to the soul, should receive reward or punishment for its deeds (as we showed before), then the wicked too will be raised, so that they may be tormented and punished. From the sacred writings, because in Daniel 12:2 it is said: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall rise. If those many were only the just, they would certainly be few, for such men are not found in great numbers. Moreover, it is at once added that some shall rise to everlasting life and others to shame, that they may always see. This is said of the evil and the impious. Add to this the testimony of the ancients, whose words in Pirke Avot are these: All Israel shall have a share in the world to come. But from all these texts they except only three kinds: first, those who do not believe in the resurrection of the dead; second, those who deny that the Law is divine; and finally, the Epicureans. Likewise it is read in Midrash Shocher Tov: הדור המבול אין להם חלק לעולם הבא [The generation of the flood shall have no share in the world to come]. The same is confirmed in Sanhedrin and in Bereshit Rabba. But if the ancient sages had believed that the wicked would not rise, why would they have excepted these individually? It appears, then, that from the order of the wicked who are to rise they excluded only those whom we have mentioned. Likewise, if elsewhere the ancients deny that all and each of the wicked and impious will rise, why do they except the generation of the flood alone? And in chapter 22 of book II, On the Resurrection of the Dead, page 241: Indeed, all the upright and pious, who have been afflicted with many miseries here, are certainly worthy of a better fortune, and will become partakers of all joy and delights; but the wicked and evil, who have passed their lives here softly and delicately, will be tormented and most severely punished. This is abundantly clear from Rabbi Moses Alshech in Torath Moshe, page 323, column 4, on Deuteronomy chapter 32: This is also one of the reasons why the blessed God will restore all the dead of Israel with the defects of their bodies, so that they may rise with that very wound which each one has, and see with what wound he who struck him is to be struck, and take vengeance; and afterwards, when the just man rejoices that he has seen the vengeance, the blessed God will heal him. Thus Rabbi Chasdai Crescas teaches that the pious will rise with the impious, but not those who were in between, according to Menasseh ben Israel, On the Resurrection of the Dead, book II, chapter 8, page 179: Rabbi Hasdai Crescas, in his book Or Adonai, moved by the authority of certain passages which we have already cited, holds that the resurrection of the dead pertains only to those who have lived most righteously or most wickedly, and not to those who were between these two. So too they affirm, in Rabbi Eliezer's Pirke, that all the dead will rise, the pious as well as the impious, except the generation of the flood, the giants, and the Gentiles, as is clear from chapter 34: Rabbi Jonathan says: all the dead shall rise except the generation of the flood, as it is said in Isaiah 26:14: The dead shall not live, the dead shall not rise. Those are the Gentiles, who are like the carcass of a beast. They shall indeed rise on the day of judgment, but they shall not live again. The generation of the flood also shall not rise on the day of judgment; hence it is said: The giants shall not rise. All their souls were made evil spirits or demons of man, and the Holy One, blessed be He, will destroy them from the world in the age to come, so that they may no longer harm Israel, according to the saying: Therefore he will visit and exterminate them, and you will blot out all remembrance of them. Thus Rabbi Bechai preaches that the resurrection of the dead is for Israelites alone, which is one of four privileges lacking to the Gentiles, as he says in Kad Hakkemach, page 8: There are four special dignities of Israel which are not to be found among the other nations: the land of Canaan, the Law, prophecy, and the resurrection of the dead.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Sunt pariter inter Judaeos modernos, qui mitiores (saltem videntur) collocantes in resurgentium numero, non omnes singulosque homines, sed omnium gentium probos, improbosque, maxime tamen Judaeorum, quod Veterum Sapientum effatum fit: Piis ex nationibus mundi pars erit in seculo venturo;
units.tr: There are also among the modern Jews some who are milder (at least they seem so), and who include in the number of those who will rise not every single human being but the upright and the wicked of all nations, especially the Jews. This is in keeping with the saying of the Ancient Sages: "A portion of the pious among the nations of the world will have a place in the age to come."

units.la: Quoc... Quodque Deus Benedictus nullam creatu- ram suo fraudet praemio, uti patet ex Rabbi Menafseh Ben Israel, qui Gentium ad vitam revocandarum causam egit maxime, uti patet ex ipsius Conciliatore in Deuteron. Quaest.2. Theolog. Judaic. cap. 15. §.10. Et ex libr. 2. de Resurrectione Mortuorum, cap.9.
units.tr: And that the Blessed God will defraud no creature of its reward, as is clear from Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, who especially pleaded the cause of reviving the Gentiles, as is clear from his Conciliator, on Deuteronomy, Question 2, Jewish Theology, chapter 15, §10, and from book 2 of On the Resurrection of the Dead, chapter 9.

units.la: Non minus verisimile est, omnes gentes ac nationes æque resurrecturas, atq; Israelitas, juxta illud veterum dictum, חסידי אמות העולם יש להם חלק לעולם הבא Pijs ex gentibus mundi pars erit in futuro jaculo. Omnes illi qui non sunt Israelitæ, vocantur gentes, seu nationes mundi, vel quia majorem numerum faciunt; Israelitæ enim pauci sunt, juxta Deut. c. VII, VIII. vel quia reguntur a proprio ac singulari principe, juxta illud Danielis, Princeps regni Persarum, Princeps regni Græcorum, &c. Israelitæ vero immediate a Deo benedicto reguntur, juxta verba illa, Deuteron. 4. 20. Vos assumsit Dominus. Ex his nationibus omnes, ac singuli resurgent, qui probe ac pie vixerunt, quales sunt, qui juxta R. Mosen, & R. Meyr Gabay observarunt diligenter præcepta ea, quæ data sunt Noachæ: cujus modi sunt, Non committes Idololatriam. Non occides. Non adulterabis. Non maledices nomini divino. Non latrocinaberis. Non comedes membrum animalis vivi. Et constitues judices, qui curent, ut sex illa præcepta probe ac diligenter observent Sf 5 ferven ferventur. Neq; illi tantummodo resurgent; sed etiam beatitudinus futuri seculi participes erunt, juxta veterum illud pronunciatum: אין הקדוש ברוך הוא מקפח שכר כל בריה Non fraudat Deus praemio ullam creaturam. Ac proinde dicunt, illis pars erit. Neq; dubium est: quin illi quoq;, qui recte de Deo senserunt, pariter q; honeste, pie, ac probe vixerunt, partem in resurrectione mortuorum obtinebunt: uti sentit R. Moses Aegyptius in epistolis suis: quamvis talis aliquis fuerit ex gentilibus, utt Socrates, Plato, &c. Idem quoq; confirmari potest ex alio antiquorum dicto, quod ita sonat: ארבעה הדיוטות אין להם חלק לעולם הבא ואלו הן בלעם דואג אחיתופל וגחזי Quatuor Ediotot non erunt participes futuri seculi, nempe Bilham, Doeg, Achitophel, & Gehazi. Ex quibus verbis in Talmudico conciliatur: בלעם הוא דלא אתי הא גוים אחריני אתו Bilhem est, qui non veniet, scilicet in futuro seculo; ergo alii gentiles venient. Non mala equidem ista consequentia est: nam si non omnes gentiles sunt resurrecturi, superfluum omnino est etiam Biliami mentionem facere. At vero quia ejus mentio fit, hinc colligere licet, quod alij etiam gentiles Bileamo similes, resurgent, nempe si digni sint resurrectione. Similiter mali atq; improbi resurgent ut cruciantur ac puniantur. Accedat huc etiam testimonium Danielis, & multi ex dormientibus in pulvere terrae expergiscentur, hi ad vitam aeternam, illi in pudorem & opprobrium perpetuum. Ecce non de Israelitis dumtaxat taxat in specie, sed in genere loquitur; non dicit enim, multi ex filiis Israelis: sed multi ex dormientibus in pulvere terrae. Ergo per multos, intelligendi etiam sunt multi ex gentibus. Praeterea in Pirque {Abot}, R. Elhazar a Kafar inquit: הילודים Qui nati sunt, ut moriantur; qui mortui sunt, ut revivisc ant; qui vivunt, ut judicentur. Ecce orationem generalem, qua omnes in universum comprehenduntur, itaut nullus quidem excludatur. Et cum dogma de resurrectione mortuorum, apud omnes gentes receptum, omnium quoque animis insitum sit, ita ut naturali quodam instinctu inclinare, ac trahi videantur ad illud credendum: ex eo, inquam, liquet, quod inter gentes improbi quoque, ac probi resurgent. Deinde in Zoar magnae auctoritatis libro legitur, quod illos, qui in captivitate bene de Israelitis meriti sunt, maneat in futuro saeculo magna felicitas. Probat praeterea Rabbi Menahem Ben Israel, improbos ex gentibus resuscitandos, quod Justitia Dei illud efflagitet necessario, uti patet ex Libr. II. de Relurr. Mort. cap. 22. pag. 258: Deinde Justitia etiam postulat, ut qui ipsos misere adeo hic afflixerunt, et interim omnibus vitae hujus delicis ac voluptatibus aetatem transegerunt, non impune id omne ferant, sed etiam Juscitentur ac resurgant, ut in oculis eorum quos afflixerunt dignas factis supplicia et poenas merita luant. Certe clare fatis id judicat futurum Joel cap. 3. 6. In diebus illis, & tempore illo, quo convertam captivitatem Juda & Jerusalaim, & congregabo omnes gentes, & descendere faciam eas in vallem Jehosaphat, & judicium subibo cum illis super populum meum, & hereditatem meam Israel, quos disperserunt in gentes, & terram meam diviserunt; Sic testatur Rabbi Mofeh Alfchech, quod Deus fit vivifi-catur quatuor Monarchias, ut puniantur ob mala Israeli illata, uti loquitur in Thorath Moiche, sol. 323. col. 4. in Deuteron. cap. 32: Ne dicatis: nonne qui devastarunt, & fecerunt principale malum, non acceperunt partem suam? Nam scitote nunc, ego vivificabo quatuor regna memorata, & revivificabo ea. Id quod dicitur juxta illud Rabbinorum, quod Israelita percussus intuens in percussorem suum dicturus sit: ecce hic percussit me manu sua, & Deus benedictus oftenfu-rus illi sit ultionem de illa manu, & analogice de omnibus membris.
units.tr: It is no less probable that all nations and peoples will rise alike with the Israelites, according to that saying of the ancients, "The pious of the nations of the world have a portion in the world to come" [חסידי אמות העולם יש להם חלק לעולם הבא]. All who are not Israelites are called Gentiles, or nations of the world, either because they make up the greater number (for the Israelites are few, according to Deuteronomy chapters 7 and 8), or because they are ruled by their own particular prince, as in the words of Daniel, "the prince of the kingdom of Persia, the prince of the kingdom of Greece," etc. But the Israelites are ruled immediately by the Blessed God, according to those words of Deuteronomy 4:20, "The Lord has taken you." Of these nations, all and each will rise who have lived uprightly and piously, such as those who, according to Rabbi Moses and Rabbi Meir Gabbai, have diligently kept the precepts given to Noah. Of this kind are these: You shall not commit idolatry. You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not curse the divine name. You shall not steal. You shall not eat the limb of a living animal. And you shall appoint judges who will see that these six precepts are kept uprightly and diligently. Nor will they rise only; they will also share in the blessedness of the age to come, according to that saying of the ancients: "The Holy One, blessed be he, does not defraud any creature of its reward" [אין הקדוש ברוך הוא מקפח שכר כל בריה]. And so they say a portion will be theirs. Nor is there doubt that those too who thought rightly of God, and lived honestly, piously and uprightly, will obtain a portion in the resurrection of the dead, as Rabbi Moses the Egyptian holds in his letters, even if such a one was among the Gentiles, such as Socrates, Plato, etc. The same can be confirmed from another saying of the ancients, which runs thus: "Four Hediotot will have no part in the age to come, namely Bilham, Doeg, Ahithophel and Gehazi" [ארבעה הדיוטות אין להם חלק לעולם הבא ואלו הן בלעם דואג אחיתופל וגחזי]. From these words the Talmudic remark is drawn: "Bilham is the one who will not come; therefore other Gentiles will come" [בלעם הוא דלא אתי הא גוים אחריני אתו]. That inference is certainly not a bad one, for if not all Gentiles are to rise, it would be altogether superfluous to make mention of Balaam at all. But since his name is mentioned, we may conclude from this that other Gentiles like Balaam will also rise, namely if they are worthy of resurrection. Likewise the wicked and the unrighteous will rise, to be tormented and punished. Let the testimony of Daniel also be added: "And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, others to shame and everlasting contempt." Note that he does not speak of the Israelites alone, specifically, but in general; for he does not say "many of the sons of Israel" but "many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth." Therefore by "many" we must also understand many of the Gentiles. Moreover, in Pirqe [Abot], Rabbi Elazar ha-Kappar says: "Those who are born are destined to die; those who have died are destined to live again; those who live are to be judged." [הילודים]. Here is a general statement by which all are comprehended in general, so that no one is excluded. And since the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead is received among all nations, and is implanted in the minds of all, so that they seem to be inclined and drawn by a certain natural instinct to believe it, from this, I say, it is evident that among the Gentiles the wicked as well as the upright will rise. Next, in the Zohar, a book of great authority, it is read that those who in captivity have done well by the Israelites will have great happiness in the age to come. Rabbi Menahem ben Israel further maintains that the wicked among the Gentiles are to be raised, because the justice of God necessarily demands it, as is clear from book 2 of On the Resurrection of the Dead, chapter 22, page 258: "Furthermore, justice also demands that those who have so miserably afflicted them here, and meanwhile have spent their lives in all the delights and pleasures of this life, should not bear all this with impunity, but should also be judged and rise, so that before the eyes of those whom they afflicted they may pay the punishments and penalties their deeds deserve." Certainly clearly enough, he judges this will happen in Joel chapter 3, verse 6: "In those days and at that time, when I shall bring back the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem, and I shall gather all nations and bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and I shall enter into judgment with them there over my people and my inheritance Israel, whom they have scattered among the nations, and divided my land". So Rabbi Moses Alshech testifies that God will bring back to life the four monarchies, that they may be punished for the evils inflicted on Israel, as he says in Torath Moshe, folio 323, column 4, on Deuteronomy chapter 32: "Do not say: have not those who laid waste, and did the chief evil, received their portion? For know now that I will make alive the four kingdoms mentioned, and will revive them." This is said according to that saying of the Rabbis, that the Israelite who has been struck, looking upon his striker, will say: "Behold, this one has struck me with his hand," and the Blessed God will show him vengeance upon that hand, and by analogy upon all the limbs.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Tandem inquirunt multis in Resurrectio-nis causam finalem, non convenientes rursus, sed valde altercantes, dum alii cum Rabbi Mofeh Maimonide in Epist. de Resurr. con-tendunt, quod non alius hujus miraculi inve-stigari debeat finis, nisi Dei voluntas, & sicuti de miraculis per Mosen patratis, nemo pru-dens dens quaeret, quare virgam in serpentem converterit, ita eodem nefas sit modo in hujus miraculi inquirere fidem, uti haec non solum refert Rabbi Ilac Abarbanel, sed pariter cum Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, libr. II. de Resurr. mort. cap. 19. refutat, cum in Nachalath Abhoth, rad. 6. sic loquitur: Patet autem, ratiocinationem magni Doctoris valde infirmam esse. Nam postea quam novimus finem miraculi generalem, qui est ut illi credatur: non quaeritur de modo miraculi, quare scilicet hac in re, non in alia peragatur, quia respondemus unam tenendam esse, in qua peragatur. Sed in argumento, de quo disceptamus, recte quaeritur, quisnam sit finis magni hujus miraculi, resurrectionis mortuorum, non quod ad specialia et modum ejus, sed quod in genere ad ipsum miraculum, et quae eo requiruntur, attinet, quandoquidem Deus cum nihil faciat sine sibi proprio fine, in miraculo tanto habebit finem notum et necessarium; Alii in numeri propterea futuram credunt Resurrectionem, ut homines pii coram judicio comparentes divino debitam deportent mercedem, cum hujus fruitione perfecta careant in mundo animarum, uti de Rabbi Saadia Haggaon, Rabbi Nachmanide, Rabbi Chasdai & reliquis Sapientibus pronunciat Rabbi Ilac Abarbanel in Nachalath Abhoth, rad. 6: Scripsit autem Haggaon, quem sequuntur Rabbi Nachman piæ memoriæ, Rabbi Chasdai, & reliqui Sapientes omnes, finem resurrectionis esse, ut judicio sistantur homines, & mercedem accipiant, cum merces vera & finis hominis ultimus non habeant locum in mundo animarum. Quomodo enim permittet divina justitia, ut cum anima & corpus junctim cultum praestiterint, sola anima mercedem illius cultus accipiat exclusocorpore? Sed illa differtur ad tempus resurrectionis mortuorum in seculo futuro, quando denuo animæ cum corporibus suis conjungentur, & intrabunt judicium magnum coram Deo, qui judicabit populos, ut det unicuique secundum vias suas, secundum fructum operum suorum; Alii rursus finem resurrectionis ponunt Judicium illud Dei, tum in pios, tum in impios, per quod alii ad vitam resurgent æternam, alii in opprobrium, judicantes injustissimum fore, si anima sola in mundo animarum præmium vel pœnam operum suorum consequeretur, cum anima & corpus simul virtuti & vitiis operam dederint, simulque refutantes solos justos resurrecturos, autore Rabbi Isaco Abarbanele, in Præfatione ad Esaiam, rad. 6: Hæc autem sententia absurda est, quia Scriptura dicit: Multi ex dormientibus in pulvere terræ evigilabunt, hi ad vitam æternam, illi ad opprobrium & contemptum æternum, Daniel 12.2. Quod si non nisi justi essent resurrecturi, illi forent pauci, quos puer posseт scribere, quomodo autem dicerentur multi. Quod majus est, Scriptura clamat: hi advitam æternam, illi ad opprobrium & contemptum æternum. Ita etiam Esaias ait, cap.66.verf.24. Et exibunt & videbunt cadavera eorum, qui à me defecerunt, quod arguit etiam ex impiis esse resurrecturos ad justinendam suam pœnam. Videbis etiam hanc fidem esse radicatam in omnibus gentibus, quasi natura hæc veritas esset illis tradita; Sic aliam præterea Resurrectionis mortuorum causam priori suæ jungit Rabbi Hac Abarbanel, referens resurrectionis miraculum idcirco futurum esse, ut Dei potentia manifestetur, & veritas ejus, ab omnibus mundi incolis agnoscatur, qui ineptarum opinionum & idololatrici cultus plenissimus erit, cum in Nachalath Abhoth, rad. 10. ita inquit: Qui finis est, ut, cum tot ubique gentium sint religiones perplexæ, capitibus differentes, phantasticæ & falsæ, neq; præcepta Dei exercituum ab illis hominibus curentur, alii Deitatem ejus negantibus, jolig; vel lunæ, vel in genere exercitui cælesti, vel alicui creaturæ attribuentibus: aliis creationem & innovationem mundi, articulum de resurrectione mortuorum & adventu Messiæ negantibus, aliis providentiam ejus se ad singula extendere, alius justitiam in præmiis & pœnis distribuendis negantibus, sicut ea multorum Philosophorum magni apud
units.tr: Finally, many inquire into the final cause of the resurrection. They do not agree with one another, and they argue vehemently. Some, with Rabbi Moses Maimonides in his Epistle on the Resurrection, contend that no other end of this miracle should be sought than the will of God. Just as no prudent person asks why Moses turned the rod into a serpent, so it is wrong to inquire into the purpose of this miracle. Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel reports this, and Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel refutes it in the second book of his work On the Resurrection of the Dead, chapter 19, where in Nachalath Abhoth, root 6, he speaks thus: It is clear, however, that the reasoning of the great Doctor is very weak. For once we know the general end of the miracle, which is that it be believed, we do not ask about the manner of the miracle, namely why it is carried out in this matter and not in another, because we answer that one must hold that it is carried out in whatever way it is. But in the question we are disputing, it is rightly asked what is the end of this great miracle, the resurrection of the dead. I do not mean its particulars and manner, but what pertains in general to the miracle itself and to what it requires. For since God does nothing without its own proper end, in so great a miracle he will have an end that is known and necessary. Others therefore believe that the resurrection is to come in order that pious people, appearing before the judgment, may receive the reward due from God, since they lack the full enjoyment of it in the world of souls. Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel reports this of Rabbi Saadia Gaon, Rabbi Nachmanides, Rabbi Chasdai and the other sages, in Nachalath Abhoth, root 6: Now Haggaon, whom Rabbi Nachman of blessed memory, Rabbi Chasdai, and all the other sages follow, wrote that the end of the resurrection is that men may be brought before judgment and receive their reward, since true reward and man's ultimate end have no place in the world of souls. For how would divine justice permit that when soul and body have rendered worship together, the soul alone should receive the reward of that worship, the body being excluded? Rather, that reward is deferred to the time of the resurrection of the dead in the future age, when souls are again joined to their bodies and enter the great judgment before God, who will judge the peoples, to give to each according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds. Others again place the end of the resurrection in that judgment of God upon both the righteous and the wicked, through which some rise to eternal life and others to shame. They judge it most unjust if the soul alone in the world of souls received the reward or punishment of its deeds, since soul and body together have devoted themselves to virtue and vice. At the same time they deny that only the righteous will rise. So teaches the author Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel, in his Preface to Isaiah, root 6: "But this opinion is absurd, because Scripture says: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, others to shame and everlasting contempt" (Dan. 12:2). If only the righteous were to rise, they would be few, so few that a boy could write them down; yet how could they be called many? What is more, Scripture cries out: these to everlasting life, those to everlasting shame and contempt. So also Isaiah says, chap. 66, verse 24: "And they shall go out and look upon the carcasses of those who have rebelled against me," which argues that the wicked too will rise to undergo their punishment. You will also see that this belief is rooted among all nations, as if this truth had been handed down to them by nature. Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel adds yet another cause of the resurrection of the dead to the former one, saying that the miracle of the resurrection will happen so that the power and truth of God may be made manifest and acknowledged by all the inhabitants of the world, which will be full of foolish opinions and idolatrous worship. In Nachalath Abhoth, root 10, he says: The end is that, since there are so many perplexed religions everywhere among the nations, differing in their heads, fantastic and false, and since the commandments of the Lord of hosts are not observed by those men, some deny his Godhead and ascribe divinity to the sun or moon, or in general to the host of heaven, or to some creature; others deny the creation and renewal of the world, the article on the resurrection of the dead, and the coming of the Messiah; others deny that his providence extends to individual things; and another denies that he distributes justice in rewards and punishments, as was the opinion of many philosophers of great name and authority among

units.la: suos nominis & autoritatis fuit sententia; illi qui hæc crediderunt per totum orbem notam faciant veritatem Dei, & legem ejus, quæq; ad mundum spiritualem ejusq; præmium & pœnam pertinent; vitaq; restituti pœnas dent coram omnibus hominibus, juxta illud: & videbunt cadavera hominum &c. Esai.66. 4. quibus conspectus in stuporem rapiantur homines, ut omnes simul veritatem confiteantur; Distinguit autem Rabbi Isac Abarbanel Resurrectionis hunc finem in Particularem, qui ad solum pertinet Israelem, & in communem, qui ad reliquos quoque refertur populos, uti liquet ex Præfatione ad Esaiam, rad.5: Propterea dico, quod statuatur in resurrectione finis alius particularis Israeli, alius illi cum cæteris communis, quodq; finis particularis sit, ut pij & amantes Dei, qui mortui fuerunt in exilio tribulatio oppressi, nec boni participes facti, digni habeantur salute Domini in liberatione futura. At vero finis omnibus populis in resurrectione communis ille est, ut, cum in terris suis invicem perplexa & falsa credant, alius solem & lunam, alius alia, quibus Deitatem vendicant, colentibus, omnibus autem a fine vero, ob quem conditi sunt, aberrantibus: constituerit Deus, ne species humana frustra esset condita, illis monstrare viam qua eant, & opus, quod faciant, ut absumantur de terra peccatores, & omnis nequitia occludat os suum, idolaq; penitus exscindantur, & cognoscant omnes incolæ terræ, Dei esse regnum, illumq; gentibus dominari; Hanc resurrectionis causam Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, non novam tantum appellat, sed neutiquam absurdam sibi videri testatur libr. II. de Resurrectione mortuorum, cap.21. pag.134.
units.tr: Those who have believed these things shall make known throughout the whole world the truth of God and his law, and what pertains to the spiritual world and its reward and punishment. Restored to life, they shall pay the penalties before all men, according to the words: and they shall see the carcasses of men, etc., Isaiah 66:4. At the sight of them men shall be struck with astonishment, so that all together they may confess the truth; Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel, moreover, distinguishes this end of the resurrection into a particular end, which pertains to Israel alone, and a general end, which also extends to the other peoples. This is clear from the Preface to Isaiah, root 5: Therefore I say that in the resurrection one end is established for Israel in particular, and another end is common to them with the rest. The particular end is that the pious and those who love God, who died in exile, oppressed by tribulation, and who were not made partakers of the good, may be counted worthy of the Lord's salvation in the coming deliverance. But the end of the resurrection common to all peoples is this: since they believe in perplexing and false things in their own lands, one worshipping the sun and moon, another other things to which they ascribe Godhead, and all of them going astray from the true end for which they were made, God has determined, lest the human species have been created in vain, to show them the way they should go and the work they should do. Thus sinners will be consumed from the earth, all wickedness will stop its mouth, idols will be utterly cut off, and all the inhabitants of the earth will know that the kingdom is God's and that he rules over the nations. Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel not only calls this cause of the resurrection new, but testifies that it does not seem to him absurd in any way. See his second book On the Resurrection of the Dead, chapter 21, page 134.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Alii denique ex Judæis hanc Resurrectionis mortuorum fingunt causam, ut justi illa observent, perficiantq; præcepta, quæ in vita priore ob interjecta impedimenta præstare non poterant, uti concludit Rabbi Joseph Albo de Fundamentis Part. iv. cap.31. sol.147: Quoniam illi justi, quos novit Deus, non potuisse præstare legem totam, non quod aliter noluerint, sed objugum captivitatis, vel impedimenta externa, vel aliam causam, sicut Moses & Aaron non poterant præstare legem totam, seu præcepta terræ Israelitica propria, quia eam non intrabant, digni habebuntur resurrectione, & tum perficient præcepta terræ Israelitica propria, & illa, quæ non poterant perficere in vita priore, & ita merebuntur præeminum magnum consequens, scilicet vitam æternam; Alii Hebraeorum rursus ajunt, hominem propterea resurgere, ut ad ultimam sui perveniat perfectionem, amissamque recuperet imaginem divinam, sicque à Rabbi Josepho Albo non multum abludentibus, uti patet ex Rabbi Menafleh Ben Israel, cum libr. II. de Refurr. Mort. cap. 19. sic loquitur: Hebraorum prima ratio, quam adferunt pro fine resurrectionis est, ut detur via, ac modus quo homo perveniat ad ultimam sui perfectionem, quia videl. ad imaginem Dei factus est. Imago autem, & simulachrum Dei, est lex divina, per Mosen populo tradita: illa enim, uti Cabalistæ observant, plena est divinorum nominum. Uti igitur lex constat ex lege CCXLVIII praeceptis affirmativis, & CCCLXV negativis: ita etiam tota corporis humani compages constat ex CCXLVIII membris, & CCCLXV nervis. Quod non aliud indicari videtur, quam quod tota hominis perfectio, ac consummatio sit accurata, ac diligenti praeceptorum observatione.
units.tr: Others among the Jews, finally, assign this cause for the resurrection of the dead: that the righteous may keep and fulfil those precepts which in their earlier life they could not perform because of hindrances in the way. So concludes Rabbi Joseph Albo, in Fundamentals, Part 4, chapter 31, page 147: Since those righteous ones whom God knows could not keep the whole law, not because they were unwilling, but because of the yoke of captivity, or external hindrances, or some other cause, just as Moses and Aaron could not keep the whole law, that is, the precepts proper to the land of Israel, because they did not enter it, they will be judged worthy of the resurrection, and then they will keep the precepts proper to the land of Israel, and those which they could not perform in their earlier life; and so they will merit the great reward that follows, namely eternal life. Other Hebrews again say that man rises so that he may attain his ultimate perfection and recover the lost image of God. This view does not differ much from that of Rabbi Joseph Albo, as appears from Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, who in book 2 of On the Resurrection of the Dead, chapter 19, speaks thus: The first reason the Hebrews give for the purpose of the resurrection is that there be given a way and a means by which man may come to his ultimate perfection, since he was made in the image of God.
